en: Preface to the *Bishuo* (Pen-Notes) of the *Chanlin Baoxun* (Precious Instructions from the Zen Forest). This single volume of the *Baoxun* consists of the intimate words from the innermost hearts of the ancients, born of their profound affection for those they nurtured.

To compose and record it was truly no less than chewing food to feed an infant; their painstaking effort was extreme indeed. Furthermore, the three hundred odes of the *Shijing* are all of such brilliant and world-transcending excellence...

His talent transcends a hundred generations. He brings forth subtle refinement from the concise and archaic, and entrusts the ultimate flavor to the plain and simple. His celestial mechanism flows freely;
though his phrasing is ordinary, when scrutinized, later practitioners find it as vast and desolate as a wilderness, making it difficult even to set foot upon.
Rarely have there been those who have treasured it and cherished it, becoming intoxicated by its spirit and drenched in its essence.
Since I first entered the path of study, forty springs and autumns have passed as I have read it; it has been like drinking clarified butter (*sarpis*) or consuming wondrous medicine.

In the moments of establishing my character and interacting with others, I have occasionally ventured to extract one or two phrases to serve as a model for conduct. Although I cannot rival the excellence of the sages of old, [I have found solace therein].
Furthermore, some do not even see it and laugh at the present age. Lately, having retired from affairs to a cold rock, I have pared away the myriad concerns;
day after day, I am but a monk who sits facing a wall, carrying a load of withered wood as my burden. As for this book, I set it aside and pay it no heed.
However, at the request of a practitioner of Zen, I said: "I am old; my sinews are weary and my bones are decayed. How could I possibly fulfill your wish again?"
Yet his request became increasingly insistent. Unable to refuse him, I was compelled to comply and ordered my two disciples, Zhu and Ying, to compose explanations on his behalf.
As days turned into months, these eventually formed a complete volume, which I titled *Bishuo* (Explanations by Pen).

From this, one may know that even if I were capable of explaining, there must be the proper occasion and the right time; such explanations have their intervals. Only the *Bishuo* is not restricted by time.

Without discriminating between places, I have continued my humble studies even as the tradition was on the verge of collapse, and I have brought forth the wondrous principles from their most accessible forms.

My words may spread like the wind through branches or the moon upon the shore throughout the valleys and mountains, yet they are merely the words of the ancients used to convey the intent of the ancients.

How could I dare claim that I am entrusting these teachings to the future to enlighten the ignorant and those who have not yet awakened? I only pray that students will apply themselves with profound and earnest dedication.

I reflect. With a subtle mind, I exhaustively contemplate and savor these words, melting the speech of the ancients into my own words and realizing the aspirations of the ancients as my own aspirations.

In this way, not only do I avoid failing the predecessors who harbored the compassionate heart of chewing food to feed an infant, but I also do not betray the humble resolve of one with white hair by the dim light of a lamp tonight.
Written by the reclusive elder Zhixiang Pingji, the Daoist Tiyun, at the Muli Hall on Yunfeng Peak during the middle summer month of the Bingxu year of the Kangxi era.
Preface to the *Cānlín Bǎoxùn* (Precious Admonitions from the Zen Forest).

Regarding the four characters of the title *Cānlín Bǎoxùn*, they are interpreted through a pairing of dharma and metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*). The character "Zen" (*cān*) is the dharma; "forest" (*lín*) is the metaphor.
The character "precious" (*bǎo*) is the metaphor; "admonition" (*xùn*) is the dharma. In Sanskrit, it is *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "meditative concentration" (*jìnglù*).

It takes tranquility as its essential meaning. Furthermore, it is called "cultivation through reflection. As for what is termed *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), concentration is spoken of in contrast to distraction;
if there is even slight distraction, it is no longer *dhyāna*. Regarding the term "forest" (*vana*), a forest consists of many trees; this is a metaphor for the various meditation masters.
Their noble words and virtuous deeds were not spoken by just one person, and thus they are likened to a forest. Comparing these elders, they have all deeply cultivated meditative concentration.
The words collected by these individuals are exceedingly numerous; hence it is called "Chán-lín" (Forest of Meditation). As for "treasure" (*bǎo*), it carries the meaning of being precious.
The common world regards wealth and silk as treasures; the gentleman regards literary expressions as treasures; and the perfected person regards the Way and its Virtue as treasures.
Therefore, the analogy is presented first so that people may know that the literary expressions of the former sages are such that every single character is worthy of being cherished and treasured.
"Xun" (訓) means instruction; it refers to admonition and teaching. This signifies that the dharma-words of the various Chan masters are all expressions of instruction and admonition.
These four characters constitute the title of this work. By obtaining its title, one can understand the meaning of the three hundred poems [of the *Shijing*].
"Xu" (序) refers to the introductory preface. Whenever a book has a preface, it is like a garment having a collar or a net having a handle.
Regarding its having a "General Outline" (Gang), it is also called the "Preface" (Xu), which describes the origins of this book.
As for the "Precious Teachings" (Baoyun), they were formerly compiled together by Miaoxi and Zhuanan when they were clearing away brambles at Yunmen in Jiangxi.
This describes the origin of the compilation of the *Chen Jibaoxun* (Anthology of Precious Teachings). The character "者" (*zhě*) has two uses: a literal and a figurative.
Here, it is used figuratively as a particle of speech. Whenever the character "者" appears in a text, its function is to distinguish and separate [the preceding clause].
"Xīzhě" (In the past) means "formerly" or "in previous generations. Miaoxi refers to Dahuì Chánshī Zōnggǎo of Jìngshān. Níngguó...

The son of the Xi family was Chan Master Fuguo Keqin; Zhuanian was Chan Master Shigui of Longxiang in Wenzhou, a son of the Shi family from Chengdu who succeeded Chan Master Fuyan Qingyuan. Both masters belonged to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue;
"clearing away brambles" and "cutting through weeds" refers to how these two masters [established their hermitages] at the ancient site of Yunmen in Jiangxi.
When Jie’an was living in seclusion at Zhi, they collected this book together.

During the Chunxi era, while traveling to Yunju, I obtained it from the elderly monk Zu’an; I regret that its latter portion was severely damaged by woodworms, leaving both beginning and end incomplete.
This is the account of how this compilation was produced. "I" refers to myself. "Chunxi" is the reign title of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty.

"You" means to travel or journey. This indicates that during the Chunxi period, I traveled throughout various regions and reached Yunju Mountain in Jiangxi, where I obtained these precious instructions from an elderly monk named Zu’an—who was the abbot of Yueshan Zu’an and had received the Dharma [from his master].
Regarding Qingyuan Weixin: he was the fourteenth generation descendant of Nanyue. The Master resided at Mount Heng for thirty years, yet no one knew of him.
He had a verse that said: "A small cauldron boils vegetables while rice steams above; The vegetables are cooked and the rice is fragrant, yet people are still hungry.
Once full, the sores of hunger are gone and there is nothing more to do; Tomorrow morning, they will paint a cat exactly as before. Because of this, the monastic disciples...
They vied with one another in admiring him. Master Zhang Wujin exerted his efforts to urge him toward the transcendental life, but [Wujin] did not comply.
He subsequently lived in seclusion at Yunju for over ten years before passing away. "To regret" means to feel pity for someone. "Zi" (字) is a term used to designate things.

"Dù" (蠧) is the name of an insect that can eat paper; its appearance resembles a fish. Formerly, during the reign of King Cheng of Zhou, a foreign state presented a memorial, which was sealed within a chest.
Three years passed. One day, the Emperor ordered the scrolls to be brought for inspection. He saw that the worm-eaten characters had formed the words "Fú" (Blessing) and "Shòu" (Longevity).

The Emperor was greatly delighted. Later, Zhe wrote a eulogy: "The silkworm-fish never dwells in clear waves; It pierces through paper and paper, heedless of sleep or food. Without intent, it forms characters that pass imperial eyes;
Throughout ancient and modern times, such treasures in book-cases are few. He remarked that although he had obtained this book, he could only regret...
Having been preserved for many years, it has been eaten by bookworms; thus the chapters are incomplete.
Some portions have the beginning but lack the end, and there are many such omissions—this is truly regrettable.
Later, I encountered [these texts] within various recorded sayings (*yulu*) and biographies. Over the course of ten years, I collected only some fifty-plus pieces;
subsequently, I further selected the legacy teachings of masters from Huanglong down to Fozhao and Jiantang, editing and categorizing them into three hundred sections.
Although these acquisitions occurred at different times, I did not arrange them according to chronological order.
This preface explains the reason for the sequence of the tantras. "Later" (*kōrai*) means after obtaining this book. "Or" (*ka*) is an indefinite term.
That which expresses the true mechanism of the secret and manifest is called "speech" (*go*). That which compiles various matters is called a "record" (*roku*).

That which extensively records the past and present is called a "biography" (*den*). That which broadly chronicles the worthy and wise is called a "chronicle" (*ki*). "Accumulated" (*shika*) means gradually collected. "Merely" (*kin*) means just now.
It is said that since obtaining this collection, I have searched through various anthologies for those whose beginnings and ends were incomplete;
it was only within ten years that I finally obtained some fifty-odd pieces. "Still" (仍) means again or as before.
Huanglong Temple is located in Longxing Prefecture, which is now called Nanchang. Chan Master Huinan was from Xinzhou.
The son of the Zhang family succeeded Chan Master Chuyuan of Shichuang. He was the eleventh generation descendant of Nanyue.
"Down to" refers to those from the eleventh to the sixteenth generations. Fozhao was Chan Master Zuguan Deguang of Yewang Monastery in Mingzhou;
he was the son of the Peng family of Linjiang and succeeded Chan Master Dahui. Jiantang was [the successor] of Guoqing.
Chan Master Sijian Xingji was the son of the Yang family of Taizhou and succeeded Chan Master Jingyuan of Huguo. Both masters belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
The term "various elders" is a phrase used to indicate that [the list] does not exhaustively encompass all of them. The term "final instructions" refers to...
Although these individuals have passed away, their recorded sayings remain. "Jie" (節) means to exercise restraint; "qi" (葺) means to gradually repair and restore.
However, masters such as Huitang of Huanglong had already collected those of the two masters Dahui and Zhuan’an;
yet, because the beginning and end were incomplete, we have been obliged to continue as before by exercising restraint over the various masters' bequeathed words.
He then repaired and supplemented it, resulting in a total of three hundred pieces across the fifty categories mentioned previously. However, what he obtained was not from a single time or place;
there was an original sequence of priority, as he recorded them as they were acquired. Therefore, he did not prioritize antiquity above all else.
The present work is intended for future generations as a means of clarification and sequential exposition;
its general purpose is to lead students to eliminate worldly power, profit, and the notions of self and other, and to pursue the Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness.
This precisely expresses the fundamental intent of the *Sūtra of the Collection of Jewels* (*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*). "Gai" (概) means generally or collectively.
"Xiao" (削) means to delete or excise. "Shi" (勢) refers to power and authority; "li" (利) refers to wealth and profit. "Ren-wo" (人我) is a term for the mutual opposition between self and others.
This indicates that the original purpose of compiling this book was primarily to cause students to completely abandon their hearts of power, wealth, and self-centeredness.
Delete it; it must not be retained. "The Way" (Dao) refers to the thorough path traversed by all sages and ordinary beings alike.

That which is the natural course of daily affairs and things is called the Way. "Virtue" (De) means attainment. To have attained realization in one's heart through practicing the Way is called virtue.
Whether a monk cultivates precepts, concentration, and wisdom, or a Confucian practices filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and good faith—all these are called virtue. Benevolence (Ren).
"Righteousness (yi)" is the virtue of the mind and the principle of affection. "Appropriateness (yi)" is the regulation of the mind and the suitability of affairs.
"To incline toward" means to approach and to adopt; it signifies that what was previously irrational should be eliminated, while what is now rational should be adopted.
It aims solely to lead scholars toward morality, benevolence, and righteousness. The word "solely" (ér) conveys the sense of reaching a conclusion with nothing remaining.
Its literary style is graceful, leisurely, and plain, devoid of any traces of loftiness, hyperbole, remoteness, or eccentricity; it is truly capable of providing assistance.
This is a grand strategy for entering the Way. Furthermore, I shall have trees carved [to record this] so that it may spread widely.
There must surely be like-minded scholars who, upon seeing it once, will grant their hearts’ assent; though I myself die old and alone in the hills and valleys, my aspirations will be fulfilled.
This extends the elucidation of the text of the Precious Teachings. "Text" (*wen*) refers to literary expression; "principle" (*li*) refers to doctrinal meaning.

"Leisurely" (*youyou*) describes a state of natural ease. "Ordinary" (*ping*) means commonplace; "easy" (*yi*) means simple and straightforward. "Lofty" (*gao*) refers to speech that is isolated, precarious, and difficult to approach;

"extravagant" (*dan*) refers to discourse that is deceptive, false, and unreal; "wild" (*huang*) refers to desolate talk lacking any basis in evidence; "remote" (*miao*) refers to what is vast and distant.
"Phrases that cannot be applied. "Deceitful" refers to words of guile and fraud; "strange" refers to expressions of the bizarre and anomalous.
It means that such words do not possess actual substance within the text, nor can their traces be found upon investigation.
Such truly authentic and non-deceptive instructions can indeed assist in the grand strategy for entering the Way. As for "strategy" (yóu): it refers to—
It is the Dharma. "Far-reaching plans" refers to profound and far-reaching principles. This preface describes its efficacy; the following clarifies the intention for its circulation.
"Qie" (且) means provisional or temporary. "Qie jiang" (且將) is a term expressing a temporary desire. "Kan mu" (刊木) refers to carving wood blocks [for printing].

This is so that it may circulate widely and far-reaching. "There will surely be those who [share this aim]" means that once this book is in circulation, there will certainly be those whose aspirations accord with my own.
Upon seeing it, such a person will surely grant me their heartfelt approval. "Approval" (許) carries the sense of consent or acceptance.
Once the book has circulated, even though I am old and decrepit and shall die in the hills and valleys, the lifelong ambition of my life will have been fulfilled.
"Yi. "Qiu" refers to a high mound of earth. "He" refers to a ravine, a valley, or a pit. "Zhi" (aspiration) is that toward which the mind is directed;

"yuan" (wish) is that which the emotions long for. The above constitutes the completion of the explanatory commentary on the preface. Following this, the name of the author of the preface is set forth.
Written by the śramaṇa Jingshan of Eastern Wu.

Anciently, the region was called the Three Wus; Eastern Wu refers specifically to Suzhou. "Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term, which in this [Chinese] language means "one who exerts effort and seeks cessation.
This signifies that one diligently practices various virtues and brings all evils to rest. Those of later generations must not simply address their predecessors by name alone; they ought to...
It says: "Purity above and goodness below" refers to the name of the author of the preface. He was a person of the Song period, a high monk of Pugu.
His family lineage and clan are unknown. As for the word "shū" (書), it means "to spread"; it signifies spreading his words and setting them down upon tablets and slips of bamboo.
*Chánlín chóngkè bǎoxùn bǐshuō*, Scroll One.
Composed by Zhìxiáng of Yúnfēng in Chùhéng.
This chapter teaches that virtue and morality are the foundation for establishing one’s character; to honor and cherish them is of the utmost urgency and importance.
Therefore, this [title] is placed at the head of the three hundred poems;
there is a specific intention behind it. Master Mingjiao Song said: "Nothing is more honorable than the Way (Dào); nothing is more beautiful than Virtue (Dé).
Where the Way and Virtue reside, even a commoner is not in straits. Where the Way and Virtue do not reside, even one who rules all under heaven is not successful."
Mingjiao was Chan Master Qisong of Furi Temple in Hangzhou. His courtesy name was Zhongling, and he styled himself Qianzi.
He was the son of the Li family of Tanjin in Tengzhou and inherited the lineage of Chan Master Xiaocong of Dongshan; thus, he belonged to the tenth generation of the Qingyuan line.

He entered the monastic order at the age of seven, received full ordination at thirteen, and began his travels to visit various masters at nineteen. He constantly carried a scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra with him every day.
He recited the sacred names one hundred thousand times, making this his constant practice. There was no secular scripture he had not perused.

He composed the *Yuanjiao lun* (Treatise on the Origin of the Teachings) in over one hundred thousand words, asserting that the Way of Confucianism and Buddhism is a single thread, thereby countering the arguments of Han Yu who sought to exclude Buddhism.
When Wang Gong Su, the Dragon Diagram Official of Kaifeng, along with Ouyang Xiu and Cheng Shimeng, submitted his work for imperial review, it was presented to the throne.

When Emperor Renzong read it, he sighed in admiration. He entrusted the work to the compilers for inclusion in the Imperial Canon, titled it *Fǔjiào piān* (Treatise on Aiding the Teaching) in three fascicles, and bestowed upon him purple robes and a square-cut cassock, along with the title "Míngjiào" (Enlightened Teaching).
"Heshang" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "one who gives birth through power. This refers to attaining the growth of the Dharma-body by virtue of the teacher's power.
It is also said to mean "relying on study," signifying that one learns and emerges [from ignorance] by following this teacher.
This is a worldly matter. It is said: "Words. [This section first clarifies the distinction between those who preserve and those who do not preserve the Way and its Virtue.
"Venerable" (zun) means to honor; "excellent" (mei) means to praise. The explanation of the Way (dao) and its Virtue (de) is as seen previously.

This means that among all things in the world, there is nothing more worthy of veneration and honor than the Way, and nothing more praiseworthy and excellent than Virtue. If the human mind is able to preserve them...
The Way: when the person is able to nourish their virtue, even if they dwell in the midst of poverty and hardship like a common man or woman, they do not consider it suffering;

therefore, it is said that this is "not being in distress. Conversely, if one does not cultivate the Way and its Virtue, and the body and mind are dissolute and wandering, then even if one’s nobility is equal to that of the Son of Heaven, one does not consider it an honor;
therefore, it is said that this is "not being successful. A "common man" (pifu) is a designation for one who is destitute and solitary. This is what is meant by...
Among the three armies, one may seize the commander; yet the will of a single man cannot be taken away.
As for the "three armies," the Son of Heaven of Zhou had six armies, with twelve thousand five hundred men constituting one army; a great state possessed three armies.
Next are two armies for a medium-sized state and one army for a small state. The character for "King" (王) is pronounced with the departing tone; one who presides over the four seas is called a King.
This first cites two types—the honorable and the humble—to establish the standard of whether one possesses virtue and morality or lacks it.
Thereafter, he brought forth his critical arguments so that people were transformed spontaneously without even speaking.
Bo Yi and Shu Qi were once men who starved to death; yet when they are now compared to these [present-day figures], everyone feels joy.
Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were former sovereigns; yet when one compares them to those [of today], everyone feels indignation.
This section cites evidence to demonstrate the reality of whether moral virtue exists or not. Boyi and Shuqi were commoners who possessed moral virtue;
yet when they are compared to people [of today], everyone feels joy. This is because they rejoice in their possession of the Way.
This is virtue. Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were rulers who possessed neither moral character nor virtue. Now, when these are compared to ordinary people, everyone feels indignation;
this is because they are angry at their lack of moral character and virtue. Bo Yi and Shu Qi were the two sons of the Lord of Guzhu.
Guzhu was the state ruled by the lord to whom King Tang of Yin granted a fief; it was located in Yongping Prefecture.
Eighteen *li* to the northwest is the City of Gulu, where the temples of Yi and Qi still exist. [Yi’s] surname was Motai;
his given name was Chu, and his courtesy name was Zichao. His son Bo Yi’s given name was Yun, and his courtesy name was Gongxin. The younger brother, Shu Qi, was named Zhi.

His courtesy name was Gongda. He was posthumously titled as "The Peerless" (Boyi) and "The Younger Peerless" (Shuqi). When his father was about to pass away, he left a testament appointing Shuqi as his successor.
Shuqi considered fraternal succession to be paramount, thinking, "If I were to occupy the throne, it would be unjust.

Boyi considered his father’s command to be supreme, thinking, "If I were to occupy the throne, it would be unfilial. Both brothers fled. The people of the state enthroned their middle son as ruler. As for those two...
Hearing that Chang, the Chief of Xi, was skilled at nurturing the elderly, they went to him and returned to serve him.

When King Wen passed away and King Wu went to war against Zhou, the two men struck the horse’s head and remonstrated, saying: "The father is dead and not yet buried, yet you are already engaged in arms; can this be called filial piety?"
"To kill a ruler with a minister—can this be called loyalty? His attendants wished to execute him, but the Grand Duke said, "This man is righteous.
They supported him out. After King Wu pacified the world and made Zhou the capital, Yi and Qi felt ashamed and would not eat the grain of Zhou;
they subsequently went into seclusion on Mount Shouyang. This is located thirty li southeast of the western city of Puzhou, at Mount Leishou.
He gathered wild herbs to eat, yet in the end he died of hunger. Shi Yong said: "Bo Yi and Shu Qi of Guzhu were ashamed of war;

seeing the dust of an approaching army, they blocked the road and requested a truce. When Mount Shouyang collapsed and became level ground, it was likely that no one would speak their names from then on.
Jie of Xia, named Liu Gui, was the son of Emperor Fa. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles): "One who harms many people and kills them excessively is called Jie."

Jie was licentious, dissolute, and unrighteous. He took as his consort a woman of the Shi clan named Meixi; he constructed towers of jasper and terraces of jade, indulging his whims to seek her favor.

He created a wine-pool where boats were navigated, and the mounds of dregs could be seen for ten li. Long Feng remonstrated with him out of loyalty, but Jie would not listen and subsequently killed him.
King Tang of Yin possessed great virtue, and Yi Yin assisted him in the campaign against Jie. Jie was defeated in battle and fled to Sanzong.
The state was located in Dingtao County, Shandong Province; there stood the Three Palmyra Pavilion (Sanzongting) therein.
Tang subsequently attacked and conquered it, banished Jie to Nancaoshan where he died. This location is ninety li from Luzhou Prefecture, in Chao County. Shi Yong said:
The obstinate and unruly [Shou] doted on his younger sister Xi. At the Jade Terrace he indulged in the Pool of Wine.

Though the nine Yi tribes did not assist him in his conquests, when Chao Fang deposed him, Shou lost his dragon limbs. As for the nine Yi tribes: Xuantu, Leiwang, Gaoli, Mandi, Fusou, Suodang, Dongtu, Woren, and Tianbu.

Regarding Shang Zhou, his name was Xin, also known as Shou. He was the son of Emperor Yi. According to the *Shifa* (Methods of Posthumous Titles), his title was given because he "harmed righteousness."
The one who ruined the good was known as Zhòu. He obtained a woman of the Sū clan named Dájǐ and doted upon her excessively.

He established a wine-pool and a forest of meat, causing men and women to pursue one another there in the nude. He constructed the Palace of Eternal Night, where one hundred and ten days constituted a single day.
He employed the "roasting and branding" punishment, disemboweling the pregnant and flaying those who had committed offenses. He built the Lù Terrace, which took seven years to complete.
He cruelly oppressed the loyal and virtuous. My uncle Bi Gan exhausted his loyalty in remonstrance and was consequently dismembered, dying with his heart torn out.
The Grand Preceptor Ji Zi feigned madness and became a slave. My elder brother, the Viscount Wei, departed and withdrew from him because he could no longer abide in such a lack of benevolence.
Later, King Wu raised an army to attack him. [Shou] was defeated at Denglutai; he covered his head and threw himself into the fire, dying. Shi Yong said:
"Grains of grain accumulated until they became dust, yet in the end, no opening was made. Who would have known that by rejecting counsel, his brilliant talent was cut short?
When King Wu’s army arose, there was no one to oppose it; thus he became but a heap of ashes on the outskirts of Shang. King Zhou of Zhou named his palace Nie. King Xuan—
My son. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who obstructs and blocks so that there is no passage is called "Dark" (*you*).

Because his administration was perilous and his rule tyrannical toward the people, Mount Qi eventually collapsed of its own accord, and the waters of the mountains and rivers dried up. He obtained a woman from the state of Bao named Bao Si and favored her;
he consequently demoted Queen Shen and the Crown Prince Yijiu. Bao Si did not enjoy laughing, so [the King] raised fires on Mount Li as a spectacle to please her.

[She] laughed. Mount Li is located three *li* southeast of Lintong County in Xianyang Prefecture. Later, Lord Shen became enraged and summoned the Qunrong tribes to slaughter [the King] at the foot of Mount Li.
Shi Yong wrote: "Relying on her favor, she was full of coquetry and enjoyed total freedom; On Mount Li, she raised a signal fire to mock the feudal lords.
How could she have known that one smile would topple the state? Unaware, the dust of the Hu tribes filled the Jade [Palace]."
Lóu ○ was Zhōu Lì, whose personal name was Hú. He was the son of Yíwáng. According to the *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who slays the innocent is called "Lì.
The king acted without the Way; he was extravagant, arrogant, and tyrannical. The people of the state slandered him, so the king appointed the *Wèiwū* (the Witch of Wèi) to oversee the slanders.

Anyone who slandered him was executed without exception. Wèi is the name of a state; a *wū* is a man upon whom a deity has descended. Duke Shāo admonished him, saying: [...]* *(Note: The original text contains a lacuna marked by ○. The provided passage concludes with the introduction to Duke Shao's admonition.)*
The officials at the frontier gates reported his transgressions to the throne, fearing they would bring calamity upon the state. The King did not listen;
consequently, the people of the realm rebelled against him, and disaster befell the King. He then fled into exile to Zhi—an ancient place name that is now Huozhou.
It belonged to Pingyang Prefecture. The Crown Prince was young, so the two dukes, Zhou and Shao, acted in harmony and cooperation to manage the affairs of state;
hence it is called the "Joint Rule" (Gonghe). The twenty-two pieces of the *Xiaoya* all concern the virtuous governance of Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang, yet by this time they were entirely abandoned.
Shi Yong said: "Violent, wicked, and arrogant, he delighted in inciting war; though his loyal heart urged repeated remonstrances..."
They did not grieve. The two gentlemen calculated that they might escape by way of Zhui; yet until their deaths they had no place to return, and no mound upon which to offer libations.

Therefore, those who study are concerned that the Way and its Virtue are not fully realized within themselves; they are not concerned that power and position do not belong to them (from the *Xinjin Ji*).
This section specifically instructs the person to recognize what they should be concerned about.

Thus, the two characters "is-hu" (is-gu) serve to carry forward the discussion of the benefits and harms of seeing and practicing versus not seeing and practicing. "Hu" (gu) means anxiety or concern. As it is said:
"For this reason, a student should be concerned that their moral virtue (*dào-dé*) is insufficient within themselves; they need not be concerned with fame, reputation, power, or status."
This does not depend on me. △ If one’s Way were full and virtue complete, such that devas and dragons paid them reverence, one would not consider this a cause for joy;
how then could power and status be a source of anxiety? One must know that moral virtue endures forever through the ages, whereas power and status perish along with the body.
Which is more important: the ages, or the body? Students should apply themselves here with vigorous introspection and profound cultivation.
It is appropriate.
This chapter instructs people that they must inquire with discernment when studying; only then can they fully develop its principles and benefit their fundamental nature.
Mingjiao said: "The learning of the sages and worthies is certainly not something accomplished in a single day. When the daylight is insufficient, one continues by night;
by accumulating it over months and years, it will naturally be perfected."

This section first clarifies the accumulation of merit. That which is spiritually luminous and possesses penetrating discernment is called "sage" (sheng). One who transcends the ordinary yet ranks below a sage is called "worthy" (xian).
When speaking of the learning of sages and worthies, one must understand that these are not mere ordinary texts, but rather words concerning the realization of sagehood and worthiness.
"Solidly" (*ko*) means "fundamentally. This refers to the fact that the foundation cannot be fully accomplished in a single day.

Even if one's daytime study is insufficient, one must continue it throughout the night. In this manner, from month to year, if one studies without weariness, then the ultimate learning of the sages and worthies will naturally be achieved. The two characters "naturally" (*jirani*) carry the sense of certainty.
Therefore it is said: "One studies to accumulate [knowledge] and questions to discern it. These words mean that learning cannot be fully elucidated without questioning and discernment.
This section cites the source of study and inquiry from the *Yijing* (Book of Changes), which states:

"The noble person studies to accumulate [knowledge], questions to discern it, dwells in it with breadth, and practices it with benevolence. Studying to accumulate and questioning to discern are means of advancing one's mastery; dwelling with breadth...
To practice benevolence is to cultivate virtue. Therefore, the phrase "it has been said" refers to words spoken by people of antiquity;
the Master now cites them to instruct others, so that they may know these are not merely my own words. The phrase "these words" means the Master again raises them to enlighten his students.
"These" (si) refers to this—that is, these words of the ancients. When studying, one must necessarily inquire; when inquiring, one must necessarily...
Dialectical inquiry. If it were not for dialectical inquiry, how could one clarify the ultimate principles of the sages and worthies?
Now, among those who study, there are rarely any who utter a single word of question or debate with others.
I do not know how they will assist their fundamental nature or achieve the benefit of daily renewal.
This section directly rebukes the student. It does not question or debate; rather, it correctly instructs people that they must question and debate.
This means that when the ancients practiced their studies, they invariably questioned and debated. Among students today, however, such things are rarely seen wherever they go.
It is too little. I have rarely seen anyone who would utter a single word to question or debate with such students.
I do not know how, at some future time, these practitioners will be able to assist those on the stage of the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) and bring about the benefit of daily renewal.
"Bì" means to supplement. As for "the stage of nature" (*xingdi*), "stage" carries the sense of a vehicle that can bring forth all things.
It is said that upon the ground of one's own mind-nature, one must rely on sacred learning to be able to give rise to all that exists; only then can it increase and renew day by day.
Now, if not a single word is uttered, there will be nothing at all that can be brought forth upon the ground of nature—how, then, could there be any benefit?
○ "Daily Renewal" appears in the *Great Learning*. "If one renews oneself on this day, one renews oneself daily, and again renews oneself daily.
△ Those who study the sages and worthies are not ordinary people; they must possess the aspiration of the sages and worthies before they can learn from them.
This chapter admonishes scholars to eliminate profit-seeking desire, as it is the source of disorder.
Mingjiao said: "When Grand Historian Sima Qian read the *Mencius* to the point where King Hui of Liang asked, 'How can I benefit my state?
he unconsciously set down his scroll and sighed deeply, exclaiming, 'Alas! Profit is truly the beginning of chaos. Therefore, the Master [Confucius] rarely spoke of profit. Constantly...
To prevent it at its source. The "source" refers to the beginning. How can one distinguish between the evils of honoring the poor and lowly versus the pursuit of profit?
This section clarifies that profit is the foundation of all harms. The Grand Historian’s surname was Sī-mā and his given name was Tán;
he served as the Grand Historian. His son, named Qiān, inherited his father’s office. Because he honored his father, he is referred to as "Gōng" (the Grand). West.
A native of Longmen in the Han [dynasty]. As for those who read him: they recite his writings. Mencius, whose given name was Ke and courtesy name Ziyu, was a native of Zou.
He composed the *Mencius* in seven chapters. King Hui of Liang—Wu Hou of Wei, whose personal name was Ji—had his capital at Biancheng;
he changed the state's title to Liang. His son, named Ying, usurped the title of King and was posthumously titled Hui. According to the *Shiji*, this was the thirty-fifth year of King Hui’s reign.

In the year of Yǐyǒu, Qi was powerful while Liáng was weak. The King of Qi established a Hall for Summoning Talents, humbling himself in his etiquette and providing generous gifts to widely attract men of superior ability.
When Mēngzǐ arrived, the King of Liáng asked him, saying: "Old man, you have come from no less than a thousand li away; will you perhaps bring some benefit to my state?
Mēngzǐ replied: "Why must Your Majesty speak only of 'benefit'? There are also benevolence and righteousness."
When the King asked about his intentions regarding matters such as maintaining a strong army and enriching the state, Mencius’s response was that he did not consider wealth to be the true benefit;
rather, he considered righteousness to be the benefit. That he did not notice [the King's presence] arose from his lack of conscious intent.
That he set down his book was because he wished to know that there was a profound resonance stirring within his breast. His long sigh was the sound of that inner resonance. "Alas!"—this was it.
This is an exclamation. When King Hui opened his mouth, he immediately brought up the word "profit" (*li*);

this was to place all people under heaven within the womb of calamity. "Sincerity" (*cheng*) means reality. It is truly and fundamentally the root of disorder. Next, he cites the Master to clarify this:
that our Master did not speak much of profit precisely reveals his ordinary, constant vigilance and maintenance [of moral order].
I am cautious, fearing that this may become the very source of inciting disorder. Why is this? It is because the Master constantly used the character "li" (profit) as a precaution;

he knew that from the Son of Heaven, who is most honored and supreme among all people in the world, down to the commoners, who are poor and lowly—though their ranks differ in nobility—the malady of craving profit is indistinguishable between them.
If those in public office take profit unfairly, the law will fall into disorder. If those in private life take profit through deception, affairs will fall into disorder.
When affairs are in disorder, people contend with one another in injustice; when the law is in disorder, the people resent it and refuse to submit. Thus, there arises perverse rebellion and strife.
"Those who disregard death set this [path] in motion from hereon. Is this not indeed the beginning of disorder?
This section clarifies the弊 (defects) of those above and below seeking personal gain. The word '夫' (fu) is a particle used to connect the preceding to the following.

Regarding 'those in public office': this responds to the aforementioned 'honoring one's peers. When those in office seek gain unrighteously, their commands will not be carried out, and the laws will fall into chaos."
As for myself, I am but one of the poor and lowly. If I were to take advantage of others through deception, my moral standing would be lost and affairs would fall into chaos.
If affairs are in chaos, there is no distinction between self and other; the strong and the weak compete until nothing can be clearly discerned.
Thus, people struggle in injustice. If the law is in chaos, it is used to oppress others, with no regard for right or wrong, so that justice cannot be vindicated.

Consequently, the people become resentful and refuse to submit. In such a state, when superiors and subordinates are in mutual disorder, even though laws and regulations exist, the people will not follow them.
"Pèi" (悖) means perverse; "guāi" (乖) means discordant; "lì" (戾) means contrary; and "wéi" (違) means to go against. Affairs lack clarity, and strife and contention immediately arise.
Thus, those who disregard death and destruction all originate from this single character, "lì" (利—profit). Is this not, indeed, like...?

One might ask: "Is this not the character for 'profit' (li)? It is truly the beginning of chaos. Only upon reaching this point does the author finally conclude the meaning of Grand Historian Sima Qian’s sighs.

Furthermore, while the sages and worthies strictly cautioned against profit and honored benevolence and righteousness as primary, even in later generations there were still those who relied on profit to deceive one another.
How many have there been who have wounded the Way and subverted the teachings? How much more so when one openly proclaims and practices the path of seeking profit?
If one desires the customs of the empire to be upright, rather than corrupt and base through greed, how could this possibly be achieved?
This section reiterates the words of the sages and worthies so that people may come to know the precepts and know what is honorable. "Profoundly precepted" means it is not shallow.
When the sages and worthies admonish people to abandon profit and desire and to honor benevolence and righteousness, their intent is by no means trivial.
Yet, in later generations, not only do they fail to follow the teachings to observe the precepts and preserve benevolence, but they instead rely on profit to deceive one another. To "rely" means—
This is also a form of dependence. Those who act in such a manner harm the moral transformation of the ancients and subvert the teachings of the sages and worthies;

there is no limit to them, as they cannot be fully enumerated—this is said to indicate their great number. Furthermore, he advances his argument one step further, saying: "It does not stop at this alone.
There is yet another kind of shameless person who practices [these things] openly. To say "openly" means in a bold and manifest manner.
They extensively promulgated the methods for extracting profit and practiced them on a grand scale. "Zhang" means to spread; "zheng" means to take.
Yet, the essential factor for rectifying and solemnizing the customs of the world lies entirely in ritual and law. Now, the path of profit is manifest while ritual and law have perished.
Yet, to ensure that the customs of the world remain upright and do not become decadent or impoverished—this is absolutely impossible.
"Decadent" (*jiāo*) means to drench; it carries the sense of being moistened. "Impoverished" (*bó*) means not substantial. The transformation of the superior [ruler] becomes the wind.
To practice the lower [teachings] for worldly profit is a delusive and frantic drug that must not be drunk; to drink it is undoubtedly to kill oneself.
This chapter admonishes students to guard against evil before it has sprouted, thereby avoiding harm.
Mingjiao said: "The evils committed by ordinary people are either manifest or unmanifest. Unmanifest evil is that which harms others;
manifest evil is that which kills people. The evil of killing is small, while the evil of harming is great."
This section first exposes their evil. Now, how could a student possibly possess the evil of killing or harming others, such that they would be cautioned against by their teacher?
Nevertheless, as people dwell on the ground of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are permeated moment by moment by fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).

When encountering objects, they give rise to emotional attachments; thus, without realizing it or being aware of it, a thought suddenly arises, producing [afflictions] within the sphere of self and other.
To what extent do jealousy, greed, and anger give rise to disputes and cause the loss of the foundation of the Way?
For this reason, it is said that the evil of harming others is great. The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "Evil with form has a definite source from which it comes;
its adversary can be resisted. Evil without form comes without warning; its harm is no small matter. Therefore, the evil of killing others is minor [in comparison].
The evil of harming others is great. Killing is spoken of in terms of outward traces; harming is discussed in terms of the mind.
Thus, within leisurely banquets there may be lethal poison; amidst laughter and jesting there may be spears and halberds; within the inner chambers there may be tigers and leopards.
In the neighboring lanes there were Rong and Di barbarians;
this section specifically clarifies evil matters. A "banquet for leisurely enjoyment" (*youyan*) is a feast where hosts and guests rejoice together in tranquility.

Who would have expected that poison was placed within the food, causing people to die before their feet could even touch the ground? The *Guangzhi* states: "The *hen* is a poisonous bird, as large as..."
The hawk has a neck eight inches long and is purple-green in color; it feeds on snakes and scorpions. The male is called *yun*, and the female is named *yin*.
If its feathers are placed in wine, flames will arise. If they are inserted into the nose, the intestines will rupture and death will follow immediately;
only rhinoceros horn can counteract this. Laughter and conversation arise without intention, yet one does not realize that a single word may be like a spear or a halberd.
It causes people to swallow their words and suppress their indignation, remaining ill at ease. The *ge* (pike) is a flat-headed halberd, six feet six inches long.
The *mao* (spear) is hook-shaped and twenty feet long; both are sharp weapons for inflicting injury. The central chamber constitutes the main hall.
The deep and secluded is called the inner sanctum (*ào*). Tigers and leopards can devour humans; yet how could there be tigers and leopards within the inner sanctum of a hall?
This refers to those capable of plotting to harm others, who are like such beasts. Five households constitute a neighborhood (*lín*); twenty-five households constitute a lane (*xiàng*).
As for the Rong and Di: these are the Western Rong and Northern Di, people who do not observe rites and laws. It is difficult to dwell together with them.
Unless one is a sage or a worthy, if one does not sever ties with them before their influence has sprouted and guard against them through rites and laws, will their harm not be exceedingly great?
This section teaches people to eliminate evil and guard against harm. The two characters "zìfēi" (自非) are used as an ironic expression. It is as if one were to say:
"If one were a sage or a worthy person, one would naturally be able to cut off [evil] before it has sprouted and guard oneself with ritual and law; thus, no evil thoughts could arise."
Therefore, there is nothing that can harm you. However, you are not yet a sage or a worthy one;
thus, you cannot cut off [evil] before it has even sprouted—where "sprouting" refers to the grass about to bud—and you further fail to restrain yourself with ritual propriety (*li*) and law.

Should a single thought suddenly arise, its consequences would be beyond description. Ritual propriety is the patterned refinement of the principles of Heaven (*tian-li*) and the regulation of human affairs.

This is appropriate. "Law" (*fa*) refers to institutions, regulations, and ceremonial codes. The *Zuozhuan* states: "It is stored within the profound and the obscure, yet it manifests at the moment of sudden crisis.
Were it not for the Sage establishing these as a defense through ritual (*li*), the human race would have perished long ago.
This supreme instruction for preventing harm and distancing oneself from evil is clearly set forth; it is simply that people [fail to follow it].
The mind is extremely treacherous; that which is familiar is difficult to forget. Be on guard!
This chapter cites a man of principle to shame greedy monks, causing them to reflect upon themselves.
Mingjiao says: When the Great Awakened Master Liaan was residing at Yuwang Monastery, two monks were quarreling over the distribution of offerings without ceasing. The abbot...
The matter could not be resolved. The Great Awakened One (the Emperor) summoned him and reprimanded him, saying:

"In the past, when Lord Bao was administering Kaifeng, there was a citizen who came forward and said, 'I had deposited one hundred taels of white gold with you; it is now lost. He has now returned it to his family, but the son will not accept it.
I hope you, my lord, will summon the son and restore it to him. Lord Bao sighed in wonder and immediately summoned the son to speak with him. The son declined, saying: "My late father..."

During his father’s lifetime, he had deposited no silver in private with other households. After the two parties had firmly declined for a long time, the Duke had no choice but to entrust the funds to temples and monasteries within the city to cultivate merit for the deceased in order to offer it as a memorial service.
Dajue was Chan Master Huailian of Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou, whose courtesy name was Qizhi.
He was the son of the Chen family of Chenzhou, Fujian, and was a dharma successor of Chan Master Letan Cheng. He belonged to the fourteenth generation below Qingyuan.
[This section first introduces his background. While he was residing at Yuyang, two monks were quarreling over wealth and profit without ceasing, and the monastery administrators...
No one could judge [the matter]. The Master summoned the two monks and rebuked them, citing past events as a lesson for the two monks.
Bao Gong’s name was Zheng, his courtesy name was Xiren; he rose to the rank of Censor. By nature he was stern and severe, never once showing a smile.
During his tenure as Governor of Kaifeng, there was a commoner named Li Jue’an who had a son named Jingwen; while the boy was still young, because—
While ill, he entrusted one hundred taels of white silver to his friend Zhang Huiming. After Juean’s death, Huiming returned the gold to his son.

The son would not accept it; on one hand, he thought that since he had received a person's deposit, he must certainly return it, and on the other hand, he thought that as his father had given no instructions regarding it, he should not accept it.
Huiming then appealed the matter to the magistrate. The magistrate marveled at the extraordinary nature of the situation.
He immediately summoned his son to return the gold, but the son resolutely refused. One insisted on returning the gold; the other steadfastly refused to accept it.

Seeing that both men were so righteous and courageous, the official had no choice but to entrust the gold to the local temples and monasteries to commission a vegetarian feast for the benefit of the deceased.
"To entrust" (ze) means to assign responsibility to others and have them carry out the task.
I witnessed this with my own eyes. Furthermore, those mired in the dust and toil of worldly life can still be so generous with their wealth and devoted to righteousness;
yet you, as a disciple of the Buddha, lack such integrity and shame. Consequently, I have expelled you according to the laws of the monastic community.

This section rebukes the monks for their lack of shame, saying: "In this matter, I have witnessed with my own eyes that even those in the midst of worldly toil, whose hearts were originally set upon wealth and profit, were still able to distance themselves from such riches and admire righteousness as you do.

The two characters 'ru' (如, 'as') are used here to emphasize, with all my might, that they possessed such righteousness. You two, having shaved your heads and donned the black robes, ought to practice the giving of alms (*dāna*)."

To cross over [to liberation] is the duty of a Buddha’s son. Yet, to return instead to quarreling over wealth and competing for profit is truly to fail in maintaining integrity and to be utterly devoid of shame.
The two characters "ruò shì" (若是) are used here as a severe rebuke for such shamelessness;

it is only right that he be expelled according to the ancient regulations of the monastic community so as not to defile the pure assembly. As for those today who struggle for money and delight in profit...
I have read it with reverence. Is it not a source of shame?
This essay reveals that the Master possesses the discerning eye to know men; thus, he has not failed the monk who possesses the potential to excel above his peers.
When Master Da-jue Lian first traveled to Mount Lu, Chan Master Yuan-tong Ne saw him at once and expected him to be a vessel of great capacity.
Someone asked, "How did you know this? Ne replied, "This man is central and balanced, leaning toward neither side; his demeanor is dignified whether in motion or stillness.

Furthermore, his mastery of the Way and his conduct are such that his words are concise yet exhaustive in their principle. Among ordinary people, few who possess such natural endowment fail to achieve greatness."
Regarding those who became vessels [from the *Jiuping ji*]:
Chan Master Junet of Lushan Yuantong, whose courtesy name was Zhongmin, was the son of the Jian family of Zizhou in Western Sichuan.
He was the dharma heir of Chan Master Zirong of Yanqing and belonged to the tenth generation below Qingyuan. Initially, when he met Dajue, Dajue recognized him as a vessel of great capacity.
"Upon a single glance": they were initially not acquainted with one another; yet, upon merely seeing each other once, it was immediately known that [the other] was a great vessel for the Dharma.

"Limit" (*ki*) means a boundary; it signifies that the accomplishment of the task is certain and beyond doubt. "Or if someone asks": this refers to the hypothetical case where someone might pose such a question.
"Why is it that one knows him at first sight? He replied: "This man’s character is central and upright, leaning toward neither side.
'Central' means not partial; 'upright' means not deviant. Whether moving or still, he maintains his own dignity and solemnity; this is how one knows the uniqueness of his physical form.
Furthermore, regarding what is maintained within his mind, he possesses the Way, possesses learning, possesses practice, and possesses virtue."
Yi. In all that he spoke, his words were concise yet exhaustive in principle; this was precisely because one knew the subtlety of his mind.

Zi and Bing—these two characters share the same meaning. Xian means "few. Generally speaking, regarding human nature and disposition, among those who possess such a character, there are few who do not become great vessels.
△ One whose knowledge possesses the eye upon the crown of the head can recognize people.
One must surely reach the ultimate in truth and beauty; this is no ordinary matter.

This chapter extols the worthy, the wise, and the broad-minded, instructing people that they should take the ancients as their model and emulate them today, being diligent at the beginning and careful to the end.

At the beginning of the Huángyòu era of Emperor Rénzǔ, a silver-inset eunuch messenger was dispatched, carrying a decree written on a single foot of silk, to summon Yuántōng Nè to reside at the Great Monastery of Xiàocí.
Nè declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise; instead, Dàjué submitted a memorial in response to the imperial summons.
This section first presents the event. "Renzu" refers to Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty. "Huangyou" is the reign title;
"chuzi" (the first characters) refers to the first and second years of the Huangyou era. "Quan zhe" (those sent) refers to envoys.

"Yindang" (silver ear-rings) and "erzhui" (ear-pendants) come in three types—gold, jade, and silver—to distinguish between ranks. During the Qin and Han dynasties, small eunuchs wore silver [pendants].
A *diao* (badger) on the right; Emperor Ming changed this to a golden *diao* on the left. Those who transmitted commands when entering or leaving the palace were eunuchs.
"One who holds" refers to one who carries an imperial edict in hand. "Green silk" refers to a green-colored document pouch.

"Chi-yi" refers to the "one-foot-one-inch" wooden tablet used during the Han dynasty to mount imperial decrees. "Zhao" (edict) means to announce; it is the command of the Sovereign. "Xiaoci" (Filial and Compassionate) refers to...

Since the destruction of the monasteries during the Tang dynasty, the two streets of temples had been restored during the Jianlong era of Emperor Taizu; these were all academies for doctrinal study (*yixue*).
Li Yunning, an envoy of the Silver Seal Office, submitted a memorial offering his residence in Bianjing to establish a Chan seat, which was granted the name Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery.
The Emperor took a keen interest in the school of emptiness (*kongzong*) and issued an edict to the Three Departments of State to deliberate on the summoning of those possessed of the Way.
The Abbot, Ou-yang Hsiu, and Cheng Shih-meng petitioned for the invitation of Chan Master Yuan-t'ung Nê. Emperor Ying personally issued an imperial decree to Chiang-chou;
however, Nê declined on the grounds of eye disease and deafness and did not go. The Emperor held him in even greater esteem and permitted him to nominate a successor.
Nê nominated Da-chueh Ho-shang, who then responded to the summons. "Gā-lan" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "monks' garden. It is...

This is a place where the community of monks dwells together. "Sū" (疏) means to explain away or clarify their inability to comply with the imperial command. "Biǎo" (表) means to present a memorial for advancement.
It signifies that the Great Awakened One is one who possesses the Way and is capable of responding to the summons and decrees of the Son of Heaven.

Someone said, "The Sage Emperor has honored and exalted moral virtue, and his grace extends even to the springs and rocks. Why does the Master so firmly decline? Nan said, "I have unworthily joined the ranks of the clergy;
my hearing and sight are no longer keen. It is my good fortune to find peace beneath the forest trees, subsisting on vegetarian food and drinking water.
Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs would not do such things, let alone others. As the sages of old said: 'It is difficult to dwell long under a great name. I—"
Throughout my life, I have practiced the principle of contentment and have not allowed fame or profit to burden me. If one’s heart is weary of worldly things, when will there ever be enough?
Thus, Dongpo once said: "To know contentment is honor; to know contentment is wealth."
This section sets forth its meaning. "Jiajie" (假借) is a figurative designation. "Jing" (旌) means to honor; "qin" (欽) means to look up to with admiration; "chong" (崇) means to revere. Some may say:
"Now the Sage Emperor honors, admires, and reveres the virtue and morality of our Master.
His grace is universally bestowed, such that even springs and rocks receive its nourishment. Why does the Master so firmly decline? To "firmly decline" means to entreat repeatedly three times.

"辭" (ci) means "to be included indiscriminately. "汎雜" (fanzá) means "miscellaneous and promiscuous. "倫" (lún) means "category" or "kind. "幸" (xìng) is the same as "倖" (xìng), meaning to obtain what one ought not to obtain.
"飡蔬" (cānsū) refers to coarse food. It is as if saying: "I am now a monk; I am merely included among the miscellaneous ranks of monks."

Furthermore, to find peace in the mountain forests is itself a stroke of good fortune. During that time, eating only vegetables and drinking only water, one may be said to be "a thousand times satisfied and ten thousand times fulfilled.
At such a moment, even if I were taught to become a Buddha or a Patriarch, I would have no desire for it;
how much less so to be the teacher of the Son of Heaven? The repetition of "ye" is a particle used to express a question. This reveals what is within his breast.
"Vast and empty, devoid of substance; pure as jade and clear as ice—how virtuous is this Master! Furthermore, he cites the words of Fan Li: 'It is difficult to dwell long beneath a great name.
How much more so for all that I have done throughout my life, every single act of which was a plan for contentment.
Fame, profit, and the nourishment of offerings truly bind and entangle a person; how could I, by means of such fame and profit..."
Yet one brings about self-entanglement. "Entanglement" means being bound and fettered. Furthermore, the greedy minds of worldly people are like thirsty deer; how could they ever find satiety?
If one desires to satisfy the mind with fullness, there will never be a day of completion. "Satiety" (yàn) here means fulfillment. Therefore, he again cites the words of Dongpo:
"To know contentment is honor; to know sufficiency is wealth. This serves to complete his lifelong understanding.
The substance of Master Zu’s conduct lay in avoiding fame and preserving his integrity, beginning well and ending well; this was attained through his perfect mastery (yuantong).
This section is intended by the compiler to praise the Master’s words, which state: "Fame is indeed what every person desires."
That the Master now avoids it may be called the perfection of virtue and the preservation of integrity. To leave the household life and become a vessel of beauty is a good beginning;
to achieve the Way and maintain a noble reputation is a good end. Such manifold excellences have been attained by the Master.
Sū Dongpo, surnamed Sū and styled Zīzhān, was a native of Mèishān. He received the Dharma from Dōnglín.
Cōng served as an official at the Hanlin Academy. Later, he built a residence east of the city walls of Huangzhou and consequently styled himself the "East Slope Recluse.
Reading his writings, one clearly perceives the skeletal remains of a man of the Way; his very sighs and laughter seem to linger before us, making it impossible for one not to envy him to death.
This chapter instructs people to maintain integrity and righteousness, and not to rely on external power.
Master Yuantong Ne said: "The life of a cripple depends on his staff; if he loses his staff, he will fall. The life of a ferryman depends on his boat."
If one loses their boat, they will drown. Generally, those who dwell beneath the trees [monastics] have nothing of their own to preserve;
those who rely on external power as their support will, the moment they lose that which they rely upon, all fail to escape the calamity of falling and drowning.

"Lame" means being crippled and unable to walk; it refers to falling down. "Drowned" means to be submerged. These terms are used metaphorically to describe the state of being dependent on something external for support.
For example, one with a lame foot relies entirely on a staff for strength; if they lose the staff while walking, they will inevitably fall.
For those who cross a river, their lives depend entirely upon the boat; if they lose the boat in the water, they will surely be submerged.

By this one may know that, in general, practitioners in the forest (recluses) ought to maintain their integrity and righteousness to honor themselves, rather than relying on power and influence to control others.

"Jia" (挾) means to support or uphold. Should the day ever come when their karma is exhausted and their blessings have ended, and their power and influence are lost, their integrity and righteousness—[will remain].
It will not remain. Whether one tumbles or sinks, how can one escape it? Those who rely on their power should suddenly turn back before they reach the point of tumbling and sinking;
once it is too late for regret, what can be done?
This chapter discusses the rise and fall of monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*); it lies in virtue, not in formal rules.

Yuantong Ne said: "In the past, the Great Wise Chan Master Baizhang established monasteries and instituted regulations, desiring to remedy the failing of the Dharma not being born during the Semblance Age.
He little realized that students of the Semblance Age would steal these regulations to destroy Baizhang’s [legacy]."
Regarding the Monastic Forests:
Chan Master Daizhi Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Jiangxi was a native of the Wang family of Changle in Fuzhou.
He was the dharma heir of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi. He belongs to the second generation under Nanyue. [This section clarifies how the Dharma led to corruption.]

"Jian" (建) means to establish; "zhi" (置) means to place; "li" (立) means to set up; and "cheng" (成) means to complete. "Cao" (草) refers to grasses; when many grow together, they form a thicket (*cong*); when many trees grow together, they form a forest (*lin*).

This is the place where the assembly of monks takes refuge and the site where one settles the mind to cultivate the Way. "Yuan" (圓) refers to the compass; "fang" (方) refers to the square ruler. These are used as models and patterns.
This means that Baizhang established the monasteries (*conglins*) and instituted their rules and regulations, intending thereby to save [sentient beings].
To remedy the maladies of the unrighteousness of people in the final age: while the Buddha dwelt in the world, it was called the True Dharma (*saddharma*);

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the images remained, it was called the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*). This is the final age. To indulge in greed, anger, and delusion, and to harbor thoughts of birth and death—all these are maladies of unrighteousness.
"Zeng" (曾) means "indeed. Those who steal the rules (*guiju*) feign public service to satisfy their private interests; they use the Dharma to commit villainy. This is indeed...
I observe that those who study in this degenerate age plunder the systems and standards of their predecessors, yet end up destroying the monastic groves established by them. Why is this?

It is because in ancient times, when teachers saw that students were unrestrained in mind and wild in spirit, making it difficult for them to enter the Way, they relied upon rules and regulations to subdue them.
However, they failed to realize that as time passes, decay arises; instead of recognizing this, they rely on those very rules and regulations as a pretext for further control.
Greed, anger, and the ego are called "fame," yet in reality, they serve as the medium for profit and desire; this is why the monastic communities have fallen into ruin.
In ancient times, although people lived in nests or caves, everyone disciplined themselves. After the era of Great Sages, although people dwell in lofty halls...
In a grand mansion, everyone naturally feels constrained. Thus it is said: "Safety and peril depend on virtue; rise and fall depend on destiny.
This section clarifies the distinctions between antiquity and the present. In ancient times, people lived in nests during the summer and dwelt in caves during the winter.
Those who lived in nests and caves had no fixed rules of their own, yet everyone spontaneously established their own rules; therefore, it is called "self-discipline" (*lǜ*). Discipline.

This is a matter of regulations and decrees. Yet people today occupy high halls a hundred feet tall and vast mansions of a thousand pillars; though these possess rules and measures, they do not follow them.
Everyone acts according to their own whims and indulges their desires, wandering aimlessly until they forget their way back. Therefore it is said that they bring about their own ruin.
By this we know that the safety or peril of a person depends on virtue, while the rise or decline of affairs depends on destiny (*shu*). As for destiny:
It is a matter of timing; it is a matter of principle and destiny.
If virtue can be sustained, why necessarily require a forest monastery? If destiny can be relied upon, what need is there for rules and regulations? (From the *Yalu*)
This passage definitively determines that teaching. "Gou" (苟) means "if. "Jiang" (將) means "to maintain.

It implies that if a student truly possesses virtue that can be maintained, they may practice anywhere—even in deep mountains or remote valleys—why must they necessarily seek out monastic communities?

If one can indeed penetrate the principles and patterns of reality, then all hardships and setbacks will become forms of ritual discipline; furthermore, why must one necessarily [seek such environments] on purpose?
"Ruler and square. What does this mean? It means that the Master’s intention lies in making the cultivation of virtue and the clarification of principle his urgent task;
it is not for the purpose of neglecting the monastic community or disregarding established rules. Students must understand this. The *Tanzi Huashu* also says:
"If virtue can be carried forth, why necessarily expand upon grain and silk? If numerical rites can be relied upon, why necessarily expand upon..."
Regarding military weapons: if one allows oneself to become self-indulgent and self-defeating, who is it that causes this? A student ought to cherish themselves;
this chapter instructs students to contemplate danger while dwelling in peace, so that they may avoid lifelong anxiety.
Yuantong said to Dajue: "The ancient sages cultivated their minds before [afflictions] had sprouted and guarded their emotions before they were disordered.

This is because when one is prepared in advance, there will be no calamity; thus, one sets up heavy gates and strikes the wooden clappers to await violent guests, taking this from the hexagram Yú (Preparation)."

This section clarifies being prepared so as to be free from affliction. "That which is called" refers to addressing someone. First, the ancient sages are cited so that people may know the correctness of the model to be followed.
"Cultivating the mind" means refining the mind. "Before it has sprouted" means prior to the movement of even a single thought;
if one waits for the mind and thoughts to act, it becomes delusion. "Sentiment" refers to the passions of consciousness. [One must] guard against them.
The mind must be preserved before it becomes disordered. If one allows the conscious mind to rush in competition with external objects, then the person will become deluded.
"Preemptively" (*yu*) means beforehand; "preparation" (*bei*) means guarding against danger. To teach that one should guard against danger beforehand ensures that no faults or afflictions arise.

Next, he cites the *Yijing* (Book of Changes), the hexagram *Lei Di Yu* (Thunder over Earth: Preemption), taking its imagery to elucidate this point: with *Zhen* (Thunder) above and *Kun* (Earth) below, there is tranquility, harmony, and joy.
Regarding the meaning of this, Master Yang said: "Once the roads and paths are open, violent guests will arrive; one must not fail to ward them off with skillful means.

Therefore, the hexagram *Yù* (Preparation) is taken as the model: by setting up double gates to ward them off and striking the wooden clappers to give warning, violent guests will have no way to enter.
The two yin lines at the top represent the image of the double gates; the single yang line at the bottom represents the striking [of the clappers]."
The image of *tuó* (the wooden clapper): three yin lines within represent the image of joy and delight. *Tuó* is made by hewing wood; it is that which is struck during night patrols.

If one prepares for an undertaking in advance, it is easy; if one acts when the crisis has already arrived, it is certainly difficult. Among the sages and philosophers of antiquity, there were those who harbored lifelong anxieties.
That one suffers not for even a single morning lies truly in this (from the *Jiupeng ji*).
This section teaches and admonishes you to be ever-vigilant and never forget it. Generally speaking, regarding all worldly undertakings, one must first regulate and prepare oneself.
Such conduct is easy [to master] when practiced gradually; if one acts with haste, the task will not be thorough. "Zhe" (哲) means "worthy.
This refers to the wise men and sagacious scholars of antiquity, who never for a single moment or instant failed to worry, strive, and exert themselves to admonish themselves.
Thus, the reason they had no anxiety regarding sudden calamities was that they possessed the wisdom of foresight. Therefore, one must prepare before the sun has declined.
These two characters—what kind of person could achieve them? Even King Wen had no leisure from morning until evening, and Zhou Gong found no rest;
only by such means might one perhaps attain them.
This chapter states that learning is the fundamental basis for establishing one's character;
it must be practiced with vigorous effort. The Great Awakened Master Liaan said: "Jade is not formed into a vessel unless it is carved; a person does not know the Way unless they study.
It is by this that the present understands the past and the later understands the former; thus, the good may be taken as a model, while the evil may serve as a warning.
This is for the sake of the precepts. First, an analogy shall be raised to clarify this: it is like jade within stone, which must rely upon carving and polishing.

If it were left uncarved, how could it become a beautiful vessel? It is the same for the student: if one does not apply oneself diligently to learning, how can one come to know its wondrous subtleties?
Principle. Just as people today can know where the ancients reached and those of later generations can know what their predecessors practiced, it is all due to the power of learning and knowledge.
These two sentences are from Han Yu’s "Memorial Presented to Emperor Shunzong of Tang.
"What was good in antiquity, I shall take as my model; what was not good among my predecessors, I shall take as a warning."
"Observe the predecessors who have established themselves and achieved renown in their time; few did not achieve this through learning and inquiry.
This section instructs one to observe the ancients. "To observe" means to look at them in succession—that is, to look back step by step at the ancients of old.
All those who possessed outstanding insight and disciplined cultivation, and who spread their fine reputations throughout their own eras, [did so through study]."
Who is it that is not so? It is through diligent and earnest effort, extensively reading the classics and histories, and consulting the wise and the sages, that one achieves accomplishment.
Therefore, students should cultivate with courageous vigor and profound dedication. The two characters "study" (xuéwèn) do not mean that one has finished once they have been spoken;
within them lies the actual merit of unremitting diligence. To stop as soon as one happens to achieve something is to fail oneself.
What is the basis for this naming? Let students strive toward it.
This chapter is a response to a letter from the Vice Director Sun Xunlao, in which [the author] asserts that the Three Teachings are fundamentally one body;
it is only because human sentiments have undergone change that internal notions of self and other arise, leading to disputes over right and wrong, and thereby causing this Way to vanish.
The Great Awakened One said: "The principle of the wondrous Way was once embodied by the sages in the *I Ching*.

However, when the Zhou dynasty declined, the laws of the former kings were destroyed and rites and righteousness perished; thereafter, eccentric words and heterodox arts emerged sporadically to disorder the customs."

This section clarifies that the establishment of the teaching occurs at a specific time. The Way is fundamentally nameless and likewise devoid of characteristics; it exhausts the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions, being neither localized nor non-localized.
Only when the single wondrous character "Jia" (加) is added does one first perceive that while its essence remains immutable, its function accords with conditions.
The sages do not increase and the ordinary people do not decrease; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving—is this not wondrous?
This is what is called the principle of the Wondrous Way (*miao dao*). "Principle" (*li*) is synonymous with "meaning" (*yi*). The sages once enshrined this within the *Yi* (the Book of Changes).
These "sages" refer to Fuxi, King Wen, and Confucius. "Enshrined" (*yu*) means "entrusted" or "deposited. The *Yi* refers to the *Yijing* (Classic of Changes); it is said that this wondrousness—
The principles of the Way are difficult to point out directly. The sages of antiquity could do no more than rely on words in the *I Ching* to manifest them;
thus, they showed how the Ultimate (Wuji) gives rise to the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji), which in turn produces the Two Polarities, the Four Images, and the Eight Trigrams.

Within these, all things and all phenomena—including birth and death, success and failure, and the mechanisms of concealment and manifestation—are fully contained. During the decline of the Zhou dynasty, [the sages spoke of] Kings You and Li.
Thereafter, as the Way of the world declined, the laws and regulations fell into ruin, and rites and righteousness perished.
When the correct has declined, the perverse inevitably manifests; thus, various strange rumors and heterodox, deviant arts emerged sporadically to disrupt social customs.
"Emerging sporadically" means they appeared privately by taking advantage of gaps and opportunities. At such a time, the transmission of the Way was nearly extinguished.
It was perilous.

When our Śākyamuni entered the Middle Kingdom, he revealed the ultimate truth (paramārtha) to people in its pure essence, yet from beginning to end he established compassion to transform sentient beings;
this, too, was a means of responding to the exigencies of the times.

This section clarifies that the teaching was established according to the occasion. "Dai" (逮) means "to reach" or "to arrive at. "Śākyamuni" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren).
This refers to the fact that when I, Śākyamuni, descended to be born in the Central Land—that is, in the land of Zhongguo (China), which is the Indian subcontinent where the Buddha was born.
"Pure" (*chun*) means being singular and unmixed. It takes the single flavor of the Middle Way as its teaching, never falling into the two extremes.
"The Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) refers to the principle of truth that is neither dual nor triple; it awakens those people from beginning to end.
All that is bestowed and all that is established are the path of compassion and kindness, intended to teach and transform sentient beings. Kindness (*maitrī*) is able to grant happiness;

compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract them from suffering. As for "sentient beings," they are produced through the arising of manifold dharmas; that is, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute their physical form.
