The reflections conditioned by the six sense-objects constitute the characteristics of the mind. "Toward" (qù) means to incline; it signifies that even the coming of a Buddha is for the purpose of inclining toward that [right] time, and all such occurrences have their causes.
One should treasure the word "time. This conveys the meaning of the medicine emerging from the golden jar to save those who are ill:
if it does not emerge at this time, when will it ever emerge? Later, the customs of the people were divided into four seasons, totaling—
All things return to winter; there is a deeper meaning here.
Since the birth of mankind, when the primal simplicity had not yet dissipated, the teachings of the Three Sovereigns were concise and plain—this was like spring.
As the apertures of the emotions were daily excavated, the teachings of the Five Emperors became detailed and ornate—this was like summer. Times and ages differ, and human sentiments follow the days.

It was transferred. Thus, the teachings of the Three Kings were subtle and solemn, like the autumn season. In the past, regarding the proclamations and oaths of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, later scholars have been unable to understand them;
yet when the people of those times heard them, they did not disobey. How different, then, is the custom from that of today?
When it reached its degeneration in the Qin and Han periods, there was no limit to what occurred. Therefore, throughout the world...
There were those who could not bear to hear this. Thereupon, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, first expounded it through the principle of life and destiny.
This section clarifies the four seasons; for since heaven gave birth to the people, their fundamental nature has been one of simplicity and purity.
Being entirely unadulterated, the teachings of the Three Sovereigns were concise and simple, like the springtime of heaven when all things are budding and latent, yet have not yet moved.
The Three Sovereigns are Taihao (the Lord of Great Radiance), Fuxi, and Yan Di.

Shennong, Huangdi, and Youxingshi—“Huang” signifies greatness. Their Way was so great that it matched Heaven; therefore, they are called the Three Sovereigns (Sanhuang). “Dou” means a cavity or aperture;
“zhao” means to excavate or open up. As the *Zhuangzi* says: "After seven days of being excavated, the Chaos died."
This refers to the fact that as one reaches the apertures of human nature, they are opened and carved according to the times, whereby the paths of affairs gradually emerge.
Thus, the teachings and laws of the Five Emperors were detailed, complete, and elegant, like the summer season when all things flourish and grow luxuriantly.
The Five Emperors were: Shao Hao (the Lord of Metal Heaven), Zhuanxu (the Lord of High Yang), and Di Ku (the Lord of High Xin).
The Clan [of Yao]. Emperor Yao, of the Táo Dáng clan. Emperor Shùn, of the Yǒu Yú clan. They presided over the altars of soil and grain (*shèjì*) and brought peace to the people;

as their conduct accorded with the Way of the Sovereigns (*dìdào*), they are called the Five Emperors (*wǔdì*). Regarding the distinction between "time" (*shí*) and "age" (*shì*): "time" refers to the four seasons or the twelve periods of the day;
it is spoken of in terms of the near. Thirty years constitute an "age"; there are the past, future, and present. "Age" is spoken of in terms of the distant.
Treatise: As time shifts and eras change, human sentiments likewise undergo transformation. When sentiments shift, they inevitably give rise to artifice;
thus, the teachings of the Three Kings were solemn, meticulous, and majestic, like the autumn season of heaven, which possesses a chilling and destructive air.
The Three Kings were: King Yu of Xia, surnamed Si; King Tang of Yin, surnamed Zi; and King Wen of Zhou.

The surname was Ji. "King" (Wang) means "to go toward"; it signifies that which the whole world turns toward. During the era of the Three Kings, the position of the Nine-Five (the throne) was no longer transmitted to the worthy but to one's own son.
It was at this point that ritual, music, literary arts, penal law, and administrative regulations reached their full perfection.
*Gào* (誥) means "to inform. To report upward is called *gào*; to issue downward is called *gào*.

It is the name of a section in the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), such as the "Zhong Hui's Gao" and the "Tang Gao" from the *Shangshu*, and the "Kang Gao" and "Jiu Gao" from the *Zhou Shu*. *Shì* (誓) means "oath" or "covenant.
Examples include the "Gan Shi" and "Tang Shi" of Yu, and the "Qin Shi" of Zhou; these were all sworn oaths made among the feudal lords. Now, regarding the *Gao*:
The text of this oath is refined in principle and complete in meaning. There are those among scholars who, though they recite and practice it, are unable to fully comprehend it.

Comparing the present with the past, one sees that at that time the people were characterized by a prevailing air of simplicity and integrity; hearing the terms of their oath, they did not dare to transgress them.
When comparing the customs of antiquity with those of today, how vast is the distance between them! As for the daily degeneration of its influence...
Descending to the Qin of Ying and the Han of Liu, they subverted principle and violated moral custom, doing everything that ought not to be done.

Instances such as ministers murdering their sovereigns and sons murdering their fathers were everywhere. The worthy scholars of the world were filled with grief and sorrow, unable to bear hearing of such unrighteous acts that harm life.
It was for this reason that our Buddha, the Tathāgata, first descended to be born among humans.

To transform and guide sentient beings, one encompasses them through the principle of life and destiny and the Way of Compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), thereby transforming their deviations into correctness and their evils into goodness.
Thus it is said that from beginning to end, one establishes compassion. It is like the winter in the Way of Heaven, which gathers and stores [the fruits].
*Buddha* in the Sanskrit language means "The Awakened One" (*buddha*). There are three types, namely: self-... [text ends]
Awakening; awakening others; and the fulfillment of awakening. As for "Tathāgata," it means one who has come from the path of suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, "such" (*tathā*) refers to original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), and "come" (*āgata*) refers to initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). Because the initial and the original are non-dual, one is called a Tathāgata.

Heaven has four seasons that circulate, thereby generating and completing all things. The Sage establishes teachings that support one another in turn, thereby transforming and perfecting the world; it is just like this.
This section generally elucidates the intention of the sages of the Three Teachings to transform and harmonize the world through mutual influence.
Heaven has four seasons that circulate; "circulate" (huan) means to complete the cycle and begin again. It is like the Way of Heaven, which begins and then ends.
Ending and beginning, flowing without ceasing, it is simply for the purpose of generating and completing the myriad things.
The sages of the Three Teachings established their teachings so as to support one another in turn. "In turn" means alternately or mutually;
it does not exceed the act of creating and completing, nurturing the human mind and nature, and transforming the world through moral influence. It is just like this:
"This" refers to the operation of the four seasons in the celestial realm.
Yet, when they reach their ultimate limit, all inevitably encounter decay. Decay refers to the outward traces; there must necessarily be sages and worthies to address this.
The world arises and one rescues it.
This section follows from Xunlao’s question regarding those who have a reputation for "cultivating themselves alone" yet engage in eccentric conduct—being artificial rather than genuine.
Therefore, the Master again answers by shifting the focus to the character "so" (rán). Ultimately, when both parties reach the ultimate limit of practicing the Way, [they are found to be one].
None can be entirely comprehensive and free from flaws. A "flaw" refers to a trace of imperfection. For instance, although Confucius was a sage, he could not rectify the faults of his sovereign;
although the Duke of Zhou was a sage, he could not restrain the deceptions within the state of Lu; and although Yao and Shun were sages, they could not transform their sons toward goodness.
Whether it be the former sages or later sages, the principle remains the same. Whether the Way is practiced or not depends on [circumstances].
The times compel it; to judge the mind of a sage by the changes of the age is either foolishness or madness.

Yet, in this degenerate and evil world, there must be great sages and supreme saints who, out of compassion for all beings, bestow their mercy and arise from within this turbid and foul sea to rescue us with all their might;
only then might the lineage of the Way be somewhat restored.
Since the Qin and Han dynasties, more than a thousand years have passed; social customs have become increasingly decadent and thin.
The teachings of the sages stand like tripods side by side, yet they mutually disparage one another. The Great Way has become desolate, with none returning to it—this is truly lamentable.
This section concludes that while the teachings are the same, the people have changed. From the Qin and Han dynasties until the present, more than a thousand years have passed;
the customs and social mores of the people have become increasingly debased. "Mimi" (靡靡) means gradually or progressively; "yu" (愈) means more or further, signifying an intensification of this trend.
This means that [the teachings] gradually become thin and diluted, declining day by day.
The Dharma taught by the Sages is displayed in the world like the three legs of a tripod; not one can be missing.

Yet today’s people not only fail to support one another, but instead revile and slander each other—*di* (詆) meaning to scold, and *zi* (訾) meaning to destroy. Consequently, the principles of the wondrous Way are increasingly neglected.
It turns toward obscurity; vast and silent, it departs and does not return. How tragic! How lamentable! Truly, it is to be sighed over.

△ This entire great text surges like billowing waves, penetrating from top to bottom. From the fundamental source of the Way, it speaks of the transformations of human emotions, all of which are gathered back into the Ultimate Way, concluding with "truly to be sighed over. This is a single needle applied to the crown of the head.
To establish the teaching and bring the dead back to life—this is truly a marvelous feat. ○ Appendix:

Letter Received △ From the Three Dynasties onwards, successive sages have maintained the continuity of governance such that administration was harmonious and the people were at peace; the lineage of the Way has been transmitted without interruption.
It was not considered a deficiency that Buddhism had not yet arrived. When the Zhou dynasty ended its mandate and the Qin was replaced by the Han, the constitutional laws were changed.
Nets and traps form nests that shroud the sky and fall upon the wilds; yet they do not reform themselves despite the arrival of the Buddhist teachings.

Throughout the four seas, factions split apart and divergent doctrines emerge with increasing speed, reaching their height from the Tang dynasty through the Five Dynasties period. Amidst the myriad affairs and ten thousand state machinations, where order and chaos are ever-shifting, what benefit is there in upholding the Buddhist doctrine?
There are those who occasionally wear grass for clothing and eat wood for food, dwelling in crags and drinking from mountain streams, yet these do no more than—

They merely seek to perfect themselves alone. Furthermore, there are those who possess fame yet act contrary to it; their claims are false rather than true, and as their transformative teachings have not been fully realized, corruption arises.
Yet a teacher must surely possess the power of discernment; we await your explanation of this matter.
This chapter instructs those who practice the Way to set aside their own benefit for the sake of others, taking non-attachment as the essential application.

The Great Awakened One said: "Now, one who serves as a leader of a region and wishes to practice the Way they have attained to benefit others must first subdue themselves and bestow kindness upon things, lowering their mind toward all beings.
Only then, regarding gold and silk as mere excrement and soil, can they [attain] the four..."
The multitude honors and returns to him.
"A single region" refers to a province, a prefecture, a district, or a village; collectively, these are called a single region.
The "master" is the one who acts as the host for the propagation of the teaching. The "Way he has attained" is the learning through which he previously investigated and realized awakening. As for...
Self-benefit. Now, desiring to awaken these people through this Way is the benefit of others. Generally speaking, those who act as teachers and models for others must possess a correct standard;
they must first subdue their own selfish hearts in order to exclusively extend their virtue to others.
Furthermore, they must humble their minds to treat all beings with patience. Only then may they employ wealth, grain, cloth, and silk...
Treat them with as little regard as excrement or soil. If one maintains oneself and engages with others in this manner, the fourfold assembly will naturally revere and submit to them.
The "fourfold assembly" consists of the two groups of renunciants and the two groups of laypeople. Throughout this entire work there are only six sentences;
the meaning of ten thousand volumes of scripture is fully exhausted within these.
This chapter admonishes people that even when secure, one must not forget danger; it should be reflected upon deeply and never treated with negligence or arrogance.

The Great Awakened One said: "Those of former generations who possessed the talent for intelligence yet lacked concern for security and peril—such as Shimen Cong and Qixian Shun—are examples by which we may be cautioned."

This section teaches that one must be cautious regarding safety and peril. Zen Master Yuncong of Shimen Temple in Xiangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Nian of Shoushan and belonged to the ninth generation under Mount Heng.
During his tenure at Shimen, he was fond of collecting calligraphic works by ancient masters.
When the Prefect visited the temple and saw them, he requested to borrow them three times after his departure; the Master did not grant permission, which provoked the Prefect’s anger.

The Prefect had severely reprimanded Master [Zhaozhou]. Once the Master returned, the assembly of monks welcomed him by the roadside. The Head Seat stepped forward to offer his greetings and said, "The Prefect has needlessly humiliated you, Master. The Master pointed at the ground and said, "A pile of bones rises from level ground. As soon as he spoke, a mound three feet high surged up right where he pointed. When the Prefect heard of this, he sent men to shave it away. Three times he did so. When the Master pointed again, the mound rose back up to its original height. The Prefect was deeply moved and apologized for his previous conduct. He then invited the Master to reside permanently at the monastery. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he told the monks, "I have been here for thirty years, yet I have not seen even a single blade of grass grow. Having spoken thus, he passed away. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Nanjun. This was the second patriarch of the Linji school. His dharma name was Zhaozhou, and his secular surname was Pei. He was a native of Taiyuan, China. He lived to the age of one hundred and seventeen. The Master’s lineage was as follows: the First Patriarch Mahākāśyapa; the Second Patriarch Ānanda; the Third Patriarch Śaṇavāsa; the Fourth Patriarch Upagupta; the Fifth Patriarch Dharmatrāta; the Sixth Patriarch Buddhanandi; the Seventh Patriarch Buddhamitra; the Eighth Patriarch Parśva; the Ninth Patriarch Punyayashas; the Tenth Patriarch Vasubandhu; the Eleventh Patriarch Manorhita; the Twelfth Patriarch Simha; the Thirteenth Patriarch Prajñātāra; the Fourteenth Patriarch Bodhidharma; the Fifteenth Patriarch Huike; the Sixteenth Patriarch Sengcan; the Seventeenth Patriarch Daoxin; the Eighteenth Patriarch Hongren; the Nineteenth Patriarch Huineng; the Twentieth Patriarch Mazu Daoyi; the Twenty-first Patriarch Baizhang Huaihai; the Twenty-second Patriarch Huangbo Xiyun; the Twenty-third Patriarch Linji Yixuan; the Twenty-fourth Patriarch Xuefeng Yicun; the Twenty-fifth Patriarch YanTou Shouzuo; the Twenty-sixth Patriarch Fayan Wenyi; the Twenty-seventh Patriarch Fenzhou Wuye; the Twenty-eighth Patriarch Yunmen Wenyan; the Twenty-ninth Patriarch Dongshan Liangjie; the Thirtieth Patriarch Caoshan Benji; the Thirty-first Patriarch Yangqi Fanghui; the Thirty-second Patriarch Fenyang Shanzhao; the Thirty-third Patriarch Yuanwu Keqin; the Thirty-fourth Patriarch Dahui Zonggao; the Thirty-fifth Patriarch Wansong Xingxiu; the Thirty-sixth Patriarch Juefan Huihong; the Thirty-seventh Patriarch Tianyi Yihuai; the Thirty-eighth Patriarch Zhenxie Qingliao; the Thirty-ninth Patriarch Xuedou Chongxian; the Fortieth Patriarch Wuzu Fayan; the Forty-first Patriarch Touzi Datong; the Forty-second Patriarch Hongzhi Zhengjue; the Forty-third Patriarch Wanshi Shoude; the Forty-fourth Patriarch Xutang Zhiyu; the Forty-fifth Patriarch Zhenxie Qingliao; the Forty-sixth Patriarch Xuedou Chongxian; the Forty-seventh Patriarch Wuzu Fayan; the Forty-eighth Patriarch Touzi Datong; the Forty-ninth Patriarch Hongzhi Zhengjue; the Fiftieth Patriarch Wanshi Shoude; the Fifty-first Patriarch Xutang Zhiyu; the Fifty-second Patriarch Zhenxie Qingliao; the Fifty-third Patriarch Xuedou Chongxian; the Fifty-fourth Patriarch Wuzu Fayan; Next, it surged up again as before. The Prefect was terrified; day and night he was ill at ease, and within a month his entire family perished in Xiangzhou.
Chan Master Xiaoshun of Yunju in Nankang, surnamed Laofu, was the son of the Hu family of Ruizhou.
He was a dharma heir of Chan Master Cong of Dongshan, the tenth generation below Qingyuan. He resided at Qixian Temple on Mount Lu. At the temple...
Later, there was a large tree. The Prefect entered the mountains and saw it; he intended to cut it down to establish a public office site, but the Master would not permit it.

Subsequently, someone harboring a grudge took advantage of a vulnerability to file a complaint. The Prefect seized the Master and interrogated him harshly, ordering him to return to secular life and stripping away his monastic robes.
Dajue realized that he had previously entered the chamber of Shun and thus went to the capital to seek him out. Dajue yielded [the position].

Shun resided in the main hall, while Liai lived in a side chamber. Emperor Renzong repeatedly issued edicts for him to enter the inner palace to inquire about the Way, yet Liai never spoke of Shun’s affairs.

One day, by imperial decree, he was ordered to provide a meal for the monks at Jingyin Monastery. There he saw Da’jue serving Shun with great reverence; upon returning, he reported this to the Emperor, who summoned him for an audience.
The Emperor then sighed in admiration, saying, "His spiritual resonance is extraordinary and magnificent; he is truly a man of realization from the mountains and forests. Thereupon...

The *Shanshu* records: Having been exonerated from blame, he became a monk and resided again at Xiqian. He was further granted purple robes and a golden bowl, and an envoy was dispatched to escort him back.
On the day Shun retired from Xiqian, two strongmen were carrying his sedan chair to the front of Luohan Temple.
The two men said to each other, "Now he is no longer the elder of our monastery; there is no need to escort him far. They abandoned the sedan chair and returned.
Once Shun had returned, he sent someone to comfort them, saying, "What you did at that time was correct. Set your minds at ease; there is no need for suspicion or fear.
Entering the monastery, he ascended the hall and said: "Without cause, I was slandered and unjustly met with misfortune;
For more than half a year, I lived as a layman. Today I return once more to Sanxia Temple; How much joy, how much anger? Now, Great... [text continues]
Regarding "Awakening and Exhortation": it is said that our predecessors possessed the capacity for intelligence. Sharpness of ear is "cleverness" (cóng), while sharpness of eye is "clarity" (míng).
They never lacked the concern that "when at peace, one must not forget danger.

For instance, Shimen suffered the humiliation of Xiangzhou because he failed to maintain self-restraint, and Qixian was pursued to Nankang because he failed to regulate himself. Were these two masters not [examples of this truth]?
Even those of naturally refined and beautiful character may possess such failings; this can truly serve as a warning for future generations.

Nevertheless, the fixed karma of human life is inherently difficult to discern clearly. If one examines its origins in detail, how could one not realize that it is the fault of negligence, arrogance, and lack of reflection?
Therefore it is said: "Calamities lie hidden in the subtle and minute, yet they manifest through what people do."
Suddenly, when observing this, one should be especially cautious and reverent;

these points of instruction must be vigilantly examined. Thus, while it is true that human beings possess fixed karmic retributions from past lives that are inherently difficult to discern and impossible to escape, if one carefully and minutely scrutinizes their origins, how could this not be regarded as negligence and indolence?
Is this not the fault of failing to reflect and examine? It is a word of doubt; out of humility, I do not yet dare to be certain. Therefore it is said:
"The calamities, harms, sorrows, and anxieties of men lie hidden within the obscure, secluded, and minute. By what means are they brought forth?
They are brought forth by a person’s momentary negligence and lack of care. Judging from the two masters, one should all the more observe reverence.
This means to be cautious and reverent. "You" (尤) means "even more so. Regarding the two terms "negligence" (忽) and "arrogance" (慢), each has its own fault.

Negligence results from a lack of refinement in the mind; arrogance results from a lack of respect in the mind. In managing worldly affairs and conducting one's conduct, one must constantly admonish oneself to be wary and reverent.
This chapter teaches that the application of one's true feeling must be cultivated in ordinary times; when such feeling reaches its peak, the matter will naturally resolve itself.
Master Yunju Shun, styled Laofu, while residing at Qixian on Mount Lu, [was visited] by the District Magistrate Huai Dugu.
"Personal resentment leads to calamity and injustice; the people will wear [the consequences]. I am going to the capital to visit Da'jue.
This section clarifies that he visited for a specific reason. Yunju was located in Nan-kang, Jiangxi, and was renowned as the preeminent monastery of the region east of the Yangtze (Jiangzuo).
This recounts the Master’s past events; thus it says, "during his stay at Qixian on Mount Lu," referring to the causal occasion.

Because of the Prefect Huai Dugu—there was an ancient *huái* tree in front of Nan’ang Prefecture, hence he was called Huai Dugu—the Master harbored private resentment, which was not in accordance with the True Dharma.
*Li* means to encounter; *héngyì* (横逆) means to act contrary to principle, as cited from Mencius. "The people shall wear [their own clothes]" refers to the clothing of the common people.
Yi (clothing). The capital, that is, the imperial city.
Upon arriving at a lodging in Shanyang (present-day Chuzhou), he was obstructed by snow. One night, a guest arrived, having broken through the snow with two servants.
Seeing the old man as an old acquaintance, the guest immediately changed his clothes and bowed before him.
The old man questioned him, and the guest replied, "In the past, while at Dongshan, I was the one who carried your belongings to Hanyang; I am your servant, Song Rong.

The old man conversed with him about their former times, and the guest sighed for a long while. At dawn, he prepared a meal and presented five taels of white silver, then called for a servant. The guest— [text ends] —[left].
He said, "This boy has traveled to and from the capital several times; he is thoroughly familiar with the hardships and obstacles along the way. You may proceed without concern, Master.
It is because of him that I have been able to reach the imperial capital."
This section clarifies the circumstances encountered by the author’s former self. While traveling along the road, he was detained by snow at an inn (*lùdì*; that is, a guesthouse).
One evening as the day was drawing to a close, there arrived another traveler bringing a servant with him. This man had come through the falling snow;
upon seeing the old man, he treated him as an old acquaintance. "Not long thereafter" (*yǐ'ér*) means before much time had passed.
He then changed his clothes and paid his respects before the old man. When the old man asked the reason for his prostration, he replied:
"In the past, while at Dongshan, I was a servant who accompanied my master as he traveled with his luggage. I went to Hanyang to attend to various affairs;
my surname is Song and my name is Rong. 'Chouxi' refers to the distant past. Together—[he continued].
He recounted the events of the past and the reasons for his misfortune. The guest sighed and lamented incessantly.
At dawn—that is, early the next morning—he prepared a meal and gave him five taels as travel expenses. He then called for a servant.
The guest said, "This son of mine has traveled back and forth to the capital several times; regarding all the obstacles, the rugged terrain, and the winding turns along the way..."
"I understand everything. You need not worry about your departure, Master. It is because of this that I have been able to reach the capital.
'Nyen' (輦) refers to the carriage used by the Son of Heaven."
"By inferring from this, one further knows what the two men harbored in their ordinary lives" (Jiupeng ji).

This section concludes by clarifying that there is a profound sentiment at work here. "Inferring from this" means that the compiler of this collection has carefully examined the causes and conditions of this passage;
I certainly know the sentiments between master and guest of those two men, as well as their private feelings of mutual affection in their daily lives.
It resides within the breast. △ One who bestows grace must necessarily possess sincerity. When a person receives grace, sincerity remains;
when sincerity remains, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
This chapter clarifies that the ancients were firm in their resolve and did not allow their practice to slacken because of old age.
Dajo said: "The Old Man Shun is simple and straightforward by nature; he knows nothing of the balancing of scales or the accumulation of wealth.
He has a fixed daily routine that he never alters, even when it comes to lighting lamps or sweeping the floor, which he performs with his own hands. He once said: 'The ancients had...'"
Regarding the precept that "if one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day," what kind of person am I? Though I am advanced in years, my resolve grows ever firmer.
Someone asked, "Why do you not employ those around you? The old man replied, "I have endured the vicissitudes of cold and heat, and my rising and sitting have been irregular."
I do not wish to weary you with this.
"Fubing" (賦稟) refers to the nature I have possessed since birth: simple rather than complex, straightforward rather than circuitous.
"Quan" (權) is the scale-weight; "heng" (衡) is the beam of the scale. To transform goods through wealth is called "huo" (貨); to accumulate and grow wealth is called "zhi" (殖).
He was entirely ignorant of all worldly affairs, such as weighing goods for trade.
His daily labors followed a fixed schedule that he never altered, even in the slightest degree. Even the most minor tasks, such as lighting lamps or sweeping the floor, he performed personally.
He constantly admonished himself, citing the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang, who exerted himself in manual labor every day.
To repay their offerings, he worked; yet when some advised him to desist, he said, "I have no virtue to weary others.
The community could not bear it and hid his tools, searching everywhere for them without success. Consequently, he ceased eating.
Thus the saying, "One day without work, one day without food," spread throughout the world. If even the ancients were like this, what kind of person am I?
I dare not give rise to indolence. It is as if he were about to pass away. Though his years are advanced, his resolve grows ever firmer. Some say:
"Why not have those who attend to you perform such trivial matters? The old man replied: "Having endured bitter cold and scorching heat, my movements and stillness are no longer constant;
there is no need to trouble them. *Ai!* Nowadays, people desire only loose robes and ample clothing.
Sleeves. How could he have ever understood where the ancients placed their feet?
This chapter states that in maintaining one's conduct, what is prized is sincerity; vanity and falsehood are of no benefit.
Old Man Shun said: "In upholding this Way, what is valued above all is truthfulness—distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox and eliminating deluded sentiments."
To cultivate the mind is the reality of practice; to recognize cause and effect and clarify sin and merit is the reality of conduct.
To propagate the Way and virtue and welcome those who come from afar is the reality of abbotship; to assess talents and appoint officials is the reality of employing men.
To examine words and deeds and determine their acceptability is the reality of seeking the worthy.
This section values all that is true. To transmit from generation to generation is called "transmission" (chuan); to earnestly uphold and maintain it is called "retention" (chi).
This Way is the unsurpassed, wondrous Way. The character "valued" (gui) is the most significant;

the two characters "all" (yi-qie) provide a general summary, while the following briefly opens up five articles so that people may know what is to be upheld and maintained. "True" (zhen) means not false; it is real and—
Regarding the first, the non-vacuous cultivation of the mind: one must first distinguish between the deviant mind and the correct mind, and between the deluded mind and the non-deluded.
That which is deviant and deluded should be discarded; that which is upright and correct should be brought to fulfillment.

This is the true essence of cultivating the mind. Second, regarding conduct: maintaining one’s resolve without alteration is called "cultivation" (操); acting in accordance with principle is called "conduct" (履).
First, one must understand that there are causes and effects of good and evil. From what do transgressions arise? By what are blessings produced?

During this time, one must be reverent and cautious, not daring to err regarding cause and effect. That which leads to sin and fault must be extinguished; that which accords with principle and produces merit must be cultivated.
This is the true essence of conduct. Third, as for the abbot: he dwells in the house of the Dharma-king and upholds...
Regarding the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, it is essential to propagate and manifest the sacred transformation and to practice virtue and morality with vigor.

One must uphold the supreme seal of the Dharma (dharmamudrā) with sincerity and steadfastness, receiving scholars from the four quarters without arrogance or pride; this is the true way of upholding the Dharma.
Fourth, as for the employment of people, one should first assess who possesses talent and strategy, and what tasks they ought to manage.

In affairs, who possesses the power and capability? What office should they hold? To harmonize and manage matters so that both internal and external affairs are joyful and contented—this is the true essence of employing men.
Fifth, in seeking the worthy, one must first examine whether their words and deeds correspond, and observe whether their inner and outer conduct are consistent.
At the critical juncture of whether a person may be employed or not, this is especially valued.
To possess foresight and clarity, yet lose vigilance even slightly, so that one’s own interests and harms are immediately revealed—this is the true essence of seeking worthy men.
To fail to maintain such sincerity and instead merely parade empty fame is of no benefit to principle. Therefore, in a person's conduct, only what is essential matters.
Sincerity. If one holds fast to it without wavering, then even amidst the level and the perilous, one may remain consistent (these two matters are straightforward;
*Tánjì*). This section concludes all matters of truth. The preceding five have been explained in general terms.
As for all that one does, if one does not maintain sincerity, it is merely peddling an empty reputation; what benefit is there for the principle? (*Xuàn*: to display and sell).
Therefore, the conduct and practice of one who holds office must be genuine.

If one can indeed uphold these two characters—“genuine” (zhen) and “real” (shi)—without alteration or deviation, then whether on level ground or through perilous obstacles, all may return to the same path;
there is no second principle. *Yu* means change. *Yi* refers to level ground; *xian* refers to perilous obstacles. As for *zhi*:
This is the principle. To have attained the two characters "Reality" (zhen-shi) is to be among the ranks of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This chapter teaches people to establish firm resolve and not harbor thoughts of fame or profit, lest they lose their supreme virtue.
Shun Laofu said to Master Fushan Yuan: "If you wish to investigate the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, when in extremity you should become even more resolute;
as you grow old, you should become even more vigorous. You must not conform to worldly customs by covetously seeking fame and profit, thereby losing your supreme virtue."

This section first clarifies the preservation and maintenance of supreme virtue. Chan Master Fushan Fayuan Yuanjian of Shuzhou was a native of the Wang clan of Zhengzhou and succeeded Chan Master Xing of Ye County.
Once, Fayuan traveled through Sichuan with Daguan Ying, Xue Datou, and seven or eight others;
they encountered several hardships and perils, which the Master resolved through his wisdom. The group recognized him as one who was well-versed in administrative affairs.
Therefore, he was titled Master Yuanlu. He taught that those who study the unsurpassed, wondrous Way—the very fruit of Buddhahood—must establish a resolute will.
Though their physical condition may be impoverished, their resolve must increase and become ever firmer;
though their years may be advanced in age, their vigor must increase and become ever more robust. By no means should they follow along with the worldly current.
"Worldly" (sú): to recklessly seek fame, profit, and material support, thereby losing one's own great virtue. "Cún" (循) means to follow. It is the appearance of being reckless and improper;
it refers to seeking comfort by accommodating oneself to others.
Now, jade is prized for its purity and luster; thus, even vermilion and purple cannot alter its substance. The pine stands out through the cold of the year;
frost and snow cannot wither its integrity. Therefore, integrity and righteousness constitute the greatest virtue in the world.
This section uses a metaphor to clarify the persistence of integrity and righteousness, as well as what is precious about jade. Jade is valued for its purity and luster. Jade possesses seven virtues:
its hardness represents benevolence (*ren*); its unchanging nature represents righteousness (*yi*); its worthiness to be worn as an ornament represents ritual propriety (*li*);

its glossy brilliance represents wisdom (*zhi*); its pure color represents trustworthiness (*xin*); its resistance to defilement represents loyalty (*zhong*); and its beauty to behold represents joy (*le*). Even if one were to apply cinnabar...
Even if one coats it with vermilion or purple, they cannot stain or alter its natural quality. "Biao" (Tablet) means endurance.
The pine endures the full force of the cold; thus, even severe frost and heavy snow cannot damage its verdant sprouts.
From this we know that a person must not lack the integrity of a jade-like nature and a pine-like resolve; this is the most essential principle within heaven and earth.
Truly, your noble character is worthy of admiration; how could you not exert yourself? As the ancients said: "The soaring wings fly alone;
solitary wind has no companion. This is surely fitting for you (Guǎnglù).
This section praises him and exhorts him to exert himself. "Vei" (惟) means "alone. "Gong" (公) refers to Master Yuan.
The master’s bearing and character are commendable and noble; how could he not strive with vigor to establish his resolve?
"Jieyi" (節義) refers to possessing integrity and conduct that accords with principle and righteousness. "Biao" (標) means "to raise up"; it describes his transcendent excellence.
This is the ultimate of establishing oneself. Self-exertion (*zìqiáng*)—the *Yī* says, "The Way of the Gentleman is to be active and vigilant all day long, exerting himself without ceasing.

To "relax" (*yì*) means to let loose; "wings" (*hè*) refers to the strength of feathers. As the ancients said, when the Great Peng spreads its wings, it rides upon the six breaths of wind to soar with its back against the blue heavens;
how could ordinary birds ever reach such heights? It is fitting that it should be so. △ Integrity and righteousness are the path of the sages.
The root of worthiness; the sacred sprout of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Students should guard it with care and cherish it.
This chapter clarifies that one must not be remiss in attending to teachers and friends; for if one is remiss, learning will not succeed.
Master Fushan Yuan said: "The ancients attended their teachers and chose their friends with such diligence that they did not dare to be idle day or night.
Even when performing menial tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying grain for grinding, they never shied away from labor."
This section exhorts people to practice diligently. It states that those who sought the Way in ancient times drew near to enlightened masters and chose virtuous friends;
they were diligent in the morning and vigilant in the evening, never daring to seek ease for themselves. "Cuan" (爨) refers to cooking;

it is called "cuan" because it takes fire to advance the process, and it is called "chui" (炊) because the steam rises upward. "Fu-chong" (負舂) refers to pounding rice. One would rather go against the ways of the world [than neglect such practice].
I did not expect such prominence; it is said that to be submerged like Lu is to be deeply hidden.

As for menial service, it is something that others find difficult to perform—tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying out the mortars—and yet I do not consider them laborious. Being submerged like Lu and performing menial service, I do not regard them as a disgrace, nor do I ever dare to give rise to thoughts of indolence, weariness, or aversion.

While I was at Ye County, I tested this thoroughly. However, if one harbors even the slightest thought of regarding profit and loss or calculating gain and defeat, one will resort to equivocation and indulgence to such an extent that there is no limit.
Furthermore, if one’s own person is not upright, how can one study the Way?
(Dharma Words by Attendant Yue)
This section provides personal testimony regarding such matters. When I was formerly at Ye County attending upon Master Guisheng, I tested these things in detail.
Chan Master Guisheng of Guangjiao Monastery in Ye County, Ruizhou, was the son of the Jia family of Jizhou;
he was a successor of Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian and belongs to the ninth generation under Mount Heng. Regarding his tenure as abbot:
Xuefeng was austere and stern; the *zhendi* (patch-robed monks) feared him. Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai, hearing of his lofty reputation, went specifically to seek an audience with him.
It happened to be a time of bitter snow and cold; Xuefeng scolded them and drove them away, pouring water on the ground so that their robes and bedding were all soaked.
The other monks departed in anger, but only Yuan and Huai adjusted their robes and sitting mats and resumed their seats as before. When Xuefeng returned, he saw them there.
He scolded them, saying, "If you do not go away immediately, wait until I beat you.

Yuanjing stepped forward and said, "The two of us have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master. How can we leave simply because you splashed us with a ladle of water?
He laughed heartily and said, "If you two truly came wishing to study Chan, then go and register as monks. You shall serve as the head cook (dianzuo). The assembly found this quite vexing.
Huishong was living in austere simplicity. Once, while Huisheng went out from the monastery to visit a village, Huairuan secretly took some oil and flour to prepare a five-flavor congee.

Just as it was nearly finished, Huisheng suddenly returned. After the meal, he ordered the *dianzuo* (the head cook) to summon Huairuan. Huisheng said, "You have stolen oil and flour; this constitutes the misappropriation of communal property.

Huairuan replied, "I did indeed take the oil and flour. I beg you to impose a punishment upon me. Huisheng then ordered that the value of the items be calculated and the proceeds used to purchase robes and alms bowls to be returned to the community.

[The punishment] was completed. [Xuefeng] struck him thirty more times with a staff and drove him out of the monastery. His fellow practitioners exhorted him to reconsider, but Xuefeng would not agree.
A friend said, "If you will not permit me to return, I beg only this: that I may stay with the assembly to listen to the Dharma. Xuefeng still did not allow it.

One day, as Xuefeng went out onto the street, he saw [the monk] standing before a guest house for travelers. Xuefeng said, "This is the corridor of the monastery's gate quarters. Why are you staying here? He ordered [him to leave].
When people pursued him for the money owed at the shop, Fayuan showed no sign of distress. He subsequently went to the marketplace with his alms bowl to beg for the funds to repay them.

Upon returning, he informed the assembly, saying, "Fayuan is truly a vessel for the Dharma of Chan. He then sent Fayuan back to the hall, where he was formally invested with the robe and the transmission of the Dharma before the assembly.
He said, "Regarding all circumstances of adversity and favor, one must experience each and every one. If I were to..."
At that time, if one harbors even a single thought of cherishing personal gain or loss, or calculates the balance of profit and failure, one will waver and vacillate;
how then could there be any certainty? "Gouxi" (to be indulgent) means to seek comfort through mere expediency;
this is from the *Liji* (Book of Rites). If one is thus, being already improper in body, how can one possibly govern the mind to study the Way?
To act in such a manner is the way of those of the highest caliber; one who masters this is a true adept.
This chapter clarifies that the essential requirement for studying the Way lies in firm resolve and diligent practice; one must not allow doubt and faith to coexist.

Master Yuan said: "Between heaven and earth, there are indeed things that grow easily; yet if one were to expose them to the sun for a single day and subject them to cold for ten days, it would not be seen that they could grow."
This section first uses the analogy that one day of heat followed by ten days of cold will certainly not produce growth.
It first cites the growth of the myriad things in the world as an analogy. "Sincerely" means truly.

This refers to the fact that even if a thing is easy to grow, were it to receive the warming influence of heat for only a single day, yet then be drenched by cold rain for ten days, its growth would still not be seen.
There are those capable of growth who, by comparison with other students, find their application of effort to be inconsistent.

The unsurpassed, wondrous Way is vividly present within the space between one’s heart and mind; thus, it is not difficult to perceive. The essential requirement lies in the firmness of one’s resolve and the vigor of one’s practice.
Success may be awaited while sitting or standing. Yet, should one believe for a single day and then doubt for ten days, or [be wavering] morning...

Thus, though they may strive in the morning, they grow weary by evening. Is this difficulty to be seen only before one's eyes? I fear that by the end of their lives, they will have turned their backs upon it.
(Written by Chan Master Yun).
This section clarifies that one who possesses a single faith yet harbors ten doubts will certainly not awaken to the unsurpassed, wondrous Way. It is "zhāozhāo"—that is, perfectly clear and manifest.
This perfect clarity resides at the gateway of the six sense organs; with light radiating and the earth shaking, how could it be difficult to see?
Nevertheless, the essential point is that one’s resolve must be firm and steadfast, like an iron stake;
one’s practice must be courageous and fierce, as if facing ten thousand enemies. If you act in this manner, you will surely attain realization on the spot.
Yet, it may happen that you possess the power of faith for a single day and then practice, only to harbor doubts for ten days and fail to act, resuming diligence only when morning breaks.
One exerts effort to practice, yet by night one stops out of fear and apprehension.
Seeking the Way in this manner, not only will it be difficult to achieve in the present life, but I fear that by the end of this lifetime, one will have gone so far astray as to never see it at all.
The acupuncture needle for the most incurable ailment and the medicine that raises the dead are both contained within the single character for diligence (*qín*).
This chapter clarifies that the abbot must carefully examine all matters of acceptance and rejection.

Master Huiyuan said: "In the essentials of abbatial leadership, nothing precedes the careful examination of what to accept and what to reject. The ultimate nature of one's acceptance and rejection is determined within;
the sprouts of safety and peril are determined without. Yet, safety is not safety for a single day, nor is peril peril for a single day."
All things arise from gradual accumulation; this cannot fail to be examined.
This section presents the general outline, asserting that for the governance of a monastery, nothing is more vital than first scrutinizing what to adopt and what to discard.
One must discern which matters are urgent and thus worthy of inclusion, and which are useless and thus ought to be excluded.

One must abandon [what is harmful]. When the tally of what is taken up and what is abandoned is firmly settled within the breast, then the sprouts of safety and peril will likewise be settled externally.
However, bringing peace to others cannot be achieved in a single day, nor can one bring peril to others in a single day;
both result from gradual accumulation and permeation, manifesting only after a long time. This is something that must be scrutinized.

Furthermore, by governing through virtue and integrity, one accumulates virtue and integrity; by governing through ritual and righteousness, one accumulates ritual and righteousness; by governing through oppression and exploitation, one accumulates resentment.
When resentment accumulates, those both within and without become estranged and turn away; when ritual and righteousness accumulate, those both within and without become harmonious and joyful.
When moral virtue accumulates, both those within and without are moved and submit.
To analyze the benefits and harms of this principle in detail, there are three points to be examined.
If, during ordinary times, I conduct myself with moral virtue while presiding over affairs, then all those who interact with me will be able to cultivate that same virtue. If I act with propriety...
Regarding the maintenance of the practice of righteousness: if those who have accumulated [merit] are all able to practice propriety and righteousness, then it will be so.
However, if I am austere toward the masses for my own benefit and exploit the virtuous and good, then everyone will utter evil words with venomous intent in their hearts;
thus, resentment will accumulate. Once resentment has accumulated, there will be no place—whether internal or external—from which separation, dispersal, and rebellion do not arise.

Regarding the mind: that which is near is discussed in terms of the internal, while that which is distant is discussed in terms of the external. Once rites and righteousness have accumulated, there will be nothing discordant or displeasing between the internal and the external.
Once the Way and its Virtue have accumulated, there will be nothing that does not respond with feeling or submit through conviction.

Therefore, when morality, the Way, propriety, and righteousness are pervasive, both those within and without will rejoice; when exploitation and resentment reach their extreme, both those within and without will grieve.
Such feelings of grief and joy provoke responses of calamity and fortune accordingly.
This section concludes the discussion on calamity and fortune. Therefore, when morality, virtue, ritual, and righteousness pervade a region, both those within and without will experience joy.
"Qià" (洽) means to be thoroughly moistened and pervasive. If one were to subject people to bitter hardship and exploitation to the extreme, then both those within and without would suffer grief.
Grief gives rise to calamity; joy ensures that fortune arrives. Indeed, grief and joy are what move [the heart].
Within, calamity or fortune will correspond without. Human nature’s choices and rejections are a critical juncture;
if one does not examine them carefully, one cannot avoid being inverted in one's experience of suffering and joy.
This chapter states that there are three essentials for maintaining the monastic community (*saṃgha*), none of which may be omitted or neglected if one is to not abandon the Way.

Master Huiyuan said: "There are three essentials for a *vihārasvāmin* (abbot): benevolence, clarity, and courage. As for benevolence: it means practicing morality and virtue, promoting education and transformation, bringing peace to those above and below, and bringing joy to those who come and go.
As for clarity: it means adhering to ritual and righteousness, discerning safety and peril, examining the worthy and the foolish, and distinguishing between right and wrong."
This is "courage. When matters require decisive resolution, one acts without doubt; the treacherous must certainly be eliminated, and the sycophants must certainly be removed.
This section first sets forth the three essentials: benevolence (*ren*), clarity (*ming*), and courage (*yong*). In Sima Guang’s *Memorial to Emperor Renzong* on Benevolence, he states:

"The benevolent person is pure in accordance with the principles of Heaven (*tianli*), possessing not even a trace of selfish desire. The clear-sighted person illuminates the nature of things (*wuli*) to distinguish right from wrong, [possessing not even a trace of...]"

Regarding the doubts concerning these matters: the courageous person, upon seeing what is righteous, will surely act upon it; hearing of what is good, they will surely transition toward it. They do not harbor a single thought of retreat or cowardice.

Those who are called "abbot" (zhuchi) must first possess benevolence (*ren*). With benevolence, one can practice and maintain the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*), and promote and propagate the teachings and transformations (*jiaohua*).
As for these teachings and transformations, they are practiced by the superior and move like a wind among those below, causing—
A person transforms their innate disposition. To bring peace and comfort to those above and below, and to ensure that all who come and go are joyful—this is the first and most urgent matter.
Next, one must necessarily be clear-sighted, able to penetrate and illuminate the principles of things so that not a single affair or object remains obscured;
only then can one practice ritual and righteousness, discern safety and peril, distinguish between the foolish and the wise, and make proper discriminations.

No. This is the second essential matter. Furthermore, one must also possess courage: being able to act upon what is righteous as soon as it is seen, and transforming toward what is good as soon as it is perceived, without the slightest hesitation or cowardice.

Only then can one act with resolute daring in all affairs, making decisive judgments without doubt, knowing that the treacherous must be eliminated and the sycophantic must be removed. This is the third essential matter.
To be benevolent without clarity is like having fields that are not plowed. To be clear-sighted without courage is like having seedlings that are not weeded.
To be courageous without benevolence is like knowing how to reap but not knowing how to sow. When these three qualities are complete, the forest flourishes; if even one is lacking, it declines.
If two of these are lacking, there is peril; if one of the three is missing, the way of sustaining the Dharma will fall into ruin (from a letter to Master Jingyin Zhen).
This section clarifies that they must not be deficient. If one possesses only benevolence (*ren*) but lacks wisdom (*ming*), it is like a person who has fields but cannot cultivate them—truly a pity.
Yet, even if both benevolence and wisdom are present, if one lacks the courage to follow through with them, [the same result follows].
It is also like worldly people who, though they have already sown their fields, fail to weed them; they shall obtain nothing.
If one possesses intelligence and courage but lacks benevolence to lead them, it is just as worldly people who know only how to reap the harvest but do not know how to sow the seed;
there will certainly be no benefit. "Cai" means to cut. Viewed from this perspective, these three qualities must not be absent.
[Omission]. If the abbot possesses all three [qualities] in their entirety, then the monastic community will surely flourish. If one is lacking, the community will surely decline;

if two are lacking, the community will surely be in peril. If all three are lacking, the Buddha-Dharma will surely be swept from the earth, and the monastic communities will naturally appear desolate.
△ Observe those who act as men in both the mundane and supramundane realms—who among them does not possess [these qualities]?
This is like a cart missing a single axle-pin.

This chapter states that for one who maintains the Dharma, the essential task is to discern between the worthy and the foolish; once the worthy and the foolish are distinguished, the Way of the Dharma will manifest of its own accord.
Master Yuǎn said: "The wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, are like water and fire that cannot share the same vessel, or cold and heat that do not coexist at the same time;

this is simply their inherent nature (*sufen*). This section demonstrates that wisdom and folly are fundamentally established by birth. The wise person receives the pure and harmonious qi, thereby producing human talent."
The wise possess clear and acute consciousness; the foolish are endowed with turbid qi, being born as people who are stubborn, dull-witted, and ignorant.

The virtuous are endowed with harmonious and warm qi, being born as people who are compassionate, frugal, gentle, and kind. The unworthy are endowed with discordant and erroneous qi, being born as people who are cruel, dangerous, treacherous, and depraved.
These four types are like light and darkness opposing one another, or the fragrance of incense and the stench of rancid herbs not coexisting; this is an absolute certainty.

This is the principle. Therefore, it is likened to water and fire not occupying the same vessel, or cold and heat not occurring at the same time; this is essentially the fixed distinction established in ordinary life.
A man of worthy wisdom—pure, refined, upright, and grave—plans his affairs according to the Way, its Virtue, humanity, and righteousness. In his speech and actions, he considers only...
I fear that this would not accord with human sentiment nor conform to the principles of nature. Those who are unworthy are treacherous, perilous, deceitful, and sycophantic;
they boast of themselves and display their own abilities, craving desires and seeking profit at any cost, disregarding everything else.

This section clarifies that the categories of the wise and the foolish are vastly distinct. Generally, those who are virtuous and wise possess a natural disposition from birth that is pure, harmonious, elegant, upright, and dignified.
Their pursuits and endeavors are centered on morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness.
They speak at the proper time and act at the proper time, ever fearing that their character may not accord with that of others or that their conduct may conflict with the principles of things.

He was not at ease; with constant apprehension and earnest diligence, he took the service of the Way as his own heart’s concern. As for those foolish and unworthy people, they are uniformly treacherous, wicked, perilous, and hypocritical.
Deceitful, sycophantic, and fawning, their speech is like that of sages and worthies, yet their conduct is truly that of demons and goblins.

They boast of themselves and harbor self-importance; they flaunt their abilities and exalt themselves; they greedily indulge in private desires and seek wealth and profit by any means, without restraint.
That which one does not do:
thus, when a virtuous person occupies the Zen grove, their moral cultivation establishes the fundamental order, and the Dharma assembly is thereby perfected.

If even a single unworthy person is interposed among them, they will stir up the multitude and bring disorder to the assembly, leaving both the inner and outer circles in unrest. Even if one possesses great wisdom and ritual propriety, what can be done?
Thus, the difference between the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, is as great as this. How can you, O bird, not exercise such discernment? (A letter from Preceptor Huili Fang).

This section concludes by establishing that one must choose between the superior and the inferior. For if even a single worthy person is found within the Zen grove, then the Way and its virtue may be cultivated and the fundamental principles will establish themselves.
"Gang" (the main rope) refers to the overarching cord; "ji" (the meshes) refers to the individual strands. By means of these, the rules and regulations are brought into order.
If it is orderly, the Dharma community will surely flourish. "Toilets" (廁) means "mixture.
If an unworthy person is intermingled among them within the assembly, they will disturb the monastic grove and confuse the multitude;
the entire monastery will be unsettled, and even if there are rules and regulations for those of great wisdom, they will be of no use. Why? Because such a person lacks a sense of shame.
It cannot be cured. Furthermore, wisdom and virtue are of one kind, while folly and lack of reflection are of another.
These two types—superior and inferior, beneficial and harmful—are as clear as day. How can you fail to exert effort in discerning which is superior?
"Inferior" means weak. Why is this so? △ By nature there is no duality; it is through habituation that differences arise. Why do people...
That they do not reflect upon themselves.
This chapter admonishes that human emotions must not be obstructed; when emotions flow freely, the Way can operate within them.
Master Huiyuan said: "The abbot resides above and should be humble and respectful in dealing with those below. Those who hold office reside below and must exert their full sincerity."
Thus they are presented to the superior. When those above and below are in harmony, the way of sustaining the community (the *zhuchi*) flows unimpeded.

If those in superior positions are arrogant and self-important, while those in subordinate positions are negligent and aloof, such that the sentiments between superiors and subordinates do not communicate, then the way of sustaining the community is blocked.
This section first indicates the pervasion and obstruction of emotional states.

It means that while the position of the abbot is inherently one of constant superiority, in practice he must be humble, harmonious, reverent, and cautious in order to receive others. As for those who serve as administrators, their position is inherently one of subordination.
At all times, one must offer sincere respect to serve those above.
When those above are thus humble and harmonious, and those below are able to serve them, the Dharma-way of the abbot will naturally circulate. However, if those in superior positions...
If one is arrogant, extravagant, and haughty in seeking self-elevation, those beneath them will inevitably become indolent,
disrespectful, and distant. When the sentiments between superiors and subordinates are thus obstructed, the Way and Dharma of monastic leadership will surely become stagnant and blocked.
When the ancient masters served as abbots, they had leisure and were free from affairs; they would engage in relaxed discussions with their students on all manner of topics.
Consequently, even a single word or half-sentence from them has been recorded in biographies and is still praised to this day.

This section now clarifies the reason why emotional resonance is possible. Therefore, it further cites those of antiquity who were able to communicate with others emotionally to illustrate this point.
Observe that in ancient times, teachers possessed of virtue and moral integrity, when they had leisure and were free from affairs, would invariably receive others with humble grace.
They would often engage in relaxed discussion with students worthy of conversation. "Relaxed" (*cong rong*) means being harmonious, gentle, and unhurried; "discussion" (*yi lun*)...
This refers to the evaluation and determination of matters from both ancient and modern times; it is the art of debate. When there is something not clearly understood, one analyzes and dissects it.

One may debate the "public cases" (gong'an) of ancient masters, or evaluate the witty sayings (jiyu) of virtuous sages. There is no aspect of worldly phenomena or Buddhist Dharma to which this does not reach.
Occasionally, the witty exchanges between teacher and disciple coincide with the ultimate principle, whether through a single word or...
A half-phrase. Though the words are few, the meaning of the speech is extraordinary; it shall surely be recorded in the biographies and praised by both ancient and modern scholars.
For example, when Dayang asked Liangshan, "What is the formless Way-place?
Shan pointed to an image of a Great Being and said, "This was painted by Wu Daozi. As Dayang was about to offer a reply, Shan said, "This one has form."
"That which is thus is formless. Yang immediately had an awakening. The Master said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase?
Yang said, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would fall upon paper and brush. The Master laughed and said, "These words shall be inscribed upon a stele."
What is the reason for this? First, it is to ensure that the sentiments of the superior reach those below, so that the Way remains free from obstruction or concealment.
Second, it allows for the prior knowledge of whether a student’s talent and capacity are sufficient, so that their advancement or withdrawal may always accord with what is appropriate.

Thus, naturally, those above and below will be harmonious and solemn, and those far and near will turn toward them with reverence. The flourishing of monastic communities is brought about by this very means (Letter to Qing Huayan).
This section concludes that the communication of sentiments ensures that affairs are handled appropriately. Yet, why must one engage in discussion with students during their leisure time?
For one reason, it allows for the free flow of sentiment between superior and subordinates, ensuring that the Way of the Dharma does not become obstructed.
For another, it allows one to know in advance whether a student’s talent, capacity, and temperament are serviceable or not—what is called "discerning the seed from the sprout."
The Abbot addresses the people through his speech; thereafter, regarding what should be advanced and what should be withdrawn, he attains the proper balance in all matters.
When mutual trust is established in this way, naturally those above and below will be harmonious, dignified, and solemn. Those far and near will follow and revere him with faith.

As for the flourishing of a monastic community (saṃghārāma), what other method could there be? It is nothing more than being brought about by the free flow of these human sentiments. △ Discussion on Leisurely Moments.
This treatise truly brings forth the hidden luster of latent virtue; it is no trivial matter.
This chapter instructs people that they ought to devote themselves to practical learning, rather than peddling empty embellishments and pretenses.

Master Yuǎn said to Dàowú Zhēn: "Those whose learning has not yet reached the Way, who flaunt their见闻 (learned knowledge), who race about with their intellectual insights, and who seek to prevail through the sharpness of their verbal eloquence, are like a latrine house that has been smeared and painted;
it only serves to increase its stench. (From *Xīhú Jìwén*)
Chan Master Zhenke of Daowu Monastery in Tanzhou was a successor of Chan Master Shishuang Yuan. He was the tenth generation under Mount Heng. He said:
"If you have not yet reached the ultimate point in studying the Way, you must by no means engage in superficiality. Do not gloss over what you have not seen and claim it as seeing;
do not embellish what you have not heard and claim it as hearing. Do not indulge in intellectual cleverness. To 'indulge' means for a horse to gallop swiftly."
It is simply because they are quick of mouth and clever of tongue that they gain many words, considering them superior.
Such people are like a latrine house painted with the five colors—*dan-gwok* being a general term for pigments.
Though it looks fine on the outside, its interior is actually so foul as to be unbearable. Such empty pretension is better left undone.
Excellent. Who would not know that this is a city of illusory silver?
This treatise teaches that one must seek subtle awakening in order to govern the mind, taking it as the foundation for eliminating delusive views and realizing the true.
Master Yuan said to the head seat Yan: "The mind is the master of the single body and the foundation of the myriad practices.

If the mind does not attain wondrous awakening, deluded sentiments arise spontaneously. Once deluded sentiments have arisen, one’s perception of principle is not clear. When the perception of principle is not clear, right and wrong become confused and disordered."
This section reveals that the mind is the fundamental source. Chan Master Fayan of Wuzhuo in Qizhou was a native of the Deng clan of Mianzhou;
he was a successor of Chan Master Baiyun Yuan and belongs to the thirteenth generation under Mount Heng.

He stated that as for the mind, it is luminous and penetrating, embodying all principles and responding to myriad functions; the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable wondrous meanings do not arise from anything other than this.
One must investigate thoroughly until one attains wondrous awakening. If the mind does not awaken, deluded thoughts and emotional consciousness will naturally arise.
When delusions arise, the discernment of principle is obscured; when principle is not clear, right and wrong will inevitably become distorted and confused.

Therefore, in governing the mind, one must seek wondrous awakening. When awakened, the spirit becomes harmonious and the vital energy tranquil; the countenance becomes reverent and the expression dignified.
Erroneous thoughts and emotional anxieties all melt away into the true mind. By governing the mind in this way, the mind itself becomes spontaneously numinous and wondrous.
Only then can one guide beings and point out their delusions—who would not follow such transformation? (From the *Fushan Shilu*)
This section teaches that one must necessarily practice and necessarily awaken. Therefore, when a student cultivates their own mind, they should seek thorough realization.

Once they have awakened and entered [this state], it causes the spirit and will to be harmonious, the breath to be tranquil, the countenance to be reverent, and the physical appearance to be dignified.
Should discursive thoughts or emotional anxieties arise, by illuminating them with this wondrous mind, they are all melted away into the true mind.
If one cultivates the mind in this manner, the mind will surely become spiritually penetrating and exquisitely refined.
Only then can one guide the multitudes and lead those who are deluded; who would not follow such transformation? △ This is the essential method for awakening.
The meaning lies beyond words and language. If you merely read it in this way, what connection will there be?
This chapter teaches pure cultivation and true virtue; do not strive for superficial splendor, lest it obscure what is essential and subtle.
Master Wuzu Yan said: "In the monasteries of today, those who study the Way fail to have their reputations spread and are not trusted by others.
This is because their *brahmacarya* is not pure and they do not conduct themselves with integrity, often acting with mere expediency."
Seeking fame, reputation, and material gain, one extensively displays outward ornamentation; consequently, one is censured by those with true discernment. Thus, the essential and subtle is obscured;
even if one possesses the Way and virtue like that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, those who hear of or see such a person will harbor doubts and refuse to believe.
On a future day, if any among you should take a mere handful of thatch to roof your head [in seclusion], you should exhort yourselves by this example (a letter to Fojian and Foguo).
This refers to those who currently serve as elders (*sthavira*) within monastic communities;
their good reputations fail to spread, and they are no different from those who lack the faith and respect of the fourfold assembly.

This is solely because their holy life (*brahmacarya*) is deficient—neither pure nor stainless—and furthermore, because in their conduct and affairs, they act without careful deliberation or stability, hastily engaging in every matter.
This is indeed so. In every matter, one’s conduct is often characterized by negligence; one greedily seeks fame and material gain.
Furthermore, one’s actions are superficial and hollow, peddling outward brilliance and glossing over one’s behavior to deceive the ignorant masses.
Consequently, one is seen through by those with clear vision, who then give rise to derision and ridicule. Because of this, how many urgent and wondrous matters have been... [lost].

It is obscured. Even if one possesses realization and divine power like the Buddhas and Patriarchs, all that is heard and seen will cause people to harbor doubts and fail to believe it with sincerity.
When you all enter the world as humans in the future, you should build a thatched hut, guard your own minds, and subdue the thoughts of others; you must take my [teachings]...
This speaks of self-exertion. △ The two characters "sincerity" (*lǎoshí*) are worth a thousand pieces of gold.
If one is frivolous and merely puts on a facade without maintaining actual practice, this is the very seed of the roots of karma.
This chapter admonishes people to value their fundamental duty and not to pursue external conditions, lest they lose the essence of the Dharma.
Master Yuanwu said: "When my late teacher first resided at Yangqi, his dwelling was an old house with dilapidated rafters that barely shielded against wind and rain.
It happened to be the end of winter; snow and sleet filled the bed, and he had no place to stay."
This section clarifies the cultivation of non-attachment to one’s own body. Chan Master Fānghuì of Yángqí Mountain in Yuánzhōu was the son of the Lěng family of Yíchūn.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Címíng Chǔyuán and belonged to the tenth generation under Nányuè.
It is said that when Master Huì first resided at Yángqí, the buildings were dilapidated and the rafters rotten; there were merely two broken rooms that barely provided shelter.

It was merely sufficient to shield against wind and rain. "適" (shì) means "to arrive at. It happened to be the end of winter, specifically the twelfth lunar month. "霰" (xiàn) refers to snowflakes or sleet.
Although snowflakes were scattered everywhere upon the beds where everyone lay, he did not allow his mind to be distracted by this;

he remained there in peace. When affairs are many, one says "there is no leisure" (bù xiá); when the mind is occupied, one says "there is no time" (bù luáng). This means that although snow had accumulated upon his bed, [he remained undisturbed].
He did not allow the hardships of the cold to disturb his mind.

When a patch-robed monk (nàzǐ) offered his sincere devotion, wishing to provide funds for construction, the Master declined him, saying: "The Buddha has said that we live in an age of decline (jiǎnjié).
High ridges and deep valleys are subject to constant change; how can one expect everything to be perfect and as one wishes? One must seek what is sufficient for oneself."
This section reveals that all phenomena are merely provisional combinations. Among the monastics, there were those with sincere resolve who wished to take charge of the fundraising;
however, the Master declined and would not consent, saying: "Have you not heard what our Buddha said?"
At this time, it is precisely the period of the kalpa of decrease (*apacaya-kalpa*). The merit and lifespan of all people also diminish accordingly.

It is said that during the ninth minor kalpa, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years; it decreased until it reached sixty thousand years, at which point Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world.
It decreased to forty thousand years. When Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world, it decreased to twenty thousand years.
When Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, it decreased to one hundred years. When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, it was therefore said: "The time is that of the kalpa of decrease.
Yet even the most precipitously high cliffs and the deepest ravines undergo shifting and transformation; yet [the mountain] remains thus.
It is impermanent. At times high cliffs collapse; at times deep valleys fill up level.
Since it is fundamentally not a firm and enduring dharma, how could it ever be as complete as one desires, allowing one to seek fulfillment for oneself?
"You have left the household life to study the Way, yet your practice is not yet stable; you are already forty or fifty years old.
How could you afford the leisure to concern yourself with building grand houses? They ultimately did not follow his advice.
This section demonstrates the study of his power. Furthermore, you who have left the household life originally did so for the purpose of studying the Way;
yet your physical movements are still not yet stable—this means you cannot maintain your grasp. It is said that your practice is still unsettled. You are already forty or fifty years old;
how could you possibly have the leisure time to go out again to solicit alms? For... (the text ends).
To beautify one's dwelling for the sake of worldly affairs: Formerly, Li Jing-gong, whose name was Hang, served as Prime Minister of the Song dynasty.
His personal frugality was extreme; he lived in a humble alleyway, and his official residence had no double gates. When his family members urged him to renovate it, Hang said:
He enjoyed a generous stipend and lived in peace and prosperity as he desired. Yet, since human life cannot be guaranteed from morning until evening, why expend such effort on grand dwellings?
[The master] ultimately did not comply.
The following day, he ascended the hall and said: "Yangqi has newly settled in; the walls of my house are sparse. The bed is strewn all over with snow-white pearls.
I shrink my neck and sigh in secret. I am reminded once more of the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees" (from the *Guanglu*).
This section clarifies the great meaning. On the following day—that is, the next morning—he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:

"At Yangqi, having newly settled, the walls of my house are thin; The entire bed is strewn with snow-white pearls. I shrink my neck and sigh in secret, Recalling once again the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees.
"Recalling once again" means turning back to pursue the ancients of old, who practiced their cultivation beneath the trees. When he encountered [this situation],...

Regarding this wind and rain: furthermore, as for the writings [of the past], down to the present day, people still require ghosts to manipulate them into acting as transformation-masters (*huàzhǔ*). Who is able to turn this back?
This chapter teaches that students must ensure their practice and understanding are in accord; they must be cautious and rigorous.
Master Yuan said: "A monk guards the city of his mind and upholds the precepts, contemplating them day and night and practicing them morning and evening.
His practice does not exceed his contemplation, and his contemplation does not exceed his practice. Having its beginning and completing its end is like a farmer who has defined boundaries."
Its faults are few. The character for "city" (城) serves as a metaphor. An ancient verse says: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city:
by day one wards off the six thieves; by night one remains alert. When the commander-in-chief of the central army can enforce his orders, peace is brought about without moving a blade. This...
This is what is meant by that. "To uphold" means to reverently follow the precepts—that is, the various codes of monastic discipline. Guarding the mind is the study of the Way;
upholding the precepts is the cultivation of virtue. To perfect both the Way and virtue, one must proceed from day to night, thinking upon them with tireless diligence.
From morning until evening, one should practice with diligent perseverance. Indeed, when practicing, one must not depart from reflection; when reflecting, one must not transcend practice.
