If a petty person were like this, every action and deed performed in their daily life would be nothing but transgression and evil, like mere rubble;
how then could they even be worth mentioning? Since ancient times, the worthy and heroic have preferred to be rebuked by others rather than [be like the base].
That people can be so receptive has indeed its reason.
This chapter explains that the Way is fundamentally non-dual; it is only because there are differences in the depth of one's realization.
Huìtáng said: "The Way of the Sage is like Heaven and Earth nurturing the myriad things; there is nothing that is not fully provided for within the Way."

The Way of all people is like the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji; like mountains, rivers, hills, and valleys; and like grasses, trees, insects, and animals—each merely exhausts its own capacity.
This section illustrates that what is realized by the sages and the common folk differs. The Way realized by the sages is most profound and most vast.
Just as heaven and earth cover and sustain all things, what dharma is not contained within them?

As for the Way attained by the multitude of people, their enjoyment of it differs according to the depth or shallowness of their own power. Thus, there are those who are like rivers; among rivers, there are three great rivers.
One flows from the east of Songlou, its waters originating from Mount Min. Furthermore, the greatest of streams is called a "Jiang" (River). Moreover, there are those who are like...
As for the River (Hé), its waters emerge from Mount Jishí; coming from the position of Qián, it flows with a bend every thousand *lǐ*, making nine bends before entering the sea.
There are also rivers like the Huái: the Huái water emerges from Rúníng Prefecture in Henán and enters the sea at Huāi'ān Prefecture in Zhílì.
There are also those like the Jì: the Jì water emerges from Chángshān. Thus, each of these four waters—

There are distinctions of distance, nearness, depth, and shallowness, yet all ultimately return to the sea. Regarding mountains and rivers: "rivers" (chuan) refers to the many streams that flow into the sea; regarding hills and valleys:
"hills" (ling) refers to large mounds, while "valleys" (gu) refers to mountain gorges and ravines. Regarding plants, trees, and insects: "kun" [refers to their collective nature].

"Zhuye. This term collectively refers to all sentient and insentient beings. Although they differ in being conscious or inert, the principle inherent within each is simply that every being exhausts its own capacity.
One does not know what lies beyond; there is nothing that is not fully prepared therein. Now, is the Way truly dual?
Is it that, depending on the depth of one's attainment, there arise distinctions of great and small? (A Letter to Zhang Wujin)

This section now brings forth the Way of Great Sameness (Dàtóng). Yet, one ultimately fails to realize that beyond what is known and seen by oneself, there exists a great realm that encompasses all and is complete in every respect.
As it is said: "The Way has no fixed direction; practitioners cannot reach it. But how could the Way possess distinctions of large or small, long or short? It is because...
Those who attain it do so to varying degrees—some shallow and some deep; thus, those who achieve it also differ in scale, some great and some small.
Its external realm is all-encompassing and complete, beyond the reach of discursive thought and conceptual discrimination. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it.
Students should investigate it with meticulous care.
This chapter teaches the methods for an abbot to navigate the world and avoid harm.
Huìtáng said: "What has long been neglected cannot be restored quickly; long-standing abuses cannot be eliminated all at once. One must not linger too long in leisurely circumstances;
human relations can never be perfectly harmonious; and calamities cannot be evaded by mere expediency. Now, as a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one must understand this.
There are five matters; by attending to them, one may traverse the world without weariness (a letter to Master Xiang).
It is said that when a matter has long been neglected, it cannot be expected to achieve success through haste; what is hastily accomplished is bound to be easily ruined.
When accumulated maladies have persisted, they cannot be eradicated all at once; to attempt sudden removal only serves to increase the malady further. This is the state of leisurely ease.
One must not linger in attachment for long; prolonged attachment inevitably leads to change. Human affairs and worldly conditions cannot always be perfectly complete;
perfection is difficult to attain. When faced with calamities and hardships, one must not seek to evade them through mere expediency.

If one merely seeks to avoid [suffering], there will inevitably be much turmoil. Now, as for those who act as good friends (kalyāṇamitra), if they attain an understanding of these five kinds of causal conditions and traverse the world, they will naturally be free from anxiety and distress. △ It is difficult to reach such a state;
once reached, one’s fortune and lifespan will surely flourish.
This chapter reveals that the ancients possessed hearts of loving-kindness, reverence, and filial piety.
Huìtáng said: "The Master’s deportment was grave and dignified; those who saw him felt awe and respect. When his disciples requested leave for various matters, he would often sternly refuse them.
Only when he heard that they were attending to their elderly parents did his countenance become serene and harmonious, his expression manifesting this on his face as he observed the proper rites."
He saw them off with great care. His love for others was as respectful and filial as this (as stated in his letter to Xie Jingwen).
He said that my late master’s deportment—whether advancing or retreating—was so majestic and dignified that there were none who beheld him without feeling reverence and awe.
When a monk requested leave on some business matter, he would often sternly refuse and deny it.
Whenever he hears of someone wishing to return home to visit their elderly parents, a serene and harmonious expression naturally appears upon his face;
furthermore, he provides them with all necessary gifts to see them safely on their way. Such is the heart of his love for others, his reverence, obedience, and filial piety.
This is the very liver and gall of the sages and worthies, beyond the reach of ordinary people. Why is this? Because it is rooted in reverence and filial piety.
This is the ultimate essential of the sages; it must not be separated from oneself for even a moment.
This chapter reveals the capacity and measure of the ancients, providing a sufficient model and standard for later generations.
Huìtáng said: "In the past, when our late master Huánglóng resided with Master Yúe of Yúnfēng at Fènglín in Jīngnán during the summer retreat, Yúe was fond of engaging in debate.
One day, while he was making a commotion with some monastics, our late master continued reading his scriptures as usual, appearing as if he neither heard nor saw anything.
Eventually, Yúe went to our late master’s desk and, glaring at him, rebuked him, saying: 'Are you here practicing the art of knowing well? "
"Is this the measure of consciousness? My late teacher bowed his head and apologized for this; he continued to read the scriptures as before (the above is found in the *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Chan Master Wenyue of Yunfeng on Mount Nanyue was a native of the Xu family of Nanchang and succeeded Chan Master Shouzhi of Dayu.
He was the eleventh generation descendant of Mount Nanyue. He said that formerly, while traveling together with my late teacher, they spent the summer retreat at Jingzhou.
At Fenglin Temple in the prefecture, Master Yue was always fond of debate.
One day, he and his disciples were making a great clamor, yet the Preceptor was reading a scripture as usual, remaining unperturbed as if he neither heard nor saw them.
After the commotion subsided, Master Yue went to the Preceptor’s desk, widened his eyes, and rebuked him, saying, "You have been here..."
To put on airs and affect the manner of a virtuous teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*)—is that how you measure things?
The former master simply offered his respects and withdrew, after which he continued reading the sutras as before. △ Yunfeng Wei was inviolable;
Huanglong Ci was irresistible. Both were naturally perfected; they cannot be fathomed by ordinary minds.
This chapter teaches students not to become so attached to external things as to neglect their own practice.
Master Huanglong Nan said: "In the past, I traveled through Hunan with Wenyue. I saw a monk carrying his travel pack on his back as he journeyed.
Wenyue was struck with wonder and frowned; then, he rebuked him, saying: 'These are the very things from within your own inner chambers that you refuse to let go.'"
"Stop! To burden others with your own heavy load—is this not excessive toil? (from *Línjiān lù*).
Hǎngluóng cited this past event to inspire his disciples, saying: "In the past, I traveled through Húnán with Master Yuè.
I saw a monk traveling on foot carrying a trunk and a basket. When Yuè saw him, he was shocked and sighed."
Considering it a strange matter, he knit his brows and furrowed his forehead for a long time. Then, rebuking the monk, he said:
"You are not even willing to set aside the things of your own private chambers. 'Things of the private chambers' refers to the objects within one's bedchamber."
This means that one’s sensory consciousness does not relinquish its attachment to external objects. This, in turn, burdens others;
to "shoulder" is to carry on the shoulders, and to "haul" is to carry on the back. How can this be anything other than exhausting oneself while exhausting others?
△ Once one has let go of the things within the inner chambers, what further matter remains to cause lingering attachment? This is truly the foremost shortcut for realizing the Way.
This chapter instructs the abbot on the necessity of communicating with those both above and below, and understanding the causes of loss and gain, decline and prosperity. Huanglong said:

"The essential requirement for an abbot is to win the hearts of the assembly; winning the hearts of the assembly requires perceiving their true sentiments. As the Buddhas of the past have said: "Human sentiment..."
Such a person serves as a field of merit for the world; indeed, it is through them that the Way of principle arises.

Thus, the decline or prosperity of an era, and the loss or gain of affairs, must depend upon human sentiment. When sentiment is either open or obstructed, decline or prosperity ensues; when affairs are either substantial or meager, loss or gain arrives.
This section first clarifies the importance of understanding human sentiments. It means that the abbot must foremost possess a deep understanding of human nature in order to comfort the assembly.
As the Buddhas of the past have said: "Human sentiment is the foremost field for producing merit in the world."
Indeed, all matters and principles, as well as all dharmas of the Path, arise from human sentiment.
Therefore, the prosperity or decline of an age, and the increase or decrease of things and events, must necessarily result from human sentiment. When sentiment is unobstructed, prosperity arises;
when sentiment is blocked, decline ensues. If an undertaking is abundant and substantial, sentiment will surely follow; thus, in such matters, there will inevitably be benefit. As for the matter...
If feelings are slight, they will inevitably become distant; thus, in matters of state, there will surely be loss. Only the Sage can penetrate the sentiments of the world.
Therefore, in the differentiation of the hexagrams of the *I Ching*: when Qian is below and Kun is above, it is called Tai (Prosperity);

when Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi (Stagnation). As for their symbolic significance: when the upper is diminished and the lower is benefited, it is called Yi (Increase); when the lower is diminished...
"When increase occurs at the top, it is called 'Diminution' (Sǔn). Now, Qian represents Heaven and Kun represents Earth.
For Heaven to be below and Earth above is certainly a reversal of their proper positions; yet it is nevertheless called 'Peace' (Tài), because the upper and lower realms interact with one another.

For the host to be above while the guest resides below is certainly consistent with propriety; yet it is nevertheless called 'Stagnation' (Fǒu), because the upper and lower realms do not interact. Therefore, Heaven..."

If the earth does not interact [with the heavens], the myriad things cannot flourish. If human sentiments do not interact, all affairs will lack harmony. The principle of increase and decrease likewise proceeds from this.
This section cites the Sage as proof; for it is only the Sage who can, of his own accord, penetrate the sentiments of the world. Why is this so?
I know this is so. Have you not seen the separate hexagrams of the *Yi*? When Qian is below and Kun is above, it is called Tai;
when Kun is above and Qian is below, it is named the hexagram Di Tian Tai. "Tai" means "pervasion. It signifies "the small depart and the great arrive. The "small" refers to Yin.
When [the sun] moves outward to dwell outside, it is the Great Yang. When it comes inward to dwell inside, the yang qi descends and the yin qi ascends;
as these two qi intersect, the myriad things are transformed and produced, and thus heaven and earth are in harmonious prosperity. To speak in terms of human affairs:

The great serves as the ruler; the small serves as the minister. When the ruler extends sincerity in entrusting his subordinates, and the ministers exhaust their loyalty in serving their superior, the wills of those above and below are communicated, and the world becomes universally prosperous and peaceful. When Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi (Stagnation).
This refers to Qian (Heaven) above and Kun (Earth) below, which is named the hexagram Pi (Stagnation). "Pi" means closure and obstruction. The great departs and the small arrives;
the Yang departs to dwell outside, while the Yin arrives to dwell inside. The Yin qi does not ascend, and the Yang qi does not descend.
Because the two qi do not interact, the myriad things do not come into being; thus, there is the stagnation and closure of Heaven and Earth. To speak in terms of human affairs:

If the ruler does not bestow his trust upon his ministers, and the ministers do not offer their service upward to the ruler, then the interaction between high and low ceases, and human relations become obstructed and stifled.
As for its symbolic representation: when the upper is diminished to benefit the lower, it is called "Yi" (Increase).

This refers to the hexagram *Yi* (Increase), with *Xun* above and *Zhen* below, known as Wind over Thunder. "Yi" means to increase or augment. *Xun* represents wind, and *Zhen* represents thunder; when thunder rages, the wind arises.
Anger. Second, they assist one another, which constitutes benefit. Speaking in terms of human affairs:
those above bestow their grace upon those below, while those below exhaust their sincerity in serving those above; this is mutual augmentation. Therefore, the fundamental meaning states:
the yang line at the beginning of the upper trigram is diminished, and the yin line at the beginning of the lower trigram is augmented. Hence it is said:

"Benefit" and "Diminution. When the lower is diminished to benefit the upper, it is called *Dun* (Diminution). This refers to the *Dun* hexagram, with *Gen* (Mountain) above and *Dui* (Lake) below, known as "Mountain and Lake Diminished.

*Dun* means to reduce or diminish. It signifies diminishing the depth of the *Dui* lake to increase the height of the *Gen* mountain; taking from within to supplement without is what constitutes diminution.
In terms of human affairs, this refers to those in superior positions taking from the people to enrich themselves, while those in subordinate positions [focus on...]
To diminish oneself for the sake of the ruler will inevitably lead to the mutual detriment of both superiors and subordinates.

Therefore, the fundamental meaning states that one diminishes the yang line at the top of the lower trigram to benefit the yin line at the top of the upper trigram; hence it is called "Diminution" (Sǔn). Furthermore, Qian is fundamentally Heaven.
Qian is fundamentally the heavens, yet it now resides below; Kun is fundamentally the earth, yet it now resides above.

In terms of their positions, this is certainly a state of contrariety; yet it is called "Tai" (Peaceful Stability) because the qi of the upper and lower realms circulate and communicate with one another.
When the host is above and the guest is below, the principle is naturally harmonious; yet [in this hexagram], it is otherwise.
That which is called "Pi" (the hexagram of obstruction) arises because the upper and lower realms do not communicate with one another.

Thus, when the vital energies of Heaven and Earth do not interact, all things are unable to grow and reproduce; when the way of human relations does not interact, all affairs fail to achieve harmony and joy.
The meaning of "diminution" and "augmentation" discussed previously is precisely what has been stated here.
Furthermore, those who occupy positions of authority over others can restrain themselves to benefit those below them; the subordinates will surely be pleased and serve their superiors.

Is this not what is called "beneficial"? Conversely, if those in high positions despise their subordinates and act with self-indulgence, the subordinates will surely resent them and rebel against their superiors.
Can this not be called diminution? Therefore, when those above and below interact, there is prosperity (*tai*); when they do not interact, there is stagnation (*pi*).
He who diminishes himself is benefited by others; he who benefits himself is diminished by others. Is the gain or loss of one's emotional state (*qing*) not a matter of no small consequence?

The former sages once used the metaphor of man as a boat and emotion as water. Water can carry a boat, yet it can also overturn it. When the water flows favorably, the boat floats; if it goes against the current, the boat sinks.

This section clarifies the communication between those above and below. Now, if those in superior positions are naturally able to exercise restraint and treat others with broad-minded tolerance, those below will surely be joyful and serve them with devotion. Is this not what is called "beneficial"?
If those in superior positions treat others with contempt while indulging their own whims, those below will surely harbor resentment and rebel against them. Is this not...?

This is what is called "diminution. Thus, when the sentiments of those above and below can communicate with one another, it is termed *tai* (thorough penetration); when they do not communicate, it is termed *pi* (obstruction). Those who willingly practice diminution cause others to increase; those who persist in their own benefit cause others to diminish. How easy is it for human nature to attain such success or failure?

A former sage once provided an analogy, as Confucius answered Duke Ai of Lu: [The Duke asked: "What is meant by 'the superior man diminishes himself'? Confucius replied: "He diminishes his own desires, yet increases his virtue. He diminishes his private interests, yet increases his public service. He diminishes his personal ambition, yet increases his contribution to the state. This is what is meant by 'the superior man diminishes himself. The Duke said: "Excellent! If a ruler can truly diminish himself, the people will naturally increase in prosperity. If he does not diminish himself, the people will suffer loss. The attainment or failure of human affairs—how could this be achieved easily? The former sages have often used such metaphors, just as Confucius answered Duke Ai of Lu.
The words compare the person to a boat and the emotions to water. Now, water is inherently capable of carrying a boat;
yet if suddenly adverse winds arise and waves are produced, the capsizing of the boat is likewise due to the water. Therefore, it is said that when the water is favorable, the boat floats;
when it opposes it, the boat sinks.

Therefore, when an abbot wins the hearts of the people, the monastery prospers; when he loses their hearts, it declines. If he fully wins them, there is full prosperity; if he fully loses them, there is total ruin.
Thus, shared goodness brings abundant blessings, while shared evil brings severe calamity. Good and evil follow one another as surely as beads on a string.
Prosperity and decline mirror conduct as clearly as observing the sun. This is the essential lesson for successive generations (from the Letter to Huangbo Sheng).
This section summarizes the thorough understanding of human sentiments. Thus, if the abbot grasps the sentiments of people, the Way of the Dharma will flourish;

if he loses the sentiments of people, all affairs will fall into ruin. When human sentiments are understood everywhere, this is called "complete attainment," and matters will consequently flourish entirely.
Conversely, if one fails to understand human sentiments in every situation and completely loses them, then no matter can be successfully managed, and everything will fail.
It is abandoned. Therefore, those who dwell with the virtuous receive much fortune; those who associate with the wicked will surely suffer great calamity.
These two types—good and evil—are fundamentally of the same category, like black and white following one another, or like pearls strung together;
they are not two distinct things. Whether one prospers or declines depends on the presence of good or evil; this principle is clear and evident.

It is like observing the sun; it is clearly visible. Whether one is good or evil, and the principles of prosperity or decline, all depend entirely on whether human sentiment reaches its full expression or not.
This single matter of applying sentiment serves as a model for all successive dynasties.
Regarding this "model" (yuantui), the *Zhuangzi* says: "At midnight, Lord Yuan of Song dreamed of a man who, with disheveled hair, peered in."
The Gatekeeper said, "I have been at the Abyss of the Lord of the Passes since I was appointed as the Superintendent of the Clear River to serve the Lord of the River.
There, a fisherman named Yú Qié caught me. When the Sovereign Yuan awoke, he sent someone to divine my nature, who declared, 'This is a divine tortoise.
The Sovereign asked, 'Is there a fisherman named Yú Qié? His attendants replied, 'There is. The Sovereign said, 'Summon Yú Qié for an audience tomorrow. The next day, Yú Qié appeared.
The next morning, the ruler asked, "What have you caught in your fishing? He replied, "In my net this morning, I caught a white tortoise;
its shell is five feet in circumference. The ruler said, "Present that tortoise to me. When the tortoise arrived, the ruler wished to kill it once, and then wished to spare it again;

his mind was filled with doubt. He divined about it, and the result was: "It is auspicious to kill the tortoise for divination. Thereupon, he cut open the tortoise and drilled seventy-two holes in it, yet there was no flaw.
The Record of the Bamboo Slips states: Zhongni said, "The divine tortoise was able to appear in a dream to Emperor Yuanjun, yet it could not avoid the net of Yuqie.
Its wisdom was such that its shell could be drilled seventy-two times without missing a single joint, yet it could not avoid the calamity of having its belly cut open.

Thus, even knowledge has its limitations, and the spiritual can have its reach surpassed. [This illustrates how] those of similar virtue and shared understanding communicate with one another; this is the way of the thousand sages.
The essential precept for maintaining one's person: it is not enough merely to know this; one should inscribe it upon the seat beside one’s right.
This chapter states that when an ordinary person undertakes a task, their resolve must be vast and expansive, so that they do not feel cramped by their circumstances.

Huanglong said to Lord Jing: "In all matters undertaken with a focused mind, one must always ensure that the path before one is wide open, allowing everyone else to pass through; only then is this the way a great man applies his mind.
If it is narrow and impassable, not only will others be unable to proceed, but there will be no ground even for oneself to set foot upon" (Zhangjiang ji).
Lord Jing’s surname was Wang; his given name was Anshi, and his courtesy name was Jiefu.

A native of Linchuan, he was appointed as Prime Minister during the Xining era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jing. He sought instruction from Chan Master Nanyuan of Huanglong. The Master said:
"When ordinary people set their minds on performing a single upright and direct deed, they must first ensure that their resolve is broad and expansive; do not..."

To take one's own private interests as right, one must broaden the path before them so that all people throughout the world—whether wise or foolish, distant or near, ancient or modern—can walk upon it;
only then can one see the place where a true man of great character applies his mind.
If one’s actions are treacherous and one’s intentions are narrow and obstructive, not only will others be unable to follow them, but...
There is an obstruction; furthermore, there is no place for one's own self to rest or set foot.
Such talk as this must be understood by people of this caliber; otherwise, it will mostly be viewed with indifference.
This chapter teaches people to be cautious and reverent in those places where others do not know, but which one knows alone, in order to eliminate deception.
Huanglong said: "In every word, silence, gesture, and action, a person claims not to deceive Heaven above, nor to deceive others without; yet within..."
"Not to deceive one's own heart" can truly be called "attaining it. Yet, one must still remain cautious and reverent even in the privacy of solitude and the most hidden recesses;
only when there is not even the slightest trace of self-deception can it be called "attaining it" (Reply to Lord Jing).

Now, "fu" (夫) is an introductory particle. Generally, in every instance of speech or silence, movement or stillness, ordinary people should have self-assurance, knowing that above they do not dare deceive Heaven, outwardly they do not dare deceive others, and inwardly they do not dare deceive their own minds.
This may truly be called attaining non-deception. Nevertheless, one must still exercise caution and vigilance when alone.

Within the most obscure and subtle recesses, examine this mind with rigorous scrutiny; if there is not even a hair’s breadth of deception or delusion, one may truly be said to have attained something.
Indeed, when there is not even a hair’s breadth of deception, one immediately enters the first stage (bhūmi).
This chapter states that since one has assumed the title of "Elder" (Changlao), one must take the practice of the Way as one's responsibility;

only then does one not render that title hollow. Huanglong said: "The office of an Elder is a vessel for moral cultivation. The former sages established the monasteries and laid out their regulations."

The regulations establish titles and positions; those monastics who possess virtue and moral integrity are selected and designated as "Elders" (Changlao) so that they may practice their virtue and morality, rather than merely usurping this title for personal gain.
This section states that in establishing titles, one must understand their meaning. The position of *zhǎnglǎo* (Elder) is also an office;
this office is a vessel for carrying the Way and a tool for mounting virtue. It is like Baizhang’s establishment of the monastic groves (*conglin*) and his setting forth of the governing regulations.
To establish the title of "Abbot" and the position of "Head of the Hall," one must first select a monk of virtue and character and appoint him as an "Elder.
This is intended for him to practice such virtue and character; it is not meant as a mere expedient to privately and improperly assume the empty name of an Elder.

The late Master Ciming once said: "Rather than remaining in the mountains and valleys to die old and alone while guarding the Way, it is better to practice the Way and lead the assembly within the monasteries.
Is this not because the virtue and morality of the Buddhas and Patriarchs reside in those who skillfully uphold the office of an elder?
(From his letter to Cuiyan Zhen).
This section clarifies that benefiting oneself is not as good as benefiting others. Our late master Ciming once said:

"For members of the monastic community, it is better to practice the Way and govern the great assembly, managing the monasteries for the sake of the Dharma, than to embrace one's principles and hide one's talents, dying old and alone in mountain retreats while seeking only to perfect oneself. Is this not being truly capable of upholding the dignity of an elder?"
Those who hold these offices must ensure that the Way and virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs endure forever without perishing.
To establish principles and define positions, one requires a core of integrity and spirit; it is not merely a matter of managing formalities or performing tasks with mere expediency.
This chapter states that while the study of the Way certainly requires dedicated diligence, it is especially essential to sever one’s cravings and attachments in order to expand and fulfill the Way.
Huanglong said to the recluse Pan Yanzhi: "The learning of the sages and worthies cannot be accomplished in a moment; it must be pursued..."
Accumulation. The essentials of accumulation are solely diligence and constancy. Banish all personal indulgences and practice without weariness;
only then can you expand and fulfill this, thereby exhausting the mysteries of the world (from the *Longshan Guanglu*).
As for the hermits who do not seek honor or renown but find joy in the Way themselves, there was one named Pan Yanming, styled the Recluse Qingyi.
He sought instruction from Huanglong, who told him that the learning required to become a sage or a worthy cannot be accomplished in haste.
"Haste" refers to acting with urgency or superficiality; the essential point lies in accumulating merit and cultivating virtue over time.
Furthermore, the essential point of this accumulation lies in being single-mindedly earnest and diligent.
Moreover, one must completely eliminate all that the mouth desires and all that the heart loves and craves. Practice this without allowing for any laxity or weariness.
After ten or five years of such practice, one may then cause the principle to expand and the scope of the mind to become fully filled; only then will it be perfected.
The ultimate subtlety in all under heaven—how could it not be magnificent? Regarding the two characters "accumulation" (jìlěi), they cannot be measured by years or months;
rather, one must focus one's gaze upon diligent application, and understanding will naturally arise.
This chapter concerns the majestic and solemnity of the Master’s Dharma; it serves as an excellent model for future generations.
When Pan Yanzhi heard that Huanglong’s Dharma way was strict and rigorous, he asked about its essential principles. Huanglong said:
"If the father is stern, the son will be respectful. Today’s regulations and instructions are the models for tomorrow."
This section states that the upholding of the Dharma depends entirely upon formal instruction.
When Yan saw Huanglong upholding the Dharma and practicing the Way with such solemnity and meticulous care, he asked him about its essential principles. Huanglong replied:

"It is like the worldly way of a father who maintains strictness so that his children and grandchildren will surely give rise to reverence; it is like when Ma Yuan campaigned against Jiaozhi and issued a letter of admonition."
My sons and nephews said, "Do not covet personal indulgences; apply yourselves diligently to your studies and duties. My sons and nephews followed this and did not dare to disobey.
Thus we know that the respect of children arises from the strictness of their fathers. The rules and admonitions I establish today shall serve as a model for others in the future.
It is like leveling the various terrains: that which is high is lowered, and that which is hollow is filled. When he is about to ascend a mountain a thousand fathoms high, I am there with him;
when he is exhausted and sinks to the bottom of the Nine Abysses, I am there with him as well.
When his skills are exhausted and his delusions are spent, he will rest of his own accord.
This section uses a metaphor to clarify the power of maintaining discipline. For example, when people of the world level the ground—raising the low and filling the deep;
wherever there is height, they shave it down to make it humble, and wherever there is depth, they fill it in to make it level.
Now, the reason I employ such strict methods is not without intention; rather, they are applied according to the individual. If that person...
Joyfully, he wishes to ascend to the summit of ten-thousand-fathom peaks; I also follow him and ascend together with him.
If he becomes weary and exhausted at the bottom of the ninefold abyss, I also follow him and descend together with him.
I wait until his skillful means for ascending are exhausted and his deluded thoughts of descending are ended; then, he himself—
However, let it rest. How could I possibly allow it to flow freely from high to low? Therefore, it is no different from the way one manages the land.
It is further said: "To nourish and foster it is how growth and reproduction occur in spring and summer; to apply frost and snow is how [harvest] occurs in autumn and winter."
"It is for the sake of maturation. May I not wish to remain silent? (Linjian Lu).
This passage shows that only when the nurturing and the fostering begin does success finally come. It further states:

"The *xu* and the *yu*—these are the means by which spring and summer bring forth and nourish life. The *Liji* says: "Heaven nurtures with qi; Earth nurtures with form. Thus, yin and yang attain one another.
It covers and nurtures the myriad things; it freezes them with frost and snow, for this is how autumn and winter bring them to full maturity.
The meaning is that although the Yin and Yang are capable of generating and nourishing all things, if they do not rely upon frost and snow, there would be no means by which to bring them to maturity.

Now that I occupy the seat of the teacher, how could I remain silent and say nothing? If I do not instruct and am not sincere, how can I enable others to achieve accomplishment? △ (The character "煅" [xiàn] signifies refining or smelting.)
To refine the holy and melt the mundane—how could this be an easy matter? It depends entirely upon the master’s refined mind and skillful hand to bring it to perfection.
This chapter reveals the master’s wondrous function, possessing a mechanism unfathomable even to Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is not something that those of shallow understanding can know.
Within the chamber of Huanglong, there were three "gate" statements (*guānyǔ*). Few monks could harmonize with his pivotal intent;

even when some offered a response, he would merely sit upright with eyes closed, showing no sign of approval or disapproval. When Yan extended his inquiry and pressed him further, Huanglong said, "Those who have already passed through the gate."
He swung his arms and departed. He went to ask the frontier official whether he might pass through; this was one who had not yet penetrated the barrier (*Línjiān lù*).
Whenever Huánglóng saw a monk come for instruction, he would immediately ask: "Every person has their own karmic affinity (*shēngyuán*);
where is yours, Venerable? Longqìng Xián replied: "In the morning I ate white congee; by evening I felt hungry again."
Ji asked again, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? Xian replied, "Playing a pipa under the moon. Ji asked again, "How is my foot like a donkey’s foot?
Xian replied, "A heron standing in the snow is not the same color. The Master used these questions to test people constantly.
For thirty years, there was rarely anyone who could grasp his essential pivot. Even if someone were to respond to him, he would simply sit upright with eyes closed, alone and solemn;
whether the response was acceptable or not, he made no distinction. For this reason, the monastic communities came to call these "the words of the three barriers.
The Master himself composed a verse on them: "Where the conditions of birth are severed, the donkey’s hoof is extended; When the donkey’s hoof is extended, it is the Buddha’s hand."

Kai said: "To report to you practitioners of Chan from the Five Lakes: once the three barriers have been pierced one by one, Pan Yanzhi could not fathom their application and thus requested further instruction from the Master.
The Master said: 'If one has already passed through the barriers, they do not ask others again;
they simply wave their sleeves and walk away. But if you wish to ask the gatekeeper whether this barrier can be passed, [you must first pass it yourself].'"
"You may pass. This means that you have not yet penetrated this barrier. △ How many people are unable to do so?
It is simply because they fail to grasp its vital point. Once it is recognized, what is it? It is nothing more than a pair of worn-out straw sandals.
This chapter speaks of those who possess resolve; it is only such persons who can exhaustively master the Way and reach its ultimate limit.
Huanglong said: "The Way is like a mountain: the higher one ascends, the higher it becomes. It is like the earth: the further one travels, the further it extends.

Those who study it with base and shallow minds merely stop when they have exhausted their own strength. Only those who are resolute in their pursuit of the Way can exhaustively fathom its loftiness and distance."
What else can compare to this? (From *Jiwen*).
A student who intends to cultivate the Way must prepare a heart of resolute determination. Yet this Way is like an exceedingly high mountain;
the higher one ascends, the higher it becomes. "Yi" means "increasingly. It is also like an exceedingly remote place; the further one travels, the more remote it becomes. [...]
As one proceeds, one travels ever further. Those who study with inferior understanding and limited vision, whose resolve is shallow and mundane, can only do their utmost and stop there.
Only those who possess a resolute will and strength for the cultivation of the Way can exhaust its heights and reach its distances.
As for the rest, with their lowly views and meager strength, who could possibly reach it? △ Study.
One must resolutely pursue this until reaching the very summit and the ultimate depths; only then is it a place of rest. Otherwise, one remains a mere common, mediocre being.
This chapter warns scholars not to loathe the old and delight in the new; if they do so, they will be far removed from the Way.
Huanglong said: "The heavens, earth, sun, and moon of antiquity are just like the heavens, earth, sun, and moon of today.

The nature and characteristics of the myriad things of antiquity are just like the nature and characteristics of the myriad things of today. Since the heavens, earth, sun, and moon certainly do not change, and the nature and characteristics of the myriad things certainly do not alter, why would the Way alone be subject to change?"

This section returns to clarify that the fundamental Way is unchanging. It means that the heavens, earth, sun, and moon that existed in antiquity are precisely the same as the heavens, earth, sun, and moon of today.
The natures and dispositions of the myriad things that existed in antiquity are precisely the same as the natures and dispositions of the myriad things of today.
The heavens, earth, sun, and moon, and the natures and dispositions of the myriad things, have been so since ancient times.
To this day, since things are neither renewed nor transmuted, why do you say that the Dharma alone is subject to change and transformation?
Alas for those who have not yet attained it: they grow weary of the old and take delight in the new, abandoning this to grasp that. They are like one bound for Yue who goes north instead of south;
truly, they may be called different from others. Yet they merely exhaust their minds and weary their bodies; such is their resolve.
"The more diligent one is, the further one's path becomes" (from the *Dun’an Bìjì*).
This section clearly shows that people do not study with sufficient effort. Alas!

It is likely because students lack the necessary vigor and cannot reach the Way, they then claim that studying the Way is exceedingly difficult and prefer to study some external books and classics, considering them easier.
It is so. This is what is called "disliking the old and delighting in the new," abandoning this and taking up that; it is merely people of the time changing for themselves.
It is like someone who has just set out for the land of Yue, instead of traveling south, turns back and heads north; the distance between north and south is vast.

Truly, this may be called being different from others. As for "going"—if a student is unwilling to exert effort in studying this Way and instead seeks out heterodox learning, they do not realize that they are merely exhausting their minds and toiling their bodies in vain.
Your resolve to study is increasingly diligent, yet you do not know that you are moving further away from the Way. Is this not to be lamented? △ Now, regarding study...
For the most part, these people are weary [of the world] and thus find pleasure in novelty. Who, then, can possess an iron-like backbone and an ice-cold heart to investigate the Way of immutability?
This chapter teaches the student to establish their resolve; while it is essential that this be focused and free from distraction, it is even more vital that it endure and remain unchanging.
This is indeed what constitutes attainment.
Huanglong said to Ying Shaowu: "Your resolve should be focused on a single point; persevere for a long time without retreating. One day you will surely know where the wondrous Way leads.
Should your mind harbor likes and dislikes, or your emotions give way to depravity and perversity, then even if your ambition and spirit were equal to those of the ancients,"
I fear that in the end I may not succeed in beholding this Way (from the *Biji*).
For those who study the Way, it is simply a matter of maintaining a single thought of sincere truth. Settle the mind upon one point; even if it takes a long time, do not falter or grow discouraged.
At some future time, you will naturally overturn everything to its very depths and will surely come to know the locus of the wondrous Way.

It is so. Should there be even a trace of likes and dislikes remaining in your breast, or if emotional consciousness has accumulated many deviant thoughts, then even if your aspirations and your spirit are no different from those of the ancients, I fear you will ultimately never see the Way.
As soon as there is a single thread of attachment, you are immediately obstructed by that very thread.
How much more so regarding what is good or evil, and what is deviant or perverse! How could the Way be attained through mere superficiality?
This chapter teaches people to know what they ought to do; thus, one may reflect upon oneself with confidence.

Master Baofeng Ying said: "The old masters of various quarters who critique the words of the predecessors and handle the public cases (gong'an) are like those who carry soil to build up Mount Tai or scoop water to drench the Eastern Sea. Yet how could they rely on these to achieve greatness or depth?
Observing their intent, they aim to augment [the teachings], yet they do not realize that what they do is inappropriate. (From the *Guanglu*).
This refers to the elder masters of various regions today who frequently criticize and analyze the words of the ancients.
Little do they realize that the minds of those ancient worthies were like precious mirrors: when objects appeared, they were reflected; when circumstances arose, they spoke.

They never gave rise to deliberate thoughts or mental constructions; all their utterances emerged from the source as words of ultimate truth. As for the current practice of dividing chapters and analyzing phrases—
To offer critical comments and pointed remarks is much like painting empty space or carving ice; it is utterly useless.
A *gong'an* (public case) is like the legal records of a government office: where the Dharma resides, the True Path governs.

It is by taking up this Dharma that one rectifies the improprieties of the world. The karmic encounters between Buddhas and patriarchs were originally intended to awaken those who have not yet awakened.
Awakening! Though hundreds of thousands of teachings have been revealed, they all transmit the ultimate principle; how could one speak of it through mere subjective views?
Those who I see critiquing *gong'an* (public cases) are like those who wish to increase the height of Mount Tai by scooping up a handful of soil with both hands.

To scoop up a single ladle of water and hope to irrigate the depths of the vast ocean—how could those ancients have relied upon your picking up and setting down, or your critical judgments, to increase their height or deepen their waters?
Observing your intent, you seek to supplement what the ancients established, yet you remain unaware that what you yourself produce is, in fact, inappropriate. △ This marks the end of the section.
This is a single dose of detoxifying powder; those who can savor its flavor will naturally find their minds and hearts cool and serene.
This chapter teaches students to recognize cause and effect and to practice this path with diligence, lest they lose the sacred seed.
Whenever Master Ying Shaowu encountered scholars who behaved with reckless abandon and showed no fear of cause and effect, he would sigh for a long time and say:
"A life of toil is like a temporary lodging; one stays according to conditions, and when one departs, it is gone. What can such people actually achieve?
You lot lack a sense of integrity and shame, violating the boundaries of social order and defiling the religious teachings to such an extent."
This section clarifies how students greedily pursue external things while forgetting their fundamental nature.

I have often observed a class of scholars who are unrestrained and heedless of the consequences of their karma, failing to recognize cause and effect. Therefore, after sighing for a long time, I said:
"People in this world are busily occupied and striving; this is called a 'toil-filled life,' like a traveler lodging at an inn, or like a boat moored [for a moment]."

"On this bank, we merely stay for a brief while; how could this be a plan for the long term? If we remain here, all things will be regarded as 'me,' and we can only enjoy them according to conditions.
If we depart, they will all be of no use. As for those who, with deluded minds, greedily seek after them—how many such people can there be?
How could one not avoid such karmic retribution? What do you all think of this?"
Lacking any sense of integrity or shame, you have ultimately violated the rites and laws of social hierarchy and brought disgrace upon the teachings of your ancestors, reaching such a state as this.
A man of great character should aim to broaden the ancestral Way and guide future generations; he ought not to indulge his private desires at will. It is improper—
That which one avoids and shuns brings calamity upon one’s own person and creates misfortune for ten thousand kalpas.
To suffer in the three miserable realms and the hells is not yet the ultimate suffering; to lose one’s human body beneath the *kāṣāya* robe is truly suffering (from the *Biji*).
This section exhorts one to harbor the resolve to propagate the Way and not bring ruin upon oneself.

If one is a true man of great character, his harbored resolve should lie in restoring and manifesting the ancestral Way, and in guiding and supporting future generations. "Guiding" (yòu) means to lead; "supporting" (yè) means to assist.

One ought not to become such a shameless monk who privately indulges in his own desires—*shàn* meaning to monopolize—and who, without any sense of restraint or avoidance, takes [what belongs to others] openly.
It is for this reason. Such greedy pursuit brings about the calamities of one's own life and creates the misfortunes of ten thousand kalpas.
You must understand this: those who suffer in the three realms and the hells do not consider their suffering to be true suffering;
yet here, beneath these *kāṣāya* robes, they lose this human body, and it is truly unknown when they shall emerge from it again. This is indeed...

It is suffering. The "matchmaker" is that which brews its transgressions; it is also that which summons them. Though there may be a thousand words and ten thousand discourses, they serve only to teach people to recognize cause and effect.
Those who lack understanding remain stubbornly deaf to this; even if a Buddha or Patriarch were to appear again in this world, there would be nothing they could do for such as these.
This chapter states that an elder should honor himself through virtue and the Way; do not invite the disdain of devas and humans.

Ying Shaowu said to Huìtáng, "Those who are called 'good knowledge-holders' (śāstrins) assist the Buddhas and Patriarchs in spreading their transformation, causing monastics to turn their minds toward the Way and changing customs and transforming social mores. This is certainly not something that those of shallow character can accomplish."
This section clarifies that those who propagate the Way must necessarily be wise ones.

Generally speaking, those designated as "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) exist fundamentally to assist in exalting the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, causing the assembly of monastics to turn their minds directly toward the wondrous Way.
I truly wish to shift this wind of wicked rebellion and reform these customs of unrighteousness;
how could such a task be accomplished by those of shallow roots and meager virtue?
Monks of the Final Dharma do not cultivate morality or the Way, possess little integrity or righteousness, and often act with sycophancy and filth, wagging their tails like dogs.
He begged for pity, pursuing fame and profit at the gates of those in power. Once his karma was exhausted and his merit had declined, the devas and humans grew weary of him;
he defiled the Orthodox Lineage and brought disgrace upon his teachers and friends. Should he not have sighed in regret? Huìtáng nodded in agreement.
This section reveals that the craving for meditative concentration is loathed by all people.

I have observed that among those in the age of the Dharma’s decline, there are certain bhikṣus—*bhikṣu* in Sanskrit meaning "one who begs"—who beg from the Buddhas for the Truth to nourish their wisdom-life, and beg from donors for alms to sustain their physical bodies.
Having already taken the title of *bhikṣu*, yet they neither cultivate the Path nor maintain [their spiritual integrity].
Virtue. Furthermore, they are unable to maintain their integrity or preserve righteousness. "Wǎngwǎng" means frequently or repeatedly.

"Bāojū" refers to wrapping up extraordinary items in gifts to offer to sycophants and flatterers in order to seek favors or recommendations. "Āngzàng" describes an appearance of seeking advantage by chance. The *Book of the Later Han* states:
"Those who lean against the gate with an *āngzàng* air wagging their tails to beg for pity are like dogs that wag their tails when seeing people."
They flatter others, seeking nothing more than pity and compassion. Such is the manner of the sycophancy and fawning of petty people;
they chase after and follow those with power and influence wherever they go. This is the conduct and character of petty people:

they seek out powerful figures everywhere, pursuing them no further than to seek their reputation and covet their material gains, which they then boast of to others, saying, "Such-and-such a high official," or "Such-and-such a person."
"Sir, this was a close acquaintance of mine who bestowed upon me generous gifts, unaware that many years had passed.
Suddenly, his accumulated karma has reached its limit and his remaining merit has exhausted. Consequently, both gods and men have come to loathe him;
not only has he brought calamity upon himself, but he has further defiled the Dharma-gate and brought disgrace upon his teachers and friends—this is truly lamentable."
"Sus" means a long sigh. "Ling" means nodding one's head in assent; it is to grant permission with the heart while remaining silent with the mouth.
△ When one reaches the point where both gods and humans grow weary [of existence], it becomes truly agonizing. Why do you not borrow a mirror to look at your own face?
You will see for yourself how shameful and loathsome it is.
This chapter states that people do not apply themselves to the fundamental but instead pursue the peripheral; the distance between these two is more than a world apart.
Ying Shaowu said to Pan Yanzhi: "Those who studied in antiquity cultivated their minds; those who study today cultivate outward traces."
However, the mind and its outward traces are as far apart as heaven and earth.

Since ancient times, those who have studied the Way have, during their daily lives, stilled all external conditions and concentrated their single mind on investigating the Way, never wavering from beginning to end.
This is why it is said that governing the mind is the pursuit of the fundamental. Those who study today, by contrast, do nothing but look outward.
In one's daily activities, all that is performed is accomplished through floating thoughts; therefore, it is said that the traces of cultivation are all merely secondary.
Yet, the nature of the mind is without form and without action; when its manifestations deviate, they become chaotic and disordered.
Therefore, it does not accord with the Way; fundamentally and ultimately, they do not overcome one another.
This is what is meant by being as far apart as heaven and earth. In the present age, those who all merely follow the traces of practice are like trying to carry a mountain on the back of a gnat;
they will certainly be unable to bear the burden.
This chapter states that studying the Way cannot be done in haste; it must rely on gradual accumulation, with the goal of entering [the path] by degrees.
Ying of Shaowu said to Master Zhenjing Wen: "Things that grow too rapidly will surely wither and die;
achievements completed too quickly will surely be easily destroyed. To disregard long-term planning and instead seek immediate success is never a far-reaching or grand undertaking."
This section teaches the establishment of a long-term resolve. Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen of Baofeng in Longxing Prefecture was the son of Lady Zheng of the Min family from Xianfu.
He was a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan and belongs to the eleventh generation under Mount Heng. It is said:
Whatever things are produced in the world that grow suddenly and rapidly, achieving completion without expectation, will inevitably perish prematurely.
Whatever great achievements or magnificent undertakings one desires to accomplish with haste and speed will ultimately be easy to ruin.
If one does not seek a long-term plan but instead creates such works that are hastily completed, none of them will be of lasting value.
This is a quality of long-term, vast, and lofty potential.
Now, even Heaven and Earth, the most spiritual of entities, require three years and an intercalary month before their work is completed and their transformation perfected;

how much more so for the subtlety of the Great Way—how could it be accomplished in haste? It requires the accumulation of merit and the building up of virtue. Therefore it is said: "If one desires speed..."

If one does not achieve success, it is because their conduct is not meticulous; yet, when things are refined and accomplished, they endure for a long time, leading eventually to lifelong planning. The Sage said:
"Maintain it with faith, carry it out with diligence, and complete it with loyalty. Though a task may be great, it will surely be accomplished."

This section clarifies that nothing is accomplished through haste. Now, even Heaven and Earth, which possess the principle of supreme intelligence, still require an intercalary month every three years and another every five years before they can fulfill their work of creation and complete their process of growth and transformation.
Regarding the term *zài* (year): the *Erya* states that in the Xia dynasty it was called a *suì*, taking its name from the sequence of the sun’s annual course. In the Shang...

It is called *si* (sacrifice), taking the sense of completing one cycle of the four seasonal sacrifices. It is called *zhou* (year) in the Zhou dynasty, taking the meaning of the ripening of the grain.

It was called *zai* (carriage/bearer) in the Tang and Yu dynasties, taking the significance of things reaching their end and beginning anew. Regarding the occurrence of a second intercalary month, Zhang Chun said:

"An intercalary month every three years makes the celestial breath (*tianqi*) slightly complete; an intercalary month every five years makes the celestial breath fully complete. This refers to the intercalary month.
It is insufficient. It is because the days have a surplus. In ancient times, a year consisted of three hundred and sixty-six days.
These were divided into twelve months, with each month having thirty days; thus, a year totaled three hundred and sixty days, leaving a remainder of six days.
Furthermore, six months were short by one day each, adding another six days. Thus, the total surplus for the year was two times six, which is twelve days.
Accumulated over three years, there are thirty-six days. After subtracting one intercalary month, six days remain.
When the subsequent two years arrive, there are twenty-four remaining days; together with the previous six days, this totals thirty days, which constitutes another intercalary month.
Thus, it is said that there is one intercalary month every three years, and a second intercalary month every five years; such is the harmony between heaven and earth.

Its merit has now become fully perfected for the first time. How much more so for the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, which is most ultimate and most profound—how could it be accomplished through sudden or violent application?
It requires that one accumulate merit daily and build up virtue year by year before one can reach its pinnacle.
Therefore it is said: "To desire haste prevents thorough attainment; to attend to minute details ensures there is no loss or error."
For those who wish to reach a place of sublime excellence, it fundamentally depends on persistence. Persistence is indeed a lifelong endeavor.
The Sage said: "Maintain it with steadfast faith; carry it out with agility; establish it with loyalty and generosity.
These three phrases are from the *Zuozhuan*, where Fan Wenzi answered Duke Jing of Jin. This is indeed true.
If one can act in this way, then even the most momentous matters can certainly be brought to a successful conclusion.
Formerly, Attendant Zhe sat through the night without sleeping, using a round log as a pillow. When he dozed off, the pillow would roll away;
upon waking, he would rise again and sit back down as before. He made this his constant practice. Some remarked that his application of mind was excessive, to which Zhe replied: "As for me..."
One’s affinity for Prajñā is naturally thin; if one does not exert oneself with bitter diligence, there is fear that one will be led astray by deluded habits.

How much more so when things are as unreal as dreams and illusions—how could they serve as a long-term plan? In the past, while I was in Xiangxi, I personally witnessed his conduct being such as this;
therefore, the monastic community honored his reputation, revered his virtue, and praised him (from *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
This section cites evidence for steadfast cultivation, taking an ancient master as a model. Chan Master Zhenru Muzhe of Daming in Tanzhou was the son of the Wen family of Linchuan in Fuzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Zhen of Cuishan and belonged to the eleventh generation under Nanyue.
It is said that in the past, when Attendant Zhe practiced the Way, he was most sincere and earnest; he would sit through the night without [sleeping].

Sleeping: Should he intend to sleep, he uses a round wooden log as a pillow. After sleeping for only a short while, as soon as the pillow moves, he awakens, immediately rises, spreads his mat, and returns to his position just as before he had slept.
He takes this as his regular practice. "Shuai" (率) means "to follow" or "to conform to.
Someone said, "Using the mind in this way seems excessive. Zhe replied, "Regarding the great matter of birth and death, [I cannot afford to be lax]."
That one has not yet attained liberation is entirely due to the fact that one’s affinity with Prajñā has been thin and meager from the outset.
If one does not apply oneself with diligent effort and sharpen one’s resolve, there is fear that one will be led astray by the habitual tendencies of deluded thoughts.
Moreover, this body of mine is like a dream or an illusion; it is fundamentally unreal. How could I possibly harbor long-term plans for a hundred-year lifespan? This—
It is evident that Master Zhe’s firm resolve was such as this. When I was formerly in Xiangyin, I personally witnessed his conduct to be thus;

therefore, those who heard of him or saw him within the monastic community all admired his reputation for possessing the Way and revered the reality of his possession of virtue, praising him on this account.
△ No one is willing to apply themselves to the arduous practice of meditation. For example:
What could possibly have been accomplished? Throughout one's entire life, one remains shrouded in darkness, harboring much self-importance.
Yet, this treatise reveals that virtue, being profound, can ultimately not be concealed; it is what is meant by "when the time arrives, the principle is manifest."
Master Zhenjing Wen had long studied under Huanglong. Initially, he maintained the vow not to appear before others.
Later, having accepted an invitation from Dongshan, he traveled through the Western Mountains to visit Master Xiangcheng Shun. Shun teased him, saying:

"Zhuge Liang of old claimed to be a recluse, yet the thatched cottage earnestly invited him to emerge from the mountains. If the pine blossoms are to be moistened by the power of spring, the roots must remain deep."
Yanyang also wrote the *Kaishi* (Opening the Eyes). Zhenjing bowed and withdrew (*Shun’s Record*).

This refers to how Master Zhenjing had resided at Huanglong for the longest time; while he was still in the stage of a student, he often said that he did not wish to enter the world to act as a teacher to others.
Later, when the seat at Dongshan was vacant, he was specially invited to preside over it. The route necessarily passed through Xishan.
He then entered the mountains to visit Chan Master Xiangcheng Jingshun. Shun was a native of Shu who had inherited the lineage of Huanglong;
later, he passed away while seated at Xiangcheng. Shun addressed him with a verse in jest, saying: "Zhuge Liang of old claimed to be a recluse."

This line correctly recounts the vow made by Zhenjing in years past. "The thatched cottage earnestly entreated him to leave the mountains" is a metaphor for the intent of receiving an invitation this morning.
"If the pine blossoms are moistened by the power of spring"—the "power of spring" refers precisely to the timing of the era reaching its peak of prosperity;
it cannot be concealed. Even when the roots lie deep within the crags, they must still bloom. This is compared to those who possess virtue.
"He ultimately remained hidden and did not stay" is a phrase expressing sincere praise. [Zhuge] was his surname; his given name was Liang, and his courtesy name was Kongming.
A native of Langye, he ploughed his own fields at West Sleeping Dragon Ridge in Nanyang and was friends with Xu Shu.
At that time, Liu Xuande was stationed with his troops at Xinye. Ji Shu saw him and informed him, saying, "Zhuge Kongming is the Sleeping Dragon.
General, you ought to go and see him. This man may be approached, but he cannot be forced.
Consequently, Xuande went to visit Liang three times before the latter finally accepted his command; he was subsequently appointed as Military Counselor. Later—

He served as the Chancellor of Shu-Han and was posthumously honored with the title Marquis Zhongwu. The historian Yong wrote: "In an age of chaos, for more than a hundred years, heroic armies have roamed;
Kongming once found joy here in plowing and tilling. Had the King of Shu not personally gone three times to seek him out, how could the Master have emerged from his old cottage?
The appearance and disappearance of the Perfect Man each have their own appointed time. If one attempts to hide when the time has arrived, it conversely becomes a cause for ridicule.
This is not wise.
This chapter teaches that students must not easily judge others as right or wrong; they should carefully examine the facts.
Zhenneng mentioned that Guangdao resided at Wufeng. Public opinion held that Guang was coarse and clumsy, lacking the talent to respond to the world. Upon reaching Guang—
As abbot, he was rigorous in governing himself and broad-minded in presiding over the assembly. Before long, all neglected matters were restored.
Monks passing through the area vied with one another to spread the news. When Zhenjing heard of this, he remarked, "How easily do students give rise to slander and praise!"
This section clarifies that the scholar lacked discernment. As for Master Xingguang of Jiufeng in Ruizhou:
he was a native of Zizhou in Western Sichuan and succeeded Chan Master Zhenjing Wen; he belonged to the twelfth generation under Nanyue.
By nature, the Master was compassionate and loved all things, never preoccupied with trivial or mundane matters; therefore, the monastic community called him "Guangwu" (Guang Without).

One day, [Foguo] Guang was appointed as the abbot of Wufeng. As the community deliberated, everyone spoke privately among themselves, saying, "Guang has always been a man of loose character and is moreover dull-witted.
We fear he lacks the talent to respond to the needs of this world; how could he possibly manage the abbacy?
However, once Guang took up residence, his self-discipline was exceedingly rigorous and his conduct toward the assembly was extremely broad-minded and tolerant. Before long—
In the interim, all that had fallen into neglect within the monastery was fully restored.
Monks passing through vied with one another to spread the news, and everyone spoke of it with praise. When Zhenjing heard of this, he said, "Why do students so easily disparage or praise others?"
Whenever I see monasteries, I overhear people whispering among themselves: "Which elder practices the Way and settles the assembly?

Which elder does not misappropriate the monastery's permanent assets, but shares both its joys and sorrows with the community? Truly, one who is called a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) serves as the master of a temple.

To practice the Way and bring peace to the assembly, not encroaching upon the permanent property of the monastery, and sharing both sweet and bitter experiences with the community—this one ought certainly to do;
what is there to say of it? It is like a scholar-official serving as a government official: to secure the state and pacify the people, he says, "I do not accept bribes, nor do I harass the people.
Now, not accepting bribes and not harassing the people—is this not merely his duty? (From *Shantang Xiaocan*).
This section further raises a common malady. Every time I see monks in the monastic forests (conglins) whispering among themselves, they say:

"Which elder is willing to practice the Way and is able to bring peace to the assembly? Which elder does not misappropriate the permanent property (sangha assets), but shares both joy and hardship with the community?
Now, since one is called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra), they have taken upon themselves the heavy responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to serve as a leader for all.
The head of a monastery practices the Way and sustains the Dharma, pacifying the great assembly and refraining from misappropriating the communal property;
sharing both joy and sorrow with all others is but what is natural and proper, much like a scholar-official serving in government.
Above, he serves his sovereign with loyalty; below, he benefits the people with benevolence—all these are duties inherent to his station. Thus he says: "I..."
To serve as an official without accepting bribes and without harassing the people—ha ha! Is not refusing bribes and not harassing the people something beyond the ordinary?
"Bribe" (*zang*) refers to the emoluments received by a functionary; all wealth obtained through improper means is termed a bribe.
To engage in groundless criticism of others is the very root of diminishing one's merit. I pray that you will cherish yourself and refrain from damaging your virtue.
This chapter shows how the ancients felt shame for themselves and reproached their own selves, thereby being able to know when to stop.
When Zhenjing was at Guizong, every year the fundraising masters would submit petitions, and bolts of cloth would arrive in clouds. When Zhenjing saw them, he frowned.

He frowned, and after a while sighed, saying: "The faith of this man is like his own fat and blood; I am ashamed that I lack virtue—how could I possibly be worthy of it? (From Li Shanglao’s *Record of Daily Excursions*).
When Master Zhenneng resided at Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu, every year the fundraising directors returned to the mountain to submit their records of offerings.
The resulting wealth—money, grain, cloth, and silk—accumulated in such abundance that it gathered like clouds.
Upon seeing this, Zhenneng knit his brows and frowned; he did not rejoice at the great quantity of what had been amassed. After a while, he sighed and said:
All such things as these are, in their entirety, the very marrow and blood of faithful donors.
I feel profound shame and remorse that I possess no virtue or morality; how could I possibly be worthy of such offerings made out of faith?
Yet there is another class of people who still find this insufficient, lacking any sense of shame or remorse; they are scarcely distinguishable from the beasts.

This chapter teaches that students must maintain a mind that is upright and unhidden; only then will they not lose their integrity and commitment to the principles of *jieyi* (integrity and righteousness).
Zhenjing said:
"In the Dharma-ending age (*mofa*), bhikṣus rarely possess integrity and righteousness. Whenever I see them engaging in lofty talk and grand discourse, they claim for themselves..."
No one was able to equal him. When it came to the favor of even a single meal, he would first treat them with distinction and later assist them; he would first criticize them and later praise them.
Few were those who sought out what was right, declaring it right and what was wrong, declaring it wrong—remaining impartial and without concealment (from the *Biji*).
This refers to the bhikṣus of the Dharma-ending age, who originally lack integrity and are devoid of righteous spirit.
They constantly observe others speaking with lofty discourse and expansive rhetoric, like clouds rising and waves surging; they claim for themselves, "I am capable of this; who else can equal me?"
As for those who receive even the kindness of a single meal from another, few are there who first treat them as distinct and later assist and support them;

few are there who first slander them and later praise them; few are there who, seeking a single point of truth, will say it is right when it is right and wrong when it is wrong, remaining resolutely undeluded by profit and desire, and maintaining impartiality without concealment. △
Those of lowly station are inherently unworthy of mention; yet these are the maxims of the ancients, and one must know shame.
This chapter instructs humanity: one’s character and bearing ought to be solemn and prudent, while the cultivation of virtue prizes practical application.
Zhenguan said: "The dharma of a bhikṣu is that one's enjoyments should not be abundant; if they are abundant, they will overflow.
Matters that accord with one's wishes should not be over-schemed; excessive scheming inevitably leads to ruin. That which is about to be accomplished will surely be brought to destruction."

This section teaches that one must be cautious regarding what is done. This refers to those who have left the household life: their use of requisites during the proper times should not be excessive or abundant.
If it is excessive, it will surely overflow; "overflow" means to spill out and flow away. Regarding all matters that satisfy the mind, one should not engage in excessive scheming;
excessive scheming inevitably leads to ruin. That success is necessarily followed by failure is the constant law of nature.

I have observed that my late master Huanglong remained in the world for forty years; whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, he never sought to ensnare the monastics of his time with mere countenance, etiquette, or literary talent.
He accepted only those who possessed a firm realization of the ground and whose conduct was rooted in the practice of truth.
He handled matters with meticulous care and deliberation, truly capturing the spirit and style of the ancients; such a person is rarely equaled among the various schools of Chan.
Therefore, when he presided over the assembly today, there were none who did not take him as their model (*Risheri*).
This section cites the conduct of the former patriarch. Whenever I have observed the late Master Huanglong, he has been manifesting in the world to benefit sentient beings for forty years.

Throughout his speech and silence, and during all moments of movement and stillness, he never once sought to please others with his countenance, nor did he ever attempt to curry favor with others through formal etiquette.
Furthermore, he never tried to ensnare people with his literary skills or scholarly learning. The assembly...
The realization of the middle fruit is stable and profound; for those who tread upon the truth, it unfolds through intricate stages—*tǔ* (褫) meaning "to accomplish" or "to bring to fruition.
In their state of vigilance and reverence, they truly capture the essential form of the ancients;
it seems that throughout all quarters, none can be found to equal or compare with them. Therefore, as I preside over the assembly today, there is [no one to rival them].
Each matter and each dharma is not to be grasped as a fixed rule. When fullness leads to overflow and excessive deliberation leads to failure, who does not know this?
Yet, when one arrives at this point, one often becomes dazed and obscured, lacking the eye of wisdom.
This chapter shows that the ancients were simple and free from greed, finding contentment and peace within themselves.
When Zhujing of Zhenjing was at Baoning in Jiankang, Prince Shu presented him with a gift of plain silk as an offering for his vegetarian meal. He then asked an attendant monk, "What is this?"
The attendant replied, "It is spun silk gauze. Zhenjing asked, "What use for it? The attendant said, "It is fit to be made into a *kāṣāya* (monastic robe).
Zhenjing pointed to the *buddhotara-saṃghāṭī* he was wearing and said, "I usually wear this; those who see it do not find it particularly offensive.
He immediately ordered it to be sent to the storehouse to be appraised and sold to provide for the community. Such was his lack of concern for finery (*Rishen Ji*).
"Jiankang" refers to the name of Baoning Temple in Jinling. Regarding "Prince Shu": Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty conferred the title of Prince Shu upon Lord Jing (Wang Anshi).
During the Xining era, Lord Jing was appointed as Chancellor; he implemented the New Policies, which brought suffering upon the people.
His son, Wang Pang, served as Grand Master of the Chongzheng Hall and assisted his father in ensuring the New Policies were strictly enforced. When Pang passed away, his father...

After he resigned from the相位 (prime ministership), during a period of leisure, he saw in a dream-like vision a ghost messenger leading Fan Pāng, who was burdened with an iron cangue and weeping before him.
The messenger said, "This is because of your father’s dedication to the New Laws. The Duke asked the messenger for a way to be released from this retribution.

The messenger replied, "By establishing a temple and providing food for the monks, you may be absolved. Thereupon, the Duke donated his fields, lands, and residences in Jinling to establish a temple, which was granted the name Baoning.
He requested that a master of pure integrity take charge of it. "Jian" refers to silk; he used plain silk to prepare for the offering at the vegetarian feast. He asked an attendant, "What is this?
The attendant replied, "It is spun-silk gauze. The Master asked, "What use is it? The attendant said, "It can be made into a *kāṣāya* (monastic robe)."
"This is called 'dust-free clothing,'" the Master said, pointing to the cotton *kāṣāya* he was wearing. "I usually wear this, and those who see it do not find it particularly loathsome.
What would you do with this? He immediately ordered it to be sent to the storehouse to be appraised and sold to provide funds for the support of the assembly.
Such was his lack of interest in fine garments and adornments. Although the matter was small, [it reveals his character].
The model is indeed true. If later generations know this, how could they not be careful about that upon which they base their emulation?
This chapter teaches that one must not allow one's resolve to fluctuate according to the difficulty or ease of a task; rather, one must apply oneself with earnestness and practice it with vigor.
Zhenjing said to Prince Shu: "In daily life, exert effort in what is right; if it is not so, firmly cease from it.

One should not allow ease or difficulty to shift one's resolve. If you now turn your head away and disregard something because it is difficult, how do you know that tomorrow it will not be as difficult as it is today? (From *Risheng ji*).
This means that regarding the activities performed by ordinary people in their daily lives: those that accord with principle should be constantly practiced with diligent effort;
those that contravene principle are not right, and one should therefore firm up one's resolve and swiftly cease them.
In all matters, inquire only into whether they accord with principle or not, rather than debating the difficulty or ease of the task. Thus, one should readily change [what is wrong].
