As for their resolve, some who find today’s difficulties daunting simply turn their heads away and ignore them.
How can they know that when their goals are achieved and their tasks accomplished in the future, there may be nothing more difficult than what they face today?
A few words of this kind constitute a swift path to the ranks of the sages and worthies; truly, they are difficult for people to practice. We must apply ourselves with fierce diligence.
It is appropriate to act for their sake.
This chapter reveals the profound sincerity with which our predecessors esteemed the Dharma and cherished others.
When Zhenjing heard that a man of the Way in a certain region had passed away, he sighed with deep compassion until his tears fell. At that time—

When Zhantang was serving as an attendant, he remarked, "All things born between heaven and earth possess a single form and substance; that they wither, die, and become decayed and infested seems unavoidable.
Why then do you take such pains to injure yourself? Zhenjing replied, "The flourishing of the Dharma depends on those of virtue to sustain it.
Now that they have all passed away, the monasteries are in decline; by this one may make an augury. (Record of Daily Immersion)

When Master Zhenjing heard that a man of virtue and wisdom in a certain region had passed away—"passed away" meaning that what once existed has suddenly vanished—he was moved with deep compassion and felt profound grief.
He sighed and lamented until he wept; "weeping" refers to tears flowing from the eyes, while "tears" (tid) refers to the flow from the nose.
At that time, Zantang served as his attendant. This took place at Letan in Longxing Prefecture. Wen Zhun.
Chan Master [Xing] was the son of the Liang family of Xingyuan Prefecture. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhenjing Wen and belonged to the thirteenth generation under Mount Heng.
Seeing his master’s excessive grief and lamentation, he said: "When ordinary people are born between heaven and earth, after the first sign has manifested, they receive this physical form.
'Sign' carries the meaning of manifesting form; yet it is withered, aged, subject to death, and perishable."
When damage is being inflicted by woodworms, none can escape it in advance. How could you, O Venerable One, find it so painful to wound yourself?
The Master replied, "The flourishing of the Dharma depends entirely upon virtuous teachers who are able to revitalize it."
It is said that when the man of the Way exists, the Dharma exists; when the man of virtue perishes, the Dharma perishes. Today, those who possess both virtue and the Way have all passed away.
Beneath the groves of monasteries, who is capable of reviving it? From this day forward, it will surely decline and fall into ruin.
△ This sincerity of cherishing the person and valuing the Dharma is inherent within the nature and constitution of sages and worthies; it is not something artificially produced.
The mind is what causes it; when the heart grieves over the decline of the Dharma, how can one endure weeping?
This chapter instructs people to sever heterodox studies and seek wondrous enlightenment, governing the mind to attend to the fundamental.
When Zen Master Zhantang Zhun first visited Zhenjing, he would often read by the light of a lamp inside his mosquito netting. Zhenjing rebuked him, saying:
"The purpose of a student is to seek the cultivation of the mind. If one studies extensively yet fails to cultivate the mind, what benefit is there in such study?"
How much more so regarding the hundred schools of heterodox learning, as lofty as mountains and as deep as the ocean—how could you possibly exhaust them all?
This section teaches the severance of heterodox learning. It refers to when Master Zhantang first attended upon Chan Master Zhenjing;
before he had attained entry into the principle, he once lit a lamp inside his curtains to read. When Zhenjing saw this, he immediately rebuked him, saying: "What..."

This refers to the student. It is not merely a matter of devoting oneself to the study of texts in order to seek [truth] externally. One must instead still all conceptualizations to cultivate the mind.
If the mind is not cultivated, then the very foundation is not established; even if one studies much, it is all like plucking leaves and seeking branches—what benefit is there?
This is especially true for the heterodox teachings of the various masters and the hundred schools. As for these "various masters," they are like...

As for the various schools of thought, such as those of Laozi, Zhuangzi, Xunzi, and Mozi, and the heterodox scholars, such as Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan, Ou-yang Hsiu, and Su Shih—each has its own particular tenets.
Like the height of mountains or the depth of the ocean, how could you possibly exhaustively investigate them all?

Now, to abandon the root and pursue the branches is like using the lowly to serve the noble; I fear it will hinder your progress on the path. You must simply cut off all external conditions and seek wondrous awakening.
When you look back upon this another day, it will be like pushing a door into a mortar—it will not be difficult.
At this juncture, you must seek wondrous awakening. To study in such a manner as you are now is precisely what is called "discarding the root to pursue the branches.
It is like a lowly person turning around to employ a noble one; it is an inversion that is improper according to principle. In truth, it hinders your spiritual practice.
From this point forward, you must strictly block off all discriminative and delusive conditions. You must...

One should single-mindedly seek wondrous enlightenment. If one were to achieve a sudden, expansive awakening all at once, then reading the classics and histories would be like pushing open a door to enter a mortar;
one may open and close it as one pleases, for it would no longer be difficult.
At that moment, Zhantang cast aside his habitual studies and focused single-mindedly on Chan meditation.

One day, hearing a monk reciting Zhuge Kongming’s “Memorial on Sending Out the Army,” he attained sudden enlightenment; his mental obstructions were instantly dissolved, and his eloquence became unimpeded.
Among his contemporaries, few could surpass him.
This section concerns the instruction on exclusive practice. Regarding the "immediate" instruction heard from Zhantang: it refers to this very day, under the present teaching and admonition.
One should immediately set aside all matters previously studied and practiced. "Setting aside" means to eliminate them. "Exclusive focus" is like pouring water from one vessel into another;
through meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), one ensures the mind does not wander. One day, while listening to a monk reciting the words of Zhuge Kongming:

The Memorial on Sending the Army. Zhuge Wuhou, having received the charge of regency to assist the Later Emperor (Liu Shan), subdued Meng Huo by capturing him seven times and thereby stabilized the South.
He then set out to lead an army against Wei. On the eve of his departure, he left this memorial to the Later Emperor, which states:

"The founding emperor began his enterprise, but before it was half completed, he passed away midway," and so forth, concluding with: "In the palace and in the government offices, let all be treated as one body."
The Master then attained sudden and complete enlightenment. All the knots and stagnations that had long accumulated within his breast were instantly dissolved like melting ice.
From this point forward, his eloquence became unimpeded. Among his peers, few could surpass him in the depth of their realization or the subtlety of their spiritual insight.
△ Cultivating the mind is the ultimate path for both the mundane and the transcendent worlds.
Study: To study extensively without governing the mind is what is called "counting sand"—it is merely exhausting and ultimately of no benefit.
Upon reaching this point in the reading, one then understands that a fine horse moves at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow; once it has reached its destination, it is not difficult.
This chapter teaches that the abbot should share in the likes and dislikes of the assembly; this accords with the principle of the Great Center and Ultimate Rectitude.
Zhantang said: "Those who possess virtue and wisdom delight in the assembly; those who lack virtue and wisdom delight in themselves. To delight in the assembly..."
That which endures is long; that which delights in the body perishes.
This section clarifies that there must be a proper object for one's delight. That is to say, any person who possesses virtue and the Way has no private interest in their own self.
When one possesses joy oneself, one shares that joy with the multitude. Those who lack virtue and morality seek only their own peace and happiness, disregarding the masses.
They fail to realize that for those who share joy with the multitude, that joy is long-lasting;
whereas for those who seek joy for themselves alone, such joy is meager and will soon perish.
Nowadays, those who hold the position of abbot often treat the assembly with favoritism and animosity; consequently, the multitude rejects them.
It is rare to find one who seeks out their virtues while recognizing their faults, or who recognizes their faults while appreciating their virtues. Therefore it is said:

"To share the same sorrows and joys as the multitude, and to share the same likes and dislikes, is righteousness (*yi*). Wherever righteousness resides, whom in the world would not turn toward it? (From *Ershi Lai Ke Zhuiyou Ji*).
This section teaches the preservation of the great meaning. Nowadays, those who are called *chujū* (abbot) often approach the assembly with their own likes and dislikes;
they do not share the same sentiments as the community, and thus are brushed aside and fail to take office.
Therefore, one must seek someone of public mind and upright courage. One must discern human relations carefully: if I am already well-regarded, why would the multitude [resist]?
Therefore, they turn back to evil. Since I am already evil, how could the multitude consequently turn to goodness? There must surely be a reason for this.
To maintain such a principle is rare in the world. As the tradition says: "To do what the good man hates, and to do what the evil man loves."

Therefore, to violate the nature of others will inevitably bring calamity upon oneself. "To violate" means to act contrary to it. Thus it is said: cold and heat, hunger and thirst—these are what all people equally suffer;
ease, leisure, satiety, and warmth—these are what all people equally enjoy; the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness—these are what all people equally love;
injury, mutilation, and exploitation—these are what all people equally hate. Regarding these four categories, the one who maintains the Dharma must be able to...

To be the same as the multitude is righteousness (*yi*). When righteousness is present, all excellences are present. Who in the world would not turn toward him with reverence? One must contemplate the character "righteousness" (*yi*) with deep attention;

it must not be read lightly or carelessly. For one who attains this, there is neither "being" nor "non-being. △ The character "righteousness" (*yi*) should be contemplated with profound reflection; it must not be read with negligence. One who attains this is neither in existence nor non-existence.

This chapter speaks of those who uphold the Dharma; its essence lies in adaptability and transformation. If one does not know how to transform and adapt, they will not even have leisure to save themselves, let alone be of benefit to others.

Zantang said: "The Way is the true authority of antiquity and the present. One who excels at propagating the Way must rely on adaptability and transformation. If one does not know how to transform..."
Those who cling to the literal teachings and become mired in appearances and attachments have all failed to comprehend the principle of skillful means (*upāya*).
This section teaches people to master such means and penetrate these transformations; it asserts that the Way is the single great instrument of authority throughout the past and the present.
It governs all things and establishes the distinction between the holy and the ordinary; it is the dharma that is universally interfused and unimpeded.

This is not a matter of resorting to desperate measures like treating a dead horse with medicine. If one is skilled in propagating this Way, one will naturally be able to master expedient means and adapt to changing circumstances.
This is what is meant by being "brilliant on all eight sides" and "penetrating through the four directions. This arises from having entered deeply into the principle.

Suppose one does not know how to adapt and transform, but instead clings rigidly to words, adheres to the scriptures, lingers in names and forms, and becomes mired in the consciousness and emotions—*ni* meaning the utmost exhaustion.
To single-mindedly handle things as if they were dead methods, what joy can there possibly be?
Therefore, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Zhaozhou replied, "I am making a cotton shirt in Qingzhou that weighs seven catties.
This shows that one need not be ignorant of expedient means to be able to respond with such eloquence as this.
This section cites ancient precedents to demonstrate the application of skillful means (*upāya*). Consider the following: A monk asked Zhaozhou, “All phenomena return to the One;
where does the One return? Zhaozhou replied, “I was making a cotton robe in Qingzhou that weighed seven *jin*.
Zhaozhou Guanyuan Congshen Chan Master was the son of the Hao family of Caozhou and succeeded Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan. Nan...

Regarding the two generations under Mount [Wutai]: if the ancients had not mastered the application of expedient means and the penetration of change, how could they have been capable of such responsive exchanges?
To respond to the host is called *chou*; to respond to the guest is called *cuo*.
The Sage said: "The deep valley is impartial, and thus it produces this resonance. When a great bell is suspended on its frame, there is no strike that does not elicit a response.

From this we know that the superior man of universal attainment, intending to return to the ordinary and harmonize with the Dao, does not cling to a single state but responds to change (Letter to Li Shanglao).

This section concludes by demonstrating that being free from partiality enables one to respond with adaptability. The "Sage" refers to Laozi, who said: "The deep valley is impartial, and thus it produces this resonance.
This means that within a deep and secluded rocky valley, if someone shouts loudly, there is a loud response; if they shout softly, there is a soft response.
This occurs because, being devoid of a mind of self and other, it responds in such a manner. It is also like a great bell.
The *jù* (supporting frame) responds to every strike without fail. The *jù* is a divine beast of the heavens with the head of a deer and the body of a dragon.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is the crossbar of a bell or drum stand; the horizontal beam is called the *xiǔ*, while the vertical posts are called the *jù*. It is thus an instrument for striking the bell.
By this, one may know that for the superior man who has attained universal realization, even the most ordinary matters are each and every one in accord with the Ultimate Way.
What is called "picking it up with the hand as it comes" means that there is nothing that is not so.
It is ultimately not like those who fixate upon a single dharma and fail to understand how to apply it according to circumstances, yet claim their transformations and adaptations are unimpeded.

△ The realm of transformation and adaptation is ultimately not easy to reach; one must have no obstructions in the breast and no entanglements on the tongue before one can respond to sounds as they arise.
This is like merely speaking with one's mouth; it is entirely like a group of blind men feeling an elephant—they have no real insight at all.
This chapter teaches that when seeking a friend, one must seek someone superior to oneself; if the person is base and unworthy, there will be no benefit.

Zantang said: "When a student seeks a friend, it must be one who is worthy to serve as a teacher. In daily life, one should constantly maintain a sense of reverence and take them as a model in all actions, hoping for some benefit.
Even if their wisdom and insight are slightly superior to my own, they may still be followed to alert oneself to what has not yet been attained.
Should they happen to be similar to me, then it would be better not to have such a companion at all" (*Baofeng Shilu*).
That is to say, when a student seeks a friend, they must find one who can serve as a teacher and model for them.

Throughout the two periods of six hours each day, they should always maintain a sense of reverence; in every action, they must take that person as their standard, aspiring to derive benefit from them.
Furthermore, even if another’s intellectual power and insight are only slightly superior to one's own, it is appropriate to follow them. There is no fault in this.
Next. Why? To warn me against what I am incapable of. If, by some chance, I were to become the same as this, it would be better not to have been at all.
As an ancient worthy said: "In choosing a good friend, one must seek those who are mature; do not form an alliance with one who is inferior to yourself.
It is like water entering muddy soil; even if it were clear, it would still not be pure. This is precisely what that refers to.
It is said thus.
This chapter requires that people truly practice and realize its meaning; to strive for mere ornamentation is not appropriate.
Zantang said: "In the late autumn of the ancestral hall, it is naturally difficult to find those among the practitioners who are not frivolous and superficial. In the past...

Zhentru (Zhenru) dwells in the ocean of wisdom. He once remarked that when he was at Xiangshan and Daowu, although the assembly was not large, there were still several veteran monks who had practiced this Way.
Since coming here from Dayue, there have been no fewer than nine hundred monks, yet not even seventy-five of them understand my words.
By this, I know that attaining people does not depend on their great number. (From the *Shilu*).
"Ancestral Hall" (Zuting) refers to the gateway of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. "The late autumn" refers to a time when the Dharma is in decline.
It is said that among students of the "grove" (monastics), those who do not engage in clamorous, frivolous, or superficial matters during this period of decline are truly rare to find.
Formerly, when Chan Master Zhenru Zhe resided at Zhikai, he once said of himself:
When he resided at Daowu Monastery to the west of the Xiang River, although the assembly was not large, there were still several veteran practitioners who maintained this Way.
Since his relocation from Daguang Miaofa Chan Monastery to Zhihai, the number of monks has never been fewer than nine hundred;
among them, there have been no fewer than seventy-five whose tongues could grasp the point where my words land.
By this one may know: that for a person to attain [the Way], it depends solely on genuine cultivation and actual practice;
it certainly does not lie in the great number of followers. Although human nature is inherently endowed by birth, there are those who rise or fall according to the times.
How many are there who do not change with the times? One must understand that the intent of the ancients lay in substance, and not in...
In China, this chapter states that human sentiments have become shallow and insincere, making it most difficult to know them. Zantang said:

"Only through a person's conduct can one truly understand them; it cannot be accomplished by a single response or a single interrogation, for how could one possibly know them all? This is because [the mind] is in the mouth..."
Those with eloquent tongues may have arguments that are not yet entirely convincing; those whose speech is clumsy and stammering may have principles that are not yet fully exhausted.
Though one may exhaust their words, I fear one has not exhausted their principles; though one can subdue their mouths, I fear one has not subdued their hearts.
That people are difficult to know is the very affliction of the sages.
This section clarifies the difficulty of knowing others. It says: In this world, there is only one true way to know a person, and it is by no means easy.
One cannot fully understand another through a single response or a single interrogation. Why is this?
It is because there are those whose eloquence and debate are sharp; when one listens to their words, they seem worthy of praise, yet when it comes to their actual conduct...
Whether such words are true or false cannot yet be trusted. Furthermore, there is another kind of person whose speech is clumsy and stammering; "stammering" here means slow and dull.
Upon hearing their voice, it seems as though there is nothing worth listening to; yet when one investigates their underlying principles to the end, they prove difficult to exhaustively fathom.
Thus, regarding those who are dull and reticent, although one may exhaust their words, I fear one cannot exhaust their underlying principles;
regarding those with clever tongues, although one may subdue their mouths, I fear one cannot subdue their hearts.
This is why it is difficult to know others—a concern shared even by the sages.
How much more so for the monks of recent times, who, though intelligent, do not strive to understand human nature; their sight and hearing are mostly occupied with watching for every flaw.

They act in opposition to the community’s desires and deviate from the direction of the Way. They honor one another with deception and overstep one another with fraud, thereby causing the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—
It has become increasingly superficial and is nearly beyond remedy (in the *Reply to Lu Zhi*).
This section addresses the current maladies of the age. Furthermore, as for what the monks of recent times have heard and seen, they do not at all take it as their business to master human affairs;
instead, they view and listen to everything with a single flavor, mostly merely waiting for others’... [text truncated]
"Passing through a crevice. A "crevice" (koku) refers to a gap or fissure. This is why one's emotional desires conflict with those of the multitude and run counter to the direction of the Great Way.
That which is venerated and pursued in this age is nothing but a mind of deceit and unreality, and thoughts of ignorance, flattery, and fraud.
To "be shrouded in ignorance" means to be thus obscured. Such conduct causes the Buddhas and Patriarchs'... [teachings] to be lost.
The Way has gradually declined; it is perilous and beyond salvation. In recent times, human sentiments have mostly favored the frivolous and the ornate;
both conduct and speech lack gravity and substance. Thus, the difficulty of knowing people is not a phenomenon of the present age alone.
My wish for future generations is that they preserve and maintain this wholesome state of mind, so as to derive benefit from it.
This chapter teaches students how to rely upon the right person, so that they may maintain themselves without delusion and achieve true character.
Zantang said to Miaoxi: "In this age of the Semblance Dharma, monks mostly pursue external things while failing to clarify their inner minds; even if they possess..."
These practices are all not ultimate; they are made so because that which they rely upon is base and vulgar.

This refers to those who follow the teachings of this degenerate age. Such scholars, outwardly merely conform to external conditions and pursue various sounds and forms—*xùn* meaning to follow or comply—and inwardly do not seek for themselves the awakening and clarity of the nature and mind. Even if such people...
There are instances of grand undertakings, yet all are hollow and unsubstantial; they are truly not ultimate. Why is this?
It is because of the base, shallow, and vulgar nature of those upon whom one relies.
It is like a gadfly that stings an ox: it can fly and alight only for a few paces; yet if it clings to the tail of a fine horse, it immediately gains the ability to chase the wind and pursue the sun.
This is the excellence of relying upon another.
This section uses a metaphor to clarify that which is supported. For example, consider a fly that has alighted on the body of an ox;
though it exerts its own strength to fly upward, it travels no more than a few paces.

However, if it clings to the tail of a *jì*—a *jì* being a fine horse—it then manifests the capacity to follow the wind and pursue the sun. This is due to nothing other than the excellence of the support upon which it relies.
Therefore, a student must choose their dwelling carefully and seek out worthy scholars in their travels;

only then can they sever ties with the heterodox and deviant and draw near to the upright and correct, hearing true words. Formerly, the Venerable Fuyan Ya was always fond of Zhenru Zhe, admiring his noble character.
However, he did not know whom he relied upon. One day, he saw him [Zhenru] together with Danning Kuan, Jiangshan Yuan, and Cuishan Zhen.

They traveled together. [Cheng] was so delighted that he could not contain himself. At ease, he said to Zhe, "You, a great being among the 'dragon elephants' of the Dharma gates, have been able to follow him in his travels.
In the future, it will be you who shall uphold the Way when it is in decline and manifest the salvation of the Patriarchal Teachings;
this truly does not depend on my many instructions" (*Rishet Ji*).

This section clarifies the evidence for relying [on others]. From this, we know that those who study must choose their dwelling place with care when residing, and choose the people they associate with when traveling.

If one’s environment is virtuous and the people one encounters are excellent, one will then be able to sever the afflictions of private bias and partiality, thereby attaining proximity to the upright and center and hearing correct words. Formerly, Master Fǎ... of Zézhōu...
Chan Master Yan Liangya was the dharma successor of Chan Master Dongshan Shouchu. He belonged to the eighth generation below Qingyuan.
He always admired the bearing and spiritual disposition of Zhenru Zhe, which were truly worthy of esteem; however, he did not know whom Zhenru relied upon for guidance.
One day, he saw that [Zhenru] was with Chan Master Daoning Daokuan of Hongzhou, who was a successor of Shishuang Chuyuan.
The Master—Chan Master Zanyuan of Jiangshan—was also a successor of Shishuang, belonging to the eleventh generation under Nanyue.
When he traveled together with Chan Master Zhen of Cuoyan, "together" (xiejie) meaning they went as companions, Master Ya was filled with boundless joy.
On a day of leisurely tranquility, he said to Zhe, "All these great beings possess profound merit and wisdom; they are truly the great [treasures] within the Dharma gate."
One who possesses great power, like a dragon or an elephant—such a person as you, my son, has now been found for me to follow and associate with.
In days to come, it shall not depend upon my repeated instructions that you support the decline of our Way and manifest the salvation of the ancestral teachings.
△ To lose oneself among the unholy is to shatter all things like broken tiles; one must rely [on the right path].

This chapter teaches that students must harbor far-reaching and great aspirations; they must not conform to worldly customs or seek mere profit.
Zhandang said to Miaoxi: "In practicing Chan, one must recognize the necessity of having lofty and distant considerations, with a spirit and ambition that transcend the mundane. When speaking..."
In conducting one's affairs, maintain integrity toward others; do not yield to power or profit through deceitful compromise.
In this way, you will naturally not be swayed by the fashions or evaluations of your peers. (Recorded in the *Baofeng Jiwen*).
This means that a practitioner of Zen must first possess lofty insight and far-reaching deliberation; their will and spirit should both be exceptionally transcendent and far-reaching.
"Far-reaching" (*yuan*) implies vastness. In all matters of speech and action, one must always maintain sincerity and establish faith so as not to cause others to harbor doubts.
Furthermore, one must not succumb to power, nor greedily seek wealth and profit, nor act with mere expediency.
If such a thing as being "bent and humbled" can truly be so, it will naturally leave those among one's peers with no way to seize upon you, to paint a portrait of you, or to grope for your essence.
Naturally, you will not be like those others; you will be one who, according to the times, may rise or fall.
△ To follow worldly customs and pursue gain with a clouded mind leads one to fall into the ranks of the vulgar.
A human being.
This chapter shows that when ancient people spoke and acted, they invariably prioritized non-deception.
Zantang said: "In the past, I was with Lingyuan, attending upon Huaitang at Zhangjiang Temple. One day, Lingyuan and..."
The two monks entered the city and did not return until evening. Huitang then asked, "Where have you been today?
Lingyuan replied, "I just came from Daling."
This section directly recounts past events. It says that I once attended upon Master Huìtáng at Zhāngjiāng Temple together with Língyuán.
One day, Língyuán happened to enter the city with two monks and did not return until evening.
Huitang asked, "Where have you come from today? Lingyuan, feeling that entering the city for no particular reason was inconvenient, simply replied, "I have just come from Daling."
At that time, Sishin was standing by his side. He rebuked him in a stern voice, saying, "One who practices Chan seeking liberation from birth and death must first ensure their speech is truthful.
Elder Qing, how can you utter such falsehoods?"
This section clarifies that a true friend does not conceal the truth. At that time, Sīxin was standing nearby in attendance.
Unable to endure his falsehood, he shouted at him in a loud voice, saying, "The purpose of practicing Chan is precisely to transcend birth and death.
When speaking, one must first be sincere and honest. Brother Qing, how can you utter such false words? Sīxin was then [named] Long... [text ends].

Chan Master Wuxin of Huanglong in Xingfu was a native of the Huang family of Shaoyou Prefecture. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zuxin of Huanglong and belonged to the thirteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
Lingyuan’s face flushed with heat, and he did not dare to respond. From that time on, he no longer entered city walls and refrained from speaking recklessly.
I knew well that both Lingyuan and Sishi were vessels of great potential (from the *Rishenji*).
This section clearly shows that those who recognize their faults must reform them. Upon hearing Lingyuan’s reproach, Dajian’s face flushed with shame; he did not dare to offer further response.

From that time forward, he did not dare to enter city walls again—whereas the outer wall is called a "guo" (enclosure)—nor did he dare to utter false words. I knew for certain that Lingyuan would surely reform his errors, and that Sishin was upright and unbending. Thus it is said: [The text continues with a verse:

*The great man of the world is truly rare;* *He does not seek fame through the marketplace.* *If one has already attained the Way,* *Why should one fear the passing years?* *The sun and moon are the eyes of heaven;* *The wind and rain are the breath of earth.* *If you can see this principle,* *Then you will know the source of the Way.* I have long known that Lingyuan would certainly amend his mistakes, and that Sishin remained steadfast and unyielding. Like... [the text ends].
These two individuals were truly excellent vessels. "Excellent" means beautiful and refined.
The ancients maintained their minds such that there was not even a hair’s breadth of deception or stinginess herein. Sīcín held his friend accountable with a heart free from self-deception;
Linyuans amended his faults with a heart free from self-stinginess. Each attained what is correct. Let students examine this carefully.
This chapter explains that the ancients were tireless in their pursuit of learning; it all arose from their innate nature (*tianzhen*), rather than through forced effort.
Zhantang said, "Lingyuan was fond of reading the classics and histories, never resting even for meals or sleep; he would only stop when he had mastered them by heart.
Huìtáng therefore rebuked him, to which Lingyuan replied, "I have heard that those who exert great effort will achieve far-reaching success."
This section concerns the profundity of the merit of dedicated study. Master Zhantang cited the exemplary learning of Chan Master Lingyuan to encourage future generations.
*Yue* means to read; *jing* refers to all the sutras and scriptures; *shi* refers to all historical records and administrative archives;

*shi* (food) refers to eating and drinking; *xi* (rest) refers to sleeping and repose. This means that Lingyuan was so devoted to learning that even during his meals and sleep— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
While sleeping, he never rested for even a moment. Whenever he read, he would not stop until he had mastered the text through recitation from memory.
Huìtáng scolded him, saying that one should not study with such bitter intensity.

Línyuán replied, "I have heard that for all matters, those who exert great effort will achieve far-reaching results. It is said in the teachings: 'Be courageous and diligent; be self-reliant and tireless.'"
For such a person, samādhi will be easily accomplished, the further shore easily reached, and perfected merit will also be attained forever.
Thus, Imperial Historian Huang Lu-zhi said: "My brother Qing loves learning as one who suffers from hunger and thirst craves food and drink;
he regards worldly gain and ostentation as if they were foul and loathsome. This is the spontaneous expression of his sincere heart, not merely something incidental" (*Zhu-wei ji*).
This section reveals the fundamental endowment of one's nature. The Imperial Historian Huang, whose given name was Tingjian and courtesy name Lu-zhi, was styled the Layman Shangu.
He received the Dharma from Chan Master Zuxin of Huanglong. Thus, he once said of Master Lingyuan:
"My elder brother Qing is fond of learning, like one who is hungry and thirsty and longs for food and drink; yet he views worldly gain, profit, and the confusion of superficial splendor as..."
This matter is like a foul odor; it is simply that his innate nature is so profoundly sincere that it manifests naturally in this way—it is not something achieved through forced effort.

Dare you say you can recite it from memory? Strive! Strive!

This chapter teaches people how to uphold the Dharma; its essential principle is to maintain a relaxed and moderate middle way.
When Master Lingyuan Qing resided at Taiping in Shuzhou, he observed that every time Foyan presided over the assembly, he was thorough and meticulous, rarely failing in his duties.
Consequently, Lingyuan asked him what his secret was. Foyan replied: "When managing affairs, it is better to err on the side of leniency than to err on the side of haste. It is better...
Do not neglect the concise; do not lose the detailed. If one is too hasty, there can be no salvation; if one is too detailed, there is no room for action.
One should maintain the Middle Way and treat others with patience and composure. This may serve as the method for managing the affairs of a community. (Supplementary Notes)
When Master Qing resided at Taiping, he frequently visited Master Fuyan. Whenever Fuyan presided over the assembly, Qing attended to all matters;
there was nothing he did not manage with thoroughness, and nothing he handled that was not meticulous, never failing to act in accordance with what was appropriate for the occasion.

Thereupon, he asked for the essential meaning of this. Fuyan replied: "In general, regarding any undertaking one performs, how can one guarantee that it will be entirely free of error? It is better to err through laxity than through haste;
it is better to err through brevity than through excessive detail. For if a matter is lost through haste, it cannot be recovered."

This is because [the former] is insufficient and [the latter] errs in excessive detail, leaving no room for others. One should simply maintain the Middle Way and treat them with the patience of providing food;
in this way, it will likely be appropriate. This may then serve as the standard for conducting affairs when presiding over a multitude.
△ The ancients laid bare their hearts and exposed their livers; their sincerity was truly no less than that of parents instructing their children.
"It is better to be lax than hasty; it is better to be concise than meticulous. These two statements exhaust the way of establishing one's character and conducting oneself in the world.
This chapter concerns the emergence and withdrawal of a practitioner of the Way; such timing exists of its own accord, and one should not force it.
Lingyuan said to Master Changling Zhuo, "The Way’s manifestation surely has its own appointed time.
In the past, when Ciming let his mind roam freely amidst the Jing and Chu regions, he endured shame and bore impurity; those who saw him disregarded him, yet Ciming merely smiled.
When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied: 'When a city of ten thousand chariots comes into contact with mere rubble, I know well in advance that it will not prevail.'"
Tianning Monastery in Tokyo. Chan Master Chánglíng Shǒuzhuó succeeded Chan Master Língyuán Qīng.
He was the fourteenth generation descendant of Nanyue. This section clarifies nurturing the Way while awaiting the opportune time.

It means that when a practitioner of the Way wishes to practice what they have attained, it is not done by force; there must be its proper time. When the time arrives, the principle manifests of itself.
This is to manifest [the truth]. In the past, Master Ciming let his mind roam freely throughout the Jing and Chu regions.

"Letting his mind roam freely" does not mean that he abandoned himself to dissipation; rather, because the time had not yet arrived, he allowed his outward conduct to appear unrestrained amidst the crowds.
Although he encountered many instances of humiliation and defilement, he simply contained and endured them all. Often, when people saw him acting in this manner, they...
He let his physical form go loose and treated him with much contempt. Ciming merely smiled and stopped.
Someone asked, "He treats you with such contempt; why do you instead smile? He replied, "When a city’s worth of jade strikes against a pebble, I certainly know it will not prevail.
(Lì means a small stone. Zhao possessed the Bianhe Jade. King Zhao of Qin wished to [exchange it]...
He traded it for twelve connected cities. Zhao sent Xiangru to deliver it to Qin.
Upon observing King Qin, Xiangru saw that he possessed only a desire for the jade disc and lacked any intention to cede the cities. He then feigned a pretext, saying, "The jade has a flaw;
please allow me to show it to you. When the king handed the jade to Xiangru, he turned back toward the pillar and stood there with his hair bristling in rage as it struck his crown.
He said, "Your servant has heard that even among commoners who have formed a bond of friendship, they cannot bear to deceive one another; how much less so in the case of a great state?

If Your Majesty is in such haste for my person, then let my head and this jade be smashed together against this pillar. The King, fearing he would smash the jade, sent men to support Xiangru and raise him up.
After he beheld the divine cauldron, his reputation spread throughout the monastic forests, and he ultimately gave rise to the Way of Linji. Alas!
The Way and its timing—how could these possibly be forced? (Bietie)
This section clarifies how transformation is accomplished when the time has arrived.

After meeting Shendǐng [Shéndìng] Hóngxīn, the Zen Master of Shendǐng in Tánzhōu—a native of Yí County in Xiāngshuǐ—who was a dharma heir of Shǒushān Niàn Chánshī and belonged to the ninth generation under Nányuè—Hóngxīn wore a single robe throughout his life to endure both cold and heat.
Later, he lived in seclusion at Mount Héng. Once, a man of noble rank came to the mountain for recreation and saw him.
The Master’s demeanor was serene and tranquil; he possessed nothing beyond a single almsbowl. He was subsequently invited to reside at Shendingsi, where for ten years he lived in austere simplicity.

There was not even a pint of rice in his quarters; each day he would collect a mere cup of food. A single bed of withered wood served as his Dharma seat, surrounded by a small number of remaining monks who never wavered in their devotion from beginning to end.
Later, his school’s influence flourished greatly, and he became a figure of supreme authority in his time. His disciples’ spirits...
He had swallowed all the quarters [of the world]. At that time, Ciming went to pay his respects; his hair was long and uncut, he wore tattered clothes, and he spoke with a Chu accent.
He announced his arrival, calling himself a "Dharma-nephew," which caused the entire assembly to laugh loudly. Foding sent a youth to ask, "Whose successor is this elder?
Ciming looked up at the roof and said, "I have come directly from seeing Fenyang in person. Foding then stepped out leaning on his staff; upon seeing him, he was delighted and asked, "Fen..."
In the province, there was a master from Xihe named Foshi. Ming pointed directly at him and shouted, "The house is collapsing!
The youth fled backward; Foding looked back in startled alarm. Ming sat down on the ground and showed him his single sandal.
Foding, being old, forgot what he had asked and also lost sight of where Ming was. Ming slowly rose, adjusted his robes, and as he walked away, spoke, saying, "I see you."
His appearance did not match his reputation. He then departed, and although Ciming sent someone to pursue him, it was impossible. [Ciming] sighed, saying, "Is there such a person as this in Fenzhou?
From that time on, Ciming’s excellent reputation spread throughout the monastic community (*conglin*), and he revitalized the Way of Linji.
Alas! These two characters refer to Lingyuan’s sigh regarding those who were compelled to enter the world [of teaching]; it means that although the Way—
It is complete. But the time has not yet arrived; what benefit is there in forcing it? △ The realization of the Way depends on oneself, but the practice of the Way depends solely on the timing.
If the time does not arrive, how can one practice that Way? As the saying goes: "Without the spring breeze, the flowers will not bloom."
This is limited by the timing [of the situation].
This chapter teaches people to prevent calamities through principle during times of leisure; if it becomes urgent, it cannot be saved.
Linyuan said to Historian Huang: "The ancients said: 'To carry fire and place it beneath a stack of firewood, and then go to sleep.'"

Above it, the fire has not yet reached it, so one remains secure; this truly serves as a metaphor for the pivot between safety and peril, and the principle of life and death, as clear as the bright sun and leaving no space for even a hair’s breadth.
This section first clarifies how the lack of wisdom leads to the failure to prevent calamities. Regarding the ancients:

in the sixth year of Emperor Wen’s reign (the *dingmao* year), Liu Chang, the Prince of Huainan, plotted a rebellion. He was demoted and confined in Shu Commandery, where he died of indignation and refusing to eat.

Jia Yi, Grand Tutor to the Prince of Liang, submitted a memorial stating: "I have privately considered the current situation, and there are matters that must be regarded as reasons for bitter lamentation."
First, there are two matters that move one to shed tears; second, there are six matters that move one to long-drawn sighs.

As for other instances where reason is subverted and the Way is harmed, it would be difficult to enumerate them all in detail. Those who offer their words all claim that the empire is already at peace and well-ordered.
I alone believe this is not yet the case. To say it is peaceful and well-ordered is either foolishness or flattery; neither is correct.

This is truly one who understands the nature of order and chaos. To carry fire and place it beneath a pile of firewood, then sleep upon it—though the fire has not yet ignited, one nonetheless considers oneself secure.
How does the current situation differ from this? The fundamental and the derivative are inverted; the beginning and the end are disordered.
The state institutions are in turmoil, lacking any semblance of order. Your Majesty cannot fail to [recognize this].
I would like to request that Your Majesty allow me to enumerate these matters in detail before you, so that I may present strategies for securing peace and order; may you examine them with care.
Master, I believe these words truly serve as an analogy for the pivotal moments of human security and peril, and the principles of life and death.
They are as clear as the bright sun shining in the sky; there is not even room for a hair’s breadth of ambiguity or obscurity here.
When a person dwells in ordinary leisure and quietude, they rarely give thought to birth and death or calamity and misfortune.
Yet, when an unforeseen event suddenly occurs, they only then stamp their feet and wring their hands in an attempt to save themselves; in the end, they can never succeed in doing so. (Bietie)
This section is intended as a self-exhortation during the present time.

I observe that when people are in their ordinary, leisurely lives, they never once give thought to death, birth, or calamity; they are just like those who sleep soundly atop a pile of firewood, feeling no fear.
Yet, once a disaster suddenly and unexpectedly arises, it is like [the fire consuming] that which has been piled up...
The fire has already risen from beneath the fuel; it is only now that one finally stamps one's feet and wrings one's hands.
"Wrings one's hands" means to beat one's breast, hoping to save [the situation], yet in the end it cannot be recovered.
△ How many people nowadays can truly regard birth-and-death and calamity as matters of concern? Those who wring their hands in pursuit [of this truth] are infinite.
This passage shows that the ancients took it as their own responsibility to propagate the Way in every thought-moment; this was the true mind of the patriarchs.
Lingyuan said to Fojian: "Whenever I received a letter from my elder brother, Master Dongshan, he never spoke of worldly matters;
he only earnestly exhorted me to propagate the Way regardless of my own life and to guide and assist future generations."

This section clarifies that the ancient masters' aspirations were centered on the Way. It is said that whenever they received letters from their elder brother, the Fifth Patriarch, they never spoke of worldly matters therein.

Their earnestness consisted solely of instruction and admonition—teaching people to forget their own bodies in order to propagate the Way, and merely to guide and attract the younger generation while supporting and assisting future descendants.
I recently received a letter stating that the various estates have suffered damage from drought. I do not worry about these at all; I only worry that the Chan community lacks eyes.
This summer, there were over a hundred people in the meditation hall discussing the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, yet not a single person understood it.
This is what I truly worry about.
This section shows how the wise person relieves others in times of urgency. I recently received a letter stating:

"Although this year's various manors have suffered from drought damage, I do not worry about it at all. I only worry that practitioners lack the eye of the Way. This summer, there were over a hundred people in the mountains;
in their meditation rooms, they raised the koan, 'Why does a dog have no Buddha-nature? yet not a single one [attained realization]."
People will surely understand this; it is truly something to be concerned about.

How profound these words are! They concern the worry that the monastery’s affairs may not be managed properly, the fear of being censured by government officials, and the anxiety that one's reputation and status may fail to flourish.
To fear that one's followers are not numerous is indeed a difference as vast as heaven and earth.
This section refers to the distinct concerns of ordinary people: those who worry about various administrative matters in the monastery not being handled properly;
those who fear the resentment and reprimands of government officials; and those who dread that their reputation and status will not be widely proclaimed. I fear that...
When compared with those whose retinues are not so flourishing, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
Whenever I reflect on these words of truth, how could I ever hear them again? My nephew is the legitimate heir;
if he can truly revitalize our family tradition, he shall fulfill the hopes of our entire clan. This is my earnest prayer. (From the *Daily Record of Attendant Xian*)
This section is an exhortation to practice this Way with diligence. I have often reflected upon these words, which are so true and to my heart’s content;
how could I ever hear them again today? My nephew is the legitimate son of my elder brother;
he will surely exert his utmost efforts to uphold our family tradition. Now, there is nothing else that the members of our own school hope for, but you alone.
This is all. You must comfort those who look to you as their kinsmen; this is what I urge with the utmost earnestness and pray for.
△ This segment of concern for others is truly unfathomable.
This chapter states that all affairs are accomplished through accumulation; one must apply oneself with profound diligence. Lingyuan said:
"In grinding and polishing, one does not see any diminution, yet eventually it is exhausted. In planting trees and nurturing them, one does not see any increase, yet eventually they become large.
In accumulating virtue and heaping up good deeds, one is not conscious of their goodness, yet eventually they are put to use. To abandon [this process]...
To act contrary to principle is to turn one's back on righteousness; unaware of its evil, one may perish at any time.

When a student weighs these matters with mature deliberation and puts them into practice, they will become a great vessel and spread a fine reputation. This is the Way that remains unchanged through antiquity and the present.
*Mò* (mó) means to grind with a stone. *Lǒng* (lóng) means to grind. *Zhǐ* (zhǐ) refers to using a whetstone to grind an object. *Lì* (lì) refers to a whetstone.
"Grinding with a whetstone" (*módǐ*) thus means using a stone to grind an object. "Grinding and sharpening" (*lǒnglì*) means grinding an object upon a stone.

Lingyuan wishes for people to understand the meaning of what is accomplished through accumulation; he says it is like the relationship between a millstone and the grinding stone—accumulating [grains].
As months accumulate into years, although one does not perceive any diminution, there comes a time when they are exhausted without one's noticing it.
It is like planting trees or cultivating melons and fruits; during the intervening period, one sees no increase, yet at times they become large.
One must know that the accumulation of virtue and the cultivation of conduct by a person is likewise so: though within each day one may not perceive it, [it continues to grow].

"Good. There are times when it is employed. As for those who abandon righteousness and turn their backs on principle, although they may not realize their own wickedness, there are times when they perish.
This entire passage appears in the "Zhengjian" (Counseling) chapter of the *Shuoyuan*.

If students can indeed reflect deeply upon these words, they will understand that good cannot be left uncultivated because it is slight, and evil cannot be left unchecked because it is slight. Relying [on this],...
If one acts accordingly, one will surely become a vessel of great achievement and spread a glorious reputation;
this is the immutable orthodox discourse of both ancient and modern times. Although the realms of sages and worthies are inconceivable, they too are attained through gradual accumulation.
This chapter teaches the maintenance of the Dharma. To eliminate private interests and expand one’s capacity is its essential point.
Lingyuan said to Master Gu: "Calamity and fortune depend on one another; good and ill share the same realm. Since these are summoned by oneself, how can one not reflect upon this?
One might focus solely on one's own likes and dislikes while being narrow in tolerance, or squander resources through private desires."
To follow what people desire is in no way an urgent matter for the maintenance of the institution;
it is truly the gradual onset of license and the fundamental source of calamity and harm. (Note)
Chan Master Huigu was a successor of Chan Master Lingyuan Qing and belonged to the fourteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
He maintained that human fortune and misfortune fundamentally depend upon one another, and that auspiciousness and calamity likewise share the same locus;

in all cases, these are brought about by the actions of the individual themselves. How can one not contemplate this minutely within the flow of time? Why say they are "brought about by oneself"? It is said: perhaps...
To focus exclusively on one's own likes and dislikes, resulting in a narrow and constricted mind that lacks the capacity for magnanimity;
or to indulge one’s private whims, wasting resources without cause while merely complying with the desires of others—
such behaviors are not the urgent duties of an abbot, but are rather the origins of unrestrained self-indulgence, which will surely lead to calamity.
This is the foundation and source of harm. △ A person with a private mind and narrow capacity is fundamentally not of the caliber to serve as an abbot.
If such a person is appointed, it will be difficult to ensure there will be no trouble.

This chapter instructs people that while enjoying peace, one must not forget danger; while experiencing order, one must not forget chaos. This is the great sovereign principle for distancing oneself from calamity and giving rise to fortune.
Lingyuan said to Master Yichuan, "Calamity can give rise to fortune, and fortune can give rise to calamity; calamity arises from within fortune."
As for those who, during times of peril and crisis, are earnest in their desire for peace and profound in their quest for the truth, they are thus able to be reverent, fearful, and conscientious;

therefore, it is fitting that blessings arise for them. As for those who, during times of security and prosperity, indulge their extravagant desires and give rein to their arrogance and indolence, becoming especially prone to negligence, contempt, and insolence; therefore, it is fitting that calamity arises for them.
This section clarifies that fortune and misfortune are experienced solely by oneself. Cheng Yi (styled Zhengshu, known as Yichuan) was a native of Henan.
He sought the Way from Chan Master Lingyuan, who said to Mr. Yichuan:
"Although calamity is an undesirable matter, it can actually give rise to blessings; although blessing is a state of joy,"

Yet it is certain that calamity will arise. Why is this? It is because when a person dwells in a time of disaster and peril, situated in a state where nothing is as they wish, they focus their efforts on seeking the means for peace and happiness, and deeply investigate the principles of liberation.
Consequently, through their profound awe and reverent caution, they remain humble and vigilant in all matters.
With wings spread, one does not cease for even a single breath; thus, merit gradually arises from this. As for how merit can give rise to calamity:
it is because when a person dwells in a time of peace and security, all things accord with their heart’s desires.

They indulge in luxury and sensual pleasures, and give full rein to arrogance, haughtiness, and negligence. Consequently, they become frequently heedless of their duties and treat others with contempt and insolence. Therefore—
Calamities will arrive from this point on without end.
The Sage said: "Many hardships fulfill one's aspirations; an absence of hardship brings about the ruin of one's person. Attainment is the beginning of loss; loss is the principle of attainment.
Thus we know that fortune cannot be repeatedly sought through luck, and gain cannot be constantly coveted. One dwells in fortune...
If one anticipates calamity, their fortune can be preserved; if one perceives gain while anticipating its loss, that gain will surely be attained.
Therefore, the gentleman remains mindful of danger even in security, and mindful of disorder even amidst order. (Biqie)
This section clarifies that gain and loss are known only by oneself. The "Sage" refers to Laozi. The "Warning to the World" chapter states:
"Through many hardships one fulfills one's will; without hardship one loses one's person. Where there is gain, there is loss;
therefore, gain is the very root of loss, and loss is again the principle of gain. From this it is known that since ordinary people reside [in the world]...
Regarding merit, one must know contentment; one must not repeatedly seek by chance. "Repeatedly" means frequently. "Seeking by chance" (*jiao*) means to seek what should not be sought;
"gaining by chance" (*xing*) means to obtain what should not be obtained. Once something has been obtained, it is appropriate to know when to stop.
One must not constantly harbor covetous expectations. To "covet" means to hope for and desire to obtain.
If, while dwelling in a time of fortune, one can anticipate misfortune, then that fortune will certainly be preserved. When seeing gain, one is then able to anticipate loss.
Thus, their attainment will surely reach its ultimate fulfillment. For this reason, those who act as gentlemen, while dwelling in security, must never dare to forget danger;
while in a state of order, they must never dare to forget chaos. This is what constitutes true attainment. [This teaches you to observe closely the origins of calamity and fortune;
it is not something placed there by another. To dwell in security and order without forgetting danger and chaos—this is the highest attainment.]
The Illuminating Instructions on Power.
This chapter teaches people to immediately forget the illumination and realize the truth, so that they do not give rise to a mind of arising and ceasing.
Lingsuan said to Master Yichuan: "People may loathe their footprints and fear their shadows, yet they turn their backs [on the source]."
As for one who runs, the more urgently they run, the more numerous their tracks become, and the faster their shadow moves;

it is better to go into the shade and stop, so that the shadow will naturally vanish and the tracks will naturally cease. If you understand this clearly in your daily life, you may advance toward this Way while sitting still. (Note)

The actions one performs are like footprints; the arising of a mind subject to birth and extinction is like a shadow. Running away from them is like abandoning [the source] and forgetting to return to the truth.

Resorting to the aggregates is like immediately forgetting the brightness of the truth—what is called "boiling the broth to stop the bubbling" is not as effective as "removing the firewood from the bottom of the cauldron."
Now, if one wishes for others not to hear, there is nothing better than remaining silent; if one wishes for others not to know, there is nothing better than non-action (*wuwei*).
Thus we know that footprints arise from thought and shadows follow the body. If one cuts off divergent thoughts, delusive traces will naturally vanish;

if one stills the illusory substance, empty reflections will likewise perish. Let the student simply understand how to turn the light back upon themselves and return to the realm to contemplate the mind; then the Dharma—
When the eye is clear, the shadows of karma naturally vanish; when the true body manifests, the traces of dust naturally cease.
If this is so, one will not be stalled at the provisional city but will proceed directly to the precious destination.
If you clarify this in your daily life, you shall attain this Way within a single sitting. △ Regarding "stopping amidst the aggregates," how do you understand it from your own perspective? If...
If you understand this clearly, then you may advance in this Way; otherwise, you will mostly be making your living in a ghost cave.
This chapter teaches people to act according to their own capacity and not to overextend themselves.
Lingyuan said: "Among those who occupy the position of abbot, few are able to see it through to the end.

This is because their merit and virtue are shallow, their capacity and judgment are narrow, and their learning and experience are vulgar; furthermore, they are unable to follow what is good and pursue what is righteous to broaden themselves, which leads to such an outcome" (from the *Rilü*).

This means that those who maintain the Dharma are those who shoulder the heavy responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If one’s strength is small yet the burden is great, they will for the most part be unable to fulfill it perfectly.

Why is this? It is because their merit and virtue are shallow, and furthermore, their aspirations and understanding are not broad, their capacity for judgment is not expansive, and all that they have heard and seen is base and unworthy. Moreover, they are unable to follow and rely upon the virtuous.
Excellent! It is essential to apply oneself to what is appropriate to the situation, yet it is through self-exaltation and self-aggrandizement that one acts thus.

△ To follow what is good and strive for righteousness is the life-course of the wise. If one exerts effort in this practice, though one be foolish, one will surely become wise; though one be weak, one will surely become strong.
This chapter explains that the Perfected Person (*zhiren*) should conceal their brilliance and obscure their traces; they must not flaunt themselves to invite ruin.
When Lingyuan heard that Juefan had been exiled to the regions beyond the passes and the sea, he sighed and said: "An orchid planted in the middle of a road will surely lose its verdancy before long;
a cassia growing in a secluded ravine will always retain its crimson hue for many years. Throughout antiquity and today, those of talent and wisdom have lost their lives through slander and calumny."
Calamities are many; those who seek to float and sink with the world while being able to preserve their own bodies are few.
This section clarifies that one who conceals their talent will necessarily be free from anxiety. At Qingyuan Temple in Ruizhou was the Chan Master Dehong Juefan.
He was the son of the Peng family of this prefecture and the successor of Chan Master Wen of Zhenjing. He belonged to the thirteenth generation under the lineage of Nanyue.
During the Southern Song dynasty, Emperor Gaozong bestowed upon him the title Baojue Yuanming (Jewel-Awakening Perfect-Enlightenment). At that time, he was renowned as the Venerable Jiyin.

Because Qin Hui monopolized power and detested all virtuous men in the realm, he slandered the Master for his transgressions and subsequently banished him to the southern frontier. Thus, he was exiled and sent into exile.
"Chuan" means to drive away or expel. Upon hearing this, Lingyuan sighed and said:
"The orchid is the ultimate in fragrance, yet because it is planted by the side of a main road, one cannot obtain even its greenery for a single moment.
The cassia is also fragrant, but because it grows amidst secluded cliffs and deep ravines, it is able to preserve its elixir of longevity."
Furthermore, among the men of talent and wisdom throughout antiquity and the present day, it has been the same. Some have lost their lives; some have invited slander and defamation;

and those who have met with misfortune and harm are exceedingly numerous. If one seeks those who did not offend the world, who followed its currents, whose feelings were harmonious and whose intentions were in accord, and who were able to preserve themselves—such individuals are few indeed.
Therefore, the Sage said: "Those in this world who are clever and profoundly observant, yet come close to death, are those who love to criticize others.
Those who are erudite, eloquent, and grand, yet bring peril upon themselves, are those who love to expose the faults of others.
This is evident in Juefan (as recorded in the *Zhangjiang ji*).
This section clarifies that one who reveals their wisdom will inevitably encounter adversity. Thus, the Sage said:
When Confucius visited Zhou and inquired about the rites from Laozi, as he was about to depart, Laozi said: "I have heard that those who are wealthy and noble give people material wealth;
those who are benevolent send people off with words. Although I am not wealthy or noble, I have stolen the title of the benevolent; now, I shall send you off."
It is because of words, my son. Among the scholars of today, those who are clever and perceptive yet come close to death are those who delight in criticizing others.
Those who are broad-minded, eloquent, and far-reaching yet endanger themselves are those who delight in exposing the faults of others.
As subjects and sons, can one not be cautious? Confucius reverently upheld his teachings;
from Zhou he returned to Lu, and his Way became ever more honored. Now, Master Linyuan cites this to express his lament, saying:
"These words of Laozi are truly found in Chan Master Juefan. Those who wish to understand such conduct will find it fundamentally impossible [to grasp].
To float and sink with the world while preserving one's integrity and staying far from harm—this requires a distinct way of looking.
This chapter maintains that in the study of the Way, wondrous awakening must come first; one must not be mired in mere words and letters.
Lingyuan said to Juefan, "I have heard that while you were in the south, you spent much time investigating the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and specifically added annotations and commentaries to it.

This is not what I, your unworthy disciple, had hoped for; for the study of words and letters cannot penetrate the original source of a person's nature, serving merely as a distraction for later students."
This obstructs the wisdom-eye of the Buddhas of the past; the illness lies in relying on others for understanding, thereby blocking the gate of self-awakening.

While one may excel in superficial learning by means of speech and rhetoric, it is ultimately difficult to reach the pinnacle of wondrous realization through the expansion of the divine mechanism. Consequently, there arises much discrepancy between practice and understanding.
Yet, in daily life, my seeing and hearing have become increasingly obscured and dim.
Lingyuan heard that Faquan was in the south of the Ling Mountains; at that time, he was minutely investigating the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. As for the Sanskrit term, it is *Śūraṅgama*.
Regarding this phrase, "The ultimate firmness of all phenomena," I have provided a special commentary (*jian*). *Jian* refers to that which has not been fully transmitted;
*shi* means to explain. This implies that although you apply yourself with such diligence, it is not what I, your unworthy disciple, hoped for from you.
For the study of words and letters cannot penetrate to the root source of one's own wondrous nature. It is merely...
Yet, on the contrary, it obstructs the wisdom-eye of the Buddhas of the past for later generations of learners. Why?
Because the illness lies in relying on other people’s words and texts to form interpretations; thus, it blocks the gateway to one’s own wondrous awakening.
If one were to consider the assistance provided by another’s eloquence, obtaining such commentaries may indeed surpass shallow learning. However, as for [attaining] the vast...
Although one may thoroughly penetrate the divine mechanism [of the teachings], in the end it cannot cause a person to reach the ultimate, wondrous realization.
Consequently, in practice and understanding, many discrepancies arise. "Discrepancy" (cānchā) refers to a lack of uniformity; it denotes a divergence between words and deeds.
Thus, in daily life, what one sees are mere words and what one hears are mere principles, while that innate, singular radiance of one's own which illuminates both heaven and earth—[is neglected].
This has become increasingly obscure and hidden. △ This is a direct and straightforward instruction for holding fast to the upward path; it should be examined with deep sincerity.
This chapter teaches that those who maintain the Dharma must fully utilize human talent; one must not allow for partial neglect due to occasional lapses.
Lingyuan said: "The scholar must be circumspect in their conduct; their words and deeds must be examined. One who speaks little is not necessarily foolish;
one with a glib tongue is not necessarily wise. One who is rustic and simple is not necessarily perverse; one who is compliant and submissive is not necessarily loyal.
Therefore, a true spiritual friend does not judge human character solely by words, nor does he select disciples based on mere personal impressions."
This section states that knowledge requires the careful examination of human nature.
It means that those who act as elders must not fail to scrutinize minutely the conduct and deportment of their students, nor must they fail to investigate their speech and actions at all times.

Those who speak little may be clumsy and reticent in speech, yet they are not necessarily dull-witted at heart. Those with eloquent tongues may possess skillful and expedient speech, yet they are not necessarily wise in their inner minds.
The vulgar and simple may be somewhat constrained and cautious in their conduct, yet they do not necessarily all act in rebellion.
Those who are compliant may be humble and respectful in both word and appearance, yet they do not necessarily all possess loyalty and integrity. Therefore:
"Good friends cannot have their human sentiments fully expressed through mere words, nor can scholars be selected based on personal whims.

Lü Zhi, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, submitted this remonstrance to Emperor Dezong of the Tang Dynasty: "An enlightened monarch cannot have human sentiments fully expressed through mere words, nor can he select jinshi candidates based on his own whims.
Advancement and dismissal should not follow sentiments of love and hatred; separation and union should not depend on personal bias."
This is like abandoning the carpenter’s line and attempting to determine right angles by mere intuition, or discarding the scale and balance and estimating weight with one's hands;
though it may be called subtle and refined, it cannot avoid error. This is why Lingyuan specifically cited this passage to demonstrate it to others.
Now, among the monks of the lakes and seas, who does not wish to seek the Way? Yet among them, those who attain awakening and perceive the principle are but one in a thousand or ten thousand.
Furthermore, to cultivate the person, exert oneself in practice, accumulate learning, and establish virtue requires more than thirty years before it can be achieved.

If one happens to commit a single error or transgression, the monastic community abandons them, such that they cannot establish themselves for the rest of their lives. This is like a pearl in the royal carriage; if it is once lost, it is gone forever.
It is impossible to be without flaws. Even a jade disc worth a city—how could it avoid being without blemish?
Among all sentient beings, how can one be without fault? You, Master, are a sage; yet you spoke of studying the *Yi* at fifty so as to avoid great transgression. Thus, the *Sūtra* says:
One need not fear the arising of thoughts; one only fears that awakening is slow. Moreover, from the sages and worthies downward, who among them has been without fault?
It is through the skillful cultivation of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that all things are left out of consideration.
This section states that students must know their own faults and examine themselves. For among the monastics from all quarters, who does not desire to seek the Way?
Yet, among those thousands or hundreds, it is difficult to find even one or two who have awakened to their own minds and thoroughly perceived their original nature.
Among such rare individuals, there are those who refine their bodies with diligence, exert themselves in their conduct, accumulate learning, and establish virtuous deeds.
To achieve the character of a true person, thirty years of diligent practice are required before one can reach such a state.
Yet, if by some chance there is a single lapse or failure in self-examination, it becomes a transgression; the monastic community will regard this as a fault and immediately cast the individual out.
This causes all the training accumulated over thirty years to be discarded at once, making it impossible for that person to ever establish themselves in the Way for the rest of their lives.
Now, the pearls that adorn a carriage cannot be without flaws; "flaws" (lei) refers here to the knots in the silk thread.
King Wei of Wei said, "I possess several pearls, each an inch in diameter, which can illuminate twelve chariots ahead and twelve behind.
The King of Qi said, "I have four ministers who can illuminate everything beyond a thousand li; how could it be merely twelve chariots? Thus, King Wei possessed [the pearls].

I am ashamed. How could the jade of ten thousand cities be entirely free from flaw? (The meaning of "explanation" is as before. Within the realm of sentient beings and consciousness, how could all be equally without fault?

Even the Master was a sage; yet he studied the *Yi* at fifty to clarify the principles of fortune and misfortune, waxing and waning, and the way of advancing and retreating, or preserving and perishing. Therefore, it can be said that even he was capable of avoiding great error.

Thus it is. In the language of India, *sūtra*; here, it is translated as "Sutra" (契經). This means it accords with principle and accords with capacity: above, it accords with the wondrous principle of all Buddhas;
below, it accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings. "Accord" (*qi*) means "to harmonize. Thus it is said: "Do not fear that thoughts will arise."
One fears only that awakening and illumination may arise too late. Moreover, from the sages and worthies downward—“downward” meaning those below them—who has ever been free from error?

It is through the patient and thorough guidance of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that all types of people—whether high or low, great or small, sharp or dull—are brought to completion without exception.

Therefore it is said: A skilled carpenter follows the utility of wheels and rafters; whether wood is crooked or straight, no material is wasted. A skilled charioteer adapts to the demands of difficult or easy terrain;
whether a horse is sluggish or a steed, neither loses its natural disposition. Since things are thus, so too should it be for humans.

If one’s advancement or withdrawal follows the sentiments of love and hatred, and one’s association or separation depends on the inclination toward difference or sameness, this is like cutting wood for straightness and curves while discarding the line and square, or abandoning the balance scale.
When weighing and comparing the heavy and the light, though it may be called subtle and refined, it cannot be without error.

In this regard, the transmission of the teaching must be impartial and upright. Thus it is said: "A skillful carpenter follows the utility of wheels and rafters; whether crooked or straight, no timber is wasted.

"Carpenter" (zǐ) refers to a woodworker. "Wheels" (lún) refers to chariot wheels. "Rafters" (guò) refers to the rafters of a roof. This means that a skilled craftsman utilizes wood [according to its natural properties].
That which is crooked may be made into a wheel; that which is straight may be made into a rafter. Thus, their material is not wasted.
Once, while Duke Huan of Qi was reading a book in the hall above, Lún Pián was planing wheels in the hall below. He set aside his chisel and asked, saying:
"I venture to ask, what books does Your Majesty read? The Duke replied, "The words of the sages. Bian He said, "Are the sages still here?
The Duke replied, "The sages have passed away. Bian He said, "Indeed, then what Your Majesty reads is nothing but dregs and chaff."
The Duke said in anger, "I am a man of letters; how dare a wheelwright criticize me? If you have a reason, it shall be accepted;
if you have no reason, you shall die. Bian replied, "Judging from my own work, when I am carving a wheel, if I proceed too slowly, the spokes will be smooth but not firm."

If it is too fast, it is painful and the wheel does not enter the socket. When it is neither too slow nor too fast, one attains it with the mind and responds with the hand; it cannot be described in words, for there is a subtle principle (shu) at work. I could not explain it to my son, and my son could not receive it from me. I am seventy years old and still laboring at the wheel-making. Of those who have made wheels in antiquity, there was no one who could transmit it to their sons. It is like this: when you look at the wheel, it seems to be moving in a circle, yet when you look closely at its motion, it is not moving. When you look at it from a distance, it seems to be moving, yet when you look at it closely, it is not moving. This is what is meant by "the movement of non-movement. Therefore, although the wheel is round, it can be stopped; although the handle is square, it can be turned. It is because there is a principle that exists within it. Thus, the ancients who made wheels could not pass on their skill to their sons. How much more so is it with the Way! How much more so is it with the Way! It is like this: when you look at the Way, it seems to be moving, yet when you look closely at its motion, it is not moving. When you look at it from a distance, it seems to be moving, yet when you look at it closely, it is not moving. This is what is meant by "the movement of non-movement. "Those who have died while transmitting [the teachings] are many. Therefore, what Your Majesty has been reading is merely dregs. Duke Huan was greatly pleased. [This concludes the passage from] the "Tian Dao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
A skilled charioteer adapts appropriately to the terrain, whether difficult or easy; thus, both the slow ox and the swift steed do not lose their natural dispositions.
