One who is skilled at driving horses is called an excellent charioteer. "Nú" refers to a dull horse; "Jì" refers to a fine steed.

Just as one who is adept at employing horses will drive a Jì across difficult terrain and a Nú across easy ground, ensuring that both slowness and speed are appropriate to the occasion, so that each does not lose its naturally allotted nature. Since all things are likewise thus.

Yet how could people not act in such a manner? If one’s advancement or withdrawal follows the sentiments of love and hatred, and one’s association or separation depends on the inclination toward difference or sameness—these two points refer to those who employ others through their personal knowledge.
Even if a loved one lacks the requisite talent, they would still advance them and join with them in their affairs; even if a hated person is truly capable, they would still withdraw from them.
"To depart" means to differ from their intent. One who acts thus is like a carpenter who discards his marking lines and rules yet wishes to fashion what is curved or straight;
or like a merchant who abandons his scales and weights yet wishes to measure what is heavy or light.
Though their skill may be refined and subtle day by day, they can ultimately not avoid error. Only one who acts in this manner becomes a true person. This is the point.
The true intention of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This chapter teaches that an abbot should take impartiality as his core principle; he must not yield to private bias for his own self-interest.
Lingyuan said: "A skilled abbot takes the minds of the assembly as his own mind; he never makes his own mind private. By means of the assembly...

A person’s ears and eyes serve as ears and eyes for others; they have never treated their own ears and eyes as private property. Consequently, they are able to communicate the will of the multitude and exhaustively grasp the sentiments of the multitude.

This section clarifies that when sentiments are communicated, there is no boundary between self and other; it refers to one who is truly skilled at acting as a presiding abbot. It is simply by means of the minds of the multitude...
To act for one's own mind is not necessarily to employ one's own mind privately;

rather, one takes the ears and eyes of the multitude as one's own ears and eyes, and does not necessarily employ one's own ears and eyes privately. Thus, one is able to penetrate the wills of the multitude and exhaust their sentiments.
If one takes the hearts of the multitude as one's own heart, then one's likes and dislikes are simply those of the multitude;
thus, what is liked will not be perverse, and what is disliked will not be erroneous. Furthermore, why rely on private confidants and willingly submit to their flattery?
Since one uses the ears and eyes of the multitude as one's own ears and eyes, then the wisdom and clarity of the multitude are all one's own wisdom and clarity. Therefore...

The enlightened perceive nothing they do not discern; the wise hear nothing they do not understand. Furthermore, why rely on private channels for one's own ears and eyes, thereby stubbornly inviting obscuration and delusion?
This section reveals that the underlying sentiment is non-dual. Indeed, when one employs the minds of the multitude as one’s own mind, then there is no [self-centeredness].
These are two matters of the heart. Therefore, what I find good or evil is precisely what the multitude finds good or evil;
thus, that which I prefer is certainly not perverse, and that which I dislike is certainly not erroneous.
Furthermore, why must I resort to private grounds to entrust my innermost thoughts to others, or willingly submit to the flattery of others toward me? Since I employ the will of the multitude...
If one regards the ears and eyes as one's own ears and eyes, then what is seen and heard will be without concealment;
thus, the intelligence of the multitude is precisely my own intelligence. Therefore, clarity will reflect everything without exception, and acuity will comprehend everything without exception.
Why, then, must one entrust matters within private secrecy to the ears and eyes of others? This would surely invite the obscurations of others.
Are you perhaps deluded by me?

In entrusting one’s innermost thoughts and relying upon another as eyes and ears, one must seek only those who are wise and far-sighted—those who strive to seek their own faults, share the desires of the multitude, and harbor no partiality or private bias.
Thus, all people turn their hearts toward them, and it is for this reason that morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness spread throughout the far reaches.

That it has come to this is only natural for those who are distant [from virtue]. Yet, the intent of the foolish and unworthy is to strive to seek out the faults of others, to oppose the desires of the multitude, and to sink into partiality and self-interest;
thus, there is no one among the people whose heart does not turn away from them. Therefore, that their ill repute and perilous conduct spread to far-off places is also only natural.

This section clarifies the reasons for both similarity and difference. Thus, there may indeed be those who disclose the innermost hearts of many people and entrust themselves to the ears and eyes of the multitude;
however, it is only the wise and accomplished who utilize such reports and observations as a pretext.
Entrusting oneself to those of like mind, one should exclusively seek out one's own faults and share one’s desires with all people without partiality or favoritism;
thus, there are none among the multitude who do not turn their hearts toward such a person.

It is therefore only natural that the virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness of the abbot should spread to distant lands. Yet, the intention of the foolish is merely to solicit favors from others.

As the heart, mind, eyes, and ears [of the community], if one is intent on seeking out the faults and transgressions of others, one will act contrary to the desires of the multitude and fall into partiality and private bias. Consequently, the hearts of all will turn away from him;
it is therefore only natural that the abbot’s ill repute and perilous conduct should spread to distant lands.
Thus we know that an abbot who shares the desires of the assembly is called a worthy sage, while one whose desires conflict with the assembly is called a mediocre person.
Generally speaking, there is a distinction in their intentions regarding whether they disclose their inner thoughts and entrust others with their ears and eyes;

yet the resulting good or evil, and success or failure, are as diametrically opposed as this. Is it not because their emotional pursuit of faults differs, and their methods of delegating authority to others vary?
This section clarifies the evidence for similarity and difference. It is known that one who acts as a steward (*sthapati*) in harmony with the desires of the multitude is a sage;

one whose desires conflict with those of the multitude is merely a common person. Generally speaking, this reflects the intent of laying bare one's heart and entrusting one's ears and eyes [to others].
There is a distinction between seeking out the faults of others and seeking out one's own faults, which determines whether one is good or evil.
The fact that success and failure are mutually inverted in their consequences is indeed as such. How could this not be a state of mind seeking out faults?
Is there not a distinction between self and others, and a difference between the public and the private in the way one relies upon others?
△ This chapter values the pursuit of one's own faults; only then does one cease to be a peer of ordinary people. If it is so, then...
The foremost and most heroic of men in the world.
This chapter states that those who serve as practitioners of the Way should regard wealth lightly and virtue highly; this can serve as a condition for gathering and transforming others.

Lingyuan said: "In recent times, those who act as elders encounter two kinds of conditions; it is often seen that their wisdom and understanding are not clear, and being touched by these two winds, they lose the essence of the Dharma.
First, encountering adverse conditions, they are mostly touched by the wind of decline. Second, encountering favorable conditions, they are mostly touched by the wind of profit.
Once touched by these two winds, the vapors of joy and anger intermingle within the mind, becoming stifling and turbulent."
A flushed complexion appears on the face; this is a dharma-gate that leads to humiliation and causes one to be ridiculed by the worthy and enlightened.

This section states that one should respond to conditions by illuminating them with wisdom. Among those who act as elders in recent times, there are two kinds of causes and conditions through which they have passed:
for the most part, they see that people’s wisdom and knowledge are not clear, and thus [they are buffeted] by these two kinds of winds of sensory objects.
When one is moved by contact, one ultimately loses the very essence of one's own mastery of the Dharma. What are these two types?
First, when unfavorable conditions that are contrary to one's wishes frequently arise, they are the "wind of decline," which is the energy of afflictions such as anger and resentment.
Second, when favorable conditions that accord with one's wishes frequently arise, they are the "wind of benefit," which is...
When the breath of craving and delight is struck by these two winds, then the breaths of joy and anger clash within the heart, and the colors of agitation appear upon the face.
"Agitated" (*yù*) refers to the expression of joy; "boiling up" (*bó*) refers to the transformation of facial color.
Throughout one's entire life, one laughs and chatters: gaining something, one rejoices; losing it, one becomes angry. This must surely be observed by a person of discerning eyes.
Such people follow along with derision and mockery, which leads them to bring disgrace upon the Dharma-gate.

Only the wise are truly able to transform this into a means of gathering and converting others, providing an excellent guide for future generations, such as was the case with the Venerable Master of Langye.

I went to Suzhou to visit Fan Xihun. Having received alms and over a thousand strings of cash from him, I dispatched people to secretly count the number of monks in all the temples within the city and sent money to them in secret.
On the same day, I prepared a vegetarian feast for the assembly of donors.
I then took my leave of Master Fan in advance. That morning, I set sail at dawn; by daybreak, the crowd realized I had already departed. Some pursued me as far as Changzhou.

That those in this province were able to see [the Master] and receive the benefits of the Dharma, thereby turning back [from worldly ways], and that by observing this single act of the Elder, the clergy and laity of Gusu were all moved to give rise to faith and their seeds of the Path were deepened—this is what is called a method for converting and gathering others through transformation.

It is truly as different as heaven and earth from those who pilfer the position of the Dharma to seek mere gain and sustenance, plotting only for their own individual interests. (Letter to the Venerable Master De)
This section clarifies that the arising of faith depends solely upon external conditions.

Only those possessing great wisdom, when encountering such circumstances, are well able to skillfully transform them into expedient means for gathering and teaching others. By means of this excellent reputation, they guide future generations;
for example, Master Langye (Xuedou Chongxian) was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Guangzhao Huijiao of Xuzhou, who in turn succeeded Fenyang.

Chan Master Zhao was the tenth generation descendant of Nanyue. He went to Suzhou to visit Fan Xihun—whose surname was Fan, given name Zhongyan, and courtesy name Xihun—a native of Runan who served as State Councilor during the Qingli era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty and was posthumously honored with the title Duke Wenzheng.
Zhao sought instruction from Langye, and when the Abbot Langye visited him, he received a religious offering and a thousand [coins].
"Yumín. *Mín* refers to a string of cash. He then dispatched people to secretly calculate the number of monks in the various temples within the city;
they all delivered money in secret. On the same day, he prepared a vegetarian feast for the assembly of donors. The Abbot immediately took his leave of Lord Fan beforehand.
It was on this very day of the feast that he set sail at dawn, unknown to anyone. By the time... [the sky] grew light.
When the assembly realized that [the Master] had already departed, some who felt an intense longing for their teacher pursued him as far as Changzhou, where they were able to meet him.
He guided them according to the Dharma, and all returned having received the benefit of his gift of the Dharma.
Master Lingyuan remarked, "Observe how this old man’s single instance of action has caused both the clergy and laity of Gusu to give rise to faith, greatly increasing the prospects for the future."
The profound path-seeds are truly what is called the method for converting and gathering [beings].

This stands in a vast contrast, like that between heaven and earth, to those who brazenly usurp the position of the Dharma, greedily seeking profit and sustenance, plotting only for their own individual interests.
I know not how such usurpers and seekers of wealth would look upon themselves were they to read this.
This chapter teaches people to cultivate virtue and practice diligence, not seeking fame or recognition from others, so that they may naturally be respected by them.
Wen Zheng Gong said to Langye: "Last year when I arrived here, I was thinking of finding someone among those living in the woods with whom I might converse. He once...
He questioned an official, asking whether there were any eminent monks on the various mountains. The official replied that the two monks Ruiguang and Ximao of the Northern Monastery were excellent.
This passage refers to those whose virtue is preserved and whose fame is manifest; it means that since last year he arrived here in Suzhou and took up his post...

He longed to find a man of the forest who could converse with him on such matters. Once, he asked an official whether there were any monks of excellent virtue within or outside the city walls and throughout the various mountains.
The official replied that the two monks Rui-guang and Xi-mao of Beisi Temple were the finest.
As for the name of Rui-guang Temple, it was derived from four auspicious omens: the bells and drums rang spontaneously, the precious pagoda emitted light, and auspicious bamboo [sprouted].
They were intermingled. Because a white tortoise listened to the Dharma there, it was called Rui-guang (Auspicious Light); this is the present-day Wofo Temple (Sleeping Buddha Temple).
Xi’s clan and lineage for the succession of the Dharma are not detailed. Mao was Chan Master Maoyue; he succeeded Chan Master Shouzhi of Dayu, being the eleventh generation under Nanyue.

I asked, "Is there no such thing apart from these various systems of Chan and Vinaya? The official replied to me, "The Confucians honor the conduct of the scholar, while the monks discuss virtue and achievement.
As for those like Xi and Mao, for thirty years they have not stepped beyond their doorsteps, wearing nothing but plain cloth."
He was entirely unattached to fame, profit, or offerings; thus, the people of the land held his conduct in high esteem and revered him as their teacher.

As for his ascending the seat to preach the Dharma and propagating the transformation on behalf of the Buddha, his spontaneous eloquence and mastery were such that those who could be called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) were beyond the comprehension of dull officials.
"This section proves that their names were real and their conduct was true. I asked, "Aside from these two men, are there no others among the various Chan masters and Vinaya masters?
The official replied, "Confucianists value the conduct of the scholar alone, whereas the monastic community mostly honors virtuous achievement."
As for the two masters Xi and Mou, for thirty years they did not step beyond their doorsteps;
they wore only plain cloth garments, and fame, profit, and worldly gain left no trace within their minds.
Therefore, the people of this commandery all held these two masters in high esteem for their integrity and conduct, regarding them with reverence as teachers. As for others...
Ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, acting as the Buddha’s representative to propagate and transform beings,
and being honored as a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) due to his mastery of sharp wit and eloquence— this is something that a dull-witted official could not possibly understand.
On a day of leisure, I visited the two venerable masters Xi and Mou and observed their conduct; it was exactly as the official had described.

Retiring to reflect, I recalled the old saying that the customs of Su and Xiu were excellent; yet now, even an aged official is still able to distinguish between the noble and the base, and the superior and the inferior.
How much more so for those who possess true realization!
This section demonstrates that the Way exists in the very act of direct perception. On a day of leisure, I went to visit the two venerable masters, Xi and Mou.
These masters were individuals who stood above others, possessing wisdom and virtue within and sublime conduct without. Observing them...
The facts of his conduct were exactly as this official had stated. I withdrew and reflected upon this:
it has long been said that the customs of Suzhou and Jiaxing are excellent. "Su" refers to Suzhou, and "Xiu" refers to Jiaxing.
If even this old official can still distinguish between the superior and inferior qualities of the gentleman and the petty man, how much more so must those who possess true discernment?
Langya said: "What this official has spoken is truly a lofty discourse. I request that it be recorded so as to enlighten those who have not yet heard it.
(From the *Langya Bielü*).
This section records these events to inform the assembly. When Master Langya heard this, he said with joy: "If this official..."
He said: "Truly, these are most sublime discussions. Please record them so that they may be made known everywhere to those who have not yet heard them.
△ Gold and white jade are precious by their very nature; what cause for concern is there that no one would recognize them? Let scholars read this.
One should know for oneself that one ought to act as a good person.
This chapter urges people to store up and cultivate themselves deeply; it is not appropriate to advance with haste in pursuit of fame.
Lingyuan said: "Master Yuan of Mount Zhongsheng did not associate with high officials throughout his life, nor did he seek after fame or profit, remaining humble."
Cultivating oneself; finding joy in the Way for oneself.

This section clarifies the commitment to reality and the preservation of truth. Master Zanyuan of Mount Zhong (originally Mount Jiang) was described by Master Linyuan in terms of his lifelong conduct and deeds, intended to serve as a warning to later students. It is said that throughout his life, Master Yuan...
He came here because he did not wish to form alliances with high officials or scholars; he did not seek fame, profit, or sustenance, but instead governed himself solely through humility.
The *Image* of the *Qian* hexagram says: "The humble and humble gentleman governs himself by means of humility. Humility is the ultimate expression of modesty.
He delighted in cultivating the Way for himself and had no desire to leave the mundane world to become a person of the clergy.
When the scholar-officials first encouraged him to engage with the world, Yuan said, "If one possesses fertile fields, why worry about a late harvest?
I only fear a lack of talent and ability.
This passage clarifies the joy of self-sufficiency; the scholar-officials admired his lofty conduct and urged him to respond to the world.
Regarding the mundane world, Yuan said: "If a student truly possesses fertile and excellent soil, the sprouts will be abundant and the fruit will be substantial;
though it may ripen slowly, it is still marvelous. Why worry about late fruition? This 'fertile field' is a metaphor for the Way that a person upholds—nothing more."
"I only fear that he lacks wisdom, talent, and the necessary implements.
When Lord Jing heard this, he said: "He flies away at the sight of color; he soars before he settles. This is what Master Yuan has attained" (*Zhuici ji*).
This section provides a judgment on the excellence [of the teaching]. When Lord Jing heard these words from Master Yuan, he said:
"It takes flight upon seeing color; it soars before it settles. Such is the nature of birds: when they perceive that a person’s countenance is not benevolent, they vanish with a flutter.
They soar back and forth, observing carefully, until they find a place where they will not be startled by arrows or slings, and only then do they settle. This means:
Duke Yuan’s discernment of the opportune moment was likewise like this. △ To have fertile fields is not to worry about a late harvest;
this is the place of ultimate utility. Why such haste?
This chapter speaks of the practitioner of the Way. Practice is more difficult than awakening and maintaining [the realization]; it is essential to diminish oneself and benefit others. Lingyuan said:
"The sages of old stated that awakening through study is difficult; once awakened, maintaining it is difficult; once maintained, practicing it is difficult.
Now, when it is time to practice, the difficulty exceeds even that of awakening and maintaining. This is because those who awaken and maintain [the realization] are refined."

Advancing with firm resolve, one should simply exert oneself in one's own person. Practitioners must necessarily maintain an impartial mind and a death-vow, taking it as their duty to diminish themselves to benefit others.
If the mind is not impartial or the vow is not firm, then the roles of diminishing and benefiting will be inverted, and one will fall into the ranks of a worldly master.
This is something for which one ought to stand in awe.
It is said that for those who study the Way in the world, the most difficult thing is simply to awaken to and realize one’s own mind.

Once awakened, it is further necessary to constantly maintain and cultivate this realization. Even so-called "nurturing the sacred embryo" by dwelling by waterside or beneath the forest trees is not easy.

Once one is able to maintain this state, it is further valued that one must put it into practice. However, when it comes to practicing these methods of the Way to guide and lead others, [it is even more difficult].
For the multitude of people, this is even more difficult than the most difficult. Why? It is because those who awaken to and maintain [this practice] advance with diligence without retreating;
after three or five years, it naturally coalesces into a single whole. Their maintenance is firm, steadfast, and transcendent, and their resolve remains non-dual.
However, this does not go beyond exerting effort in practice; it requires nothing more than being diligent and untiring within one's own person.
Those who would follow this path must do so with a mind of equanimity and firm resolve, and furthermore, they must take it as their responsibility to diminish themselves and benefit others.
If the mind is not impartial and the vow is not firm, yet one instead harms others to benefit oneself, [one cannot succeed].
This is acting with inverted views. Not only will one fail to glorify the ancestral Way, but one will also fall into the ranks of a common, worldly teacher.
Such are the stakes involved; one must therefore revere it with profound awe.
"Only" (*qi*) means "great. The difficulty of practicing the Way is not something known by those of coarse minds;
it is only the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) who can fully investigate it. Students should examine this closely and practice it with diligence.
This chapter reveals that the ancients possessed the function of guiding beings through the light of humility; they were especially modest and did not dare to rely upon themselves.
Linyuan said: "Brother Dongsan was exceptionally gifted by nature; his speech and silence were always measured, and he habitually manifested his words."

The principle of his phrasing was naturally superior; those in all quarters who wished to emulate it found that anything other than being unconventional led to vulgarity and meanness, such that they could never reach his level.
Even seeking among the ancients, one could find no equal. Yet he remained humble and radiant in guiding others, as if driven by hunger and thirst.
He once said, "I have no Dharma; how can I fail to be diligent? You disciples are truly sinners within the gates of the Dharma."
Master Lingyuan cited the practical conduct of Master Yuan as an example to exhort later students, saying:
"My elder brother from Dongshan possessed a natural endowment that was exceptionally outstanding and extraordinary. Whether speaking or remaining silent, he always accorded with the Dharma.
In his daily life, whenever he uttered a word or spoke a phrase to instruct others, its underlying principle naturally transcended [the mundane]."

Excellent! Even if those from all quarters were to attempt to emulate him, they would find nothing but deceitful and vulgar speech, or licentious and narrow-minded talk; in the end, none could equal him.
Not only could his contemporaries not reach such heights, but even if one sought among the ancients, such a person would be hard to find. Nevertheless, he remains humble and modest.
He guided all beings; he was no different from one who is truly hungry or thirsty. He once said: "I possess no dharma. 'Ning' (寧) means 'how could';

'qi' (豈) means 'how could'; 'ke' (克) means 'to be able. How could I possibly urge my disciples to diligence? Since I cannot urge students forward in their studies, I may be called a true sinner within the Dharma-gate.
Regarding such a personage as this, one must know that his source has its origin and that his influence is vast and great.
Yet it is not fixed; it is not something that ordinary people can learn through study. The ancients compiled this as a model for practice.
Upon reading it, one should feel a sense of deep reverence.
This treatise teaches the essential conduct of an abbot: that practice and understanding must correspond, and that one should not be obsessively attached to fame or profit.
Lingyuan’s Way, learning, and conduct were characterized by pure sincerity and profound virtue, possessing the style of the ancients.
He was composed and spoke little, earning the highest respect from scholars and officials alike.

This section recounts the life and deeds of Master Luyuan. The Way realized by the Master, the learning he cultivated, and the principles he practiced were of a single flavor—pure, sincere, and truthful;
they were neither adulterated nor false. His virtue was exceedingly profound, truly embodying the spirit of the ancient sages.
In his daily conduct, he was composed and spoke sparingly, further exemplifying the character of a great scholar.
What my husband has revered and honored he once said:

"That which the multitude neglects is that which the sages are careful about. How much more so for one who is the master of a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) and assists in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation;

if one’s practice and understanding are not in accord, how can one possibly fulfill this role? The essential point is to examine and reproach oneself at all times, lest one’s reputation [be tarnished]."

If even a slight inclination toward gain and honor arises in the mind, and if perhaps the Dharma has not yet been fully realized by others or the monastics have not yet been won over, you should reflect inwardly and cultivate virtue to await those who come later.
I have never seen one whose own person was upright yet whose monastic community was not well-ordered.
This section further clarifies that the Master’s teaching requires the correspondence of practice and realization. The Master often said to others:
"Generally, those places where ordinary people let their minds run wild and neglect their conduct are precisely the grounds where the sages are most cautious and vigilant.

This is especially true for one who is the master of a monastic community; since his primary purpose is to assist in proclaiming the Buddha's transformation, if he does not possess the correspondence of practice and realization,"
How could one dare to perform this lightly? It requires that one constantly examine and reproach oneself.
One must by no means allow fame, profit, or sustenance to stir within the mind.

If one maintains such meticulous care, yet the Dharma one practices still fails to inspire conviction in others—*fu* meaning "to believe"—or fails to win the submission of fellow monks (*nàzǐ*), one should naturally withdraw.

When one’s reflections are profound and one cultivates the Way and its Virtue, it is impossible to force others to follow oneself; rather, one must await the time when they will naturally submit to transformation.
I have never seen a case where the person themselves was upright, yet the monastic community remained disordered.
This refers to what is called "observing the countenance of a person of virtue, which causes the turbidity of one's mind to melt away.
The reality truly lies herein (from *Jiwen*). This section cites the "person of virtue" (*de-ren*) as proof.

That is to say, when one observes the countenance of a person possessed of virtue, the reason why the defilements within the heart melt away like ice is none other than that their reality resides solely in virtue. (Tian)
Zifang’s name was Wuzhe. He replied to Marquis Wen of Wei, saying, "My teacher is Dongguo Shunzi. The Marquis asked, "Why have you never mentioned him?
Zifang said, "As for his person, he has the appearance of a Perfected Man (*zhenren*) while being natural (*tian*).

He is empty yet responsive, preserving his authenticity. He is pure yet accommodates all things. When people lack the Way, he rectifies his countenance to awaken them, causing their minds to become compliant."
It is also exhausted. How could I, Wuze, be sufficient to describe it? (From the "Outer Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*).
△ To examine and reproach oneself from time to time is to be a person of the highest caliber. When others do not respond, one should hold oneself responsible; this is a truly marvelous remedy.
This chapter teaches people to nurture themselves and not act recklessly, so as to avoid inviting calamity or disgrace.
Lingyuan said to Yuanwu: "Although a monk may possess the potential for insight into the Way, if he does not store it deeply and cultivate it thoroughly..."
If he were to act upon this, his conduct would surely be abrupt and violent; it would not only fail to benefit the teaching, but would likely invite disaster and disgrace.
Chan Master Foguo Keqin of Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu, whose secular surname was Luo and who hailed from Pengzhou, was named Yuanwu.

The successor of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Xian, said: "Generally speaking, although those who are monastics possess the innate capacity for realizing the Way, if they are unwilling to store it deeply and nurture it thoroughly so that it may be brought forth in practice, their every action will ultimately be precipitous and violent.
To act in such a manner not only fails to provide any benefit to the teaching,"
[End of] Gate. I fear that in days to come you will surely invite calamity, slander, and disgrace. A monk must not fail to be cautious.
Only deep accumulation and mature cultivation constitute true benefit; what is the use of impetuous advancement? You should examine this most earnestly.
This chapter teaches the student that sincerity and faithfulness (*chengxin*) must be taken as the foundation;
they must never be abandoned for even a moment. Zen Master Yuanwu said: "The study of the Way depends on faith; establishing faith depends on sincerity.
Once sincerity is maintained within, one can then prevent others from being deluded. When faith is maintained within oneself, one can teach others without deceit. Only through faith and sincerity..."
There is no error in supplementing this.
This section takes sincerity (*cheng*) as the foundation. Sincerity is the reality of the mind; it is the essence of faith (*xin*).
Faith is the reality of speech; it is the function of sincerity. It means that one who studies the Way must first maintain the character for "faith. Establishing faith depends entirely upon—
Regarding this single character "sincerity" (chéng): if a person can maintain ultimate sincerity within their heart, then they will cause others to have no cause for confusion.
By maintaining ultimate trust within oneself, one can instruct others without any deception.
Thus, sincerity and trust truly benefit oneself and do no harm to others.
Thus we know that if sincerity is not singular, the mind cannot be preserved; if trustworthiness is not singular, one's words cannot be carried out. As the ancients said:
"Food and clothing may be dispensed with, but sincerity and trustworthiness must not be lost. It is only the *kalyāṇamitra* who should teach people through sincerity and trustworthiness.
Furthermore, if one's mind is not sincere and one does not believe in the matter, can one be called a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)? The *I Ching* says:
"Only the most sincere in the world is able to fully realize their own nature. Being able to fully realize their own nature, they are then able to fully realize the nature of others."
This section teaches that one must be sincere and faithful. Thus we know that a person’s sincerity is not uniform; it naturally possesses degrees of weight, and if so, this mind cannot be preserved.
The power of faith is not uniform; it naturally possesses degrees of diligence or negligence, and if so, what is spoken cannot be put into practice.
The *Analects* says: "Clothing is essential to the body, for it can ward off the cold; food is essential to life..."
This is done to stave off hunger. Even if it seems that neither [alternative] can be abandoned, one must still be able to abandon [the former].

As for the two characters "sincerity" (cheng) and "trustworthiness" (xin), one must never lose them even at the cost of death. Only those who are true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) will surely teach others through ultimate sincerity and move others through ultimate trustworthiness.
If one's mind is deluded rather than sincere, and one's actions are deceitful rather than trustworthy, how could such a person be called a true spiritual friend?
Is this not so? The *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* say: "Only those who possess the ultimate sincerity in the world are able to fully realize their own nature.

Being able to fully realize their own nature, they are then able to fully realize the nature of others. Being able to fully realize the nature of others, they are then able to fully realize the nature of all things."
One who can exhaust the nature of things is able to assist in the transformative nourishment of Heaven and Earth.

Being able to assist in the transformative nourishment of Heaven and Earth, one is then able to form a triad with Heaven and Earth. The commentary states: "Nature" means that there is no virtue that is not fully realized.

Principle is complete in its entirety; thus, there is no private bias of human desire. One who is able to exhaust this principle possesses knowledge that is without lack of clarity and acts in a manner that is never inappropriate.
When the world speaks of the virtue of the Sage, none can surpass him. "To assist" means to act in concert with Heaven and Earth;
"to participate" means to stand side by side with Heaven and Earth.
If one cannot fulfill oneself, yet desires to fulfill others, the multitude will surely deceive and not follow.
If one is not sincere before, yet claims to be sincere afterward, the multitude will surely doubt and not believe.
This section clarifies that one must first perfect oneself in order to be able to perfect others.

Suppose you yourself are unable to exhaust sincerity and maintain integrity within yourself, yet you desire others to exhaust sincerity and maintain integrity; all people will surely deceive you and not follow you.
"Deceive" (紿) means to cheat. If you yourself cannot exhaust sincerity and practice it before others to serve as a model, yet you say:
My practice of sincerity must lie in what follows. The more people see this, the more they will fall into doubt and fail to believe.
This is what is meant by saying that when one cuts one's hair, it should reach the skin; when one trims one's nails, they should almost reach the body.

Truly, if sincerity does not reach its goal, things will not respond; if self-sacrifice does not reach its limit, benefit will not arrive. It is clear, therefore, that sincerity and trustworthiness must never for a moment depart from oneself.
(Letter to Vice Censor-in-Chief Yu).
This section uses an analogy to show that from sincerity one can reach the state of faith. It is as they say: "One who shaves their hair must necessarily reach the skin;
one who splits their fingernails will naturally penetrate the flesh. This is truly because if my own sincerity and faith are not...
If one does not reach the ultimate limit, people will be unable to be moved or won over, just as shaving the hair cannot reach the skin.
If my reductions do not reach the ultimate limit, they likewise cannot lead everyone to the goal, just as clipping the nails cannot penetrate the body.
"Zhen" means "to arrive at. It is clear that sincerity (*cheng*) and trustworthiness (*xin*) are one in essence and one in function, and must never for a moment be separated from oneself.
"For a moment" (*si xu*) refers to a brief interval. Nowadays, many are neither sincere nor trustworthy;
if they wish to act as teachers and models, how can they possibly put this into practice and move others to respond?
This chapter states that the wise are able to reform their faults and shift toward goodness, causing their virtue and character to renew themselves daily.

Yuanwu said: "Who among men is without fault? To be able to reform one's faults when they occur—nothing is greater than this goodness. Those of antiquity all praised the reforming of faults as being worthy;
they did not consider the absence of faults to be the mark of excellence."

This section first clarifies that reforming one's faults is a source of excellence. It means that in this world, regardless of whether one is worthy or unworthy, a gentleman or a petty person, who can claim to be entirely without error?
Should there be even slight transgressions, if one is able to reform them of one’s own accord, no goodness could be greater than this.
The sages and worthies of antiquity all praised those capable of reforming their faults as being truly virtuous.
Virtue has never regarded the absence of fault as being truly praiseworthy;
therefore, in the conduct of human beings, errors and transgressions are frequent, and neither the most intelligent nor the most ignorant can entirely avoid them.

Only the wise are able to reform their faults and turn toward goodness, whereas the foolish often conceal their errors and gloss over their wrongdoings. When one reforms and turns toward goodness, their virtue is renewed daily.
This is what is called a gentleman. To gloss over one’s transgressions causes those evils to become even more manifest; this is what is called a petty person.
This section clarifies that no human being can avoid having faults. Thus, in the course of their actions, there are many instances of error and deviation.
This is something that cannot be avoided by either the superior sages and gentlemen above or the common people and petty persons below.
Exemption. Only those possessed of wisdom can reform themselves, shift toward goodness, and clarify their principles;

whereas the ignorant and deluded mostly conceal their errors and gloss over their faults. If one can shift toward goodness, then their virtue and achievements will renew daily, and they are called a "gentleman" (junzi).
If one glosses over their errors, then their evil traces will become manifest daily, and they are termed [a petty person].
I am a man of no talent.
Therefore, to hear of righteousness and be able to move toward it is difficult for ordinary people; to see goodness and joyfully follow it is what the virtuous esteem.
I hope you will forget me beyond words, as is fitting (for you, Magistrate Wen).

This section cites ancient precedents to exhort those who understand the value of speech. Thus, being able to transform oneself upon hearing virtuous words is something difficult for ordinary people to achieve.
"Transform" (徙) means to shift. To immediately rejoice in and follow virtuous conduct upon seeing it is what the worthy and virtuous esteem.
Confucius said: "If virtue is not cultivated, if learning is not discussed, and if one cannot transform upon hearing of righteousness..."
That goodness cannot be reformed is my concern. The commentary states: "Virtue must be cultivated before it is perfected; learning must be discussed before it becomes clear.
To perceive righteousness and be able to shift toward it, and to reform one's errors without stinginess—these four are the essential points for daily renewal."
If one is unable to achieve this, even the Sage still feels concern, let alone a student.
What I have said here consists of the words of the ancients’ sincere instructions. I hope you will forget me beyond the realm of words.
It is sufficient merely to grasp my meaning. △ The two characters "rectifying errors" (kaigō) are the shortcut for transforming delusion into awakening and turning objects into the Way;
one must not fail to practice them with deliberate intent.
This chapter states that an abbot should move others through virtue, causing people to admire and love him. Yuanwu said:
"The former master spoke of those who serve as elders: there are those who move others through their moral character, and there are those who subdue others through their power.
It is like the flight of a phoenix, which all birds love; or the prowling of a tiger or wolf, which all beasts fear. Its...
In their resulting sense of reverence and submission, they are one and the same;
yet their respective categories are as different as heaven and earth. My late teacher, Master Yan, said:

"Among those who serve as elders, there are those who move others through their virtue and character, and there are those who subdue others through their authority and power. Those who move others through virtue are like the soaring of phoenixes."
The hundred birds love him and follow him. Those who submit through force act like tigers and wolves; the hundred beasts fear them and avoid them.
They come because they are moved by him, and they depart because they have submitted to him. Thus, though being moved and submitting are two distinct states, in this case they are not different.
The difference between the application of virtue and the application of power is such that their names, ranks, and realities are as far apart as heaven and earth.
This analogy reaches the height of clarity. Observe the distinction between being moved and being submissive; how do they differ in their actual experience?
This chapter states that what the wise follow is solely the Way; thus, the emotions are harmonized and the Dharma is governed.
Yuanwu said to the Abbot Long: "If one wishes to manage a monastic community (conglin) but does not strive to understand the sentiments of its people, then the community cannot be managed.
If one strives to understand the sentiments of the people but is not diligent in receiving those below, then the human sentiments cannot be understood."
It is possible. If one strives diligently to welcome those below but does not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy, then those below cannot be welcomed.

If one strives to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy but detests hearing of their faults while delighting in compliance with oneself, then the worthy and the unworthy cannot be distinguished.
Only the sagely and enlightened person does not detest hearing of faults nor delight in compliance with themselves; they follow only the Way. This is how one attains the hearts of others and—
The management of monastic communities (*conglin*) is thus established (*Guanglu*).

Chan Master Shao Long of Tiger Hill in Pingjiang Prefecture was a native of Heshan in Hezhou. He was a successor of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin and belongs to the fifteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
He maintained that the proper administration of monastic communities depends upon gaining the hearts of the multitude; for it is the hearts [of the people] that matter.

If one cannot do so, how can the monastic community (saṃgha) be governed? However, if one wishes to grasp the true nature of people, it depends primarily on treating beginners with diligent hospitality.
If one is not diligent in receiving others, one will likewise fail to understand human nature.
To be diligent in receiving others, one must necessarily distinguish between those who are virtuous and those who are unworthy. If one does not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy...
The worthy and the unworthy become indistinguishably one; thus, those below cannot be engaged. One must distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy.
It is not that one dislikes others speaking of one’s own faults, nor does one delight in others being submissive to oneself.

If you were to cause others to dislike speaking of your faults while delighting in their submissiveness to you, then even the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy could not be discerned. Only the truly wise and accomplished do not harbor such dislikes.
When people speak of their own faults, one does not take pleasure in others conforming to one’s own preferences; rather, one follows only the Way.
This is how one gains the hearts of the multitude, causing the monastic community to naturally become harmonious and solemn, and its regulations to naturally be brought into order.
△ The phrase "following only the Way" is a crucial point of importance; furthermore, one must turn back and examine oneself to see it.
How can one’s emotions be brought into accord? Knowing this, one can practice the Way.
This chapter teaches that the abbot’s sole pursuit should be goodness; by attending to minor details of conduct, one preserves great virtue.
Yuánwù said: "The abbot takes the wisdom of the assembly as his own wisdom and the mind of the assembly as his own mind.

He is constantly apprehensive that even a single thing may not have its true nature fully expressed, or a single matter may not accord with principle. Thus, he diligently seeks out and receives [advice], pursuing only that which is good."
This section states that what is sought is solely the good. To discern right from wrong is called wisdom (*jñāna*); it is to master all principles and govern all things.
It means that one who acts as a presiding official (*sthavira*) should take the wisdom of the multitude as their own wisdom, and take the mind of the multitude as their own mind.
One must always reflect with careful scrutiny, fearing that there may be even a single person whose needs have not been fully met.
I am concerned that there may be some matter that cannot be resolved through principle. To be "zealous" (zizi) means to be earnest and persistent.
Seeking out the worthy and accepting remonstrance—this alone is what I must strive to achieve.
One should inquire into the rightness or wrongness of the principle; how could one concern oneself with the magnitude of the matter?
If the principle is correct, even if the expenditure is great, what harm is there in undertaking it? If the matter is incorrect, even if the cost is small, what injury is there in abolishing it?
For the small is the precursor to the great, and the subtle is the sprout of the manifest; therefore, the worthy are cautious at the beginning, and the sages maintain their vigilance.
This section concerns the application of logic: in all matters one undertakes, one should inquire only whether they accord with principle or not, regardless of whether the action is great or small.

If a particular matter accords with principle and benefits the monastic community while bringing fulfillment to the assembly, what harm could there be in carrying it out even if the expenditure is extremely great?
If an action is contrary to the Way, even if its expenditure is slight, what harm is there in eliminating it?

Even if one were to say that because the usage is slight, it need not be eliminated—yet one must know that the small is the gradual advance toward the great, and the minute is the sprout of the manifest.
Therefore, the wise and accomplished are cautious in their conduct from the very beginning; the most sagely persons exercise restraint and vigilance at the outset.
It is subtle.
If a tiny trickle is not stopped, it will eventually transform a mulberry field. If a flickering flame is not extinguished, it will ultimately consume the plains and wilds.

Once the spreading fire has become intense and the calamity is already complete, though one wishes to save it, it is truly too late. As the ancients said: "If one does not take care of small matters, they will eventually accumulate into great trouble."
"Venerable Sir, this is what is meant [in the Letter to the Buddha].
This section now clarifies the point by means of an illustration. 'Jiānjiān' (涓涓) refers to droplets. It is like one who manages water:
if they do not stop it at its very first drop, it will eventually become a current that will surely transform even a mulberry field. The heat..."
"Flame" refers to a spark from fire. Furthermore, if one does not extinguish a fire at its initial stage as a single spark, then when it blazes up, it will inevitably consume the plains and wilds.
When water flows and fire fans out, the momentum is already great, and the calamity is already accomplished; though one wishes to rescue it, it is truly beyond reach. As the ancients said:
If one does not maintain meticulousness in minor conduct, one will ultimately suffer setbacks that impair great virtue.

This is precisely what is meant by these words. The Book says: "Alas! From dawn until night, there must never be a moment of lack of caution. If one does not attend to minor details, it will ultimately impair great virtue.
To build a mountain nine *ren* high, the effort may be frustrated by a single basket of earth. The commentary states: "Or" (*huò*) means "perhaps" or "at any time. (Lüshi Chunqiu)
It is said: "This is the work of diligent virtue. The single word 'or' (or) is most full of meaning;
if one ceases even for a moment, it is no longer diligent virtue. *Jin* (矜) means to maintain or uphold. *Xi xing* (細行) refers to minor matters.
△ This chapter emphasizes seeking only what is good and paying close attention to not being negligent in minor matters. If one contemplates this deeply, its meaning will become clear of itself.

I have observed this chapter, which states that the Elder takes the salvation of others as his primary concern; he is one who serves as an instrument for assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma transformation.
Yuanwu said to Yuan Budai: "In all matters concerning the duties of an Elder, one should assist in proclaiming the Buddha's transformation and constantly reflect upon it."
To have the welfare of others as one’s heart-mind, and to act without self-conceit, ensures that those reached will be broad and those aided will be many. However,

if there arises even a single thought of self-aggrandizement or the display of one’s own ability, the notion of seeking personal advantage will emerge, and the mind of the unworthy will take birth (from the Shuanglin Stone Inscription).
Yuan Buidai was Chan Master Cihu Ang Jinge Yuan of Huguo Monastery in Taizhou.
He was the son of the Zhang family of Nanxi in Yongjia and a successor to Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin. He belonged to the fifteenth generation under the lineage of Mount Nanyue.
Because the master habitually walked about carrying a cloth bag, people called him "Bagu Daihe" (Cloth-Bag Layman). This was considered the customary duty of those titled "Elders."
This chapter is no ordinary matter; it is to assist the Buddha in proclaiming his transformational teachings. How could this be an easy task?
At all times, one must constantly keep in mind the aspiration to benefit others and save the world.

When engaged in such transformative work, one must also remain free from thoughts of self-importance or self-reliance; only then will those reached be broad and those saved be many. Yet, in a single moment...
If one harbors a mind that prizes oneself and displays one's own abilities, the desire for gain through luck will arise, and an unworthy state of mind will immediately take root.

The malady of self-exaltation is extremely difficult to eliminate; I hope that you all will constantly examine yourselves with a sense of humility, so that over time, this fault will naturally vanish.
This chapter states that a person should be cautious at the beginning and prudent at the end in order to achieve a good reputation.
Yuanwu said to Miaoxi: "In all matters of conduct, one must be careful from beginning to end. Therefore, those who are skilled at initiating a task will surely be skilled at completing it;
those who have a good start will surely have a good finish. If one is as careful at the end as at the beginning, there will be no failure."

This section teaches the importance of being careful from beginning to end. That is to say, in all matters of human conduct—whether in movement or stillness—one must invariably be cautious at the outset and prudent until the conclusion.

Therefore, those who are skilled in undertaking tasks will surely be able to bring them to successful completion; those who are skilled in being cautious at the start will surely be able to conclude well.
If one maintains such care until the very end, just as at the beginning, without any difference between the two, then regarding that task...
One will certainly not suffer defeat through such grasping. An ancient saying goes:
"Alas, the robe was not yet finished when it was turned into a skirt; the journey of a hundred li is completed by its ninety.
These are all lamentations over having a beginning but no end. Therefore it is said: "There is nothing that does not have a beginning, but few are able to reach the end."
This section cites actual events as verification. An ancient saying goes: "Alas! Those who began making an upper garment failed to complete it and instead changed course to make lower trousers.
It is also like a traveler who sets out for a hundred li but turns back at fifty, or even one who turns back after having traveled ninety li.
These are all lamentations over having a beginning but no end. Thus, the Classic of Poetry says:
"There is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end.
Long ago, the elder Master Huìtáng said: "The Venerable Hángbó Shèng was also an extraordinary monk; it was only in his later years that he went astray."
"Observe how he first attained it; one cannot call him merely 'worthy' (Yunmen’s Collected Works).
This section cites a person to provide verification. Formerly, the old master Haitang said: "On Mount Huangbo was Chan Master Weisheng."
He was a son of the Luo family from Tongzhou and succeeded Master Nanhua Huanglong Nan, being the twelfth generation under Mount Heng.
During his days of training under Huanglong, he stood out with such exceptional brilliance that everyone hailed him as a marvelous monk.
Yet, when it came to his later conduct, his actions became flawed and he fell short of his former standard. Observing his beginning, how could one not call him worthy? △ For this reason.
Observing this, can one not be earnest and vigilant, diligent from dawn to dusk, and careful in the end as one was in the beginning?
This chapter states that in all matters, taking antiquity as one's instruction prevents the error of relying on mere conjecture.

Yuánwù said to Fójìàn, "Master Báiyún’s conduct and actions were invariably modeled upon antiquity. He once said: 'If one does not examine antiquity in one's affairs, it is called being contrary to the Dharma.
I have extensively studied the words and deeds of the past, and thus I have fulfilled my resolve. However, this was not merely a fondness for the ancient;
rather, it was because people of the present day are insufficient as models."

This section states that all affairs must rely on antiquity. Formerly, my late master Baiyun, in all his daily activities, invariably examined the precedents of the sages and worthies of the past to establish his standards. He once said:
"If an ordinary person undertakes an action without investigating the past, it is called being without a standard. I have extensively gathered the words of former worthies for this purpose.
The conduct of the sages of antiquity has thus fulfilled the aspirations of my life. The *Hexagram of Great Accumulation* (*Dazhu*) in the *Book of Changes* states:
"Heaven within the mountain is Great Accumulation. The noble person extensively knows the words and deeds of the past to accumulate his virtue.
The commentary notes: "Words and deeds of the past" refers to the speech and conduct of the ancient sages. By observing their words and examining their deeds, one achieves virtue.
This is the meaning of "Great Accumulation" (Dàxù). "Accumulation" (chù) means to gather and complete. However, it is not that I am personally intent on antiquity;
rather, people of the present age truly do not suffice to serve as a standard or model.
My late teacher used to say: "The Master (Shiweng) clings to antiquity and does not understand the changes of the times. The Master replied:
"To change the old for the sake of novelty is the great affliction of people today; I shall never do so" (*Chanheshang Rilu*).
In this section, he further argues for adhering to antiquity. His former teacher often said, "The Master is excessively attached to antiquity;

in the end, he does not know how to adapt and change with the times. The Master replied, "To intentionally alter what has been established and to change the constant Dharma is the great affliction of people today. I shall never engage in such acts of alteration. △ People today most...
I fear clinging to antiquity. To not cling to antiquity is what is called being a man of refined elegance (*fengliu*). How extraordinary!
This chapter shows that the ancients maintained their integrity with firm resolve, never degrading their principles in pursuit of fame.
When Fojian invited Master Qin to move from Taiping to Zhihai, the Prefect, Mr. Zeng Gongyuan, asked who could succeed him as abbot.
Fojian recommended the Head Seat, Mingben. The Prefect wished to meet him in person, but Fojian said, "Mingben is a man of stern integrity;
he remains aloof from the world and has no worldly attachments. Even if we were to invite him, I fear he would not comply, so how could he ever come of his own accord?"
Lord Ye firmly invited him. Yanbing said, "This is what is called a 'long-lived elder who presents his body [to the world]'"; he ultimately fled to Mount Sīkong.
Lord Ye looked at Fojian and said, "No one knows a son better than his father. He immediately ordered the various monasteries to issue a formal invitation;
having no other choice, Yanbing finally accepted the summons. (From the *Daily Record of Attendant Xian*)
Formerly, when Master Fojian moved his seat from Taiping to Zhihai Temple, the Prefect, Mr. Zeng Gongyuanli, asked:
"Since you have departed, who will be able to succeed you as the abbot of this seat? Fojian recommended Chan Master Zhibing of Nanhua in Shaozhou;
a native of Yongkang in the Shu region, he was stern and severe by nature, and was thus known at the time as "Bing the Iron."
[Daoyin] succeeded Master Foguan as his dharma heir; he was the fifteenth generation descendant in the lineage of Nanyue. When Mr.
Zeng wished to have him come so that he might seek an audience with the Master, Foguan said, "Faying is a man of firm resolve and upright integrity; he remains aloof from worldly affairs."
"With a mind of profound detachment, he has no personal preferences. Even if invited, he would likely refuse your command;

how could he ever come of his own accord? Although you have repeatedly extended invitations, Baeng said, 'This is what is called a "self-presenting" elder who seeks fame for himself and sells his own interests.
He ultimately fled to Sikong Mountain, located in Taichou County, Anqing."
This was the place where the Second Patriarch transmitted the robe to the Third Patriarch. "Elder" (*zhǎnglǎo*) is a title for one of venerable virtue;
having thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and possessing wisdom and merit within, he causes those who study to revere him, and is thus called an Elder.
The Master looked at Fojian and said, "No one knows a son better than his father; indeed, you are truly father and son. These were words of mutual praise.

He immediately commanded the various mountain deities to make a firm request; "to suppress" means to coerce or to bend. Only after being repeatedly and forcefully coerced did he finally grant his consent to the command.
Those who have always been self-respecting are the ones others come to respect. Do not ever say that such a person is out of touch with the times.
This chapter states that within the breast of a person of lofty character there is a fixed sovereign; thus, they are not moved by honor or disgrace.
Fojian said to Xun Fudeng: "A man of noble character does not regard fame or rank as an honor. One who has attained the principle..."
A person who is not distressed by suppression or frustration, who exerts effort upon receiving favor and offers sincerity when seeing profit—
these are all the actions of those of middling or inferior capacity (from the *Rilü*).
Chan Master Shouchun Fodeng of Heshan, Anji County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang Province.
He was the son of the Shi family of that same prefecture and succeeded Chan Master Fojian Qin. He belongs to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue. [He] said:
"Whenever there are gentlemen of superior insight and discernment who fully understand that the world is illusory and false rather than real, although they possess names..."

One does not regard [high] status as glory or splendor. A person who has attained thorough understanding of the ultimate principle does not regard even the most numerous instances of suppression, humiliation, or frustration as misfortune.
"Suppression" (yī) means to constrain; "humiliation" (qū) means to degrade; "frustration" (cuò) means to crush or break.

There is a certain type of person who, upon receiving another's kindness, immediately hastens to serve them with all their strength and, seeing that the other gains advantage, offers their utmost sincerity.
To treat them with such reverence is the conduct of those who are mediocre or below; what is there to say of it?
△ If you harbor the mind of one who is mediocre or below, you will surely fail your own innate capacity—the measure of humanity that fills heaven and earth. Take care, take care!
This chapter states that an elder must not follow his own private preferences, as he would then be deluded and distracted by external things.
Fojian said to Chief Seat Bian: "In all who are called elders, it is essential that they have no attachment to any single thing.
Should they have attachment to anything, they will be plundered by external objects."

The Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) serves as a model for the monastic community and acts as the eyes and mind for humanity and the heavens. By sharing the seat to preach the Dharma, he guides future generations.

This section teaches people to purify their minds so that they have no attachments. Generally speaking, those who are called "Elders" must have a heart that is vast and empty, possessing not a single object of attachment.
If one possesses even a single attachment, it is as the saying goes: "A single speck of dust arises and obscures the sun."
Emptiness is immediately plundered by that which one cherishes, for these become its thieves.
If one cherishes sensual desires, the mind of greed and attachment arises; if one cherishes gain and offerings, the thought of vying and scrambling arises;

if one cherishes compliance, sycophantic flatterers gather around; if one cherishes victory and defeat, the mountain of "self" and "other" becomes high; and if one cherishes oppression and exploitation, [the calamity follows].
Sighs of lamentation arise.
This section reveals that a wholesome mind changes according to circumstances. If one is fond of sensual desires, the thief-like mind of craving and attachment arises;
if one is fond of gain and offerings, the thief-like thought of vying and scrambling arises; if one is fond of compliance and obedience, then [the thief-like mind of] flattery...
When the thieves of deceitful and sycophantic petty men come to join one, and one delights in victory and defeat, then the mountains of the thieves of self and others grow ever higher.

"Pou-ke" means to amass and collect; it refers to the ruthless stripping away of the people's wealth. When one delights in such exploitation, the sound of the thieves of lamentation and resentment immediately arises.

To summarize and investigate this thoroughly: it does not depart from the one mind. If the mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas naturally vanish. What you have attained throughout your life does not exceed this.
You should exert yourself in this; provide guidance and correction for those who come to study. (Southern Capital Stone Inscription)
This section concludes that the single mind undergoes no transformation. To investigate this thoroughly: how could external objects ever harm me?
In reality, they do not depart from my own mind. If the mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas naturally vanish.
Nothing I have known or attained throughout my life exceeds this. You should exert yourself and cultivate it deeply; by means of this—
It is possible. One may set a standard for those who come to study. If one has no attachment to anything, their purity and integrity can be known.
But if one has even a single attachment, they will lose themselves to unrighteousness. Is this not something to be deeply cautious about?
This chapter cites the conduct of the Master to admonish people to abandon extravagance and follow frugality.

Fojian said: "The former Master was temperate and frugal; his single alms bowl bag and his shoe bag had been patched a hundred times and mended a thousand times, yet he could not bear to discard them.
He once remarked: 'These two items have accompanied me since we left the Pass; it has been barely fifty years. How could I ever be willing to cast them away midway?'"
This section is from Chen Jie-jian. "Jie" (節) means restraint; "jian" (儉) means to eliminate extravagance and follow simplicity.
This refers to how our former teacher was most restrained and frugal in his conduct, while other matters are set aside for now. Let us examine his single alms-bag.
There was a single shoe bag, patched a hundred times and mended a thousand times. "Patched" (zhuì) means joined and repaired. He could not bear to discard it, once saying:
"These two items have accompanied me since I passed through the Kui Pass; it has been barely fifty years. How could I bear to abandon them midway?
This clearly demonstrates his possession of the virtue of frugality.
There was a senior monk named Quan-nan Wu who sent a garment of coarse cloth, saying that he had obtained it from overseas;
he claimed that when worn in winter it was warm, and when worn in summer it was cool. My late teacher said, "When this old monk is cold, I have firewood, charcoal, and paper quilts;
when hot, I have pine wind, water, and rocks. Why should I keep this? In the end, he refused it. (From the *Rilü*).

This section clarifies the absence of craving. Above, that which was worthy of discarding was not discarded; here, that which is worthy of taking up is not taken up—only then does one perceive its wondrousness.
There was a Venerable Master named Wushang from Quannan who sent a robe made of coarse cloth. This was a fabric woven from the fur of two types of mice:
the "ice-mouse" and the "fire-mouse. When the fire-mouse enters the flames, it is not burned; its fur is about a foot long. If it becomes soiled, [it is cleaned with]...
It is washed in fire. In the north there is ice a hundred feet thick, beneath which there are mice that feed only upon this ice;
their fur grows several inches long and can be woven into cloth. When these two are combined, it is warm in winter and cool in summer. This is recorded in the *Shenyiji* (Records of Divine Marvels).
He claimed to have obtained it from overseas; when worn in winter it was warm, and when worn in summer it was cool. This was seen as an extreme marvel.
My former teacher said, "When this old monk is cold, I have firewood and charcoal, and I have paper quilts—paper quilts being quilts made by stitching paper together.
When it is hot, I have the pine wind and water over rocks. What is the use of hoarding such things? Ultimately, he declined [the gift] and departed.
He rejected it. His frugality was such as this. Had he not possessed the subsequent section [of his character], he would have been nothing more than a miserly old man.
Knowing this, one can clearly see the resolve of the sage: he was not moved by external things.
This chapter shows that the ancients cherished people for the sake of the Way; it is not merely a matter of ordinary grief and lamentation.
Fojian said: "When our former teacher heard that Zhenjing had passed away, he prepared a seat and offerings and wept with excessive ceremony, sighing:"

Such a person is difficult to find. He saw the very roots of the Way, devoid of branches and leaves; it is regrettable that he died so young, and I have not yet heard of anyone who has succeeded to his path.
From this point on, the monastic communities of Jiangxi will surely fall into silence (from the *Rilu*).
The Master related how the Fifth Patriarch, upon hearing that Zen Master Zhenjing had passed away, prepared an altar for offerings and wept with excessive grief.

Commenting that the rites of lamentation were too extravagant, he sighed, "A person such as this is truly difficult to find. His realization of the Way penetrated directly to the very root and foundation.
(In botany, the root of a flower is called the *di*, and the root of a tree is called the *ji*. In his preaching of the Dharma, he did not carry any branches.)"

[The Master] sighed, "Leaves! What deity has failed to grant protection? To lament his early passing—amidst the present age, I have heard of no one whose realization and penetration equal that of this Master.
As for those who shall continue the Way and the Dharma, the monastic centers (conglin) of Jiangxi will, from this point forward, likely fall into desolation. [The Master continued:
"To obtain a hundred mediocre men is not as good as obtaining one worthy man. Once he is lost, it is not merely the grief of a single individual."
Who would not grieve?
This chapter sets forth the virtues and deeds of the former patriarchs so that later generations may take them as models, remaining content in poverty to preserve the Way.

Fojian said: "The late master spoke of Master Baoyun, who throughout his life was open and unreserved, devoid of any pretension or guile; yet when it came to matters of righteousness, he was resolute."

Regarding matters that ought to be done, he would leap forward with joy, taking the lead with his own person. He delighted in drawing forth and promoting the worthy and capable, and took no pleasure in forming attachments through fickle or superficial alliances.
Alone upon a single mat, he was serene and composed, sitting upright throughout the entire day.
This section reveals the purity of his innate nature. It is said that throughout the Master’s entire life, his mind was open and unobstructed, retaining not a single thing.
A "citadel" (*chengfu*) refers to a place capable of concealing and hiding;
to say he had "no citadel" means we know this elder’s breast was vast and expansive, with nothing hidden and nothing covered. Whenever he encountered matters that were righteous and reasonable...
He would leap with joy, leading them by his own person. "Leaping with joy" describes the appearance of advancing with delight.

By nature, he was extremely fond of attracting, drawing forth, and elevating men of talent and ability. That which he did not like was this class of people who sought association only for their own profit:
those with wealth they would attach themselves to, while those without resources they would abandon; such were the sort who sought union through expedient means.
During the time [of meditation], there was only a single mat; he remained in a state of *xiāo* (serene detachment), as if at ease, sitting alone in a precarious yet solitary manner. *Xiāo*:
like a bird flying alone, he was naturally composed.
He once said to Attendant Ning, "To preserve the Way and remain content in poverty is the natural lot of a patch-robed monk (*nàzǐ*).
One who allows their steadfastness to be shifted by success or failure, by prosperity or adversity, cannot yet be said to speak of the Way" (from the *Rilù*).
This section clarifies embracing the Way and maintaining virtue. The preceding was the actual practice; this is the earnest exhortation. He once said to Attendant Ning:
"To embrace and maintain the Way and virtue while dwelling peacefully in poverty is the fundamental duty of a patch-robed monk.
If one alters their integrity and resolve based on fortune or misfortune, gain or loss, they are not yet fit to be spoken of as a practitioner of the Way. △ Observe this.
He has reached the ultimate depths; he is a master of the school in its true essence. Who can ever equal him?
This chapter teaches that one should maintain profound integrity and long-term foresight, practicing with diligent austerity and advancing in cultivation.

Fojian said: "If one does not worry for the sake of the Way, the cultivation of the mind will not be far-reaching; if one always seeks ease for the body, the application of the will will not be great.
The ancients underwent hardships and experienced perils before enjoying lifelong peace. This is because when affairs are difficult, the will becomes keen;
when one undergoes austerity and suffering, one's reflections become profound. Thus, they were able to transform calamity into fortune and transform external things into the Way."
This section clarifies that through enduring hardships, one's resolve becomes firm.

It means that for those who practice the Way, if they do not harbor anxiety or form mental preoccupations during their time, one knows that their mind for practicing the Way is not expansive and far-reaching.
If they dwell in their bodies constantly seeking ease and comfort, one knows that the will they employ is not broad and great. How much did the ancients endure when practicing the Way?
Difficulties. One must first encounter many perils and obstacles; only after the path of practice is perfected can one enjoy lifelong peace.
For when a task is difficult to perform, one’s will and spirit become all the more courageous and sharp; when one exerts oneself through austerity, one’s reflections grow ever more profound.
Thus, by practicing with fierce diligence, one is able to transform calamity into fortune and transform external objects [into aids].
This is the Way.
I have often seen students pursue external things while forgetting the Way; they turn their backs on light and cast themselves into darkness.

Thus, they gloss over their own inadequacies and deceive others by pretending to possess wisdom; they force others to reach what they cannot attain and insult them to establish their own loftiness. It is for this reason that—
One deceives others, yet remains unaware that there are those with prior awakening whom one cannot deceive;

one uses this to conceal one's faults, yet remains unaware that there is public opinion which cannot be suppressed. Therefore, the wise consider themselves fools, and the base consider themselves superior.
This section clarifies that those who deceive others by adorning their faults will surely perish.

It is often observed that scholars of recent times pursue external objects while completely forgetting the Way they have studied; this is precisely like turning one's back on light to cast oneself into darkness.
Internally questioning their own minds, they lack clarity regarding principle, yet instead seek to adorn their own deficiencies and treat others with contempt and deception. This causes—
People say of me, "This man is wise. Originally, I was no match for others, yet I was driven by a compulsive desire to surpass them, believing that they could not equal me.
Thus, I treated others with contempt and arrogance, regarding myself as superior.

Little did I realize that in doing so, I was deceiving others through my own lack of wisdom, remaining entirely unaware that there are those of prior awakening who cannot be deceived. By means of this deception—
They treat others with contempt and conceal their own faults, yet they remain unaware that there exists an impartial public judgment which cannot be concealed.
Therefore, when one wishes to appear wise, others perceive them as foolish; when one wishes to appear humble, others perceive them as arrogant.
The wise person, however, is not like this. They recognize that affairs are dispersed and inexhaustible, while human capacity is limited and finite.
To attempt to encompass inexhaustible affairs with finite wisdom results in partiality of consciousness and exhaustion of the spirit;
thus, regarding the Great Way, there will inevitably be deficiencies.
This section states that the worthy person preserves sincerity and thereby realizes the Way. Only those who are truly sagacious and enlightened are not like this.
It is said that worldly affairs are myriad and diverse; how could they ever come to an end? Yet human intelligence is inherently limited.
If you now wish to encompass these infinite affairs with a finite intellect, then your cognitive awareness will— [The sentence is incomplete in the source text.]
However, if one’s efforts are not thorough, there will be partiality; if the spiritual intelligence is left to its own devices without universal discernment, it will encounter obstacles.
When consciousness is biased and the spirit is constrained, one cannot fully realize the Great Way and remains deficient within oneself.
