△ Among those who have achieved the Way throughout past and present, who has not undergone hardships and tasted adversity? Not so.
However, standing in the snow and severing one's arm are both matters of secondary importance.
This treatise maintains that when engaging with the world, one must take the three keys as primary; if these are lacking, the task will not succeed.
Fojian said to Master Longya Cai, "If you wish to reform the faults of those who came before, you must not act with haste;

you must reform them through specific circumstances so that the common folk do not become suspicious, and thus there may be little cause for resentment. I have often said that there are three essentials for a *zhuchi* (abbot):
discerning the situation, being able to act, and having decisive resolve. If one of these three is lacking, then one’s discernment of the situation will be unclear, and in the end, [one will fail]."
When petty people become negligent and disrespectful, the leadership of the monastery will fail to flourish.
Zen Master Zhicai of Longya Temple in Tanzhou was a native of the Shi family of Shuzhou;

he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Foguan Qin and belonged to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage. He maintained that if one wishes to reform the defects of those who came before, one must not act with haste.
"Go! Hurry! means with urgency. One must reform a matter by means of a single method so that base people do not give rise to doubt or confusion, nor cause resentment.
Regarding the three precepts for a resident monk: the first is to view all matters as they truly are.

The first is like the bright sun in the sky, with not even a hair’s breadth of obscuration. The second, which one should practice, is like a great elephant crossing a river, proceeding straight ahead.
The third, the discernment of right and wrong, is like a clear mirror set upon its stand, wherein both beauty and ugliness are reflected together.
If one of these three dharmas is lacking, then one's perception of affairs will not be clear, and in the end, it will lead to [confusion].
If petty people are negligent and disrespectful, they will prevent the Way of the Abbot from being revitalized.
△ These three precepts are talismans for protecting the person. If one loses them, the body will not be at peace and affairs will not be prepared.
This chapter instructs that an abbot should maintain pure conduct and uphold trust with others; this constitutes the true standard of character.
Fojian said: "In being the master of a monastery, what is most valued is the purity of one's practice and conduct, maintaining great integrity to await [the community]."
If monks from the four quarters harbor even the slightest trace of vulgar or improper conduct within themselves and fail to remove it, they will be scrutinized by petty people;
even if their virtue and realization match those of the ancients, students will harbor doubts and refuse to believe them (from *Shantang Xiaocan*).
That is to say, for one who serves as the master of a monastery, what is most esteemed is that he himself maintains pure and stainless conduct in his observances and practice.
In responding to circumstances and engaging with others, he must uphold great faith and strength to welcome monastics from the four quarters.
If there were even a hair’s breadth of vulgar or defiling conduct that one had not eliminated from within oneself,
one would be scrutinized by petty people— “scrutinized” meaning they would investigate and observe. Thus, although one’s Way may be lofty and virtues complete,
no different from those of the ancients, when students observe one’s actual conduct, they will harbor doubts and fail to have faith.
Indeed! △ His conduct was pure and serene. How could this apply only to the abbot? Who would not desire it to be so?
Yet when indulgence and desire arise, and arrogance takes root, the single mechanism of great faith is brought to ruin and destruction.
This chapter reveals that the ancients were upright and possessed integrity and righteousness; few people can equal them.

Fojian said: "Among the disciples of Foyan, only Ga’nan was steadfast and unbending, refusing to conform to worldly sentiments. He had no personal indulgences and acted without seeking partisan support.
Pure, strict, reverent, and cautious, he established himself through fame and integrity from beginning to end—truly a man of antiquity."
Regarding this tradition, among the monastics of recent times, few can be compared to him (as stated in his letter to Geng Longxue).
It is said that among the dharma heirs of Master Foyan, there was only Gaofeng Wu, who was vigorous, robust, and upright.
Furthermore, one does not show favoritism toward others out of private affection; rather, one refrains from greedy attachment for the sake of self-indulgence.
In conducting affairs, one avoids forming factions or seeking alliances. Moreover, one maintains purity and strictness, remaining upright, respectful, and conscientious from beginning to end.

All of them established themselves through fame and integrity; they truly possessed the character and风范 of the ancients. Among the monastics of recent times, few can be compared or ranked alongside them.
These individuals are the foremost models for conduct and behavior in the present age;
one should strive with all one's heart to take them as teachers.
This chapter concerns the abbot presiding over the assembly. It is essential that he never be lacking in vigilance for even a single moment;
yet when facing specific affairs, it is especially vital that he consult widely in order to perfect his conduct.
Master Foyuan said: "The demeanor when presiding over the assembly must be more solemn on ordinary days than during formal occasions;

the speech used when addressing guests should be more dignified in private moments than in public. When one who dwells beneath the forest trees speaks, acts, or undertakes any measure or deed, they must first deliberate and reflect before proceeding.
Do not act with haste or reckless impulsiveness."
Chan Master Fuyan Qingyuan of Shu Prefecture was the son of the Li family of Linqiong. He was a successor of Chan Master Wuzu Faian and belongs to the fourteenth generation under Nanyue.
[This section instructs that] when a *zhuchi* (abbot) is about to undertake a task, he must first exercise careful deliberation before proceeding.
This refers to "Approaching" (Lin). It means the manner in which one approaches the great assembly. It does not consist in momentarily assuming an air of authority or affectation;
rather, it requires that on all occasions of leisure, one must be upright and solemn. The way to establish oneself is to be firm within and gentle without.
In the demeanor of presiding over a multitude, one must receive from above and accord with those below. If one is not harmonious, one cannot engage with others;
if one is not solemn, one cannot govern subordinates. Regarding all speech when addressing guests, the essential point is to speak truthfully and honestly at all times;

how could one possibly feign such refinement at the moment of encounter? As for those with whom one is intimately acquainted, this applies during times of leisure and private solitude—such as when walking in the forest.

As for the person of lower capacity: when revealing a single word or enacting a single deed, or in the midst of any movement, stillness, or deliberate action, they must first calculate and reflect until it is perfectly settled before proceeding.
They must not act with haste or impulsiveness, lest they lose their own wholesome benefit.

If one is unable to reach a decision on one's own, one ought to consult the elders and extensively inquire of the ancient sages to broaden one's knowledge and experience, thereby supplementing what one has not yet mastered and illuminating what one does not yet understand.
How can one vainly display an air of authority and exclusively indulge in arrogance, only to manifest one's own flaws?
If a single action fails at the outset, then even a hundred subsequent virtues will be unable to conceal it.
(To Zhenmu). This section clarifies that I am unable to decide for myself; I must consult the sages of old.
When it comes to the moment of action, if I am unable to reach a decision on my own, I ought to seek counsel and instruction from the elders, inquiring extensively and questioning broadly.
Regarding the sages of the past, one should broaden one’s own knowledge and experience through them, supplement what one has not yet mastered, and illuminate what one does not yet understand;
only then may one be considered a person who employs the mind well. How could one merely display empty prestige and indulge solely in arrogance to manifest one’s own ugliness?
If there is even a single instance of unrighteous conduct that is exposed before the multitude, [the consequences will follow].
Even if one possesses a hundred virtues, they cannot be concealed or glossed over in the end. △ When facing affairs, do not disdain minute scrutiny;

this is how one prevents small matters from becoming grave and stops gradual developments from escalating. Furthermore, by extensively gathering what is seen and heard, and by not being arrogant toward those with empty status, what cause for concern could there be regarding the loss of what one possesses?
This chapter states that profit and desire are difficult to guard against; one should rectify one’s body and mind through the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*).
Foyan said: "When humans are born between heaven and earth, they receive the qi of yin and yang to form their bodies.
Unless one is a Perfected Being (*zhengzhen*) appearing in the world by virtue of the power of compassionate vows, it seems impossible to suddenly eliminate the heart of profit and desire."
This section states that profit and desire are difficult to abandon suddenly.
It means that when human beings are born within the creative transformation of heaven and earth, they receive the endowment of yin and yang qi to form this physical body.

Being inherently ordinary persons by nature, how could they immediately sever the habits of the three poisons accumulated over distant kalpas? Furthermore, they are not the true manifestations of sages who, riding upon...
As for those who, through the power of their compassionate vows, manifest themselves by taking birth in this human world,
it seems that their minds of wealth, profit, and sensual desire cannot be eliminated all at once.
Only the Sage knows that one cannot eliminate people’s desires for profit and pleasure;
therefore, he first rectifies their minds through the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*), and subsequently uses benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom to instruct and restrain them.

Through this daily progress and monthly advancement, he ensures that their desires for profit do not overcome their benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom, thereby preserving their integrity of the Way and its Virtue. (From a Letter to Geng Longxue)

This section clarifies that the sages possess profound knowledge and far-reaching insight. Thus, the sages of antiquity deeply understood that all sentient beings possess irreducible desires for profit and pleasure;

yet, if they were now to seek to transform them from ordinary beings into sages, they would first employ the Way and its Virtue (*moralò*) to cause them to practice and study it, thereby rectifying their minds. Thereafter, they would follow this with...
Humanity, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom—these four beginnings are taught and transformed to serve as the means of embankment and defense.
After such a long time, through the accumulation of years and months, with daily progress and monthly advancement, one becomes unaware and unknowing;

thus, the mind that covets profit and pursues desire can no longer overcome the will toward humanity, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, and therein the Way and its Virtue attain complete perfection.

△ The habitual tendencies of delusion are deeply rooted. How could they be removed all at once? Only by strictly governing the body and rigorously practicing conduct can one eliminate these flaws and bring the Way and its Virtue to completion.
This chapter teaches students to realize their own minds in reality; one must not become mired in words and letters.
Foyan said: "Students must not become mired in words and letters. For words and letters are interpretations based on others;
they obstruct the gate of self-awakening and prevent one from transcending the realm of speech and symbols."
This section clarifies that written characters can obstruct the gate of awakening.
It means that students must not become mired or stagnant within the realm of words and language. For characters and language are merely the dregs of the ancients.
To rely on the speech of others to form one's own interpretations, only serves to obstruct one’s own wondrous realization.
In the end, none can transcend the realm of language and writing.
Long ago, when Daguan Ying first met Master Shimen Cong, he displayed his verbal eloquence within the meditation hall.
Cong said, "What you have spoken is merely talk from paper; as for the subtle and profound essence of the mind, you have not yet glimpsed its depths."
One should seek wondrous awakening.
This section shows that written words have no power in true cultivation. Formerly, Chan Master Tanying of Jinnshan in Runzhou was a successor of Master Shimen Cong;
he belonged to the eleventh generation under Nanyue. Initially, when he first saw Shimen in the meditation hall, [Shimen said:]
He often indulged in the dialectical debates of verbal eloquence. Cong said, "What you have been discussing is merely talk from books.
As for the profound depth and subtle intricacy of your own mind, you have not yet personally witnessed its mysteries.
You ought to seek direct and wondrous awakening."
Upon awakening, one transcends and stands preeminent; one does not ride upon words nor linger in phrases.

Like the roar of the lion king, which causes all beasts to tremble with alarm, when one surveys the study of written characters from this lofty perspective, it is more than merely a matter of ten to a hundred, or a thousand to ten thousand (from *Longmen Jiwen*).
This section reveals that after awakening, one realizes that words and letters are not real. If one has awakened, then one can naturally transcend and stand out as preeminent;
whatever one says does not merely follow the traces of written language nor linger in the constraints of phrasing.
Unhindered in every direction, it is like the roar of the lion king, at which all beasts tremble.

Fearing such alarm and shock, when one reaches this stage, looking back upon the study of written characters from former days, it is not merely a matter of ten to a hundred or a thousand to ten thousand.
△ Written characters are not the truth and cannot be taken as the ultimate study; they are merely distinguished by their being the "branch" (the secondary) rather than the "root" (the primary).
The ailment lies in becoming mired in the characters themselves. Being mired therein prevents transformation and penetration, thereby obscuring one's own nature.
This chapter instructs people that they should use the compass and square to restrain their emotions and remedy defects; it serves as the stairway for entering the Way.
Foyan said to Gaofeng: "The *Baizhang Qinggui* generally aims to rectify the correct and examine the deviant, providing a model for things and bringing order to the assembly."
Thus, one must regulate the sentiments of later generations according to the times. Human sentiment is like water; ritual and law serve as its embankments.
If these embankments are not firm, the water will inevitably break through and overflow. If human sentiment is not restrained, it will run wild and cause disorder.
Therefore, to eliminate sentiment and cease delusion, and to prohibit evil and stop deviance, one may never for a moment dispense with ritual and law.

This section concerns the regulation of the mind through rules and standards. The general purport of Baizhang’s desire to establish the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules) was simply to manifest the True Dharma, restrain deviant conduct, provide a model for people according to the Dharma, and bring order to the great assembly;
it was merely to adapt to the times and thereby regulate the mental dispositions of future generations. Furthermore, as for human beings...
The nature of human emotion is like water. Rules, compasses, and ritual laws serve as embankments to guard against it.
Should the earth and stone of these embankments not be firm and solid, that water will surely cause a surge and break through.
Human emotion is likewise; if one does not restrain unruly passions, they will inevitably run wild and become licentious.
To bring disorder to these is why one must eliminate emotional consciousness, cease delusive thoughts, restrain evil intentions, and halt deviant conduct;
one must not for even a single moment or instant lose sight of the prescribed rules.
Thus, how could the compass, square, rites, and laws possibly prevent human emotions entirely? They are, rather, steps that assist one in entering the Way.
The establishment of these rules and measures is as manifest as the sun and moon; those who look toward them will not be lost. They are as expansive as the Great Way;
those who walk upon them will not be confused. Although the institutions established by the former sages differ, they do not diverge when returning to their source.
This section clarifies that practice resides within the person. If this is so, how could rules, standards, rites, and laws possibly prevent all of human emotion?
This, too, is merely a means of borrowing these [institutions] to assist people in creating a staircase for entering the Way, like a vermilion-paved courtyard.
Thus, one may reach the gateway. The establishment of the compass and square is as manifest as the sun and moon in the sky;
those who gaze upon them are not lost. Its vastness is like a great highway before one; those who walk it are not confused.
Although the establishments of the former sages each differ, they all collectively aim only to lead people to the realm of the wondrous Way.
What is meant is that returning to the source is without distinction.

In recent times, within the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*), there have been those who strictly enforce the rules of labor, those who cling dogmatically to the rules, and those who hold the rules in contempt.
All of these turn their backs on the Way and lose proper decorum; they act thus because they indulge their passions and pursue evil, never having considered the former sages.
It was established for the purpose of rescuing the decay of the Dharma-ending age, restraining the emotions of negligence, blocking the source of craving and desire,
and cutting off the path of depravity (from the *Donghu ji*).

This section clarifies the failure to comprehend the underlying intent. In the monastic communities of recent times, there are those who focus exclusively on outward appearances and laboriously enforce formal regulations;
there are those who fail to grasp the flexibility of expedient means and cling dogmatically to regulations;
and there are those who do not follow ritual laws and treat regulations with contempt. Such views as these all constitute a departure from the Right Path and a loss of Proper Ritual.
To act thus is merely to follow private passions and pursue evil intentions.

One ultimately fails to contemplate the intent of the former sages, who originally established these rules to remedy the accumulated defects of the Dharma-ending age, to prohibit the reckless emotions of negligence, to block the source of human craving and desire, and to cut off the path of human depravity and perversity. △ Do not, by any means, [neglect this].
Misunderstanding the intent of the ancients, you are taught to follow the rules and regulations; this is precisely how one honors their own character.
Those who have silently received its benefits throughout past and present are universal.
This chapter teaches people to reproach themselves and be lenient toward others; one should reflect inwardly and know this for oneself.
Foyan said to Gaocun: "One who can see the tip of a autumn hair does not see his own eyelashes;
one who can lift a weight of a thousand *jin* cannot lift his own body. This is like a student who is clear about reproaching others but ignorant of being lenient toward himself.
"Not a little different" (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
Chan Master Shangu Wuzu of Yunju Hermitage in Nankang Commandery was the son of the Li family of Pan Prefecture.

He was a successor of Chan Master Foyan Yuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation below [Master] Huairang of Mount Nanyue. Regarding the phrase "the autumn hair": Zhuangzi said, "In autumn, the beast grows its fur."
It is extremely subtle. Mencius said: "One whose vision is clear enough to discern the tip of an autumn hair may yet fail to see a cartload of firewood.
This refers to people in the world who possess such keen visual acuity that they can perceive the minute tip of an autumn hair, yet do not see the eyelashes upon their own eyes.
*Jie* (睫) means eyebrows. Furthermore, there are those of great strength and vigor who can lift a thousand [weights].
A *jun* is heavy, yet one cannot lift it by oneself. Thirty *jin* make one *jun*.

Comparing these two cases is like a student who is most clear-sighted when criticizing others, yet becomes blind when applying the same standard to himself—just like someone who fails to see the eyelashes on their own face.
"Not raising the whole body" means there is no difference. Not seeing oneself, not raising oneself—this is a state that cannot be reached by verbal explanation.
Try to see for yourself: where do clarity and obscurity reside? If you understand this, you may be spoken with.
This chapter instructs students that they must possess the eye of a seeker to recognize the character of those who are truly authentic.
Master Wuzu Fayan said: "When I first traveled to the ancestral mountains, I attended a small public sermon by Fojian, in which he said:
'Greed and anger are worse than enemies; one should oppose them with wisdom. Wisdom is like water: if it is not used, it stagnates; if it stagnates, [it becomes turbid]. "
He did not flow [with worldly passions]. When one does not flow, wisdom does not function. As for his greed, desire, anger, and hatred—what were they?
At that time, although I was young, I knew in my heart that he was a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). I then requested to be enrolled as a resident monk under him.
It is said that when I first set out on my travels as a wandering monk (*chánghé*) and arrived at Mount Zu, I witnessed Master Fojian’s informal discourse (*xiǎocān*), in which he said:
"Greed and anger are more dangerous than a vengeful enemy; their harm is no small matter. One must resist them with wisdom."
The wisdom of a person is like water: if it is not used, it becomes stagnant; if it stagnates, it does not flow;
and if it does not flow, wisdom cannot function. Alas, what can be done about greed, desire, anger, and hatred? Having heard this instruction, I was deeply moved.
Although he was young in years, in his heart he knew him to be a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
He then requested to hang his alms bowl and don his robes to rely upon him as a disciple. △ When the tiger was three days old, it already had the scent of beef;
as soon as it emerged, it possessed the eye that discerns people—how magnificent!
This chapter teaches people to maintain a mind that is upright and great; it serves as the foundation for entering the Way.
Gao’an said: "If what a student maintains is central and balanced, then even if they undergo a hundred setbacks, they will remain grandly free from anxiety.
If, however, their orientation is biased and deviant, and they spend their days and nights busily scheming for profit and status, I fear that this magnificent person will come to nothing."
"To abide between heaven and earth" (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
This means that for any student, what is maintained within the breast must be central and not biased, upright and not depraved.
Even if one should encounter various difficulties at any time, and even if subjected to a hundredfold setbacks and humiliations, one must ensure—
The vast and boundless spirit of *haoran* (magnanimity) must always be present; there must be absolutely no thoughts of anxiety or concern.

Only this constitutes the true form of a monk (*shramana*). Should one’s direction become biased or deviant, and for morning and evening one busily schemes to pursue gain and sustenance as one's primary plan—this "busily" refers to a base and petty state, much like being merely mediocre—I fear that such a person is merely a hollow shell.
If one’s person is thus, there will be no place in heaven and earth where one can find peace in the future.
△ This is but a single drop of water from a willow branch; it has revived many people.
This chapter teaches that one should eliminate delusion and remove obstructions in order to perfect virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness.
Gao’an said: "Virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness are not possessed by the ancients alone; they are also present in people of today.

It is only because their wisdom and knowledge are not clear, their learning is not extensive, their spiritual capacity is impure, their resolve is narrow and inferior, and they do not practice with vigor."

Consequently, one is moved by sounds and forms, rendered unconscious of this state. This is because deluded thoughts and emotional attachments have accumulated through long habituation and cannot be suddenly eliminated;
for this reason, one fails to reach the level of the ancients (Letter to Geng Longxue).
That which is called benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom is the innate goodness inherent in human nature. It was not only possessed by people of antiquity;
even today, it has never been absent from humanity. Since all possess it, how can there be a distinction between the ancients and the moderns?
It is simply because the knowledge and understanding of modern people are not clear, their learning is not extensive, and their spiritual faculties are turbid.

It is impure; one’s will and spirit are narrow and base. Furthermore, one’s practice lacks vigor, and one’s mastery is unstable, such that one is ultimately moved away by external objects of sound and form, leading to a lack of self-awareness. Yet, where does the illness lie?
It is simply because a person’s deluded thoughts are many and their mental afflictions are heavy; it is the habitual tendencies accumulated throughout one’s life.
The karmic vapors are so dense that they cannot be removed all at once; this is why one fails to reach the station of the ancients of old.
△ How wondrous is this instruction! Should one not purify the mind and drink it in?
This chapter states that bhikṣus should hold frugality and austerity as supreme; they ought to take the ancients as their model.
When Gao’an heard that Cheng Kugumu resided at Jīnshān Monastery and lived in such luxury and extravagance, he sighed for a long time and said:

"The dharma of a bhikṣu prizes frugality and austerity. How could one act in such a manner? It merely serves to encourage the younger generation to pursue lightness and fatness [of lifestyle], increasing their worldly attachments."
In your insatiable quest for gain, do you not feel shame before the ancients?

Chan Master Fucheng (Famen) of Jingyin Monastery in Dongjing was a native of Hexi. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Daokai of Furong and belonged to the twelfth generation of the Qingyuan lineage.
Throughout his life, he delighted in practicing "withered-tree Chan" (*kumoku zen*), and thus he became known as "Withered Tree."
When High-an Wenhong heard that during his tenure at Mount Jinshan, the master’s personal requisites were luxurious and wasteful, he sighed for a long time and said:
"The principle governing a bhikṣu’s use of things is that what is most valued lies in integrity and frugality."
How could it be appropriate to indulge in such luxury and enjoyment? If one acts as a master [of the household], such opulence is in vain;
it merely provides for those of the younger generation who habituate themselves to lightness and fatness, only increasing their insatiable desire and causing them to seek everywhere.
Will they not feel shame before the ancients who wore grass garments and ate from trees? Regarding "lightness and fatness": this refers to...
This refers to riding in a carriage drawn by fat horses and wearing light furs. An ancient saying goes: "Riding fat horses and wearing light furs, one strolls leisurely through the neighborhoods;
though one may gain the pity of the market folk, one is still despised by those who truly understand.

I often see people of later generations who desire nothing but fine clothing and delicious food, yet they do not know how to enjoy them. When they cannot properly enjoy them, the harm is profound indeed.
This chapter states that the abbot serves as a model for others and must prioritize the monastic regulations.
Gaofeng An said: "The fundamental principle of an abbot is to treat the monastery as his home; he must distinguish roles appropriately and entrust responsibilities to those who are fit vessels."
One’s actions determine the principles of safety and peril; success or failure concerns the source of transformation and education. As a model for others, how can one afford to be casual?
This section clarifies that the abbot has a fundamental essence—that is, the great essence of the abbot’s role—wherein one must not harbor private interests. One ought to...
Taking the monastic community as one’s family inheritance, whatever actions one undertakes must be carefully distinguished to ensure they are appropriate.
The transmission of the Dharma must be entrusted to a worthy vessel; for every movement and every pause, the principles of safety and peril are at stake.
Within the context of gain and loss, these matters collectively constitute the source of spiritual edification. To serve as a model for others, how could such a task be undertaken with ease?
Yes. During the course of one's duties, one must surely act as if walking on thin ice or treading over a deep abyss.

I have never seen a *zhuchi* (abbot) who could cause his disciples to submit through laxity and indulgence, nor one who sought to restrain the arrogance within the monastic community while the legal codes were in decay.
In the past, Chanlin Cheng of Yuyang dispatched the head seat, and Xuanwei of Yangshan demoted his attendant; these accounts are recorded in the classics.
This text serves as a model for emulation.

This section concerning the methods of a teacher must be strictly observed. In this world, we have yet to see one who acts as a teacher while being lax, negligent, or unrestrained, yet is still able to instruct his disciples so that they hold him in reverence and follow him.
Since the rules and regulations have already fallen into decay, how could one possibly restrain them?
To cease the横行, violence, contempt, and arrogance within the monastic community. In the past, there was Chan Master Wushi Jiechen of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture.
He was the son of the Zhang family of Wenzhou and received the Dharma from Chan Master Changling Zhuo. He belonged to the fifteenth generation under Nanyue.
By nature he was stern and resolute, earning him the reputation of having an "iron face. One day, while leading the communal labor (*pǔqǐng*), he first...

The Abbot feigned illness. After the assembly had departed, the Abbot went with his attendant monk for tea and conversation outside the monastery grounds. When the administrative official (Kanjishi) saw this, he questioned him.

The Abbot spoke back defiantly and opposed the official. The official reported this to Zenji (the Head Priest). Zenji ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the community and reprimanded the Abbot, intending to expel him.

The assembly pleaded for mercy on his behalf. Zenji then ordered the Abbot’s office to be vacated, and he was made to serve as an attendant in the Shokumokudō (Hall of Selecting Trees) for guests and officials.
Dazuo was haughty and appeared unhappy. One day, when the Prefect arrived, Dazuo did not go out to welcome him; instead, he conversed idly with an old attendant monk.
Chen (the Prefect) grew angry, summoned the two men, severely reprimanded them, and expelled them. *Chanshi Xingwei of Qushan in Yuanzhou was a native of Heshuo.
He was a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan and belonged to the twelfth generation under Nanyue.* Regarding his character:
He was by nature stern. When presiding over affairs, he maintained strict discipline; when he assigned a certain person to handle a specific task, no one dared to disobey.
Once, he gave the names of twelve individuals to the *vinaya-dhara* (rector), instructing him to have them all arrive at the abbot’s quarters the following day to receive detailed instructions.
When the time for the tea assembly arrived, however, one person was missing. Daowei asked who it was, and the assembly replied, “Sengyuan of Yongtai in Suizhou. Daowei said, “The Head Seat—”
As Tai had not yet returned from his mountain excursion, Wei invited another monk [to take his place]. Shortly thereafter, someone reported that Tai was actually there;

the head seat (shouzuo) had concealed him. Wei assumed a solemn expression and ordered a search, which confirmed Tai’s presence. Tai confessed his own incompetence, fearing he might fail in the duties entrusted to him, and stated that the head seat was truly unaware [of his whereabouts].
Wei then ordered the bell to be struck to assemble the community and declared: "I have been deceived..."

"To deceive the assembly with one's own mind is something others should not even attempt; how much less so for the Head Seat (śrāmaṇera), who occupies the seat of honor and transmits the Way—a position bestowed by the Master himself.
To destroy it from within? Both men were punished and expelled from the monastery. Consequently, the assembly submitted to his impartiality.
Daowei Tai later inherited the Dharma and resided at Huangbo Mountain; the Head Seat was none other than the Great Miao Ancestor of Tanzhou."
Chan Master Xun was the son of the Wu family of Fuzhou. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Daopei Xiu of Dayue, being the thirteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
His record, as preserved in the canonical texts, appears in the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha), and it is sufficient to serve as a model for the Dharma gate.

Now, each person pursues their own private desires, causing the regulations and rules of Baizhang to fall into great ruin. They are negligent in rising early and frequently fail to observe the rites and laws of communal assembly.
Some indulge in greed and gluttony without restraint; others provoke clamorous strife for the sake of gain and sustenance.

As for sycophancy and depravity, there is nothing that does not exist among them. Alas! To look toward the flourishing of the Dharma-gate and the prosperity of the religious teachings—how could this ever be?
"Can it be so? (*Longchang ji*).
This section clarifies that the methods of the masters have not been established [correctly]. Furthermore, those who serve as abbots today do not act in this way;
each follows their own desires, acting according to their whims and passions. They greatly ruin the rules, standards, and measuring lines established by Baizhang. To "ruin" means to destroy.

Furthermore, in the monastic communities (conglin), morning and evening attendance (zao can and wan can) has been the established custom from the beginning. To rise late means to neglect the morning attendance;
moreover, it often results in a deficiency regarding the ritual protocols of daily communal assemblies. Some individuals indulge in gluttony without restraint:
to seek more than one’s need is called greed (tan); to crave more than one’s satiety is called voracity (tao). This may arise from such greedy acquisition.
For the sake of gain and offerings, they fall into clamor and contention; there is nothing among all other fawning, depraved, and loathsome matters that they do not engage in.
Alas! How can such people hope for the flourishing of the Dharma-gate or the prosperity of the religious teachings?
This is truly lamentable. When acting as a teacher to others, one should, during the cold... [text fragment ends]
In times of smoke and rain, look closely at what kind of person you yourself are and what your conduct is like;
this alone constitutes propriety.
This chapter uses the expectations held by parents, elders, and teachers to stir the will of the student, causing them—
This is the result of unremitting diligence.

Whenever Gao-an was at Yunju and saw a monk in his quarters whose realization did not accord with his own, he would immediately seize him by the sleeve, assume a stern expression, and rebuke him, saying:
"Your parents raised your body; your teachers and friends have fulfilled your aspirations. You are free from the pressures of hunger and cold."

"There is no labor of conscription or service here; yet if you do not cultivate the work of the Way with firm and resolute diligence, what face will you have to show your parents, teachers, and friends on another day? When the monastics heard these words, some wept incessantly.
Such was the strictness and severity of his commands.

When Master Gao’an resided at Yunju, whenever he saw a practitioner enter his room for instruction who was unable to respond in accord with his spiritual capacity, he would immediately seize them by the hem of their robe, straighten their countenance, and rebuke them, saying:
"Your parents gave birth to and nurtured this body of yours; your teachers and friends have helped you achieve your aspirations. Furthermore, you rely upon and dwell within this monastic community."
Having received the offerings of faithful donors, one is no longer pressed by hunger or cold.

Once having completed the renunciation of the household life, one relies on the power of the Buddha-dharma and is no longer exhausted by military service or corvée labor—military conscription being termed "service" (*zheng*) and civilian levies being termed "labor" (*yi*).

At this time, when the body is at ease and the mind is tranquil, if one is unwilling to establish a firm and resolute will and give rise to a mind of diligent effort (*vīrya*), [one fails to achieve liberation].
"Having accomplished the path-work of our own house, at some other time or another day, with what face shall we go to see our parents, teachers, and friends?
When the monks heard these words, there were those who wept and could not stop. Such was the orderliness of his commands and the severity of his instructions.
△ Hearing these words and shedding tears is the manifestation of the true, original mind.
When one instructs and exhorts them in this manner, who would not leap forward with enthusiasm?
It is evident that the success or failure of human talent depends for half its measure upon the presiding official’s skill in cultivation. How can one not be cautious?
This chapter speaks of how the ancients nurtured people through virtue; their love was ultimate and their compassion profound.
When Gao’an resided at Yunju, he heard that a monk who had fallen ill was moved to the Yanshou Hall.

He sighed with deep lamentation as if the illness were his own, inquiring after him morning and evening, even to the point of personally boiling and cooking for him. He would not eat until he had first tasted the food himself. This was so even when the weather...

If it is slightly cold, he pats the person on the back and asks, "Are you not wearing too few clothes? If it happens to be hot weather, he observes their complexion and asks, "Are you not suffering from excessive heat?

If they are unfortunate enough to pass away, he does not inquire whether they have any possessions; rather, the monastery’s permanent funds are used to provide full funeral rites and escort them to their destination.

If an administrator attempts to decline this duty with some excuse, Gaofeng An rebukes him, saying: "In the past, Baizhang established the monastery's permanent funds for the sake of the elderly and the infirm. You [should not neglect this]!"
The sick shall not die.
This section concerns the preservation of sincerity through compassion. When the Master resided at Yunju, whenever he heard that a monk was ill, he would have him moved to the Yanshou Hall.
As for the name "Yanshou" (Prolonging Life), it was a place for providing comfort to the elderly and the infirm. Such has been the tradition of the monastic communities since ancient times.
The elderly were sent to the Anle Hall (Hall of Peace and Happiness), and the sick were sent to the Yanshou Hall (Hall of Prolonging Life), which is today also known as the Nirvana Hall.
The Master then sighed with deep emotion, as if the matter were his own; he regarded the sick as if they were his own children.
Day and night, he personally attended to them in inquiry after their well-being, even going so far as to decoct medicines and cook food himself, always serving it to them with his own hands.
Regarding the sick: one should first taste [the food] oneself; if one has not tasted it, one should not give it to them for eating.
If the weather happens to be somewhat cold, one should pat the back of the sick person and ask, "Are you not wearing too few clothes?

If it should happen to be hot at that time, one should observe their facial expression and ask, "Is it not too hot? If, unfortunately, their allotted lifespan has already come to an end, there is no further...
Regarding the principles for the deceased, one does not inquire whether the person had robes or an alms bowl; everything is provided from the permanent endowment (sangha property).

Following the standard protocol of the monastic community, they are escorted with full rites. However, the administrative officers (karmadāna) may sometimes use other excuses as a pretext to avoid their duty.
The Master immediately rebuked him, saying, "In the past, Baizhang originally established the permanent endowment for those who were aged or infirm.
Does it mean that you are neither ill nor dying?
Those from the four quarters who recognized his character held him in high esteem. When he retired from Yunju and passed through Tiantai, many *zhendi* (monastic disciples) followed him.
There were only fifty people; among them, some who were unable to go away wept and took their leave.
Such was the power of his virtue to move others (from the *Shantang Xiaocan*).
This section concerns the presence of supreme virtue. Those with wisdom and insight from the four quarters revered him as a man of sublime excellence.
When he retired from Yunju and traveled to Tiantai, the monks who followed him numbered barely fifty;
some who were unable to go with him wept as they parted. This was because his teacher’s magnificent virtue moved them deeply.
How regrettable! Lately, in the monastic communities, it would be sufficient simply not to disdain or resent those who are ill.
I do not know where the heart of compassion has gone.
This chapter shows that a practitioner of the Way may find joy anywhere and need not be selective about their dwelling in order to achieve self-contentment.
When Gaoyuan retired from Yunju, Yuanwu wished to restore Foyin’s Wulong Hermitage as a place for him to rest and retire.

Gaoyuan said, "For one who dwells beneath the forest trees, if there is the joy of the Way and righteousness, the physical form can be cast aside. For me, this is a matter of following the heart's inclination."
It was his year [of passing]. Like the morning moon at Changgeng, how long can its light and shadow endure?

Moreover, the western mountains and Mount Lu, with their forests and springs stretching out before one, are all places for my retirement in old age. Why must one possess them personally before they can be enjoyed?
Not long after, he took up his staff and traveled to Tiantai, where he eventually passed away on Mount Huading (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
After Master Gao’an retired from Yunju, Zen Master Yuanwu treated him with the utmost honor and affection.
He wished to renovate Wolong Hermitage, which had been founded by Chan Master Foyin, to serve as a place for leisure and retirement in his old age. The Master said:
Those who study the Way beneath the forest trees take virtue, morality, integrity, and righteousness as their true joy;

they can cast aside their physical forms as matters of secondary concern—how could such things be worth cherishing? Moreover, I have now reached the age where one follows the heart’s desire, and my remaining years are not long.
Confucius said, "At seventy, one follows the heart's desires without overstepping the boundaries," meaning that in all matters—
To act according to one's desires without transgressing the laws and measures. When one reaches such an age, it is like the morning moon or the long-ke (the evening star):
how much longer can its light and shadow endure? To the east is the "Opening Light," called Venus;
to the west is the "Long-Ke," called Mercury. Venus appears when the sun rises from the west; Mercury appears when the sun sets from the east. Furthermore, first...
The sun rising is called *qīmíng* (the Illuminator); the sun setting behind it is called *chánggēng* (the Long Tail).
As for the morning moon—such as that of the twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth day—it is said that as soon as it appears, dawn has already broken; thus its radiance does not endure long.
Furthermore, at Mount Lú in the Western Hills, where mountain forests, springs, and rocks lie one after another and face one another, all of these places are suitable for me to rest in my old age.
Why must one necessarily find joy only in a place that one governs oneself? Before long, he took up his staff and traveled to Tiantai.
Later, he passed away on Mount Huading. △ Not only does the motherwort (*shanyao*) dispel sorrow;
by reading this, one will naturally find joy.
This chapter states that the abbot should diligently guide and assist [the students], enabling them to bring their excellent potential to fruition. Gaoyuan said:

"Among the monastics, there is no distinction between the worthy and the foolish; it depends entirely upon the spiritual mentor (kalyāṇamitra) to cultivate their virtue and practice through patient and thorough instruction."

They were tested through successive trials to bring forth their talents and abilities; they were honored with rewards to give weight to their words; and they were treated with exceptional care to preserve their integrity.

As the years accumulated, both their reputation and their actual accomplishments flourished. Indeed, all people possess a spiritual nature; it is only through diligent guidance that it is brought to fruition.

This section clarifies that the cultivation of talent depends upon the teacher’s skillful and gradual molding. Generally speaking, among monastics there is originally no fixed distinction between the wise and the foolish;
it lies solely with the master to guide them through subtle and indirect means so that they may advance in virtue and cultivate their practice.
During their daily activities, the master should exert them through diligent labor and test them through various tasks, thereby causing their excellent potential and talent to emerge.
It can be done. Furthermore, one must honor and commend them, thereby revering the words they have uttered;
and one must also treat them with special favor and affection, thereby fully preserving the conduct they maintain.
In this way, from year to year, accumulating day by day and month by month, after a long time, their reputation and their actual practice will both flourish.
Is this not the skillful means by which a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) brings one to completion? For all people inherently possess the nature of enlightened awareness;
this nature is the seed. To assist in the sprouting of the sapling of enlightenment, one must rely upon external conditions.
Therefore, one must diligently entice and guide them.

It is like jade within its ore: if it is merely tossed aside, it remains a mere tile or stone; yet if it is polished and refined, it becomes a *gui* or *zhang* ritual vessel. It is also like water at its source.
When obstructed, it becomes muddy silt; when dredged and cleared, it becomes a river and marsh.

Thus we know that in this age of semblance, it is not only that the worthy are neglected and left unused, but that in the ways of nurturing and encouraging them, there has likewise been a failure to reach the mark.
This section uses a metaphor to clarify the necessity of encouraging and praising the worthy. It is like a fine jade gem within its raw stone matrix;
if it is cast aside, it will ultimately become nothing more than a common tile or stone. "Casting aside" means to discard.

However, if it should encounter a skilled craftsman who polishes and carves it, it will surely be fashioned into a *gui* or a *zhang* ritual vessel. "Polishing and carving" refers to the treatment of jade and stone; once it has been carved...

Furthermore, one polishes it; this means that although it is already refined, one seeks even greater refinement. A *gui* is circular at the top and square at the bottom, fashioned from auspicious jade.
The Duke holds the *huang gui* nine inches long; the Marquis holds the *xin gui*, and the Earl holds the *gong gui*, both seven inches long.
Half of a *gui* is called a *zhang*. It is also like the source of water: if it is obstructed, it becomes silted up.
"Mud. Suppose there were someone to dredge it; then it would surely become a stream or a marsh. "Ai" means to block; "jun" means to deepen.
Viewed from this perspective, among those in the age of the semblance dharma, it is not only that their worthies are neglected and left unused;

rather, how can one help but lament that the sentiments of the teachers who provide care, nourishment, and upbringing, as well as the methods for exhorting, inspiring, and guiding them, have been lost?
They have not yet arrived.
During times when the monastic forests were flourishing, those who were considered discarded timber in the declining age became wise once the era of prosperity dawned.

Thus it is said: "All people possess the spiritual essence; it is only through diligent guidance that they are brought forth. From this we know that the talents of scholars rise in accordance with the times.
If one encourages it, it arrives; if one promotes it, it becomes lofty; if one suppresses it, it declines; if one rejects it, it is severed.
This is how the virtue, conduct, and talent of scholars wax and wane (Letter to Li, the Transport Commissioner).

This section concludes by establishing the merit of diligent guidance. During times when the monastic communities were flourishing and harmonious, those who were then regarded as discarded materials of a degenerate age—how could they have been anyone else?
Thus, it was the ignorant who, in a degenerate age, found no one to nurture them; yet it was the wise who, during a time of revival, served as their guides and instructors.

Therefore it is said: "All people possess the spiritual essence; it is only through diligent guidance that they are brought forth. Thus we know that the talents of a student depend entirely upon how the master employs them.
When employed at the proper time, they ascend; when discarded at the improper time, they descend.
Therefore, if the master treats the student with kindness and beauty, students from all four quarters will gather together; he must encourage and guide the student in their studies.
Thus, they will be revered without being constrained. If one were to suppress them, the people would decline;
if one were to expel them, the people would sever their own ties. This is precisely what causes the morality, virtue, and talent of scholars to either diminish or flourish.
A fine man is not to be pitied. I wish that those who act as teachers would be earnest and sincere.
This concerns seeking out worthy individuals and bringing them to fulfillment.
This chapter discusses serving as a model for others; its essence lies in self-discipline, so that what is commanded above may be practiced below.
Gaoyuan said: "In the great work of teaching and transforming others, nothing takes precedence over morality, virtue, ritual, and righteousness.
If the abbot honors morality and virtue, then students will prize respectfulness; if he practices ritual and righteousness, then students will feel shame at greed and competition.

If the abbot displays the arrogance of improper demeanor, then students will fall into the vice of insolence and violence; if the abbot engages in disputes with agitated expressions, then students will likewise [succumb to strife]."
Regarding the calamity of strife and combat, this section clarifies that in the practice of transformation and education (*śāsana*), one must preserve the fundamental principle.

That is to say, among all essential matters in carrying out transformation and education, nothing takes precedence over rectifying the mind through morality (*dharma*) and virtue (*mārga*), and further cultivating the person through benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*). This applies to those who maintain the teachings.
If the master honors the Way and its virtue, then the student will also honor the Way and its virtue, and what they harbor within will be reverence.
If the master practices ritual and righteousness, then the student will also possess ritual and righteousness, and will naturally feel shame regarding greed and competition.
If the master lacks noble magnanimity and displays the arrogance of improper demeanor, then the student will immediately resort to insults and violence.
Such were the evils that arose. Had the abbots not been dignified and grave, but instead displayed agitation and contention, then students would have fallen into the calamity of assault and strife.
The former sages, perceiving this before it occurred, consequently selected men of wisdom and sagacity to preside over the monasteries, so that all might look up to them with reverence.
They transformed others through non-explanation. Thus, during the era when the Way of Shitou and Mazu flourished, eminent and heroic figures emerged;

their deportment was gentle and refined, and they were harmonious and solemn. Whether in speech or in issuing commands, even a glance of the eyes or a raising of the eyebrows could serve as a model for posterity—this was only to be expected (as stated in the Letter to Sīxin).
This section shows that the realization of the Path of Vision depends upon wisdom. This is why the ancients possessed foresight;
they prevented problems before they arose by selecting men of wisdom to preside over the monastic communities (*senglin*). Thus, all people were enabled to gaze up in reverence.
