He succeeded Master Nian of Mount Shou; he was the ninth generation under Nanyue. "Ji" means to stimulate; "yang" means to raise up.

This follows the principle of "stimulating the turbid and raising the clear": those who are muddled are stimulated so that they may exert themselves, while those who are pure are raised up so that their excellence may be more easily seen.
"Chou" refers to responding; "chang" refers to chanting in harmony. This means that these various great elders received his...

They inspired and exalted one another, responding to each other's verses in turn; these instances are recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), all of which can be verified by historical facts.
For example, there was Yang Wude’s study under Baiyun Yuan and Zhang Wujin’s meeting with Doushuai Yue.
This Doushuai Yue was Chan Master Congyue of Doushuai Temple in Longxing Prefecture; he was surnamed Xiong and was a native of Ganzhou.
His disciples succeeded Master Wenzhenjing, all of whom knocked upon the essential gates where it is difficult to pass yet they were able to pass;
they struck at the obstructed joints where there was no penetration yet they were able to penetrate. This means they struck its pivotal mechanism and struck its vital joints.
He upholds the seal of the patriarchs and reveals the true function, enabling others to rejoice throughout their lives and thoroughly realize the profound depths of the source;
how could this be in vain? Recently, there was the Vice Minister Zhang Wugou, whose name was Jiucheng, his courtesy name Zishao, and his style name the Layman Wugou.
A native of Yanguan in Hangzhou, he attained the Dharma from Chan Master Miaoxi Gaofeng.
The Participant in State Affairs Li Bing, style name Hanlao, received the Dharma from Chan Master Miaoxi.
The Hanlin Academician Lü Benzhong, style name Jurin, sought the Way from Miaoxi; thus it is said that both had "seen the hall and entered the chamber."
Students requested further instruction and inquired about the Way, consulting him to resolve their doubts. They ascended to the meditation hall and entered the inner sanctum.
As for those who are "friends in the Way beyond the mundane," they have emerged from the confines of worldly toil and are liberated from the constraints of ordinary sentiments.

Therefore, they are called "friends beyond the mundane world. Within their respective minds, should there arise even the slightest thought of love or hatred, or encounter circumstances of adversity or favor, they immediately and resolutely cast them aside.
It is like a stroke of lightning sweeping everything away, allowing no room for anything to settle or linger.
The true fruit is liberated and transcendent, unbound by worldly sentiments or vulgar airs, and free from all hesitation or constraint.

Whenever anyone witnesses such conduct, who would not fold their robes and draw back in awe and trepidation, as if beholding the great ocean, whose boundaries and shores are impossible to perceive? Yet, he possesses a name.
Even those who are gentlemen of high station still seek out the great elders of the Zen forest in secluded places,
on the shores of solitude, by watersides or beneath the trees, intending to measure whether they might surely wish to settle this mind within the tranquility of Zen,
awaiting its manifestation as the wondrous nature inherently possessed from the beginning. Part One.
The essential point is to make people know that those who are good should be emulated. Next, it teaches that those who are not good should be avoided.
In later generations, people no longer look to the models of former virtuous ones, but instead devote themselves solely to flattery and seek advancement through crooked means.

Generally, when those serving as abbots recommend someone for the title of "Elder" (Laozhe), they often write on their calling cards (shaci) to address them as "gate-monks" (menseng) and treat their predecessors as "benevolent lords" (enfu).

They seize the property of the *cāturdīśa* (the Sangha of the four quarters) and present it as bribes to flatter those in power; the wise look upon this with pity and laughter, yet these people remain complacent and feel no shame.

This section describes how there are none who uphold the Dharma. The preceding section enumerated the liberated states and images of former sages who attained transcendental awakening to their own nature;
this section fully details the manner in which sycophants seek favor and bring ruin to the Dharma-gate—each has its respective purpose.

This is a matter of gravity. It refers to people of later generations who, failing to see the exemplary conduct and models of the former virtuous ones, ultimately do not sustain themselves through the Way, but instead devote themselves solely to the art of clever speech, insincere countenance, and flattery toward famous officials. They employ such devious means.
There is no one who does not excessively seek power and influence, striving only for advancement and high status.
Among the monastic communities, those who recommend others by name to serve as abbots or elders are themselves not the actual individuals [who hold such positions].
Yet they do so by force. Regarding "writing a *cì*": it refers to writing one's name upon a slip of bamboo or wood, which is called a *cì*.
They often write such letters, referring to themselves as "monks under your gate" (*ménxià sēng*) and addressing those of noble lineage before them as "Honored Family, Great Donor" (*ēnfǔ dàtányuè*).
As for "taking what belongs to the community," this refers to wrapping up rare and precious items to present as offerings. "Baojū" (bundles) means to wrap up rare treasures to offer.
This is flattery and sycophancy. Therefore, it causes those of wisdom to feel pity and break into derisive laughter.
Yet, in the end, they themselves remain complacent and do not know shame. "Complacent" (tián) means peaceful and at ease.
Alas! We, the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya, travel like clouds and birds with but a single flask and a single bowl;

we are not pressed by the hardships of cold or hunger, nor do we harbor attachments to children, jade, or silks. Yet why must we bend our waists and sweep the ground, shivering in misery and crouching in fear, bringing such humiliation and degradation upon ourselves?
This section laments their lack of shame. The two characters "O-hu" (Alas! express deep sighing over the extreme ignorance of those people.
However, I am a śramaṇa; I am a son of Śākyamuni. It is only right that I emulate the Buddha:

with a single flask and a single bowl, like clouds emerging from a mountain peak, like birds soaring high into the sky. As it is said: "A single bowl receives offerings from a thousand households; a solitary body [wanders] through ten thousand..."
Wandering through the villages, he is neither oppressed by hunger and cold, nor does he have children, jade, or silks to which he is attached.
Originally a man of carefree spirit, for what reason has he now come to bend his waist and sweep the floor?
Why has he reduced himself to such a state—so cramped and miserable, bringing humiliation upon himself and seeking out lowliness for himself? *Bending the Waist* (Zhéyāo)
This refers to the posture of breaking at the waist. During the Jin dynasty, there was Tao Qian, styled Yuanming and nicknamed Yuanliang.

Five willow trees grew before his gate, so he called himself Master of the Five Willows. He served as the Magistrate of Pengze; by nature simple and noble, he would not privately curry favor with his superiors.
One day, a district magistrate’s supervisor (*duyōu*) was dispatched by the superior to the county. The officials said that Tányuáng should put on his formal belt to receive him.

Tányuáng sighed and said, "How could I, for the sake of five *dǒngǔ* [measures] of rice, stoop my waist before the petty children of my hometown? That very day, he untied his sash and resigned from office, composing the "Return Home" (*Guīqùláicí*) poem.
The historian Yǒng remarked: "How could such a man of talent and distinction be forced to submit to a low-ranking post? At his gate... [he planted five... (text fragment).
The affairs of Liu [Zhang] were desolate; the phoenix does not compete with the chicken for food. Do not take offense at this gentleman’s laziness in bowing his waist.
One who "holds the broom" is one in the form of a sweeper. When Emperor Gaozu of Han ascended the throne, he visited his father once every five days.
The Grand Duke (Tang Gong) treated him according to the rites between father and son. The Grand Duke’s household steward said to him: "Though Gaozu is your son, he is now the sovereign."
Furthermore, although the Duke of Tai was the father of the Emperor, he was nonetheless a subject. How could one who is a sovereign bow before a subject?

If this were done, the gravity of imperial authority would not be maintained. Later, when the High Ancestor (Gaozu) visited the Duke of Tai’s court, the Duke swept the path with a broom and retreated backward as he approached the gate.
The High Ancestor was greatly startled and descended from his carriage to support the Duke. The Duke said, "The Emperor is the sovereign; how can I [be treated otherwise]?"
The laws of the empire were thrown into disorder. Thereupon, the High Ancestor honored the Grandfather as the Emperor of the Most High.

He approved the words of the House Steward and bestowed five hundred catties of gold upon him. "Sour and cold" (*suanhan*) refers to a state of terror; it means the body shivers and the heart is chilled. *Ju* means to bend the body.
*Ji* means to take small steps by placing one foot upon the other. These terms describe a person in a state of fear, such that they dare not move freely.
He stretches his limbs, yet dares not relax his feet; he bends his waist into an eight-character posture, exhausting every possible expression of sycophancy and flattery.
To address someone as "Enfu" (Lord of Grace) is merely a private invention of one's own, lacking any basis in principle.

One foolish and vulgar person initiates it at the front, and a hundred such fools harmonize with it from behind; they vie with one another to offer it up, truly acting like petty and lowly creatures who weaken their own integrity.
In matters of social influence and moral instruction, nothing is more severe than the presence of sycophants. These are truly the precursors of villainy, depravity, and deceit.

Even upright men and virtuous scholars, if they are skillfully drawn into their influence, will find themselves ensnared in unrighteousness and fall into irremediable loss of virtue. Is this not to be lamented?
This section again brings forward the common man. The title "Enfu" (Lord of Grace) originated from the private interests of sycophants;
it originally has no basis in fact. When one reckless and vulgar person initiates it first, hundreds of reckless and vulgar people harmonize with it thereafter.
Anticipating their mutual flattery and servility, these are truly nothing but base and lowly petty men.
There is no sycophant more capable of weakening the noble traditions and holy teachings of our ancestors than these individuals.
Furthermore, one must understand that this is precisely the origin of all treachery, wickedness, and deceit.
Even upright men and virtuous scholars, when skillfully manipulated by them, will join their ranks; consequently, an entire class of good people will cause themselves to fall into ruin.
This is the land of righteousness. That one should lose virtue amidst a state of no rescue—is this not to be lamented?

These bhikṣus who destroy the Dharma are the locus of demonic influence; they are shameless in their deception and self-assurance, falsely assuming the physical marks of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), taking the great elders of the Zen groves as their lineage masters, and flattery-seeking after the powerful and noble of the path as their kinsmen. They extend [their influence] without being invited...

I respectfully submit that you have initiated the ruin of the Dharma. That laypeople ascend the dais and prostrate themselves beneath it is a perverse violation of the sacred regulations and a great disgrace to our school’s tradition.
The decline of our Way has reached this extreme. Alas! To be struck by Heaven’s punishment and recorded in the registers of the spirits—how could ten thousand deaths atone for this?
Are these not indeed sycophants?
This section severely rebukes such sycophants. Those who are a class of bhikṣus who destroy my path of the Dharma are all possessed by demonic influences;
therefore, they are uniformly deceitful, boastful, and arrogant, remaining entirely without shame.
Deceiving others, he manifests the physical form of a learned master and points to a renowned elder of a Zen forest as his own lineage teacher;
he flatters high-ranking officials to claim them as his own kinsmen in the Dharma, proffering unsolicited respect that is entirely a deception of others.
He initiates the beginning of the destruction of the Dharma, unaware that he is only bringing ruin upon himself.
The layperson ultimately went ahead and ascended the seat, while the monk of preceptual conduct returned to prostrate.

This was a perverse violation of the Buddha’s regulations and a great disgrace to our school’s tradition. Alas! How could I have expected that the decline of our Way and Dharma would reach such a point all at once?
The two characters "Wu-hu" (Alas! express lamentation; they represent the utmost depth of my grief and resentment. Master Guiyun said: "This one..."

Such are the seeds of karma. When celestial beings come to kill others or spirits come to seize them, leading them to ten thousand deaths, who else but a sycophant could commit such unforgivable crimes?
Those who come after should know this and ought to guard against it with deep sorrow.
Master Song’s *Yuanjiao* states: "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, those who met the Son of Heaven did not act as subjects.
When receiving official decrees, they were addressed as 'Duke' or 'Master. Sengyuan of Mount Zhong did not rise from his seat to welcome the imperial carriage when it reached his gate.
Huairan of Tiger Creek did not leave the mountain despite an imperial summons when the Emperor visited Xunyang. In their time, the world honored such men and revered their virtue."
Therefore, the Way of the Sages is sustained.
This section clarifies that the Perfected Person values themselves highly, advancing the matter one step further so that people may know that the Buddha-dharma is thus revered;
it is simply that none but the Perfected can practice and preserve it. Master Mingjiao has an original [text] on this.
The *Jiaolun* states: "In ancient times, eminent monks did not perform the etiquette of subjects before the Son of Heaven; rather, the Son of Heaven admired these eminent monks.
Whenever there was an imperial edict or decree addressed to them, he invariably honored them by referring to them as 'Duke' or 'Master.

In the eighth month of the first year of the Jianyuan era (the Gengchen year) of Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty, the Master Sengyuan of Zhongshan had an audience with the Emperor, who arrived at Zhongshan in person."

Mount [Shan]. By chance, Emperor [Wu] visited the śramaṇa Sengyuan. When the Emperor inquired after him, Sengyuan remained seated on his bed, declining to welcome him on account of his old age and illness.
Gaozu intended to go beneath the bed to see him. His attendants said, "The room and the couch are too narrow to accommodate a palanquin or a canopy."
He then halted his carriage to inquire after him with great courtesy before departing. Furthermore, Huiyuan resided in the mountains for over fifty years. At first, his provisions were insufficient;
for more than twenty years, he drank from mountain streams and ate only forest fruits. People from all quarters admired his lofty character.
On the day of his death, a memorial was submitted to the Emperor, who subsequently honored him as his teacher and provided an imperial burial at Mount Zhong. —From the *Lushan* (Mount Lu) section.
The Chan Master Huixi (later known as Huiyuan) of Lintusi in Shandong was the son of the Jia family of Loufan in Yanmen.
He was extensively versed in the Six Classics and was particularly proficient in the *Book of Changes*. Once, together with his younger brother Huichi, he visited the seat of Dharma Master Dao’an;

upon hearing him expound the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he sighed in joyful admiration, saying, "The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are but mere chaff. He then shaved his head and left the household life.
Taking it as his own responsibility to uphold the Great Dharma, when the region of Guanzhong fell into turmoil, the Master traveled south to Xunyang.
Upon seeing Mount Kuang, he took a liking to it and built a thatched hut among its peaks. The local governor, Yuan Huan, revered his virtue and morality, and established a vihāra for him there.
At that time, the Jin dynasty was in decline, and many men of extraordinary talent throughout the realm remained in seclusion and did not serve in office.

The Master established the Lotus Society, gathering several hundred scholars and monks to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. When Emperor An of the Eastern Jin arrived at Xunyang, he issued an imperial decree for Huiyuan to appear once before him.
The Master declined on the grounds of old age and illness and did not go forth; the Emperor’s respect for him increased all the more, and he issued an edict to Jiujiang.
The Prefect provided him annually with provisions and travel requisites. The Master chose to reside there for thirty years, his shadow never leaving the mountains.
He set the Tiger Creek Bridge as the limit beyond which he would not escort guests. He authored the *Kuāngshān Collection* in thirty fascicles, which circulated widely throughout the world.
Among the eighteen worthies of the Lotus Society, the presiding master was the Great Master Huìyuǎn of Dōnglín, known as Biànjué; he was from Yànmén.
Dharma Master Huizhi; Great Master Jueji Huiyong of Xilin; Buddhabhadra (Juexian) from India; Buddhayaśas (Jueming) from Kaśmīra;
Great Master Dao-sheng of Donglin, who brought universal salvation;
Dharma Master Tanheng; Dharma Master Sengrui; Dharma Master Tanshun; Dharma Master Daobing; and Dharma Master Tanxian.
Dharma Master Daojing; Zhang Xuanxiu Shishuo of Nanyang; Zhou Xuzhi Daodan of Yanmen;
Liu Yimin Zhongsisi of Pengcheng; Lei Cizong Zhonglun of Yuzhang; Zhang Yaocai Minmin of Nanyang;
and Zong Bing Shaowen of Nanyang—when these men were active, there was no sovereign who did not take the Buddha-mind as his own mind.
If one cannot revere a high monk, it is because he is not a monk of ultimate virtue;
nor can such a person move the Son of Heaven. Only when there is both such a person and such virtue does the Way of the Sages flourish.

Those who admire the lofty character of such eminent monks in later generations may associate with high officials and ministers, yet they still cannot even participate in the rites accorded to a low-ranking scholar.
In their conduct both in public and in private, they do not even approach the self-contentment of an ordinary man;

how much less could one compare them to Sengyuan’s audience with the Emperor, or Huìyuǎn’s composure? If we hope for the flourishing of our Way, can the cultivation of us people truly be attained [in this manner]?
Alas! To preserve the teachings while not having the person [to embody them]—what benefit is there in preserving them? Thinking of this alone, tears have never failed to fall.
In the Dingyou year of the Chunxi era, I retired from my duties at Xian'en Temple and took up residence in a small valley on the western mountains of Pingtian.

Observing what I saw and heard there daily, I found that affairs were largely hypocritical and the ancient style had fallen into decay; thus, my words would neither add weight nor diminish their faults.
I have recorded this briefly to admonish myself (An Auspicious Event in the Forests).
This section speaks of the absence of true monks in later generations. Those in later ages who admire eminent monks do so based on nothing more than hollow reputations.
Even when people today associate with high officials and great scholars, they cannot even receive the courtesy due to a commoner of the lowest rank. As for all of these...
When he went out, whether at the proper time or place, he was so cautious and constrained that he did not dare to act according to his own will;
he was not as free and easy as ordinary people. How could he have met with the Son of Heaven on the same couch and seat like the monk Sengyuan?
How much more so when, like Huiyuan, messengers arrived with imperial commands yet he remained composed?
Since you do not attain self-mastery as ordinary people do, there is no one to nurture the Way.

Under such circumstances, how can you hope for the flourishing of our Dharma-gate or the cultivation of its practitioners? Though the teachings may still exist, no master of true practice is to be seen.
I have not seen anyone who possesses true devotion; what benefit would there be in preserving [this work]?
When the Venerable Founder brought this to my attention, I thought upon it and could never help but feel heartache and shed tears.
In the *dingyou* year of the Chunxi era, I first declined the affairs of Xian'en Temple and took up residence in a small valley in the western mountains of Pingtian. Recently...
Regarding various matters I have occasionally seen or heard, there is much hypocrisy and the ancient style has fallen into decay;
my words are not enough to carry weight or lightness, yet I have recorded them briefly for my own admonition. The ancients gave their whole heart and their full strength.
As for that which is utterly beyond human power, it serves only to let future generations know what is truly held in high esteem. Alas!
Who could ever unify the secular with the pure beneath a single word?
The essential purpose of this treatise is for people to follow the teachings and practice the Way, so as not to betray the intentions of the ancients.
The Reverend Yuanji Cen appended a postscript stating: "The Buddha’s era is remote, and the True Dharma has grown faint. A spirit of decadence prevails, reaching its limits everywhere.
The predecessors have passed away, and the younger generation lacks renown. The established standards of the monastic community (Conglin) are nearly swept from the ground. Even if..."
There are those who attempt to support and rescue [the truth], yet they instead regard it as the "barbarian speech" of a petty king.

Now, observing Master Shushan Ben’s *Discriminating the Sycophant*, its phrasing is far-reaching and its meaning vast, profound, penetrating, and illuminating; it is most capable of diagnosing their ailment. However, those who are reckless and vulgar possess dark and limited understanding;
being intoxicated by the realm of the wicked and sycophantic, they will surely mistake the finest clarified butter for a poisonous drug.
Chan Master Yanying Yuanji Yanqin of Taiping Prefecture was a native of Taicheng in Fuzhou.

He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yunju Faru and belonged to the sixteenth generation below Nanyue. The preceding portion is titled "Preface" and the following is titled "Postscript," which states:
"Since the Buddha passed into nirvana, the distance has grown ever greater; the True Dharma has likewise become faint and thin. The winds of decadence and superficiality have overflowed."
They act without anything they do not reach. Those former generations who were mature, steadfast, and dignified have all withered and passed away.
The younger generation and late learners have nothing upon which to model themselves; the exemplary standards within the monastic community (*saṃgha*) are nearly swept from the ground.
As Mencius said: "Tai Jia overturned the statutes and precedents of Tang; they were swept from the ground. These "statutes and precedents" refer to—
This refers to the sage’s righteous method for suppressing the violent, eliminating chaos, punishing evil, and encouraging good.
Even if there were one or two who supported and rescued him, they instead regarded him as a "barbarian king. This is a regional expression meaning a slave within the Dharma-gate.
Now, observing Master Shushan Ben’s “Essay on Discerning the Sycophantic,” the phrasing is extremely profound and the intent is most significant.
Extensive. Furthermore, it penetrates deeply into the principles of truth and clearly elucidates the Buddha’s intent. It is most capable of correcting and eliminating the toxic diseases of humanity;

"zhēn" (箴) is synonymous with "zhēn" (鍼), meaning a needle, and also implies admonition or instruction. However, there is a certain class of frivolous and mediocre people whose intellect and knowledge are inherently dim and shallow.
They are intoxicated—meaning they are in a state of stupor—and their minds are deluded by the realm of the wicked and sycophantic. They must [be guided] by the supreme...
To call the finest cream (amṛta) a poisonous drug is a perverse statement. This postscript is like adding flowers to brocade;
it is intended solely for people to vie with one another in its appreciation.
Through this chapter, we see how the ancients were cautious and self-respecting, such that they could truly bear the title of masters of the monastic groves (saṃghārāma).
Dongshan Master Kōng replied in a letter to Yu Caìmào regarding the loan of porters, saying: "I am deeply grateful for your previous visit and the great kindness you showed me.
Since parting, I have received your letter once more, which only increases my sense of shame. I am originally a man of the mountain caves, indifferent to the world;
Caìmào likely knows this. Although I now serve as an elder residing in the abbot’s quarters, I am still the same 'Kōng' from those former days."

"Venerable Elder, matters concerning the permanent assets—whether their existence or non-existence—are entirely entrusted to the administrative officer. Records of income and expenditure do not pass before my eyes.
I do not store robes or alms bowls, nor do I use the monastery's property. I do not accept invitations from outside, nor do I seek external assistance;
I dwell according to circumstances. I never make plans for the morrow. Since Cai Mao has already been renowned as a veteran of the Way, we should simply forget ourselves within that Way."
This section first clarifies his own conduct. Chan Master Dongshan Huikong of Xuefeng in Fuzhou was a native of the Chen clan of that prefecture.
He was a successor of Chan Master Litan Shanqing and belonged to the fourteenth generation under Mount Nanyue. In a letter he replied, he wrote:
"In the past, I brought you humiliation when you condescended to visit me; I am deeply grateful for the profound affection you have shown. After parting...
Having received your letter once again, my feelings of gratitude and shame have only increased further.
However, I am but a man dwelling among crags and caves, indifferent to the affairs of the world; you likely already know this of my dull nature and lack of talent.
Although today I serve as an elder residing in the abbot’s quarters, in truth, I am merely the same Venerable Huikong from the day before yesterday. Among the permanent residents of the monastery—
All matters regarding the presence or absence of wealth and property were entirely entrusted to the administrative monks; the ledgers for income, expenditure, and disbursements never passed his eyes.
He never accumulated capital for robes or alms bowls, nor did he dare to encroach upon or misappropriate the monastery’s permanent assets.
Furthermore, do not accept invitations from others, nor seek external assistance. All day long, it is best simply to abide as circumstances permit, never making plans for the morrow.
Since Cai Mao has been praised by me for his long-standing devotion to the Way, we both are indeed fellow travelers on this path. We should therefore forget ourselves within the Way.
Thus it is said: "Outwardly, one conforms to the world; inwardly, one dwells in the Dao. *From the "Xin Xue Pian" (Chapter on New Learning) of the *Liezi*.*
The *Zhuangzi*, in the "Dazongshi" chapter, states: Confucius said, "Fish forget one another in rivers and lakes;
birds forget one another in the void; humans forget one another in the Way and its arts. The commentary notes: "When the water is deep, they swim; the fish find their joy therein."
Therefore, they forget one another. In the unobstructed void, the bird finds its joy; therefore, it forgets itself. The Way is vast and boundless;
where both self and other are extinguished, the person finds their joy; therefore, they forget one another.
I have now sought several porters from among those listed in the register. I do not know whether these porters were provided by the monastic estate (chángzhù) or by Master Kōng.
If they were provided by Master Kōng, what resources does Master Kōng possess? If they were provided by the monastic estate, this constitutes the private use of communal property;
once it is used privately, it becomes theft. How could a true spiritual friend (shàn zhīshí) engage in the theft of communal property? Since you, sir, have entered the imperial court...

One should seek good deeds within one's own community; it is not appropriate to undertake such matters in a monastery. You are a native of Fujian, and what you have seen and known are all the practices of the elders of Fujian’s monasteries:
once they take up residence, they plunder the permanent assets of the monastery and make them their own property.

They use these funds either to cultivate relationships with powerful officials, or to provide support for lay families, or to entertain their personal acquaintances. They do not consider that these [assets]...
This refers to the property of the *sāṃghika* community, which is eternally present throughout the ten directions.
This section sets forth the matter at hand: now, within this letter, you seek several porters from me.
However, it is not known whether these porters are to be provided from the permanent property of the monastery (*sthavira-saṃgha*) or from the personal funds of the Venerable K'ung. If...
If it is taken out for personal use, I have nothing at all. If it is taken out for the sake of the permanent endowment (*sangha*), I would then be using the permanent endowment privately.
Once it involves private use, it constitutes theft. How could there be a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who would steal and misappropriate the permanent endowment?
Now that you have entered the imperial capital, your original desire was to seek advancement.
It is certainly inappropriate to seek such matters within the Three Jewels of a monastery. You are originally a man from Fujian;
everything you know and see is merely the fixed abode of an elder from Fujian, where all the permanent property has been plundered.
They treat it as their own property. Some use it to cultivate friendships with noble persons; some use it to provide for lay households;

and some use it to entertain and accompany their acquaintances. They fail to reflect that what they are using was originally the property of the Sangha of the ten directions, belonging to the *caitya* and the resident community.
Those who now shed their fur and wear horns to repay their debts are all people such as these. Since the Buddhas of the past spoke clearly of this, how can one not be afraid?
In recent years, temple buildings have fallen into ruin and the ranks of monks have become sparse; all of this is the fault of those like you.
I pray that you will not place me among such a class. If you truly grant me your trust, then I shall decline everything offered by other temples.
If you do not take [this advice] to heart, then your future career remains immeasurable. I do not know what you will think of these words that are contrary to the ear.
The weather is cold; take care of yourself on your journey. (From the *Yulu*)

This section truly exhorts one not to do what ought not be done. Those who today wear horns and shed hair to repay their debts are mostly such individuals who misappropriated the property of the Sangha.
The Buddhas of the past spoke clearly: the law of cause and effect is manifest and undeniable.
Is this not something to be feared? In recent years, monasteries throughout various regions have fallen into such ruin and desolation, and the ranks of monks have likewise become sparse;
all of this is due to the transgression of stealing the property of the Sangha.
I pray that you will not place me among such a class of people. If you truly place your trust in me, then regarding the foot-allowance permitted by other temples—
If you were to go and apologize to all of them and none would accept [your offer], then your future career and upward advancement would be immeasurable.
These words of yours do not accord with common sentiment; they are indeed harsh to the ear. I do not know what you intend by this.
As the season is at its coldest, I pray that you may take good care of yourself on your journey and eat well. This is my prayer. △ Said.
Fluttering and wafting like flowers falling from jade branches—truly enough to cause one to desire to kill, to envy to kill, and to feel shame to kill.

Regarding Dongshan’s reply to Cai Mao, the Master remarked, "This is truly a pardon for the release of a criminal from before the hall of King Yama."
The masters of the various quarters today who possess the eye of the Way—upon seeing this book, one does not know what they will truly think within their own breasts.
If you can believe and be convinced, upholding and practicing it according to its instructions, there will be great benefit to be gained in the future.

Chan said, "The mountain also says: 'Permanent assets and grain, once set aside for the purpose of providing for the assembly, are like the poison of a *he* bird;
if the abbot or those who manage their disbursement and receipt so much as touch them, their entire bodies will rot away. This is recorded in detail in the Vinaya texts.

This section clarifies that one must strictly observe the precepts regarding causes and effects. Chan Master Fo-zhen Liao-can of Jingzhong Monastery in Zhangzhou, known as Yishan Can, was the son of the Luo family of Quannan.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Foguan Qin and belongs to the sixteenth generation under Nanyue. It is also said:
"Regarding the permanent assets of gold and grain, apart from what is used to provide for the assembly, even a single thread or a tiny speck [must be treated with utmost care]."
Regarding the poison of the *hen* bird: if the abbot or those who manage his affairs are even slightly tainted by it, their entire bodies—bones and flesh alike—will disintegrate and rot away.
The gravity of this peril is recorded in great detail within the Vinaya scriptures.
An ancient example is Chan Master Zibao of Dongshan in Ruizhou, a native of Luzhou, who was a successor of Chan Master Wuzu Jie of the Qingyuan lineage.
Nine generations later, there was one who was stern and meticulous. He once served as the head of the storehouse at the Fifth Patriarch’s monastery.

When Master Jie fell ill, he ordered an attendant to fetch fresh ginger to decoct for medicine. Baoshou rebuked him. The attendant reported this to Master Jie, who told the attendant to take money back and purchase it himself.
Later, when the abbot’s position at Dongshan in Junzhou was vacant, the Prefectural Governor, who was a lay disciple of Baizhang, requested him to recommend a virtuous person to take charge.
Baizhang said, "A man who sells fresh ginger can hold the post. He was subsequently invited to serve as abbot. Later, he moved to Guizong Temple.

One day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw someone riding a horse with a proclamation banner. The master asked, "Who is that? The reply was, "It is the County Magistrate; please clear the way. Baizhang stood to one side.
By the side of the road, his horse suddenly knelt down. Ba said, "Do even beasts recognize humans? The magistrate bowed twice and departed. Later, he moved to Yunju Monastery.
One night, a mountain deity carried him on a palanquin around the temple. Ba said, "Carry your old father up to the Abbot’s quarters.
He once composed a eulogy for Bodhidharma, which was widely praised throughout the monastic community; it is now recorded in the *Zhengzong*.
Within the Treasury of the Dharma Eye, those who currently occupy the abbot’s quarters do not merely scrape away the contents from the bowls of others to indulge their own appetites;
they further employ such means to cater to their own superficial social obligations. At worst, they even gouge out and seek to purchase rare and precious items.

He extensively cultivated personal favors, hoping to be transferred to a great monastery; he only feared that one day Old Yan with the Iron Face would settle the accounts with him (from the *Nianya Manlu*).

This section clarifies how those who lack wisdom bring about their own ruin. Those today who occupy the seat of the abbot in the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters) do not merely scrape away from the bowls of others to indulge their own appetites;
they further employ these resources for their personal companionship and use them improperly to cultivate social favors.
Even more egregious still, they dig out and search through [the community's assets] to satisfy their own desires.

He purchased rare curiosities and extensively cultivated social favors, hoping to be transferred to a major monastery. (In Sanskrit, *kṣetra* means "site," which here refers to a "pole"—that is, a banner pole.
According to the *Chuyao lan*, whenever a śramaṇa attains the Way, he erects a banner to announce it to the four quarters.
This is indeed correct; however, I only fear that one day Old Man Iron-Face Yama will settle accounts with you item by item.)
In the future, I do not know how you will dispose of this matter. △ The preceding chapter was as clear as autumn water;
this chapter is as stern as severe frost. Having read it several times with great care, how could I not revere and stand in awe of it?
This chapter clarifies the essentials of selecting worthy individuals to succeed to the seat; it is a great event for those dwelling beneath the pines.
When the Venerable Xuetang Xing was residing at Jianfu Monastery, he once asked a visiting monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Fuzhou. Xuetang said, "Along the way, did you see any fine elders? The monk replied, "Recently I passed by Boshan in Xinzhou."
"Although I have never had the honor of meeting Abbot Ben, he is a fine elder," said a monk. Xuedang asked, "How do you know he is good?
The monk replied, "The paths leading to the monastery are cleared and open; the corridors and eaves are well-maintained; incense and lamps are lit without ceasing in the halls;
the bells and drums are clearly struck at dawn and dusk; the morning and evening gruel and meals are pure and clean; and when the monks see people, they show them proper courtesy."
This shows that he was a fine elder. Xuedang laughed and said, "Ben is indeed worthy; however, you too possess the eye.
This passage illustrates how one’s character can be discerned through inquiry. At Mount Wugu in Quzhou was the Chan Master Xuedang Daowen.
He was the son of the Ye family of Xunzhou and the successor of Chan Master Foyuan Yuan. He belonged to the fifteenth generation below Nanyue.
While he was residing at Jianfu Monastery, one day he asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Fuzhou."
Xuetao said, "Along this route following the river, have you encountered any particularly fine elder? The monk replied, "Recently I passed by Master Wuben, the abbot of Boshan in Xinzhou.
He is a native of Jiangzhou and is a successor of Chan Master Dahui in the sixteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
Although I have not yet paid my respects or met him in person, he is indeed a fine elder."

Xuetang said, "Since you have never bowed in formal greeting to him, how can you know that he is good? The monk replied, "I know it through six matters: the paths leading to the temple are cleared and open, which shows his preference for a fine location;
the corridors and eaves are well-maintained, showing his preference for a well-established foundation;

the incense and lamps are never extinguished, showing his preference for repaying kindness; the bells and drums are distinct and clear, showing his preference for the proper administration of the Dharma; and the rice gruel and meals are pure and clean."
"Enzhong, you are good. The Sangha’s conduct is full of propriety and its regulations are excellent. For this reason, I know you are a fine elder.
Xuetang laughed and said, "Bengu is indeed a man of virtuous character. Furthermore, you too are a monk with discerning eyes."
He conveyed these words directly to District Magistrate Wu Gong Fupeng, saying: "This monk’s argument is somewhat like the case of Fan Yanling recommending Zhang Xiyan;
yet your honor’s virtue does not fall short of that of Lord Zhang Zhongding. This old monk is advanced in years;
I pray you appoint the current abbot [Běn], so that this may become a great achievement for our community. Magistrate Wu was greatly pleased, and Běn—
Daily he moved to Jianfu Temple (the matter of Fan Yanling from the *Huangchao lueyuan* in the *Donghu ji*).

At this juncture, he further prayed for the transfer of the funeral offerings to his former master. It was precisely because of these words that they reached the ears of Wu Gong Fupeng, the Prefect of Raoyou, who said:
"The arguments held by this monk are quite similar; they are roughly the same. "Lü" means roughly or approximately.

On the Matter of Fan Yanling’s Recommendation of Zhang Xiyen During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty, Zhang Xiyen served as the magistrate of Pingxiang County, while Fan Yanling held the rank of Dianzhi (Palanquin Guard).
While escorting troops through Jinling, Fan Yanling was designated as "Vanguard" at the front of the formation and "Palanquin Guard" at the rear of the army.
When Zhang Yong was appointed by imperial decree to govern Jinling, he questioned him, saying: "Your Imperial Majesty’s Envoy..."
"Did you see any good officials along the way? Fan replied, "Yesterday we passed through Pingxiang; the county magistrate, Zhang Xiyan, is a good official.

Yong asked, "How do you know he is good? Fan said, "From the moment we entered his jurisdiction, the bridges and roads were well-maintained, the fields and gardens were wide and open, there were no idle farmers in the wilds, and no gambling in the markets. At night, the watch-drums were heard clearly."
Knowing that there was indeed a man of excellent governance, Zhang Yong sang: "To emulate Yan Hui is certainly the mark of a worthy man; Your Majesty’s appointed envoy is likewise a fine official.

That very day, they were jointly recommended to the court. The Emperor praised them, saying, "Both are outstanding envoys of the state," and subsequently promoted Yan Ling to the rank of Grand Secretary (Geda Hou) and appointed Zhang Yong as the Commissioner for Grain Transport (Fayun Shi). Zhang Yong’s courtesy name was Fuzhi, and he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ding.

"State Duke (Guogong). Your Excellency (Gexia). These are honorific titles for the Three Dukes (Sanguo) and denote a majestic and lofty appearance. The Three Dukes are: the Grand Preceptor (Taishi), who is the teacher of the Son of Heaven;
the Grand Tutor (Taifu), who instructs and assists the Son of Heaven; and the Grand Guardian (Taobao), who protects and secures the Son of Heaven. Furthermore, the *Yulu* states:
"The Chancellor, the Three Dukes, and the Prefectural Governor are all addressed as 'Your Excellency'. Regarding the virtue of the Venerable Xuetang, he [addressed him] as "Your Excellency."
"Under the guidance of Lord Zhang Zhongding, this old monk has grown advanced in years. I humbly beg that you request Master Ben to serve as the abbot of Jianfu Temple;

There, the commands were strict, the rites and laws were complete, and the ancient traditions were fully preserved. Furthermore—

This chapter teaches students to firm their resolve and practice with certainty, thereby benefiting both themselves and others.
Xuetang said: "A golden embankment spanning a thousand *li* may be breached by an anthill; the beauty of a white jade璧 (bi) may be marred by a single flaw.

How much more so for the Unsurpassed Sublime Way, which is not merely like a golden embankment or a white jade璧! And how much more so for greed, desire, anger, and hatred, which are not merely like anthills or flaws!
The essential point lies in being upright and prudent in one's resolve, diligent in one's practice, firm and certain in one's maintenance, and perfect in one's cultivation."
Only after [one has cultivated] beauty can one benefit oneself and benefit others (Letter to Wang Shípéng).
*Dī*: a riverbank. A "golden embankment" (*jīndī*) does not mean an embankment made of gold; it takes its name from its solidity, as if made of iron.
It is said that even a solid embankment extending for a thousand *lǐ* may be destroyed by a single ant hole. The most beautiful of white jade—
That which is to be abandoned is merely a single flaw. To "abandon" means that when people perceive this flaw, they cast it aside.
Furthermore, the unsurpassed, wondrous Path is the most noble and the most firm and resilient;
yet it does not compare to the solidity of a golden embankment or the beauty of a white jade disk. Moreover, the harm caused by the greed and anger of worldly people—

Compared to the crumbling of ant-hills or the flaking away of flaws, [the consequences of failure] must lie in the student’s resolve being unsteady and lax, their practice lacking diligence, their maintenance of precepts lacking firmness, and their cultivation lacking perfection.
Only by acting thus can one benefit oneself and subsequently benefit others. △ If it is not so, the golden embankment will collapse and turn white.
"The jade disc is broken; he has no leisure even to save himself—how could he reach others?
This passage shows that the ancients were resolute in their aspirations and profound in their cultivation, such that they were not swayed by external circumstances or internal states.
Xuetao said: "When I was at Longmen, Tieweiian was abbot at Taiping.
Someone mentioned that when Bian had been away from his home province on pilgrimage for not long, he heard that his own monastery had caught fire one night and was completely reduced to ashes.
Upon receiving this letter, Bian threw it to the ground and said, 'This merely disturbs the mind in vain. (From the *Donghu ji*)
I say: when I was at Longmen, Yuanbing Tiewen was residing at Taiping.

Someone told me that when Yuanbing was first traveling as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*), not long after leaving his hometown, he suddenly heard that his preceptor’s monastery had caught fire one night and was completely reduced to ashes—“ashes” meaning that nothing remained of the fire. Yuanbing received a letter from his preceptor, but had not yet opened it.
He read it and immediately threw it to the ground, saying: "This is merely a futile attempt to disturb my mind.
Unless one possesses a heart of iron and stone, one will ultimately be entangled by worldly passions; thus, the matter cannot be accomplished."
This chapter concerns the undertakings of sages and worthies. Their excellence lies in centrality and rectitude;
if one is biased or deviant, one is far removed from the Way. Xuetang said to Master Huichan Guang: "In my early twenties, I heard the words of the Gentleman Who Spoke of Solitude:

'If there is no master within, one cannot stand; if there is no rectitude without, one cannot act. These words should be practiced throughout one's life. This is the undertaking of sages and worthies."

This is complete. I have treasured these words: to cultivate oneself while at home, to study the Way after leaving the household, and even when leading oneself and presiding over the multitude, one must be like a balance scale or a set of weights that determine heavy and light, or like a compass and square that produce the square and the circle. If one departs from this, every matter will lose its standard (from the *Guanglu*).
Chan Master Huiguang of Guifeng in Xinzhou, whose secular surname was Wei, was a native of Jianning. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuedang Xingji.

In ancient China, it was said that a man reached the age of "weak-crown" (*ruogan*) at twenty, when he first donned the ceremonial cap. The layman [in question] was none other than the father of Xuedang.
It is said: In all that one does in life, one must by no means allow a lack of mastery within the mind to take root;
nor must one by any means perform outwardly improper acts. These words should be put into practice throughout one's entire life.
Thus, the undertakings of the sages and worthies are complete. "Pai" (the girdle) refers to the great sash.

In ancient times, whenever one encountered sublime words or virtuous deeds, one would immediately record them upon the girdle to demonstrate that they were not forgotten. Xuetang told me that he recorded such sayings on his girdle;
while at home, he used this to cultivate himself, and when leaving the household life, he used it to study the Way. Even upon entering the world [as a monk], he likewise...
Using this to govern oneself and face the multitude is like using a balance scale or a steelyard to determine weight, or using a compass and square to form squares and circles;
there is nothing that does not perfectly accord with the standard. If one abandons this, then every matter will lose its proper measure.
These two lines from Layman Du alone have been transmitted through the ages; they simply express a true realization that penetrates to the core.
This chapter states that students should emulate the words and deeds of the ancient sages; only then will they succeed in not failing their aspirations.
Xuetang said, "Whenever Gaowan presided over the assembly, he would invariably say, 'Among you, there must be those who possess true understanding. I therefore asked him about this."
Therefore, Gao’an said: "Have you not seen how Guishan spoke? 'In your conduct, look to those of superior caliber; do not vainly follow the mediocre and base.
Throughout his life in the monastic community, those who did not sink into the ranks of the ignorant and foolish all emerged from these words."
This section states that within the assembly, one must recognize those who are superior men. Every time Master Gaofeng addressed the assembly, he would invariably say:
"In the midst of a great multitude, one must know that there are good people. When I asked him the reason for this, Gaofeng replied: "Have you not seen how Guishan said:
'In the conduct and gestures of a student, one must look for those of the highest caliber'? He added, "Do not give them empty praise."
Pride is the same. It refers to a state of mind that cannot be disregarded, yet follows after what is vulgar and base. Gao'an said:
"Throughout my life, the reason I have not sunk into the level of the ignorant masses has all been due to these words."

In a dense crowd and amidst a vast multitude, the vulgar are many while those with discernment are few. The vulgar are easy to associate with, whereas those with discernment are difficult to approach.
If one can indeed exert one's own will amidst them, like a single person facing ten thousand enemies, the power of vulgar habits will be exhausted.

Truly a man of extraordinary integrity and boundless capacity! I have followed his words throughout my life, and only now do I feel I have not betrayed my vow to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*).
(From the *Guanglu*) This section clarifies that one who seeks to emulate [the masters] must possess discernment; for among the vast multitude of common people, I am the most base.

They are many, yet those who truly understand them are very few. Moreover, while it is easy for ordinary people to practice [worldly ways], those with wisdom and insight are extremely difficult to find.
One must possess self-mastery; indeed, one must be able to rouse great resolve amidst the throngs of common people.

It is like a single person contending against ten thousand men; after a long time, the habitual tendencies of stubbornness, mediocrity, and vulgarity are completely eliminated, and one truly becomes a peerless great man of boundless capacity.
Xuetang said: "I have practiced these words throughout my life, and only then did I become worthy of this birth."
The Aspiration of the Householder. △ The essential point of this chapter lies in the phrase: "As if one man were facing ten thousand enemies.
Observe how force is applied here. One who understands this can teach others to look out from beyond the heavens.

This chapter concerns the careful examination of one’s speech and conduct so as to ensure they accord with the Middle Way; it is appropriate to scrutinize and take responsibility for one’s own body and mind.

Xuetang said to Qian’an: "In performing your duties, you must weigh the relative importance of matters. When speaking, you must first reflect and deliberate, striving to accord with the Middle Way and avoiding partiality or bias.
If you act impulsively or recklessly, success will rarely be achieved; even if something is accomplished, [it will likely lead to further complications]."

In the end, it could not ensure complete success. While among the multitude, I observed both its benefits and its defects in full detail. Only those possessed of virtue can win over others through magnanimity.
I constantly hope that those of future generations with the will and capacity to act will examine this carefully before putting it into practice; only then will it become a source of true benefit.
This section states that those appointed to administrative duties must necessarily possess virtue. Chan Master Zhouchen Shouren of Changlu in Zhenzhou was a native of Shangyu in Yue;
he succeeded Chan Master Xuetang Xing and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.

He stated that those who preside over the Dharma must weigh the gravity and lightness of the individuals they employ as administrators. If one who ought to be highly esteemed is instead treated lightly, it is a failure of judgment.
When those who treat matters lightly instead act with gravity, their undertakings will find it difficult to succeed. One must first deliberate before speaking;
if one acts with haste and recklessness, there are few who can successfully accomplish the task.
Not to mention failure, even if success is achieved, one will ultimately be unable to ensure its perfection. While among the multitude, I have observed this clearly and in full detail.
This is beneficial for those who are ill. Only those possessing virtue can naturally win over others through their broad and magnanimous capacity.
It is my constant wish that future masters with the resolve and strength to undertake this must examine it carefully and practice it in detail;
only then will it become a source of supreme benefit.
Lingyuan once said: "Ordinary people are often able to understand clearly when reflecting inwardly in their daily lives;

yet, when they engage with external affairs, they immediately lose their state of harmonious integration and forfeit the essence of the Dharma. If one truly desires to succeed to the responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to enlighten future generations, one must constantly examine and reproach oneself. (From the *Guanglu*).
This section clarifies that engaging with the world entirely depends upon the illumination of wisdom. Master Lingyuan once said:
"When ordinary people dwell in seclusion and remain alone, they gather their minds to illuminate within; every single thing is clear and nothing remains obscure.

Yet, when they encounter worldly conditions and engage with external objects, they immediately deviate from the path of tranquil illumination and harmonious fusion, losing the essence of the Dharma. If...
Those who possess the vast power of aspiration must surely desire to contemplate inheriting the heavy responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to enlighten and guide future generations.
They must constantly restrain their bodies and scrutinize their minds. △ The discordance between inward illumination and outward pursuit—wherein does this ailment lie?
There is not even room for a hair’s breadth in the interval; should there be even one...
To covet is to be stained by worldly sentiments.
This chapter shows that you, a person of honor, regard others through their virtue and are not entangled by worldly appearances.
When Master Huigan Hua resided at Mingguo, Xuedang never failed to visit him for even a single day; occasionally, there were those who stole [his teachings].
The deliberators said: "My nephew Huar is a man who does not delight in profit or seek fame; he does not praise first and later disparage, nor does he flatter or compromise for convenience;
he does not employ sycophancy or clever speech. Furthermore, his realization of the Way is clear and lucid, and his coming and going are carefree and spontaneous.
Such a person is rare among the monks; I certainly hold him in high esteem. (From *Qian'an Yishi*)
Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Wang family of Qizhou.

He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huiqiu Long and belonged to the sixteenth generation below Nanyue. While he was residing at Mingguo, Xuedang frequently visited his quarters to associate with him.
Occasionally, there were private discussions that seemed to lapse into a lack of formal etiquette regarding their respective ranks; however, Xuedang remarked: "Although..."
Thus, while there are distinctions in rank and order, what I value most is virtue. My nephew Huar is a person of extreme integrity;

he takes no pleasure in profit nor does he pursue fame. In his dealings with others, he does not praise them first only to disparage them later, nor does he flatter to gain favor or seek a superficial harmony with people.
He does not put on the countenance of a sycophant, nor does he employ clever artifice to manipulate others.
His speech was refined, and his insight into the principle was profoundly clear. In his every movement—whether departing or staying, rising or sitting—he was remarkably free and unencumbered.
Among the assembly of monks, it would be most difficult to find another like my nephew Hua;
this is why I hold him in such high esteem. Herein, one finally understands the single-minded sincerity of the ancients.
To reach such a state of forgetting emotions, one must strive to emulate it.
This treatise argues that the vital energy (*qi*) and the will (*zhi*) of a person must not exist in partiality; if they are partial, there is no benefit.
Xuetang said: "Among scholars, if the vital energy overcomes the will, one becomes a petty person; if the will overcomes the vital energy, one becomes an upright and correct person."
The scholar’s qi and will must be equalized to become a worthy sage who has attained the Way.
This section teaches that one's qi and will must be balanced. "Will" (zhì) refers to the mental resolve; "qi" (qì) refers to the vital breath and blood.

By nourishing the mental resolve through principle, it does not become clouded; by leading the qi with the will, the qi does not fall into disorder. As the *Lun* says: "Qi listens to the commands of..."
The mind is the noble person; the mind that obeys the vital energy (*qi*) is the petty person. Now, vital energy is the culmination of the will (*zhi*);
the will is the commander of the vital energy. If the mind follows the fluctuations of the vital energy, then the vital energy conversely becomes the commander of the will.
When the vital energy acts as commander, the will of my mind declines; this is what it means for the mind to be enslaved by the vital energy. The Sage...

The worthy gentleman governs his vital energy (*qi*) with his mind, rather than being governed by his vital energy; he shifts his vital energy with his mind, rather than being shifted by his vital energy.
Xuetang said: "Generally, among students, those whose vital energy prevails and whose will (*zhi*) is weak can never accomplish great matters.
To employ vital energy exclusively is the way of the petty person. If the will is strong..."
As for those whose vital energy (*qi*) is weak, though they may be upright men and virtuous scholars, this is still a case where the will has reached its goal while the vital energy has not;
there is still a deficiency. If, however, one’s will and vital energy are balanced and equal, such a person will certainly attain the Unsurpassed Way and become a sage or a worthy.
Why is this? Although a person may possess the will to become a sage or a worthy, if their vital energy does not prevail, [they cannot succeed].
If one does not practice with vigor, how can one sever the deepest delusions and eliminate the heaviest obscurations?
This is why it is necessary for both will and energy to be balanced; only then can one sever delusion and realize the Truth.
There are those who are stubborn and fierce, refusing to accept counsel or admonition; this is caused by their temperament.
A person of upright character, even if forced at gunpoint to do what is not good, would rather die than waver; this is caused by their resolve. (From the *Guǎnglù*).
This section clarifies the differences between the influence of temperament (*qi*) and the influence of resolve (*zhi*).
Nowadays, there is a certain type of person within the monastic community who is stubborn and fierce, refusing to accept discipline or instruction; this is driven by their temperament.

A person of upright character, however, will not change their conduct even if they are forcibly compelled to engage in unwholesome deeds, even at the point of death; this is the power of their resolve.
These are what they are moved by. Will and vital energy (*qi*) are what we inherently possess. Observe how those who follow and practice them act:
if one prevails over the other, success or failure will immediately manifest; if both are brought forth without contradicting each other, the undertakings of the sages and worthies are achieved.
This chapter states that while a fine vessel is inherently formed by nature, its capacity cannot be restricted or diminished.
Xuetang said: "When Gaofeng An resided at Yunju, Puyun Yuan was the head seat (śrāmaṇera) and Yicai Seng was the secretary."
Baiyang Shun served as the Abbot; Tong Wutou served as the Guest Prefect; Xian Zhenmu served as the Rector; Huazhi served as the Vice-Abbot;
and Yongzhi served as the Chief Administrator; all of them were men of virtue and accomplishment.
This section generally lists various masters. Chan Master Ziyuan of Puyun in Nankang Prefecture was the son of the Yong family of Mianzhou;
he succeeded Chan Master Gao’an Wuzhuo and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng. His role as head seat (shouzuo) has been explained previously.
One master, whose name is unknown, may refer to Shuian (Shui’an), who served as a secretary (shuji) and managed literary affairs, including all the temple’s public notices.
Correspondence, petitions, and prayers—all such matters belong to this category. Chan Master Fayun of Baiyang in Fuzhou was a native of the Wen family of Mianzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Foyan Yuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:

"Adverse conditions are easily encountered, while the work of the Way is difficult to accomplish. If one does not understand the myriad distinctions of present conditions, [the path will remain obscured]."
I see only the winds of sensory objects raging, withering the forest of merit; the fires of the mind blaze fiercely, consuming the seeds of Bodhi.
If your aspiration for the Way were equal to your affection for your kin, you would have attained Buddhahood long ago; if you treat the multitude as you do yourself, [you will surely succeed].
When matters are settled between each other, one sees neither the faults of others nor one's own righteousness; naturally, those above show respect and those below show deference.

Thus, the Buddha-dharma manifests from time to time, and afflictions are liberated at every dust mote. As for the Librarian, he oversees the treasury of scriptures while simultaneously mastering their underlying principles.
The catalogs of the cases and volumes are constantly checked and compared; those that are missing are supplemented, and those that are torn are mended with paste.
○ Fǎtōng of Běishān in Zhēnzhōu, whose courtesy name was Tōngwū, was a successor of Chánmāster Zhēnxiè Qīngliáo of Chánglú.

The fourteenth generation under Qingyuan. The Guest Master (Zhike): responsible for attending to guests; when monastics and laypeople meet, he must ensure that his responses and reception are always orderly and dignified.
Chan Master Zhenmu Zhengxian of Nanguang Temple in Nankang Commandery. Born into the Chen family of Tongzhou, he was a dharma heir of Chan Master Fuyan Yuan.
He belongs to the fifteenth generation under Nan Yue. The Rector (Weina): responsible for the Chinese and foreign (Sanskrit) liturgical services.

He concurrently held these offices. He maintained the discipline of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) and applied himself with meticulous care to its administration; there was no matter, whether internal or external to the monastic affairs, that he did not oversee.

**Assistant Steward:** Responsible for the permanent assets of the monastery, including gold, grain, currency, silk, and rice. He maintains ledgers for all receipts and disbursements according to their timing.
**Yongzhi (Director of Use):** Chan Master De Yong of Shuanglin in Wuzhou. A native of the Dai clan of that prefecture, he was a dharma heir of Gao’an.

The Wudeng (Awakening) Master; the Jiansi (Superintendent). In Sanskrit, this is called *karmadāna*, which here means "Abbot. This official diligently attends to the incense and lamps day and night and receives visiting officials.
Those appointed to this post must be upright, capable, and honest in all their duties, and must be free from resentment among both those inside and outside the monastery.
These seven aforementioned positions are all held by individuals of virtuous conduct and spiritual practice.
Dharma Uncle Yong was always frugal and economical; he would not even use the monastery’s oil for lamps.

One day, Dharma Uncle Hua teased him, saying, "When you become an elder in the future, you must have a straight nose before you can succeed. How can you expect to achieve it by this alone? Dharma Uncle Yong did not reply.
This section discusses integrity and frugality alone. As for how Master Hua’s nephew usually conducts himself, he is most upright and most frugal.
To take one very minor example: he did not use the monastery’s cooking oil.
Master Hua teased him, saying, "In the future, when you become an elder, you need only have your nostrils straight and your fundamental principles clear. How could you possibly..."
"Is it by means of such trifles that one attains [realization]? Using Zhi did not answer.
Although Using Zhi was frugal in his own conduct, he was exceedingly generous toward others; he received those who came from the four quarters without the slightest hint of weariness.

One day, Gao’an saw him and said, "It is truly rare for a *jian-si* (superintendent) to apply himself with such diligence; furthermore, you must look after the monastery's permanent assets (*changzhu*) and not allow them—"

Gaoseng was negligent. When someone pointed out his oversight, saying, "Sir, you have committed a minor transgression," Gaoseng replied, "In a master like me, who honors the worthy and treats scholars with respect—whose magnanimity is as vast as the sea and as accommodating as a mountain—to not inquire into such trifles is truly the mark of a Great Virtue. Ga'ān merely smiled.
Thus, he became known in the monastic community (conglin) by the nickname "The One with the Large Bowl" (an anecdote).
This section clarifies the fundamental principle: although his personal conduct was most frugal, he was exceedingly generous toward others.
He received monastics coming from all directions without ever showing a sign of weariness.
One day, Gao’an saw him and said, "It is truly rare to find one who applies himself with such diligence as you do; furthermore, you must..."
"Attentively oversee the permanent property so that nothing is neglected or lost. Regarding the use of the term 'nephew' (zhí):

if it refers to someone such as Jiǎ, even if there were negligence, it would still be considered a minor fault; however, in the case of the Upādhyāya, one must certainly show respect for his worthiness and virtue."
He favored the wise, his capacity being like the great ocean that receives the hundred rivers, or like mountain valleys that store the myriad things;
he did not inquire after trivial or minor matters. This is truly what constitutes the virtue of a great abbot.
Gao-an simply smiled. For this reason, there is the saying in the monastic forests regarding the "large bowl," which is no empty boast. To speak of "great" is...
As for the bowl, it is because it can contain many things. The multitude of eminent talents has gathered, and the great virtue is fully manifested;
this is truly a time when the clouds and dragons meet. It may be called an encounter as rare as once in a morning or evening.
This chapter speaks of the harmonious accord between master and disciple; it is certainly not accidental, for there is a momentum like that of wind and clouds meeting. Xuetang said:
"When a student does not know where the Way is directed, they seek out teachers and friends to inquire and investigate it.
A virtuous teacher cannot transform others through the Way alone; therefore, they rely on the student to provide assistance and support. Thus, the master invites [the student].
To establish a community of the Dharma, there must first be a teacher endowed with virtue and morality; and to sustain it, there must necessarily be disciples who are worthy and wise.
This is what is meant by "when the tiger roars, the wind becomes piercing; when the dragon soars, the clouds arise."
This section emphasizes that the core value between teacher and disciple lies in mutual resonance.
It means that if a student does not know the direction in which the wondrous Way tends, they must seek out an enlightened master and visit virtuous friends to inquire and receive instruction.

When a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) wishes to practice this Way, how could they transform others through their own efforts alone? Therefore, it is essential to rely upon the assistance and support of students.

They assist and support him. Therefore, when one who presides over a *caitya* (monastery) is a master of virtuous conduct and meritorious deeds who establishes a Dharma community, there will naturally come monks of talent and wisdom to provide assistance.

This is what is meant by the saying: "When the tiger roars, the wind must be piercing; when the dragon soars, the clouds must arise. "Roar" (*xiao*) refers to the sound of blowing air; "piercing" (*lie*) refers to the cold air.

*Xiáng*: The appearance of leaping upward and soaring far. In the *Yi* (Book of Changes), Qian Hexagram, the fifth line of the nine says: "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man.
What does this mean? The Master said: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another out. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. When the sage arises, all things behold him. That which is rooted in Heaven..."
That which is rooted in Heaven is related to that which is above; that which is rooted in Earth is related to that which is below. Thus, each follows its own kind.
In the past, Mazu of Jiangxi manifested his great capacity and great function through Baizhang and Nanquan;
Shitou of Nanyue realized his great wisdom and great capability through Yaoshan and Tianhuang. Therefore, they formed a union once in a thousand years—thus it is said.
His discourse was free from doubt; it rose up like a swan’s down encountering the wind and surged forth like a giant fish leaping into a valley.
All were manifestations of natural momentum. Thus, he established the meritorious achievements of the monastic groves and increased the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This section reveals that while the Master was eminent, his disciples were formidable.

Thus, in the past, although Mazu of Jiangxi was originally a teacher of virtue and character, it was because he obtained Baizhang, Nanquan, and their peers that he became a master of wise and noble monastics.
Thus, his great capacity was revealed and his great function was unleashed. Furthermore, Nanyue Shitou was a master who had attained the Way;
because he encountered the wise and sagely monastics Yaoshan and Tianhuang, he manifested his great wisdom and perfected his great capabilities.
○ Chan Master Yueshan Weiyen of Lishu was the son of the Han family from Jiangzhou.

He received the Dharma from Chan Master Shitou Xiqian; he was the second generation descendant of Qingyuan. As the Master was about to pass away, one night he went up the mountain for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).
Suddenly the clouds parted and he beheld the moon; he let out a great roar, the sound of which reached about ninety li to the east of Liyang.
The next morning, the local residents questioned one another until they reached Yaoshan, where they finally learned that it had been the Master.

The Sound of Whistling. Li Ao, the Prefect of Langzhou, presented him with a poem that said: "Having chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments, Throughout the year there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain, And beneath the moon, parting the clouds, let out a single whistle.
Dharma Master Huangtian Daowu of Jingzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou. He attained [enlightenment]...
Master Fa was a disciple of Chan Master Shitou Xiqian; he belonged to the second generation under Qingyuan.

Initially residing at Mount Ziling in Dangyang, Jingzhou, his disciples followed one another in such numbers that they crowded shoulder to shoulder, and people from the capital flocked there, drawn by his reputation.

At that time, a monk from Chongye Monastery submitted a formal petition to the local prefect, requesting that the Master take up residence at Tianhuang Monastery to the east of the city. The Master had long been...
Regarding welcoming and seeing off guests, regardless of their rank—whether noble or humble—the Master would always sit while bowing to them.

When Lord Pei, the Magistrate of Jiangling, prostrated himself and inquired about the Dharma, the Master received him without showing any special marks of courtesy; yet Lord Pei’s reverence increased all the more.

From this, the Way and Dharma of Shitou flourished to the utmost. Such a master and disciple may truly be called a rare encounter spanning a thousand years, finding perfect harmony in a single day. Therefore, in all matters...
Discourse: Whenever there is a statement, as soon as the Master raises it, the disciple immediately understands it clearly and without doubt.
To be "winged" (yì) is like the great Peng bird: as soon as it spreads its wings, if it suddenly encounters a great wind, it will surely soar far upon its momentum.
The term "péi-rán" (overflowing) is like a great fish about to stir up the waves that suddenly encounters a torrential downpour and thus courses through the valley.
The "valley" is none other than the great ocean; all of this is the natural course of events.

Likewise, when a master and his disciples come together, they are able to establish monastic communities (*cónglín*), perform meritorious deeds, and increase the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—all of which are likewise the natural course of events.
My late teacher resided at Longmen. One night he said to me, "I lack both virtue and achievement; I cannot lead these young monks back to the vast ocean of the Tides.
In the end, I am ashamed before the old man of Dongshan. Having finished speaking, his voice broke with tears. I have often reflected on this:
those who act as teachers and models for others today are separated from the ancients by a factor of ten thousandfold (Letter to Zhuanan).
This section clarifies self-effacement in order to manifest the virtue of the Master. When our late Master was residing at Longmen, one evening he said to me:
"I possess no virtuous conduct and my cultivation of the Way is meager; I am unable to attract the monastics from across the lakes and seas with a grand and imposing presence."
"I am truly ashamed and filled with self-reproach. How could I possibly match the assembly gathered by the Elder of the Eastern Mountain?
Having finished speaking, his tears flowed down. Xuetang said, 'I have often reflected on this: those who act as teachers and models today are indeed far removed from the ancients;
it is not merely ten thousand times less. [Only] when there is a sage teacher will there be a worthy disciple."
The son arrived; the resonance followed and the sounds harmonized. This is truly sufficient to establish a glorious legacy for ten thousand generations—how could it be a mere coincidence?
One must know that the reason he came as a guest to the eight quarters of the world was solely due to his virtue and wisdom.
This chapter shows that a man of the Way understands the critical moment and recognizes what is appropriate; he will never be cowed by power or influence.
Xuetang said: "When I was at Longmen, Lingyuan was residing at Taiping. The authorities disturbed him with ill-intentioned interference."
Lingyuan wrote in a letter to his former teacher: "To walk the Way straightforwardly is perhaps impossible to achieve; to serve as an abbot by compromising one's integrity is truly not my aspiration.
It would be better to let my mind roam among the thousands of crags and myriad valleys, daily satiated with fodder and grain to fulfill the remainder of my life.
Why then should I be so anxious? Less than ten days later, he received an order from Huanglong and accordingly set out.
Xing returned to Jiangxi (as recorded in the notes of Chan Master Cong).
He told me that when he formerly resided at Longmen in Shuzhou, Master Lingyuan was serving as the abbot of Taiping Temple.
An official harassed and harmed him with ill intent. "Ill intent" means to inflict harm upon one who is innocent. Ling...
Yuan wrote a letter to the late Master Fuyan, saying: "A straightforward mind and straightforward conduct are the foundation of practicing the Way.
