Yet, if one finds that such conduct cannot be carried out, it is likely because of the circumstances. To act by compromising one's integrity is truly not the original intention of a practitioner of the Way. As Liu Xiaohui said:
'If one serves others with a straightforward path, where can one go without being dismissed three times? But if one serves others by compromising the path...'"
"Why must one leave the land of one's parents? If you insist that I must humble myself to serve others, what benefit would there be?

It would be better to let my mind roam among the thousands of crags and ten thousand gullies, where each day I am satiated with fodder and grain—fodder and grain being food made from wild plants—and thus find contentment, fulfilling the aspirations of my remaining life. Why?
Feeling sorrowful and distressed, he made this decision to depart. "Juan-juan" means to be weary and distressed. Ten days constitute a *xun*; twelve days constitute a *jia*.
Within that interval—neither a full *xun* nor a *jia*—he received the command of the Yellow Dragon to request the Master to reside and preside over the monastery.
Thereupon, seizing the momentum, he ultimately returned to Jiangxi. The Way-person's mind is like a straight bowstring; being circuitous is not what is appropriate for him.
This is so. As a general rule for one who serves as the master of a monastic community (*sēnlín*), it is fitting to act in this manner.
This chapter speaks of how a student should perform their duties: they must reflect with care and not employ them recklessly. Xuētáng said:
"Língyuán compared the various types of *nàizǐ* (monks) to the words of the ancients, which say: 'It is like making figures of wood or clay.'"
When making a wooden puppet that resembles a human being, one first desires the ears and nose to be large and the mouth and eyes to be small. People may criticize this, saying:

"The ears and nose can be made smaller, and the mouth and eyes can be made larger. When making an earthenware puppet, one first desires the ears and nose to be small and the mouth and eyes to be large.
People may criticize this, saying: "The ears and nose can be made larger, and the mouth and eyes [can be made smaller]."
"It may be considered small. Now, although these words concern what is small, they can serve as a metaphor for what is great.
When scholars face matters requiring choice, they should not tire of reflecting three times; thus, they may become persons of loyalty and integrity (*Jiwen*).
Master Lingyuan was fond of using analogies from the natural world for his disciples, saying: "The ancients had a saying:
'It is like having something in the world made of earth or made of wood that resembles a human being. He added, "By chance," [it might happen].
It is the same with making wooden images. The person who fashions them must first intend for the ears and nose to be large, and the mouth and eyes to be small.
Should someone criticize this, asking, "Why is it done like this? one must understand that the ears and nose were originally large, which are then pared down and trimmed until they become small.
As for the apertures of the mouth and eyes, which were originally small, they are opened and carved out [to enlarge them].

This is later arrogance. It is also like someone making a human figure out of clay: if they first desire the ears and nose to be small, or the mouth and eyes to be large, others will surely criticize them.
One must understand that although the ears and nose are initially small, by molding and shaping them, they can subsequently be made large;
and although the mouth and eyes are initially large, by reducing and pinching them, they can subsequently be made small. Lingyuan said:
Although these words concern a trivial matter, they can actually serve as a parable for how a person may ruin a great undertaking through a lack of care.
Generally speaking, when scholars face matters requiring choice between taking and rejecting, they must not disdain reflecting three times over.
Only then can one become a person of loyalty and integrity. The phrasing is plain, yet the meaning is subtle; how could this be...?
It was surely in response to such agitation that he spoke thus. To admonish others against recklessness and a lack of reflection can be called the ultimate instruction.
This chapter cites those of virtuous character as a model for people today, serving as a warning to those who seek fame and profit.

Xuetang said: "When Wan’an sent Gāo’ān to Mount Tiantai, upon his return he told me that there was the head seat Deguàn, who had lived in seclusion at Jingxing Rock for thirty years without ever venturing beyond the mountain.
When Lord Geng, the Dragon Scholar, served as the regional governor, he specifically sent an invitation from Ruiyan Temple to welcome him.
Deguàn declined with this verse: 'For thirty years I have kept my door closed alone; How could an official summons ever reach here?'"
Qing Shan said: "Cease using the trivial affairs of the human world to exchange for my lifelong leisure beneath the forest trees.
Although the imperial summons arrived once more, I ultimately did not comply. Geng Gong sighed and said: "Today’s Yan Shanzhi!"
This section clarifies that the aspirations of the ancients were directed toward the Way.

Chan Master Wanan Daoyan of Donglin in Jiangzhou was the son of the Xie family from Tongzhou and was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao. When he escorted Gao’an to Tiantai, upon his return he said to me:
"In that place there is a man named Deguan, formerly the head seat Shouqi; he is a native of Chengdu and received the Dharma from [Dahui]."
Chan Master Foyuan Yuan was the fifteenth generation descendant of Nanyue. When Yuan ordered him to share the seat and preach the Dharma, the Master firmly declined, saying:
"This is no small matter; it is like piercing the eye with a golden needle—if even a single hair's breadth is off, the pupil will be destroyed."
He vowed, "In every life, may I dwell in the stage of learning and refine myself. He expressed his resolve in verse: "The Way is found only through frequent retreating;
Humility and harmony naturally habituate the turning back of light. Unaware that one already stands atop the azure clouds, One still further lowers the body into the depths of the multitudes.
Later, he lived in seclusion at Jingxing Rock for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountains even in shadow.

This means that while the form remains unmoving, the shadow does not flow. When Master Geng was serving as the Prefectural Governor, he specifically invited [Master] Guan to the Ruiyan Chan monastery.
Guan declined with a verse, saying: "For thirty years I have kept my door closed alone; how could an official summons reach these green mountains?
The *fu* (summons) was a Han dynasty institution, made of bamboo six inches long, divided into two equal parts.
These are merely tokens of appointment. Xiu considers trivial human affairs to be the many fragmented and petty matters of an elder;
they are all worldly concerns. They cannot exchange my lifelong leisure beneath the forest. My contented and secluded life in the woods shall not be traded for your offerings.

Even if you insist on sending messengers with invitations again, the Master will ultimately— (Note: The original text ends abruptly with "師終" [the Master finally...], indicating an incomplete passage.)
He did not comply. Master Geng sighed at this and said, "This master could be considered one of the 'hidden dragons' of the present age, like those of Mount Liu.
Wan’an said, "There was an elder who could recall his words; he said: 'If one does not realize the root of the Way, one will remain submerged in delusion.'"

Regarding birth and death: when the mind arises upon encountering objects, thoughts stir according to one's emotions; with a wolf’s heart and a fox’s intent, one uses flattery to deceive others, aligns oneself with power through sycophancy, pursues fame at the expense of integrity and seeks profit by any means.

To deviate from the truth and chase after delusions, to turn one’s back on awakening and unite with the dust of the world—this is something a practitioner of the Way beneath the forest trees would never do.
I said: "Guan is also one of the vital spirits among the monastics" (anecdote).
This section clarifies that the practice of mantras by those who have reached the Way is essential. Wan’an said:

"There was an old master there who could recall the words with which the Master addressed the assembly: 'If you do not realize the fundamental source of the Way, you will drown in birth and death; you will give rise to the mind upon encountering objects and move your thoughts according to circumstances.
A wolf’s heart and a fox’s intent—wolves are full of greed and foxes are full of doubt; both are things that harm others. [Flattery...]"
To practice deception means to use flattery and sycophancy to mislead others;

to curry favor by aligning with those in power, to pursue fame and seek profit at all costs, and to deviate from the truth while chasing after delusions, turning one's back on awakening to unite with the dust of the world—such things a practitioner in the mountain forests would never do.

Upon hearing these words, one immediately understood the character of Zhigan. When Xuetang heard this, he remarked, "Zhigan was also a man of 'intermediate vital energy' (*jiānqì*) among the monastics.
To say he appeared 'in an interval' implies he was like Yi Yin or the Duke of Zhou—such a person is said to transcend the ordinary and have no concern with the mundane world.
△ A man of virtue does not need to be found among thousands or tens of thousands.

To surround oneself [in seclusion] is to attain [the Way]. To establish merit and achieve great deeds, there are other excellent paths. The character and style of those dwelling in mountain caves inspire such reverence that others can hardly reach them.
This chapter demonstrates how one maintains integrity and self-restraint, remaining unconcerned with worldly things.
Xuetang was born into a family of wealth and nobility, yet he never displayed an air of arrogance. He lived a life of frugality and simplicity, remaining fundamentally detached from worldly affairs.
While residing at Mount Wugu, a monk presented him with an iron mirror. Xuetang said, "The mountain stream is clear and limpid;
even one's hair can be reflected in it. What is the use of keeping this? In the end, he declined the gift. (From his *Xingshi*)
Venerable Xuetang was born into a family of great wealth and status, yet he possessed no air of arrogance or extravagance.
In his daily life, he practiced moderation and frugality;
though his character was refined and elegant, he never allowed himself to be preoccupied with rare or beautiful objects. How is this known? When the Master resided at Wu...
During the time of Gushan, a monk presented him with an iron mirror; it was a rare object.
Xuetang said, "The stream here is clear and limpid—'limpid' (cǐ) meaning water that is pure. One could reflect even one's hair and beard in it.
What is the use of keeping this? He ultimately declined and would not accept it. From this, we know that his lack of concern for material things was such as this. [End of Section] West.
The King of Shu was named Zongshou. While digging the earth, he discovered a single iron mirror; it was dull and nothing could be seen in it.
One day, suddenly light burst forth from it, shining across a thousand li. Coincidentally, a small boy dressed in green appeared and asked for the mirror, saying, "This mirror is my dwelling;
how can you hide it away? The king took the mirror out, and the boy entered the mirror and vanished from sight. From this, he knew [it to be a supernatural object].
It is a divine object. △ People of wealth and status generally have many habitual tendencies toward fondly playing with objects;
that he possesses a divine mirror yet does not hoard it is sufficient proof that what he does hoard is the Dao, which is most profound, and virtue, which is most substantial.
This chapter clarifies that the essential resolve for studying the Way must be firm and free from delusion, employing benevolence and compassion as its function.
Xuetang was benevolent, compassionate, loyal, and forgiving; he honored the worthy and respected the capable. Even in jest or casual speech, coarse words rarely escaped his lips;

he was neither haughty nor obstructive, nor did he ever display violent anger. Yet, when it came to matters of departure or arrival, he was exceedingly upright and pure. He once said: "When the ancients studied the Way..."
He was indifferent toward external things and had no personal preferences, even to the point of forgetting his rank and position and abandoning fame and sensory pleasures;
it seemed as though he could do this effortlessly. Yet, when scholars of today exhaust all their clever efforts, they ultimately cannot achieve such a state. What is the reason for this?
Their resolve is not firm and their focus is not singular; they treat the matter as something merely ordinary (Biographies).
The nature bestowed upon him by his Master was characterized by benevolence and compassion, as well as loyalty and reciprocity. Loyalty means to exhaust one's own sincerity;
reciprocity means to yield to others. The worthy revere it, and the capable honor it. As for all forms of jesting and merriment, [he remained steadfast].
Vulgar speech and worldly expressions rarely escaped his lips. His countenance was free from any appearance of arrogance or harshness;
his deportment was devoid of any air of violence or anger. Even at the moment of departure, he felt no lingering attachment.
He was exceedingly upright and pure, once saying: "When the ancients studied the Way, they were serene and indifferent toward all things external to the self."
Regarding one's inclinations: that one is able to forget rank and position and abandon fame and sensory pleasures seems effortless, yet it is simply natural to be thus.
As for scholars of the present day, I see that they have exhausted every artifice; "artifice" here refers to being skillful and possessing many talents.
Yet, in the end, these cannot withstand the pull of rank, position, fame, and sensory pleasures. They are unable to forget these things. Why is this?
There is no difference; it is simply that their resolve is not firm and their practice is inconsistent, treating it as something merely ordinary.
To say "pi-si-jian" (匹似間) in the local dialect means "not important. The words and deeds of a perfected person, when heard by others, all sound like the resonance of metal and stone;
how could they be compared to anything superficial? Although this is innate, it also relies upon cultivation.
This section reveals the application of the mind of one who possesses true knowledge; whether in opposition or accord, all is earnest and authentic, and thus one attains the character of a person.
Xuetang said: "When Sīxī resided at Yúnyán, he was fond of scolding and reviling within his quarters; the monks would all retreat upon seeing the cliff."
This section clarifies that the tongs and the hammer are fundamentally distinct. It cites the time when Master Sīxin resided at Yunyan;
whenever anyone entered the room for an audience, the Master would habitually scold and revile them. Now, such scolding and reviling are certainly not something people desire to receive.
This single word "desire" (好) already carries a profound meaning. The assembly of monks did not understand the Master’s intent, and none dared to [engage him].
"Near. This refers to what appears to be a steep precipice from which one cannot advance.

Attendant Fang said, "One who acts as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and practices the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to command and transform devas and humans ought to regard students as their own infants.
Yet now, you are unable to bestow the sorrow of compassion or grant the grace of consolation; you employ the Middle [Way]..."
"The teaching of harmony—how can it be treated like an enemy? To see it and then revile and abuse it—is this the way a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) applies his mind?
This section sets forth the reason for the inquiry. The attendant Fang was Chan Master Chaozong Huifang of Heshan in Jizhou;
he was a successor of Chan Master Xinfeng of Huanglong and belonged to the fourteenth generation under Nanyue. Thereupon, he said: "Now,"...
As a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one who ought to practice the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and issue commands to humans and devas should regard students as newborn infants.
A "newborn infant" refers to a child just born, who is most pitiable.

"Carpaṭa" (慘怛) means grief; it is the mind of compassion and empathy (*karuṇā*). "To console" (*fǔ*) means to bring peace; "to follow" (*xún*) means to accord with. This conveys the intention of humbling one's own dignity to approach those of lower status.
Now, since you, O Monk, are unable to exercise the compassionate concern of empathy and mercy, [how can you claim to be a teacher?].
Furthermore, you are unwilling to bestow the grace of compassionate nurturing and compliance, nor do you employ the teachings of "Centrality and Harmony" (*zhonghe*).

Centrality means that in principle there is no partiality; harmony means that in practice there is neither laxity nor urgency. Moreover, when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested, it is called "Centrality";
when they are manifested and all accord with the proper measure, it is called "Harmony. Yet, instead, you treat [us] as if we were enemies. Enemies—!
This is the mindset of one harboring resentment and seeking retribution. Whenever anyone came to see him, he would immediately become enraged and revile them in such a manner;

how could this be the way a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) applies his mind? How wonderful! Were it not for Master Fang’s petition, how could we have witnessed the sublime function of the spiritual friend?

Sishin dragged his staff and pursued him, saying: "With such a level of understanding as yours, it is certain that one day you will flatter those in power and position, sycophantically curry favor with the influential and wealthy, and cheaply sell the Buddha-dharma to deceive the ignorant masses.

It was because I could not bear this that I used these heavy words to rouse you; there is no other intent. I wish for you to know shame, reform your errors, cherish these teachings without forgetting them, and act rightly in the future."
This is based on human hearsay (*kimon*).
This section expresses the intent of "Angry Rebukes. When Dashi (Sishin) Wuheshang heard the words of Attendant Fang, he immediately seized his staff and chased him away, saying:
"Do you have such a view? If you go out to guide others in the future, it will certainly..."

To use flattery to curry favor with those in power and position, and to offer sycophancy to the influential and wealthy out of mere expediency—this is surely to trade away the Great Dharma of our Tathāgata and to deceive the ignorant masses.

I cannot bear that such people remain complacent and ignorant, failing to exert courageous effort or clarify the ultimate Way; therefore, I have used these weighty words to stir them to action. This...
This is truly my sincere expression of grief and sorrow, and my sincere bestowal of compassionate care; my intent does not stop at merely weeping and shedding tears.
What else could it be? It is truly my desire that others may come to know integrity and recognize shame, so as to renew themselves and reform their faults.
By hearing these stern words of mine, may they cherish them and never forget them, so that in the future they may become—
A fine monk has departed! △ Whether acting in opposition to or in accordance with the Way, his celestial mechanism is unfathomable.
How profound and sincere is this private effort at cultivation!
This section speaks of the master of the house; if he loses virtue and transgresses propriety, he will have no means to serve as a model for others.
The late Master Xinxin said: "Xiu Yuan-tong once remarked: 'To wish to correct others while one cannot correct oneself is called a loss of virtue;
to wish to show respect to others while one cannot show respect to oneself is called a violation of propriety.
Now, as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), if one loses virtue and violates propriety, how can one serve as a model for future generations? (This was written to Lingyuan)."
Chan Master Fǎxiù Yuántōng of Fǎyún Monastery in Bìliáng was the son of the Xiṁ family of Lóngchéng in Qīnzhōu.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiānyī Huái and belonged to the eleventh generation under Qīngyuán. Master Fǎxiù once said:
"For one who acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), if their own body and mind are not upright while they merely demand that others be upright, this is called a loss of virtue. From himself...
If one is personally lax in body and mind at home, yet demands that others be respectful and diligent, this is called a violation of ritual propriety (*li*).
Now, as a teacher and exemplar for humans and devas, having already lost virtue and violated propriety, one does not know what standard to provide as a model to bequeath to posterity.
Reading this causes the hair on one's body to stand on end; those who are neither upright nor diligent will naturally find no place to remain.
The Section on the Ground of the Body. This chapter instructs the student that the mind must not harbor external objects, for fear that they may harm its rectitude.
Sishin said to Chen Yingzhong: "If you wish to seek the Great Way, first rectify your mind; if there is even the slightest trace of anger or resentment,"
If one does not attain correctness, it is because of a slight indulgence in desires; this too prevents one from attaining correctness.

However, unless one is a sage or a worthy who has appeared in the world, how could one be without love, hatred, joy, or anger? One must simply not place these before oneself so that they harm one's correctness;
in this way, one attains it. (From the *Guǎnglù*)
This means that if a person seeks the unsurpassed Great Way, they must first rectify this mind. Do not harbor doubts or obstructions;
if even the slightest external object is allowed to remain within it, this mind will become unrectified. *Fen* (忿) is the extreme of anger.
"Enmity (*chì*) is the stagnation of anger. If there is even a slight trace of resentment within the breast, this mind will become biased toward anger.
If there is even a slight trace of craving within the breast, this mind will become biased toward craving.
Thus, unless one is a sage or a holy one manifested in the world, how could one be without the minds of love, hatred, joy, and anger? Even if such states were to arise,"
One must simply not harbor it within one's breast, lest it harm the rectitude that I maintain. One who acts thus may be said to have attained it.
△ The subtlety here lies in the single phrase: "one must simply not place it before oneself."
If this is indeed so, what cause for concern is there regarding the mind’s lack of rectitude or the failure to accomplish the Way?
This chapter maintains that in studying the Way, frugality is the essential; only by means of it can one reach its ultimate realization.
Sishin said: "Frugality and letting go are the most direct paths for entering the Way. I have often seen students whose minds are full of indignation and whose mouths are choked with words;
who among them does not wish to follow in the footsteps of the ancients? Yet when one observes their practice of letting go and frugality, not even one in ten thousand succeeds.
It is exactly like the sons and grandsons of secular families who refuse to study books but desire to become officials—though they may be three feet tall," [they still fail].
Child, know that one who cannot let go is necessarily incapable of practicing this.
Frugality is itself letting go; if one cannot let go, one cannot relinquish. How, then, can such a person be called frugal?
One must understand that while moderation and frugality are minor matters, the two words "letting go" (fangxia) are most weighty.

As the Buddha said to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), "I teach you to let go of the six internal sense organs, the six external objects, and the six consciousnesses in between; even that which lets go must itself be let go.
From this, the non-Buddhist attained awakening and entry [into the Way]. Thus, one knows that letting go is the most direct path for entering the Way.
This is a swift path. I have often seen scholars whose minds are filled with frustration;
they wish to penetrate [the truth] but cannot, and their mouths are full of yearning; they wish to speak but cannot. Who does not desire to follow in the footsteps of the ancients?
Yet when one observes their ordinary conduct, they lack that which allows for a state of ease and proper moderation.
Those who practice frugality and restraint are as rare as finding one person in ten thousand.
They are like the sons and younger brothers of worldly families who refuse to study books, desiring only to become officials;

not only would the wise find such behavior laughable, but even a child of three feet height knows that this will certainly never happen and cannot be achieved. △ The two characters "let go" (fangxia).
Within this there are hundreds of thousands of gates of liberation and hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi; those who realize and enter them are indeed near-sages.
This chapter maintains that a student must possess talent, discernment, and noble magnanimity; those who harbor depravity and pursue power are of no use.
Sishin said to Zhantang: "Among students, those who possess talent and discernment, as well as loyalty, integrity, and a sense of honor, are the highest grade.

Those whose talent may not be great but who are prudent and possess a broad capacity are the next. As for those who harbor depravity and wait for opportunities, changing their course according to circumstances—"
"This is truly a petty person. If he were placed before others, he would surely destroy the monastic community and defile the Dharma-gate" (Shilu).
Master Sijian (Sishin) said to Master Zhantang: "In general, the temperaments of those who study are not uniform; some possess talent..."
Those who possess learning, insight, and discernment, as well as loyalty, trustworthiness, integrity, and righteousness, are the highest.
Furthermore, those whose talent and insight are not particularly high, yet are able to be respectful, prudent, and possessed of great capacity, are next.

As for those of a certain kind whose inner thoughts are private and depraved, who observe and spy upon others, and who change their stance according to the momentum of victory or defeat—[they are the lowest].
As for such a person, they are truly a petty man. If one places such a type before the assembly, they will surely destroy the grove and defile the courtyard of the Dharma’s transformation.
One must not fail to be cautious. (The character *du* means "to confuse" or "to mix.
By citing this essential point, may each person know what to maintain; only then will one see that practice and wisdom grow together, and transformation and the mind develop in tandem.
It is accomplished. Yet, whose fault is it when virtue is ruined?
This chapter maintains that for a *chuzhi* (abbot), sincerity and trustworthiness must be the foundation; thus, one’s influence upon others will surely be profound.
Sishin said to Caotang: "In the duties of a *chuzhi*, whether in speech or action, the essential requirement is sincerity and trustworthiness. Regarding these words:
If one is sincere and trustworthy, that which is moved will necessarily be profound; if one’s words are not sincere and trustworthy, that which is moved will necessarily be shallow.
Even among the common people in ordinary life, they cannot bear to engage in insincere speech or untrustworthy conduct, fearing they will be deceived by their fellow villagers;

how much more so for one who is the master of a monastic community, representing the Buddhas and Patriarchs to propagate the Dharma? If one’s speech and actions lack sincerity and trustworthiness, then [the consequences] will be like a lake...
"Among the sea-robed monks, who would follow him? (From the *Huanglong Shilu*).
One who holds the office of abbot is no ordinary person; in their speech and conduct, they must prioritize sincerity and trustworthiness.
If one’s words are honest and thus command the trust of others, those who are moved by them will surely be deeply so. As for the words...
If one lacks sincerity and trustworthiness, one’s influence upon others will certainly be shallow.
As for insincere speech and untrustworthy conduct, even ordinary commoners and the sons of the people would not dare to practice them. Why? Because they fear being deceived by their neighbors;
ten thousand two thousand households constitute a *xiang* (district), and five hundred households constitute a *dang* (ward). How much more so for those who live in a *cong* (a cluster of villages)!
The Master of the Forest (the abbot) is originally one who acts as a representative of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to proclaim the Dharma and its transformation.
If his speech and conduct lack sincerity and integrity, then among the monastics from all quarters of the world, who would follow him?

△ When sincerity and integrity are present, one is upright and not deceitful; who would not be moved by such righteousness? Conversely, if one encounters objects [with insincerity], [they will not be moved].
Thus, they stand apart and do not harmonize.
This chapter states that the Way (*dào*) and profit (*lì*) cannot be practiced simultaneously; this is an established principle. Sīxīn said:
"Those who seek profit cannot be given the Way; those who seek the Way cannot be given profit. The ancients were not... [so].

One cannot possess both; for their natures are incompatible. If profit and the Way could be practiced simultaneously, then even merchants, butchers, and commoners who carry goods for sale in the villages would all be able to seek them.

Why, then, must one follow the ancients who renounced wealth and honor, forgot fame and achievement, extinguished their worldly desires, and stilled their intellects amidst empty mountains and vast marshes, subsisting on water from mountain streams and food from trees until the end of their lives?
It is a matter of the person. One must say that the pursuit of profit and the practice of the Way are not mutually obstructive;
yet, it is like holding a leaking cup to pour water into a parched cauldron—one can achieve nothing by way of salvation (Letter to Han Jizang).
The Master said: "Those who seek profit possess a worldly mind; knowing only the desire for gain, they cannot be spoken to about the Way.
Those who seek the Way already know that profit is an instrument that harms the Way; how could they be spoken to about profit once again?"
It is not that the ancients were unable to practice both of these together in the world;

rather, it was because their circumstances made such coexistence impossible. If profit and the Way could be pursued simultaneously without contradiction, then everyone in the world could practice them—whether walking as a merchant, sitting as a trader, or even as a butcher.

As for those who sell wine: even the common folk at the gates of the hamlets and lanes, and the peddlers who shoulder and carry their loads to buy cheaply and sell dearly, are all capable of attaining this Way. Why need it necessarily be the ancients?

It requires only that one cast aside wealth and honor, forget fame and achievement, extinguish the worldly mind, and dissolve the cleverness of artifice, entering deeply into the empty mountains and vast marshes.
"Drinking from mountain streams and eating from wooden vessels to spend this entire life seeking the Way—is this truly so?
Suppose there were someone who could definitively explain how benefit and the Way are compatible; it would not hinder our joint practice, nor would they be in contradiction.
What would such a person be like? It is, for example, like a person holding a broken, leaking wine cup in their hand, wishing to pour [it out]."
To attempt to save a large cauldron that is already glowing red—how could one possibly succeed in such a task? A "leaking cup" (*lòuzhī*) is a vessel for pouring wine;
an ancient saying holds that even the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers cannot fill a leaking cup. As for the "glowing cauldron," it refers to the past when Qin attacked Zhao.
Zhao sought assistance from Qi, but Qi was not clear-sighted. Zhouzi said: "If Zhao perishes today, the calamity will reach Qi tomorrow. Thus, he urged them to save Zhao.
This is an urgent matter. It would be as if one were attempting to fill a cauldron on Mount Jiao with water from a leaking cup; how could such things possibly be pursued simultaneously?
If Śākyamuni were truly capable of pursuing both at once, he would be deemed unwise. Why then did he necessarily abandon the royal palace to enter the Snowy Mountains?
To insist on pursuing both would be either foolishness or madness.
This chapter shows that when one possesses virtue, people will naturally feel admiration and longing for them;
such is the case here. Sishin said: "In the past, when the late Master Huītáng traveled to Eastern Wu, he saw Yuánzhào being invited to Jìngcí Monastery.
The monastics and laypeople of Suzhou and Hangzhou vied with one another without ceasing. One said, 'This is my teacher; why do you snatch him away? Another said, 'Now, it is mine...'"
"Master! What do you have [to offer]? (One version of this appears in the *Línjiān lù*).
This refers to when the late Master Huìtáng was traveling in Gūsū, Eastern Wú, and met Chán Master Yuánzhào Zōngběn of Huílín Monastery in Dōngjīng.
He was the son of Guǎn of Wúxī, Chángzhōu, and succeeded Chán Master Tiānyī Huái. He was from Qīng...
The eleventh generation descendant of Yuanxia, Master [Xuedou Chongxian], was invited by Li Fugui, the Commissioner of Grain Transport, to open a dharma seat at Ruiwang Temple.
Chen Xiang, the Governor of Wulin, offered him the choice between two monasteries, Chengtian and Xingjiao, for him to reside in.
As he traveled toward Hangzhou to accept the invitation from Jingci Temple, the clergy and laity of both Suzhou and Hangzhou vied with one another to detain him along the road.
They would not stop. The people of Suzhou said, "This is our master. Why do you seize him from us? The people of Hangzhou said, "He has now accepted our invitation;
he is therefore our master. What right do you have to him? The Magistrate of Hangzhou sent a formal letter to the people of Suzhou, instructing them:
"We have borrowed this master for three years to plant roots of merit for the people of our state. We dare not presume to occupy his person for long. Suzhou...
People first look at it [the triangle] wondering what kind of rare treasure it is, vying for it without ceasing;
yet in the end, they realize that what can be vied for is something the person lacks alone while the teacher possesses alone.
This chapter shows how the ancients dealt with people according to the Way and righteousness, without any private partiality.

While Sīti-citta resided at Cuiyan, he heard that Juefan had been exiled to the overseas regions; when the latter passed through Nanchang on his way, Sīti-citta invited him to return to the mountains.
He was welcomed for several days and escorted with generous hospitality. Some remarked that Sishin’s moods were inconsistent, to which Sishin replied, "Juefan is a virtuous monk.
Previously, he spoke excessively, so I stripped away his sharp edges. Now that he has encountered such adversity, it is simply his natural lot.
I have dealt with this according to the principles of the monastic community as I have always practiced. Those who understood him said that Sishin harbored no private bias toward others.
Thus it is recorded (in the *Xishan Jiwen*):
When Sīxīn was residing at Cuiyan in Jiangxi, he heard that Juefan had been banished and exiled overseas.

As Juefan’s route passed through Nanchang, Sīxīn sent someone to invite him to enter the mountains of Cuiyan. He hosted him for several days, and as they were about to part, [Sīxīn] gave him everything...
He performed the funeral rites to escort him [to the afterlife]. Some said that Master Sīxīn’s moods were inconsistent.
Sīxīn replied, "Jiǎoguàn is a monk of great virtue. 'Xiāng' (鄉) and 'xiàng' (向) are homophones.
That I previously refuted him with all my might was precisely because I cherished him; I intended to prevent him from exposing his sharp edges to the outside world, hoping—"
That he might have escaped calamity and hardship was his lot; now that he has suddenly encountered such adversity, it is simply his own destiny and cannot be avoided.
I am now treating him according to the principles of monastic conduct as practiced in our community during ordinary times; truly, there is no other motive.
Those who understand will hear this and say that Master Sijian’s heart was one of singular integrity and impartiality, devoid of any private interest.
Therefore, it is as it is. △ Regarding the reality of the Perfected Person (zhiren): truly there are no two functions.

Because people use love and hatred to model themselves after them, they measure the Perfected Person with ordinary sentiments and fail to comprehend the reason for their sameness. Students should deeply contemplate and realize this.
This chapter states that human beings possess an innate nature of birth and growth, which cannot be forcibly altered to make them good or evil.
Sishin said to Caotang: "The late Master Huaitang said that a person's breadth and kindness are obtained through their heavenly nature. If..."
To constrain them with severity will certainly not endure for long. If severity does not endure, it will instead lead to being treated with contempt by petty men.
Furthermore, whether one is depraved or upright, good or evil, these qualities are obtained through one's innate nature and cannot be altered.
Only the nature of the mediocre person is easily moved upward or downward; they can be transformed through guidance. (Shilu)
The late Master Huìtáng said: "Among the natures bestowed upon people by the world, those that are expansive, magnanimous, and grave are all fundamentally rooted in Heaven’s creation;
they cannot be achieved through forced effort. If one's nature is inherently gentle, yet one compels it to be fierce,"
Since it is not one's original nature, it cannot endure for long. If one attempts to raise oneself up with sudden force even once, before long, one will collapse and cease;
one will instead become an object of contempt for petty people, who will say that your willpower has declined.

It is simply that their practice is not constant. However, it is not only this; even the depravity or rectitude, the goodness or evil of a person, are all obtained through their innate nature (*t'ien hsing*) and cannot be forcibly altered.

Only for those of a middle capacity can the nature be transformed by being permeated with the influences of depravity or rectitude, goodness or evil; thus they may easily ascend or easily descend, and may follow accordingly.
This is the manifestation of transformation in accordance with its kind. While the nature bestowed by Heaven is indeed fixed, it is an error to suppress that nature and act against it.
Whether one is of superior intelligence or inferior folly, neither can easily be altered. One must understand that following one's nature is not merely the subtle function of the wise.
This chapter teaches that one should govern the mind before afflictions have even sprouted; once emotions arise and thoughts are produced, it is difficult to manage them.
Master Qing of Caotang said: "The fire that consumes the plains begins from a tiny spark; the torrent that destroys mountains originates from a single drop.
When water is minute, a handful of earth can block it; yet when it is in full flood, it drifts away timber and stones and submerges entire hills."
A spark is the smallest form of fire; a mere ladle of water can extinguish it. Yet when it reaches its full intensity, it scorches entire cities and burns down mountains and forests.
How does this differ from the water of craving and attachment, or the fire of hatred and anger? They are never different.
This section cites an event to verify its subtle meaning. Chan Master Shànqīng of Cǎotáng in Lóngxīng Prefecture was the son of the Hé family of Nányōngzhōu.
He was a successor of Chan Master Zǔxīn of Huánglóng and belonged to the thirteenth generation under Nányuè.
He said that worldly people inherently possess the water of greed and desire and the fire of anger and hatred, which are extremely difficult to subdue and manage.
Therefore, an analogy is first presented for clarification. *Liao* means to burn; *ying* refers to a spark.
It is like a fire burning across a vast plain, which begins from a single spark, or water collapsing a hillside, which starts from a single drop.
When water has not yet burst forth, it exists as a minute drop in a slender stream, such that a handful of earth can block and cut it off.
Yet when it reaches its full magnitude and arrives, it will drift over timber and stones and submerge hills and mounds without ceasing.
When fire has not yet ignited and exists as nothing more than a tiny spark, a single ladle of water can extinguish it.
When their ferocity arrives, they scorch the capital cities and burn the mountains and forests without ceasing.
That which the Son of Heaven inhabits is called a "du" (capital); the *Rites of Zhou* states that four counties constitute a "du," and four "wells" (*jing*) constitute a "yi" (village).
Yet how can the water of worldly craving and the fire of anger be any different from these?
When the ancients governed their minds, they guarded against thoughts before they had arisen and against emotions before they had been stirred;

thus, the effort required was extremely subtle, yet the achievement was immense. When, however, emotion and nature became disordered and love and hatred began to clash, one’s own life was harmed and others were injured;
this was perilous and imminent, beyond the possibility of rescue.
This section teaches the defense of the emotions to rectify the beginning.

However, when the ancients cultivated their minds, they prevented thoughts before they had arisen and severed emotions before they had emerged; thus, while the effort exerted was extremely subtle, the actual achievement was immense.
If one allows emotions and nature to become entangled within sensory objects, and if love and hatred attack one another therein—

The mind: if one harms it within oneself, one injures one's own life; if one harms it in others, one injures fellow human beings. Its peril is certainly inevitable; how could one ever hope to rescue it?
Is it truly that humans have no feelings? As for what is called "preventing" and "governing" [the mind], it refers to this.
One must restrain the waters and fires of anger and attachment; they must not be allowed to run wild. If they run wild, disaster will spread without limit and can no longer be remedied.

This chapter states that if an abbot wishes for his legacy to endure through great traditions for a long time, it is essential that he examine human nature and understand the relationship between superiors and subordinates.
Cao Tang said: "For an abbot, there is nothing else required than to examine human relations and thoroughly understand those above and below.
When human relations are examined, those within and without will be harmonious; when those above and below communicate, all affairs will be orderly. This is how an abbot finds peace.
If one cannot examine human relations, and the sentiments of subordinates cannot reach the superior, then those above and below will be discordant and all affairs will fall into contradiction."
This is why the position of abbot falls into neglect.
This section takes the examination of human sentiments as its function. For an abbot, there is no other method:

one need only examine and scrutinize the sentiments of the multitude with thorough sincerity. By comprehensively and deeply understanding and harmonizing the intentions of those above and below, then—
The task can then be accomplished. If people can thoroughly understand human nature, then there will be no discord between the inner and outer circles.
If those above and below can communicate fully with one another, then all affairs will naturally be brought into order. This is why the abbot remains at peace.

If people are unable to examine matters with discernment, such that the conditions below do not communicate with those above, causing the upper and lower levels to become estranged and contradictory, then all affairs will naturally fall into conflict; this is why the administration of the monastery falls into ruin.
Should the ruler, relying on his own clever endowments, take pleasure in clinging to biased views and fail to understand the sentiments of others;

should he set aside collective deliberation to exalt his own authority and discard public discourse to dispense private favors; he will cause the path for the advancement of the virtuous to gradually narrow.
The Way of entrusting it to the multitude has become increasingly obscure. They disparage what they have not seen or heard, and remain settled in their habitual prejudices and delusions.

To desire that the scriptures be maintained and the transmission endure for long is like walking backward while seeking to go forward; in the end, it is impossible to reach the goal. (Letter to Shantang)
The essential teaching of this section is to eliminate one’s private biases and obscurations.
Those who act as leaders may, relying on their own possession of clever and qualified attributes, single-mindedly favor clinging to their own partial views and fail to understand human sentiment.
They disregard the public consensus of the multitude (*śāṃ*) and instead value their own private authority, furthermore subverting the common good.

To prioritize one's own private, petty favors over the correct discourse of the multitude leads to the gradual narrowing and obstruction of the path for the advancement of goodness, while the great Way of the masses becomes increasingly diminished.
Consequently, one becomes a person of narrow learning and meager knowledge; regarding matters that were originally neither seen nor heard, one instead slanders them as such.
No. This is the fault of being obscured by what one has personally practiced; yet instead, one complacently regards it as correct.

If this is the case, even if one wishes to ensure that the Way and the Great Tradition endure for a long time, it is like turning one's back and walking away while still wishing to reach the destination ahead—it can never be attained. When Confucius was in Wei, Ran Qiu spoke to Ji [Shi].
Sun said: "If a state possesses sages yet cannot employ them, yet seeks to achieve order thereby, it is like walking backward while seeking to move forward;
how could such a goal ever be reached? If one thoroughly examines human nature and understands the righteousness of superiors and subordinates, there will be no situation where they do not harmonize;

wherever they go, they will succeed. To fail in righteousness and rely solely on cleverness, remaining complacent within one's own obscurations, is merely to follow the dictates of prevailing power and circumstance."
There is nothing that will not lead to failure.
This chapter teaches students to maintain an upright mind; then they will not fall into the ranks of those who hold divergent opinions.

Caotang said: "When a student establishes their character, they must ensure it is correct and proper, so as not to give others cause for private criticism. Once one enters the realm of divergent arguments," [the path is lost].
Then one will be unable to establish oneself for the rest of one's life. Formerly, the attendant Dàyáng Píng was highly esteemed by the monastic community for his mastery of the Way;
yet because his inner heart was not upright, those who discerned the truth condemned him, leading to a lifetime of misfortune and leaving him with no place to turn at the time of his death.
How much more so, then, for one who serves as a master of a particular region—it is all the more necessary to be reverent and cautious. (A letter to a Secretary).
Master Caotang said: "A student who wishes to establish their character for a lifetime must be upright and correct, ensuring that others do not engage in private, surreptitious criticism.
If one falls into heterodox views even once, then for the remainder of that life, one will be unable to stand firm.
In the past, Attendant Taiyang Ping resided in the quarters of Ming’an for many years; although he had mastered [the teachings] completely...
Their intent was solely to take the doctrine of birth and cessation as their own burden, seeking to undermine their colleagues and envying those who surpassed them.
At that time, Langye Guangzhao and Gong’an Yuanjian were among the assembly; when they were at Fenyang, Chan Master Zhao instructed them to investigate the fundamental tenets of Ming’an.
Ming’an said, "To revive the school of Dongshan, it will be none other than Yuan and Jue. The two masters replied: [and proceeded to do so].
The attendant Ping was present. Huian pointed to his chest with his finger and said, "This place is not good.
He then pressed his thumb between his fingers and showed it to him, saying, "Ping, you shall die here in the future.

After Huian passed away, he left a final instruction, saying, "If there are no obstacles for ten years after my body is interred, you should perform a memorial service for me at Taiyang Mountain. When the time comes to enter the stupa, my disciples..."

Fearing that Hyŏngp’yŏng might bring misfortune to the monastic community, [the abbot] inscribed upon the stupa inscription the description of the yellow and white ritual vessels bestowed by Nihu Wen-dui, though in reality none existed.
Later, while Hyŏngp’yŏng was residing at Taeryang, he suddenly declared, "The geomantic orientation of my late master’s remains is unfavorable;
I shall remove them and cremate them. The senior monks of the monastery earnestly admonished him, but Hyŏngp’yŏng replied, "It is for my own sake."

This was an obstacle. He then opened the stupa and saw that the Master’s countenance was as if alive; even as the firewood was exhausted, the body remained solemn and intact. The assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement.
Hui Ping broke open the Master’s skull with a pickaxe and added more oil and fuel, whereupon it was soon reduced to ashes. The assembly reported this matter to the authorities.
Hui Ping was charged for plotting to seize the contents of the stupa and for his lack of filial piety, and he returned to lay life. Later, Hui Ping referred to himself as "Young Scholar Huang."
He went to visit Langya. Langya said, "In years past you were Attendant Ping; today you are Scholar Huang.
When I was at Taiyang, I saw what you have done, so I will not accept you. He then visited Gong’an, who responded in the same manner.
Ping wandered on without refuge until, later, he was encountered and eaten by a tiger at a three-way intersection; in the end, he could not escape Taiyang.
The record of his hand-crossing gesture is truly lamentable. Furthermore, when one examines the path of his scholarly learning, it was indeed held in high esteem by the monastic community.
Yet, because his inner disposition was not upright, he was censured by the wise; consequently, his life remained full of misfortune until the end.
"Kǎnkě" (坎坷) describes a state of unevenness and adversity. Upon his death, he had nowhere to turn. But how could this be the case for scholars alone?
As the host of this region, you must be even more cautious and reverent in your conduct and actions.
When the mind is sincere and the person upright, one’s vital energy (qi) can overshadow mountains and rivers;
how could one who secretly harbors such thoughts ever manifest such power? Those who are insincere and unrighteous lose their very selves; they have no place within heaven and earth.
This chapter teaches that an abbot should personally associate with the worthy and distance himself from the sycophantic; doing so constitutes grasping the fundamental principle.
Caotang said to the Abbot: "The late Master Haitang once remarked that among the vast crowds of people, the worthy and the unworthy follow one another in succession.
Because the gate of transformation is so expansive, it allows for no distinction between the intimate and the distant within its midst. It simply requires that you apply a little more refinement."
In selecting [monks], if one whose talent and virtue accord with public expectation cannot be distanced simply because you are angry with him,
and if one whose insight is mediocre and whom the masses detest cannot be favored simply because you love him,
then the worthy will naturally advance and the unworthy will naturally withdraw; thus, the monastic community will be at peace.
Chan Master Faru of Daochang Monastery in Anjī Prefecture was the son of the Xu family of Qúzhōu.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shǒuzhì of Yúngài and belongs to the thirteenth generation under Nányuè. This section follows the principle that [truth] must necessarily be attained;
as my late teacher Huìtáng said: "In the midst of a vast multitude, so-called dragons and snakes are intermingled, and the worthy and the unworthy come into contact."
"Following in succession to dwell together. "Following in succession" means that their footsteps follow one another.

Because this dharma-gate of transformation is vast in its precincts, it admits no discrimination between those who are close and those who are distant. It depends solely upon the master to exercise a degree of careful selection;
if a monk truly possesses talent and virtue, and is capable of meeting the high expectations of the assembly, [he shall be admitted].
One should naturally be close to them; one must not distance oneself from them simply because of one's own anger.

If they are indeed of mediocre or common character and are thus detested by everyone else, one should naturally distance oneself from them; yet even then, one must not do so merely because of one's own personal affection.
By treating them with such personal intimacy, the worthy will naturally advance toward you, while the unworthy will naturally withdraw.
Thus, the monastic community will immediately find peace and happiness.

If the leader delights in indulging his private whims and exercises his own likes and dislikes in the advancement or dismissal of others, then the worthy will remain silent while the unworthy vie for promotion;
the disciplinary regulations will fall into disorder, and the monastic community will perish.

This section contradicts reason and is self-defeating. If a ruler delights in indulging his private whims and advances or dismisses others solely according to his own likes and dislikes, then the worthy will remain silent. "Jian" (緘) means to seal; "mo" (默) means not to speak.
At that time, when Confucius was observing the Zhou dynasty and entered the temple of Houji, he saw a golden man with his mouth sealed by three locks.
The inscription on its back reads: "If the mechanism of Heaven were not secret, how could the four seasons proceed? If the mechanism of Earth were not secret, how could the myriad things be born?
If the mechanism of Man were not secret, how could myriad affairs be accomplished? This was the man of antiquity who was cautious with his words.
The unworthy, however, compete for advancement, whereby the fundamental regulations fall into disorder and the monastic communities are brought to ruin."
These two are the true essence of sustaining the Dharma. If one can truly examine and practice them, those nearby will be delighted and those afar will spread the word.
Then what concern would there be that the Way would not prevail, or that practitioners would not come to admire it? (From the Shushan Stone Inscription)

This section generally clarifies the fundamental principle: to be close to the worthy and wise, and distant from the unworthy and base. These two points are truly the great principles for maintaining the teachings.
If one can indeed examine them carefully and act accordingly, such that there is a proper way of distinguishing between the near and the distant, then those who are close will be filled with joy.
When this is proclaimed far and wide, what need is there to worry that the Way will not prevail,

or that practitioners will not come forward with admiration? To treat the intimate and the distant with propriety is the essential secret for perfecting one's person and the great achievement of excelling above the common.
The master of this chapter was skilled at employing people; he will surely cause the Way to flourish and the Dharma to prosper.
Caotang said to the Senior Seat-holder Kung: "Since the beginning of the monastic communities, none have been as successful in attracting talent as Shitou, Mazu, Xuefeng, and Yunmen.
In recent times, there have been only the two elders Huanglong and Wuzu who were truly able to gather them in."
The eminent monastics from the four quarters, according to the depth of their capacity and the nature of their talents, were brought forth and employed.
It was as if riding a light carriage drawn by four fine horses: by holding the six reins and exerting the whip and goad, the restraining and releasing occurred within the span of a single glance;
thus, how could one fail to reach the destination? (From the *Guanglu*).
Cao Tang Heshang said to the Head Seat Xingkong— Xingkong being the dharma heir of Huanglong Wuxin—
that "one who is skilled at acquiring people must also be skilled at employing them. Since the beginning of the monastic communities (*sōnglin*),
none have been as preeminent in acquiring disciples as Shitou, Mazu, and Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Nan'an Lu.
The master’s son succeeded Zen Master Xuánjiàn of Dēngshān; he was the fifth generation descendant of Qīngyuán.
Zen Master Wényǎn of Yúnmén was the son of Zhāng of Jiāxīng; he succeeded Zen Master Cúnxión of Xuěfēng and was the sixth generation descendant of Qīngyuán.
In recent times, there have been only Hánglóng Nán and Wǔzǔ Yǎn—these two elders were truly able to gather in [the disciples] from all quarters.
All those who are handsome and refined monastics—those whose wisdom surpasses that of a thousand men—are called "refined" (*jun*).

Furthermore, he is able to assess the capacity and scale of each person, measuring their depth and breadth, as well as whether their talent, strength, and temperament are capable or not, thereby developing and selecting them.
This is like one riding a light carriage who drives it with a team of fine horses; when four horses are at the yoke, they are said to be "driving."
*Jùn*: An excellent horse. A single carriage drawn by four horses is called *sì*. One who holds all six reins: the carriage has four horses;
each has two reins, totaling eight. The two inner reins of the two outer horses (*cán*) are fastened to the front rail (*shì*).

The two outer reins of the two outer horses, along with the four reins of the two inner horses (*fú*) flanking the axle, are distributed between the two hands to constitute the six reins. To exert [them].
He governs them with the whip—the *ce* being a horse-whip, used to strike the horse.
Whether restraining or releasing, whether slow or swift—all occurs within the span of my looking left and right. "Looking" (*guàn*) means turning one's gaze.
If one acts in this manner, where would there be a place one could not reach? △ [This refers to] gathering people together.
One must not harbor even a hair’s breadth of falsehood; there must be nothing but sincerity and earnestness. If one possesses deep compassion and vast wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be managed.

This chapter instructs the abbot not to listen to only one side or to act on his own authority; by carefully examining what is appropriate and what is not, he will succeed in putting it into practice.
Cao Tang said: "The abbot has no other task than to be cautious regarding the faults of partiality and autocracy.
If he does not allow himself to be dominated by the words of those who have first entered his ear, then the slanderous flattery and sycophancy of petty men will not be able to delude him."
For the dispositions of the multitude are not uniform, and impartial discourse is difficult to perceive. One must examine their benefits and harms and deliberate upon their acceptability;
only then may one proceed to implement them (from the *Shushan Shilu*).
In serving as an abbot, there is no other purpose than to guard against partiality in listening and to be cautious of unilateral authority;
these two are great maladies. Furthermore, one must not take what has first entered the ear as being correct, but must instead evaluate it through reason.
In this way, the flattery of petty people and their attempts to ingratiate themselves by echoing the slanders of others will be prevented.
It shall not be possible to delude or confuse you. For the temperaments and dispositions of the multitude are not uniform;
therefore, a most impartial discourse is exceedingly difficult to perceive. It must depend upon the presiding authority to examine the strengths and weaknesses of each individual.
Examine the person’s suitability; only then may you proceed with confidence that no error will occur. △ Listening to one side is a malady of folly;
acting on one's own authority is a malady of arrogance. Both are terminal conditions. If one can exercise restraint and vigilance, the vitality of life remains.
This chapter teaches people to determine right from wrong through principle, so that the treacherous and sycophantic cannot delude them.
Caotang said to Shantang: "In the affairs of the world, as long as right and wrong are not yet clear, one must be cautious.

Once right and wrong are clear, decide upon them according to principle; let the Way alone be the guide, and resolve matters without hesitation. If one acts thus, the treacherous and sycophantic will [be unable to cause harm]."
One may be deluded; even forceful sophistry cannot shift [one's conviction] (from the *Qingquan jiwen*).
In worldly affairs, there are always both the right and the wrong. If right and wrong have not yet been clearly distinguished, one must exercise self-restraint.
Once right and wrong are already clear, one must further resolve them through correct principle (*zhengli*). Correct...
Principle is precisely where the Way resides. Once you have resolved a matter through principle, you must further ensure that your judgment is free from doubt.

When your sovereign authority is thus firmly established, those who are treacherous and sycophantic shall be unable to delude your intelligence, and those who are eloquent and contentious shall be unable to shift your settled standard. The location of the Way is like the fixed balance of a scale.
As for external things, how could they ever affect me? It is simply that one must not be partial; for if one is partial, then right and wrong arise.
This chapter states that the Way-person takes the fulfillment of their nature as joy, such that even fame cannot move them.
When Master Zhèn of Shāntáng first declined the summons from Cáo-shān, the Prefectural Governor sent an official letter urging him to accept.

Shāntáng declined, saying: "If I were to eat fine rice and chew fatty meat, becoming a monk who covets fame, it would be better to wear clothes of grass and eat wood for sustenance as a wild man of Yǐn-shān. (Recorded by the Master of Quánquán Cáiyuàn).
Chan Master Shantang Daozhen of Huanglong Mountain in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Zhao family of Jinling.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Letan Shan and belonged to the fourteenth generation under Mount Heng. Although he was invited by Caoshan, the Master refused to accept.

When the local Governor sent an official letter urging him to enter the world [as a public teacher], Shantang declined, saying: "If you wish me to leave my home, let it be as if I were leaving my fine rice."
"Biting into the fat and fine grain. "Biting" means to chew; "fat" means oily. This refers to plotting for exquisite food.
To become a patch-robed monk who craves fame is, in fact, not as good as being a wild man of Mount Yin, wearing clothes of grass and eating from the trees—would that not be joyful?
△ In ancient times, people did not eat official stipends but ate *wei* (cranesbill plants).
His physical form was not stout, yet his reputation was stout; even after a thousand autumns, this man remains resolutely prominent.
This chapter asserts that forgetting artifice is itself the ultimate Way; it is when one harbors doubt toward others that others themselves become doubtful.
Mountantang said: "Snakes and tigers are not natural enemies of hawks and vultures; why then do hawks and vultures shriek at them?
It is because they harbor different intentions. Oxen and pigs are not ridden by magpies; why then do magpies gather and perch upon them? It is because they harbor no different intentions.
Long ago, when Zhaozhou visited a hermitage master, he happened upon him serving rice. Zhaozhou said, 'A crow chick.'"

Seeing people, it would fly away at great speed. The master was bewildered. He then repeated his previous words and questioned the Prefect. The Prefect replied, "It was because I harbored a murderous intent.

This passage distinguishes between whether one's underlying state of mind is different or not; [the former refers to] snakes, tigers, and other malevolent insects and beasts, while [the latter refers to] hawks and vultures.
These are also predatory birds. Although snakes, tigers, and hawks or kites harbor no mutual enmity, each possesses a distinct nature;
thus, upon seeing one another, they cry out and pursue each other. The "mynah" (yīngquè) is the same as the "eight-sister" bird (bāgē).
Although oxen and pigs are not creatures that can be ridden by magpies, because they lack such animosity, the magpies are able to gather and mount them. Formerly, at Zhòuzhōu—
While visiting Master Yizhan, he happened upon the master serving rice. Yizhan asked, "Why does the crow fly away when it sees people?
[The Master replied,] "Crows and ravens are the same. The abbot was bewildered and could not fathom this; he then repeated his previous question to Yizhan.
Yizhan replied, "It is because I harbor a murderous intent."
Therefore, those who harbor suspicion toward others will themselves be suspected by others; those who forget about external things will themselves be forgotten by them.
The ancients who dwelt as equals with snakes and tigers were those who thoroughly understood this principle. As Master Laopang said: "The iron ox fears not the lion’s roar;
it is like a wooden man beholding flowers and birds. These words encompass it all (from his letter to Layman Zhou).
This section clarifies that whether emotions are forgotten or not, both states are empty. Therefore, it is not the case that I fail to forget my emotions and yet doubt others;
nor can others fail to forget their emotions and yet doubt me. Since I am already free from the mind’s obstruction by external objects, [there is no room for such doubts].
Things are inherently without mind; it is only when they obstruct me that they become impediments. For instance, Master Dakong had two tigers that attended upon him.
Venerable Yan-yang allowed snakes and tigers to come into his hands to eat from them, treating them as his equals.
Five people gathering together is called a "wu" (伍), which also means a companion or partner. These are all examples of being skillfully attuned to the principle of forgetting emotions. [Xiangzhou]
The layman Pang Yun, courtesy name Daoxuan, was a native of Hengyang. He received the Dharma from Mazu. He had a verse that said:
"Only by being personally without mind toward the myriad things, How could the myriad things hinder one’s constant surrounding?

An iron ox fears not the lion’s roar; It is just like a wooden man seeing flowers and birds. The essential nature of the wooden man is itself devoid of emotion; When flowers and birds encounter this person..."
Nor am I startled. When the mind and its objects are in suchness (*tathatā*), this alone is it. Why worry that the path to Bodhi will not be accomplished?
Master Pang’s words may be said to exhaustively capture the principle of forgetting emotions. As a former Buddha said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise.
I was previously harboring doubts about others' minds, yet others were already harboring doubts about me.
I have only just harbored a sense of resentment toward others, yet they have already resented me first.
How swift is this resonance within!
This chapter states that rewards and punishments must be administered according to the Way (*dào*). If one exceeds these bounds, arrogance and resentment will arise. Mount Tang said:

"In the method of governing subordinates, favor (*ēn*) must not be excessive; if it is excessive, they become arrogant. Authority (*wēi*) must not be overly severe; if it is severe, they become resentful.

If one desires to bestow favor without inciting arrogance, and to exercise authority without causing resentment, that favor must necessarily be bestowed upon those who have performed meritorious service. It must not... [be given otherwise].

To unjustly impose [punishment] upon others is to ensure that majesty is directed only toward those who have committed crimes; it must not be indiscriminately extended to the innocent. Thus, though one’s kindness may be profound, people will not become arrogant;
though one’s majesty may be stern, people will harbor no resentment. Even if a merit is insufficient to be praised, one rewards it generously;
even if a crime is insufficient to be censured, one punishes it with the utmost severity. Consequently, petty people will deliberately give rise to arrogance.
"An enemy! A driver!
A servant!"—these refer to the methods for governing people. Grace and awe must both be applied, but they should be directed toward those who possess the Way.
One should always bestow grace upon others, yet it must not exceed what is deserved by their rewards; if one bestows it excessively, it will instead cause them [to rebel].
In human life, there is pride and luxury. When using authority to control others, one must not exceed the bounds of what is strictly necessary.
If one governs by reversing this [pride], people will inevitably give rise to resentment.

If one wishes to possess benevolence without appearing arrogant to others, and to exercise authority without causing resentment, how can this ultimately be achieved? There is indeed a way; however, benevolence must...
Bestow rewards upon those who have merit; do not grant them arbitrarily to those who are unworthy. When employing force, apply it surely to those who have committed crimes;
do not let it extend indiscriminately to innocent persons. If those with merit receive favor and find peace of mind, what pride could they possibly harbor?
If those without merit receive favor, they will inevitably become arrogant. If those with crimes are made to...
One who receives favor with a willing heart dares not harbor resentment; one who is unjustly implicated against the innocent will inevitably feel resentment.
Therefore, though kindness may be profound, people do not become arrogant; though authority may be strict, people do not harbor resentment.
Each has its own proper way. When another’s merit is small and inherently unworthy of mention, yet they are rewarded generously—such a person...
The offense is light and originally not worth reproaching, yet the punishment is so severe that it inevitably causes the petty person to give rise to arrogance and resentment.
A skilled driver knows how to adjust the reins with proper method, so that both dangerous and level terrain can be traversed together.
When one’s feelings are not comprehensive and one’s wisdom does not reach far, there is no case where arrogance and resentment do not arise.
This chapter states that maintaining one's person depends solely on moderation and caution, and that one must not be reluctant to reform one's errors.
Mount Hall said: "The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs does not go beyond attaining the Mean. To exceed the Mean is to become biased and deviant. Among the affairs of the world,"
One must not indulge one's desires to excess; for excessive indulgence leads to calamity and disorder.

Among people of all times, past and present, there have been many who, through lack of moderation and vigilance, nearly met with ruin and death. Thus, who is without fault? Only when the wise and accomplished reform their errors without stinginess can they truly be called excellent.
This refers to the Way transmitted and upheld by the Buddhas and Patriarchs, which is nothing other than attaining the Mean.
To attain the Mean is to grasp the ultimate principle of the Middle Way. To exceed the Mean is to depart from this principle, thereby resulting in partiality and deviation.

Among the myriad affairs of the world, there is no pursuit that can be fully realized through intentional striving; to strive with such intent is to overstep one's proper bounds, which leads directly to calamity.
Chaos! Among people of both ancient and modern times, many fail to recognize their own adherence to correctness and fail to recognize their own prudence;
consequently, they frequently come to ruin themselves and lose their livelihoods. Thus, who is without fault? Even though one has faults, it is only right that one knows how to reform them.
Only those who are virtuous, talented, and adept at understanding principle will recognize their errors and reform immediately without hesitation;

it is only in this way that one may be called truly admirable. For a practitioner of the Way, one must not overstep the bounds of principle when seeking the underlying truth, nor exceed one's proper station.
These are truly excellent words for warning the world, which one must not fail to investigate with meticulous care.
This chapter shows that when wise men encounter hardships and perils, they all possess a presiding master.
In Mount Tang, together with the Minister Han Zicang and the Head Seat Wannan Yan Xianzhunmu, they sought refuge at Yunmen Hermitage.
Minister Han then asked Wannan: "I have recently heard that you were captured by the soldiers of Li Cheng; what plan did you employ to [escape]?"
Tuo said, "Yesterday I was bound and shackled; for days I suffered from hunger and cold, and I thought I would surely die.
By chance, a great snowfall buried the house, and the wall of the room where I was tied collapsed for no apparent reason. That night, more than a hundred people were fortunately released.
The official asked, "When you were under arrest, how did you manage to dispel [the suffering]? Wan’an did not answer. The official questioned him again, and Wan’an—
He said, "What is there to say about this? We who study the Way take righteousness as our substance; there is only death. What is there to fear?
The official nodded in agreement. From this, one knows that when the seniors of former generations encountered worldly calamities or faced life and death, they all possessed a clear resolution.
In the Mountain Hall, Wuan Yan, the Head Seat, along with Xian and Zhenmu—four people in total—sought refuge from banditry at Yunmen Hermitage together with Han Shangshu Zicang.
Master Han’s name was Ju; his courtesy name was Zicang, and he held the rank of Minister (Shangshu).

He sought instruction at Mount Wudang. In the first year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song Emperor Gaozong, Li Cheng incited a rebellion, gathering over one hundred thousand bandits from various parts of Zhejiang.
He seized control of more than ten prefectures along the Yangtze and Huai rivers and styled himself "Li the Heavenly King.
After plundering Xiangyang, he was defeated by Yue Fei; the number of those who threw themselves into the river is unknown.
Li Cheng was defeated and fled to the Jin. From that time on, Xiangyang and Han were entirely pacified.
Master Han then asked Wan’an, “I have heard recently that you were captured by Li Cheng’s military officials; I wonder what stratagem you employed to escape.
Wan’an replied, “Yesterday I was seized and bound by them. Having suffered from hunger and cold for several days, I calculated that I would certainly die.”

It happened that a heavy snowfall buried the buildings. The walls to which he was tied collapsed all at once without cause—"without cause" meaning it was not seen that anyone intentionally caused them to fall, but rather it was a manifestation of the vital energy (*shengji*) of the Dharma.
That night, by great fortune, more than a hundred people escaped. The official said, "At the very moment you were being held captive, you were a man of the Way (*daoren*). He did not...
[The Master] asked, "Knowing this, how do you dispel it? Wan’an replied, "It is not appropriate to answer immediately.
The Master pressed him again. Wan’an said, "What is there to say about this matter? We who are practitioners of the Way take benevolence and righteousness as our substance;
it is merely a matter of death. What is there to fear? You seem to think that death is—"

"What difficulty is there? The Duke nodded his head. From this, one may know that when the ancients of old traversed the world, they possessed their own sovereign mastery in all matters concerning calamity and harm, life and death, and were able to resolve them accordingly.
△ It is because one has not yet attained mastery that the mind which fears death is ever-present in ordinary sentiment; one simply does not realize that those who have attained it are otherwise.
To regard death as returning home—what is there to fear? This sovereign mastery is not something attained by ordinary people.
This chapter shows that the Perfected Person never loses their rectitude; every movement and gesture is in accord with the Way.
Shantang withdrew from Bai Zhang and said to Han Zicang: "In antiquity, those who advanced possessed both virtue and destiny;
thus they would proceed after three invitations and withdraw after one refusal. Those who advance today rely solely on power and force.
One who knows when to advance and when to withdraw without losing their integrity may truly be called a worthy and enlightened person" (*Jiwen*).
When the Master retired from Baizhang, he said to Han Zicang: "In antiquity, those who advanced to serve as abbot first selected for virtue and second awaited their mandate;
thus they would proceed only after three invitations and withdraw immediately upon a single refusal.
The ancients said, 'They advance after three refusals and withdraw after one. This speaks to the self-respect of the scholar. Nowadays, those who seek advancement..."
Those who hold office rely solely on their power and employ others through force; this is why they lose their integrity.
