To seek one who understands when to advance and when to withdraw without losing their integrity—such a person may be called a worthy and enlightened man.
A true man and a gentleman does not strive for advancement at all costs; he advances only through virtue and further advances only by the mandate of Heaven. To act contrary to this is not [the way].
This refers to the Perfected Man.
This chapter speaks of how the abbot must maintain impartiality and lack private bias, so that no depravity may enter.
Shantang said to Yean: "In maintaining one's mind as an abbot, one must be fair; in conducting affairs, it is not necessary that they originate from oneself."
To regard what is right as wrong means that likes and dislikes, or differences and similarities, will not arise in the mind;
thus, the vapors of violence, arrogance, and depravity will have no way to enter (from the *Huàn'ān jí*).
Chan Master Zutuan Zuxuan of Shiting Wild Hermitage in Longxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao; he belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng.
He maintained that the essential principle for one who holds the position of abbot is to be public-spirited and upright.
Regarding all matters of conduct, he did not consider what originated from himself to be right while regarding what came from others as wrong; rather, he followed a single, uniform path.
Through correct principle, the mind that discriminates between love and hatred or difference and sameness will not arise.

This causes the outwardly violent, arrogant, and deviant energies to naturally find no way to enter. The two characters for "uprightness" and "justice" prevail throughout the world as brightly as the sun and stars;
where could one conceal their private interests? When there is no private interest, the Dao proceeds of its own accord.
This chapter cites an ancient person whose capacity and integrity were both exquisite, such that few others could equal them.

Mount Hall said: "Li Shanglao remarked that Miaoxi’s bearing was profound and far-reaching, his sense of principle and righteousness surpassed that of ordinary men, and he pursued learning with tireless diligence.
He followed me at Baofeng for only four or five years; if we did not see one another for ten days, he would invariably send someone to inquire after me."

Question: An old man’s entire family was suffering from swelling. When Miaoxi passed by his house, he personally prepared the broth and cooked the meals for them with the same etiquette one uses when serving a father or elder brother.
Upon his return, the Head Seat (Yuanshou) reprimanded him; Miaoxi simply responded with "yes, yes" and accepted the instruction. Those who discerned this knew him to be a vessel of great capacity.
This section clarifies that the person’s integrity and righteousness are beyond compare.
Shantang cited Li Shanglao of Mount Lu, who often remarked that the Master Miaoxi’s talent, capacity, and magnanimity were profound, clear, and far-reaching;
moreover, his integrity and righteousness surpassed those of others. He was devoted to learning without ceasing and accompanied this old man at Baofeng for four years.

It has been five years now, and human sentiments here are likewise profound and meticulous. If we were separated for ten days without seeing one another, they would certainly send someone to inquire after our well-being.
Recently, my household disturbed the earth during construction work and thereby offended the local earth deity; consequently, the entire family fell ill with swellings.
Though we sought medical treatment, it was to no avail. When Miaoxi arrived at my home, he personally prepared the medicinal decoctions for us. It was as if—

The younger generation observed the rites for serving their fathers and elder brothers with such diligence and reverence that they were moved to burn incense, observe fasts, and recite the *Candragarbha-rāja-mantra* to pray for deliverance.
Before seven days had passed, they dreamed one night of an old man dressed in white robes riding an ox;
the ox sank into the earth and disappeared. The following day, the entire family’s illness was cured. Once Miaoxi had returned, Yuan...
The head seat reprimanded him in accordance with the established protocols of the monastic community.
This Yuan was none other than Chan Master Dao-yuan of Zhaojue, a successor of Chan Master Foguo Qian and the fifteenth generation in the lineage descending from Mount Heng.

Upon hearing the reprimand, Miaoxi responded with "wei wei," accepting the instruction. "Wei" signifies a prompt and unhesitating response; adding a second "wei" expresses the utmost compliance. Those who understand this...
By this, one knows that he was a great vessel for the Dharma-gate.
Zantang once said, "Attendant Gaomo is a person who has returned for a second birth; I regret not having lived to see him.
After Zantang passed away, Miaoxi traveled a thousand li on foot to visit the Layman Wujin at Zhugong to request an inscription for his stupa. Zantang—
"The final segment of light is the power of *Miaoxi* (Wondrous Joy)" (*Rishen Ji*).
This section reveals that the Dharma-eye discerns all things without omission. Zantang once said, "Attendant Gaomo is one who has returned for a second birth.
I am advanced in years; it is a pity I did not live to see his character. Subsequently, Zantang passed away.
Huà. Miaoxi requested Juefàn to record his life and deeds. Furthermore, he obtained a letter from Chan Master Zàorán of Lóng'ān to serve as an introduction.
An "introduction" (jièjiào) refers to providing mutual assistance. Consequently, he traveled a thousand *lǐ* with blistered feet.
"Blistered feet" means that the skin on the soles has been injured and peeled away like thick silkworm cocoons. In ancient times, when the state of Chǔ intended to attack Sòng, Mòzǐ...
He hurried from Lu to Chu for ten days and ten nights; his feet were swollen like large silkworm cocoons, yet he did not rest.

He traveled specifically to Jingzhou to visit the Layman Wujin (Wu Zhiyuan) to request an inscription for a stupa. Upon first meeting Wujin, the latter asked, "Why have you come such a great distance on foot wearing these straw sandals?
Miaoxi replied, "I have come from several hundred li specifically to see you, sir. The Master [Wujin] said: [This is what I expected].
The official asked, "How old are you? Xì said, "Twenty-four. He asked again, "And how old is the water buffalo? Xì replied, "Two.
The official said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? Xì said, "Today I have seen the Excellency in person.
The official laughed and said, "Sit and drink tea. As soon as he was seated, the official asked again, "What business brings you here from so far away?"
The master stepped forward and said, "Venerable Master Zhantang has passed away. During his cremation, his eyes, teeth, and rosary remained unburnt, and countless śarīras were obtained.
The senior monks of our monastery all wish to have a great calligrapher like you, Excellency, compose an inscription for his stupa to inspire future students.
We have come from afar specifically for this purpose, daring to trouble your esteemed hearing. The official replied, "I am currently under sentence."
"I have never composed written texts for others. Now I have a question; if you can answer it, I shall write an inscription for your stupa.
If you cannot, I will give you five strings of cash and you may return to Tuṣita to wrap your feet and practice Zen.
Xì said, "I request that you, Excellency, ask the question. The official asked, "I have heard that Old Zhǔn’s eyesight is not impaired—is this true? Xì replied, "It is. The official—
Dongshan said, "I am not asking about this eye. Xiangxiu said, "What eye are you asking about?
Dongshan said, "The Adamantine Eye of Righteousness (Vajra-cakṣus). Xiangxiu said, "If it is the Adamantine Eye of Righteousness, it is already upon your honor’s pen.
Dongshan said, "In that case, I shall then manifest its brilliance for you, so that it may illuminate both heaven and earth. Xiangxiu [nodded].
He then bowed and said, "Our late Master was most fortunate to receive the Prefect’s stele inscription for his pagoda. The Prefect merely nodded and smiled. The inscription read, in brief:

"As for *śarīra*, it is not mentioned in the books of Confucius or Laozi. After the World-Honored One, the Buddha, entered *parinirvāṇa*, his disciples collected his *śarīra* and erected pagodas to make offerings to them.
In the case of Chan Master Chouzhou Congshen, the *śarīra* were exceedingly numerous."
Ten thousand grains [of relics]. In recent times, wherever the smoke from the incense reached the dwellings of Longqing Xian and Baizhang Su, all were transformed into śarīras.
Generally speaking, those who have left the household life do so because the matter of birth and death is great; yet, when birth and death actually arrive, they do not know where it will lead.
This is not as good as the man of few concerns from a village of three families, who, at the moment of death, gives instructions with complete clarity:
"The physical body of the four elements is a provisional union of various conditions. From the very beginning, how could the *śarīra* (relics) possess any inherent nature?

If one’s pure conduct has been clean and one’s wholesome karma firm, then the spiritual luminosity will be vast and penetrating; one will know in advance that the retribution of this life is ending, remaining neither startled nor terrified."
Thus, the two retributions—the primary and the secondary—will not miss their mark by even a hair’s breadth.

If one possesses a worldly, coarse mind and fails to attend to these fundamental matters throughout the twelve periods of the day, then as subtle, continuous currents of delusion give rise to great arrogance, this is like an "empty-ghost of karma" coming to borrow one's dwelling.
Under such conditions, how could one hope that the *śarī* rosary will remain intact and the sense faculties unimpaired? How could it possibly be so?
Is it so? Thus, the final segment of Master Zhantang’s radiance was attained through the power of Miaoxi’s loyalty and filiality.
△ His noble capacity was extraordinary; his great principles were manifest, emerging spontaneously from the midst of his innate nature.
This is not something that can be approximated by ordinary people.
*Benshuo*, Scroll II of the *Cane Lin Baoxun*.
*Benshuo*, Scroll III of the Re-engraved Edition of the *Cane Lin Baoxun*.
*Chū Kōunpō* (Cloud Peak of Chu), composed by Zhixiang.
This essay shows that the ancients held noble virtue in high esteem, being so respectful, modest, and frugal.
Master Miaoxi Daogao said: "Whenever Tanzhang obtained a letter or calligraphy from a former sage, he would invariably burn incense before opening and reading it. Or...
An inscription was carved upon stone, stating: "How could one bear to cast aside the sublime reputation and magnificent virtue of the former sage? Such was his refined character.

Thus, at the time of his passing, he possessed no accumulation of even ten gold pieces; there were only two bamboo baskets containing the calligraphic works of various worthies from the Tang and Song dynasties.
Monks vied with one another to compose verses in his honor, obtaining over eighty thousand coins to assist in the funeral rites of cremation (*Kān'ān jí*).
This refers to Master Zhantang, who, whenever he obtained the collected writings or calligraphic drafts of former sages, would invariably burn incense before unfolding and reading them.
He would sometimes have them engraved upon stone, saying: "These are all the magnificent virtues and noble reputations of the ancient saints;
how could I bear to cast them aside on a high shelf and fail to ensure they endure forever in the world? Such was his refined love for them.
Such was his reverence for his seniors that on the day of his passing, he was found to possess no accumulation of even ten *jin* of gold.
He held nothing but two bamboo baskets of calligraphic works and inscriptions by various scholars of the Tang and Song dynasties.
At that time, the assembly of monks vied with one another in composing verses of tribute, obtaining over eighty thousand coins to provide for his cremation.

"Ritual. In Sanskrit, this is called *chavī* (or *dhyāpī*), which here means "cremation. To honor the former sages and preserve their remaining virtue is precisely how one perceives their expansive and noble character;
such sincerity and reverence are truly difficult to emulate. How could those who are slaves to wealth and grain ever attain such a state?
This chapter states that the distinctions between superiors and subordinates must be rectified; they must not be neglected. Miaoxi said:
"When the Buddha-nature resided at Dayue, a practitioner was scuffling with a groundsman. The Buddha-nature wished to punish the practitioner, but the Patriarch [Dongshan] intervened, saying:
'If you let the groundsman continue to humiliate and insult the practitioner, it will not only result in a loss of the proper hierarchy...'"

[The Master] gave his name and title. He feared deeply that a petty person might take advantage of the occasion to act with arrogance, whereby the matter would not be carried out; thus, he did not allow [the other] to hear of the Buddha-nature.
Before long, as expected, a tenant farmer murdered the administrator (from the *Kakuan-shū*).
Chan Master Fóxìng Fǎtài of Dàméi in Tánzhōu was a native of the Lǐ clan of Hànzhōu.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fógǔ Qín and belonged to the fifteenth generation under Nányuè. While he was residing at Dàméi, a monastery attendant and a laborer were fighting.

"Local tenants" refers to the tenant farmers. The Buddha’s nature desired that those who practice according to the monastic rules of the forest dwellings be treated with respect; however, Master Zu Chao was unwilling to comply.

He therefore said: "If you allow these tenant farmers to insult and humiliate practitioners, it will not only result in a loss of the proper distinction between superior and subordinate, but I fear that these petty people will seize the opportunity to incite trouble, showing contempt for their masters and slighting the monks. In that case, the permanent property (*sangha-rāma*)—"
Such matters were not permitted to be carried out. How much more so for a practitioner, who is like a son of the Buddha, versus a tenant farmer, who is of lower status;

each has their designated rank and position, which must not be lost. The Buddha-nature does not permit this, and one must certainly consider that how could members of the Sangha ever engage in hand-to-hand combat with others? One should handle the matter accordingly. Not long after, there was indeed a tenant...
Regarding "a subordinate murders a superior official": to kill one of higher rank is termed *shi*. This illustrates how those with discernment are so transcendent.
When the abbot adjudicates matters, his decisions must surely be appropriate; he must not lose his authority.
Furthermore, since petty people do not understand the law, their passions must not be indulged. If one loses control or indulges them, the various conditions for disorder will arise.
This chapter concerns the craftiness of petty people; one should anticipate this.
Miaoxi said: "When Chan Master Chaoran was residing at Mount Yang, a tenant stole the monastery's grain.

Chaoran had long resented the tenant and intended to dismiss him, so he ordered the storekeeper and an attendant to draft a formal confession on his behalf. The attendant wished to protect the tenant..."

The guest observed Chao Ran’s haughty demeanor and attempted to suppress it by forcing him to rise from his seat and leave; he then sent a messenger back to summon him again, yet Chao Ran refused to comply with the reprimand.
Chao Ran grew angry that the practitioner had usurped his authority, and both men were merely struck with bamboo canes.
It appears Chao Ran was unaware that he had been secretly plotted against by the practitioner. Alas! Such is the cunning of petty men (from the *Ke’an ji*).
Chan Master Wenzu Chaoran of Furi in Lin’an Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tianyi Huai and belonged to the eleventh generation of the Qingyuan lineage.
While he was residing at Yangshan, a tenant stole the monastery’s stored grain. Chaoran had long harbored a strong aversion toward tenants and intended to dismiss him;
consequently, he ordered a warehouse attendant to falsely accuse the tenant of stealing the grain.
I specifically submitted a formal petition to have him removed, so as to facilitate his expulsion. However, I did not realize that the official in charge was also a petty man;
not only did he fail to submit the petition, but he instead sought to protect the local guest.

Having discerned that I intended to decisively compel the local guest to provide a statement of departure, he went so far as to force the local guest to cry out in protest, refusing to comply with the statement.
He presented his grievances. Chaoran became enraged, for Xingxun had usurped authority and acted on his own behalf, even returning to treat the local residents as his subjects.
Thus, the two men could only resort to striking each other with bamboo canes to settle their disputes; in the end, neither could be dismissed.
This was because Chaoran did not realize that the faction of petty people had already formed secret conspiracies behind his back, and he was ultimately unable to expel them.
Alas! The treachery and guile of the petty man can reach such extremes. To be "guileful" means to be wickedly stubborn and full of deception.
The ancients cited this chapter as a model for laws and edicts for later generations;
one must understand that the heart and liver of the petty man are exceedingly perilous and evil, and thus cannot fail to be scrutinized.
This chapter states that one must not lightly trust likes and dislikes, as they can obstruct the greater purpose.
Miaoxi said: "Liking and disliking, difference and agreement—these are the common sentiments of humanity;
only the wise and the highly enlightened are not turned by them. Formerly, when Yuanwu resided at Yunju and Gao'an retired from the East Hall, those who loved Yuanwu detested Gao'an."
Gaofeng was at odds with Yuanwu; consequently, the monastic communities were thrown into a state of confusion, resulting in factions of Yuanwu’s followers and Gaofeng’s followers.
This section states that one must carefully examine what is heard. It means that love and hatred are opposites, and difference and agreement are distinct;
this is the constant condition of human nature. Only those who are truly worthy, discerning, and enlightened are not swayed by these emotions.

Regarding this turning [of events]: formerly, when Master Yuanwu resided at Yunju and Chan Master Gaofeng An retired from the East Hall, there were those who loved Yuanwu and consequently hated Gaofeng, while others who sided with Gaofeng found Yuanwu strange.
Because of this, throughout the monasteries, there was everywhere a state of clamor and confusion. Thus, there were those who favored Yuanwu and those who favored Gaofeng.
Regarding their factional affiliations:
I have observed that the great reputations of these two great men spread across the seas cannot be compared to those of ordinary mortals.

It is a pity, however, that they were clouded by misplaced trust in the sycophantic words of petty men; thus deluded in their wisdom, they became objects of ridicule for the discerning. Therefore, it was only natural that they should be enlightened [by this].
The masters of the Zen school, such as those of the lineage of Yinzhan, were men of noble character.
This section speaks of how placing undue trust in others inevitably leads to entanglement. I humbly observe these two great beings (*mahāsattva*);

"great being" is a title for one possessed of virtue, meaning one who constantly acts on behalf of the heroic and wise, whose aspirations transcend the common herd, whose talent surpasses the sentiments of the masses, and who propagates the Way to benefit all living beings.
Therefore, they were called "Great Beings" (Mahāsattvas). These two elders spread their great fame throughout the land; they could not be compared to ordinary people.

It is a pity that they trusted the flattery of petty men, thereby deluding their own intelligence and becoming objects of ridicule for those with true wisdom. From this we see that it is most difficult to be a person.
It is better to withdraw from the world than to emerge within it; thus, to seek loftiness through seclusion is indeed appropriate.
Master Liang and those like him who hid on Longshan were truly men of noble character. Master Liang was a native of Western Shu.

He had extensively lectured on the sutras and śāstras, but upon meeting Mazu and realizing the Great Matter, he went into seclusion at Mount Yunju in Hongzhou, after which no further news of him was heard.
During the Zhenghe era of the Northern Song dynasty, there was a scholar named Xiong who traveled to Mount Luofu and passed through Cuiyan to pay his respects to the Elder Simen.
Since both the Elder and the scholar were natives of Poyang, he dispatched two strong men to carry him on a palanquin.

As they passed through the forested valleys where the trees and vegetation grew in dense shade, they happened to see a monk whose appearance was ancient and whose spirit was pure, with bushy eyebrows and hair as white as snow.
He wove leaves into a garment and sat upon a flat rock, appearing like the image of the Buddha depicted on the wall beside Fotudeng.
Fotudeng was a man from the Yuezhi; there was a hole by his side, about four or five inches in circumference, which he plugged with silk cloth.
After the fast, he went to the water’s edge, took out the intestines and stomach, washed them, and returned them to their orifices.
At night, he removed the silk wrappings. As he recited the sutras, the light illuminated the entire room. Xiong said to himself, "In these times, there are no such monks as this.
I have heard that Master Liang was once hidden in the Western Mountains; I suspect he may still be alive. He stepped down from his carriage, approached with trepidation, and said, "Is it not..."
"Is this Master Liang? The monk pointed toward the east with his hand. Xiong Fang and his two companions followed the direction of the hand and looked eastward;

when they turned back, they had lost sight of where the monk was. At that time, the light rain had just ceased. Xiong climbed onto a rock and saw that the place where [the monk] had sat was still dry.
He gazed about in all directions, sighed deeply, and said: "My past karmic conditions were not sufficient; though I encountered him, I did not encounter him."
Yanshan was the Chan Master Longshan of Tanzhou. He also studied under Mazu and realized the essential point of the mind.
Later, he lived in seclusion at Longshan. One day, while Dongshan and his senior companion, Master Mi, were wandering the mountains, they saw vegetable leaves floating in a mountain stream.
"Is there any practitioner of the Way living here? He then pushed aside the grass and followed the stream for six or seven li, when he suddenly saw the Master before his hut.
He asked, "There is no path to this mountain; from where have you come, Reverend? Dōng said, "Let us set aside the matter of the path."
"From where have you entered, Preceptor? The Master said, "I do not come from the wandering waters. Dongshan asked, "How long has it been since you have resided on this mountain?
The Master said, "I do not involve myself with spring and autumn. Dongshan asked, "Did you arrive before this mountain, or did you arrive before the Preceptor?
The Master said, "I do not know. Dongshan asked, "Why do you not know? The Master said, "I do not follow after others."
Tianlai asked, "Master, what principle have you realized that you have come to dwell on this mountain? The Master said, "I saw two earthen oxen fighting and entering the sea;
until this very day, there has been no news of them. Dongshan remained silent for a long while, then assumed his formal demeanor and bowed.
He then asked, "What is the Lord among Lords? The Master said, "He never leaves his door throughout his entire life. Dongshan... [continued].
[Dongshan] asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Green mountains shroud white clouds. [Dongshan] asked, "How far apart are guest and host?
The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the long river. [Dongshan] asked, "When guest and host meet, what words are spoken?
The Master said, "A clear breeze brushes over white clouds. Dongshan took his leave. The Master then composed a verse, saying: Three bays...
The sprout-house has always been his dwelling; a single path of divine light leaves the myriad realms in tranquility. Do not bring right and wrong to debate with me;
the artificial constructions of this floating life have no concern with him. Thereafter, he burned his hermitage and retreated into the deep mountains, where his whereabouts were unknown.

For this reason, he was called "Hidden Mountain" (Yinshan). [The terms] "appearing in the world" and "avoiding the world" each have their own specific function; they cannot be discussed in a general way.
While not coming forth may be considered a mark of loftiness, one must most urgently investigate the two characters "light" and "trust."
This chapter states that one who abides in the teachings can transform toward the good and reform their faults; this is truly sufficient to serve as a model. Miaoxi said:

"The ancients would shift toward the good upon seeing it and reform themselves when they had faults. They led themselves by virtue and followed right conduct, striving with reflection to remain free from blame.
There is nothing more grievous than not knowing one's own evils, and nothing more admirable than being fond of hearing one's own faults. However...
Could it be that the wisdom and talent of the ancients were insufficient, or their insight and vision unclear, such that they acted in this way?
Truly, it was intended to serve as a warning for those in later generations who seek to broaden themselves while narrowing their regard for others.
This section cites ancient laws as a warning. Ancient people, upon seeing the goodness in others, would immediately transform themselves to follow it;
when they themselves had faults, they would immediately reform and repent them. "Shuai" (率) means to follow and cultivate.
They followed and cultivated their virtue, maintained and practiced their conduct, and constantly thought of striving to remain free from fault. This is what people [should do].
Among the ailments of humanity, none is more severe than failing to recognize one's own faults; among what is admirable, none is more excellent than delighting in hearing of one's own transgressions.
If one were thus cautious and prudent, would it be that the wisdom and talent of the ancients were insufficient, or their insight unclear, such that they acted in this way?
It is not so. Truly, it was because they wished to prevent future generations from becoming self-important and arrogant while looking down upon others.
This is what constitutes the precepts.
Now, the vastness of monastic communities and the multitude of people across the four seas cannot be known by a single individual alone;

one must rely on the ears, eyes, thoughts, and deliberations of those around them to fully grasp their principles and skillfully manage human relations. If one were to merely occupy a position of honor and remain self-important, [the community would fall into disorder].

One is meticulous regarding minor details while neglecting the grand principles. The worthy do not perceive this; the unworthy do not examine it. When a matter is wrong, they do not reform it; when a matter is right, they do not follow it.
They act recklessly according to their own whims, showing no sense of restraint or dread. This is truly the foundation of calamity and harm; how can one not stand in awe of it?
Even if there are indeed no persons to consult at your side, you should still take the former sages as your model. How could it be otherwise?
"Is it not like a fortified city with a strong army that cannot be entered by oneself?
This is hardly what is meant by 'receiving the hundred rivers to form the great ocean' (Letter to Master Baohua)."

This section clarifies that one must be cautious and reverent in matters. Now, the vast scale of a monastic community’s establishment and the great number of its peers throughout the four seas are certainly not something that a single individual can know alone.
Ultimately, it is necessary to rely upon the eyes and ears of those around one and the deliberations of the multitude;
only then can one fully realize the principles of constant propriety and effectively manage the assembly of monks.
As for human nature: if a master dwells in high station and regards himself with great importance, he may fail to attend to minute details while neglecting matters of great significance;
thus, even the virtuous cannot perceive it, let alone the unworthy.
One does not know to reform when one’s own actions are improper, nor is one willing to follow what the multitude does correctly.
One acts recklessly and arbitrarily, showing no restraint whatsoever. This is truly the fundamental basis for cultivating calamity and harm;
how can one not fear it? If one were to ensure that the ears and eyes of those around one, as well as the reflections of the assembly, found nothing at all to criticize—
Those who seek instruction should take the established words of the ancient sages as their standard.
How could one allow one's own views to remain self-enclosed, like a city under strict siege, where even valiant soldiers find no gate or path by which to enter?
Taking the ancient sages as one's model is itself a path. If the abbot is unable to take them as a model...
Regarding the former sages, how could they have lacked the magnanimity of gathering the hundred rivers to form the great ocean?
To be self-satisfied and arrogant is a malady difficult even for the finest medicine to cure; yet, if one can reform and transform oneself, one may ascend to the realm of the sages.
Students must not fail to understand this.
This chapter discusses the importance of selecting individuals who are noble and upright; this can remedy the defects and benefits of the present age. Miaoxi said:
"When various quarters select elders, they must select those who maintain the Way and remain tranquil and withdrawn. By so selecting them, their will and integrity will become even firmer;

wherever they go, they will not destroy the permanent property [of the monastery], but will instead bring the monastic community (saṃghārāma) to fulfillment. This is also how the masters of the Dharma may rescue the present."
This is the decadence of our age. Furthermore, those who are deceitful, sycophantic, and cunning do not know shame;
they naturally flatter and serve those in power and position, forming alliances at the gates of the influential and noble. Why, then, must you [raise this matter] (a letter to Zhuan’an)?

This means that when elders from various regions are now being nominated to serve as the presiding masters of their respective quarters, it is essential that those selected possess moral virtue, integrity, and a sense of duty, as well as a tranquil and retiring disposition; only such persons are fit for the role.
For once such a person is nominated, the resolve they maintain and the integrity they preserve will become even more steadfast. In all cases...
Wherever he goes, things will naturally remain intact and endure; every matter will be brought to perfection, and he will establish a flourishing monastic community.

This is also because the current presiding master possesses the ability to discern the worthy and has secured a virtuous person to succeed him in the seat—this is precisely how to remedy the maladies of our present day. If, however, it were one of those types of deceitful and sycophantic...

Those who are sycophants and devoid of shame—if they were appointed to office, they would surely seek to flatter those with power and position and form alliances at the gates of the influential and noble. What purpose would there be in employing such as these? Therefore, they need not be recommended.
Those who recommend others should examine them with meticulous scrutiny and reflection; even the slightest deviation from the law brings no small harm.
The matter is no small one.
This chapter maintains that if a person is promoted within a monastic community (chónglín) in accordance with public consensus, they will naturally be free of deficiency.
Miaoxi said to the Layman Chaoran: "In the world, only public consensus must not be discarded; even if one attempts to suppress it, it cannot be done."
How can the public consensus be disregarded? Therefore, when a monastery promotes a man of the Way, those who hear of it will surely rejoice and offer congratulations;
yet if they promote one who is not upright or worthy, the multitude will surely sigh with sorrow. In truth, there is nothing else at stake:
it depends on whether the public consensus is put into practice or not. Alas! By this, one may divine the flourishing state of the monastic community.
*Shuaiyi* (From the *Ke’an ji*).
Prince of the Commandery Zhao Lingjin, styled Biaozhi and titled the Recluse Chaoran, served as the Governor of Nankang and was the dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin.
He maintained that public discourse represents the correct judgment of all time and the world, and must not be discarded.
Even if one were to struggle to suppress it, what can be done against public opinion?

Therefore, when a person of virtue, moral integrity, and righteousness is appointed as an abbot or established in a senior office within a monastic community, it is public opinion that those who hear of or see this will surely respond with joy and offer their congratulations. However, if one is appointed whose conduct and practice are not authentic...
When a person of substance appears, the multitude will surely sigh with sorrow. "Sorrow" (qí) means grief.
There is no other reason for this than that public opinion has either prevailed or failed to prevail. Alas!
By inferring from public opinion, one can prognosticate the future flourishing or decline of the monastic community. Generally speaking, all matters of right and wrong...
One must not dogmatically cling to either the true or the false; there exists public consensus. When public consensus prevails, the ultimate correctness of the world is established.
This chapter clarifies that in cultivating oneself and entering the Way, frugality is the essential requirement.
Miaoxi said: "Frugality and relinquishment are the foundation for cultivating the self and the essential requirement for entering the Way.

Looking back through the ages at the ancients, there are few who did not practice frugality and relinquishment. In recent years, monks have traveled through Jingzhou and Chu to purchase woolen mats, and passed through Zhejiang to seek spun silk; are they not ashamed before the ancients?"

People of the world are harmed by the poison of greed; they have been entangled by it for kalpas. Now, if you wish to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, the foremost requirement is to be able to let go.

To possess self-restraint and the capacity for simplicity and frugality—what is called the sudden relinquishing of worldly toil—is the very foundation for cultivating the person and the essential point for entering the Way. Observe closely those of antiquity: who among them was not capable of this?
Regarding those who are frugal and able to let go: in recent years, monks traveling through the Jing and Chu regions have immediately gone to purchase several pieces of woolen mats and felt;
those passing through the region south of Zhejiang have likewise gone to buy some spun silk and fine silks.
Traveling as a mendicant in this manner—how could one not feel ashamed before the ancients?
This passage exhaustively describes the faults of contemporary people who cannot let go; readers should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
This chapter teaches that an abbot (zhuchi) should maintain the fundamental integrity of the institution and act in accordance with public consensus.
Miaoxi said: "In ancient times, virtuous abbots did not personally manage the monastery's assets; they entrusted all affairs entirely to the administrative officers (zhishi).

In recent times, however, those in charge have relied on their own superior talent and power, ensuring that no matter how great or small the matter, it is brought before the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang), while the administrative officers..."

It is merely a hollow reputation. Alas! If one, with the resources of a single person, truly desires to grasp the affairs of an entire institution—ensuring that petty people do not cause obstruction, that the administrative regulations remain orderly, and that the discourse accords with supreme public principle—is this not indeed difficult? (Letter to Shantang)

It is said that when the ancients established the position of abbot (*zhuchi*), it was originally intended solely for the purpose of upholding the Great Dharma and encouraging the monastic practitioners (*nazi*).

Fundamentally, they did not instruct the abbot to personally manage the affairs of the monastery’s permanent assets; rather, everything was entrusted to the administrative officers (*zhishi*) to oversee and control.
This is the fundamental principle. Nowadays, those who act as masters rely on their own superior talent and strength;
they insist that every matter, regardless of its magnitude, must come under the control of the Abbot. Meanwhile, the administrators possess nothing more than empty titles.
Alas! If one merely wishes to maintain authority and dominance through the power of one’s own individual resources alone—

Regarding the affairs of a single institution, if one wishes to prevent petty people from coming to cause obscuration and ensure that laws and regulations do not fall into disorder, while also requiring that they accord with the discourse of ultimate public justice—how could this possibly be achieved? In all matters, it is of the utmost importance to accord with public opinion;
as soon as one involves oneself in private interests, it is sufficient to manifest the air of a petty household.
This chapter teaches that the Way must be pursued in a timely manner; time and opportunity must not be wasted. Miaoxi said: "When Yang reaches its extreme, Yin arises;
when Yin reaches its extreme, Yang arises. Prosperity and decline follow one another; this is the natural law of Heaven and Earth.

Only when there is abundance and success is it appropriate for the sun to be at its zenith. Therefore it is said: 'When the sun is at midday, it begins to set. When the moon is full, it begins to wane."
"Deficiency. Heaven and earth have their waxing and waning in accordance with the rhythms of time; how much more so for human beings?
This section clarifies the principle of the alternating transformations of yin and yang, stating that the cycles of the world do not transcend the numerical patterns of yin and yang.
For instance, when pure yang is exhausted, a single line of yin arises beneath it; when pure yin reaches its limit, [a line of yang arises].
One Yang is generated at its base; there is waxing and waning, mutually multiplying and dividing, which is the fixed and natural number of Heaven and Earth.
Only when abundant and prosperous is it appropriate for the sun to be at midday. Above is Zhen, representing thunder; below is Li, representing fire.
This is named the hexagram Lei-huo Feng (Thunder over Fire). Feng means "great. To act with clarity brings about greatness and abundance.

This is the natural course of things. Therefore, its hexagram contains the way of prosperity (*heng*). Yet, when fullness reaches its extreme, decline is imminent; thus, it also contains the way of anxiety (*you*).

The Sage considered that mere anxiety was of no benefit, and so he maintained constancy to avoid reaching excessive fullness. Thus, the *Tuan* (Judgment) says: [The text continues with the specific hexagram].
"At midday, the sun declines; when the moon is full, it wanes. The fullness and emptiness of Heaven and Earth correspond to the waxing and waning of the seasons;
how much more so for human beings, and even more so for ghosts and spirits? This speaks of the difficulty of maintaining abundance and constant vigilance against complacency.
When the sun reaches its zenith, it must decline into twilight; when the moon is at its peak of fullness, it inevitably suffers deficiency. Such is the waxing and waning of Heaven and Earth.
One must still adjust according to the times; how much more so for human beings born between heaven and earth, for whom ghosts and spirits are but the vital breaths of heaven and earth.
During times of abundance, this serves as a warning, desiring that people maintain the Mean and avoid excessive prosperity.
The way of abiding in abundance is by no means easy. When the Yin dies, it is called "dissipation"; when the Yang dies, it is called "cessation.
Therefore, when people of antiquity were at the height of their physical vigor, they considered how the light of time passes so swiftly;

thus, from morning until evening they reflected and contemplated, exercising caution and ever-increasing vigilance. They did not indulge their passions nor yield to their desires, but sought only the Way. Consequently, they were able to—
One must preserve one’s good reputation. As for those who ruin it through indolence and lust, or bring it to ruin through unrestrained passions—it will likely be beyond redemption;
by then, it would be too late to stomp one's feet and wring one's hands in regret. For such moments are difficult to encounter and easy to lose.
(Written at Xianglin.)

This section reveals how earnestly the ancients investigated their minds. Thus, when the ancients were young and their vital energy was at its peak, they already lamented the ease with which time passes.
Since the years and months are inherently difficult to retain, they contemplated the Way in the morning and reflected upon the Way in the evening;
they were invariably cautious and observant, adding further a sense of dread, not daring to indulge themselves in self-indulgence.
Regarding the seven emotions, he did not dare to be dissolute in the five desires; at all times, he took only the preservation of the Way as his concern.
Thus, he was able to preserve the fine reputation of his entire life. Had he allowed himself to be unrestrained in the five desires, his body would have been ruined;
had he indulged in the seven emotions, his mind would have been shattered. His peril and ruin would surely have reached this point.
It is a ground from which there can be no rescue. Only then, when one stamps one's feet and wrings one's hands, it is already too late to pursue [the opportunity].
This clearly shows that the character "time" (時) is of the utmost importance. Time is difficult to obtain and easy to lose. Li Zuojun said to Han Xin:
"Achievements are difficult to accomplish but easy to ruin; time is difficult to obtain but easy to lose. He spoke thus of "time, oh time! (時乎時).
Ah, it will not come again! The ancients said: "That which is difficult to settle is an affair; that which is easily lost is time.
Unless one has attained a thorough realization through profound meditative concentration, one will ultimately fail to reach such a level of subtle refinement.
Be careful not to treat this lightly as something to be skimmed over.
This chapter teaches that students must establish their own reputation and integrity, and then personally contemplate how to enter [the path].
Miaoxi said: "In ancient times, people first selected those of virtue and character, and secondly promoted those of talent and learning before advancing them at court.

If one was not a vessel of excellence yet placed oneself before others, many would disparage one upon seeing or hearing of it. For this reason, monastics (nazi) reflect upon themselves to sharpen and polish their own conduct."
One establishes oneself through reputation and integrity.
This integrity takes moral character, talent, and learning as its foundation. It is said that when the ancients selected scholars, they first chose for moral character;
one must have a clear understanding and upright conduct before their talent and learning were considered. And...

Advancement and employment must be accorded at the proper time. If one is not a vessel of excellence, placing them before the multitude will likely cause most who see or hear of them to treat them with contempt and disdain.
For this reason, a monastic must reflect upon themselves and necessarily polish their character, establishing themselves through the maintenance of integrity and reputation.
Recently, I have observed that the monastic communities are withering away. Students disregard morality and virtue; they lack integrity and shame.

They deride those who are pure and simple as being vulgar and crude, while they prize those who are noisy and frivolous as being talented and quick-witted. Consequently, the younger generation’s insight remains clouded;

they merely engage in superficial reading and transcription to fuel their verbal sophistry. As this has increased day by day and month by month, it has ultimately resulted in a degenerate and corrupt atmosphere. When it comes to speech—
Regarding the Way of the Sages, one is as bewildered as if facing a blank wall; this is likely beyond redemption (in a letter to Han Jizang).
This section conversely reveals that the person must engage in genuine study. Recently, I have observed that the monastic communities are in decline;

those who study do not pursue authentic learning, and their virtue is not truly cultivated. They lack integrity and shame, yet they go so far as to mock and deride those whose natures are pure and simple.
Such people regard those who are humble and simple as base, while they prize and admire those who are noisy, obstinate, frivolous, and shallow as being talented and quick-witted.
Consequently, the understanding of the younger generation is clouded, much like wading through water to catch fish or climbing mountains to hunt beasts.
In the east, people engage in copying and transcribing, scheming to amass a few words and texts as if they were substantial learning, using them merely to aid their verbal disputations.
Day by day these are nurtured, and from day to day they grow; after a long time, a style of frivolous and shallow learning is thus established.
When it comes to questioning them about the ultimate Way of the Sages, their mouths are like stone millstones and their eyes are as if blind.
Blind; their four directions are obstructed as if they were looking at a wall. For such people, it is almost impossible to save them. The *Analects* states:
The Master said to Bo Yu, "Have you studied the *Zhounan* and *Shaonan*? He replied, "Yes."
If a person does not study the *Zhōu-nán* and *Shào-nán*, is it not as if they were standing with their face against a wall?
This means that they see nothing and cannot take even a single step forward. △ This is what scholars call "thoroughly investigating the mind.
Only after attaining the mind can one harmonize the differences of the world into unity and integrate the divergences of the myriad categories.
My dear friend, the study of mere transcription merely wastes one’s time; what benefit could it possibly bring?
This chapter serves as a warning for those who come after, so that each may know what to uphold, making the benefiting of others their primary concern.
Miaoxi said: "In the past, Huitang wrote the 'Record of the Inscriptions at Huanglong,' stating:

'Those who studied in ancient times lived in mountain caves, ate earth and wood, and wore skins and grass. They did not set their minds on fame or profit, nor did they register their names with government offices.
It was only from the Wei, Jin, Qi, Liang, Sui, and Tang dynasties onward that monasteries were first established to gather disciples from all quarters. He then selected...

The worthy provide patterns for the unworthy, and the wise lead the ignorant and deluded. From this, the roles of host and guest are established, and the distinction between superior and subordinate arises.
This section states that one must rectify names and positions; as recorded in the "Record of the Inscription of Names at Huanglong" composed by Heitang in the past:
Those who studied the Way in ancient times dwelt in high crags and deep caves; for food they ate wild vegetables and fruits from trees; for clothing they wore tree bark and leaves.
They paid no heed to fame or profit, nor did they submit their names to government offices. These were truly the idle men of heaven and earth.
Since Cao Cao claimed the title of Wei and Sima Yi claimed the title of Jin, [the world has changed]—Piao... [text truncated]
During the Qi dynasty when the Way was established; during the Liang dynasty when Xiao Yan reigned; during the Sui dynasty when Yang Jian reigned;
and during the Tang dynasty when Li Yuan reigned—since these successive dynasties began, monasteries (*zhāotí*) were first constructed, gathering the vast multitude from the four seas.
Those of virtue were selected to guide the unworthy, and those of wisdom were appointed to lead the ignorant and deluded. Thus, guests...
The master established [the order], and it was divided into upper and lower sections.
Now, for the vast multitude from all under heaven to gather in a single monastery—those who undertake such a responsibility truly find it difficult to achieve.
The essential point lies in grasping the great while relinquishing the small, prioritizing the urgent while deferring the slow, and acting not for private gain but for the benefit of others. Thus...
Those who are busily preoccupied with schemes for their own persons alone differ from others as much as heaven and earth.

Now, Huanglong has had the names of successive abbots inscribed upon this stone, so that those who come hereafter may see them and observe: "Who possessed virtue and wisdom? Who possessed benevolence and righteousness?
Who was impartial toward the multitude? Who sought only his own benefit? Alas! How can one not be filled with apprehension? (Stone Inscription)

This section states that one must fully embody moral integrity. Now, for many people from across the four seas to gather in a single courtyard and shoulder such a great responsibility is truly not something that can be easily accomplished. It requires grasping the general principles while discarding minor details;
prioritizing what is urgent while deferring what may be delayed; and furthermore, refraining from making private calculations for oneself, focusing solely on the public good.
To prioritize the benefit of others and compare it with those who are preoccupied with scheming for their own personal enjoyment is like the distance between heaven and earth.
Now, Huanglong has inscribed the names of successive abbots upon this stone so that future successors may see them and ask: "Who among these was truly possessed of the Way?"
As for "virtue": who possesses benevolence and righteousness? Who can act with public-mindedness toward the multitude? And who seeks only private benefit for themselves? Alas!
As those who serve as abbots, how can you not stand in awe? This title is enough to strike fear into people; it is difficult to bear, truly difficult to bear.
If one does not reflect with care and exert oneself in practice, one will inevitably fail to preserve one's integrity in this world and will merely become a common person obsessed with worldly gain.
This is a term of contempt.
This chapter states that those appointed to lead must be the right individuals; otherwise, they will be of no benefit to the Dharma-gate.
Attendant Zhang Zishao said to Miaoxi: "The office of the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) in a Chan monastery is the selection of the worthy."
Position. Nowadays, throughout all quarters, regardless of whether one is worthy or unworthy, people generally regard this as a shortcut to fortune and advantage;
this, too, is the fault of those who preside over the Dharma. Thus, in this degenerate age, it is indeed difficult to find such a person.

However, if one were to select someone whose conduct is somewhat superior, whose talent and virtue are somewhat complete, and who recognizes shame and integrity, and have them occupy this post, they would still be far superior to those who seek advancement through treacherous means.
"Excellent! (From the *Ke'an ji*). He said:
"The office of the head seat (*shouzuo*) within the monastic community is the eye and mind of humanity; it is truly a position for selecting worthy talent.
Yet nowadays, in all quarters, they fail to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy, treating this position as a matter of mere luck."

Regarding the path of the ferry: by relying on this to seek fame and ensnare profit, they destroy the established order; this is entirely due to the failure of those who uphold the Dharma in their selection of personnel.

Although it is difficult to find truly excellent people during the Age of Dharma Decline, one must still select those whose conduct and practice slightly surpass others, and whose talent, capability, virtue, and achievements slightly exceed one's own. One must recognize this.
There are some who possess a sense of shame and integrity; only those who occupy this position with such qualities can truly be said to be qualified for their office.
Compared to those who recklessly compete for advancement, they may be considered slightly superior. △ Lately, however, those occupying this position have become even more shameful.
They disregard the fundamental principles of the Dharma and remain ignorant of the worldly consequences of their actions. They are truly like snakes...
The tiger glares at its side; the cricket and the sparrow pay no heed to its rear.
Alas! This chapter sets forth men of virtue as a model for later students.
Miaoxi said to his disciple Zishao: "Among those who have presided over the Dharma in recent times, none is like Zhenru Zhe;
as for those who skillfully assisted the monastic communities, none is equal to Yangqi."
This section marks two excellences simultaneously: namely, that among those who uphold the Great Dharma in recent times, none has equaled Chan Master Zhiren;
and as for those who skillfully assisted the monastic communities, none has surpassed Master Yangqi.
Critics said that Ciming was straightforward and simple, yet negligent in his affairs and entirely lacking in restraint.

Yangqi, however, served him selflessly, fearing only that things might not be thorough or that they might not be accomplished. Even when braving the cold and the heat, he never once displayed haste for his own sake or a look of indolence.
Beginning with Nanyuan and ending with Xinghua, this spanned barely thirty years; throughout this entire period, they held the reins of the monastic discipline until the passing of Ciming.
This section clarifies the actual conduct of these supporting ministers. Regarding those who offer commentary, it is said that Ciming was a man of sincere integrity.
In general, when performing tasks, he was diligent and never evaded or shied away from anything. Yangqi forgot his own person in order to serve his duties;
he feared that even a single matter might not be fully attended to and worried that even a single dharma might not be perfectly prepared.
Although he braved bitter cold and humid heat, he never once showed signs of haste to cherish himself or allowed himself to succumb to indolence.

Beginning with his acceptance of the invitation from Huang Shou-dan of Nanyuan to serve as the Governor of Yichun, he subsequently accepted the invitations of the śramaṇas Benyan and Dowu of Dinglin. Later, he moved to Shishuang and Foyan, finally passing away at Xinghua;
throughout these various monasteries for nearly thirty years, he presided over the monastic communities, upholding the regulations and discipline until his final days.
He continued until the end of his life before finally ceasing; from this, one may know the reality of his role as a counselor and assistant.
As for Zhenru, he began by traveling on foot with his belongings bound about him, and reached the point of presiding over disciples in the world; for the sake of the Dharma, he forgot his own body.
He was as if he could never satisfy his hunger or thirst. Even in moments of haste or distress, he did not show sudden changes in expression nor speak with hurried words.
In summer he would not open the windows; in winter he would not sit near a fire. His single room was serene and secluded, with layers of dust covering the desks. He once said:
"If a monk lacks lofty insight within and is deprived of strict teachers and virtuous friends without, it is rare for him to become a vessel of accomplishment."
This section clarifies the purity and strictness of the Master’s adherence to the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding his state as True Suchness (*tathatā*):

beginning from the time he left home, packed his belongings, and traveled on foot to become a Chan practitioner, up until his emergence in the world to lead the assembly, guide his disciples, and propagate the Dharma while forgetting himself.
It is not merely like one who, when hungry or thirsty, seeks food and drink.

Even in moments of haste and negligence, or at times of being overturned and wandering in exile—on such occasions, he does not show a sudden change in his countenance nor utter words with hurried urgency.
In summer he does not throw open the windows to seek coolness; in winter he does not... [seek warmth].
He would seek warmth by sitting near a brazier; his single-zhang room was serene and empty, with nothing within it except for dust accumulating on the desk.
From this, one could know the sincerity of his devotion to the Dharma. He once said: "The home of a patch-robed monk is within his own mind."
Lacking lofty insight and vision, and furthermore being deprived of strict masters and virtuous friends outside [the monastery], it was rare for anyone to become a vessel of the Dharma.
Thus, at that time, those who were stubborn and perverse—such as Fu Tiejiao—and those who were headstrong and arrogant—such as the masters Xiuyuan and Ruantong—all bowed before his reputation.
Alas! These two elders truly serve as a mirror for the monastics of a thousand years to come. (From *Kean Jiwen*)
This section summarizes the model [of conduct]. Thus, at that time, there was one as stubborn as Fu Tiejiao.
"Fu" refers to Chan Master Yongfu of Changlu Shengtian, who was a successor of Chan Master Haitong of Letan and belongs to the fourteenth generation under Qingyuan.
"Obstinate" means being rigid, haughty, and unsympathetic toward human feelings. When the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at an inn one night;
there was a courtesan who had been coerced and seduced by her mother. The Master sat in meditation until dawn.
The woman informed her mother, who sighed and said, "A true son of the Buddha. Because the Master enjoyed wandering about, it is said that throughout his life he was like tempered iron.
"Feet. The reputation of his Way resounded throughout the universe. He was as stubborn as Xiu Yuan-tong. "Stubborn" (倔) means rigid; "obstinate" (強) means solitary and hard.
"The various masters" refers to the various spiritual teachers who appeared in his own time, such as the two masters Jianzhen and Yangqi.
Seeing him take things so seriously, they all bowed down before his influence. "Bowed down" (偃) means to fall prostrate; it means to lie flat. — Kong.
The Master said: "The virtue of the noble person is like the wind; the virtue of the common person is like the grass. When wind blows over the grass, it must surely lie prostrate. Alas!
By this, one may know that the two great elders, Zhenshu and Yangqi, truly serve as divine tortoises and precious mirrors for the monastics of a thousand years hence.
A tortoise knows the misfortunes and blessings of the future; a mirror reflects.
Regarding the present beauty and ugliness: from of old, the fragrant breeze of the virtuous has brushed against people, providing more than sufficient cause for joy;
even after a thousand or ten thousand years, it remains refreshingly cool and never ceases. Why then do people not act accordingly?
This chapter states that those who practice the Dharma disregard their own bodies; this is because the meaning lies therein.
Zishao, Miaoxi, Wan’an, and three others went to the quarters of the former Hall Head, Benchouze, to inquire after his health.

Miaoxi said, "For one in the 'groves below' [the monastic community], the body must first be at peace before one can study the Way. Wan’an directly disagreed, asserting that it was certainly not so. He insisted that—
"One who studies the Way should not look back at their own body. Miaoxi said, "You fool, you are mad again!
Although Zishao respected Miaoxi’s words, he ultimately felt that Wan’an’s statement was more appropriate (Recorded Sayings).
This refers to when three people went together to the former meditation hall to inquire after the health of the original Head Seat (the "Ben"), who was Boshan Wuben.
Miaoxi said, "A person in the 'groves below' must first have physical well-being before they can study the Way.
Wan'an spoke directly and without equivocation, disagreeing with him, asserting that if one truly intends to advance in this Way, one should not look back at such things.
"Regard this body as precious; only by forgetting the body can one study the Way. Miaoxi said, "Are you, Master Han, being deluded again?
We have come here specifically to comfort the mind of the sick person, yet you speak in such a manner.
Although Zishao respected Miaoxi’s words, he ultimately cherished Wan’an’s statement, considering it—
"Appropriate. The character "dàng" (當) is pronounced in the departing tone; it means that one's speech hits the mark.

△ Miaoxi speaks in terms of the penetration of emotion, while Wan’an discusses solely from the standpoint of principle. Each has their own insight; be careful not to become dogmatically attached to them.

This chapter concerns the abbot’s role in securing disciples so that the Way of the Dharma may flourish and his own duties be fulfilled. At that time, Wan’an was seated in the assembly; he disagreed, arguing that one must calculate the income of the monastery’s permanent endowment. He said: "If one does not manage the funds properly, the monks will have no means of livelihood. Without livelihood, they will not stay; without staying, they will not practice; and without practicing, the Dharma will perish. Therefore, the first priority is to ensure the stability of the monastery's resources. Miaoxi then said, "If you can provide for their livelihood, you have already accomplished half the task. Wan’an then asked, "What is the second priority? Miaoxi replied, "To teach them the Way. Wan’an then asked, "What is the third priority? Miaoxi replied, "To establish a lineage. Wan’an then asked, "What is the fourth priority? Miaoxi replied, "To transmit the Dharma. Wan’an then asked, "What is the fifth priority? Miaoxi replied, "To pass on the robe and bowl. Wan’an then asked, "What is the sixth priority? Miaoxi replied, "To entrust the Dharma to a successor. Wan’an then asked, "What is the seventh priority? Miaoxi replied, "To retire from office. Wan’an then asked, "What is the fifty-sixth priority? Miaoxi replied, "To ensure the Dharma is not outcasted in advance. Wan’an then asked, "What is the fifty-seventh priority? If one can restrain frivolous expenditures and employ resources according to the Way, then money and grain will be beyond counting;
why then should this be a cause for concern? Nevertheless, the current abbot should prioritize the recruitment of monks who embrace the Way.

Even if an abbot possesses the wisdom and strategy to store ten years' worth of provisions, if there are no such monks beneath him, what the former sages called "sitting and wasting offerings" applies here.
"Looking upward, I am ashamed before the dragons and devas; what benefit can I provide as abbot? Zishao said, "What the Head Seat has said is most appropriate.
Miaoxi looked back at Wan’an and said, "Every one of you is just like you. Wan’an then withdrew. (The above is found in the *Kakan ji*).
Zi Shao asked Miaoxi, "Among the abbots currently presiding over monastic communities, what do they consider their primary task to be?
Miaoxi replied, "To provide for the Zen practitioners; it amounts to nothing more than seeking silver, money, rice, and grain.
At that time, Wan’an was present in the assembly and disagreed, saying, "If one speaks of money and grain, there are capable administrators who can manage the permanent endowments."
There may be more or less [wealth], but one must be well able to exercise restraint. As for restraint, it means measuring one's income and regulating one's expenditures so as not to allow for waste.
If one uses resources according to the proper way, then money and grain will be more than sufficient;
why then should this be a cause for concern? Nevertheless, among the abbots of today, those who can first embrace and uphold a monk of moral character are the most essential.

Diligence. Even if a resident abbot possesses wisdom and strategic planning, and is able to store ten years' worth of provisions, if there is no one among his followers who can embrace and maintain the Way and its Virtue, the former sages would call this "sitting and wasting offerings.
One would look up with shame before the Dragon Kings and Heaven; what benefit would such a person bring to the abbot? Zishao praised this, saying: "First..."
"What you have said, Zuo, is most appropriate. You are truly not mistaken as the Eye of Humanity and Heaven.
Miaoxi turned his head and looked back at Wan’an, saying, "The depth and shallowness of people’s understanding differ; one by one, they all seem just like you.
Wan’an then withdrew, silently accepting this. △ The sages and worthies appear in the world originally for the purpose of bringing matters to a conclusion.
In matters of great importance, securing the right person is essential. Failing to secure such a person was the hidden anxiety of the ancients.
This chapter states that those who uphold the Dharma must maintain self-respect and must not speak with casual disregard.

Master Wanan Yan said: "When our late teacher Miaoxi first took up residence at Mount Jing, during a night discourse he spoke incessantly regarding the various schools and the tenets of the Caodong tradition.
The following day, Venerable Yin said to the Master, 'Entering the world to benefit sentient beings is by no means a trivial matter.
If you truly intend to uphold and revitalize the religious teachings, you must address current deficiencies as they arise; it is not necessary [to dwell on the past]. "

"To seize the pleasure of the moment. "The Master was a Zen monk the day before yesterday; even when he was debating with those from all quarters, he could not have been reckless, let alone now that he has ascended the Jewel Flower King’s Throne and is called a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend).

The Head Seat said, "The learning of the sages and worthies is rooted in their innate nature; how could it be undertaken so impulsively? The Master said, "That was merely what I spoke for a single moment last night.
The Head Seat said, "The study of the sages and worthies is based on one's heavenly nature; how can it be done haphazardly? The Master said, "The Master..."
He bowed his head in apology. Yet the Head Seat continued to speak of it without ceasing.
Master Wanan Daoyan of Donglin in Jiangzhou was a descendant of the Xianyu clan of Tongchuan and a successor of Chan Master Dahui.
He said, "When our late teacher Miaoxi first resided at Mount Jing, during a night assembly, he maintained a discussion regarding the methods of various masters."
The Way possesses varying depths. Regarding the discussion of the fundamental tenets established by the Cao-Dong school, one could speak of them without end.
As for Cao-Dong: this refers to Chan Master Benji of Mount Cao in Fuzhou, who succeeded Chan Master Liangjia of Dongshan.
Initially departing from Dongshan, he entered Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral stupa, and upon returning to Jishui in Jizhou, the reputation of his name resounded among the masses.
He then requested that the Dharma be opened [to him]. The Master modeled himself after Caoxi; wherever he resided, he established "Cao" as his lineage title.
Because Dongshan’s Way was greatly propagated by this master and he was honored by all quarters, it is called the Caodong School. On the following day, the head seat Yin said to the former master:
"Now, appearing in the world is fundamentally for the benefit of sentient beings; it is by no means a trivial matter. It must..."
One must uphold the Dharma-gate and greatly propagate the teachings of the five schools; it is appropriate to act according to the times to remedy the accumulated defects of the Dharma-ending age.
It is not necessary to speak merely to satisfy one's own immediate whims or temperament.
When you were a Zen student in the past, traveling among various quarters to hold forth on doctrine, you still could not have been reckless, for I fear there might have been errors.

"Your words are excessive. How much more so today, when you have ascended the Treasure Flower King Throne (*ratnapadma-rāja-āsana*) to propagate the Great Dharma and are called a 'Good Friend' (*kalyāṇamitra*).
My late teacher said: 'Last night was merely a casual remark made at a single moment. The Head Seat said:
'The study of sages and worthies fundamentally arises from the innate nature of humanity. How can one speak so recklessly? To speak recklessly..."* (text breaks off)
"Such a person is negligent. The former master bowed his head and apologized for this. The Head Seat continued to speak without ceasing.
△ The Head Seat possessed the sincerity of one who speaks directly and dares to offer counsel; the Abbot possessed the magnanimity to accept such counsel with broad tolerance.
Both may serve as models for humans and devas.
This chapter describes how even when a man of virtue faces adversity, people continue to long for him without ceasing.
Wanan said: "When the former master was exiled to Hengyang, the attendant Xian recorded the words of his banishment and displayed them before the Sangha Hall.

The monks were as if they had lost their parents; weeping and sighing in grief, they could not find peace in their dwellings. At that time, the Head Seat Yin went to the various quarters and announced:"
He said: "In the life of a human being, calamities and misfortunes cannot be avoided at will.
Had Miaoxi spent his entire life like a woman or a girl, submerged and hidden away, remaining silent and saying nothing, then these events of today would not have occurred.
Furthermore, what the former sages were called upon to do did not stop at this alone. Why do you all distress yourselves so?"

This section demonstrates his original disposition. Formerly, when the late Master [Zhaozhou] was conversing with Zhang Jiucheng, a Court Gentleman who had not yet passed the examinations, he remarked that the profound and subtle attainments of scholars such as Yang Wenyong and Lü Weizhong were all reached through the study of Chan.
Thereupon, he came to admire the study of Chan. Having heard of the reputation of Chan Master Baoyin Chuming, he respectfully went to visit and seek instruction.
Chuming presented him with the "Cypress Tree" koan and instructed him to contemplate it constantly. One day, upon hearing the cry of a frog, he attained sudden enlightenment.
There is a verse that says: "A single sound of a frog under the spring moon Breaks through heaven and earth; all share one family. At such a time as this, who can understand?

Xuefeng’s feet ache at the head of the ridge—there is Xuansha. On the eleventh day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, an imperial edict was issued for Miaoxi to reside at Nengren Temple on Mount Jing. This continued until the eleventh year of Shaoxing.
In that year, Zhang Jiu-cheng went with several high officials to pay their respects. They discussed the topic of "investigating things" (*gewu*).
Miaoxi said, "Gentlemen, you know only of 'investigating things,' but you do not know of 'things being investigated' (*wugé*). The gentlemen were at a loss, and Miaoxi laughed heartily.
The Duke said, "Can you explain this to me? Xī replied, "Have you not seen it recorded in a short story? During the Tang dynasty, there was a rebellion by Ān Lùshān.
This man had previously served as the Governor of Làngzhōu, and a portrait of him was there. At that time, the Tang Emperor Mínghuáng was visiting Shǔ;
seeing the portrait, he became enraged and ordered an envoy to strike it with a sword, whereupon the head of the image fell off. At that moment, the man [who had been the governor] was in hiding."
While staying at Shanxi, a head suddenly fell to the ground. Upon hearing this, the Master (Zhaozhou) immediately grasped the profound meaning. He inscribed a verse on the wall of the hall, saying:
"Zishao [attains] the patternization of things; Miaoxi [attains] the patternization of self. If you wish to know the single thread, it is two times five hundred.
Miaoxi highly esteemed his realization. At that time, he ascended the hall and said: "A single shot from a longbow pierces through a thousand layers."
Jiǎ: The old monk picked it up and looked at it, saying, "What is the use of this stinking leather shoe?

At that time, military and state affairs were being discussed regarding the deployment of the Shen-bi-gōng (Shen-armed bow). The Chancellor Qin Huì considered this to be a satirical critique of the administration.
In the fifth month, Mínfó Rì was exiled to Hénghuáng, and Jiǔchéng was demoted to Nánkāng Jūn. Miàoxǐ [arrived] from Shàoxīng in the seventh year...
He resided at Mount Jing for several years. In the fifth month of the eleventh year, he was demoted to Hengyang County in Hengzhou Prefecture.
His attendant, Liao Xian—who had succeeded Chan Master Dahui—recorded the decree of demotion and posted it before the Sangha Hall.
To "post" means to hoist up and display. Upon seeing this, the monastics were as if they had lost their parents; they wept, sighed in sorrow, and remained there in grief.
Feeling uneasy in his quarters, the Head Seat Yin went to the monks' hall and informed the assembly, saying:
"When human beings are born between heaven and earth, calamities and hardships can never be avoided at will.

Suppose that throughout his life, Miaoxi had been like a woman or a girl, possessing only the aspirations of the inner chambers and no mind for the world beyond; or suppose he were like Lu [Shoujing]..."
Those who practice the water-dwelling asceticism and occupy the lowest rank seal their mouths and remain silent;

it is for this reason that the events of today did not occur. Furthermore, when the former sage, the Venerable Siṃha, encountered hardship, and the Second Patriarch repaid his debts at the capital of Ye, these were both acts they ought to have performed as demonstrations for the sake of others—how could it have been merely this? You all...
Why do you inflict such suffering and pain upon yourself?
In the past, Ciming, Langye, Guquan, and Dayu formed a group to study under Fenyang; it happened that the northwest was engaged in military conflict at that time.
He then changed his clothes, mingled with the fire brigade, and departed. Now, Mount Jing and Mount Hengyang are not far apart;
the roads are free from obstacles, and the mountains and rivers present no difficulties. If one wishes to see Miaoxi, how could it be difficult?
Thereupon the entire assembly became silent, and on the following day they followed one after another in succession (*Lushan Zhilin Ji*).
This section clarifies that it is not difficult to see [the truth]. Formerly, there were Ciming and Langye; Nanyue, Bajiao, An, Daodao, and Chan Master Guquan.

Chan Master Guquan was a native of Quanzhou and succeeded Chan Master Shanzhao of Fenyang; he was the tenth generation descendant of Nanyue. Chan Master Shouzhi of Dayu Mountain in Ruizhou also succeeded Fenyang.
He formed a group to visit Fenyang, who was— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at "who was—", indicating an incomplete source.)
Zen Master Zenjō of Taishi-in in the province was a son of the Yu clan of Daibara. He was a dharma successor of Zen Master Enkan of Shuzan, belonging to the ninth generation under Nanyue.
At a time when military conflict was raging in the northwest, the region around Luan in Zezhou was occupied by troops such that no one dared to travel there.
The six men of the Compassionate One (Jikyō), disregarding danger and obstacles, crossed the Rongzhe River and ascended Mount Tai.

He traveled by mountain path, changing his clothes to blend in with military units, sleeping in the open air and lodging in the grass without shrinking from toil or hardship, in order to go and visit Fenyang.
Now, Mount Jing and Hengyang are not very far apart; the roads between them are naturally free of obstacles and have no hindrances.
Furthermore, the mountains and rivers present no difficult barriers; one can travel directly there. We ought to meet once again.
"What difficulty would there be in [going] to Wondrous Joy? Because of this, the great assembly remained silent. The next day, they departed one after another.
△ Zhuangzi said: "That the piglets do not suckle at their dead mother is not because they love her physical form, but because they love that which animates her form.
That the monastics (nàzǐ) hasten toward Hengyang is due to the power of virtue."
This chapter concerns the evaluation of human character. One must examine the origins of the mind through outward traces; it cannot be judged by occasional lapses or disparaging remarks.
Wan’an said: "When the former master moved to Mei-yang, some among the monks privately criticized him. Yun Shouzuo said: 'The Great..."
In evaluating others, one should seek for the absence of fault within their faults; how could one possibly seek for faults within their faultlessness?
Indeed, if one fails to examine the heart and instead suspects the outward traces, how can this truly console the public judgment of the monastic community?
After Miaoxi was demoted to Hengyang, he compiled the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma) in three fascicles.
Because he was again slandered by others, he was further demoted to Meiyang County in Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong. Not long thereafter, an imperial edict restored his lay attire.

At that time, various quarters offered him vacant seats to entice him to accept them, but he did not comply. In the eleventh month of the twentieth year of the Shaoxing era, an edict ordered him to reside at Ayuwang Temple in Mingzhou.
