At Wangsi Temple. In the twenty-eighth year [of the reign], an imperial decree was issued for him to reside again at Mount Jing.

On the first day of the eighth month in the first year of Xiaozong’s Longxing era, he passed away. During the Song dynasty, once Qin Hui monopolized state power, all scholar-officials of reputation were exiled to remote regions;
yet those who were petty, effete, and lacking in vigor would ascend to positions of authority as soon as they found common ground with him in a single word.

The Prefectural Governor still stopped short of dismissing one official; this was called "accompanying attendance. If the official uttered even a slight word of dissent, he was expelled without exception, no different from a slave.
This section states that those who evaluate others must not engage in frivolous criticism.
Among the monastics, there were some who spoke privately, saying: "In general, when evaluating a person, one should focus on their faults and shortcomings."
One seeks a single principle free from fault so that the faults possessed by others may be reformed;
how could one, within that which is faultless, instead seek out its faults? This is irrational.

Indeed, failing to examine the intention behind the compilation of the *Miaoxi ji* (Collection of Wondrous Joy) while merely doubting the traces of a second demotion—how can this truly provide comfort?
This is the public consensus of the monastic community.
Furthermore, Miaoxi’s virtue, character, and talent are innate; in his conduct and actions, he follows only what is righteous.
His capacity surely exceeds that of others. That the Creator now restrains him must surely have its reason; how could one not know this?
Is this not the merit of a different time for the Dharma-gate? Those who heard it thereafter no longer engaged in such debate (from the *Zhilinjiji*).
This section clarifies that when encountering difficulties, there must be a underlying principle. Furthermore, Miaoxi’s virtue, talent, and capacity were innate;
in his personal conduct and actions, he followed only what was righteous. His magnanimity and breadth of character naturally surpassed those of others.
Today, the Way has intentionally suppressed it; there must surely be another underlying principle.
Who knows that this matter may not become a blessing for the Dharma-gate in the future? After hearing this, those who had previously discussed it no longer did so again.
△ Among those with faults, one seeks out those without fault; only Nityapradīpa (Constantly Non-Light) was such a person. This is subtle indeed.
None of these individuals are fit to be spoken to regarding this matter.
The Master of this school should receive people with impartiality and justice; he must not involve himself in private interests.
The Head Seat Yin said to Wan’an, "One who calls himself a 'Good Knowledge' (Sanzhi Shi) ought to cleanse his mind so that it is characterized by supreme public-mindedness."

Upon reaching the ultimate correctness, one receives those who come from the four quarters. Among them, if there are those who embrace virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness, one must admit them even if they harbor enmity or resentment.
Conversely, if there are those who are treacherous, wicked, or base, one must distance oneself from them even if they have rendered private favors.
This ensures that all who come know what to uphold, so that they may be of one mind and shared virtue, and the monastic community will be at peace. (From a letter to Miaoxi)

It is said that one who is called a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) and proclaims the Great Dharma must first purify their own mind, ensuring that not even a single trace of defiled habitual tendencies remains within the breast.

Only then, by means of the law of supreme impartiality and the path of ultimate rectitude, should they receive students from the four quarters. Among them, if there be those who cherish and uphold the Way and its Virtue...
Regarding benevolence and righteousness: even if one has some enmity or grievance with another, one must still recommend and promote them;
yet if that person harbors wickedness, treachery, or meanness, even if they have some private kindness toward me, one must certainly dismiss and distance oneself from them.
In this way, those who come from the four quarters will each know their own place.
This is what they maintain. Whether others possess virtue or lack it, one follows accordingly.
Even if there are a thousand or ten thousand people among them, if they all cultivate virtuous conduct with a single mind, then the monastic community will naturally be peaceful and secure.
To split the measuring bowls and break the scales is simply to achieve self-leveling; when one is supremely impartial and upright, what more need be said?
This chapter teaches that an abbot should rectify himself to benefit others, maintaining sincerity and profound virtue.
It further states: "Among those who serve as abbots, who does not wish to establish a monastic community (*saṅghārāma*)? Yet few are able to truly revitalize it.

This is because they forget the Way and its Virtue (*moral*), neglect benevolence and righteousness (*ren-yi*), discard the laws and regulations, and allow private sentiments to prevail. One must truly contemplate the Dharma.

As the members of your household have suffered through death and decline, you should rectify yourself and treat others with humility. Select the worthy to assist you, honor those of long-standing virtue, and distance yourself from petty men.
Cultivate frugality within yourself and extend the benefits of your virtue to others; only then will those whom you employ as attendants [behave appropriately].

Those who are somewhat mature and experienced should be retained; those who are sycophantic and flattering should be distanced. This is to ensure there are no slanders of the ugly or evil, nor the chaos of partisan factionalism.
If one acts in this manner, one may be equaled by Mazu and Baizhang, and even reach the level of Linji and Deshan (from the *Zhilin ji*).
This means that once one has become a master who maintains the Dharma, who would not wish to establish monastic groves and bring glory to their lineage?

Yet, in the end, few are able to truly uphold the reputation of their house. This is for no other reason than that their human path is not yet authentically realized and their virtue is not truly cultivated;
furthermore, they have abandoned benevolence and righteousness and cast aside the laws and regulations of the Dharma. Moreover—
Furthermore, by not reforming their private attachments, they have caused their family reputation to decline.
If one truly perceives that the Dharma is fading and the lineage is becoming desolate, one should first rectify one’s own mind and treat others with humility.
From among the gathered multitude, one should select virtuous, upright, and worthy individuals to serve as assistants and supporters.
One must promote and honor those who are elderly and virtuous, while distancing oneself from petty people of ignorance.
Furthermore, one should cultivate the self through frugality and bestow kindness upon others.
Subsequently, among those who attend to and serve at one's side, one should retain those who are more mature and experienced, and distance oneself from those who are sycophantic and fickle.
Why is this? Because its value lies in being free from the slander of the ugly and evil, thereby avoiding the turmoil caused by factions of the biased and depraved.
If one can achieve this, even the teachings of Mazu and Baizhang may be ranked as equal to them, and the reputations of Linji and Deshan may likewise be attained.
Chan Master Yixuan of Linji Monastery in Zhenzhou was the son of the Xing family of Nanhua in Caizhou.
He was a successor of Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo and belongs to the fourth generation under Nanyue. Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Dingzhou...

Jianzhou asked a disciple: "The successor of Chan Master Longtan Chongxin, who was the fourth generation under Qingyuan, was one who managed the monastic community by upholding the Way and concealing his virtues;
he was truly a great master of the public lineage and its fundamental source. Furthermore, he could select the worthy and distance himself from the sycophantic;
he cultivated his own person and benefited all things, so that naturally the multitude of talents gathered around him. How could he have worried about the failure of the Way?"
This is not so. This chapter teaches people that knowing worry and toil are good medicines; that calamities and misfortunes cannot be escaped.
Master Yinshou said: "The sages of antiquity took the absence of disaster as a cause for fear, saying: 'Does Heaven perhaps abandon me, the unworthy?'"
Fan Wenzi said: "Only the sage can be free from anxiety both internally and externally. For anyone other than a sage, external tranquility necessarily implies internal worry.
The worthy and enlightened of past and present have known that one cannot escape this; thus they were careful at the outset and established their own defenses.
Therefore, if a person’s life involves even a modicum of worry and toil, it may not fail to become a blessing for a lifetime. This is because calamities, misfortunes, slander, and disgrace—"
"Even Yao and Shun could not escape it; how much less others? (In a letter to Miaoxi).
The supreme persons of antiquity often felt fear upon seeing themselves free from calamity and affliction, and they would say to themselves in self-reproach:
"The Way of Heaven is impartial. How could it be that it alone has abandoned me, the 'not-valuable' one? 'Valuable' (穀) means 'good. 'Not-valuable' refers to an unvirtuous person;
it is also a term for having committed offenses. This implies that I have committed offenses, and thus Heaven seems to abandon me rather than pitying me.
Lord Wen Zhengfan said: "Only a sage can be free from anxiety both internally and externally. Unless one is a sage..."

A person may have peace in their external body, yet their inner mind will inevitably be anxious. Wise men and sagely scholars of both past and present have known for themselves that they cannot escape suffering and affliction;

therefore, they constantly take the two paths of *śīla* (precepts) and *kṣānti* (patience) as their walls and fences, and the *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom) as their armor and staff, with which to protect themselves.
Thus, when one is born into this world, there is inevitably some degree of anxiety, toil, and affliction.
This is difficult to say; it may not fail to become a blessing for one's entire life.

For as for the calamities and misfortunes of human existence, and the slanders and insults of the world—even the most sagely sages like Yao and Shun could not escape the slander of being unkind or the disgrace of being unfilial. Thus, such things cannot be avoided.

How much more so for people today, who are of ordinary capacity! One must understand that much toil and much suffering are themselves the Mohe-mo (Mojie) sword for whetting one's desires and eliminating depravity;
they can certainly not be avoided. Within this toil and suffering lies infinite enjoyment; one should investigate this deeply.
This chapter concerns the essential conduct for maintaining the Dharma, which requires that practice and understanding be in accord; one must not seek fame or profit at any cost.
Master Wanan Yan said: "I observe that in the monastic communities today, there are utterly no mature and accomplished masters.

Wherever they go, whether in groups of three hundred or five hundred, one person takes the lead as the leader while many others act as his companions. They occupy the throne of the Dharma King, wielding the mallet and brandishing the whisk, [only] to compete with one another."
Deceptive and deceitful; even if there is discourse, it does not touch upon the classical teachings.
It is therefore no wonder that there are no mature, experienced elders. This section serves as a counter-illustration: the monastic community must rely on those who are mature and experienced.
This refers to what I have observed in monasteries recently—there are, in fact, very few people who are seasoned and authentic. Wherever I go, perhaps three...
Whether there be a hundred or five hundred people dwelling together in a single courtyard, they appoint one person as their leader, while the many serve as his companions.
This leader himself lacks right view, yet he ascends the throne of the Dharma King and speaks in barbaric gibberish.
The head monk strikes the gavel and the elder brandishes the whisk; everyone joins in a chaotic clamor, mutually deceiving one another. Even if there were some words of substance...
Their discourse is entirely fabricated and fails to touch upon established precedents;
this is all because they lack mature, experienced men who act according to their own whims and personal inclinations, creating disorder at will.

Now, to transcend the world and benefit sentient beings, acting as a representative of the Buddha to propagate his transformation, one must clarify the mind and penetrate the fundamental source, ensuring that practice and understanding correspond;

how could one dare to undertake this otherwise? It is like a person who falsely claims the title of Emperor and brings about their own execution; how much more so for the Dharma-King—how could one recklessly usurp such a position? Alas!
As the distance from the Sage has grown ever greater, those like the "cranes in the floodwaters" have proliferated everywhere, causing the former Sages’... [teachings to be obscured].
The gate of transformation is daily sinking into ruin; how could I wish to remain silent?
This section precisely clarifies the upholding of the Dharma, which necessitates the correspondence of practice and understanding. Indeed, to transcend the world and benefit sentient beings—
This is originally a matter of acting as a representative of the Tathāgata to proclaim the Dharma and transform sentient beings.
Unless one has clearly realized one's own mind, thoroughly penetrated its source, and possesses a mutual correspondence between practice and understanding, how could one dare to presume to do so?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Suppose there were a person who falsely claimed to be an emperor; he would bring his own execution.

How much more so for one who aspires to be a Dharma King transcending the world—if they have not seen the stage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and lack true virtue and morality, how could they dare to arrogantly and falsely usurp this title?
Alas! As the distance from the Buddha’s era grows ever greater, there arises a certain class of people, like cranes wading in shallow water.

...belonging to [this category]. Everywhere he was praised and extolled as "Zheng," moving freely through the world. Long ago, when Ānanda went to the Bamboo Grove, he heard a bhikṣu reciting a verse:

"If a person lives for a hundred years And does not see the cranes at the marshes, It is not as good as living for a single day And being able to behold them. Having heard this, Ānanda sighed with sorrow and said, "The Eye of the World..."
"It has ceased! How sudden it was! These afflictions and various evils—how could they have arisen so quickly? They contradict the holy teachings; they arise of their own accord and then vanish.
Lacking the light of wisdom, they dwell perpetually in the darkness of delusion. They shall forever wander through birth and death. Then he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is not to be practiced. You should now know that there are two kinds of people who slander the Buddha: first, those who..."
First, though possessing great learning, one gives rise to false views. Second, though understanding profound meanings, one explains them erroneously and falsely.
Possessing these two qualities, one brings about self-destruction and cannot lead others to escape the three evil realms. You should now listen as I recite the Buddha’s verses.
"If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the law of arising and ceasing, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining full comprehension.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke thus to his teacher, who said: "Ānanda is aged and infirm; his words are full of errors."
"This is not to be trusted. You must return and recite it as before. Later, Ānanda heard the bhikṣu reciting the previous verse again and asked him the reason for this.
The bhikṣu related his teacher's words in full. Ānanda reflected that the man might have slighted his words or perhaps received other teachings;
he immediately entered *samādhi* to seek out someone of superior virtue who might be able to turn back that man's mind, but he saw no one capable of doing so. He then... [proceeded to act].
He thought to himself: "How strange! How strange! It is no longer upright; one shall surely fall into the three miserable realms.
This passage appears in the *Aśokarāja-avadāna*. Relying upon the gateway of the teachings of the former sages, [the world] declines day by day, sinking and drowning away. How could I not speak out?

Taking advantage of my leisure while dwelling in a mountain hermitage, I have set forth several points regarding how certain practices harm the tradition and subvert the teachings, the most egregious of which are one or two instances that have spread throughout the monastic community.

This is intended to ensure that future generations and latecomers to the path will know that their predecessors were ever-vigilant and earnest, making it their primary concern to uphold the Great Dharma.
It is like walking upon jagged ice or running across the edge of a sword; it is not for the sake of seeking fame or profit.
Whether they understand me or condemn me, I have no words to offer in response (from the *Zhilinjiji*).
This section entrusts [the reader] with the responsibility of upholding the Great Dharma. "To encounter" means to meet [this opportunity].

It is precisely while residing in a hermitage free from worldly affairs that one may set forth these articles. "Setting forth" refers to arranging regulations and establishing methods in order to remedy the defects of the Final Dharma Age.
Thus, my setting forth of these articles concerns the many instances in recent monasteries where customs have been violated and the teachings have been brought to ruin.
The harm that has reached its utmost severity is such that I shall briefly set forth several instances for circulation within the monastic communities (*saṃgha*).

This is so that later generations and those of humble standing may know how the predecessors who upheld the Dharma were ever cautious, as if treading on thin ice fearing they might sink, and ever vigilant, as if walking upon the edge of a sword fearing they might be wounded;
their sole concern was to shoulder the Great Dharma, never acting with mere expediency.
They seek his empty fame and covet his wealth and profit. Those who understand me will consider my words to be right; those who condemn me will consider my words to be wrong.
As for this charge of being judged as right or wrong, how could I dare to decline it? Regarding those who understand me and those who condemn me:
Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Chunqiu*) to embody the royal law. Its essential principles were all matters pertaining to the Son of Heaven.
Those who understand Confucius say that the composition of this book stemmed from his profound and far-reaching concern for future generations;

it was intended to stem the flood of human desires and preserve the principles of Heaven where they had already been extinguished. Those who condemn Confucius, however, argue that he lacked the proper authority.

Yet, by entrusting the authority of the southern-facing ruler for two hundred and forty-two years, he caused rebellious ministers and treacherous sons to restrain their desires and not dare to act recklessly—this was truly a matter of profound sorrow.

One must understand that the single-minded, blood-red heart of the ancients was entirely intended only to teach people to become world-transcending men of integrity and not to allow themselves to sink into ruin; what else could it have been?
This chapter states that the Dharma has long since fallen into decline. Be careful not to take arising and ceasing as your primary concern.
Wanan said: "When the ancients ascended the hall, they would first present the essential principles of the Great Dharma and examine the assembly.
Students would then come forward to request instruction, whereupon questions and answers ensued."
This section clarifies what is logically required. It means that the reason the ancients ascended the hall was originally to "extract nails and pull out wedges" for the sake of their students;
they would first present the essential principles and core tenets of the Great Dharma and then interrogate the assembly to see whether anyone among them understood its meaning.
Because the students did not understand its meaning, they would step forward from the assembly to request instruction.
Seeking benefit, they eventually give form to it through questions and answers; this is the natural principle of things.

Nowadays, people fabricate four-line rhymed verses and call them "hooked talk" (*dōwa*). Another person suddenly steps forward before the assembly and loudly recites a couplet from an ancient poem, calling it a "verbal battle" (*bajin*).
How vulgar, how depraved! It is truly lamentable and painful. May my predecessors take heed.
"The matter of birth and death is great. To resolve doubts before the assembly, he has already clarified this so that the mind of arising and ceasing does not yet stir.
This section clarifies that such [actions] are irrational and fabricated. People today do not act thus;
rather, the elders first compose their own rhyming four-line verses and call them "hooks" to entice scholars. "Du-zuan" (杜撰) means to block off and fabricate. To "zuan" (撰) is to create.
It is a fabrication; it is a mere imitation. It means to create something on one’s own while failing to understand the ancient methods.
This is like the Daoist Du Guangting, who plagiarized Buddhist scriptures to compose Daoist texts.
Suddenly, there might be a person who emerges before the multitude and loudly recites two lines of an ancient poem, calling this a "stance for mutual abuse" and treating it as the Dharma.
To engage in combat—does such a principle exist? This is the ultimate depravity of the secular world; it is a matter of lamentation and sorrow that the Way of the Dharma is in decline.
Ultimately, they do not realize that for their own predecessors, the failure to clearly comprehend birth and death was the most pressing concern.
Wherever they go, they simply set down their packs and come to seek out masters, whether during formal sermons or informal sessions.

"San. He then resolved his deep doubts before the great assembly. Having attained the illumination of the great matter of one's own person, how could there ever have been even a hair’s breadth of a mind subject to arising and ceasing, or the view of self and others?

△ This chapter reveals that those who have served the Dharma throughout antiquity and the present are like bright mirrors set upon a stand, leaving no place for anyone to escape. Students may [reflect upon this].
Is this not a lack of care?
Those who teach the Dharma in this chapter must know that the etiquette between guest and host is not to be neglected.
Wanan said: "When a venerable master of great reputation arrives at the monastery, the host shall ascend the seat and express gratitude with humble courtesy. He then bowed.

The Honored One descends from his high position to a lower one to speak words of increasing gravity. The junior monks join the senior seat-holder (shouzuo) and the assembly in requesting him to ascend the seat, so that they may hear the essentials of the Dharma.
This section first teaches the principle of propriety: whenever a venerable elder or spiritual teacher of virtuous conduct and renown arrives...
In the monastery, the master must first ascend the seat for him and preach the Dharma; this is called "introducing the seat.

He must act with humility, harmony, and deference, expressing gratitude for the other's honor in descending to visit. Whether in terms of monastic rank or seniority, he should yield his own dignity to accord with the other's lower status.

In speaking, one should employ increasingly grave and weighty language. When the teaching has been concluded, the assembly descends from their seats and, together with the head seat (śrāmaṇera), requests the venerable elder or spiritual friend to ascend the seat.
"Shu" (庶) means to hope; it signifies the aspiration to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
This is the correct principle.

I have frequently observed that in recent times, people emulate one another by citing ancient *gong'an* (public cases) and commanding others to critique them before an assembly, calling this "testing others.

You must absolutely not harbor such a mind. The former sages forgot their own emotions for the sake of the Dharma; together they established the transformation of the Dharma, responding to one another in song so that the Dharma might endure for a long time.

How could they have allowed thoughts of arising and ceasing to arise, or given rise to such evil intentions? Reverence takes humility as its primary principle; you should be profoundly mindful of this.
Reflect upon this.

This section clarifies what is "unreasoned. I have often observed those who follow contemporary customs and trends taking up the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients and having other venerable seniors come forward to critique and judge them before the assembly, in order to examine the depth of their insight.
Is there such a thing as this ritual? Those who act as hosts hereafter must strictly avoid harboring such a competitive spirit, for it harms social customs and moral transformation.

The former sages were so earnest in their concern for the Dharma that they forgot all personal attachments; their fundamental aim was to jointly erect the banner of the Dharma and promote the flourishing of the teachings.
It was not intended that they should necessarily engage in mutual recrimination, thereby causing the Buddha-Dharma to endure long in the world.
How could he possibly allow his mind to give rise to birth and extinction, or harbor such an evil thought?
Furthermore, the etiquette between guest and host is fundamentally based on humility; one should reflect deeply upon this matter.

Knowledgeable ones originally intend to help others untie their adhesions and remove their fetters, yet they instead turn the Dharma into a pretext for craftiness—I do not know what kind of mind this is.
This is the practice.
This chapter teaches that in receiving and protecting outsiders, one must maintain the fundamental principle; do not allow extraneous branches to sprout beyond the core.
Wan’an said: "Recently, I have seen instances where officials—whether provincial inspectors or district magistrates—enter the mountain. On the following day, they order their attendants..."

"Regarding the matter of 'the elder being covered,' today [the Master] specifically ascends the seat for the sake of such-and-such an official. This one point should still be considered with threefold reflection.
This point clearly concerns the great principle of awaiting external protection.

It refers to what has been observed recently regarding scholar-gentlemen, various high officials, and local supervising officers—whether they be the Prefectural Governors of their respective commanderies—and how, due to certain matters..."
When an official arrives to enter the mountain monastery, the head administrator reports it to the attendant on the following day.
"Taking up the *fù* (covering)" refers to reporting the name of the official to the Elder. This means taking up the title of the official to inform the Elder.
Today, a certain high-ranking official has specifically ascended the seat for this occasion; this matter must not be handled carelessly, but should be considered with threefold reflection.
This is indeed so.
Although such matters have been recorded in the volumes of the past, they were all instances where scholar-officials sought out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Consequently, the abbot, during the course of their formal inquiry, briefly offered guidance to protect the teachings and expressed his intention to bring glory to the springs and rocks. Since this is already our own home...
A host should speak a few plain words at home to inspire respect in their guest.
This is exemplified by the visits of Guo Gongfu and Yang Cigong to Baiyun, and the meetings of Su Dongpo and Huang Tingjian with Foyin; these serve as models.
How could this be a deliberate act of pretension intended to invite the ridicule of the wise?

This section refers to the visiting of scholar-officials (*shidafu*). Although records from ancient times contain accounts of abbots ascending the hall for officials, one must understand that these were all instances where such officials, out of admiration for the Way, came to seek out a spiritual teacher (*zhishi*) for instruction and guidance.
Once the abbot had finished providing the formal words of inquiry (*can-yu*) requested by them, he would subsequently offer a brief [discourse].
To protect the outer gate of the Teaching and illuminate the spirit of the springs and rocks:
if there are those who belong to the Dharma, one should speak a few words of the Dharma to them that may seem devoid of flavor, thereby causing them to increase their reverence and faith.
This is like Guo Gongfu and Yang Cigong visiting Baiyun at Haihui in Shuzhou. (The account of Gongfu follows.)

The traces [of his life] appear as before. Yang Cigong (Yang Cigong) rose to the rank of Minister of the Ministry of Rites. At night, he felt a lack of spiritual support and thus took pleasure in Buddhism.
He studied under twelve teachers in succession, yet failed to grasp their essential teachings. Later, hearing that the reputation of Baiyun was flourishing greatly, he went to visit him.
It happened that Baiyun was entering the room for meditation with the assembly at the third watch of the night; Gong requested an audience, but Baiyun did not grant it.
The Master [Yunmen] was at his window imitating the crowing of a rooster. Yunmen said, "A thing that does not know the proper season may indeed confuse all quarters.
He ordered an attendant to seize and kill him. As the attendant dragged him into the abbot’s quarters, the Master continued to crow without ceasing.
Yun made the sound of a dog. The Master then stopped and extended his neck before the teacher. Yun seized the Master by the whiskers and said, "Long hair like a tail.
The Master asked, "When you discard the hair and take the tail, what is it like? Yun said, "Watch the chicken. The Master let out a single crow.
Yun grabbed him and pushed him away, saying, "The chicken is in the coop; why seek a bowl? Thereupon, he shut the door.
He summoned him again, saying, "Next Master. The Master responded, "Yes. Yun said, "Have you emerged from the cage yet?
The Master was speechless. An attendant said, "Sir, please rest for now; come see the Master again tomorrow. The Master then withdrew.
Sōtō visited Mount Jinshan and encountered Fuyin (Foyin) while he was conducting a private interview with his disciples. Fuyin said, "There are no seats here. Sōtō replied:
"May I temporarily borrow the four elements of the Buddha’s body as a seat? Foyin said, "I, a mountain monk, have a question. If you, Layman, can answer it, you may sit;
if you cannot, you must forfeit the jade belt at your waist. Su Shi joyfully replied, "Please do so.
Foyin said, "Just now you said, 'May I temporarily borrow the mountain monk's four elements as a seat. Now, as for the mountain monk himself—"
"The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist. Where would you sit? Su Shi was unable to answer.
Zhenjing summoned his attendant and said, "Take this jade belt and keep it forever to guard the mountain gate. He then presented Su Shi with a monastic robe. Su Shi composed a verse, saying:
"My sickly bones cannot endure the encirclement of a jade belt; My dull faculties still fall short of the 'arrow-point' pivot. I wish to beg..."
He ate at the Courtesan’s Quarters. Thus, with his old monk’s robe from Yunshan, [he was like] Huang Taishi, who saw Foyin sitting upon the meditation platform and asked:
"After the extinction at Śāla Grove, who is the Buddha? Who is the Sealing Seal that radiates light from the Ocean?"
Yin said, "The melon of Jiangnan is planted in Jiangbei; the watermelon of Jiangbei is grown in Jiangbei. Shi remained speechless. That night he could not rest.
The next day, during the meal, Yin said, "Heaven and earth are dark and yellow, yet we have not yet seen the yellow.
Shupan built the village gate, yet we have not yet seen its solidity. What is the Yellow Court's hardness? Shi rose from his seat and stood with palms joined. Yin said, "I..."
The one who did not ask was Huang Tingjian. Shi said, "How could there be two? Yin said, "Blind! And so forth.
As for these various masters mentioned above, they all came seeking the Way as those of their own household; they spoke the language of the household, which serves as a model.
How could this be the case for those who are ignorant? It is not something done on a whim; it is without cause. Furthermore...
I ask you again: why do you ascend the hall without being asked? To act in such a frivolous manner is bound to invite derision from those who possess true discernment.
Not only do you now insist on ascending the hall for others, but you even go so far as to seek out various opportunities to show off, fearing that you might not have enough chances.
Were Wan’an to hear of this, I do not know what he would say.
Regarding the master of this chapter: do not suppress people with the Dharma; you must preserve ancient regulations. Wan’an said:

"In the past, when entering the room [for formal instruction], one would first have a plaque hung up. Each person, regarding the great matter of birth and death, would come with eager anticipation to seek decisive resolution.
I have often seen that nowadays, regardless of whether they are old or sick, everyone is made to come and surrender their submission. If there is musk...
This is natural fragrance. Why must it be suppressed by public regulations? Because of this, artificial formalities arise, leaving both guest and host uneasy.
Those who uphold the Dharma should reflect upon this.
This refers to the ancient masters of the Dharma who, in refining their students, required them to enter the room [of the master].
First, they would have the attendant hang up a notice to inform the assembly that the student regards the matter of birth and death as paramount.

Consequently, the student would naturally come with great enthusiasm and joy to seek the Master’s guidance in resolving their doubts and obstructions; this is the correct principle. However, in many of the modern monasteries...
Regardless of whether they are elderly or ill, one must have them come to submit their surrender. "Surrendering one's doubts" refers to the appearance of offering one's sincerity and utmost respect.
Should there be those who do not comply, it is said that they fail to follow the rules and treat the Abbot with contempt.
Why is this so? You are indeed a man of knowledge who has penetrated both heaven and earth.
As the saying goes, "The musk deer naturally exudes fragrance. Why must you publicly establish boundaries to restrain it and forcibly compel its arrival?
For this reason, it is called "needlessly creating complications" and "falsely inventing categories," which leads to unease between guest and host.
Thus it is. Those who preside over the Dharma should reflect deeply upon this. Reverence arises from sincerity; through sincerity, one looks up to virtue.
If I were truly endowed with virtue, even ghosts and spirits would come to my chamber, let alone human beings.
This chapter states that the source of the Way lies in emulating the ancients and honoring the predecessors; there is nothing to be discriminated. Wanan said:
"The First Patriarch of Shaolin transmitted both the robe and the Dharma. At the sixth generation, the robe was no longer transmitted.

By taking those whose practice and understanding corresponded [to the truth] to inherit the family vocation, the ancestral Way became ever more radiant and the descendants multiplied. After Dajian, Shitou..."
Mazu was the legitimate grandson of both; this is precisely what is meant by the prophecy of Prajñātāra that "it must be realized through the feet of one's descendants.
The profound words and wondrous sayings of these two Great Beings have spread throughout the world, and those who have secretly conformed to and secretly realized them are found everywhere.

This section clarifies that the source of the Dharma has its own origin. It means that from the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs until its transmission and proclamation within our land of Zhendan (China), Master Bodhidharma of Shaolin was regarded as the progenitor. Therein, the transmission of the robe and the conferral of the Dharma proceeded in tandem.
It was not until the Sixth Patriarch that it was declared that the robe was a cause for contention and was no longer transmitted; henceforth, only conduct was taken up.
It is in accord with liberation. Regarding the phrase "both practice and teaching reach [the goal]": "to reach" means that their family vocation is sustained through successive generations.
Because of this, the ancestral Way becomes increasingly magnificent, and descendants become ever more numerous.
Following the Sixth Patriarch, Dajian Huineng, both the Chan Master Shitou Xiqian and the Chan Master Mazu Daoyi received his direct instruction.
Having received the Dharma directly from Qingyuan and Nanyue, he was the legitimate grandson of the Sixth Patriarch.
This precisely accords with the prophetic omen of Prajñātāra, which stated that the work must be carried out "under the feet of his descendants.
After Master Bodhidharma attained the Dharma, he asked Prajñātāra: "To which country should I go to perform the Buddha-work? The Patriarch [Prajñātāra] said: [He should go to the land of China].
He said, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay in Southern India for now. Wait until sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa;
then you shall go to China to bestow the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties. Be careful not to travel too far, lest you suffer decline under the sun.
He asked again, "Will there be Great Beings in that land capable of being vessels for the Dharma? [The Master replied,] "After a thousand years, there will be."
"Will there be obstacles? The Patriarch said, "The number of those you have converted who have attained Bodhi is beyond counting.

Sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa, that country will face difficulties; the waters will overflow and spread everywhere. You must skillfully subdue them. When your time comes, do not remain there.
That country values only conditioned merits and does not perceive the principle of the Buddha. Listen to my verse:"
It is said: "Traveling along the road, one crosses water and again encounters sheep. "Traveling along the road and crossing water" refers to meeting Emperor Liang Wu, whose name was Yan.
"Again encountering sheep" means that Emperor Wu of Wei was a Qiang person. "Alone and desolate, he crossed the river in the dark" refers to the incident of plucking the reeds.
"Under the sun, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses": "under the sun" refers to Luoyang; "how pitiable" refers to the pair of elephants.
"Ma" refers to Emperor Wu of Liang and Emperor Wu of Wei. "Two young cinnamon trees flourishing for a long time" refers to the two schools of Linji and Caodong.
It is further said that there will be a minor hardship after one hundred and fifty years. Listen to my verse: "In the heart there is auspiciousness, while outside there is misfortune.
In the heart there is auspiciousness—this is the character 'Zhou' (周). Outside there is misfortune—this refers to Emperor Wu of Zhou's suppression of the Sangha. *Chuan* (川) [End of volume].
The lower monastic quarters are called Bu Zhong. "Below the river" refers to Taixian County. The monastic quarters named Bu Zhong refer to Sikong Mountain.
"If one encounters a venomous dragon, a martial son is born"—if one encounters a venomous dragon, Emperor Ming was the father of Martial King (Wu Wang).
"A martial son is born" refers to Emperor Wu. "Suddenly encountering a small mouse, its stillness is infinite"—"suddenly encountering a small mouse" means:
In the year of the Mouse, Emperor Xuan ascended the throne and greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma. As for Jiqiong, he was extinguished by Yang Jian, who established the Sui dynasty.
It is further said: "After this, you shall see a man beneath a forest tree who will attain the fruit of the Way.
Listen to my verse: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; one must rely on the feet of his descendants to travel it. This refers to Mazu Daoyi.
This refers to Shitou. Regarding the "Golden Cock that released a grain of millet": it is said that Nanyue Huairang was a native of Jinji County;
he made offerings to the Arhat monks of the ten directions. It is said that Mazu Daoyi was a monk at Luohan Temple in Shifang County, Sichuan;
because Mazu inherited the Dharma of Nanyue, this is so. It is said that Prajñātāra had issued a prophetic prediction concerning Shitou.
Mazu was the patriarch of the Cao-Dong and Linji schools. The profound and mysterious words and the exquisite, subtle sayings of these two great masters have already circulated throughout the world.
"Latent conformity" refers to that which accords in secret and is realized through silent resonance beyond the realm of speech.
Regarding "secret realization," the *Mingjiao* states: "Secret does not mean the absence of speech..."
It is the secret testimony; it is the true esoteric transmission. This refers to the outward transmission of the robe of faith and the inward bestowal of the secret testimony;
this is the authentic and profound esoteric Dharma of our Buddhas and Patriarchs. The phrase "it occurs frequently" means that those who possess the tallying testimony are constantly found.

Since the methods of the masters were manifold, students did not specialize in a single school. Although the lineage of Caoxi branched into five streams, they were like water taking different forms according to its vessels while remaining identical in its essence.
Each enjoyed a fine reputation and diligently fulfilled their own responsibilities; in their daily conduct, they would casually impart a single word or issue a single command.
They gathered scholars together, and the monastic centers were as bustling as boiling cauldrons; this was no mere coincidence.
From this, they engaged in mutual exchanges of verse, manifesting the subtle and elucidating the profound. Whether tempering or uplifting, they assisted in the transformation of the Dharma.

Their words lacked flavor, like a soup boiled from wood chips or rice steamed from iron nails, which they chewed upon with their juniors, calling it "picking up the ancients" (*niangu*). These verses began with Fenyang and continued through Xuefeng.
Dongguo Hong makes its sounds resonant and its principles manifest; it is vast and boundless.
This section clarifies the branching of the lineages. Since the methods of the masters were so numerous, students had no single, fixed dharma-gate upon which to train;
thus, the single current of the Caoxi source was divided into five streams.
Although the school is divided into five houses, the Dharma does not differ. It is like vessels that may be square or round, yet the substance of the water within them is one and the same.
Nevertheless, each of the five houses has specialized in its own gate of teaching and edification, each possessing a distinguished reputation.
Furthermore, each has exerted itself to fulfill its own responsibility. In the course of ordinary life, they might utter a single word or perform a single act.
The term "wǎngluó" (net and snare) carries the sense of gathering and encompassing. By netting and snaring scholars from the four quarters, the monastic groves flourished like boiling cauldrons;
how could this have been in vain? Consequently, the five houses engaged in mutual dialogue and song, manifesting their subtlety and elucidating their profound depths.
Whether they suppressed and took away, or elevated and let loose, it was nothing other than [the pursuit of truth].
These two merely assist one another to aid in the completion of their dharma-gate of teaching;
whatever words they utter are all devoid of meaning, like boiling wood shavings for soup or cooking iron nails for rice.

To provide material for later generations to chew upon is called *niangu* (picking up the ancients), so named because it involves picking up and presenting the public cases (*gong'an*) of past masters.
As for what is known as *songgu* (verses on the ancients), this began with Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao and Chan Master Xuedou Chongxian of Mingzhou.
The latter was a native of the Li clan from Suzhou; he succeeded Chan Master Zhimen Guangzuo and belonged to the lineage of Qingyuan.
The Nine Generations. From these two patriarchs onward, their teachings were widely propagated and their essential principles clearly manifested.
As for how they expounded upon those meanings, they were as vast and expansive as the great ocean, beyond all bounds;
this too was entirely due to the magnificent talent and extensive learning of these two patriarchs.
Later authors galloped after Xuedou to compose their own works, regardless of whether they possessed any moral virtue;

they strove only for brilliant literary splendor and mutual display of elegance. Consequently, they prevented later generations and junior students from being able to perceive the ancient sages' essence of pure simplicity and complete perfection.
This section clarifies the fallacy of deviating from the fundamental tenet.

Those who later sought to imitate this method and forcibly composed verses on ancient cases (*sung-ku*) galloped after Xuedou’s style in their creation. To "gallop" is like two horses racing side by side;
they ultimately disregard what their own insights are like, focusing exclusively on flowery rhetoric and novel phrasing.

It is extraordinary that they fail to understand the fundamental intent of the sages, thereby causing later generations and those of recent advancement to be unable to perceive the ancient sages' spirit of holistic integration, profound sincerity, and complete perfection.

Alas! When I traveled through the monasteries and met with my predecessors, there was nothing they would not study except for the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the ancients, and there were no commands of Baizhang that they would not carry out.
This was not merely a fondness for antiquity; it was because those of the present day are not worthy of emulation.
I trust that men of broad learning and far-reaching insight will understand me beyond my words.

This section teaches that one should take the ancients as one's model. Alas! When I was traveling on foot and visiting various monasteries, and when I encountered other senior masters of former generations, they would never look at anything unless it were the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the ancients, nor would they ever practice unless it were the commands of Baizhang.
Was this merely because they were fond of antiquity? It was simply because people of recent times are not sufficient [to serve as models].
This is the standard for the Dharma. As I have spoken these words, it will suffice if those who are wise and discerning understand my intent beyond the literal language.
△ The flavor of the Way is originally *amṛta* (clarified butter); through three transformations, it becomes mere water.
To obscure the source while seeking the blossoms—what can one possibly attain of the principle of the total, profound, and complete?
This chapter teaches students that they must be broad-minded and open-hearted, and not allow themselves to be obscured by biased views.

Wanan said: "Lately, I have observed that monks are fond of clinging to biased views and fail to understand the nature of things. They are easily swayed by what they lightly believe and difficult to turn back from their ways;
they love others only when those flatter them and distance themselves from those who oppose them. Even if they possess some fragmentary understanding, they are instead hindered by these [biases]."
Obscured by such evil habits, many reach their white-haired old age without achieving anything (the above is found in the *Zhilín jí*).
This refers to what I have frequently observed among monastics lately: they delight in stubbornly clinging to their own biased views and ultimately fail to comprehend the sentiments of others;
as soon as a single word enters their ears, they fail to examine its right or wrong and instead place blind trust in it themselves.
Once their conviction is fixed, it is difficult to turn them back. Furthermore, they delight in being flattered by others;
when things accord with their wishes, they are joyful and draw others close to them, but when things oppose them, they become resentful and distance themselves.

Such practitioners, even if they possess some fragmentary understanding, are instead obscured by these evil views and habitual tendencies, such that they fail to attain [realization] until their very end.
Those who become fit vessels are many. A skilled physician does not rely on medicines from distant lands;
by taking up any single flavor at random, he can awaken the frantic and the deluded. One who masters this single chapter can accomplish all matters.
This chapter refutes heterodoxy to reveal the orthodox. It is essential that people maintain sincerity and preserve faith.

Wanan said: "In every monastery one visits, heterodox teachings flourish. They claim that the precepts need not be observed, meditative concentration and wisdom need not be practiced, the Way and its virtue need not be cultivated, and sensual desires need not be abandoned. He further cited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Awakening of Faith* as [justification].
[Zheng] praised lust, anger, ignorance, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the Brahma-faring. Alas! These words will not only bring harm to the monastic communities of today;
they are truly a calamity for the Dharma-gate for ten thousand generations.
This section states that the harm caused by false teachings and ignorance is no small matter.

It means that in the present-day monastic communities, the True Dharma is not being upheld or propagated by anyone; yet wherever one goes, various kinds of erroneous doctrines flourish like a blazing fire that will not be extinguished.
They then say: "The precepts are extremely cumbersome and restrict the body; they are unnecessary."
This is "retention. Concentration and wisdom are the meditations of those who seek minor fruits; they merely serve to still the mind and need not be practiced.
Virtue and the Way are one's original endowment; why must they be cultivated? Desire and craving are the common condition of humanity; why must they be eliminated?
Fearing that people might not believe this and would take it for the words of a demon, he further cites the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where the layman Vimalakīrti expounds upon the Mahāyāna.

It is said that Bodhisattvas enter brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire, and that although they may have wives and children, they constantly practice the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), and so forth.

Furthermore, the *Nirvana Sutra* (Yuanjue liao yi) states: "All obstacles are ultimate enlightenment," and even that "all precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are collectively the Brahma-faring. [The opponent] uses such statements as evidence.

In the end, they do not realize that those great and powerful sages manifest traces in the world to benefit sentient beings, employing the means of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*) as a form of gathering.
How could the intent of the sutras be so clear, yet heterodox and deluded persons instead use this to deceive others, unworthily receiving their veneration? Alas!
Such talk does not merely incite immediate harm within the monastic community;
it truly constitutes a threat to the Dharma for ten thousand generations.

Furthermore, ordinary people of this world are possessed of greed, anger, desire, the notion of self and other, and ignorance; their every thought clings to external objects like a cauldron of boiling water—how could they ever become clear and cool?

The ancient sages, reflecting that there must be something of great power in this regard, established the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to restrain them, hoping thereby to turn [the mind] back [from delusion].
Yet now, those of later generations who have entered the path do not maintain the precepts, nor do they cultivate concentration or wisdom.

They do not practice [the Way]. They do not cultivate moral virtue. They devote themselves solely to extensive learning and forceful debate, agitating the common people and leading them away so that they cannot return.
This is precisely what I mean when I say that such talk is a calamity for ten thousand generations.
This section states that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have heavy afflictions and must rely upon the transformative power of the Dharma. "The broad ground" (*bodhi*) refers to the great earth.

"Greed" (*rāga*) means insatiable attraction and grasping; it is also synonymous with desire. It arises from the mind’s attachment through the faculty of love. "Hatred" (*dveṣa*) refers to the intensity of anger and also to ferocity.
It arises from the interaction between the mind and the vital energy (*prāṇa*). Now, the mind belongs to the element of fire, while the vital energy belongs to...

Gold. This is because the fire of the mind becomes increasingly fierce and the metal of the vital energy (prāṇa) becomes increasingly rigid. As for "delusion" (moha), it refers to being bewildered and lacking knowledge;

it is also a state of ignorance. It arises from arrogance and self-reliance. Furthermore, the greed, anger, craving, and desire of worldly people, along with their ignorance regarding self and others, do not cease from moment to moment.
They are like a cauldron of boiling water; how could they ever attain clarity?
Cold. The former sages contemplated that the three poisons of sentient beings are most difficult to subdue;
they must employ a great method of subduing before these can be eliminated. Therefore, they specifically gave rise to great compassion for the sake of ordinary beings.

To bring about great benefit, he then established the three trainings of precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) to regulate them. Restraint of wrongdoing and cessation of evil is called precepts;
the stilling of all conditions is called concentration; and the destruction of delusions and realization of the truth is called wisdom.
These three are the gateways for entering the Path. If one possesses these three dharmas, the three poisons may perhaps be turned back. Hereafter, for future generations...
Those who entered the path late do not maintain the precepts, do not practice meditative concentration and wisdom, and do not cultivate virtue and the Way.

They focus exclusively on using extensive learning and eloquent disputation to delude and toy with those lacking wisdom, and to unsettle the common folk. Once they have led them away by feigning strangeness, the people do not turn back.
This is precisely what I mean when I say that such talk is a calamity for ten thousand generations.
Truly, a high-minded traveler of the Way should resolve the single matter of birth and death. Upholding sincerity and maintaining faith, one must not be led astray by such people.
One should say: "These words are not to be trusted; they are like the excrement of a poison-hen or water drunk by a snake.
If even hearing or seeing them is forbidden, how much more so consuming them? They will undoubtedly kill a person. To those who possess discernment, this will become self-evident.
"One stays far away from it" (as stated in the Letter to Cao Tang).
Those of clear wisdom know this to be wrong and naturally distance themselves from it; there are only those whose minds are upright who [act accordingly].
Originally, my practice as a wandering monk was characterized by lofty aspirations and far-reaching vision.
With the sole intent of resolving the single matter of birth and death, I maintained sincere devotion and guarded my right faith;
thus, I could naturally not be led astray by such practitioners of worldly karma. I declared: "These kinds of false discourses are utterly untrustworthy, like the excrement of a poison-bird."
It is like the water drunk by a venomous serpent; it is unfit even to hear of or see, let alone desire to drink.
Were a single drop to touch one, it would undoubtedly kill a person. Only those gentlemen of wisdom and discernment can naturally keep far away from it.
Since the true wind has fallen and great hypocrisy has become manifest, who does not feel their head ache and heart grieve? Myriad...
Master Ān: Such an act of denouncing the turbid and exalting the clear serves as a warning and model for ten thousand generations.
This passage shows how the host’s strict purity and propriety led to emulation from those below.
Wan’an said, "Among the disciples of Caotang, only Shantang possesses the style of the ancients.

During his tenure at Huanglong, whenever an administrative official had business to attend to, he would invariably assume a dignified demeanor and visit the abbot’s quarters to receive instructions on the details; only then would he prepare the tea and soup offerings.

He maintained this practice from beginning to end without change. There was a senior monk named Zhien who, for the sake of performing merit for his deceased mother, offered two gold coins. After two days—"
The attendant Sengcai of the Holy Monastery found it while sweeping the floor. A "Lost and Found" sign was hung up, and only then did the entire assembly come to know of it.
This was because the one presiding over the Dharma was pure; thus, those above set the example for those below to follow.
This refers to the disciples of Cao Tang. Only at Shantang did the transformative influence of the ancients remain. How is this known?

During his tenure at Huanglong, whenever an administrator had an official errand for the monastery, they would first assume a dignified demeanor and go to the abbot’s quarters to receive instructions;
only then would they prepare the rites of tea and soup to offer their thanks and reply. This was the beginning [of the tradition].
In the end, it was not lost. Among the assembly was the Elder Zhien, who had performed funeral rites for his mother to commemorate her kindness.
He had moved two gold coins to a lower location, but after two days, they remained undiscovered. A novice attendant named Caishi found them while sweeping the floor.
He hung the gold on the "Lost and Found" board. When the assembly saw it, everyone recognized that this was the Dharma.
This ensures that what exists remains so. This is likely because one knows that the master of the Dharma is pure; thus, when what is above is practiced, what is below will surely follow.
△ It is not difficult to disregard gold while plowing or to refuse to pick up gold when it is found.
What is truly difficult is simply not to deceive others.
This chapter shows that the ancients maintained their practice with principle, causing each person to know what they must uphold.
When Wanan practiced frugality during his small and general sermons, some among the monastics privately criticized him.
Upon hearing this, Wanan said: "To enjoy rich delicacies in the morning and grow weary of coarse food by evening is but human nature. Since you all are mindful of birth..."

The matter of death is great; yet you seek one another on the shores of desolation. You should reflect that your spiritual practice remains unfulfilled and that the time since the Sage passed away is far distant;
how can you continue to occupy yourself with gluttony day and night? (From the *Zhenmu ji*)
Wan’an was frugal and thrifty; he would occasionally provide small *prasaṃkhyāna* (private sermons) or *pūsè* (public lectures) as offerings.
These were true offerings, for it was because he upheld the Dharma and truly realized the Way that he was able to act in such a manner. Among the monks, there were some who privately discussed this.
When Wan’an heard of it, he said: "Generally speaking, when people of the world consume rich delicacies for breakfast, by evening they..."

"To loathe coarse food is the common sentiment. Since you have come to seek me here amidst these secluded mountains and waters, out of a profound concern for the most momentous matter of birth and death, I must not disregard your purpose in coming.
You should instead take the Dharma as your sustenance to nourish your life of wisdom. You, too, should reflect upon this."
The path of practice remains unaccomplished and the time since the Sage departed is remote; only by striving in true cultivation can one manifest the resolve and integrity of a man of honor.
How could it be right to make the pursuit of food and drink one’s sole concern through morning and evening gluttony? To covet wealth is *tāo* (greed); to covet food is *tiē* (gluttony).
Even when Bodhisattva Samantabhadra provides offerings as various and vast as Mount Sumeru, he still considers them [insufficient].
Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme; yet those who now wish to engage in private criticism are truly gluttonous scoundrels.
This chapter reveals the opportune moment with exquisite subtlety, enlightening people as clearly as if they were looking upon it with their own eyes.
Wan’an Tianxing was by nature benevolent and generous. He lived a life of integrity and frugality. In his daily teachings, his words were concise yet their meaning was profound.
Widely learned and possessing a powerful memory, he investigated the principles of the Way with thoroughness; he would neither stop halfway nor follow others blindly.

When discussing matters of antiquity and the present with others, it was as if he had personally experienced them himself. Those who listened understood clearly, as if they were witnessing the events with their own eyes. A monk once remarked: "Throughout the entire year..."
In studying under a teacher, it is better to listen to the master’s discourse for even a single day (Recorded Sayings).
Master Wanan was naturally endowed with benevolence and compassion, as well as loyalty and integrity. He lived with the utmost frugality and restraint.
In his daily speech and instructions to others, although his words were concise, their underlying principles were most refined.
His learning was most extensive and his memory exceptionally strong. He was well able to exhaustively investigate and minutely interrogate the essential meanings within them.
Regarding both principle and phenomena, he never ceased until he had reached a definitive resolution; nor did he speak falsely or merely follow the words of others.
Whenever he discussed matters of antiquity or contemporary affairs with others, his explanations were most clear and lucid, as if he himself had personally experienced them.
In an instant, it causes the listener to understand as clearly as if seeing with their own eyes. A monk once said:
"Our years of study and practice are not equal to a single day of listening to the Master’s discourse, for therein one gains profound realization.
△ Having reached this state where one is thoroughly proficient and unimpeded, whatever words are spoken naturally become like the exquisite, wondrous brocade of heaven; when one beholds them—
This must surely be "Sweet Eyes.
This chapter teaches people to maintain a straightforward mind and straightforward conduct, rather than pursuing trends or profit.
Wan’an said to Chan Master Bian: "The venerable teacher Yuanwu once said: 'Nowadays, few among the Zen practitioners possess integrity.'"
Do not be ashamed of the meaning [of these words]. Many scholars and officials hold such things in low esteem.

Should you, at some future time, unfortunately become one of these sorts of creatures, always walk within the lines of propriety; do not pursue trends or profit, nor the countenances of flatterers, even in the face of life-and-death calamities.
Leave everything as it is; this is precisely not departing from the realm of Māra to enter the realm of the Buddha (Dharma Words).
Chan Master Dabian of Zhaojue Temple in Chengdu Prefecture was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Fatai of Dayue, the sixteenth generation under Nanyue.
He said that our late teacher, Elder Yuanwu, remarked: "In these times, Chan..."
Wahzi lacks both integrity and a sense of shame; it is for this reason that many scholars and officials treat her with contempt—this is her own doing.
You all, in years to come, should you find yourselves in unavoidable circumstances, must likewise adopt such maneuvers.
That which has feet is called an insect (*chóng*); that which has no feet is called a *zhài*. You must always remain within the bounds of propriety.
Walk uprightly upon the path with rectitude. It is utterly improper to hasten after power and profit or to put on a fawning countenance for others.
When it comes to the moments of birth and death, or of calamity and misfortune, one should simply let all things be without any rejection. If one can act in this way, [one will be at peace].
This is precisely not departing from the realm of Māra while entering the realm of the Buddha.
△ To possess such mastery, one must be that person; otherwise, one will continue as before to follow along with them.
This chapter shows that those who see the Way do not value outward adornment; they simply seek self-contentment.
Chan Master Bian, the Head Seat, took up residence at Qixian on Mount Lu. He would often carry a single staff and wear a pair of sandals as he traveled through the Nine Rivers.
When the old man of Donglin saw this, he scolded him, saying, "A master is a model for others. To behave in such a manner—how can you not be self-deprecating?
Your conduct toward your host is utterly lacking in propriety. Bian laughed and said, "In human life, one takes the satisfaction of the mind as joy;
what fault is there in me? He took up his brush and wrote a verse before departing. The verse said: "Do not say that Qixian is in poverty; though my person is poor, the Way is not."
Exhausted. Grass sandals fierce as tigers; staffs alive as dragons. When thirsty, they drink from the waters of Caoxi; when hungry, they swallow the thorny chestnuts.
These men with copper heads and iron brows—all dwell within my mountains. Upon reading this, Huirong felt ashamed. (From the *Yueku ji*)

When Bian, the Head Seat, emerged from seclusion to reside at Qixian on Mount Lu, whenever he left the mountain, he would carry only a bamboo staff and wear straw sandals as he passed through the Nine Rivers and proceeded to Donglin. There, he met the Elder Hunrong, who was the Librarian Puyong.
A native of Fuzhou, he received the Dharma from Chan Master Wuzu Yan. He was the fourteenth generation descendant in the lineage of Nanyue.
While serving as the Librarian at Wuzu’s monastery, whenever anyone arrived, he would recite vernacular sayings using the Min dialect; people called him "Hunrong" (the Merged One).
One day, when he saw Bian, he rebuked him, saying: "A teacher is a model for others;
every movement and gesture should be worthy of being taken as a standard by people. Your conduct—how can you not be so self-deprecating?
Moreover, regarding the etiquette of a host, it is utterly lacking in decorum. Bian laughed and said: "In human life, one values fittingness."
"Nature itself is joy. I simply act and abide according to my own nature; what fault could there be? Thereupon, he took up his brush and wrote a verse before returning home.
The verse says: 'Do not say that dwelling at Xian is poverty; This state of poverty— Who can equal it?
The body may be poor, but the Way is not poor. Take from it and it is inexhaustible; Use it and it is never-ending. How fierce is the straw sandal!'"
Like a tiger, he tramples all under heaven; his staff is as lively as a dragon, capable of stirring up great waves and billows.
When thirsty, he drinks from the waters of Caoxi, swallowing it all in a single gulp; when hungry, he devours the *liji* thorn, chewing it to pieces until nothing remains.
Yangqi addressed the assembly, saying: "If you can pass through the diamond circle and swallow the *liji* thorn, then you are one with the Buddhas of the three periods."
The Buddha walked hand-in-hand with him; the patriarchs of successive generations share the same nostril.

If this is not yet so, you must practice true practice and realize true realization. Men of bronze heads and iron brows, measured by cartloads and bushels, all dwell within my mountains, swimming at ease.
Upon seeing this verse, Old Hunyong felt deeply ashamed. *Weifeng (Awe-inspiring Phoenix)*
A fine falcon can never be matched by a common field sparrow perched on a fence.
This passage instructs monastics that they should cultivate genuine practice and must not rely upon superficial splendor.
Master Bian said to Hunrong: "A painted dragon cannot bring rain; how can a drawn cake satisfy hunger?
A monk who lacks inner virtue yet relies on external artifice is like a leaking, dilapidated boat coated in vermilion and cinnabar;
if a puppet were made to drive it while it rests on dry land, it would indeed be quite impressive to behold. But should it venture upon the rivers and lakes and encounter a storm—"
Tao: "Is it not perilous to do so? (from the *Yueku ji*).
This means that if one were to create a dragon similar to those made by worldly people—meaning a mere likeness—how could it raise clouds or spread rain?
It is also like a painted cake; how could it satisfy the stomach or fill the bowels? This is because they are not real.
The Master used this as a metaphor for those in the Zen community. When one examines their virtue and conduct, they possess nothing within;
yet on the outside, they vainly rely on a few flowery words and clever phrases to deceive others.
Such people are much like a rotten ship, which may be painted with five colors and made to look perfectly neat, and even have a wooden figurehead fashioned for it.
A mechanical puppet is driven upon it; when placed upon dry land, who among those who see it would not believe it to be a beautiful sight?
Yet, were it suddenly cast upon a river or lake, and once it encountered wind and waves, it could only sink along with them.
How could it avoid being in peril? Those whose minds are as fine as brocade and whose speech is as embroidered as silk are just like Yang... [text truncated]
Flowers and willow catkins: a light, single touch causes one’s pain to penetrate to the very marrow of the bones. As for that which is neither true nor real, I do not know what course it would take.
This passage means that when a leader undertakes a task, they should exhaust their sincerity and must not choose between profit and harm.

Master Bian said: "Those who are called elders act as the Buddha’s representatives to propagate his transformation of the world. The essential requirement is to purify oneself when presiding over the assembly;

in performing one's duties, one must exhaustively observe the precepts. How could one allow the consideration of profit or harm to divide the mind? If it is something I ought to do, it must certainly be done in this way.
As for whether it will succeed or fail, even the former sages could not guarantee it—how then could I act with such recklessness? (From the *Yueku ji*)
It is said that one who acts as an elder is fundamentally there to propagate the Dharma on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

this is valued because they must purify their own body and mind when facing the great assembly. In all matters, one should be straightforward and without pretense, exhausting the utmost sincerity of one's being.
One must not discriminate between benefit and harm to divide the mind; in this matter, it rests upon my utmost sincerity.
To act with this mind is what the principle dictates. As for whether an undertaking succeeds or fails, there is a fixed destiny;
even the sages and worthies of antiquity could not necessarily ensure its success—how then could I, in my present state, force it to succeed through mere expediency?
"A foot of water, a ten-foot wave": this leaves one with no footing to stand upon. If...
To speak of this is easy, yet in practice it cannot be carried out; it truly places people in a situation where there is nothing that can be done.
This chapter aims to encourage people to value integrity and refrain from empty pretension.
Master Fozhi said, "The Buddha’s wisdom resides in meditation; a patch-robed monk must strive to be orderly and disciplined.
Only Shuian was by nature simple and unadorned, maintaining an extremely frugal lifestyle. He stood tall and dignified amidst the crowd, never deigning to give it a thought.
Seeing this, Fozhi rebuked him, saying, "How can you be so shabby and unkempt? Shuian replied, "It is not that I do not like fine things to use; it is simply that—"
"Because I am poor and lack the means to act, even if I had money, I would still wish to perform one or two superficial acts to join the ranks of the assembly.

Since I am poor, there is truly nothing that can be done about it. Fozhi laughed at him, thinking that he could not be forced [to change his ways], and so he let the matter rest (from the *Yueku ji*).
Chan Master Fozhi of Yuwang Temple in Qingyuan Prefecture was a descendant of the Prince of Wu and Chu. He succeeded Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin.
Chan Master Shuian Duanyi of Jingci Temple in Lin’an Prefecture was the son of the Ma family of Wuzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Fozhi. He belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng and was known as Master Fozhi.
When I was residing at Xichan, the attendant practitioners all required that their deportment be dignified and solemn, and their clothing and hats be neat and orderly;
yet Water-Arn alone, by his innate nature, was fundamentally open, empty, and detached, maintaining an extremely frugal lifestyle.
His spirit was lofty and defiant; amidst the great crowd, he did not disparage himself nor did he feel any anxiety.
"Lofty" (*āṅ-āṅ*) describes an air of self-assured elevation. When the Buddha’s wisdom perceived this, he rebuked him, saying: "How can you be so *ruò-rú*?
*Ruò-rú* is a term used by people of the Central Plains to describe those from Shu who do not follow established norms. — Water-Amban (Shuian)
He replied, "It is not that I do not like fine things to enjoy; it is simply that everything is this very character for 'poverty.
There is nothing by which one can achieve full possession. This single character for 'poverty' has great mastery. If I were to have money..."
"It would be better for you to go and acquire a bit of 'hair and skin' [worldly goods] and join the ranks of the common folk. It would be better to follow the crowd and keep company with the masses.
Since you are poor, there is truly nothing that can be done about it. When Fozhi heard this, he laughed, knowing in his mind that this man did not set foot upon the path through outward appearances;
thus, he did not force him to do so, and the matter was left at that. △ [The patched robe] (Nà)
Monastics ought to keep their every thought fixed upon the Way, as if their heads were on fire.
How could they have the leisure to adorn those perishable vessels?
This chapter speaks of subduing delusive thoughts; it requires the power of awakening-illumination.
Master Fozhi said: "When a fine horse gallops at full speed, it does not dare to let its feet run wild because it is restrained by the bit and bridle.
When a petty person is violent and overbearing, they do not dare to indulge their passions because they are constrained by laws and punishments.

When the consciousness drifts and wanders, it does not dare to cling to external conditions because of the power of awakening and illumination. Alas! If a student lacks the power of awakening and illumination, it is like..."
A fine horse has no bit or bridle; a petty person has no laws or punishments. By what means, then, can one cut off greed and desire and govern delusive thoughts?
(From a Dharma Talk with Layman Zheng)

First, let this be clarified through an analogy: the nature of a swift horse is such that it could overtake the wind, yet it does not dare to run wild and unrestrained because there are bits, bridles, and reins to restrain it. A petty person is most fierce, stubborn, and violent.
That one does not dare to indulge recklessly in sensual desires is due to the restraints of the state’s legal codes and punishments.
That the human consciousness—like a violent torrent or fierce waves—nevertheless dares not seize upon delusive conditions is due to the power of awakened awareness (*juezhao*).
Alas! If a student lacks this awakened awareness during their practice, they are truly like a swift horse without a bit.
The reins: if one is like a commoner who lacks laws and punishments, by what means can one cut off all greed and desire and govern all delusive thoughts?
When both principle and phenomena are fully revealed, there is nothing that does not enter the wondrous. Yet, how many people in this age are able to awaken and reflect?
If you wish not to fail the ancients and to preserve your own integrity, how would this differ from picking out the moon from among the stars?

This chapter discusses the fundamental principles and their applications of monastic leadership (*zhuchi*). It holds that through the cultivation and expansion of virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness, one may fulfill the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Fozhi said to Shuian: "There are four aspects to the essence of monastic leadership: first, moral virtue; second, conduct and speech; third..."
Humanity and righteousness, the four rites and laws, and moral conduct and speech constitute the root of teaching. Humanity, righteousness, rites, and laws constitute the branches of teaching.
Without the root, one cannot stand; without the branches, one cannot achieve completion.
This section first sets forth four dharmas as essential. That is to say, there are four dharmas that constitute the great substance of being a presiding master:
first, moral virtue; second, speech and conduct; third, benevolence and righteousness; and fourth, ritual and law. Moral virtue and speech and conduct are the root of edification;
