benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and law are the branches and leaves of edification. Without the root, [there can be no growth].
Why is this established for the person? Without the fundamental roots, how can the branches and leaves accomplish their tasks?
Seeing that students were unable to govern themselves, the former sages established monasteries (*conglin*) to provide them with peace and appointed abbots (*zhuzhi*) to preside over them.
Thus, the dignity of the monastery was not for the sake of the abbot, nor were the four requisites provided in abundance for the sake of the students.
All of this is for the sake of the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

This section precisely clarifies the reason for establishing [the monasteries]. Seeing that students lacked the power of discernment and could not govern themselves, the former sages established *conglin* (monastic communities) so that they would have a place to which they could return. Furthermore, they established those who possessed moral virtue and integrity.
This person acts as the abbot to govern and manage the community, ensuring that the nature of the students has a direction.

Thus, that which is honored within the assembly of the monastic grove is not the honor accorded to the person who serves as abbot; rather, it is because the four requisites—food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—are all abundant and excellent.
These are provided not solely for the personal enjoyment of the students, but for the sake of the entire community.
Because one wishes for people to practice and uphold the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must honor and provide for them.
Therefore, those who serve as abbots must first honor the Way and its Virtue and maintain their words and conduct;
those who are scholars must first preserve benevolence and righteousness and follow ritual and law. Thus, an abbot cannot be established without a scholar, nor can a scholar exist without an abbot.

This is not the case. The abbot and the students are like the body and its arms, or the head and its feet; they are perfectly proportioned to one another without conflict, and thus they must proceed in mutual dependence.
Therefore it is said: "The students preserve the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), and the monastic community preserves the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*).
If the abbot lacks the Way and its Virtue, then the monastic community will surely fall into ruin" (Shilu).

This section specifically exhorts the cultivation of virtue and integrity. Therefore, one who serves as an abbot must first and foremost revere virtue and integrity, and carefully guard their words and deeds.
One who serves as a student must first and foremost cherish benevolence and righteousness, and abide by ritual propriety and the law.
Thus, if an abbot lacks the assistance of students, they are like a single hand clapping alone.

Nanming: How could one possibly succeed by standing alone? If a student does not engage in the maintenance of the tradition and the transformation of others, they will be like a root or a sprout without rain;
how could they ever achieve fulfillment on their own? Thus, the master who maintains the tradition and the student must rely upon one another and cannot be separated.
"Must" (須) means "provisional utility. It is like a human body having arms and a head having feet;
when large and small parts are mutually appropriate and harmonious, they do not conflict, but rather assist one another in functioning. Therefore it is said:

"That which the student must preserve is the monastic community (叢林), and that which the monastic community must preserve is virtue and morality (道德). If the abbot does not reverently maintain this..."
Ethical conduct. Be scrupulous in guarding your words and deeds. In the future, the monastic orders will surely witness their decline.

△ Like a fine thread or a strand of silk, it must be maintained without interruption. One must simply uphold and follow ethical conduct. Will those who wield authority and hold the mandate not feel a sense of trepidation in their hearts?
This chapter states that birth and death are the great afflictions of humanity; it is right to prepare for them in advance.

Master Yishan said: "The *I Ching* says, 'The gentleman contemplates affliction and provides for it in advance. Therefore, the ancients contemplated the great affliction of birth and death and provided for it through the Way;
thus they were able to pass through great trials and transmit their legacy far into the distance."
This section states that the ancients contemplated the Way in every thought-moment. It refers to the *I Ching*, the hexagram of "Water and Fire in Perfect Balance" (*Ji Ji*), which says:
"The virtuous gentleman, having perfected his character, constantly contemplates potential calamities in his heart and provides for them in advance.
Therefore, the ancients reflected upon birth and death as the great affliction of humanity; thus, they took up the Great Way of the Sage that points out the wayward.

One must maintain constant mindfulness in the heart and establish a dike of defense against [unwholesome states]. Therefore, what one accomplishes will necessarily be great, and what one transmits and upholds will necessarily endure for long.
People today claim that seeking the Way is迂闊 (yūkuò—remote and impractical), and that it is not as appropriate as seeking profit.

Consequently, they compete to practice superficiality and splendor, calculating over the most minute details; they hope for matters of the immediate present and harbor expedient schemes. This is why none are willing to act [for the sake of the Way].
If this is the state of affairs regarding the regulations for a single year, how much more so must one contemplate the concerns of life and death?

Consequently, students become increasingly base day by day, the monastic groves fall into ruin day by day, and the disciplinary codes decline day by day, until they reach a state of decay and collapse that is nearly beyond salvation. Alas! How can this not serve as a warning?
This section states that people today compete for profit at every turn. People of the present day do not act otherwise;
they claim that seeking the Way is exceedingly circuitous and vast, difficult to apply to the immediate urgencies of food and clothing, and thus it is far more appropriate to seek wealth and profit.
Consequently, this competitive scrambling has become a habit, leading them to indulge in extravagant expenses and live with wasteful luxury.
They calculate down to the finest details of a hair’s breadth, seeking only immediate matters while failing to maintain a long-term vision.
They harbor nothing but a mind of greedy pursuit for profit and sustenance; they manage each day as it comes, yet even a constant rule for the end of the year has not been established.
How much less can there be any contemplation of the origin of life and the anxieties of death? Therefore...
The learning and insight of scholars grow increasingly base and vulgar day by day; the ritual laws of the monastic groves (conglins) decline more and more;

the regulations and commands fall into ruin daily. "Lingyi" (陵夷)—*ling* meaning to erode and *yi* meaning to level—refers to the imminent collapse of the Dharma-way, like a hill or dune gradually wearing down until it is flat.
In such a state of upheaval and wandering, it is almost impossible to save. Alas! For those with resolute wills...
Should one not examine this with a clear mirror? An ancient said: "Those who cultivate virtue are meticulous in their minor conduct;
those who plan for governance are concerned with what has not yet occurred. How much more so should this apply to birth and death, which are most grave and most urgent?
For a person to fail to value that which is truly important, while instead valuing that which is unimportant, is to be doubly deluded.
This chapter states that the essential core of the mind for studying the Way must be perfectly upright; do not allow it to fall into partiality or deviation. Shu’an said:
"In the past, while traveling to Yunju, I witnessed Gao’an’s night discourse. He declared that the direct path to the Ultimate Way does not conform to worldly sentiments.
One must possess a sincere heart and a correct intention, and must not engage in artificiality, partiality, or deviation. Artificiality leads to guile and flattery; partiality..."

If one is heterodox, then one is neither correct nor centered; thus, one is entirely at odds with the ultimate Way. I privately reflected that his words were close to the truth and proceeded to practice them with deliberate intent.
It was only upon meeting the late Master Fozhi that I attained a vast and profound realization;
only then did I feel I had not betrayed my lifelong vow to travel as a wandering monk (Letter to Yuetang).
I said: "In the past, when I was traveling on pilgrimage and arrived at Yunju, I saw High Hermit (Gao'an) Worthy’s night discourse, in which he said:
'The Ultimate Way is direct and upright; its momentum does not conform to human sentiments.

Students must study this Way with a sincere heart and a correct intention, and must not engage in pretension, falsehood, or the embellishment of partiality and private depravity. Pretension and deceit are closely related."

"Proximity [to the truth] requires that one be free from partiality and deviation, for only then can one be centered and correct. These [views] are all human sentiments that run contrary to the Ultimate Way;
thus, they do not accord with it. When I heard these words, I reflected upon them in private and found them to be profoundly reasonable.
I engraved them upon my mind and practiced them accordingly. It was only later, upon meeting the late Master Fozhi, that I first attained realization beneath a single word."
This vast and great penetration is entirely rooted in this. Only by means of this can one truly not fail the lifelong vow of traveling on pilgrimage.
One must know that applying oneself with deliberate intent is precisely the foundation for attaining great penetration and great enlightenment.
How many people, upon hearing this, simply set it aside as something irrelevant? How can they hope to penetrate it thoroughly?
This chapter warns people not to indulge in worldly desires, for fear that they will breed further faults and entanglements.
Shuian said: "When Yuet-tang served as abbot, he took the practice of the Way as his sole responsibility. He did not dispatch fundraising emissaries nor did he engage in formal visits to patrons.
Each year, the expenses for the community were used solely from what the monastery itself obtained. Many monks who were determined to serve as fundraisers were turned away by him. Someone asked:
'The Buddha's precepts for bhikṣus state that they should maintain their lives by means of the alms bowl. Why does your teacher refuse them?'"
Yuetang said: "This might have been acceptable during the time of our Buddha; however, were it practiced today, there would surely be those seeking profit who would go so far as to sell themselves.
Thus, one reflects that Yuetang’s foresight in preventing small evils before they become great was profound, clear, and far-reaching.
"His words of truth remain ringing in our ears even now. Looking at it from today’s perspective, how could it be merely a matter of self-promotion?
(Dharma Words). Chan Master Dàochāng of Yuètáng at Jìngcí Monastery in Lín’ān Prefecture was the son of the Wú family of Bǎoxī in Cháozhōu. He succeeded...
Chan Master Miaozhanhui was the fourteenth-generation descendant of Qingyuan. He was known as Master Yuetang. By nature he was upright and resolute.
During his tenure as abbot, wherever he traveled, he took the practice and propagation of the Dharma as his sole primary responsibility.

He did not dispatch fundraising emissaries nor did he visit high-ranking officials. His conduct was consistent with the fundamental principles of the school, and his words were spoken every year... [text truncated]
The sweet and savory food required [for the community] shall entirely be obtained from the permanent assets and established regulations of the monastery;
it is used according to its abundance or scarcity, whether more or less.

If there are monks who, seeing the difficulties of the monastery, wish to act as fundraisers, they are mostly discouraged and not permitted to do so. Or it may be said: The Buddha’s precepts for the bhikṣus...
"Every morning you rely on alms-begging to sustain your life; why do you, Master, reject me and refuse to accept me?
Wudeng said, "That would have been acceptable when our Buddha was alive.

To engage in such practices today, there must be those seeking personal gain who take advantage of people's deep-seated habit of greed, causing the wasteful expenditure of the faithful's generous offerings."
"To invite future suffering as a retribution—is this not causing a person to sell their own body?
It is not to benefit others, but rather to bring harm upon oneself. Therefore, I do not permit it for the sake of such conditions.
Suian remarked that because he contemplated the subtlety of Yuetang’s precautions, he sought to block the gradual encroachment of faults; this is profound and urgent, direct and clear. (Tangqiu)
Zhi said: "To dwell in security while anticipating danger, and to guard against the minute to prevent the gradual:
this was how the ancients were deeply concerned and far-sighted, guarding against potential calamities before they occurred. I have heard these words called true and authentic;
even now, they still ring in my ears. Yet, when it comes to the abbots of the monasteries today and those who solicit for donations, they employ a hundred schemes to..."
Investigate further: How could it be that one merely sells oneself? [The Master says: "Who would dare to sell a Zen practitioner?
It is only fitting to sell oneself. Yet, one does not know for what purpose the thing sold will be used. Reflect upon this, and you will naturally find a myriad of heart-stirring realizations."
This chapter shows how the ancients forgot their own persons for the sake of the Dharma, not shrinking from toil and hardship.
Shui-an said to Minister You Yanzhi: "In the past, Dayu, Ciming, Guquan, and Langye formed a group to study under Fenyang.
The region of Hedong was bitterly cold, and everyone else shrank from it; only Ciming set his mind solely upon the Way, [practicing] morning and night."

He was never indolent. Once, while sitting at night, he felt drowsy; he drew a metal awl and pricked himself, sighing, "The ancients took the matter of birth and death as so great that they neither ate nor slept.
What kind of person am I, yet I indulge in such negligence? To live without benefiting the age and to die without leaving a name for posterity—this is self-abandonment.
One day, when he took his leave to return home, Fenyang sighed and said, "Chu-yuan is now departing; my Way shall spread to the East."
(From the *Xihu Jiwen*): The Minister’s surname was You, his given name was Pou, and his courtesy name was Yanzhi. He styled himself the Layman Suichu.
He sought the Way from the Chan Master Shu’an Duan-yi. The Monk Shu’an cited the ancient masters’ sincerity in their pursuit of the Way and [spoke] to You Yanzhi.
It is said that in the past, Dayu Zhi, Cimeng Yuan, Guquan Dao, and Langye Jue formed a group to study under Chan Master Fenyang Shao.
Hedong is the region belonging to Fenzhou in Taishan. It was the dead of winter and bitterly cold;
most of the assembly were filled with dread, yet only Cimeng’s resolve and strength were profound and vast, keeping his every thought fixed on the Way day and night.
I did not dare to indulge myself or give rise to thoughts of indolence. Every night I sat in meditation, striving to investigate this Way.

Whenever I felt drowsy, I would immediately draw a needle and prick my thigh. He further lamented: "The ancients regarded the matter of birth and death as so great that when they applied themselves to it by day, they forgot their food;
when they applied themselves to it by night, they forgot their sleep. What kind of person am I?"
In talent, we fall far short of the ancients; yet we instead indulge in negligence and laxity, giving rise to a mind of heedlessness.
Consequently, during our lifetime, we derive no personal benefit, and thus contribute nothing of value to the world. This state continues until after death.
Because he had personally lacked the practice of the Way, there was nothing for later generations to hear; I am truly and deeply ashamed of this.
When the time came for his achievements to be fulfilled and he finally took leave of his teacher to depart, Fenyang sighed, saying:
"Now that Chu-yuan has departed, my Way and Dharma shall also follow him eastward. Long ago, Ding Kuan of Shandong studied the *Yi* (Book of Changes).
Regarding Tianhe: one day he took his leave to return home. Tianhe said, "My Way shall go east. [He] rode upon ten-thousand-li clouds, piercing through the waters of the great ocean;
he may truly be called one of solitary wind and peerless companion. Yet, even a thousand years later, his skeletal remains of the Way still stand with chilling majesty.
This chapter teaches that one should be sincere in conduct and must not be negligent or self-indulgent.
Shui-an said: "When the ancient worthies served as abbots, they led themselves by example to practice the Way; they never were negligent or self-indulgent.
In the past, Fenyang often lamented that in this degenerate age, students are difficult to transform. Ciming replied, 'That is very easy; the only concern is those who preside over the Dharma.'"
Fenyang said, "They were unable to guide them well. Fenyang continued, "The ancients were pure and sincere; it still took them twenty or thirty years before they achieved realization.
Ciming said, "This is not the discourse of a sage. One who skillfully cultivates the Way requires the effort of a thousand days.
Some claimed that Ciming was speaking falsely and would not listen to him.

This section states that the Way is neither difficult nor easy, but depends on the person. It says that those who served as abbots in antiquity first honored themselves by personally practicing this Way.
In all matters they were duty-bound to perform, they never acted with negligence or oversimplification, nor did they give way to self-indulgence.
In the past, Fenyang often sighed that the age of the semblance Dharma was extremely degenerate.
"Students are indeed difficult to transform," [Zhaozhou] said. Ciming replied, "It is not difficult;
what I worry about is that those who preside over the Dharma are unable to skillfully provide guidance.

Fenyang added, "Even for people of antiquity, whose natures were pure and simple and who were moreover sincere and earnest, they still required twenty-three years of effort before they could accomplish this great matter."
"How could it be easy? Ciming replied, "This is not merely the ultimate discourse of the sages and worthies.

If one is willing to exert courageous effort to investigate true practice and is capable of deeply penetrating this Way, it will take no more than a thousand days of work for one to become thoroughly proficient and well-versed in it.
Some may say that Ciming’s words are reckless, hollow, and exaggerated, and thus insufficient [to be taken seriously].
He consented to preach.
However, as the Fen region was very cold, he consequently canceled the night assembly. A certain extraordinary bhikṣu said to Fenyang, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) in this assembly;
why do you not preach the Dharma? Three years later, it indeed came to pass that six individuals attained the Way. Fenyang...
Yang once composed a verse that says: "The foreign monk with his golden staff radiating light Sought the Dharma at Fenyang. Six men became great vessels;
I entreat you to proclaim it far and wide. (Recorded in the *Xihu Jiwen* and the *Sengbao Zhuan*)
This section demonstrates that his spiritual responses were authentic and not false. Furthermore, the region of Fen was close to the north and very cold;
there were those who stood outside at night until their feet were cracked and bleeding, leading him to cancel the evening assemblies.
Suddenly, a strange bhikṣu—who was in fact a holy monk—said to Fenyang, "There are currently six great beings (mahāsattvas) within this assembly; why have you stopped the practice?"
He did not preach the Dharma. Having finished speaking, he immediately vanished. Less than three years later, there were indeed six who attained the Way:
namely, Ciming, Dayu, Langye, Guquan, Fahua Ju, and Tiansheng Tai. Fenyang once had a verse that said:
"The Central Asian monk with his golden staff’s radiance came to Fenyang to request the Dharma; six men attained greatness."
Vessel. I exhort you to spread this teaching far and wide. A lion follows the lion’s gait; an elephant follows the elephant’s stride.
How could a lame donkey ever traverse the waves and cross the sea, or gallop across the land of China?
This chapter reveals the lofty character of the master through his disciples.
When the Venerable Touzi Qing had a portrait of Shuian painted, he requested a eulogy, saying: "The Chan practitioner Qing-si is solitary and resolute, without rival."

He maintained a single fast from dawn to dusk and did not let his side touch the mat. He entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) until he transcended the inhalation and exhalation of breath. His reputation reached the Nine Palaces;

when the Emperor discussed Chan and selected virtuous monks, he was greatly pleased by him. The Emperor bestowed upon him gold and silk, but he declined three times. The Sovereign then praised him with admiration.
A true man of the Way! Though plants and trees blaze with brilliance, they have transmitted this humble form of mine. I offer incense and request a eulogy;
this is truly what is meant by "the green comes from the indigo, yet it is greener than the indigo" (as seen in the portrait).
Chan Master Yiqing of Mount Touzi in Shu Prefecture was the dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanyi of Shuian;
he belonged to the seventeenth generation under Nanyue. He painted a portrait of Master Shuian and requested a eulogy for it. Shuian’s eulogy read: "Chan Master Qing is my dharma heir.
His solitary fortitude is such that no one in the world can rival him. Every day, he does nothing but..."
He observed a single fast and took no further food. His side never touched his mat; he sat only in a motionless, upright posture.

He entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and became detached from inhalation and exhalation, demonstrating the profundity of his absorption. If there were still inhalation and exhalation within that meditative concentration, it would not be called "deep concentration.
His fame reached the ninefold palace—the residence of the Son of Heaven, which has nine layers—where he was discussed in terms of his mastery of *dhyāna*.
"Selecting Virtue" (Xuande) refers to being summoned into Xuande Hall to inquire about the Way. The Emperor’s countenance was greatly pleased, and he bestowed upon him gold and silk.
If a gift was conferred, he accepted it without considering himself superior; yet he declined three times with vigor. The Sovereign then praised him with admiration.
"Sovereign" (Shang) is the title used for all rulers; here it refers to Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty. He admired Touzi as a true [master].
O Daoist Master, by the single word of the Son of Heaven, not only does the Dharma-gate possess good fortune, but it has caused even the grasses and trees to soar forth in brilliance and emit light.
You have transmitted this to my humble person and again burned incense to request my encomium; I find no place for my words to alight.
One such as you is what is called "blue emerging from the indigo plant," yet the blue surpasses that of the plant itself.
[Also from] the "Encouragement to Learning" chapter of the *Xunzi*: "The color blue is dyed from indigo, yet its hue is deeper than the indigo itself.
A disciple who studies without ceasing surpasses his teacher; this is the case where a later sage excels a former sage.
△ One who is skilled at speech—what is called "entering the room and wielding the enemy's halberd, requiring no further effort"—such a style of writing is the very best.
It is not easily obtained.
This chapter states that benefiting sentient beings depends entirely on obtaining the right person; it cannot be accomplished by one's own power alone.
Shui-an said: "Master Fozhi once related that Dongshan Yanzu told Chancellor Geng Longxue: 'This mountain monk...'"
There was Yuanwu, who was like fish having water or birds having wings. Thus, the Prime Minister, Layman Ziyuan, praised him, saying:
"The mutual compatibility between teacher and disciple is rare to encounter in a single lifetime; as for their bond from beginning to end, who could ever intervene?
Layman Ziyuan may truly be called one who knows how to speak.
This section clarifies the harmonious union between teacher and disciple. Master Fozhi Xianshi said: "The Patriarch Dongshan once told Chancellor Geng Longxue:
'I, this mountain monk, have Yuanwu; it is like fish having water, or birds having wings. This reveals the mutual trust found in his acquisition of such a person.
There is a compatibility like that of water and milk, or a needle and a grain of mustard seed—just as fish have water."
This refers to when Liu Xuande obtained the Marquis of Wuhou (Zhuge Liang), both Yunchang (Guan Yu) and Yide (Zhang Fei) were displeased.
Xuande said, "My having Kongming is like a fish having water. I hope you will not speak of this again. He spoke thus to honor Kongming and to enlighten the two men.
Prime Minister Zhang Jun, whose courtesy name was De-yuan and sobriquet Ziyuan Jushi, [lived during the] Shao...
At the beginning of the Xing era, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of He. He sought the Way from Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin, for whom he once composed a eulogy, saying:

"In general, when a teacher and disciple are able to attain mutual resonance through their respective characteristics, and their transmission and reception correspond, it may be called a rare encounter of a thousand years, one not met often, like the simultaneous appearance of clouds and dragons, or wind and tigers. From beginning to end, they were in perfect accord.
One's fixed and inherent lot—who could possibly obstruct it? The words of Layman Ziyuan may indeed be called "words that know the person.
Regarding the term *shizi* (teacher-disciple): a teacher is a model for others, a leader among people, and a standard for instructing all things.
A disciple (*zi*) means "to assist"; it refers to assisting in the development of one’s own practice and conduct. Furthermore, the teacher transmits the Way.
Regarding disciples: a disciple studies under a teacher; this does not mean they are merely master and servant.
Lately, I have observed that venerable elders in various regions employ crafty schemes to manage their novices, while the novices exploit power and profit to serve those elders.
When host and guest trade benefits and superiors and subordinates engage in mutual deception, how can the Dharma-gate flourish or the monastic communities (saṃghārāma) thrive?
(In a letter to Mei Shan Run).

This section clarifies that those above and below deceive one another. "Bi" means "to reach" or "to encounter. It refers to encountering various venerable masters of the quarters who employ clever mental tactics to manage their disciples (*nàzǐ*).
"Yù" means "to employ" or "to use. Yet, what the disciples themselves possess is nothing but power and profit.
By serving one's seniors, one ensures that all those with whom the host and guest interact are benefited;
yet when those above and below harbor mutual deceit, how can the Dharma-gate flourish or the monastic communities (conglins) thrive?
Where teacher and disciple are in accord, there is a power that cannot be split even by swords or axes; if those above and below practice deception and insult, [the lineage will perish].
That he did not lose his mind and turned his back on principle is sufficient; how could there have been such a profound accord as this?
This chapter cites the ancients to teach their sons that honoring the Way and saving the world are the most urgent tasks.

Shuian said: "To move others through words, one must ensure they are sincere and earnest. If the words are not sincere and earnest, what is felt will necessarily be shallow; who would be willing to harbor such [teachings]?
Formerly, when Master Baoyun sent the Master to reside at Shimian, he exhorted him, saying: 'The ancestral Way is in decline, as precarious as stacked eggs.
Do not indulge in negligence or dissipation, nor waste your time, thereby ruining your supreme virtue. You must be broad-minded and tolerant.'"

To measure the situation, benefit all beings, and sustain the community, one upholds this matter to repay the kindness of the Buddhas and patriarchs. At that time, who among those who heard it would not have been moved to grief?
This section speaks with such clarity and urgency that it can stir people; let alone the leader, how could anyone fail to be moved?
It is said: "Words must be noble, true, essential, and appropriate. If words are not true, essential, and appropriate, then even if they can move others, they will surely be superficial;
who would then be willing to cherish and admire them? Long ago, when Master Baiyun sent Master Yan to reside at Simian, he earnestly entrusted him with these instructions, saying:
"The ancestral Way is in decline. To say it is in decline means it is withering away.

This is failure. Its peril is truly like stacking eggs. When Duke Ling of Jin was constructing a nine-story tower that remained unfinished after three years, his minister Xun Xi remonstrated, saying, "I am able to stack twelve chess pieces and further place nine eggs upon them.
The Duke said, "That would be perilous! Xun Xi replied, "It is not perilous. The Duke then proceeded to build a nine-story tower.
If this continues for three years without success, men will not plow and women will not weave; the peril will be extreme. Upon hearing this, the Duke stopped [the practice].

"Mu" means "do not. It signifies that one must by no means allow the mind to run wild, thereby neglecting the Way and indulging in licentious conduct, thus vainly wasting time and inevitably ruining one's own supreme virtue.
Furthermore, one should instead employ a broad and magnanimous capacity to embrace [others].

"O assembly, to benefit others and preserve others is truly of the utmost urgency. To constantly maintain this one great matter and repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—this is my vow.
When the Ancestor thus gave these instructions, who among those present at that time was not moved and did not grieve for him with deep longing?

That you were summoned for an audience in the Imperial Court yesterday was truly a blessing for the Dharma-gate. You must earnestly humble yourself and honor the Way, making the salvation of others your primary concern.
You must not boast of your own virtues or belittle others. The sages of antiquity were modest, gentle, reverent, and cautious;

they preserved their persons and perfected their virtue, not regarding power or status as a source of glory. Thus they were able to stir purity in their time and leave a legacy of beauty for ten thousand generations. I am concerned that—
The time remaining is not long; we shall no longer meet face to face. Therefore, I entrust this to you most earnestly (as seen in the *Touzi Shu*).
This section demonstrates that his virtue was perfected and he was able to benefit all beings. What follows are the words of Master Shui-an to Touzi:
"Yesterday, you were summoned by the Sagely Son of Heaven for an audience in the Imperial Court. The 'Imperial Court' refers to the North Star of the Son of Heaven..."
This is truly a fortunate event for the Dharma-gate. You must certainly humble yourself and honorably practice this Way, making it your primary aim to benefit others and rescue all beings.
You must not boast of yourself or rely upon your own status and influence.
Observe the virtuous predecessors of old: who among them was not humble, gentle, and reverent, thereby preserving their person and perfecting their virtue?
Although the sages of old held positions of power and rank, they did not consider themselves honorable or illustrious for that reason.

This is why they were able to leave a pure reputation resounding through their own era and a beautiful name disseminated for ten thousand generations. Are they not, indeed, great men who achieve both the beginning and the end?
I am old now, like the morning star or the moon at dawn; I fear my remaining light will not last long. I dread that—
Since there will be no further opportunity for us to meet face-to-face, I have thus earnestly charged you with this.

△ A single tongue of the Perfected One is the wondrous medicine that transforms the ordinary into the sacred. When it speaks of the ultimate truth and reality, it involuntarily causes one’s heart to feel as if washed by water.
This chapter features Chen Gu, whose innate character was extraordinary. He took the practice of the Way and its establishment as his core purpose.
Shui’an was youthful yet bold and unconventional; he possessed great ambition and esteemed integrity. He did not engage in frivolous luxury nor adhere to petty formalities.

His mind was as vast and deep as a mountain gorge; he followed righteousness even at the cost of his own life. Though calamities and harms converged before him, he showed no sign of dejection or distress. He resided at—
He presided over eight monasteries and traveled through four prefectures; wherever he went, he was cautious and reverent, making the establishment of the Way his primary concern.
In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he retired to Jingci Monastery on West Lake, where he composed this verse: "For six years I have swept and cleansed the imperial capital temple;
The rubble has been transformed into the palaces of Śakra and Brahmā. Today the palace is complete and I depart; From the tip of my staff, a pure wind rises from all eight directions."
The officials and commoners blocked his path, trying to detain him, but he would not stop. When the small boat reached Tianning Monastery in Xiuzhou, he soon fell ill;

bidding farewell to the assembly, he passed away (as recorded in his *Xingshi*). "Tidang" means outstanding and extraordinary; it refers to one who is refined, generous, and carefree without worldly constraints. This describes Shuian.
When the Master was young in years, he was already capable of acting with such self-assurance and magnanimity that he appeared entirely composed.

From birth, he possessed far-reaching and lofty ambitions, and he was further able to maintain a high standard of integrity. He did not concern himself with superficial refinement, nor did he scrutinize the slightest detail.
His breast and mind are vast and expansive, like a high embankment or a deep valley; they cannot be fathomed or measured. *Xun* means to follow.
He follows righteousness solely with his person; even if extreme calamities and harms assail him from before, he shows no sign of dejection or distress.
The *Ruxing* chapter states: "He does not become dejected or distressed by poverty and low station. The commentary notes: "It is like the shedding of bamboo sheaths (*tu*)."
Yet they drift and scatter, like grain that has been harvested and withered. Furthermore, "to perish" (*yun*) is as if falling; "to harvest" (*huo*) is as if being reaped.
This is the appearance of one who is distressed, constrained, and has lost their resolve. [He] presided over monasteries in eight locations.
Having traveled through and transformed the four prefectures, wherever he went, he never failed to maintain a sense of profound vigilance and earnestness as he practiced the Way and taught others.
It was his primary responsibility to establish monastic centers (*conglin*). In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he retired from Jingci Monastery on West Lake.
Ascending the hall, he spoke this verse: "For six years I have swept and cleaned the Imperial City temple; The rubble and debris have been overturned."
The palaces of Śakra and Brahmā were completed; today, as the palaces are finished, he returns. From the eight facets at the head of his staff, a pure breeze arises.
Though the officials and commoners earnestly sought to block him and detain him, they could not stop him. He then traveled by small boat to Tianning Temple in Xiushui County, Jiaxing.
Not long after, he manifested illness, took leave of the assembly, and passed away. (The remains of the wise man and noble gentleman.)
Every joint of his head is fragrant; standing before others, he causes them to admire him incessantly until their saliva dries up in their throats.
This chapter teaches that students should follow the ritual laws of the former sages and must not act according to their own whims or transgress the prescribed boundaries.

Master Gattō Shō said: "In the past, the Great Wisdom Master (Dazhi Chanshi), concerned that monks in the末法 (mofa) age would become arrogant and indolent, specifically established rules and regulations to prevent this.
According to their capacities and abilities, he assigned specific offices to each. The abbot resided in the *zhàngshì* (private quarters), while the assembly resided in the *tōngtáng* (common hall).
He arranged ten administrative bureaus headed by senior officers, making them as solemn as a government office. Those in superior positions oversaw the broad outlines of the administration."

Those of lower capacity manage the various branches so that the upper and lower parts support one another, just as the body directs the arms and the arms direct the fingers, such that none fail to follow.
This is why the predecessors have followed and upheld [the tradition], serving it with earnest devotion;
it is because the legacy of the former sages has not yet vanished.
This section clarifies that former masters followed this practice without deviation.

It is said that in the past, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang constantly worried that people of the末法 (mofa) age would be prone to arrogance, luxury, and indolence; how then could they achieve the unsurpassed, wondrous Way?
Therefore, he specifically formulated rules and regulations to serve as a bulwark against such tendencies, according to the capacity and talent of each individual.
Each was assigned a specific task to take charge of. The presiding master resided in the Abbot’s Quarters (fangzhang), while the community resided collectively in the Hall.
Among the assembly, ten head officials (shoudu) were appointed to oversee various departments, namely the two Head Seats (shouzuo) of the two halls.

The Secretary, the Librarian, the Guest Master, the General Manager, the Abbot’s Assistant, the Vice-Abbot, the Rector, and the Chief Cook—each shall perform their respective duties with strict discipline and solemnity, as if the state possessed a rigorous system of law.
The presiding master sits above, upholding the great principles; this is the law. The officers of duty sit below.
To organize the various categories of the community is the matter of administrative affairs.
It ensures that those above and below receive one another in succession, just as the body directs the arms and the arms direct the fingers, such that all are governed and follow one another.
This was the original foundation established by Baizhang. Subsequently, his predecessors have continued to uphold the models he formulated and the ritual laws he established.
There are none who do not treat it with reverent awe and carry it upon their heads, nor fail to wear it upon their hearts with earnest devotion and put it into practice.
All of this is due to the transformational influence bequeathed by the former sages, which still persists and has not yet been extinguished.

Recently, I have observed that the monastic communities are in decline. Those who study prize versatile talent while disparaging those who maintain their integrity; they esteem the superficial and the ornate while slighting the genuine and the simple.

Day by day and month by month, things gradually sink into a state of moral corruption. At first, people merely seek a temporary ease, but as this habit becomes long-established, they come to regard it as the natural order of things.
They do not consider it unrighteous, nor do they consider it contrary to principle. Even those in positions of authority remain apprehensive.
Yet they fear those below them. Those below watch their superiors with wide-eyed suspicion. In ordinary times, they use sweet words and humble postures to flatter and please them;
when they find an opportunity, they employ a cruel heart and deceitful schemes to slaughter and deceive one another. The victor is deemed wise, while the vanquished is called a fool;
no further account is taken of the order of rank or the principles of right and wrong. Once the other has done this, then this person...
They imitated it. Once those below had spoken of it, those above followed; once those before had practiced it, those who came after inherited it. Alas!

Had it not been for the Master of Sages, who, through his power of vows, accumulated merit for a hundred years, its evils would surely have remained unaltered and could not have been reformed. (Letter to the Monk Shun)

This section cites contemporary corruptions where people indulge their passions and violate reason. From what I have observed in monasteries recently, the Way has declined and the Dharma has been supplanted;
those who study take mere proficiency in talent and learning as precious, while they regard the maintenance of integrity and righteousness as base and lowly.
That which is revered and esteemed is empty vanity and ornate display; that which is slighted and disparaged is genuine simplicity.

Through this, day by day and month by month, they gradually become unaware as they enter a state of decadence. "Decadence" (*jiāo*) means to pour water; "corruption" (*lí*) means water seeping into the earth.

At first, it did not go beyond the mutual theft of peace between superiors and subordinates for the duration of a single moment. Yet, once they became familiar with and indulged in [such practices]...
Having long been accustomed to such practices, they instead claim that principle dictates it must be so;

they believe that while a person’s talent and insight must necessarily be comprehensive, their integrity and righteousness need not be maintained. Ultimately, they fail to realize that such conduct is neither righteous nor rational.

"Chui-chui" (惴惴) means anxiety. Those in superior positions, being preoccupied with petty gain and seeking only immediate ease, constantly harbor feelings of distress and resentment out of fear that those below them will scrutinize them.

"Kui-kui" (睽睽) is the manner of squinting or looking askance. Those in subordinate positions, likewise preoccupied with petty gain and acting against their own conscience, constantly engage in spying and peeping to await any lapse or flaw on the part of those above them. When there is leisure... [text ends]
At the time of their dealings, they employ sweet words and pleasant speech, lowering their countenances and bowing their bodies to flatter and curry favor.
Yet, after a short interval behind one's back, they harbor wolfish hearts and crafty schemes to butcher and plunder. "Butcher" (*tu*) refers to slaughtering;
"plunder" (*jue*) refers to killing—both carry the sense of plotting harm. If there is anything they can accomplish in their affairs, they immediately claim it as their own.
The worthy, if they happen to deviate slightly from propriety in a matter, are immediately labeled "fools.

Thus, one ultimately fails to inquire into the order of people according to their rank—whether noble or base—and their wisdom or folly, nor the principles of right and wrong, or good and evil, regarding their actions.
Once one person has acted in such a manner, those who follow will inevitably imitate them. When those in subordinate positions have already spoken such reckless words...
This is chaotic speech. Those in superior positions ultimately follow one another and do not dare to disobey;

those who come before initiate the practice, and those who follow merely imitate it, none of them examining whether it accords with principle or reason. Alas! Such is the state of affairs at this time.

Were it not for a virtuous and holy teacher who, by virtue of great vows from previous lives, further accumulates the transformative merit of a hundred years, one could only enter the Way through conversion and guidance;
otherwise, their depravity and stubbornness would be so entrenched that they could not be reformed.
△ The lingering influence has declined and perished, leaving chaos and ruin everywhere; from the highest to the lowest, all resort to mere empty formalities.
Adorning one's appearance while living together—how could this restore the regulations of the former sages?
This chapter demonstrates that the transmission and reception [of the Dharma] are not undertaken lightly; it shows the gravity with which they treat the Way.
Master Yuetang resided at Jingci for the longest time. Some have said, "The Master has practiced the Way for years, yet we have not heard of anyone [attaining realization] under his guidance."

"Disciple, have you not attained the wondrous and profound stillness? Yuetang did not answer. On another day, the disciple spoke of this again, and Yuetang said, "Have you not heard of the man of old who planted melons?
His love for them was so intense that during the midday sun of the height of summer, he would water them."

Before long, the melons withered and perished. Why was this? It was not that their love for them was not diligent; however, they watered them at the wrong times, which was precisely what caused their ruin.

Likewise, when elders of various quarters take up novices under their guidance, they do not examine whether the novices' spiritual practice is internally full or whether their talent and capacity are vast and far-reaching;
they merely desire to hasten their maturation as persons. Yet, when their character and virtue are scrutinized, they are found to be depraved and defiled.
If one examines his words and deeds, they are perverse and contrary; if one deems him upright and impartial, he proves to be sycophantic and deceitful.

Is this not perhaps because my affection for him has exceeded its proper measure? This is truly like watering a melon at midday. Fearing deeply that those who possess true insight might laugh at me, I have refrained from doing so (from the *Beishan Jiwen*).
It is said that Master Yuetang resided at Jingci for many years, yet there had been no successor to carry on the Dharma lineage.
Someone asked him, "Master, you have practiced the Way for many years, yet we have not heard of any disciple under your guidance who has received transmission and inherited the fundamental tenets.
Is this not a failure to honor Master Miaozhan? This was Master Miaozhan Sijian of Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
Chan Master Hui was the son of the Yu family of Qiantang. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yunshan Shenben of the Qingyuan lineage, the thirteenth generation from [National Teacher] Huairang.
Once, he spoke to Yuetang, who did not respond. On another day, he spoke of it again, and Yuetang said, "Do you not recall that in the past there was a man who planted melons?
He loved them so dearly that he wished for them to ripen quickly. During the height of summer... (The text ends here).
During the month of July, at the time of extreme heat, if one irrigates [the melons] at midday, those melons will not only fail to grow quickly but will also flourish [only to perish];
before they can even take a step forward, the melons become mired, ruined, and withered. Why is this?
Although the love [with which they care for them] is not lacking in diligence, because the irrigation is untimely, it serves only to bring about the opposite result.
This leads to failure and ruin. It is the same with the elder masters of various quarters today as they nurture and guide their disciples;
they do not consider whether the other’s virtue, wisdom, merit, and insight are sufficient, nor do they regard whether his talent, intelligence, and capacity are far-reaching and great.
They merely desire to force him to emerge and become a man as quickly as possible. By the time he finally makes his appearance—
If one examines his morality, it is licentious, depraved, and foul beyond endurance; if one scrutinizes his words and deeds, they are perverse, contradictory, and improper.
To speak of him as being upright and impartial is actually to describe one who is private, wicked, sycophantic, and shameless.
Everything about him is thus entirely hollow and superficial—is this not because one’s affection for him has exceeded its proper bounds?
This is exactly like the case of one who attempts to water melons at midday; it is no different. I fear deeply that I shall be ridiculed by those who possess true knowledge.
Therefore, I do not engage in such a matter of false and delusional transmission. △ It is impossible to cast [the seal] in gold.
It is not that brocade and embroidery are unsuitable; rather, what else could be used? Simply these four characters suffice for selection:
Virtue, Way, Speech, and Conduct.
This chapter reveals how the ancients revered their teachers and esteemed the Way, reaching the height of utmost sincerity.
Yuet Tang said: "When Huanglong resided at Jicui, he was confined by illness for three months and did not come out.

Zhenjing prayed earnestly night and day, even to the point of burning his crown and cauterizing his arm, looking upward to pray for divine assistance. Hearing this, Huanglong rebuked him, saying, 'Life and death are surely my own lot;
yet you, who practice Chan, have failed to grasp the principle to such an extent. Zhenjing replied composedly, 'The monastic community may well do without me...'"
"Kewen, one cannot do without a *upādhyāya*. Those who understand him say that Zhenjing respected his teacher and honored the Dharma;
his sincerity reaches such a point that he will surely become a great vessel in the future" (*Beishan Jiwen*).
This refers to when Master Huanglong was residing at Jicui. He had been ill for three months without recovery and had not yet emerged from his quarters.
At midnight, Zhenjing went before the Triple Gem and prayed with such sincerity that he even burned incense upon the crown of his head.
He held a lamp between his arms as an offering, praying with uplifted devotion that the Master’s divine power might secretly provide assistance so that the Master’s illness would be cured;
for if the Master were to recover, the Dharma would have something upon which to rely. When Huanglong heard of this, he rebuked him, saying: "Birth and death are indeed my fixed lot;
how could they possibly be avoided? You are a monk who practices Chan, yet you do not even understand the fundamental principles—how can you reach such a state?"
Zhenjing responded with composure: "In a monastic community, one may be without a 'self' to establish the written records, but one must certainly not be without a *ho-shang*.

The intent behind offering prayers is that upon which the source of the Dharma depends. Those who understand remarked that Zhenjing’s reverence for his teacher and gravity toward the Dharma reached such a point of sincerity;
thus, it goes without saying that he would one day become a vessel of great capacity. △ This.
Such matters cannot be brought about by the influence of others; they must all arise from sincerity and faith.
Alas, how painful it is that the contemporary heart of revering one’s teacher and honoring the Dharma has, for the most part, collapsed like a crashing wave and fallen into ruin!
This chapter speaks of treating others with utmost sincerity, so that the Way proceeds of its own accord. Yuetai said:
"The Imperial Historian Huang Luzu once remarked that Chan Master Huanglong Nan possessed a profound and vast capacity that was not swayed by external circumstances.
Throughout his life, he was free from artifice; among his disciples, there were none who ever saw him display joy."
As for those who are angry: even toward those who serve as messengers or laborers, he treated them all with sincerity.

Thus, he was able to give rise to the Way of Compassionate Clarity without raising a sound or a breath; this was no mere pretense (according to one edition, this is seen on a stone inscription at Huanglong).
The Layman of the Mountain Valley once said: "Master Huanglong’s vessel was deep and unfathomable; his measure was vast and all-embracing.
He was not moved or altered by any external phenomena. Throughout his entire life, he acted without pretension or artifice.
Among the disciples who resided with him for a long time, there were those who never saw their teacher display either joy or anger."
As for those who possessed such a character, even toward those who served as messengers or laborers, he treated them all with a sincere heart, never harboring a dual intention.
Therefore, without making any outward show of voice or demeanor, he naturally caused the Way and Dharma of Ciming to flourish.
How could this have been achieved through mere expediency or in vain? △ Huang Taishi recounts the story of Master Huanglong.
The record of his life’s conduct is much like Mount Sumeru; it remains unshakable.
Thus, from antiquity until the present day, it continues to cause people to feel a mixture of deep admiration and shame.
This passage shows that the ancients did not act with duplicity when facing peril, regarding death as returning home.
Yuetang said: On the Shangsi day of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era, Zhong Xiang rebelled in Liyang.
Chan Master Wenshu Dao was beset by this calamity. As the rebels' power grew formidable and his disciples fled, the Master said, "Can disaster be avoided? He then stood firm.
Nevertheless, while staying in his small chamber, he was ultimately killed by bandits.
This section clarifies that when a master encounters peril, it cannot be avoided. It was the *Shangji* (Upper Third) day of the *Jiyou* year of the Jianyan era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty;
*Shangji* refers to the third day of the third lunar month. Zhong Xiang was the name of the bandit leader. This occurred in the fifth year of the Shaoxing era at Dongting Lake.
Hu Zhong rose in rebellion, styling himself the Heavenly Emperor, Great King. He brought suffering and ruin upon the people until he was defeated and killed by the troops of Zhang Jun.
Liyang—referring to Liyang Prefecture in Changde, Huguang—was where Chan Master Wenshu Dao was beset by hardship.
In the spring of the third year of the Jianyan era, the Master addressed the assembly, citing Linji’s final instructions before his passing to his three disciples.

The "Holy Circumstances" (Sheng Yinyuan) states: "The treasury of the true Dharma-eye has been extinguished by the blind donkey. Where did Linji ever say such a thing? People of all times, past and present, have all falsely transmitted this.
Do not believe it; simply wait and see after three months. Indeed, when the third month of the following year arrived—
When Zhong Xiang’s troops arrived, his disciples wished to flee south with their master. The Master said, "The purpose of studying the Way is to bring an end to birth and death;
why should one seek to avoid it? *Yi* means resolute and decisive. The Master then remained steadfastly in his chamber. Shortly thereafter, the rebels arrived.
The Master said, "Let me be killed quickly so that you may satisfy your desires. The rebels raised their spears and stabbed him.
The blood all turned into white milk. The bandits were greatly alarmed;
they covered it with their mats and departed. The layman Vimala inscribed this Dharma discourse upon it, saying: "Now, to love life and fear death is the common sentiment of humanity.
Only the Perfected One realizes that [life] is fundamentally unarisen; thus, though living, he has nothing to love. He penetrates the fact that [death] has never ceased; thus, though dying,"
He was fearless; thus, even when facing the calamities of death and rebirth, he did not waver from his principles. Should one not take him as a model?

He took the teacher’s moral virtue, integrity, and righteousness as his own, sufficient to transform the monastic community and provide a paradigm for future generations. The Master’s name was Zhengdao;
he was a native of Danling in Meizhou and a successor of Fojian (according to one version, this is seen in the *Record of the Great Master Hui of Mount Lu*).
This section judges that the master’s integrity must surely serve as a model. The layman Vimala appended these words of Dharma:
"Now, to love life and loathe death is the common sentiment of worldly people; however, only those who have realized the ultimate truth understand that they are fundamentally unborn.
Though they live, there is in fact nothing to love; they penetrate the fact that they are fundamentally unceasing, and though they die, there is in fact..."
Being fearless, he was able to face the calamities of death and rebirth;
even when a white blade was pressed against his body, he never wavered from the path he upheld. Master Dao is precisely such a person.
The moral integrity and sense of righteousness maintained throughout his life are sufficient to edify the monastic community and serve as a model for future generations.
World, how much more so this final segment of divine traces? The Master’s name was Zhengdao;
he was a native of the Xu clan of Danling in Meizhou and a successor of Fojian. △ It is said: "Calamity should be avoided by seeking refuge"—this is the风范 (fengfan:
exemplary conduct) of a gentleman. It is also said: "Calamity cannot be avoided"—this is the 作略 (zuolüe: strategic resolve) of a man of stature. As the Master said:
"You shall soon be put to death; let your heart's desire be fulfilled. Thus, he regarded his own body as firmly like a floating cloud and viewed death as equal to a child’s play.
This sufficiently demonstrates that the efficacy of studying the Way is such as this.
This chapter speaks of the masters of the original school who are exceptionally capable of diagnosing the ailments of others and enabling them to attain the Way.
Master Xinwen Ben said: "Among the practitioners of the patched robe, many fall ill because of Zen. There are those whose illness resides in their ears and eyes."
Those with a malady in their eyes take staring with raised brows, baring their teeth, tilting their ears, and nodding their heads as Zen.

Those with a malady in their mouths and tongues take gibberish, inverted speech, and wild, chaotic shouting as Zen. Those with a malady in their hands and feet take stepping forward and retreating, pointing east and scratching west as Zen.
Those with a malady in their hearts and bellies take the exhaustion of the profound and the investigation of the subtle, transcending emotion and departing from views, as Zen.
Regarding Chan: to speak according to reality, there is nothing that is not a sickness.
Zen Master Xīnwén Tánbēn of Wànnián Temple in Tàizhōu was a native of Yǒngjiā and succeeded Zen Master Jièchén of Yùwáng.
He belonged to the sixteenth generation under Nányuè. The Governor of Sìmíng invited the Master to preside over Xuědòu.
The Master took his leave with a verse, saying: "In the noisy monastery, we were just beginning to find respite; But now the drum has been struck and will not cease.
Do not take the thousand-fathom snow of Milk Peak To trade once more for my pair of eyes. This section speaks of the lack of authenticity in cultivating the Way.
One day, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Nowadays, practitioners of the patched robe, because they study Chan, instead end up..."
Sick people are extremely numerous. There is a certain type of person whose illness lies in their ears and eyes;

they stare with furrowed brows and bulging eyes, tilt their heads and nod, and with these few clumsy antics, they immediately claim to be "emitting light and shaking the earth" at the gates of the six sense faculties.
They take this to be Chan. There are those with a sickness in their mouths and tongues who, using inverted speech and nonsensical talk, shouting "Hu-he" and "Luan-he" at random, deceive the ignorant.
They claim that saying "this thing" is the severing of entanglements and is the most direct pointing; they take this to be Chan.
There are those with a sickness in their hands and feet who, by stepping forward and retreating, pointing east and marking west, immediately call it—
It does not pass through the throat, lips, or mouth; this unconventional family style is what they take to be Chan.
Those who have an ailment in their hearts and bellies take the exhaustion of the profound and the investigation of the subtle, transcending emotion and departing from views, as their practice.

They immediately close their eyes and concern themselves only with forming conceptions within the ghost cave, claiming that to be free from characteristics and names is Chan. If one were to rely on the truth...
In truth, from the perspective of the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) indicated by the Buddhas and Patriarchs, all such [conceptualizations] are collectively termed "illnesses.
Only a master of the authentic school (zongshi), perceiving the subtle nuances with clarity, knows through direct observation whether one has attained realization or not upon entering the gate.

Having distinguished between those who have arrived and those who have not, one then employs a single point of piercing and a single thrust to strip away all lingering attachments, to strike at all stagnations, to verify what is true and what is false, and to determine what is substantial and what is empty;

yet one must not cling to a single expedient means or remain ignorant of adaptive transformation, ensuring that the practitioner ultimately treads the path of peace, joy, and non-action before finally resting. (From the *Shilu*).

This section clarifies that the true teacher is not deceptive. Only those who are authentic masters of the school and possess the clear eye of the Way can, by themselves, discern with clarity at the most subtle and minute level.

As soon as they meet him, they immediately understand whether he is one who understands or one who does not. The moment he enters the gate, they can distinguish and know whether this is one who has arrived home.
For those who have not yet reached the destination, one must subsequently strike a single blow at their painful spot and apply a sharp probe to their depths for those who have not yet met or arrived.

This shall cause the lingering, continuous entanglements to be cast off all at once, and the stubborn, unresolved stagnations to be fully exposed and driven out. Furthermore, one must verify whether what has been attained is true or false.
One must ascertain whether the practice being undertaken is genuine or false. If it is not so, one must employ other skillful means;
it is not a matter of stubbornly adhering to a single method while remaining oblivious to the adaptive flexibility required for benefiting others.
Ultimately, one must ensure that students tread upon the realm of peace and ease, the field of great rest and repose, before ceasing; only then is it the true essence.
This is the master’s strategic method for saving others. △ To apply a remedy while being bound by fixed rules is undoubtedly like killing a person.

One must observe what kind of person it is, what kind of illness they have received, what kind of prescription is required, and what kind of medicine to administer; only then is one a skilled physician.
However, although illnesses are inexhaustible, medicines are likewise infinite. To employ the "Fragrant Su Powder" (Xiangsu San) as the sole remedy is by no means the skillful hand of a physician.
This treatise teaches people to diligently study and accumulate virtue; its fundamental principle is to discard the hollow and embrace the substantial.
Xinwen said: "The ancients said that the most outstanding among a thousand people is called an 'Eminent' (ying), and the most eminent among ten thousand people is called a 'Heroic' (jie).
If a monk possesses wisdom and conduct renowned throughout the monastic community, is he not one who approximates such an Eminent or Heroic person?

Provided that he can diligently investigate with earnestness, discard the empty to grasp the real, and each attain their own function, then regardless of whether the monastery is large or small, or the assembly numerous or few, all shall follow [this path]."
This transformation has occurred.

This section states that in selecting people, one must recognize their sincerity. The ancients said: "Only when the refined vital energy (*qi*) of a thousand people is accumulated within a single individual can one be called an 'Eminent' (*ying*);
only when the talents of ten thousand people are accumulated within a single person can one be called a 'Heroic' (*jie*). All..."
When a patch-robed monk gains a reputation for wisdom and virtuous conduct that is heard throughout the monastic communities, is he not one who approaches the caliber of a heroic and eminent person?
It simply depends on his ability to cast away what is false and preserve what is real;
then each person’s wisdom and conduct can be applied as they are attained. If this is so, it matters not whether the monastery is large or small, nor does it matter the size of the assembly.
To whatever extent they may differ, all can be transformed by following this teaching.
In the past, there was Bai Ding of Fengxue, Niu Lan of Yaoshan, Damei of Master Chang, and Jingchu of Ciming.
At such times, if those who were merely idle commoners had sought [the truth] based on rank or appearance, they would have surely looked upon these men with disdain.
Once they occupy the teacher’s seat and ascend the lotus throne, surrounded by ten thousand fingers, they illuminate the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs for this degenerate age;
who among the monastic communities would not bow before their influence?

How much more so when our predecessors, possessing such magnificent talent and heroic spirit, were yet able to remain humble during their unmet times, enduring shame and defilement while blending with the world like waves upon the sea.
If this is so, how much more so for those of lower status?
This section clarifies that, as it is not the proper time [for such actions], one ought to maintain self-restraint. Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue was a native of the Liu clan of Yuhang in Qiantang;
he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huiyong of Nanyuan and belongs to the seventh generation under Nanyue. "Baiding" is the name of his local place.
In Yingzhou, there were many commoners. Due to the chaos of banditry, Fengxue lived in seclusion for several years, and no one knew of him.
Niulankou is the name of a mountain located to the northeast of Yanjing; Yaoshan lived in seclusion here.
Chan Master Fachang was the son of the Zheng family of Xiangyang. After meeting Mazu, he lived in seclusion seventy li south of Ning County. The Great [Mountain].
Meishan. Before Chiming emerged in the world, he was lodging his traces among the regions of Jing and Chu.
At that time, when these four elders had not yet met their destiny, ordinary people of the world who saw them regarded them as nothing more than common teachers.
If one sought them by their status, they were still at the stage of a student; if one took them by their appearance, they seemed merely ordinary.
People generally treat such a person with neglect and arrogance; "yí" (詒) here means arrogance.

Yet, one day, when the dragon and devas push him forth, he occupies the master’s seat and ascends the precious *padmavikrāmin* throne, surrounded by ten thousand fingers [of disciples], manifesting and clarifying the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This is the "later age," which refers to the *mappō* (the final dharma). At the juncture of this final dharma, he erects the great banner of radiant light. All...

Throughout the monastic forests, who would not bow down at the mere sight of his reputation? Moreover, the predecessors all possessed talents that were magnificent, extraordinary, and grand—*guī* being synonymous with *guāi*;
*guāng-guī* ranks just below jade. Furthermore, they were *wěi*: "extraordinary" meaning both marvelous and great—and moreover, they possessed the spirit and bearing of heroic excellence.
This is what is meant by saying "Heaven has sent forth such a person," yet even so, amidst the common crowd...
Even when they have not yet met with fortune, they constantly bear the shame of others and endure the defilements of others;
they mingle with the human world, flowing along with its currents in this manner—how much more so those who are below them?
Alas! The past is like the present; this is like that. If one must wait for those such as Yaoshan and Fengxue before taking them as masters, they are encountered but once in a thousand years.
If one must wait for those such as Damei and Ciming before befriending them, they appear but once in a hundred generations.

For indeed, affairs proceed from the minute to the manifest, and merit is achieved by accumulating small acts into the great. One has never seen anyone achieve success without learning, nor reach preeminence without cultivation.
If one realizes this principle, then teachers may be sought, friends may be chosen, the Way may be studied, and virtue may be cultivated;
then what task in the world would be impossible to undertake? As the ancients said: "Truly, knowing men is difficult."
"If even the sages were subject to illness, how much more so others? (Letter to Zhuan’an).
This section states that one's character and integrity depend entirely on diligent study. Alas! People of antiquity were just like people of today.
This world is just like that world. If you insist on waiting for someone like Yaoshan or Fengxue before you can take them as a teacher, you may encounter such a person only once in a thousand years.

If you insist on waiting for someone like Damei or Ciming before you can take them as a friend, such a person will only appear once in a hundred generations. Yet, it is not necessarily so; for indeed—
Originally, things proceed from the hidden and subtle to the manifest; achievements grow from the slight to the vast.
All are accomplished through accumulation; one has never seen anyone in the world who could succeed without learning or reach mastery without cultivation.
If one realizes this principle that necessitates both learning and cultivation, then a teacher need not be sought for their eminence.
One may seek them; friends need not wait for extraordinary circumstances to be chosen. The Way need not wait for the right time to be studied.
Virtue need not wait for the right person to be cultivated. Thus, in all matters under heaven—every single thing and every single principle—what could one not accomplish?
From this we know that it depends on the person, not on the method. As the ancients said: "To know a person is truly difficult; even the sages [found it so]."
This is already a source of concern; how much more so for others? The Buddha was not created by birth, and the sages were made by humans.

If you wish to distinguish between the holy and the ordinary, or to debate the present and the past, you further distance yourself from your own nature. Who is not a Yao or a Shun? It is simply that one suffers from a lack of sharp resolve.
This chapter states that the Ultimate Way is not complicated; to alter it is to turn it into something flawed.
Xinwen said: "The Way of the Separate Transmission outside the teachings is most simple and essential. From the beginning, there has been no other doctrine.
The predecessors practiced it without doubt and maintained it without alteration."

This section clarifies that the Way is fundamentally not difficult. Regarding the so-called "separate transmission outside the teachings," it means that this Way is inherently and spontaneously possessed by every person;
it is something that cannot be reached through the explanations and commentaries of the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) of the holy teachings.

There is a distinct occasion of "holding up a flower" which constitutes the essential core of the separate transmission. This matter is most simple and not complex; it is most essential and precisely appropriate. Thus spoke the First Patriarch.
When this was transmitted to China, it was simply called "the correspondence of practice and realization. From the beginning, what was there to say?
The predecessors honored and upheld this Way; they practiced it without doubt and maintained it without change.
During the Tianxi era, Xuedou, with his erudite and versatile talent, employed refined artistry to seek novelty and polish subtlety.

Continuing the tradition of Fenyang, he composed verses on ancient cases (*songgu*), captivating the scholars of his time; from this point on, the style of the Chan school underwent a complete transformation.
This section clarifies the initial transformation of the school’s style. Tianxi was the reign title of Emperor Zhenzong, the third emperor of the Song dynasty.

Xuedou possessed the talent of vast erudition and grand eloquence; it is praised that he transformed the underlying intent and began to manipulate it, seeking novelty within the meaning of the ancients and refining it with ingenious artistry.
He continued the tradition of Fenyang by composing *songgu* (verses on ancient cases), thereby ensnaring [the practitioners].
The scholars of that age were ensnared like birds in a cage or horses in their bridles and halters, unable to attain freedom;
from this point on, the patriarch’s influence and transformation underwent a complete change.
By the time of the Xuānzhèng era, Yuǎnwù further expressed his own views and separated [the original material] to produce the *Bìyán jí*.
At that time, even veteran masters of ancient and pure integrity—such as the deceased Níng Dàozhě, Shēnlíng, Xīnyuán, Fójian, and other elders—were all unable to overturn his arguments.
Consequently, junior monks and later generations came to prize his words, reciting and practicing them morning and evening, regarding them as the ultimate study.
None realized that this was erroneous. How tragic! The mental faculties of scholars have been corrupted.
This section refers to the flow into scholastic learning (*yixue*). "Xuanzheng" was the reign title of Emperor Huizong, the eighth sovereign of the Song dynasty.
Master Yuanwu further expressed his own views by providing critical commentaries on the *gusong* (verses on ancient cases) of Master Xuedou Xian.
He proclaimed it and divided it into sections, naming it the *Biyán jí* (Blue Cliff Records). "Blue Cliff" is the name of a mountain;
because Master Yuánwù resided there while composing his commentaries and songs, he gave it this name.

At that time, there were still great elders from various quarters who could transcend the present and surpass the past—all men of pure and complete virtue and character. For example, the monk Níng was from Kāifú Monastery in Tánzhōu.
Chan Master Daoning was the son of the Wang family of the Xi River. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wuzu Fayan, belonging to the fourteenth generation under Nanyue.
Furthermore, figures such as Sijian, Lingyuan, and Fojian were all likewise unable to turn him back from his practice of commentary and exposition (*pingchang*).
Consequently, when those newly entering the Dharma and junior students of later generations encountered these commentaries, they perceived them as having a rational path (*yilü*).
One may seek [this teaching]. All should cherish and respect its doctrine, reciting it in the morning and practicing it in the evening; this is called the ultimate study.
Yet, there is not a single student who awakens to this and realizes it is otherwise—how tragic! The student’s mind should embody the Way and its arts.
All were harmed by their scholastic pedantry and could not be saved.

At the beginning of the Xiangshu era, Furi entered Min and saw that scholars were being dragged along without turning back, racing forward day after day and month after month until they gradually became corrupted.

He immediately smashed their printing blocks and refuted their doctrines, thereby dispelling delusions, rescuing those drowning, pruning the profuse, clearing away the chaotic, and crushing [their errors].
The heterodox was exposed and the orthodox was specially revitalized. When the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas) came to realize their error, they no longer aspired [to such ways].

However, had it not been for the Buddha-Sun’s lofty brilliance and far-reaching vision, which, through the power of his compassionate vows, rescued the world from the defects of the Dharma-ending age, there would have been much to fear within the monastic communities (saṃghārāmas).
(From the "Letter to Zhang Zishao," Part II, from the *Guanglu*).
This section now clarifies the rectification [of errors]. "Shaoxing" was the reign title of Emperor Gaozong, the tenth sovereign of the Song dynasty.
"Furi Temple" (Buddha-Sun Temple) is the name of the monastery; it was the site of practice for Master Dahui. "Min" refers to Fujian.

[The author] observes that students are led astray by a single copy of the *Biyan ji* (Blue Cliff Record), which they study and practice without ceasing. They gallop about, all rushing toward conceptual meanings, racing day after day.

One day, [the teachings] spread like the moon moving through the sky for a month; as they progressed further and further, they became increasingly pervasive, soaking into things like water moistening objects until they had become a settled malady.
Consequently, Master Dàhuì personally went to Fújiàn and immediately smashed the printing blocks.
He then published his own *Shōyu* (Pointing at the Moon) to refute those doctrines; thus, he was able to dispel the deluded attachments of students and rescue them.
He pruned away its excesses and set aside its complexities—“complexity” meaning that which is excessive or extreme.

By suppressing the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox, he caused the Way of the Special Transmission to rise up with particular vigor. Consequently, the monastics gradually came to recognize its errors and no longer envied this book.
Thus, it was not due to the lack of Ming-hsi’s lofty intelligence and far-reaching insight.

I observe that, while riding upon the vow of universal salvation through great compassion to rescue the defects of scholasticism in the Dharma-ending age, there are many things in the monastic communities that are truly fearsome;
their disorder is evident. It cannot be said that the intention of the ancients was not good.
I only regret that students practice this without regard for the proper time, abandoning the root to pursue the branches, and thereby bringing blame upon their teachers.
