The Buddha-sun awaits the Dharma, not the person; it is precisely for the sake of Elder Yuanwu to manifest boundless radiance.
This chapter reveals that a vessel of great capacity is inherently formed by nature; it cannot be conceived through the ordinary workings of the mind.
When the Venerable Fotiao Guang of Zhuo’an first visited Xuetang at Jianfu Monastery, a physiognomist beheld him and recognized his potential, saying to Xuetang:
"Among the assembly, the senior monk Guang has a perfectly square head, a broad forehead, and full cheeks. Seven...

He resided in a level and full position. It was destined that one day he would become a teacher to an emperor. At the beginning of the Chūxi era of Emperor Xiaozong, he was summoned for an audience and pleased the Emperor’s mind.
He was retained at the Neiguan Hall for seven nights, receiving treatment of exceptional excellence that surpassed all previous precedents. The Emperor bestowed upon him the name Fozhao.
Recorded from what was heard throughout the realm:
Chan Master Fozhao Deguang of Yuyang Mountain in Qingyuan Prefecture was the son of the Peng family of Linjiang Commandery.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue. Initially, he went to visit Master Xuedang at Jianfu Temple.
At Fusi Temple, there was a physiognomist who, upon seeing him once, sighed and said, "This is a vessel of great beauty.
He then said to Xuetang, "Among the assembly, there is the Elder Guang; he is a man born with a noble destiny. Observe his skull and cranial bone: they are square and upright.
His *sang*—that is, the forehead—and his *yi*—that is, the jaw—are such that the forehead is broad and the jaw is full. Furthermore, add the two hands and the two... [feet].
The soles of his feet, his two shoulders, and the crown of his head—these seven places were all perfectly full and even.
This man would surely become the teacher of an emperor in the future. At the beginning of the Chūxi era of Emperor Xiaozong, the Emperor summoned the Master for an audience;

indeed, he met with the Emperor’s approval. He was invited to stay at the Neiguan Hall for seven nights. The hospitality extended to him was exceptionally generous and distinguished, and the Emperor held him in high regard. [He was ordained.]

"Transcendence" (yuè) means to go beyond. This refers to transcending all the sincerity with which emperors and kings from the past have honored their teachers and revered the Dharma, as well as bestowing upon the Buddha the name "Illuminator" (Fozhao), which has become renowned throughout the world.

I see a certain class of people who give rise to many strange and eccentric thoughts, desiring to go forth and become National Teachers (Guoshi), yet they do not realize that the Five-Phoenix Pavilion remains high above them.
This chapter maintains that the Way cannot be discussed in terms of wisdom or folly; it is only when one encounters the right person that it is perfected.
Zhu'an said to Prime Minister Yu Yunwen: "The Great Way is transparent and luminous; fundamentally, there is neither folly nor wisdom.
For example, Yi Yin and Lü Shang rose from plowing fields and fishing to become teachers of emperors and kings—how could they be measured by the gradations of wisdom and folly?"
Although he was not a great man, who else could have been his equal?
Yǔn Wén’s surname was Yú, his given name Yǐn, and his courtesy name Bīnfǔ. At the age of ten, he was skilled at composing poetry and prose, producing words that startled the world.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Xiāozōng, he was appointed as Chancellor. He established the Qiáo Village Guest House to entertain scholars from all quarters.
Zhu’an said to the Chancellor: "The way to select the worthy lies in a person's virtue, not in judging them by their name or rank.
Furthermore, the substance of the Great Way is empty and void, devoid of partiality. As for human nature, there is originally no distinction between the dull and the wise.
For example, Yi Yin lamented that China lacked a virtuous sovereign and sighed that this Way was not being practiced; thus he lived in seclusion, tilling the soil."
"In the wilds of Xin. This refers to delighting in the Way of Yao and Shun. Youxin was the name of an ancient city, located fifty li east of Kaifeng.
Tang went three times to summon him and appointed him as Prime Minister. He said of himself: "If there were no sovereign like Cheng Tang in the world, I would have remained in the wilds of Youxin;
I would never have bent my principles to seek favor. It is also like Lu Wang (Liu Bang).
A man of the Eastern Sea, surnamed Jiang, named Shang, with the courtesy name Ziya.

He fished at Panxi Creek in Baoji County. When King Wen of Zhou was about to go hunting, he divined the matter and said: "What we shall capture will be neither a bear, nor a brown bear, nor a leopard, nor a tiger;
it will be an assistant to a hegemon-king. Having gone out, he captured Jiang Shang on the northern bank of the Wei River. Conversing with him, the King was greatly pleased.
The King then said, "My late predecessor, Duke Tai Gong, once remarked that a supreme man would surely come to Zhou;
could you be this person? Shang replied, "Indeed. The King said, "Duke Tai Gong has long looked toward you. Thus he was styled Taigong Wang (Duke Tai Gong Who Waits).
He was appointed as his teacher and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lü. Later, he assisted King Wu in the campaign against Zhou. As Hu Zeng wrote in a poem: "The river grasses are lush and green..."
The Wei River flows on; from this place, Zi Ya alone cast down his hook. At that time, he had not yet entered the omen of the "Bear and Tiger" [to be summoned by the King];
for a while, he must have sighed toward the setting sun over his white hair. These two men may truly be said to have been "morning field-labourers and evening guests at the Emperor’s hall.
How could they be compared by the gradations of the wise and the foolish? Although this is so—
Regarding the discourse on wisdom and folly: were it not for such great men as Yi Lu, who could possibly equal them?
△ The Great Way fundamentally cannot be discussed in terms of wisdom and folly; rather, those who attain the Way emerge beyond the realm of wisdom and folly.
If one insists on discussing the Way through wisdom and folly, those who truly attain it will be few indeed.
This chapter speaks of how the Perfected Person values themselves, such that their daily activities and rest are non-dual.

Zhu’an said: Xuanyeyan often remarked that Chan Master Huanglong Nan was broad-minded and generous, loyal and trustworthy, reverent yet compassionate, profound and far-reaching in his discernment, and widely learned with vast erudition.
He frequently traveled through the Lake and Xiang regions with Yunfeng Yue, once seeking shelter from the rain beneath a tree.
Fayue sat with his legs spread out in a loose-legged posture facing him, while Nan alone sat upright and alert.
Fayue glared at him and said, "The wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not the kind of dead expression worn by the local deity in a village shrine.

Nan bowed his head in thanks and sat even more upright than before. Thus, Imperial Historian Huang Tingjian (Luzhi) praised him, saying: "In both movement and stillness, Master Nan never forgot reverent respect."
He was truly a master of the monastic community (*Huàn'ān jí*).
Master Chan Master Yě’ān Zu Xuán was a successor of Chan Master Dàméi Guǒ; he belonged to the eighteenth generation below Nányuè.
He often remarked that the nature bestowed by Chan Master Huánglóng Nán was broad and generous, loyal and trustworthy, and his person was most reverent and humble.
He was solemn yet compassionate toward others; moreover, his discernment was profound and far-reaching, and he was extensively learned and well-informed.
Once, while traveling with Master Yunfeng Yue through Huxi and Xiangyin, they took shelter from the rain beneath a tree.
Yue sat facing him in the *jizu* posture—squatting with both legs extended and both hands resting upon his knees, the shape of which resembles a winnowing basket (*ji*). (Southern Dynasties)

The Master sat alone, looking grave and composed. Yuanze immediately glared at him with his eyes and said, "The subtle and wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was never meant for the local guardian spirits of some rustic village shrine.
Why do you put on this pretense of being a dead man? Nanping bowed his head in apology; thereafter, he resumed his grave posture once more.
It grew even more profound. Thus, Imperial Historian Huang Ru-zhi praised him, saying: "Master Nan never forgets reverence in either motion or stillness;

he is truly the master of the monastic community. Indeed, his true insight was broad and generous, his nature was composed and far-reaching, and he lacked even the slightest attachment to forms. That Master Yue refined him in this way—truly a virtuous friend.
This chapter states that in studying the Way, awakening through wisdom must come first; to lose this is to fall into disorder.拙菴 (Zhu’an) said:
"To lead oneself and preside over the assembly, one must rely on wisdom; to dispel delusions and eliminate attachments, one must first awaken.

To turn one's back on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses leads to the mind becoming obscured; when the wise and the foolish cannot be distinguished, affairs fall into chaos. (Written by Chanter-in-Chief Zhòu).
Whenever a monk places himself before the great assembly, he must take wisdom as his primary guide.
Furthermore, in order to dispel deluded thoughts and eliminate emotional consciousness, he must take awakened illumination as the very foundation.
If one turns one's back on awakened illumination and merges with sensory objects, this mind will become obscured. This is especially true when among the great assembly...
If the wise and the foolish cannot distinguish between them, affairs will surely fall into disorder.
These few words alone are much like a three-hundred-jin burden that no one can lift; let those with strength try to lift it.
This passage reveals the profound and subtle wisdom and capacity of the ancients; both host and guest possessed the Way.

Zhu’an said: "When Fojian resided at Taiping, Gao’an served as the *vina* (steward). Gao’an was young in years and bold in spirit, looking down upon those from all quarters, finding few who could satisfy his mind.
One day, during the midday meal, when the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) was struck, he saw an attendant using a separate vessel."

He placed the food before the Buddha-mirror (the portrait of the Buddha). Gao’an emerged from the hall and said in a stern voice, "A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of five hundred monks acts with such conduct;
how can he serve as a model for future students? The Buddha-mirror, as if he had neither heard nor seen anything, did not react.

When Gao’an went downstairs to inquire about it, he discovered it was pickled vegetables. This was because the Buddha-mirror had long suffered from spleen disease and did not eat oil. Gao’an felt ashamed.
He went to the Abbot’s quarters to take his leave. Fojian said, "What the Rector has said is very appropriate.

Since Huiqin’s illness is such as this, I have often heard the words of the sages that one should use principle to resolve all obstacles. As his food is not substantial, there is consequently no cause for suspicion regarding the assembly.
The Rector’s spirit and character are clear and far-reaching; he shall one day serve as a pillar and foundation for our school. I hope you will not harbor resentment over this matter."
When Fojian moved to Zhikai Temple, Gao’an succeeded him at Longmen; he later became the dharma heir of Foyan.
Formerly, when Fojian resided at Taiping, Gao’an served as the *karmadāna*. Although Gao’an was young in years, his ambition and spirit were exceptionally bold;
he looked down upon the venerable elders of all quarters, as if no one existed who could match his resolve. One—
As the wooden gong was being struck at dawn and it was time to receive the precepts, Gaoan suddenly saw an attendant place food in a separate vessel before the Buddha’s mirror.
Not knowing what kind of object it was, Gaoan immediately stepped out from the assembly and said in a stern voice:
"A spiritual friend of five hundred monks, practicing such conduct—how can you possibly serve as a model for future students?"
Fojian remained silent as if he had neither heard their voices nor seen their forms.
When they descended from the hall to inquire further, it turned out to be watered pickled vegetables; this was because Fojian had long suffered from spleen ailments and did not dare to eat oil.
Ga’nan immediately felt ashamed and went to the abbot’s quarters to request his resignation. Fojian said, "What the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Na) has said..."
This is most reasonable. It is simply because Huìqín was ill that he acted thus. I have often heard the sages say:
"Only through principle can one penetrate all obstacles. Now, since what I eat does not exceed that of the assembly, why should anyone harbor doubts?
The Venerable Karmadāna’s spirit and character are exceedingly lofty and far-reaching; in days to come, he shall surely become a pillar of our school.
The Liang dynasty supported the Great Dharma as firmly as a massive boulder. I hope you will not allow yourself to be obstructed by these few minor words of today.
"Jièdì" (芥蔕) refers to a prickling obstruction; it is like a bone stuck in the throat. It describes how people find direct speech difficult to receive, as if a bone were lodged in their gullet.
Furthermore, one hopes for a person's magnanimity, saying: "I hope you will not harbor such petty resentment."
When Fojian succeeded as abbot at Zhihai, Ga’an immediately went to Longmen; he later became the dharma heir of Foyan.
Ga’an possessed a majestic and formidable spirit, capable of seizing the banner amidst a crowd of ten thousand men.
Had it not been for Fojian’s capacity—vast as the sky and the sea—there would surely have been a rift between master and disciple.
This chapter concerns discussing the Way with government officials; its purpose is to eliminate their intellectual understanding so that they may transcend directly and enter [the truth].

Zhu’an said: "In general, when engaging in discourse and exchange on the Way with officials, one must strip away their conceptual knowledge and not allow them to remain settled within their habitual nests;
one must strive solely for the direct clarification of the single point that points upward. My late teacher Miaoxi once...
He said: "When gentlemen meet, one should respond when questioned; it is improper not to do so.
Furthermore, one must be a person of this caliber before it is acceptable. These words are beneficial for the times and do not harm the dignity of the abbot;
you should reflect upon them deeply. (A letter to Xinghua Puan).
Whenever an abbot discusses the ultimate Way with lay patrons or officials, he must not allow his discourse to become entangled in trivialities during the exchange of greetings.
He must strip away their mental calculations and intellectual interpretations, ensuring they do not remain ensnared in a thicket of complications.
He must directly and simply present the pointing-out instruction to reveal to them that supreme state which transcends all.
This is precisely the essential character of a patch-robed monk (*śramaṇa*). My late master Miaoxi once said:
"Whenever I meet with scholars and officials, if they have a question, I must respond in accordance with the Dharma; if they do not ask, there is no need to force conversation upon them.
Furthermore, when engaging in discussion, one must first recognize that the person is among those who follow the Way before one can speak of the inner meaning with them."
[The Master] said: "Not so. To speak otherwise would be of no benefit. This saying of my former teacher truly provides benefit for the present age;
it serves to ensure that the dignity of the abbot is not compromised. All who preside over the Dharma should reflect deeply upon this point.
△ I have often observed that when receiving scholar-officials (shida-fu) these days, the attendants do not care whether the guests believe or not, but merely focus on...
The platter was passed forward, yet alas, he cast it away like spittle. How pitiable, how pitiable!
This passage instructs the master of the house to properly nurture scholars, so that the Dharma-gate may be made magnificent and radiant.
Zhu’an said: "The beauty of the earth lies in its ability to nurture all things; the benevolence of a ruler lies in his ability to nurture his scholars.

Today, those who hold the position of abbot for the most part do not take the interests of the community to heart. They act only on their own immediate desires, loathe hearing virtuous words, delight in concealing their faults and evils, and willfully carry out depraved conduct.
While they indulge their own whims for the sake of momentary gratification, they are instead exploited by petty people who seize upon their likes and dislikes."
If one acts thus, how could the way of the abbot not be endangered? (Letter to Old Master Hong).

For example, just as the most fertile lands in the world are necessarily able to grow fine crops, so too is it an immutable principle that an abbot who possesses benevolence and compassion will inevitably be able to nurture wise men. In these times...
Those who hold the title of "abbot" (zhuchi) generally do not take it as their primary concern to maintain the community with benevolence and compassion.
Instead, they constantly prioritize their own personal preferences as urgent matters. Whenever they encounter virtuous words, they feel aversion and refuse to listen or accept them.
They invariably conceal their own faults and transgressions, acting arbitrarily upon all improper deeds, even if they bring them personal gratification.
For the time being, this has allowed a class of petty people to seize upon these vulnerabilities, catering to their own likes and dislikes to achieve their ends.
If this continues, how could the way of the abbot avoid falling into peril?
△ To nourish the monks with benevolence and love is the most appropriate course for the world; yet they have usurped this authority.
For private use. To lose one's mind and turn away from reason—may you fortunately not tread the same path; ruin follows before one can even turn back one's heels.
This chapter means that the sharp edge of one's brilliance must not be too exposed, for fear of inviting injury or deficiency.
Zhu’an said to Yeshan: “The Minister, Layman Ziyán, remarked that our late teacher Miaoxi throughout his life prioritized virtue, morality, integrity, and courage.
He was one who could be trusted but not distanced; who could be approached but not pressured; and who could be killed but never humiliated.
In his private life he was not licentious, and in his diet he was not gluttonous. When facing death or calamity, he regarded them as non-existent.”
As the saying goes: "The swords Ganjiang and Moye are difficult to contend with; one only fears being wounded or impaired.
Later, it was just as Ziyuan had said (Recorded in the *Huanchan Jiwen*).
Formerly, the Prime Minister, Layman Ziyuan, said: "Throughout his life, Master Miaoxi cultivated his person and regulated his mind solely through the Way and virtue.
Thus, because this body was upright and possessed of propriety, this mind was likewise upright and accorded with righteousness."
In all his actions at any time, he always prioritized courage, vigor, and resolute daring.
Thus, as a person, he was like what is described in the "Conduct of the Scholar" (*Ru Xing*) chapter of the *Analects*: a scholar may be intimate with but not distant from;
one may draw near to but not press upon; it is better to be killed than to be disgraced. As the *Book of Rites* says: "When living at home, he does not indulge in excess."
"Food and drink are not glutted. "Yin" means to drift and dissipate; to indulge unrestrainedly in the pursuit of flavors is called "gluttony" (*ru*).

Even if one were placed amidst the vicissitudes of life and death or the midst of calamity and disaster, such a person regards them as if they did not exist. To maintain oneself in this manner is truly what is meant by saying:
"Who could compete with Ganjiang and Moye for sharpness? "Yu" means anxiety; it is merely a fear that some unforeseen misfortune may arise.
This is merely a matter of injury and deficiency. Later, it indeed turned out as Ziyan had said.

According to the *Biographies of Filial Sons* (*Xiaozizhuan*), the consort of King Xiang of Chu was enjoying the cool air in summer when she embraced an iron pillar and became pregnant. She gave birth to an iron mass. The King ordered the master smith Ganjiang to forge swords;
after three years, two swords, male and female, were completed. He concealed the male sword and presented the female one to the King. The King...

He placed it in a casket and kept it secret. Whenever he heard a mournful cry, the King questioned his ministers. A minister said, "The sword has both male and female blades; that which cries is the female yearning for the male.
The King was greatly incensed and wished to execute Ganjiang. Ganjiang, knowing he would surely die, hid the sword within a pillar of his house.
His wife, named Mo-xie, was pregnant and about to give birth. Ganjiang entrusted her with a letter, saying: "On the day..."
He went out the door toward the east. On the southern mountain there was a pine tree; the pine grew from a rock, and a sword was within it.

He further said, "If you give birth to a son, tell him of this when he has grown up. Later, his wife indeed gave birth to a son. There was a red mark between his eyebrows, so he was named Mei-jian-chi (Red Mark Between the Eyebrows).
When he reached the age of fifteen, he asked his mother, "Where is my father? His mother took out the slip of paper and showed it to him, saying: [text follows].
"Your father was unjustly executed. Upon hearing this, Chi became enraged and contemplated day and night how to take revenge for his father.
He then went out of the gate three times, looking toward the mountain pines, but seeing none, he lay down dejectedly in the hall. Suddenly, he saw a pine-patterned pillar on the wall of the hall;
upon reflecting on it, he split it open and found a sword. King Pre had previously dreamed of a small boy with something red between his eyebrows, who said, "I shall avenge my father."
Mencius said: "The King was afraid and issued an edict: 'Whoever can capture Mengjianchi, or whoever obtains his head, shall be handsomely rewarded.
When Mengjianchi heard this, he fled into the mountains. There he unexpectedly encountered a woodcutter, who saw him and asked, 'Are you not Mengjianchi?
He replied, 'Indeed. The man said, 'I am a native of Zengshan. I recently heard that the King has ordered your arrest; you must certainly [flee further]..."
"It is difficult to escape. Why not hand over your head along with the sword to me? I shall avenge you. Chi replied, "I am most fortunate.
He then took the sword and cut off his own head, giving it to the guest. The guest concealed the sword on his person and presented the head to the King.
The King was greatly pleased. The guest said, "This is the head of a brave warrior; I fear there may be future trouble. It should be cooked in oil."
The king was greatly pleased. He then prepared an oil cauldron and boiled [the head] for three days and nights, yet it did not decompose; its mouth and eyes opened and closed as if alive.
A guest invited the king to observe it, whereupon he drew his sword and struck off the king’s head, which fell into the cauldron. Thereupon, the two heads bit each other.
Fearing that the "Red Head" would not prevail, the guest then took his own life by cutting off his head to join them. Thus, the three heads bit one another for a moment.

In time, they all rotted away; the ministers could no longer distinguish them, so they divided the flesh from the broth and buried it. Thus, they are collectively known as the Tombs of the Three Kings.
They are located in Yichun County, Runan Prefecture. A sharp blade for slicing hair requires skill and effort to grind it;
if the Creator did not polish and sharpen it, it would remain dull and obstructive.
This chapter teaches that for one who holds the position of abbot, it is essential to have those of virtuous character assist them;

only then will the Way flourish. Zhu’an said: "When I was the abbot at Yeshan, I understood the beginning and end of human affairs and clarified the fundamental principles of the monastic community (conglin).
I once told my disciple: 'One who serves as the leader of a region must select monks of ambition and integrity to assist and support him.'"
A comb for the hair and a mirror for the face allow one’s ailments and beauty, or flaws and excellence, to be revealed without concealment.
Thus, when Ciming obtained Yangqi, and Mazu obtained Baizhang, it was like pouring water into water—nothing could obstruct it (from the *Huanchan ji*).

It is said that Master Yeshan served as the abbot. He was exceptionally adept at understanding human nature, maintaining integrity from beginning to end, and possessed a profound understanding of the fundamental principles of the monastic community (*saṃgha*). He once told me:

"One who serves as the leader of a region must necessarily select those monks who possess great resolve and vigor, whose practice of the Way is diligent, and with whom he may together promote and support the teachings."
"To assist" means to support and aid. If one obtains good people to serve as assistants, then for the abbot it will be like having a comb for one's hair or a mirror for one's face;
all matters—every benefit and harm, every good and bad—will be impossible to conceal.
It was like when Ciming obtained Yangqi, such that no task remained unattended, or when Mazu obtained Baizhang.
There is no dharma that is not perfectly round; all these are in accord with the mind, like water poured into water—how could there be any further opposition?
If a person of noble wisdom were placed before such a situation, they would discern the colors black and yellow as clearly as with their own eyes and count odd and even numbers with their hands;
how then could any trace of corruption be concealed? Thus, the way of maintaining the Dharma will be expanded boundlessly.
This chapter teaches that one must exhaust the very depths of the Path before one can discern the profound and fathom the distant. Zhu’an said:

"Those of superficial learning and shallow reception merely value what they hear while disparaging what they see; thus, they are ultimately unable to investigate its mysteries and subtleties. Therefore it is said:
A mountain does not disdain being high, for within it lie layered cliffs of accumulated greenery; the ocean does not disdain being deep, for within it lie the four seas and nine rivers."
Yuan: "If one wishes to investigate the Great Way, the essential point lies in exhausting its heights and depths;
only then can one illuminate the subtle and obscure, responding to changes without end" (Letter to Master Jin).
This refers to people in the age of the Dharma’s decline who are unwilling to investigate the fundamental source deeply; all that they study are merely superficial efforts on the surface.
The *Tōkyō Fu* (Eulogy of the Eastern Capital) states: "Those of late learning receive only the superficial; they value what they hear and despise what they see. Here, "fū" (膚) means skin.
The reception of the Dharma through the skin implies a lack of deep study. What is received externally is shallow and thin; what exists internally is truly nothing at all.
Those who value their ears delight in hearing, while those who despise their eyes are lazy regarding reading.

They claim that as soon as they have heard a few words of plain talk from another, they consider themselves to have attained realization. Thus, although there are the words of instruction from predecessors, they ultimately do not pass beyond them.
In such cases, one will inevitably be unable to exhaustively reach the most profound and wondrous state. Thus it is said: "The mountain does not weary of being high;
because it is high, that which it contains is also vast, possessing within it the secluded wonders of layered cliffs and accumulated emerald verdure.
The sea does not weary of being deep; because it is deep, that which it receives is also abundant, containing within its midst the four oceans and nine rivers."
The vastness of the abysses: the four *míng* (oceans) refer to the four seas of the east, west, south, and north;

their waters are black, hence they are called *míng*. Regarding the nine abysses: *Lèizi* says that the swirling eddies of the *kūn* fish form an abyss; still water that does not swirl forms an abyss;
the eddies of flowing water form an abyss; the eddies of overflowing water form an abyss; the eddies of drenching water form an abyss... [and so forth].
Yuan. When the waters of Ji overflow, they form a yuan; when the waters of Yong overflow, they form a yuan; when the waters of Qian overflow, they form a yuan;
when the waters of Fei overflow, they form a yuan. These are known as the Nine Yuans. A yuan signifies depth; it is where water comes to rest. Where water swirls and turns is called a yuan.
A student who wishes to investigate and clarify the Great Way must ultimately exhaust its limits, reaching the highest and the most profound.
Only after reaching such depth can one spontaneously illuminate the subtle and obscure, naturally attaining the infinite subtlety of skillful means and adaptive transformations.

To value what is heard while despising what is seen is a universal malady of the age. Those who are able to investigate deeply and know the far-reaching, thereby forging the character of Yao and Shun, are truly the rare vital breaths bestowed by Heaven.
This chapter states that the learning of the sages and worthies values persistence, for this is free from error.
Zhu’an said to Minister You: "The intention of the sages and worthies is such that their principles are clear through a gradual pace, and their affairs are manifest through leisurely progress.
Regarding the matters they employ, they do not expect rapid accomplishment but permit sustained endurance; they do not require inevitable advancement."

Yet he granted [the possibility] with the hope that it might be so; by thus inferring the intention of the sages and worthies, one is able to maintain [this principle] throughout ten thousand generations without error—such is the case (from the *Huan’an ji*).
This refers to the fundamental intent established by the sages and worthies: it values being moderate and relaxed so that the underlying principles may be clarified;
it also values being unhurried and self-possessed so that practical affairs may be made manifest.

Regarding all matters undertaken, one must not act with haste or expect rapid completion; rather, one permits people to take persistence as the essential, and does not permit them to rely on certainty.
They strive with one another, yet they grant others the hope that they may approach [the goal].

If one can apply this effort, elaborating upon the intent of the sages and worthies, and attaining their method of solemnity and long-term persistence, then one will be able to maintain it throughout ten thousand generations.
Thus, by preserving it without error, one is able to achieve such a state. △ [The Way of] the Sages and Worthies.

This mind is formed through many lifetimes; how could it be attained through impetuous haste? If you truly wish to realize the intent of the sages and worthies, you must cultivate a heart and liver as enduring as a kalpa-stone;
then, naturally, there will be merit that shall not be worn away for ten thousand ages.
This chapter uses ancient sayings to admonish people, hoping that they will follow them with faith and put them into practice.
Minister You said: "Before the time of the Patriarchs, there was no office of abbot. Later, when they appeared in the world to propagate the Way, they were driven by necessity.
Yet, as for their dwelling, it was merely a thatched hut sufficient to shield them from wind and rain; as for their food, it was coarse and simple, enough to satisfy hunger."

Through hardship and emaciation, there were those who could not endure their grief; yet among the princes and high officials, there were even those who desired to see him but could not obtain the opportunity.
Therefore, all that he established was vast and magnificent, shaking heaven and moving earth.
This section clarifies that the ultimate person (zhiren) finds joy in the Way for themselves. Master Yougong recounted the words of Miaoxi as an admonition for his contemporaries, saying:
"Prior to the Patriarchs, there was originally no established position of abbot. It was only later that those who appeared to manifest in the world and practice this Way were all revered by people;
they were compelled by the presence of those possessing the Way and could not help but do so."
Thus he first appeared in the world. However, his dwelling was merely a thatched hut; he wove thorns to form a gate. As the *Ruxing* says:
"The Confucian has a courtyard of one mu and a room with walls of ten paces on each side. His gate is made of woven thorns with a small opening like a ruler's edge;
his door is of rushes and his window is shaped like a jar. These serve only to shield him from wind and rain. His food is coarse and unrefined; this serves only to satisfy his hunger."
Time and again he gathered firewood and cultivated his own crops, toiling his body and withering his mind.
To the outside world, he appeared to bear an unbearable burden of sorrow; yet, though his physical form was weary, his moral virtue was truly full.
Among kings, lords, dukes, and high officials, there were those who wished to seek an audience with him but could not obtain it. Therefore, whatever these predecessors established—
They stand firm, all vast and unimpeded like a cascade of boulders tumbling down without obstruction.
These are all metaphors for the marks of a great man: nothing can stagnate within his breast, just as one passes straight through amidst a thicket of spears and shields.
Amidst the thicket of brambles, he strides forth with a wave of his hand;
beneath his heels there is no five-colored thread, upon his tongue there is no cross-barred gate, at the tip of his nose there is no trace of mud, and in his eyes there is no gold dust.
His lifelong practice is such that it can truly startle heaven and shake the earth.
In later generations, it was not so. Living in high halls and vast mansions, wearing fine garments and eating sumptuous food, they had their every whim satisfied by a mere gesture.
Thereupon, the followers of Pāpīyas began to be moved by such splendor; they loitered at the gates of power, wagging their tails to beg for pity.
Worse still, they practiced crafty seizure and violent plunder as if snatching gold in broad daylight, no longer recognizing that there is such a thing as cause and effect in this world.
This section states that fools vied with one another to practice superficial splendor; those of later generations were not like this.
With high halls and vast mansions, fine clothing and abundant food, they merely moved their chins—*yi* means "chin"—and waved their fingers.
In every glance and gesture, there was nothing that did not accord with their desires. Consequently, there arose a class of followers of the *pāpīyas* Māra.
Their greed and seeking are insatiable; their minds are moved by a vast, overflowing restlessness. "Vastly overflowing" describes the manner of being dissolute and wandering.
They loiter at the gates of those in power; "loitering" means wishing to advance but not doing so. They wag their tails to beg for pity; what is more egregious than this?
Employing every kind of artifice to take by stealth and relying on power to seize by force, it is like plucking gold in broad daylight; one does not even notice those looking on.
"Plucking" (攫) means to seize with the claws. The *Liezi* says: "Formerly, there was a man from Qi who desired gold.

At dawn, having dressed in his cap and robes, he went to the marketplace and approached a place where gold was being sold. He stole the gold and departed. The owner of the gold caught him and said, 'Everyone else was here...'"
"How is it that you snatch gold from another? He replied, "At the very moment I took the gold, I saw no one.
By this, he meant that worldly people merely covet profit while forgetting their shame; they see the benefit and forget the harm.
Knowing only how to seek falsely, they ultimately no longer understand that there are matters of good and evil cause and effect within the world.
This letter of Miaoxi is not merely intended for Boshan; it exhausts the habitual tendencies inherited from all quarters since time immemorial, leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
It is like drinking the "upper-pool" water of Master Canggong, through which one sees the internal organs clearly. If you can believe and accept this, and uphold it...
"Practice! What use is it to seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere? (Inscribed on a stone at Lingyin).
This section was specifically used by Master Gong to offer encouragement. This letter from Wuxi Wenhui was not written solely for the sake of Boshan;
in truth, it completely uproots the habitual tendencies that all elders of the various quarters have harbored since time immemorial.
As for the vital energy (*qi*), not a single thread or hair shall be lost. It is like a person who has drunk Master Cang Gong’s water from atop the pond:
they can see clearly through the liver, the diaphragm, and all the internal organs. If a person can faithfully accept these words of Miaoxi, [they will likewise perceive all things with clarity].
There is no need to seek the various Buddha-dharmas elsewhere. Regarding the "Water of the Upper Pond" of Master Cang:
ancient records state that to the east of Luoyue there was a man named Bian Que, surnamed Qin and given name Huan, a native of Bohai Commandery; therefore, he was called Master Cang.
In his youth, he served as a steward for a household. A guest named Zhang Sangjun, who had long admired Bian Que’s singular talent, frequently sought him out.
Over the course of more than ten years, one day while sitting in private with Bian Que, he said to him, "I possess a medicinal formula.
Now that I am old, I wish to transmit it to you; do not let it leak out. Bian Que respectfully agreed. The guest then took the medicine from within his robe and gave it to him.
He gave it to him, instructing him to drink water from the "upper pond. The upper pond refers to the dew upon bamboo and trees.
After twenty-one days, he was to see things for himself. He then bestowed the entire medicinal formula upon him and suddenly vanished;
only then did [Qie] realize he had been an immortal. Qie followed these instructions and took the medicine; after twenty-one days, he was able to see people on the other side of a wall.

Regarding "Matter": later, when examining illnesses, one perceives clearly the five viscera and their pathologies; thus, it is specifically through the examination of the pulse that this [method] gained its name.
△ To feel the past and grieve for the present—every word flows from within a heart of great compassion. How many people can they truly acknowledge with joy and accept in faith?
This chapter states that a leader must be humble and uphold the Dharma so that later generations have a standard to follow.
Minister You Gong said to Zhu’an: "In the past, when the Way of Linji was in decline, Miaoxi revitalized it;
yet his character remained humble and open, never flaunting his realization of principle. Throughout his life, he did not pursue power or status."
Gou Liangyang once said: "In all matters, one must not act with negligence or indolence, nor maintain a lifestyle of extravagance.

There are things that benefit the times and facilitate affairs, yet there are those that result only in excess without any merit. If one indulges in such extravagance and sloth, nothing will be achieved.
I, the unworthy, have taken these words to heart and have made them a lifelong admonition.
This section cites ancient words as a warning. "Restoration" (zhongxing) refers to reviving what had been abandoned;
it is like Emperor Guangwu’s restoration of the Han enterprise, or how in former times Master Miaoxi restored the Way of Linji during an autumn of decline and decay.
As for the nature he inherited, that which he revered was solely humility and emptiness. Although this was so—
He perceived the profound depth of the Path, yet never indulged in self-conceit or boastfulness.
Throughout his life, he refused to curry favor with those in power and did not seek gain or sustenance through expediency. He once said:

"Of the myriad affairs of this world, one must not act according to one's whims or for the sake of gratifying the senses; they must be undertaken with diligent effort. Furthermore, one must not be extravagant."
One must maintain a sense of pride through one's conduct, yet employ it with frugality and restraint. Worldly affairs are diverse and manifold;

indeed, they are not of a single kind. Generally, there are certain undertakings that can benefit the times and accord with the needs of things, while there are another class of activities whose pursuit only increases one's faults and yields no merit. If one were to...
If one acts solely out of a desire for luxury, ease, and pleasure, then one's undertakings will certainly not succeed.
I, the unworthy one, have taken these words to heart and adopted them as a lifelong admonition.
Yesterday, the Master encountered the Sovereign, who granted him lodging at the Guantang Hall; this is truly a blessing for the Buddha-dharma.
We earnestly hope that you will not weary of your compassionate vows, so that the path toward goodness may be illuminated and the Way of benefiting all beings may expand ever further.

In this way, future generations and junior disciples may refrain from seeking petty associations and instead each harbor far-reaching ambitions. Would this not be a source of great benefit and salvation for the monastic community?
(However, according to the records of the attendant).

This section exhorts one to practice the Way with vigor. That the Great Master was recently favored by the extraordinary grace of His Majesty and permitted to stay overnight in the Inner Contemplation Hall is truly a great blessing for the Buddha-Dharma. I earnestly hope that you will not grow weary in your compassion.

I pray that you do not forget your compassionate vows, so that the path for humanity to advance toward goodness may become ever more illuminated, and the way for monastics to serve the multitude may grow increasingly vast.
In this way, future generations and those of later years will each know where to direct their efforts;
naturally, they will cease their petty and narrow habits and each harbor a pursuit of the far-reaching and great. Will this not truly benefit the Sangha?
The benefit of the forest is to universally rescue all living beings. Master Miaoxi’s broad and open mind served as his own great precept;
he further exhorted others to practice compassionate salvation, establishing a model for future generations. Truly, he was like the master chef Ding with his miraculous skill.
This chapter teaches that those who practice should know that they ought to revere ritual propriety (*li*).
Master Mianjie said: "The flourishing or decline of monastic communities depends upon ritual law; the excellence or deficiency of scholars depends upon their habitual practices.
If the ways of the ancients—who dwelt in nests and caves, drank from mountain streams, and ate from trees—were put into practice in the present age," [it would lead to chaos].
It is not possible. Suppose people today were to wear fine, colorful garments and eat fine rice with fatty meats; if this were practiced in ancient times, it would likewise be impossible.
What is the reason? It is simply because of familiarity and lack of familiarity. For what a person sees morning and evening becomes the norm.

One must say that the affairs of the world ought indeed to be thus. If one were suddenly to drive them away from here and toward there, not only would they harbor doubts and fail to believe, but it is feared they would also refuse to comply. Judging from this, human nature finds comfort in what it is accustomed to.
"It is only natural that people are startled when they have not yet seen this; what is there to marvel at? (From the Letter to Imperial Censor Shi).
Zen Master Mitan Xianjie of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture was a native of the Zheng family of Fuzhou.

He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ying'an Hua and belonged to the seventeenth generation under Mount Heng. It is said: "In general, regarding the rise and fall of monastic communities, what indeed is the cause?"
This is not due to anything else; it depends solely on whether the rites and laws are present or absent.

If the presiding master is upright and the regulations are strictly maintained, such that the relationship between superiors and subordinates is harmonious, the monastic community will naturally flourish.

Conversely, if things are the opposite of this, decline is inevitable. Whether the practitioners are excellent or base is not determined by some separate method, but rather by their prevailing customs.
This is what is practiced. If one habituates oneself to the good during ordinary times, it becomes beautiful; if one habituates oneself to what is not good, it becomes evil.
Those ancients dwelt in nests, lived in caves, drank from mountain torrents, and ate from trees;
these were all practices of their respective times that each considered comfortable. If one were to make people of today perform such acts, they would certainly—

It is simply that they were unable to do so. Given that people today wear fine garments of colorful patterns, eat fine grain, and chew fatty meats, it would be impossible to force the ancients to act in such a manner.
Is there some separate path that causes such a vast disparity between the people of antiquity and those of the present? No; it all depends solely on the habits of the people.
It is simply because one has not practiced it. Generally, from morning until evening, people take what they see and hear as ordinary matters;
they then assume that the affairs of the world ought to be conducted in this way, regarding them as things that are naturally so.
Suppose, however, that one day someone were to drive them away from these fine garments and elegant finery, and compel them to...
As for those who wear grass for clothing and eat from trees, it is not only that people harbor doubts and do not believe them;
rather, it is feared they will certainly not follow what has been sent forth. Observing this, one sees that human nature finds comfort in what it is accustomed to during ordinary times;

to be startled by what has never been seen or heard is merely the common condition of humanity. How, then, is it worth being considered strange? △ Regarding the student’s [inquiry] concerning stillness and profundity:
In the middle of the night, purify the mind and reflect back upon yourself to examine what kind of luminous state your habitual practice has produced and what kind of experience you have attained.
After doing this for a long time, a coldness will naturally arise in your very bones and ribs.
This chapter instructs people to maintain the Middle Way and remain inconspicuous, not to be deluded by fame or profit.
Miyuan said to Chief Seat Wuzhuo: "Among those in the monasteries, only those from Zhejiang are weak and lack firm resolve.
Your talent and capacity are vast, your temperament is profound and dignified, and your aspirations are upright and certain; furthermore, your realization is stable and secure. In the future—"
The *I Ching* says: "Simply remain concealed and obscure; do not expose your sharp edges. Break the square to fit the round, maintaining the Middle Way.
Do not yield even slightly to power or profit; this is precisely to perform the work of a Buddha without leaving the realm of worldly toil" (Letter to Xia’an).
Chan Master Wuzhu from Wuyun in Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Wuxing on the Tiāoxī River.
Master Mian said to him, "Within the monastic communities, only those from Zhejiang are habitually negligent and weak; few are able to stand out with distinction.
Although you are from Zhejiang, your talent, strength, and innate character are all grand and expansive. Furthermore, you possess great capacity..."
He has crossed the profound abyss and encompasses all things. His spirit and resolve are noble, and his demeanor is dignified and steadfast.
Furthermore, his realization of the Way is exceedingly secure; it would not be easy to describe the full extent of his future manifestations.
However, one must further conceal one's brilliance and obscure one's traces. Do not expose your sharp edges. You must indeed "break the square to fit the tile" (huīfāng wáhé). As the *Ruxing* says:

"The Confucian is extensively learned without exhaustion, practices his teachings with diligence without weariness, admires the worthy while being tolerant of the masses, and breaks the square to fit the tile.
One who is broad-minded and generous is like this. The commentary states: [The text provided ends here.]
It is like a ceramic tile: initially it is round; when split into four, its shape becomes square.
This is destroying the round to create the square, and joining the square to become round again. Within this process of containment and transformation, there has never been a lack of distinction.
This is why one is taught not to be biased toward one side, but to maintain the Middle Way.
Furthermore, one must not be subjugated by power or profit. If one can act thus, then it is possible to perform the deeds of all Buddhas without leaving the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*).
One dwells in peace wherever one happens to be, and there is nothing that does not accord with the Way. △ His talent and capacity are vast and his realization is stable;
he has already transcended the ranks of ordinary beings. If he can exercise forbearance and avoid being self-righteous, then he enters the state of the Sages.
This chapter states that the worthy and the unworthy must be distinguished; one ought to exercise self-restraint. Mian said:
"The late Master Ying'an once remarked that the worthy and the unworthy are opposites and thus cannot but be distinguished.

The worthy establish themselves by upholding morality, righteousness, benevolence, and propriety; the unworthy employ themselves in affairs by monopolizing power, profit, deceit, and flattery. The worthy...
Those who attain their ambitions will surely put into practice what they have learned. Those of inferior character who occupy positions of authority often act on private whims;

they envy the virtuous and resent the capable, indulging in desires and seeking wealth until there is nothing they will not do. Therefore, when the worthy are obtained, the monastic community flourishes;
when the unworthy are employed, it falls into ruin. If either of these conditions prevails, the community can never remain in peace (as seen in the letter of Master Yue).
He said: "Our late teacher Ying'an once remarked that the worthy and the unworthy are opposites. As a host, one must exercise discernment.
If the guest is a worthy person, they will naturally be able to uphold the Way and its Virtue, maintain benevolence and righteousness, and establish themselves."
The unworthy have no sense of integrity or shame; they employ power, profit, deception, and flattery as their sole means of action.
When a worthy person attains their aspirations, they necessarily put into practice the morality, benevolence, and righteousness they have studied.

However, once an unworthy person occupies a position of authority, they mostly indulge solely in their own private interests, harboring jealousy toward the virtuous and envy toward the capable, while craving desires and seeking only personal gain. They are devoid of—

These are things one must not do. Therefore, when a worthy person is obtained, the monastic community (*saṃgha*) will surely flourish; by employing those who are unworthy, the laws and regulations will fall into ruin.

If even a single one of such petty people is present within the assembly, they will stir up turmoil and cause harm to the community, rendering both the internal and external spheres unable to find peace. △ When the ancients spoke and established their principles, it was originally...
It is essential that those who lead others uphold the correct path and recognize the great principles. Whether one is worthy or unworthy is not fixed or immutable;
it depends on what a person habituates themselves to. If one is content to be cast aside by the world, whose fault is that?
This chapter teaches the master of the house regarding three matters that one must know.
Miyuan said: "A monastic has three 'do nots': when affairs are numerous, do not fear them; when there are no affairs, do not seek them out; and when faced with right and wrong, do not debate them."
If an abbot realizes these three matters, he will not be deluded by external things (as recorded in the notes of Attendant Hui).
An abbot must recognize these three "mores. In any monastic community (*sōrin*), a hundred affairs accumulate.
You must not fail to regulate and manage each thing accordingly. Do not harbor fear at all; for if you fear, the matter will not be resolved.

At times when there is nothing to do, and both within and without are quiet and still, you will find natural ease and contentment. Do not seek this out at all; to seek it is to invite further entanglement.
Regarding all matters of right and wrong, and every kind of favorable or adverse circumstance, simply let them be as they may. Do not...

One must discern. Through discernment, the myriad capacities of sentient beings arise. If a monastic head (zhuchi) understands these three points, they will naturally not be deluded by external things.
The three instances of the word "must not" contain how wondrous a principle! It is simply difficult to put into practice.
If one can put it into practice, how could external things ever delude me?
This chapter states that a person’s hidden evils are more serious than their outward depravity; one must therefore subject them to rigorous inspection.
Mian said: "When a monk’s conduct is depraved and he has long possessed traces of unwholesome behavior, this is known among all within the monastic community."
This is not what is truly despicable; rather, it is truly despicable when the multitude deems someone virtuous while that person is inwardly unworthy (Letter to Puci).
The conduct and practice of ordinary monks are not particularly upright.
If they have consistently displayed traces of unwholesome behavior, everyone knows it of one another; this is not sufficient to constitute evil.
Why? Because they are simply not of the right vessel. Yet there is only one kind of person whom everyone calls "worthy," and...
This person is inwardly truly unworthy; this is indeed a most loathsome and detestable condition.
△ When others are virtuous while I am myself unworthy, it is a terminal illness. Even if Bian Que were to stand at one's door, he would have no place to apply his hand.
It is truly a pity.
This chapter states that for a person to preserve their nature, they must be profound and steadfast; one must not rashly set forth one's own limited views.
Miyuan said to Shui'an, "When one encounters insult or humiliation, one should accept it with equanimity; how can one lightly listen to mere rumors?"
I venture to set forth my humble observations. Generally speaking, those who are sycophantic and fawning are of a certain type; those who are devious and artful employ many stratagems.

Those harboring treacherous and biased intentions delight in venting their private whims, while those prone to suspicion and jealousy will unilaterally suppress public deliberation. This is because such individuals are narrow-minded in their inclinations and short-sighted in their vision;

they certainly regard their own eccentricity as being beyond the common crowd, and consider the obstruction of debate to be a mark of distinction. Yet, once they realize that I am employing [such people]...
In the end, it is so; yet slander naturally resides with the other party, and after time, the truth will manifest of its own accord.

There is no need for further clarification, nor is it necessary to insist upon one's own correctness by exposing the faults of others. Only then may one be considered a true recluse beneath the forest trees.
The Master said to Shuian, "When someone slanders or brings disgrace upon me, I should simply accept their intent and endure it.
One must not hastily listen to whatever they say and then immediately indulge in all sorts of deluded thoughts.
This is a sign of narrow vision. As for 'tunnel vision,' it is like looking at the sky through a tube; one sees only what is within that tube."
This is not an exaggeration. These words refer to how human knowledge is dark and limited, lacking lofty insight or far-reaching vision;

they fear that [such ignorance] might harm the essence of the Dharma. Generally speaking, those who are sycophantic originally have their own factions, and those who are wicked and artful possess many shifting schemes of mind.
Those who harbor the treacherous and the perverse: "perverse" refers to unbalanced speech, which is also synonymous with sycophancy.

This means that where there are treacherous and sycophantic persons, there will inevitably be flatterous and deceitful words. Consequently, they delight in indulging their private whims, giving rise to suspicion, jealousy, and hatred.
They forget the great kindnesses of others while recording their minor faults; they exalt themselves and disparage others, thereby arbitrarily subverting public discourse. Such individuals as these—

Their inclinations are exceedingly narrow, and what they perceive is extremely dim and short-sighted. Because they cling to their own views as being far removed from those of others, they claim to be "transcending the crowd.
Because they obstruct the deliberations of the multitude and do not share the sentiments of the masses, they claim to be "standing out from the crowd.
This is how they differ from the gentleman (*junzi*). Nevertheless, once one understands the workings of one's own mind...
To employ this is the Way and the Principle; yet that which one slanders is in fact nothing but self-slander and self-destruction.

After time has passed, it will clarify itself of its own accord; there is no need to further analyze and explain it to others, nor is it necessary to insist on one's own correctness to attack, expose, or provoke others.
If one acts in this manner, one may perhaps be considered a true recluse beneath the forest trees.
There is a saying: "Human emotions are easy to arouse but difficult to restrain; none is more extreme than anger.

Those who can patiently endure humiliation were all considered worthy by the ancient sages; thus, those petty people will instead turn their own words against themselves and bring about their own ruin."
This chapter states that if a person can direct themselves toward the Way with utmost sincerity, even if they are dull-witted, they are nonetheless a fit vessel and may be employed.
Master Huiguang said: "In general, if a monk is sincere and directs himself toward what is correct, he may be employed even if he is dull-witted;

if he is sycophantic and harbors evil intent, he will ultimately cause harm even if he is intelligent. For the most part, those who dwell in the forest have impure intentions; even if they possess talent, [it is of no avail].
"It is possible, yet in the end it cannot be established" (as seen in the *Jiantang shu*).
Chan Master Zide Huahui of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was a native of the Zhang family of Kuaiji.

He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhengjue of Tiantong and belonged to the sixteenth generation below Qingyuan. He said: "In general, when a monk possesses utmost sincerity within his breast..."
All that they pursue is the Way and its Virtue (Dao-de). Even those who are dull-witted may be employed; why? Because they have a foundation.

If, however, one is full of flattery and deceit in speech while harboring evil in their heart, then even if they possess knowledge and insight, they will ultimately cause harm and must never be employed.
Generally speaking, those within the monastic community maintain their integrity...
If the mind is not upright, then even if one possesses talent, learning, and capability, it will ultimately lead to great harm.
Should such a person be established as the ruler of a region, they will surely bring ruin to the monastic community. A pearl from a nine-holed oyster, though small, is still cherished by people;
whereas a mere piece of *wǔfū* stone, however dazzling its luster may be, is of no use at all.
This chapter states that practitioners must embody the rectitude of the root while regulating the branches, solemnly upholding the Great Dharma.

Daizide remarked: "The Chan Master Dazhi specifically established these pure rules (qinggui) to support and remedy the defects of the bhikṣus in the Final Dharma (mofa), who have lost their integrity.
Consequently, former worthies have respectfully inherited and diligently practiced them; they possess instruction, they possess order, and they possess a beginning and an end."
At the end of the Shaoxing era, there were still mature elders within the monastic communities who could maintain the established traditions and dared not depart from their side for even a moment.
This principle clarifies that the former sages followed the teachings, stating that Master Dazhi specifically intended to establish formal rules and regulations.
Why is this? It is fundamentally for the purpose of rectifying the accumulated corruptions of the bhikṣus of the Final Dharma (mofa).
For this reason, the sages of old followed and upheld it, reverently practicing it with earnest devotion. Consequently, within the Dharma-gate there was instruction;
the superior acted and the subordinates emulated, resulting in order. "Order" (tiaoli) means regulation; "order" (li) means governance. Beginning with order and ending with order—thus it emerges.
During the end of the Shaoxing era— the latter years of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty—

there were still mature and venerable figures within the monastic communities who were able to uphold the precedents and statutes of the former sages, never daring to let them depart from their side for even a moment.

In recent years, its fundamental lineage has been lost; the guiding principles have not been maintained as principles, nor the disciplinary codes as codes. Even if such principles and codes exist, how can they be rectified?
Thus it is said: "If one guiding principle is upheld, all the details will unfold; if one mechanism is slackened, ten thousand affairs will fall into ruin.
Alas, the guiding principles and disciplinary codes are not being revitalized, and the monastic communities are not flourishing.
This section reveals that people of the present day have lost the fundamental tenets. In recent years, these have gradually declined;

their essential principles have been lost and their orderly succession has been destroyed. Those who preside over the Dharma fail to form a true net, and the threads of universal principle fail to form a true cord.
Although the framework of the net and cord still nominally exists, how could anyone like Baizhang arise once more to rectify them? Regarding this...
Because he is the presiding lord: if one main cord is raised, all the meshes naturally expand.
If the master relaxes even a single mechanism—"relax" meaning to neglect—then ten thousand mechanisms will all fall into ruin. Alas! The fundamental order can no longer be revitalized.
The rites and laws will likewise perish along with it; how then can the monastic groves flourish?
Only the ancients embodied the fundamental to rectify the derivative; they merely feared that the legal statutes were not strict, rather than fearing that students would lose their proper direction.

Their standard for correctness lay in public integrity. Today, however, the leaders of various quarters confuse the public with the private and seek to rectify the derivative with the derivative itself.
At the highest level, those who seek profit do so without regard for the Way; at the lowest level, those who harm others do so without regard for righteousness.

When those above and below are in error and confusion, and when guests and hosts are intermingled, how can monks turn toward what is correct and cause the monastic community to flourish? (From a Letter to Minister You)
This section clarifies the distinction between the ancient and the modern. Only the Sage investigates its root and rectifies its branches.
He need only worry that the master’s laws, regulations, and prohibitions are not strictly maintained;
he need not worry that students fail to find what they should uphold. Yet, in what does his method of rectification truly consist? It lies in impartiality.

It is simply a matter of integrity. Yet today, those who preside over the Dharma in various quarters entirely mix their private interests with public justice and use official affairs to satisfy their personal sentiments; thus, both the root and the branches have become inverted.
Those above merely seek gain and sustenance without regarding virtue and morality as their concern, while those below pilfer wealth and desire without knowing benevolence.
Taking the meaning as the foundation, both the superior and the subordinate fall into confusion; guest and host are entirely muddled.
If this is how the Dharma is maintained, how can one lead the monks toward the correct path and bring about the flourishing of the monastic community?

△ The words become increasingly plain, yet the intent becomes increasingly fierce; like vast surging waves, their momentum cannot be restrained. The point where true power is found lies solely in upholding justice and maintaining integrity.
It is simply to propagate the Way and save the world.
This chapter speaks of promoting the worthy and employing the capable; it depends upon the wisdom and discernment of the master. As it is said:
"Before fine jade is cut, it is no different from common tiles and stones; before a famous steed has galloped, it is indistinguishable from a sluggish hack. Upon reaching...
When it is cut open and polished, and when it is put to the test by being driven, then the jade and the stone, and the thoroughbred horse and the common steed, are distinguished from one another.

This section first uses a metaphor to explain this point, saying: "In the world, when a fine gem still harbors its raw luster (*bǎopó*) and has not yet been cut open, how does it differ from tiles and stones?
When a famous thoroughbred is among a herd and has not yet been driven, how does it differ from a common, sluggish horse?"
When the stone is split open and the jade emerges, its brilliance, purity, and luster become apparent;

when it is put to the test by being driven at full gallop, one immediately knows that it can pursue the wind for a thousand li. Thus, the jade and the stone, the thoroughbred and the hack, are clearly distinguished from one another.
Now, when a patch-robed monk possesses virtuous character yet remains unemployed, he is indistinguishable from the common crowd; how, then, can he be identified?
It depends upon men of lofty intelligence to recommend him through public consensus, entrust him with official duties, test him by his talent, and hold him accountable for accomplishing tasks.
Only then will he be far removed from the ranks of the mediocre.

This section now clearly reveals such a person. As for those practitioners who possess talent and virtue yet have not been recommended, how can they be distinguished from the common crowd? It depends on the master to possess the eye that discerns people;
a truly eminent and wise individual must raise them up through an impartial evaluation. Let others...

By means of their official duties, one examines the talents possessed by others and holds them accountable for accomplishing their tasks, thereby enabling both their talent and virtue to be fully displayed.
Only then does one realize that they are vastly different from the common masses. It is like selecting a single pearl from among a thousand or ten thousand;
its value naturally becomes many times greater than ordinary ones. This is truly due to the skill of the merchant.
He was a man of refined mind and exquisite skill.
This passage shows that he maintained his hidden traces and held himself in high esteem, remaining unmoved by fame or reputation.
When Master Oran Ti first visited Tiantai Huguo to consult with Yuan Budai, the following occurred during a formal lecture:
He recited the verse by Pang Mase on "Selecting the Buddha," arriving at the line: "This is the field for selecting the Buddha. Ciyuan shouted at him, and Chan’an attained great enlightenment.

He offered this verse of realization: "At the limit of deliberation, one sees the title; At the end of the road, one enters the examination hall. Grasping the tip of the brush, wind and rain rush forth;
Turning back now, I shall not be a 'Plum-Blossom Official' (the first graduate). From then on, he concealed his traces in Tian...
The Chancellor, Lord Qian, admired his character and urged him to take up the position of abbot at Tianfeng Temple to engage with the world.
Upon hearing this, Hui’ou said, "I do not understand hanging up the head of a sheep while selling the meat of a dog. He then fled that very night.
Chan Master Or-an Shi-ti of Jiao-shan in Zhenjiang Prefecture was the son of the Luo family of Taizhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ci-an Jingyuan and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Nanyue.
It is said that when Or-an first visited Chan Master Ci-an Yuan of Bu-dai at Huo-guo Temple on Mount Tiantai, Master Ci-an ascended the hall and cited the story of Pang Jushi.
The layman asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "When you can suck up the waters of the Yangtze River in a single draught, I will tell you. At these words, the layman attained sudden and great enlightenment and presented this verse:
"The ten directions gather together, Each and every one practicing non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; When the mind is empty..."
"Returning after passing the imperial examination"—this refers to the phrase "the field for selecting Buddhas. When Caan uttered a loud shout, Wuan heard it and attained sudden, great enlightenment.
He composed a verse on his realization, which says: "At the limit of deliberation, one sees the title; At the end of the road, one enters the examination hall.
Raising the tip of the brush, wind and rain rush forth; This time, I shall not seek to be the first to pluck the flowers."
Lord, from that time forth, he concealed his traces on Mount Tiantai. Prime Minister Qian Xiangzu, whose courtesy name was Xiangxian, sought the Way from Chan Master Huan’an.
Admiring the Master’s character, he invited him to take charge of Tianfeng Temple, urging him to emerge into the world.
Upon hearing this, Huan’an laughed and said, "I do not understand."
"Hanging up a goat's head while selling dog meat. That night, he simply fled and disappeared, concealing his person.
△ The one who has realized the truth does not set foot upon names or positions. Observe his departure: what was his intention?
If one were a person of the present day, one would only fear being too late.
This chapter is intended to identify people by their words; it seeks out and highlights those who have transcended the world.
At the beginning of the Qiandao era, Xiatang was residing at Guoqing Temple. There, he saw Huikan’s eulogy for the image of Yuancong, which said: "He does not rely on the original..."
[He] divided [the teachings], causing distress and confusion among sentient beings. Looking up to him, those with eyes were as if blind. The wind and moon of Chang’an pervade both past and present;
what man would walk groping along the walls? Xiatang, filled with surprise and joy, exclaimed: "I never thought this Chan Hall had such a son!"
He searched for him everywhere and eventually found him at the heart of the river. He firmly requested that he be appointed to the first seat among the assembly.
"Qiandao" was the era name of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty. Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan of Lingyin Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture was the son of the Peng family of Meishan.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin, belonging to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage. Because...
Seeing the image of Ananda in the Hall of Universal Worthy (Ciyuan-tong), he said: "Not abiding in his own station, he troubles and confuses sentient beings;
those who gaze up at him have eyes like the blind. The wind and moon of Chang'an penetrate both past and present—what man would grope along the walls?"
When Xia Tang saw this eulogy, he was both startled and delighted, saying, "I did not expect Ci'an to have such an outstanding child who transcends his peers.
He immediately sought him out everywhere until he found him at Jiaoshan Temple on Jiangxin Island.
From among the great multitude, he requested that he serve as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò) to act as the eyes for gods and men—this is called "the name following the reality."
When reality arrives, the name manifests of itself; what need is there to strive for it? Let students exert themselves!
This chapter shows that the instructions of the Perfected One (zhiren) are unfailing; when the time arrives, they correspond perfectly.
In the early years of the Andong era, Huikan suddenly visited Xiatang at Mount Huqiu.

When the monastics and laypeople of Gusu heard of his lofty reputation, they went to the prefecture to petition for him to reside at Juebao Monastery in the city. Upon hearing this, Huikan said, "This was the instruction my late master gave me:
'In the future, when you encounter Old Shou, stop there. Now it is as if two seals have met. He then joyfully accepted the invitation. Indeed...
Juebao was formerly known as Laoshou An (according to the *Huiqiu Jiwen*).
"Pian" describes the manner of a bird flying swiftly, or it signifies spontaneity.
Hearing that Oran possessed a spirit of lofty integrity, the monks and laypeople of Gusu went to visit Master Xiatang at Huqiu Temple; they even reached the Prefectural Governor.
When he was invited to reside at Juebao Temple in the city, Chan Master An heard of this and said, "This was the instruction my late master gave me:
'In the future, when you encounter Old Shou (Old Age), you shall stop there. It is as if the tally from the past has now been joined with its counterpart.
He then joyfully accepted the invitation; for Juebao had formerly been named Old Shou Hermitage. △ Although this was so...
Matters possess a fixed principle that does not shift. Why, then, do you say it stops when encountering an old man?
You must know that the wisdom-eye is so sharp and lucid that it penetrates everything without omission.
This chapter clarifies how supreme words move people; who would not revere and love them?

Once, after Master An had entered the monastery, a donor requested a *xiaocan* (small discourse), saying: "The Way is eternal and never changes, yet worldly affairs have their decay and must inevitably transform.
In the past, the various patriarchs of Nanyue in Jiangxi took antiquity as their instruction; let us examine what was appropriate and what was not. Holding [this view], he said:

By means of the Middle Way, he strove to harmonize with the human heart, taking awakening as his standard; thus, the original spirit remains lofty and has not faded even to this day. However, if we speak from the standpoint of the patch-robed monks:
to gain realization prior to words is to do a disservice to our school’s tradition; to have clarity within a single phrase is to bury the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, it is said: "When walking, one reaches the end of the water; sitting, one watches the clouds arise. For this reason, the monastic community...
Suo was delighted to hear what he had never heard before; those who returned were as numerous as at a marketplace (this account differs from the *Yulu*).
After Huigan entered Juebao Monastery, a patron invited him to preach the Dharma. Ascending the seat, he said:
"The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs penetrates through all time, fundamentally unchanging. The affairs of the world, however, move from name to profit and naturally undergo change."
In the past, when the various patriarchs such as Mazu of Jiangxi and Shitou of Nanyue engaged in any activity, they all examined the methods of former sages to serve as instruction and admonition;
they investigated what was permissible and what was not to establish the fundamental principles of their school.
Uphold this by means of the Middle Way; exert yourself single-mindedly to harmonize with the human heart, and ensure that awakening is taken as the standard of instruction.
This is why the spirit of pure simplicity remains majestic and still persists today without having faded.

Yet, if we speak in terms of the "one critical phrase" (or "one point") within the Gate of the Monks, even if you were to realize it prior to words, you would already be falling short of our school’s tradition. If you further...

The meaning was clear beneath every phrase; yet, as time passed, even Buddhas and patriarchs were seen to be buried within it. Nevertheless, "When the path to the water's end is reached, sit and watch the clouds arise.
Having spoken thus, he descended from his seat. Because of this single discourse on the Dharma, both monastics and laypeople rejoiced at hearing what they had never heard before.
From that time on, those who returned to pay their respects came and went like the constant flow of people through a bustling marketplace.
△ Gold has its price; white jade has its luster. Neither is obtained from others.
This chapter speaks of knowing people through the Way, like water poured into water.
Once Huikan had taken charge as abbot, the gentry and commoners flocked to him in great numbers.
When word of this reached Tiger Hill (Húqiū), Xiatang remarked, "This mountain barbarian and clumsy fellow is letting loose his 'blind' Chan to deal with that pack of wild fox spirits."
Upon hearing this, Huikang responded with a verse: "The mountain barbarian Du Ao has gained the ability to hate; Leading a multitude and guiding disciples as if he had never done so before.
Transcending conventions, he turns the handle of the broom upside down; Blindly practicing Chan, he treats the wild fox monks.
Xiatang merely laughs. (Recorded in *Jimu*)
