After Master Huikan took over as the abbot of Juebao, scholars and commoners flocked to him like a swarm of birds;
they came in great numbers, coming and going in harmony to seek his guidance. News of this reached Tiger Hill, where several monks spread the word.

Upon hearing this, Xiatang was delighted. He remarked playfully, "This mountain barbarian, Du-aozi—'Du' meaning he does not follow the established tracks, and 'Ao' meaning he is contrary to human sentiment—has come here to let loose some of his blind Zen."
"Patting" means to stroke. When a blind person cannot walk by themselves, they must have someone pat their shoulder as they go;
this is said because they are not "carefree. This group of wild fox spirits you are dealing with is exactly like that.
These words seem like a jest, but in truth, they are earnest—expressing the utmost praise and envy. Upon hearing this, Or-an replied with a verse: The mountain barbarian Du...
He twisted it so that the monks were unable to withstand him; this thief recognizes a thief. Leading his assembly and managing his followers, he seems as if he has never done so before.
Do not try to follow or evade him by any means. Transcending the ordinary, he turns the handle of the broom upside down—how brilliantly revealed!
He treats wild fox spirits with the blunt force of Zen; how many among them could truly know this? Xiatang merely laughs. It would be enough to kill a man. (The words emerged spontaneously.)

Thus, his true feelings were fully revealed; it was indeed a meeting like that of two canopies leaning toward one another. Those who do not understand the flow of the discourse, how could they recognize the subtle excellence of these two masters?
This passage states that in studying the Way, one must maintain equanimity; being either too light or too heavy is equally unsuitable.
Master Or-an said to Minister Zeng Gong Dai: "The essential point of studying the Way is like using a balance scale to determine the weight of objects:
one simply maintains its equilibrium. How could partiality or imbalance be permissible? To shift the weight forward or pull it back is equally biased.
By understanding this, one can study the Way. (As seen in the letter from Master Zeng.)
He said to Master Zeng: "The ultimate essential of studying the Way is like one who weighs objects:
one takes balance alone as correctness. A bias is not permissible, nor is heaviness. To lean forward is called 'heavy'; to lean backward is called 'biased.
Both are errors that result in a lack of balance. Long ago, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'Studying the Way is like tuning a lute string.'"
Regarding the Dharma: if it is too tight, the strings will easily break; if it is too loose, the sound will be discordant. It is appropriate that the tension be balanced between these two extremes.
Understanding this, one can learn the Ultimate Way (Zhidao). Diligence in the morning and indolence in the evening is a universal malady. I wish for this to serve as a standard;
yet, maintaining evenness in a single phrase is the most difficult thing to achieve. Unless one is earnestly devoted to the Ultimate Way, this will not be possible.
In the end, it can never be settled.
This chapter refers to those who uphold the Dharma; they should know that the monastic community (*saṃgha*) is the foundation, and must not abandon or disdain the *śramaṇas* (monks).
Wuzu An said: "Virtue and Way are the root of the monastic community; the *śramaṇas* are the root of virtue and Way. The abbot is [the one who sustains this]."

To cast aside and weary of the monastics is to forget the Way and its Virtue (*moral*). Once the Way and its Virtue are forgotten, by what means can one cultivate transformation and edification, maintain the monastic community (*saṃgha*), and guide those who come to study?

The ancients embodied the fundamental to rectify the derivative; they were concerned that the Way and its Virtue would not be practiced, rather than being concerned that the monastic community would lose its proper place.
Therefore it is said: "The monastic community is preserved by the monastics; the monastics are preserved by the Way and its Virtue. To dwell [in this way]—
"If one fails to uphold the Way and virtue, then the monastic community will fall into ruin" (as seen in the writings of Jiantang).
It is said: "If a person can maintain the Way and preserve virtue, they truly constitute the great root and foundation of the monastic community.
Just as eminent men and wise scholars are able to perfect what they have studied, so too are the monastics the very foundation of the Way and virtue. Thus he resided there.
If those who hold office do not encourage and guide their disciples, they are abandoning and detesting the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*).
Once the Way and its Virtue are forgotten, what dharma will the administrators have to practice for cultivation and transformation, or to organize the monastic community and attract students?
Those of antiquity embodied the fundamental to rectify the derivative; what they worried about was that their Way and its Virtue would not be put into practice. Ultimately, they did not...

I am concerned that the monastic communities (chōrin) may or may not find their proper place. Therefore, it is said: "The monastic community was originally established for the sake of the *natsushi* (monastics);
thus, those whom it protects are the monastics. Monastics are people who practice the Way and its Virtue (*dōtokku*), and what they protect is, in turn, the Way and its Virtue.
If the abbot does not protect the monastics, and if the monastics lack the Way...
Virtue. When both of these are lost, the monastic community will surely witness its decline.
△ The words and intent of this chapter flow smoothly, strung together like beads; they all aim solely to teach people how to recognize the fundamental source.
This chapter states that the essential point for a ruler lies in recognizing the worthy. Once the worthy are obtained, the Dharma has a successor. Master An said:
"To be a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the essential lies in recognizing the worthy, not in considering oneself worthy. Therefore, one who harms the worthy is foolish;
one who conceals the worthy is ignorant; one who envies the worthy is deficient. To obtain the glory of a single lifetime is not as good as [obtaining the glory] of an entire age."

Fame: To attain fame for a single lifetime is not as good as finding a single virtuous monk-disciple, so that future students have a teacher and the monastic community has a leader (Letter to Yuanji).
To be a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one must possess the clarity to discern others; one must recognize who among the multitude is truly virtuous and worthy.
Such a person is a true host to the virtuous. Originally, being virtuous does not consist in regarding oneself as virtuous, but in recognizing the virtuous as truly virtuous.
If one were to harm or disparage such a person, who would there be to provide support? One cannot avoid falling into folly.
When one errs, who will inform the worthy sages of this concealment? It is difficult to avoid the affliction of ignorance.
When one envies the worthy, who will provide mutual encouragement? It is difficult to avoid the reproach of being shallow and limited.

Even if one were to attain the glory and distinction of a single lifetime, it would not be as good as attaining a beautiful reputation for all generations. Furthermore, attaining a beautiful reputation for all generations is not as good as attaining [the state of] One.
It is even more admirable when such a virtuous patch-robed monk appears. Why is this?

It ensures that future students have a true and authentic teacher, and that the monastic community has a master who practices the Way. To find and appoint such a person is truly a magnificent achievement.
If one can indeed find a true practitioner of the Way who establishes the fundamental principles and regulations, standing preeminent throughout the age, they will be able to continue the lineage.
What joy there is in a glorious reputation lasting for a thousand years!
This verse reveals how the ancients came and went with ease, unattached and free from lingering ties.
It was on the fourth day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Chunxi era that Or-an moved to Jiaoshan; this is what he first showed.
He was slightly ill. He then wrote by hand and gave a single inkstone to part with to the District Magistrate, Vice Minister Zeng Gong.
By midnight, he passed away. The Magistrate lamented him with this verse: "Lightly fluttering, a pair of sandals followed the wind; Not a single thing remained within the cloth bag.
Leaving behind only this 'Tao-hong' (inkwell)—what will it be used for? This old man has no brush to judge the void."
Or-an resided at Mount Jiao for his third year. This day was the fourth of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Shaoxing era (1178).

On the eve of his passing, he manifested a slight illness; he composed a letter and prepared an inkstone to bid farewell to the Prefectural Governor, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Lord Zeng Dai.
That very night at midnight, he entered parinirvāṇa. When morning dawned, Lord Zeng—
When he arrived, the Master had already passed away. He then composed a verse to mourn him, saying: "Fluttering, the single sandal pursues the west wind.
This line refers to the Master’s return, like that of the First Patriarch. "Not a single thing remains within the cloth bag."
This phrase further states: "Like a foolish cloth bag, all things are placed within the bag, yet the Master’s cloth bag contains not a single thing;
this reveals his freedom of coming and going. The line, "Leaving behind the clay inkwell—what will you use?
refers to the *táohóng*. *Táohóng* is the name for an inkstone; there are varieties such as the *bǎohóng*, *shíhóng*, and *hánxīnghóng*. This phrase describes the Master’s final moments.
In the end, he sent me a seal-stone. Regarding the phrase "intending to use it as a base," this means that while I have no use for the Master’s seal-stone, I do not possess one myself.
Thus he said: "This old man has no brush with which to judge the void. This sentence is both the Minister’s own expression of humility and a word of supreme praise;
it means that the Master’s Way is as vast as the great void, and that I likewise lack such a thing.
The brush can delineate this empty space; such is the skill of the master and his guest.
Yet within this, there is a place where life and death are not mutually related. Can a person know it? If they know it, one may converse with them.
This chapter states that the capacity and aptitude of a person are inherently determined by their own lot and cannot be forcibly taught.
Master Xiatang Yuan said to Huan’ou: "The talent and capacity of people naturally vary in size;
truly, they cannot be taught. Thus, one with small paper cannot carry a large load; one with a short rope cannot draw from a deep well; and the owl can only catch its prey at night."
One may discern the finest tip of autumn hair, yet by day one may stare with wide-open eyes and fail to see hills and mountains;
this is because one's lot is fixed (*fen-ding*). This section clarifies that human beings inherently possess a fixed lot. It says: "The talent, strength, and capacity of human beings..."
Innate capacity has its own magnitude; once one's nature is established, how could it be taught to become large or small?
For example, a small sheet of paper cannot possibly contain a large object. Paper is the bark of trees; when Cai Lun used it to manufacture paper, he was limited by its nature.
A short rope cannot draw water from great depths. Thus it is said: "The small cannot contain the large."

In the "Zhilè" (The Ultimate Joy) chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, it is said that the *chīxiū* is a strange bird; when it cries, it rains. By day its eyes see nothing, yet by night it can discern the finest hair of an autumn down.
This is also found in the "Qiūshui" (Autumn Floods) chapter of the *Zhuangzi*. It is now cited here as a metaphor:
although this bird belongs to the class of feathered creatures, why is it that in the deepest darkness of night, it can pluck a flea and examine the finest hair?
Even under the bright daylight, if one opens their eyes wide, they cannot see even a mound or a mountain standing directly before them.
Why is this? It is because the boundaries of one's innate constitution are fixed.
In the past, Jing of the Southern Hall transmitted the Way of Dongshan; his realization of the profound and subtle was deep, penetrating, and clearly manifest.

Yet, when he came to serve as the abbot of various monasteries, his influence did not flourish wherever he went. When our late master Yuanwu returned to Shu, he visited Dazui together with Master Tongfan.
Huijing was seen to be negligent and lax; he had fallen into a state of general indolence and neglect. When Master [Huai]gan was about to pass away, he did not question Jing at all.
Upon returning to the middle of the road, Daofan said, "Jing is a fellow practitioner and dharma friend of yours; why did you not offer him a single word of instruction?

The Master replied, "In governing the world and presiding over a community, the primary requirement is for laws and regulations to come first. The implementation of these laws depends on one's wisdom and capability. Whether one is capable or incapable," [is determined by this].
"Given their inherent dispositions, how could they be taught? Fan nodded in agreement (*Hǔqiū Jìwén*).

This section states that once a disposition is fixed, it is difficult to force a change. While the preceding passage used material objects as metaphors, this one uses human beings to illustrate the point.
Formerly, there was Chan Master Nántáng Yuánjìng of Dàsuí in Pěngzhōu; he was a great scholar from Yùshān in Lángzhōu.
He was the son of Zhao Yuezhong and the successor to Zen Master Wuzu Fayan. He transmitted the Dharma of the Dongshan lineage and was renowned for his sharp insight;
his understanding of the profound and subtle principles was both deep and clearly manifest.

Dongshan once certified him, saying, "The essential pivot-points of all quarters of the school shall not escape your grasp. When he eventually emerged from seclusion to serve as an abbot, in all that he did—
Everywhere he went, he was unable to revitalize the Dongshan tradition. When our late master Yuanwu returned to Shu, he visited Dawsui together with Master Juefan.
There they saw Master Jing, who was generally negligent in his affairs;

the grand principles of the monastic community and all its various regulations had completely fallen into disuse. Our late master, recognizing that such was his talent and capacity, [proceeded as follows].
He did not question them at all. Upon returning to the halfway point, Fàn asked, "Jìng and I are fellow practitioners and dharma friends.
Yesterday I saw that he was entirely disorganized in every respect; why did you fail to offer him even a single word of inspiration or guidance?

The former master replied, "In general, when responding to the world, practicing the Way, presiding over a community, or leading disciples, it is essential that one prioritizes the enforcement of discipline."
The decree that its laws must be implemented depends solely upon the wisdom, knowledge, and capability of individuals.
Whether one is capable or incapable is determined by one's own long-standing disposition. It is not that others do not know [the law]; it is simply that they are unable to carry it out.
Since they cannot carry it out, how could I possibly instruct them? When Fan heard this, he nodded his head. To nod means that there is something in one's mind [that is agreed with].
He wears his collar high; his gaze is lofty and his stride is broad. This is the bearing of a great man, majestic and dignified—whom would not recognize him?
Yet, alas, it cannot be faked. There must not be even a hair’s breadth of deviation from the truth. Students should regard this with profound trepidation.
This chapter states that one who studies the Way must first rectify the mind; when the mind is rectified, all things follow its transformation.
Xiatang said: "A student of the Way must first rectify their own mind, and only then can they rectify themselves and others."
Once the mind is rectified, the myriad things are settled. I have never heard of one whose mind is disciplined yet whose body remains in disorder.
The teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs proceeds from the interior to the exterior, and from the near to the distant. External sounds and forms are the ailments of the four limbs;

deluded passions arising within are the ailments of the heart and belly. I have never seen one whose mind is not rectified who can nonetheless govern external things, nor one whose body is not rectified [who can do so].
Yet they are unable to transform others.

This section teaches that one must first rectify one's own mind. That is to say, anyone who wishes to give rise to the supramundane mind and study the Unsurpassed Way must first establish this very mind in accordance with the teachings so that it is upright, and cleanse it until it is pure; only then...
One can rectify one’s own body and mind, and likewise rectify the body and mind of others.
When the mind is upright, all things follow suit and become upright. It has never been heard of anyone whose mind is already disciplined [who cannot do so].
Yet this body is still something in disorder. The teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs all proceed from within to without, and from the near to the distant.
Sounds and forms are what delude the person; the afflictions of the four limbs are external maladies.
The passions of deluded thoughts are maladies of the heart and belly, internal diseases.
I have never seen one who possesses peace and tranquility within their own mind yet cannot govern others, or one who is upright in their own person yet cannot transform others.
Indeed, the single mind is the root, and the myriad things are the branches and leaves. When the root is strong and substantial, the branches and leaves flourish;

when the root is withered and parched, the branches and leaves perish prematurely. One who learns the Way skillfully first governs the internal to resist the external, rather than coveting the external to the detriment of the internal.
Therefore, the essential for guiding others lies in purifying one's own mind. To rectify others, one must first rectify oneself. When the mind is upright, the self is established.
"Yet there has never been a case where the myriad things do not follow this transformation" (Letter to Vice Minister Yan).
This section clarifies that the mind is the root. For the single mind is the root, and the myriad things are the branches and leaves.

If the root is robust and full, then the branches and leaves will naturally flourish and grow luxuriantly. If it is... [if it is not so]... [the branches and leaves will wither].* *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.)*
If the root is withered, the branches and leaves will inevitably perish. Therefore, one who studies the Way well must first rectify the internal.
Once the internal is rectified, one can naturally withstand all external conditions. One must not greedily pursue external defilements, for they will instead harm one's own mind.
Those who wish to lead others away from delusion must first purify their own minds; if they wish to remove [delusion], they must first establish what is correct.

In governing others, one must first ensure that one is correct within oneself. Once the mind is correct and the self is established, it is impossible for there to be any principle by which the myriad things would not respond to one’s transformative teachings.
To rectify the mind and cultivate sincerity is the very foundation for transcending the world.
If this foundation is not established, all affairs will fall into neglect and ruin.
This chapter shows that the practice of the Way has its proper timing; when nourishment arrives, the flavor is naturally complete.
Master Jiantang Ji resided at Guanshan in Fanyang for nearly twenty years, eating only mugwort soup and millet, as if he had severed all intent toward honor and advancement.
Once, while descending the mountain, he heard the sound of wailing by the roadside. Jiantang was moved with compassion, and upon inquiring into it, [he learned...]

A family was stricken by a cold epidemic, resulting in the death of two members. Being too poor to afford the necessary funeral implements, they specifically borrowed coffins from the market to bury them.
The local people sighed with deep emotion and could not stop their lamentations.
This section clarifies that although his outward traces were obscured, his benevolent heart was naturally manifest.
Master Jiantang resided at Guanshan in Poyang County, Raozhou, for nearly twenty years. He ate wild amaranth and dock leaves for vegetables, and millet and sorghum for grain.
Within his breast, he never harbored a single thought of seeking honor, splendor, or high office. Whenever he descended the mountain and heard the voices of people by the roadside...
There was the sound of mournful weeping. Jiandang felt deeply moved by it. Upon inquiring into the matter, they replied, "At that time, two people died of cold-related illnesses;
because our family is poor and lacks the means for coffins and burial, we are grieving.
The Master went to the market and borrowed coffins for them to bury the deceased. The local people sighed with admiration without end.
Minister Li said to the scholar-officials, "The Elder Ji from our province is a monk of great realization. Furthermore, he bestows compassion upon all beings;
how could he remain long at Mount Guan? It happened that the Grand Councilor Wang was touring the various circuits as a Pacification Commissioner.
Upon reaching Jiujiang, he informed the Prefect Lin, who vacated the Dharma seat of Yuan Tong to welcome him. When Jian Tang heard this command, he said:
"My Way is being practiced! he exclaimed, and with joyful cheer, he trailed his staff as he arrived. Ascending the seat, he preached the Dharma, saying:

"The Universal Penetration does not open a pharmacy for the living; it sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. Who knows which one, free from calculation, will eat it and have cold sweat pour down their entire body?
The monastics and laypeople were struck with wonder, and from this point on, his Dharma assembly flourished greatly (*Lan’an Ji*).
This section clarifies that once the time had arrived, the transformation of the Way manifested spontaneously.

Minister Li Gong, whose given name was Hao, courtesy name De-yuan, and style name Chun-nian, read the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* in his youth as if visiting a familiar land. Upon attending upon Master Ying’an, he attained a profound realization.
He said to the scholar-officials: "The Elder Ji of our district is truly a man of virtue and a monk of great character.
Furthermore, he bestows benevolence and kindness upon others. How could this small mountain retreat suffice for the Master’s long-term residence?

He then summoned the State Councilor (Shumim) Wang Mingyuan—whom we now call a Director of the Court of Judicial Inspection—and the Pacification Commissioner (Xuanfu)—who is now known as a Circuit Inspector.
In various regions, what the Song dynasty called a *lu* (路) is now termed a *fu* (府).
He sent a letter to Lin Gongsuda, the Prefect of Jiujiang County, requesting that he be welcomed to the Dharma seat of Yuan Tong at Mount Lu.
Upon hearing this summons, Jiantang said, "The Way shall now proceed," and joyfully took up his staff and came. Ascending the seat, he preached the Dharma, saying: "Yuan Tong does not open..."
A medicine shop that sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. This refers to when a monk asked Caoshan, "What is most precious in the world?
Caoshan replied, "The head of a dead cat. Danxia’s verse says: "Foul-smelling and red-rotting, it is unbearable to hear;
Wherever it moves, it lightly soils the body with blood. For what reason does no one offer a price? It is because it is not [a living thing]."
"A world-treasure" is a metaphor for matters that transcend the ordinary. Who knows which one is free from calculation? Upon consuming it, cold sweat flows over the entire body.
When both the monastics and the laity heard of this, they were all struck with wonder. From this, the Dharma assembly was greatly revitalized.
For twenty or thirty years, the ancients dwelt in the cold reaches of mountain corners, without a single trace of heat; suddenly, they were pushed forward by others.
When it comes forth, it immediately permeates the heavens and scorches the earth; how could it be compared to those things nowadays that are merely steamed and sold for profit?
Those who study this chapter should maintain the grand principle and not be拘泥 (confined) by minor details.

Jiandang said: "In antiquity, when cultivating the person and governing the mind, one shared the Way with others; when initiating undertakings and establishing enterprises, one shared the merit with others;
and when the Way was perfected and achievements were manifest, one shared the fame with others.
Thus, the Way was never obscure, merit was never unaccomplished, and fame was never not honored."
This section speaks of how the ancients were pure and without private interest.

It means that after the ancients cultivated their persons and regulated their minds, and once their persons were upright and their minds had attained penetration, they did not privately appropriate the Way for themselves, but instead shared this Way clearly with all people.
Whether initiating a single matter or establishing a single enterprise, once the task was accomplished and the work completed, they did not privately claim its merit.

Thus, one shares the manifestation of its efficacy with all people. Once the Way is perfected and its efficacy is manifest, one does not privately claim its fame, but rather shares the glorification of its name with all people. Therefore, when speaking of the Way, there is no aspect of the Way that is not clarified;
when discussing its efficacy, there is no achievement of efficacy that is not realized; and when recording its name, there is no renown that is not honored. This is why...
It is only natural that [the Way] remains undiminished throughout a thousand or ten hundred generations.
Modern people, however, are not so. They cling exclusively to their own way, fearing only that others might surpass them;
furthermore, they are unable to follow what is good or pursue righteousness to broaden themselves. They monopolize their own merits and do not wish for others to possess them, nor can they...
To employ the worthy and the capable yet to consider oneself great; to monopolize one's own reputation and not share it with others;

and furthermore, to be unable to lead others through humble brilliance so as to achieve one's own realization—therefore, the Way cannot avoid being obscured, merit cannot avoid being diminished, and fame cannot avoid being disgraced.
This is the great distinction among scholars of both ancient and modern times.
This section states that people today are exclusively private and lack public spirit. People today are not like this.
They practice their own way alone, fearing only that the ways of others might surpass their own; furthermore, they are unwilling to humble themselves and follow what is good.
They strive only to conform to their own righteousness, seeking merely to expand their own self-importance. Even when establishing merit, they seek solely to obscure the merits of others. Not...
They do not share [their achievements] with others, nor can they entrust capable and virtuous men to assist them.
They seek only to exalt themselves. Even if they achieve fame and undertake great tasks for the sake of self-display, they are unwilling to share them with others.
Furthermore, they cannot practice humility and accumulate virtue, blending their light with the dust of the world to welcome and guide others; they seek only—
This is what it means to be self-attained. With such a private mind, even if one possesses the Way, one cannot avoid being obscured by that private mind;
even if one possesses merit, one cannot avoid being diminished by that private mind; even if one possesses fame, one cannot avoid being disgraced by that private mind.
These two types of learners constitute a definitive and fundamental distinction between the ancients and the moderns. — Public (Gong)

I have made this single judgment. There is a vast difference between categories, as profound as that between heaven and abyss. It is you who have caused your fame to spread throughout the world and whose Way has been exalted through both past and present.
As for those who harbor private ambitions and rely on themselves, it is said that their roots are shallow and thus not firm; their foundations are thin and thus easily endangered.
Consequently, their Way becomes obscured and their achievements suffer loss and disgrace—this is an inevitable principle.

This chapter states that one who studies the Way must cultivate it with diligent resolve and profound practice; only when one’s internal resources have been nurtured to a state of abundance and greatness can they be brought forth for use.
Jiantang said: "Studying the Way is like planting a tree. If you cut it down while it is just beginning to flourish, it may serve as firewood."
If felled while it is flourishing, its timber can be used for rafters and eaves; if felled when it has reached moderate maturity, it can serve as pillars and beams;
if felled when it is fully grown and large, it can become lintels and ridgepoles. Is this not taking advantage of distant labor while securing great utility?
This section first clarifies the matter through an analogy. The practice of the Way is like a worldly person planting a tree:
as soon as it flourishes and grows, they wish to cut it down; though it serves no great purpose, it can still provide firewood.
When it has grown somewhat large and flourishing, one cuts it down; it can be used for rafters and eaves. In the state of Zhou they are called *chuī*, and in Qi they are called *jué*;

these are the same as the *chuān* (purlins). When it has become somewhat robust and solid, one wishes to cut it down; it can serve as pillars and beams. A *yíng* is a column; a *bǎng* is a lintel or beam-head.
When it is old and large before being cut down, it can be made into a ridge beam or main beam. The wood at the very top of the roof is called the *jīmù*.
The ridgepole; that which supports the ridgepole is called the beam. Is this not taking a distant task and yet achieving great benefit?
Therefore, the ancients held that their Way was inherently vast and not narrow, and their resolve was far-reaching and profound rather than shortsighted.

His words were sublime and not base. Although they encountered friction with the times and he was reduced to the extremities of hunger and cold, nearly perishing in the mountain ravines, his lingering influence and remaining legacy have endured for a thousand years;
even now, later generations still take them as a model and transmit them.

Had he instead sought to accommodate himself to narrow paths, pursued immediate goals to seek conformity, and used humble speech to serve the powers of the age, his benefit would have been limited to the glory of a single person.
"How could there be any remaining grace to be widely bestowed upon future generations?
(The Two Letters to Assistant Minister Li). This section precisely clarifies that the Way must be truly cultivated.
Therefore, those of old who studied the Way knew only that this Way is inherently vast and boundless, and cannot be learned through a narrow or limited capacity; thus, what they established—
His aspirations were lofty and profound, rather than shallow or mundane. The words he uttered were honorable and expansive, rather than base or petty.

Although he encountered adverse circumstances—“adverse circumstances” (zhuyu) meaning the teeth of men meshing so that one moves forward while the other recedes, a metaphor for the sense of being beset by misfortune—he may have been reduced to the extremities of hunger and cold, even reaching the point of perilous ruin in mountain valleys.
Although the person has passed away, the way and spirit they left behind, and their enduring legacy, remain undiminished for a thousand years;
later generations still take them as a model, transmitting them from generation to generation without ceasing.
Had it not been for this, if one were to view this Way as narrow and trivial, or act with mere expediency and compromise during the practice of its observance—
Regarding oneself, with shallow and mundane ambitions, one flatters others to seek their favor; with lowly and trivial words, one serves those in power.
Even if some slight benefit is obtained, it can only bring glory and distinction to a single person.
How could there be any remaining grace or benevolence that extends to a thousand or ten thousand generations thereafter? The metaphor is thus made clear.
The explanations are thorough and clear, yet it is a pity that no one puts them into practice.
This chapter reveals that the meaning of the Way is in perfect accord, no different from water and milk blending together.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Chunxi era, Jiantang [Zhao] traveled once more from Mount Jingxing in Tiantai to Yinjing.
There, the Grand Secretary Lord Wu, retired in leisure, composed thirteen poems in the style of Yuanming (Tao Qian) at the Xiuxiu Hall to see him off; the first reads:
I have retired to the forest depths and have long since grown distant from the world. Fortunately, there is a spiritual friend who frequently visits my humble cottage;
he accompanies me as we discourse on the Way and delights in my reading of the Buddha’s scriptures. Now that he has ascended to the mountain crags, I too shall prepare my carriage for the journey.
I wish now to set forth my alms-bowl and follow my Master to partake together of the vegetarian meal. Having cast off these worldly burdens, I shall dwell forever among the crags and rocks.
These cliffs are indeed lofty, rising prominently above the maps of mountains and seas; yet if compared with the loftiness of my Master, these cliffs fall short by comparison.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Chunxi era, Master Jiantang accepted a second invitation from Yijing Temple, departing from Jingxing Rock on Mount Tiantai.
Wu Gong Fu, a Grand Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel and an eminent Confucian scholar of the Song dynasty, had retired to live as a recluse in the Xiuxiu Hall;
he composed thirteen verses in the style of Mr. Tao Yuanming to be presented to Master Jiantang.
Farewell. The first [verse] says: Since I retired from official service and returned to live beneath the trees, I have long been estranged from the world.
Fortunately, I have relied upon you, Master, who are a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

You frequently visit my thatched cottage to speak for me of the words of the sublime Way that transcends the world. Furthermore, you cherish that I am able to read the sutras of the Buddhas of the past.
The letter reads: "When you, Master, returned to the mountain crag, I also prepared oil for your carriage and went with you.

Once we reached the cave, you spread out your bowl and ate from it before me; I too was fortunate to share the simple vegetables with you, thereby casting off the burdens of worldly toil and all vulgar, evil habits.
I only wish that I may dwell here on this crag with you forever. And so it ends.
Thus, this cliff is indeed exceedingly lofty and precipitous; it stands out prominently, far beyond the scope of any map or painting of mountains and seas.

Although the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) contains maps that exhaustively depict the famous mountains and magnificent landscapes of the world, even these cannot capture the sublime excellence of this cliff.
If one were to compare this to the loftiness of our Master’s virtue, even this cliff would fall short.

I was born within a mountain cave where the four sides are rugged and steep; there is a cliff named Gyeongseong (Star of the Landscape), and though I have longed to reach it, how many years have passed?
Now, for the first time, I believe this place is truly marvelous. Upon surveying Xiaozhong Mountain, I have further found you as my master; these two wonders are not easily described.
The second is this: I have taken rest from further rebirth within a mountain cave, where on all four sides there are rugged and precipitous forms.
The rugged and imposing peaks possess a most lovely appearance. There is another cliff named Jingsing (Auspicious Star), which I have long desired to visit but have been unable to reach;
I have harbored this wish for several years. Having arrived today, I finally believe with my own eyes that it is indeed marvelous and extraordinary.
How can one see its marvel? Let us observe it for a moment: the myriad mountains stand tall and upright.
The myriad waters all flow together and merge into something small; is this not truly marvelous?
Not only is the cliff itself wondrous, but we have further obtained our Master as its lord. With these two excellences, it is not something that can be spoken of lightly.
My home lies upon a lake and mountain; wherever my eyes turn, there are forests and hills. If compared to the splendor of this mountain, even a small hillock is truly beyond comparison.

From its clouds and peaks, one can see for a thousand li; its springs and rocks flow through the four seasons. Having arrived here for but a single visit, I have already surpassed the excursions of the Five Lakes.
The third said: "My family has constructed our residence upon a lake-side mountain. Whatever meets my eyes is nothing but green waters and blue peaks;
with its secluded forests and rolling hills, it may be said that we have found our proper place.
Yet, compared to the towering loftiness and exquisite beauty of this cliff, my dwelling is like a mere molehill—how could it possibly be its equal?"
"Pai-p'ou" refers to small mounds. Why is it that they cannot be compared [to this place]? Observe for a moment as you cast your gaze upon it:
the clouds and mountains of a thousand *li* are visible at once. Furthermore, what is most delightful is that the springs and rocks flow constantly through the four seasons.
I have only just arrived today, yet its secluded charm is already so serene that it surpasses those of the past.
I have roamed the Five Lakes;
I am now seventy-five years old. Like a lingering sunset hanging from the treetops, even if my life has not yet ended, how could it last much longer?

I still hope to dwell among the forest trees and share the final light with you, Master. Suddenly a solitary cloud emerges for a moment, and those near and far are struck with a sense of hurried alarm.
The fourth [point] says: "I am now seventy-five years old. My remaining vitality is like a single fragment of the setting sun hanging upon the tip of a tree branch.
Even if this body remains and does not yet depart, how could it possibly endure for long?
It is said that there are not many days left; though I have grown old, my heart still harbors hope."
While dwelling in this forest, he shared in the master’s final radiance. Although the master now departs for another place, it is like a solitary cloud momentarily appearing;
those both near and far are all struck with alarm and confusion. "Cānghuáng" (蒼黃) describes the appearance of urgency and haste.

Long ago, during the time of King Tang, there was no rain for seven years. Suddenly, a solitary cloud briefly appeared; the dogs barked and ran wild, and all were thrown into a state of frantic confusion.

My love for mountains has been a constant part of my nature, yet I am pitiable for being bound by worldly conventions. Recently, while serving as the governor of Dangtu Prefecture, I did not know of Yijing Mountain.
I envy the Master for coming and yet departing; ashamed of myself, what more can I say? I still hope you will not stay long, so that you may return to see me out my remaining years.
The fifth verse says: My love for mountain forests is truly the nature of my original disposition; to be bound by worldly sentiments—
Truly, this is pitiable. When I previously served as the governor of Dangtu, I was tirelessly immersed in the sea of officialdom;
I did not realize that there was such a place of seclusion and tranquility there, which would be considered extraordinary and wonderful. All of this was due to being constrained by worldly affairs.
I alone have envied my Master, who once came from that place of seclusion and is now departing for it, truly attaining [the state of peace].
As for the joy of seclusion and tranquility, I am ashamed not to know it; what more can be said? Though you are departing, I only hope that you will not stay away for long.
I pray that you will return to see me through this final fragment of my remaining years.
The Master’s mind is like extinguished ashes; his form is like withered wood. Why does he respond to the returning monk as an echo answers from a valley?
Beholding my defiled body, I am now waiting for a bath of *amṛta*. I pray further that you will kindle the Buddha-lamp to serve as a bright candle for me.
The sixth [point] says: "My Master’s mind has forgotten all worldly concerns, becoming like extinguished ashes;
since the mind is thus still, the body is likewise withered. As Zhuangzi said, when Ziyou asked Nan-guo Ziqi:
'How is it that the mind can truly be made like extinguished ashes, and the body truly be made like withered wood? Thus, both mind and body [are at rest]."
"Ji, for what reason have you become one to whom the monastics from the four quarters turn? This too is like an echo responding in a valley;

it accords with things without a mind of its own. Behold my body, defiled by the dust of worldly toil; I truly desire to wait upon the Master so that he may bathe me with the essence of *amṛta* (clarified butter).
I further pray that our Master will illuminate the heart-lamp of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to act as my representative."
Its radiance illuminates me.
The trees, spreading and lush upon the crags, have all cast their shade since summer began. What was once a wasteland of thorns for many years has, in a single day, become a verdant forest.
I and this monk together listen to the sound of the ocean tide. In human life there is much gathering and dispersing; this sudden parting startles the heart. The seventh verse says:
The trees upon the cliff, one by one sparse and interlacing, have since the arrival of summer grown lush and formed a canopy.
They shade the interior of the cliff, which may be called the height of coolness. In former times, it was but a thicket of brambles.
The land where we were born—within a few years, we did not realize that it had suddenly become a Buddhist sanctuary.
Just now, I and the monks who have come from the four quarters listened to our Master’s preaching of the Dharma, like the sound of the ocean tides, never missing its appointed time.
It is fortunate that we have gathered here, yet we must soon part. Generally speaking, for those born into this world, suffering is many and gatherings are rare.
It is already over; yet today you speak again of parting. How could anyone not be startled by this sudden turn of events?
Although the years since I have come and gone with you, Master, have not been long, we have looked upon one another as two elders, and our refined rapport has been extraordinary.
The Master sat in meditation upon the cliff while I was gathering provisions. "If you, Master, could return early, this joy would still not have reached its end.
The eighth [verse] says: Although the years since I and the Master have been coming and going together have not been long, looking at one another, we have both become two old men.
Now that we are both old, as for comparing our respective styles of elegance—
He was unlike ordinary people. In the past, when the Master arrived, he would sit silently and in meditative stillness upon the rock;
I would then gather provisions to serve as the host of offerings. Had my teacher returned sooner, such joys would not yet have come to an end.
Those who flock to study Chan run about vying with satchels at their waists; as soon as they can speak of tangled vines, their deluded minds become self-important.
To find one whose virtue and character are truly honored is as rare as finding a master. I pray that those who transmit the Supreme Vehicle will forever bring glory to the lineage of Linji.
The ninth point says: Amidst this chaotic clamor, there are countless seekers who study Chan;
yet, with their packs on their backs and straw hats upon their heads, they race and drive about, rushing south and running north, until in the end not a single one is a true seeker of the Way.
After two or three years, they have learned a few phrases from their mouths—nothing but entangling weeds and utter delusion.

With such a mind, one naturally becomes conceited, thinking they have grasped the Way; those who seek a teacher whose realization is more exalted and whose virtue more superior than their own are truly rare.
I further wish that you, Master, in transmitting this Way, must select those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna, so that it may be perpetually glorified and sustained in the lineage after Linji.
In my district, there are many monastics, vast as a sea of clouds. The Great Capacity has long since vanished; we rely on the fact that the Small Capacity still remains.
Furthermore, bestow one more upon Chen; let both be complete and without regret. These two eminent Chan masters stand forth with dignity; all within the realm look toward them with high expectation.
The tenth [point] says: Within my own native district, those who have donned the dyed robes and shaved their heads are exceedingly numerous;
they are as vast as clouds arising or the ocean surging, beyond counting. Daji was Chan Master Chongji Mingzhen of Tiantong Temple in Hangzhou.
A native of Taizhou, he was a successor of Chan Master Xiansha Shibei and had already passed away long ago.
Fortunately, there remains a "small mechanism" (xiao ji). This "small mechanism" refers to Chan Master Jiandang Xingji.
Furthermore, there is yet another "peak" (cen), namely Venerable Yuanji Cen. These two elders are true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) whose Way is pure and whose virtue is complete;
they are free from both fault and regret. The spiritual influence of these two masters is grand and magnificent.
Prosperous! Throughout the land, the stream of Chan practitioners has gathered together, awaiting one another.
In antiquity, there was no institution of abbotship; one merely transmitted the essential teachings. If one is able to awaken to the emptiness of form, one may transcend birth and death.

Ordinary monks are oblivious to their original nature; how could they recognize the path back to the source? They purchase certificates to sit upon the meditation platform—what reliance can they have on the Buddha-dharma?
The eleventh [verse] says: From of old, there has never been such a thing as the office of abbot. It is simply that each person, through what they themselves have realized, transmits mind-to-mind;
this is the essential principle of the transmission of the Dharma. If any student of the Way is truly able to awaken...
Upon reaching the state where all forms are empty, one may transcend birth and death. As for the mediocre monk, he is distressed by food and clothing and preoccupied with fame and profit;
he knows nothing of his coming from life nor his departure in death—he is merely one of the common run who subsists on morning gruel and evening rice.
In the end, he remains ignorant of and loses the innate, original nature of his own true self. Even of himself, he is not yet aware...

How could one know it? Furthermore, how could one know the Great Intent of the West? Since the intent of his coming cannot be known, let alone the fact that he departed for the West with his sandals—this remains even more unknown.
When Master Bodhidharma was interred at Mount Xiong’er, Emperor Wu of the Wei dynasty sent Song Yun to the Western Regions.
Upon returning, Yun encountered the Master on Mount Congling, who was holding a single sandal in his hand. Yun then...
When asked where he was going, the Master replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven. Yun returned and informed the Emperor. The Emperor ordered the tomb to be opened;

there was only an empty niche with a single shoe remaining. Furthermore, in these degenerate times when the Way has been lost, people go so far as to send precious gifts and purchase recommendation letters from nobles and elders to have them recommended for a seat on the meditation platform. Such is their falsehood; the Buddha-Dharma is about to...
On what can one rely to achieve such a resurgence?
Among the monks there are eminent monks; among the lay scholars there are also eminent scholars. Although I am not considered eminent myself, my coarse mind is capable of knowing when to stop.
The Master is one of those very people; my only concern is that he does not act for you. How fortunate it is that both I and the Master are children of the same neighborhood.
The twelfth [chapter] says: Among those who have left the household life to become monks, there are indeed eminent monks whose Way is full and virtue complete.
Within our Confucian scholars, there are likewise eminent gentlemen who transcend the crowd and rise above their peers. Although I cannot be such a high-minded person, [I shall strive to be so].
Yet this mind, though coarse, is capable of knowing contentment. "Coarse" means "brief" or "general. My Master was originally one outstanding man among eminent monks;
wishing to conceal his traces, he specifically refused to dwell in high status.
A person such as this is truly difficult to find a peer for. I do not know by what karmic affinity I have had the good fortune to encounter my Master.
We were born as neighbors; we dwell in seclusion upon the same mountain; we share the same joy in the Way.

My teacher was originally a monk who lived in poverty, and I too am a scholar who has reached the depths of destitution. Our resolve to endure this poverty is now complete; having grown old, we are content not to return.
"Though we part for now, Master, do not harbor suspicion toward this spring and these rocks. It is merely that I have returned to you for the sake of conditions;
how could you, Master, have any ulterior motive? The thirteenth [verse] says: "That your will can remain steadfast even in such poverty—this is a monk who is truly capable of enduring poverty."
I, too, firmly maintain this very poverty. This is the kind of poverty that even a scholar can attain.
As for the mind that endures poverty, both of us have already thoroughly penetrated it; one might call us people who possess unimpeded liberation.
Since both of us have been able to realize and enjoy the meaning of this word "poverty," and we are now old, how could we possibly refuse to turn our hearts toward this joy?
Yes. Although the Master shall now be temporarily separated from us, I have therefore informed those who dwell among the springs and rocks:

please do not harbor suspicions. The Master is currently responding to the conditions of that [other] realm; this is merely my way of replying on his behalf. How could he truly be one who goes with a deliberate intention?
△ A renowned Confucian scholar of the School of Principle, who has profoundly plumbed the depths of the Way, is moved by what is not yet manifest. Liberation.
The Master’s manifestations are boundless; he responds where there is no need for response. That these two gentlemen encountered him so auspiciously—was this not a blessing for a thousand years?
This chapter reveals how he withdrew from the world to maintain his integrity; when the fruit ripens, its fragrance wafts forth, for the Way is great when free of artifice.
Gong Ji Shi, the Duke of Wu, said to Jian Tang, "The ancients extinguished their worldly desires and stilled their intellects amidst thousands of crags and ten thousand ravines;
they drank from mountain streams and ate from the trees as if they had severed all intent for fame and office. Yet, one day, they received the imperial decree sealed in purple clay.

They concealed their brilliance and hid their traces beneath the lowly labor of the grain-pounding miller, having no initial thought of honor or advancement, yet in the end, they were destined to transmit the Dharma."
It is arranged like a row of lamps. Therefore, when attained through a mind free of intention, its Way is great and its virtue is vast;
yet when calculated in terms of seeking something, its name is base and its ambition is narrow.
This section clarifies that for the ancients, the Way manifested spontaneously through non-intentionality. Master Wu addressed Chan Master Jiantang, saying:
"The students of antiquity extinguished their minds like cold ashes and obliterated their intellects.

They hid deeply among thousands of crags and ten thousand gullies, drinking from mountain streams and eating herbs and trees. How could they have ever harbored any intention regarding fame or achievement?"
Regarding gain and offerings: when his Way was perfected and his virtues complete, his fame spread far and wide. One day, he received an imperial edict sealed with purple clay from the Son of Heaven.

As for "purple clay," this refers to the six seals of the Son of Heaven, all of which were sealed with purple clay from Wudu to enclose their boxes and caskets, so that even ghosts and spirits would not dare to look upon them.
Wudu is the present-day Jie Prefecture; the waters and mountains there are all red.
Therefore, he used it as ink for his seal; thus he concealed his brilliance and hid his traces, sometimes even among the lowly laborers who grind grain with mortars.
Originally having no heart for honor or advancement, he later ultimately joined the ranks of those who transmit the lamp—not out of any hope or expectation.
This is not a matter of seeking; rather, it must all be attained through a state of no-mind. Therefore, the Way becomes ever greater and its virtue ever more vast.
If one were to employ calculation and effort in pursuit, the reputation gained would instead become base, and the principle maintained would grow increasingly narrow.

Truly, the Master’s discernment was profound and far-reaching; following in the footsteps of the ancients, he was able to dwell at Guanshan for seventeen years, thereby becoming an excellent vessel for the monastic community.
The patch-robed monks of today lack internal self-restraint and pursue external splendor;
they lack long-term vision and possess no sense of great principle. Consequently, they are unable to support the religious teachings, and thus fall far short of the Master’s achievements.
This section serves as proof that Master Jian’s profound internal cultivation caused his virtue to manifest naturally.
Only because the Master’s capacity was so vast and far-reaching could he continue the lineage of wisdom and follow in the footsteps of the ancients.

He lived in seclusion at Guanshan for seventeen years, contentedly maintaining his proper station, thereby becoming an excellent vessel for the Dharma. Recently, when fellow monks observed his inner state...
Lacking genuine virtue, they pursue external splendors and compete for fame and profit; few have long-term plans regarding the Dharma-gate, and they entirely lack the grand principles of edification.
Thus, they are unable to support the religious tradition. Compared to such people, [the Master] was truly far superior.
△ To contend over strength and superiority as the ancients did, and to add to the habits of hatred for those of today—truly...

There is a sense of indignation and resentment; this precisely names the phenomenon to point toward its reality, so that people may know there are things in the world that are held in honor and things that are treated with contempt.
This chapter teaches that in conducting one's affairs, one must preserve the correct principle and not indulge private desires.
Jiandang said: "In the ordinary human condition, it is rare to be free from delusion.

Generally, people are obscured by what they believe, hindered by what they doubt, negligent regarding what they deem trivial, and submerged in what they love. When belief is biased, one fails to examine the reality of what is heard;
thus, there arise words that are excessive. When doubt is extreme, one refuses to listen even to the truth; thus, there arises the loss of reality."
If one holds a person in low esteem, one neglects the matters that ought to be valued; if one cherishes those matters, one retains the persons who ought to be discarded.

These are all instances of recklessly indulging private attachments and failing to examine the principles of the Way. Consequently, one forgets the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and loses the spirit of the monastic community (*saṃgha*).
Thus, what is held in low regard by ordinary people is precisely what is esteemed by the sages and worthies. As an ancient worthy said: "In planning for the distant..."

One who seeks to verify the distant must first examine what is near; one who strives for the great must be diligent regarding the minute. This requires extensive gathering of information and careful discernment of its essence;
it certainly does not consist in admiring the lofty or delighting in the eccentric (Letter to the Official of Wu).
It is the common nature of worldly people that they encounter objects according to their own emotions;
few are not deluded by them. Generally, there are four ways one is deluded: first, upon hearing the words of others, one fails to examine whether they are right or wrong;
this is being obscured by blind credulity. Second, when encountering an affair, one either wishes to act or does not wish to act; this is being hindered by doubt.
Third, one may harbor contempt for others; this is to neglect what one looks down upon. Fourth, one may pursue objects and self with excessive intent;
this is to be submerged in what one loves. When faith is thus biased, the words one hears will certainly not be examined for their truth or falsehood.
Consequently, there arise words that exaggerate the facts as well as those that fall short of them. Its...
The first delusion is this: since I harbor doubts regarding that person, I am unwilling to listen even if their words are correct and accord with reason;

thus, I fail to hear the truth. This is the second delusion. If I treat that person with contempt, I will likewise cast aside and refuse to employ whatever truly worthy matters they may possess. This is the third delusion. I...
If one deeply loves a matter yet does not inquire into it, such a person is truly one who should be abandoned.

To place one's trust in a person merely because of their affairs—this is the fourth delusion. These four are all instances of acting with negligence to indulge private emotions rather than examining the true principles;
consequently, they lead to forgetting the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and falling into contravention.
The minds of the great multitude—those things which ordinary people habitually treat with contempt—are in fact what the sages and worthies regard as most important.
An ancient master said: "If one wishes to plan a far-reaching and grand undertaking, one must first test it through small and immediate matters;
if one wishes to perform a vast and expansive deed, one must first exercise caution in the most minute details. Regarding all affairs...
One must extensively gather knowledge from many sources and then exercise careful discernment in its application. As the *Shijing* says: "Toiling the mind in extensive gathering and adoption.

This certainly does not consist in admiring what is lofty or delighting in what is eccentric. To indulge one's passions and turn one's back on reason, or to admire the lofty and delight in the eccentric, results from a failure to study.
"Toiling the mind in extensive gathering and adoption" is the teaching of the Sages. Reflect upon it, reflect upon it!
This chapter shows that the ancients found self-contentment through the Way; external circumstances could not shift them.
Jiantang was clear, pure, and level-minded, showing compassion and kindness toward all beings. If a monk made even a slight error, he would shield and protect him.
Thus he perfected his virtue. He once said, "Who among men is without fault? It is in rectifying them that one achieves beauty.
This passage illustrates his conduct and speech, indicating that Master Jiantang was throughout his life clear-sighted, upright, and serene.

Purity means being upright and untainted; clarity means being well-versed in discerning the worthy from the unworthy. Being broad-minded and even-tempered, he further extends compassionate grace and benefit to others.

Regarding errors—that is, transgressions—if there is even a slight lapse or mistake among his disciples, he immediately provides them with protection and care, secretly leading them to repent and reform so as to perfect them as human beings.
Master Deheng once said, "Who among men is without fault? It is in the rectifying of them that one finds beauty.

While he was residing at Guanshan in Poyang, it happened to be the height of winter, with snow and rain falling continuously. His supply of thick gruel and rice porridge was exhausted, yet the Master acted as if he had neither heard nor seen it.
Thus, he composed this verse: "The hearth-stove has no fire, the traveler’s bag is empty; The snow falls like willow blossoms through the passing year."

In poverty, he wrapped his head in a hempen robe and burned firewood; unaware that he was dwelling in solitude. Throughout his life, he had found contentment in the Way and did not strive for fame or honor.
On the day he accepted the invitation to Mount Lu at Yuan Tong, he carried nothing but a staff and straw sandals.

Those who saw him perceived his dignified countenance and understood his liberated mind. When Lin Gong Shuda, the Governor of Jiuyang Prefecture, beheld him, he remarked: "This is one among the Buddhadharma..."

He was a bridge and a ford for others; thus his reputation spread throughout the four quarters. His conduct in both retiring from office and entering public service truly embodied the standards of the former masters.
On the day of his death, even the messengers who had served him diligently shed tears for him.
This section clarifies the actual facts. While he was staying at Guanshan in Poyang, it happened that during the final month of winter, snow and rain fell continuously for many days without ceasing.
"Zhān" refers to thick porridge. When zhān and porridge could not be sustained, it was as if his meals had been cut off entirely;
yet the Master remained composed, as if hearing or seeing nothing at all. Thus, there is a verse that says: "The hearth-stove has no fire, the traveler’s bag is empty; The snow is like..."
Willow flowers fall as the year draws to a close; with a patched robe covering his head, he burns firewood logs.
Unaware that he dwells in solitude—these "firewood logs" (*geudeok*) are short pieces of wood from trees stripped of branches and leaves. From this, one knows the height of his integrity and purity.
Throughout his life, he took delight in attaining the Way for himself and did not strive urgently for fame.

On the day he traveled to Mount Lu at the invitation of Yuan-tong, he carried nothing but a staff and straw sandals. Those who beheld the Master’s deportment found that people’s countenances became respectful and solemn;
their vulgar thoughts were dissolved and dispelled. Upon first meeting him, Lin Gong, the Prefect of Jiujiang, remarked:
This was a ferryboat and bridge within the Buddha-dharma. Because of this, his reputation spread throughout the four quarters.
The Master’s conduct—his coming and going, his advancing and withdrawing—truly captured the standard of the ancients.
On the day he entered nirvana, even those who were ordinary laborers did not fail to weep and shed tears in bitter grief; such was the way his virtue moved people. △
Whenever a student reads a book, they must identify within each chapter what constitutes the essential point.
For instance, when it says here that snow and rain fell continuously, and that one neither heard nor saw them—could this have been achieved through mere forced effort?
By observing this, one will see that all virtues are naturally and fully prepared.
This chapter teaches that one should know the proper time, recognize the capacity of others, and abide according to conditions.

Zhang Gong Xiaoxiang, the Court Gentleman for Ceremonial, sent a letter to the Elder Chan Master Yan of Fengqiao Bridge, stating: "Among the patriarchs of old, there was no such thing as acting as an abbot.
Opening the gates to receive disciples was done only out of necessity. As the Semblance Dharma declined, it even came to include the practice of hereditary succession by sealed grant."
Regarding the submission of a formal petition and the theory of purchasing a monastery: these matters are as numerous and prevalent as those at Fengqiao in the past.
This section clarifies that ordinary people lack wisdom. Zhang Xiaoxiang, a Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, sent a letter to Fengqiao in Suzhou.
The bridge is located in front of Hanshan Temple. The Elder Yan was Chan Master Zongyan of Tuna at Huazang Monastery in Changzhou.
He was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou and received the Dharma from Chan Master Dahui; he belonged to the sixteenth generation under Nanyue.
Xiaoxiang asked his teacher about the Way, saying: "Among the successive patriarchs of old, there was no such thing as establishing the position of abbot.
Whenever someone founded a mountain monastery or accepted a multitude of disciples, it was always because they could not help themselves and were compelled by others to do so.
In this age of semblance, when the Buddha-dharma has declined, there have even appeared those who seek fame."
There are those who, having formed alliances with powerful officials along the route, seek to convert their original documents in order to obtain official seals, bestowed titles, or honorary names.
Furthermore, there are those seeking profit who rely upon local gentry and merchants to present their circumstances;
they engage in fraudulent sales and purchases to ensnare money and silk. These matters have long been a source of turmoil within Fengqiao Temple.
Those who engage in endless chatter, prattle on about long and short matters, and do not cease their sharp-tongued disputes—all are of this same sort of person.

As for your public conduct, everyone knows it thoroughly; the moment of the chick pecking and the hen pecking is simultaneous, requiring no effort at all. When the conditions are right, you shall stay.

When the conditions for life are exhausted, one must depart. If those who merely peddle goods wish to create the karma of hell on this very ground, it would be better to simply entrust both hands [to the Buddha] rather than that.
(Inscribed on a stone tablet at Hanshan Temple)

This section clarifies Master Yan’s career as a monk, both in active ministry and in seclusion. As for his various periods of engagement with the world or withdrawal from it, leading assemblies and practicing the Way, everyone is well aware.
Regarding the term "cup-zuo" (pricking and pecking): it is like a hen brooding her eggs; when the chick is about to emerge, it uses its beak to peck at the shell, which is called "cup."
The mother, knowing it was about to hatch, pecks at it with her beak, saying "peck. This is said to mean that the meeting of human conditions is also like this.
If the "sucking" and the "pecking" were simultaneous, there would originally have been no need for human effort. When there is a karmic affinity, one simply abides according to that affinity;
when there is no affinity, one takes up the staff and departs. If those who are like petty peddlers wish to harbor greed and attachment to this...
The earth-spirit skillfully employs its cunning mechanisms; this is precisely what constitutes the karma of hell.
It would be better for you, sir, to entrust both hands to him instead. Regarding the term "peddler" (*baifan*): *bai* is a weed that resembles rice but is not rice.

In common parlance, it refers to weeds among a fertile field or thorns within a pine forest. It is also written as "beneficial peddler" (*bifan*); in this case, the character *bi* is pronounced *bei*.
"Fu" (Affiliated) means to affiliate oneself with my Dharma while trafficking in the Buddha-dharma for the sake of profit and offerings. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Trafficking in the Tathāgata, they create all manner of karmas. This single chapter of discourse surpasses a great treasury of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*;
it can, by itself, cause you to eliminate calamities and obtain blessings.
This chapter praises those who possess genuine virtue and do not change with the shifting world.
Master Cishou Shen addressed Master Jingshan Ne, saying: "In the past twenty or thirty years, the Chan school has been desolate and truly pitiful to behold.
Elders from all quarters have fled south and run north in countless numbers, dispersing like smoke."
The assembly was filled with such people; yet only you, Elder Brother, remained unmoved in spirit, sitting in tranquil ease. How could you be compared to those who are merely mediocre?

I admire and revere you deeply! This present circumstance could not have occurred unless one’s Way were full and virtue substantial, and practice and understanding were in accord—how could such a thing be easily found?
I further hope that you will exert yourself to guide and inspire future generations, so that the Cao Yuan [the source of the Dharma] may flourish.
Dried up, it swells again; the withered tree awakens to spring once more. This is truly the earnest hope of my humble heart.
(By Bitie) Chan Master Cishou Huishen of HuiLin Temple in Dongjing. Born to the Xia family, he was the dharma heir of Chan Master Chongxin of Changlu.
Thirteenth generation descendant of Qingyuan. [Seal of] Miaokong Zhi of Jing Mountain, Lin’an Prefecture.
Master Nü also succeeded Master Xìn of Chánglú. Upādhyāya Císhòu praised Jìngshān, saying:
"In recent two or three decades, the Chan school has gradually become desolate and silent; it is truly distressing to behold.
Those who serve as elders in various quarters are obsessed with the two characters 'fame' and 'profit'; they do nothing but rush south or flee north."
To the north, there were those beyond counting who were likewise like this. Furthermore, there was another kind who lacked willpower;
they would either disperse the incense smoke or scatter the assembly. Such people filled the eyes everywhere. This entire scene of light and environment was truly pitiable.
Only you, elder brother, remained with both spirit and emotion utterly unmoving, able to sit and enjoy peace on your own.
"Exquisite! These enjoyments—how could they ever be spoken of as being on the same level as those who are merely mediocre and commonplace?

To 'admire and admire' is the height of respectful submission. This particular circumstance could not easily be found unless one’s moral virtue were full and one’s practice were in accord with realization.
To cultivate while dissolving conceptual understanding is called 'practice. When the mind is luminous and penetrating..."
I say: "Understood. What I further hope for is that you will diligently exert your spiritual power to guide and attract those who come to study.
For the source of Caoxi is now on the verge of drying up; only the Dharma-flood from your person can cause it to swell again.
The Bodhi tree of awakening is now on the verge of withering; only the wind of your Way can cause it to bloom once more."
This is truly the humble aspiration of my lowly mind. "Qūqū" (區區) denotes a small appearance; it is a term of self-deprecation.
This chapter does not emphasize praising the virtue of the virtuous person, but rather emphasizes exhorting future generations to exert effort.
It is said that even when a source is about to run dry, it may swell again; and when a tree is about to wither, it may spring forth anew once more. One’s hope for this is not slight.
This treatise instructs people to endure slander and cease calumny, and not to engage in strife or competition.
Master Lingzhi Zhao asked: "Are slander and defamation the same or different? He replied: "Slander necessarily relies upon defamation to be accomplished.
There may be those who defame without slandering, but one has never seen one who slanders without defaming. As for the arising of slander—"
It begins with hatred and jealousy, yet ends in blind trust. Those who act thus are sycophantic and petty men.
Among the ancients, there were those who offered loyalty to assist their sovereigns, practiced filial piety to serve their parents, and embraced righteousness to form friendships.
Even when sovereign and minister attained mutual understanding, father and son shared mutual affection, or friends shared mutual intimacy, for a single day—
When slandered by others, people may turn their eyes in resentment, roll up their sleeves in anger, cast out the accuser, and sow discord, until they regard one another as enemies.
Even among the ancient sages and worthies, this could not be avoided. Yet, there are those whose innocence cannot be proven at first but becomes clear after time;
those who cannot prove it while alive but have it vindicated after death; and those who cannot prove it even unto death, remaining so forever.
Those who cannot perceive this clearly are beyond counting.
This section strictly admonishes people not to believe lightly. Dharma Master Yuanzhao Zhanran of Lingzhi Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Tang family of Yuhang.
When he received the precepts from Dharma Master Huicai, he was moved by the sight of the Avalokiteśvara image emitting light. The Master...
He poses a question of his own: "Are calumny (*chán*) and slander (*fěi*) the same or different?
Calumny refers to the use of artful and piercing words to harm the virtuous and good. Slander refers to speech that is not so piercing, but merely speaks of a person's faults."
Answer: Generally speaking, those who slander and harm others must first rely on defamation to achieve their ends.

While there may be those among the world's people who engage in defamation without proceeding to actual harm, I have never seen one who slanders and harms another without first resorting to defamation. As for the origin of slander, it always begins with hatred.
He harbors malice, envy, and jealousy toward others, yet ultimately follows the light-minded counsel of those around him.
Those who speak such words are originally sycophants and flatterers; they must not be listened to. This situation is not merely so today;
it was likewise in the past, when there were those who served as ministers, sacrificing their bodies and facing death to offer their loyalty.
My Lord: As a son, one serves one’s parents with humble compliance and the utmost filial piety;
as a companion, one assists in virtue, embraces righteousness, and exerts the full heart to maintain mutual affinity.

Yet, at such moments when emotions are harmonious and principles accordant, the perfect rapport between ruler and minister, the mutual love between father and son, and the deep intimacy between friends may be said to reach their ultimate height. Suddenly—

Yet, once slandered by petty men, it causes fathers and sons to give rise to anger and turn against one another, brothers to quarrel and roll up their sleeves in defiance, and sovereigns and ministers to become estranged and cast out. When they meet, they regard each other as enemies.
As Mencius said: "If the ruler regards his minister as mere weeds or chaff, then the minister will regard the ruler as an enemy."
These circumstances, though unavoidable even for the sages and worthies of antiquity, all stem from the slanderous calumnies of petty men.
Yet, there are those who initially do not realize they have been deceived by such petty people into creating this estrangement, only discovering it after a long time;
and there are others who, throughout their entire lives, are unable to clear their names, only coming to know the truth upon their death.
There are also those who come to know later; yet there are even more who, even after death, are unable to discern [the truth].
Indeed, those who remain ignorant until the end of eternity are beyond counting.
Ziyou said, "To be too frequent in serving one's ruler brings disgrace; to be too frequent in dealing with a friend leads to estrangement.

This was intended as a warning for people to distance themselves from slander. Alas! Slander and defamation must be scrutinized. Furthermore, they are recorded in the Classics and Histories such that they are not obscure;
scholars who read them all know their wrongfulness. Yet, time and again, individuals personally fall into the mouths of slanderers, choking upon them.
To remain resentful until death, unable to vindicate oneself, is surely due to the failure of those who receive the slander to investigate, and to the flattery and sycophancy of those who slander.
When a pack of petty people arrive before one and again slander others, yet one listens to them and deems it so—can this be called being wise?
Indeed, those skilled at slandering are clever and artful in inciting strife and instigating discord, merely seeking to curry favor.
To be obscured and deluded until one is as if possessed by a ghost, such that some cannot discern the truth for their entire lives—this section teaches people to clearly examine what is false.
This follows from the preceding discussion on loyalty to one's sovereign and trust in friends, stating that the harm of slander is no small matter.
It then cites the words of an ancient to provide proof; Ziyou was a disciple of Confucius.

"Zi" is his surname; "Yan" is his given name, and "Ziyou" is his courtesy name. "Shu" means to be frequent or repetitive. When serving a ruler, if one's remonstrance is not accepted, it is permissible to leave.
However, if one repeatedly and excessively remonstrates, the listener will become weary and annoyed. A petty person may then take advantage of the situation to slander him;
at best, he will lose his rank, and at worst, his life will be harmed. This is to seek honor and instead return with disgrace."
This is what is meant by "serving one's lord with excessive frequency leads to disgrace. If a friend does not accept your guidance, you may simply stop.
However, if you repeatedly urge them to sell [their property], the listener will become weary and annoyed. A petty person will then seize the opportunity to slander you;
