at the minor level, they will agree with their lips while harboring anger in their hearts, and at the major level, they will feel resentment and seek revenge. This is to seek intimacy and instead end up with estrangement. Therefore it is said: "Friends..."
Friends become increasingly sparse because of this; it is for this reason that one must warn others against slander. Alas! One must not fail to subject slander and defamation to profound scrutiny.
It would be appropriate for all such matters to be recorded in the classics and histories and annotated therein, so that they are not left unexplained.
Each instance should be clearly set forth, so that all scholars who read and examine them will surely understand and heed them.
Slander and defamation ultimately ruin one's virtue. We often see people fall into the mouths of slanderers;
"throttled" (*ē*) refers to being choked in the throat, while "oppressed" (*yù*) refers to the distress bound within the heart.

There is no difference between those who, until their death, remain unable to examine themselves and clarify the truth—it is because they were momentarily provoked by a slanderer’s words during a fit of anger and failed to discern the reality.
Having scrutinized the facts, one ultimately accepts the flattery and sycophancy of slanderers.
When a multitude of petty people stand before me and further slander others, I again listen with increasing ease and believe them all the more, taking it to be true.
Having myself accepted their slander, I then in turn believe their slanders when directed at others. Can this be called being wise? Indeed, it is merely being skilled at slandering.
Those who slander employ many varieties of expedient guile and numerous skillful methods. They incite discord between two parties and curry favor with others to win them over.

They delude and obscure the truth for others, causing people to become as bewildered and deluded as if possessed by a malevolent spirit, such that they remain unable to discern the truth until the end of their lives, being utterly lost to the slanderer’s influence.
They delude my mind. How tragic! Confucius said:

"There are slanders that seep in like moisture and accusations that come from immediate personal experience. When such words of seeping infiltration arrive, they do not allow people to perceive them beforehand;
even if Zeng Shen were the most filial of sons, his mother would surely suspect him of murder. A marketplace is no forest retreat, yet people will surely harbor suspicions.
If there were tigers [in the path], and some among them failed to proceed, they would be called enlightened and far-sighted gentlemen.
This section teaches people to anticipate the implications of their words. This, moreover, follows upon the preceding discussion on filial piety toward one's parents;
it speaks of how the harm caused by slander is not small, for it can cause even a most filial son to be suspected by his virtuous mother. Confucius—
His surname was Kong, his given name was Qiu, and his courtesy name was Zhongni.

He was born on the fourth day of the eleventh month in the twenty-first year of the gengxu cycle during the reign of King Ling of Zhou, at Pingxiang in Jinchang Village, Zou County, Yanzhou, within the state of Lu.

His father was Shuliang He, and his mother was Lady Yan. During the Tang dynasty, under the seventh emperor, Xuanzong, he was posthumously honored with the title Wenzhuan. His son was Zhang Wenming. His son...
It is said: "When slander that seeps in like moisture and accusations that are personally felt do not gain entry, one may be called enlightened. The commentary states:
"Seeping in like moisture" refers to being like water that irrigates and nourishes, soaking in gradually rather than suddenly.
"Slander" refers to destroying a person's conduct. If one destroys another's conduct gradually rather than suddenly, the listener will not perceive its entry. And...
The depth of one's faith is profound. "Superficial reception" (*fūsu*) refers to what is received through the skin;
it means that gain or loss touches one’s very person. "Sù" (愬) is the same as "sù" (訴); "sù" means to recount one's grievances.

This describes how when a person recounts their grievance with such urgency and intensity that the listener does not have time to provide detailed scrutiny, the matter is exposed with sudden force. Both of these cases are difficult to discern; if a person can perceive them, then...
One can see how clear and far-reaching his mind was, unobscured by the immediate. ○ Zeng Shen, styled Zixing, was a disciple of Confucius from Wucheng.
He was profoundly filial; it was because of him that Confucius composed the *Classic of Filial Piety*.
Gan Mao of Qin said: "A man in Lu had the same name as Zeng Shen and committed murder. Someone told his mother:"
"Your son has killed a man. The mother said, "My son is benevolent and filial; he would not kill a man," and she continued weaving at her loom as before.
After a short while, another person reported that Zeng Shen had killed someone. The mother again remained composed. Yet another person reported it to her.
She then threw down her shuttle, descended from the loom, leaped over the wall, and fled. Now, my virtue does not equal that of Zeng Shen, and Your Majesty’s trust in me is likewise not [as firm].
"And as for my mother—those who suspect me are not limited to three people; I fear Your Majesty will set aside the ladle [and stop the cooking].
This was said because King Wu of Qin was entrusting Gan Mao with the mission to attack Han. *The Mozi* says:
"Pang Cong was serving as a hostage for the Crown Prince of Wei in Handan. He said to the King of Wei: 'Suppose one person says there is a tiger in the market.'"
"Does Your Majesty believe it? The King said, "No. He asked, "Do you believe what two people say? The King said, "I am doubtful of that.
He asked, "Do you believe what three people say? The King said, "I believe it, Sire. [The Master] said, "It is clear that there are no tigers in the marketplace;
yet when three people speak, their words are believed. Now, Handan is much farther from Daliang than the marketplace is. Those who discuss me exceed even those three men."
"Regarding these three men, I pray that Your Majesty will examine them. The King said, "I shall know for myself.
Just as he was about to take his leave, there were indeed slanderous words brought before the King.
There were some who, being neither suspicious nor believing such talk, ensured that the calumny could not proceed. These may be called high-minded and far-sighted gentlemen.

Because I am foolish, clumsy, and indolent, I have no fondness for flattery or for feigning pleasure with others; consequently, I have often been the subject of slander and calumny by those around me.
Upon hearing such things, I have reflected in private, saying: "If what they say is indeed true, I shall reform my faults; then they are my teachers.
If what they say is indeed false, it is merely their idle talk; how could it defile me? Thus I have listened.
Although I have heard these things, my mouth has never once debated them. Whether a scholar or gentleman examines them or not depends solely on whether their talent and insight are clear or obscure.
How could I possibly vindicate what is crooked or straight by seeking recognition from others?
Yet, one does not know whether they will become clear after a long time, or in a future generation, or whether they will remain obscure forever. Wen Zhongzi said: "How can this be?"
"Cease the slander; call it 'inability to debate. I shall take these words as my task" (*Jituji*).

This section marks the emergence of his own words. This is Master Lingzhi’s own account of the reasons for enduring calumny, citing Wen Gong’s "ceasing of slander" as a means to extinguish it himself. He says: "By nature I am dull and clumsy; as a person..."
I am scatterbrained and indolent. Throughout my life, I have had no fondness for flattery, sycophancy, or seeking to please others through falsehoods;
consequently, I have frequently been the subject of slander by petty people. Upon hearing such words of slander from others, I privately reflect and examine myself, saying:
"If what he says is correct, I shall personally acknowledge my error; that man is indeed my teacher.
If what he says is incorrect, then he merely acts in vain and reaps the consequences of his own delusions. [The character] *měi* means "to defile" or "to pollute.
Furthermore, how could he possibly defile me? Thus, although he heard these words with his ears, his mouth never uttered a word of refutation. Master Shi—
Whether you are able to examine me with discernment or not depends solely on the clarity or lack thereof of that person’s own innate talent and insight.
Why should I necessarily seek to clarify whether I am wrong or right, seeking to be known by scholars and gentlemen?
Nevertheless, it may be that what is unclear today will become clear after a long time. Or perhaps there is.
Furthermore, there are those who are not enlightened in this life but become enlightened in future lives;
there are even those who remain unenlightened throughout eternity. Wen Zhongzi said: "How can one stop slander?"

He said, "Do not argue. I shall accept these words and practice self-restraint. Wen Zhongzi (The Master Wen): His secular surname was Wang, his given name was Tong, and his courtesy name was Zhongyan.
He was a native of Longmen in Luoyang. After his death, his disciples conferred upon him the posthumous title "Master Wen."
He traveled to Chang’an and presented twelve strategic proposals for peace and prosperity to Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, who was greatly pleased.
After returning home, nine years later, he completed his extensive revision of the Six Classics. When Jia Qiong asked, "How does one quell slander? Master [Wang] said, "By not defending oneself.
When asked, "How does one stop resentment? he said, "By not contending. He then remarked, "One who hears slander and feels resentment is a victim of calumny."
"Yòu. To rejoice upon seeing praise is the harbinger of flattery. By eliminating the yòu and removing the mediator, calumny and flattery will stay far away.
"Yòu" (pronounced wéi) refers to a bird used as a decoy. △ How vast and expansive was the spirit of the ancients!

To dwell amidst circumstances most difficult to manage requires nothing less than a Perfected Person. This constitutes one who truly knows repentance; it is simply the ultimate reach of sincere intention.
This chapter teaches authentic inquiry and genuine study, investigating the ultimate reason for such practice.
Master Lanyan Shu said: "A practitioner of the Way should take awakening as their goal. They must seek out a true and virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to resolve their doubts.
If even a thread-thin trace of emotional views remains unexhausted, it is the very root of birth and death. Once these emotional views are exhausted, one must investigate further."
The reason for this exhaustion is like a person who always stays at home, worrying about why household affairs are not being managed.
This section concludes with the sudden enlightenment of Chan Master Lǎn'ān Dàoshū of Língyǐn Monastery in Lín'ān Prefecture.
He was a successor of Chan Master Jūhuì of Dào-chǎng and belongs to the eighteenth generation under Nányuè. It is said that if one wishes to produce a transcendent measure...

Indeed, one must take full enlightenment as the goal. Furthermore, it is essential to have a truly enlightened master who can dissect my doubts and delusions for me and discern between what is heterodox and what is orthodox.
As it is said, "After awakening, one must specifically seek out a true person.
If even a single thread of emotional consciousness or discursive thought remains unexhausted, that is the very root of birth and death. When one reaches the point where [emotional]...
Having seen the point where all things end, one must further seek the ultimate reason for that final exhaustion. As the ancients said:
"Do not say that 'no-mind' is the Way; even 'no-mind' still leaves behind a single barrier. It is like a person who always resides within their own home;
why should they worry about whether the various affairs of the household are being managed?

Guishan said: "People of the present day, although they may attain sudden enlightenment into the fundamental principle through conditions, still possess the habitual tendencies from beginningless time that cannot yet be suddenly exhausted.
One must teach them to purify the flowing consciousness of current karma; this is what is meant by 'cultivation.
It is not that there is some other gate of practice to which they are directed. Only an ancient Buddha like Guishan could utter such words. If it were otherwise...
Not so. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one cannot avoid being flustered with hands and feet; it remains like a crab falling into boiling water.
This section cites the authentic practice of the Patriarch Guishan Lingyou, who said: "Though practitioners of the Way nowadays follow conditions..."

Once one has attained sudden enlightenment through a single thought-moment and realized the fundamental principle, there still remain the habitual tendencies of the three karmas and ten evils accumulated since beginningless kalpas that cannot be eradicated all at once.
One must therefore instruct them that throughout the two-and-six periods of the day and night, they should simply purify and completely eliminate their current active consciousness;
the subtle arising and ceasing within this state of drifting and wandering is itself cultivation.
It is not that there is some other separate dharma-gate to cause them to turn toward it. Only an ancient Buddha like Guishan could utter such words;
were one to recklessly accept them, wait until the time when the light of the eyes falls to the ground.
One cannot avoid being flustered and confused; one remains like a crab that has fallen into boiling water.
How lamentable! △ A single grain of the elixir of immortality can turn iron into gold; what need is there for thousands of words?
If one merely upholds the single phrase "purifying the flowing consciousness of present karma," one can attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
This section shows that objects belonging to the *jātidīpa* (the universal monastery) must not be used lightly; the workings of cause and effect are clearly manifest.
Lan’an said: “The Vinaya states that there are four kinds of monastic property: first, permanently fixed property; second, property belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions;
third, property belonging to the present assembly; and fourth, property belonging to the present assembly of the ten directions.

Regarding these permanently fixed assets, one must not commit even the slightest transgression, for such an offense is no small matter. From the sages of antiquity to the sages of later times, they have not failed to issue this earnest admonition.”
This section states that monastic property must not be diverted for private use. The Vinaya says: "There are four kinds of monastic property.

First is 'permanently fixed permanently' (zhǒngcháng zhǒngcháng), referring to the dwellings, utensils, trees, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, rice, wheat, and other such items belonging to the community of monks.
Because their substance is restricted to a specific location and does not extend to other boundaries, they may only be used; they are not permitted to be divided or sold."

Therefore, it is stated again that it is "permanently abiding, permanently abiding. Second is the "permanently abiding of the ten directions," which refers to food, drink, and other items provided for the monastic community within a temple.
Their substance belongs to the ten directions and is not restricted to their original location. As the *Śīlasamuccaya* states:
To eat without striking the bell constitutes the offense of theft. Now, in all monasteries, residents dwell together and eat together;

once the food is prepared, the bell and drum are struck, which serves to clarify that the Sangha of the ten directions has a share in it. Third is the "present resident property" (*pratyutpanna-sāṃghika-vastu*).
This is of two kinds: first, the presence of a specific object; second, the presence of the monastic community. However, as for this object...

This is because it is given to the *saṃgha* present at this location. Fourth is the "present and permanent" (*pratyutpanna-sthāvara*) of the ten directions, which refers to the property of deceased monks.
Because light objects are common to the ten directions, only those currently present at the original site are entitled to a share.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "If one steals the property of deceased monks, against whom does one incur the fundamental offense? It answers: "Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed..."

Regarding "grinding" (or processing): it is obtained from the assembly where the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed. If the *karmavācanā* has not yet been performed, it is obtained from the entire assembly that correctly expounds the various Dharmas.

Now, to examine the distribution of the property of a deceased monk: those monks who have come from the ten directions and are present before the number [of the assembly] for the *karmavācanā* obtain [the share];
those who arrive after the *karmavācanā* does not obtain it. Furthermore, as for the property of the permanent endowment (*saṃghika-vastu*), not even a single thread or speck may be [taken].
There are transgressions. Should one commit even a single offense, the suffering of that sin is not light.
The former sages, such as the Buddhas, and the later sages, such as the Patriarchs—who among them did not earnestly warn against this matter of permanent possession?
Often those who hear this are not necessarily able to believe it; those who believe it are not necessarily able to practice it.

Whether I, this mountain monk, am in the world or in seclusion, I have never failed to keep this matter earnestly in mind, fearing that there may still be something I have not yet attained. Therefore, I have composed these verses to admonish myself:

The property of the Sangha from the ten directions is as heavy as a mountain; Throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, how easily can it be repaid? The Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] speaks of it together [with all].
Never having believed, how can one avoid the gates of the Iron City in years to come? This human body is difficult to obtain; reflect upon it well.
Once the horns have grown, the years and months will be many. It is laughable to covet another’s single grain of rice, only to casually lose half a year’s worth of provisions.

These instructions and admonitions must be faithfully believed with utmost sincerity. Often, whether it be an abbot or an administrator, upon hearing these earnest words of instruction and admonition, they may not necessarily believe them.
Even if they do believe and recognize that the retributive suffering of hell is no light matter, they may still not be able to act accordingly.
Whether I was traveling as a wandering monk or residing at a monastery, in all my comings and goings—
In the intervals [between my duties], there has never been a time when I have not kept these communal possessions of the Sangha earnestly in mind.
They must not be lightly violated; yet, fearing that there may still be points where my practice falls short, I have composed this verse to admonish myself:

"The property of the Sangha of the ten directions is as heavy as a mountain; Throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, how easily could it be repaid? Though the Golden Mouth spoke of it together with others, I once failed to believe."
"In other years, how can one avoid the Iron City Gate? The "Golden Mouth" refers to the mouth of the Great Awakened Golden Immortal;
it is the Buddha’s teaching. Human life is difficult to obtain; reflect upon this well. When the horns of youth first appear, the years and months pass swiftly.
It is laughable that for the sake of a single grain of rice, One carelessly loses half a year's worth of provisions. △ This is like the sound of a midnight bell; one does not even realize it.

This causes those in a great dream to be startled awake. Yet there are others who remain submerged in the land of intoxication; even if they hear this, they will not awaken. What can be done for them?
This treatise clarifies that Chan and the Teachings are not two separate things; they are fundamentally one principle.

Lan’an said: "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: 'If a person hears a single phrase or a single word of the Great Nirvāṇa, and does not form a conception of words, does not form a conception of phrases, does not form a conception of hearing, does not form a conception of the Buddha, and does not form a conception of preaching—such a meaning is called the characteristic of no-characteristic.
That the Great Master Bodhidharma came across the sea and did not establish written words was precisely because..."
The principle of signlessness is not something newly devised by Bodhidharma nor a separate school he established;
this section generally clarifies that the Buddha’s intent is without deviation. The Buddha said:

"If there is anyone who hears my teaching of the Great Nirvāṇa—Nirvāṇa in Sanskrit, which here is translated as 'extinction' (mièdù)—it means the extinction of afflictions and the crossing over the sea of birth and death."
Furthermore, "Nir" means non-arising and "vāṇa" means non-ceasing; the principle of neither arising nor ceasing is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Whether one hears a single phrase or a single syllable, if in that interval one does not form the conceptualization of syllables, one knows that the nature of letters is empty.
If one does not form the conceptualization of phrases, one realizes that the nature of speech is empty. If one does not form the conceptualization of hearing, one is able to...
I have heard that the nature of things is fundamentally empty. That which does not manifest as the form of a Buddha is empty;

the person who is able to speak is also empty, for they do not manifest as the form of a speaker; and the Dharma that is spoken is also empty. Such meanings refer to the five kinds of emptiness mentioned above;
this is the characteristic of the signless. Bodhidharma was the second son of King Xiangzhi. He...

He was the twenty-eighth patriarch in the Western Heaven and the First Patriarch in this Eastern Land. It is said that the Great Master came across the sea by boat and sat facing a wall at Mount Song.
He pointed directly to the human mind for the realization of one's nature and attainment of Buddhahood, without relying on written words;
this was based on the teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to clarify the principle of formlessness, not something newly devised as his own personal opinion by the First Patriarch.
It is simply the opening of a distinct Dharma-gate of formlessness. Thus, the Tathāgata spoke in this manner, and the Patriarchs taught people by means of this;
how could there be two different versions?

Scholars of recent times have failed to realize this principle; they believe that the Chan school is a distinct dharma-gate, such that those who take Chan as their primary focus do not follow the Teaching, while those who take the Teaching as their primary focus do not practice Chan. Consequently, two separate schools of thought have come into being.

They revile one another, clamoring incessantly and unable to restrain themselves. Alas! That what I have heard is so shallow and superficial as to reach this state—whether it be foolishness or madness, it is truly lamentable (from the *Cittadharmamukha*).
This section states that ignorance gives rise to deluded discrimination. Scholars of recent times, with their coarse minds, fail to realize that the Buddhas and Patriarchs share a single principle;
they claim that the Chan school is a distinct type of dharma-gate. Those who take Chan as their primary focus rely solely on Chan and thus are not people who study the teachings.
Those who take the teachings as their primary focus rely solely on the teachings. Furthermore...
Those who do not practice meditation have thus formed two distinct schools of thought.
Not only do they demarcate boundaries and establish separate domains, but they have even gone so far as to engage in mutual slander and clamorous disputes. Alas!
To sigh for these people who do not penetrate the Great Way; their learning is base and shallow, and moreover vulgar and crude, as they contend with one another.
They slander [the Dharma] to such an extent. One must know that such people are either fools or madmen; it is truly lamentable.

△ After the three hundred poems [of the *Shi Jing*], this one chapter appears, encompassing all the many previous discourses and returning them all to the essence of formlessness (*animitta*). If a person can understand the intent of the scripture...
The meaning of the Patriarchs is perfectly clear and free of doubt; then even the three hundred odes of the *Shijing* would all be superfluous words.
How profound these words are! *Zenrin Hōkun Hitsusetsu*, Scroll Lower (End).
By Zhang Zhao, Dayan Jushi, Former Censor-in-Chief.

**Preface to the "Treatise on the Mind" (by Your Subject)** In my youth, I recited the *Shi* and *Shu*; I mastered only their literal phrases. In my maturity, I have gazed upon the yellow silk and white paper, yet I have done nothing but confuse myself with vain blossoms.

Since the obstructions of principle (*li-zhang*) are profound and deep, and the roots of desire (*yu-gen*) are firm and solid, my circling through the realms of pleasure has only served to further increase the bitter roots of suffering. This is my intention.
The filaments open in profusion; the burning at the crown of my head is truly painful. Having heard the teachings of our school, I was able to find coolness in the ground of the mind.

Thereupon, I examined the scriptural texts, browsing through the precious treasuries of the Dragon Palace. For the first time, I understood that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are fundamentally born of delusion, and that earth, water, fire, and wind are originally formed from illusion.
This single body does not exist; what else can be said beyond this? Yet, regarding light and darkness...
Form is emptiness. Dust upon dust is in harmonious union; the body, the people, and all things are clearly present before one.

If one seeks to cast them away, they are all non-existent; how could they be the same if one were to remain mixed with them? To abandon one thing while grasping at another never ceases this frantic pursuit.

"Three before" and "three after" only further increase one's calculating deliberations. Believing oneself satisfied with meager gains, one halts at the *parīttābha* (small reward) city; yearning for the sage and loathing the ordinary, these two...
The fortress is upon one's head; it is through body, speech, and mind that they intersect at every step.

Greed, anger, and delusion penetrate layer after layer, extinguishing this life only to give rise to the next, with no end in sight. Mistakenly regretting what was done before, how can one ever attain mastery?
Fortunately, through the vast cultivation of the field of merit over ten lifetimes, one has encountered [this opportunity].
The singular sovereign extends his compassionate grace.

We reverently contemplate Your Majesty, who assists the Three Non-beings and governs the myriad existences. Employing the canons and rules of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, you have brought about the harmonious concord of the ages of Yao and Shun.

Though dwelling in the innermost palace, you roam as if among mountains and marshes; though your bounty spreads to the eight extremities of the world, you regard all things as equal to floating clouds.
Like clouds merging with the profound clarity of the great void, and like the bright illumination of the radiant sun, he manifested in the body of a sovereign to preach the Dharma.

Within a single mote of dust, he revealed the Tathāgatagarbha; having long ago harmonized with the source of the mind’s single thread, he extensively expounded the wondrous intent of the separate transmission.
Without ever speaking, he has already thundered the sound of the dragon’s roar, universally manifesting [the truth].
Awakened by Your constant bestowal of the ambrosia of Dharma, You have pity for this servant who, lost in delusion, mistakes his head for a shadow.

For my sake, You untie the knots and unfold the cloth, thereby enabling me—like a frog emerging from a well—to lift my head and gaze toward the heavens, and like a bee piercing a gap in paper, to flutter its wings and draw near to the brilliance of the sun.
Only then do I realize that the fundamental nature is thus, and that this gate is non-dual. As for the Way of Great Learning, it is indeed the means of governing the world.
The *Zhizhi* (Direct Pointing) transmission is the essential core for clarifying the luminous mind.

Without the orderly arrangement of human relations, the practice of ordinary rites, the cultivation of government, and the clarification of punishments, how could one master the dharma-characteristics of this mind?

Without shattering delusion, merging with the true, and attaining universal penetration and universal awakening, how could one fathom the spiritual source of the myriad transformations? Emptiness and existence depend upon each other to arise; once existence is exhausted, [emptiness remains].
Perfect emptiness and illusion are different names for the same reality. Only by treading upon that reality does one first realize that the causes of illusion—names and forms—are empty flowers.

This is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in *nirvāṇa*. If one has not yet reached this limit of reality where not even a single thread is attached, how can one gather the empty flowers of the myriad virtues?
In both the mundane and supramundane realms, do not grasp at a single dharma; cast the empty into the empty.
At this juncture, I have set aside all worldly concerns;
though it would take kalpas of time to repay such kindness, the Great Trichiliocosm ultimately returns to a single principle.
Now, having received Your Majesty’s decree, I respectfully compose this "Heart赋" (Xin Fu) in one chapter for Your Imperial Inspection.
Please peruse this preface, wherein I set forth the origins and details of my own resolve. As for that which is called "mind," no metaphor can be applied and no description can exhaust its nature.
Even when an infant opens its mouth, it has already realized the fundamental source; yet when Buddhas and patriarchs consult one another, none can utter a word.

If the golden needle is already in hand, how could one possibly grasp the shifting hues of the clouds to perform the work of tailoring? Even if one wields a brilliant brush that soars above the clouds, how could one— [The text ends abruptly.]

Taking the Great Purity (*Mahāśuddha*) as a canvas for painting, a single thread-hole is perfectly the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumagarbha*), and the thousand Sumeru mountains are no different from a single hair.
Every thing is fully perfected; every point is manifest. How could this [work] of mine, this composition, alone not be the mind?
The mind, too, is not the mind; the composition, surely, is not a composition. It is merely like a parrot that has clipped its tongue yet learns to speak, or an earthworm that beats its drum.
The crane calls out with joy; yellow chrysanthemums display their faces toward the sun; green bamboo pipes its melodies in the wind—thus it is said. The verse says:
Without birth and without extinction, without abiding and without transition. After Maitreya and before Bhīṣmagarjitasvarakalpa, it stands solitary and eminent.

Abiding yet detached from both that and this, it is profoundly still and eternally present, neither central nor peripheral. Only through perfection is there awakening; only through awakening is there perfection.
In perfection, one does not perceive perfection; in perfection, one encompasses the other and the self. In awakening, there is nothing to be awakened to; yet awakening pervades humans and devas.

Were one to lift up the empty space of the ten directions, it would be insufficient to measure its greatness; were one to exhaustively count all myriad existences as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could not equal it.
This is insufficient to speak of its totality. Within the eye of a mustard seed, the waters of the four great oceans are contained;
in the time it takes to bend and extend an arm, eighteen thousand years are directly traversed. To claim this as one's own possession, one calls it the "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.

To accommodate human sentiment through expedient means, one calls it the "Direct Pointing" or the "Separate Transmission. What is vulgar and what is ordinary? What is sacred and what is wise? What is delusion and what is...

Awakening! What dharma? What meditation? The six realms and the three miserable paths are entirely encompassed within the true essence. The ten bodies and four wisdoms are not separated from delusive conditions.
Arising yet without birth, all Buddhas enter nirvana within the ocean of sentient beings' consciousness.
Quiescent yet constantly moving, sentient beings fall into birth and death within the mind-source of all Buddhas. There is not a single speck of dust that does not enter [it], like the Great...
The perfect mirror: there is not a single land that is not real; it is the adamantine circle. Like a mass of great fire in the void, it is difficult to approach even with washed hands;
like mercury falling to the ground, it vanishes in an instant. All phenomena rely upon it to manifest as reflections.
Like a mani-jewel whose substance is not of a single color, yet from which every object derives its radiance;

like a net of precious threads, layered and interconnected, extending throughout the six realms of existence while simultaneously encompassing that which lies beyond them—thus its outer boundaries are immeasurable.
It can be shattered into minute particles, yet it dwells within each of those very particles—thus its inner essence is unfathomable.
Firmly established, every form is fully manifest; in every instance, all is revealed. Vast and signless, yet myriad phenomena intersect and cross;
silent and soundless, yet the multitude of sounds issues forth together. Should one seek its ultimate limit, even the most supreme wisdom cannot fathom it.
If one seeks its origin, it cannot be traced back even to the time of Dīpaṃkara. If one wishes to flee to avoid it, the nine heavens and nine earths meet everywhere.
If one wishes to seize it for observation, it cannot be encountered throughout a thousand kalpas or a thousand lifetimes.
It is vast and traceless; where could it be defiled? It pervades the great trichiliocosm; where could it find protection? Great or small—[it is beyond all such distinctions].
Equal in measure: equal in degree whether high or low, identical in essence whether existent or non-existent, co-dwelling in both arising and ceasing;
it is both "is" and "is not," both rising and falling, both distant and near, both black and white. To comprehend it, one finds a single path of uniform evenness;

to cling to it, one finds a thousand divergent paths each established. One revolves within earth, water, fire, and wind, and is dazed and whirled about by sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Consciousness is entangled in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is mired in the past, future, present, and antiquity. It is deluded by the saliva of foxes and the drool of wildcats;
it searches through broken books and fragmentary records. It is lost in the vast emptiness and profound obscurity; it calculates in terms of inches, spans, and feet.
It toys with the conscious spirit, yet it is cut off and extinguished in the ignorance of wood and stone.
They loathe and reject the concepts of person, self, and sentient beings; they are buried within the darkness of emptiness and form.

They arrange themselves within Buddha-lands and sites of enlightenment, yet they stumble over the fetters of worldly truth. They habituate themselves to the illusion of flowers appearing when one presses on the eye;

they foolishly cling to what is like a discarded gold coin while picking up pebbles. They are confounded by the pursuit of joy and the flight from aversion; they are distracted by gain and loss, benefit and harm. O!
It is neither black nor white. Since beginningless kalpas, there have been traces of names and forms: the path is called black and the path is called white;
the crane is purely white and the crow is purely black. When the six knots are centered in the heart yet remain unadjusted and crooked, one doubts whether they are white or black;

thus, wherever attachment arises, one becomes stuck. They entangle one another and cannot be untied. It is like casting glue into lacquer so that the lacquer also becomes glue, or like welcoming a guest with a guest.
The guest is entirely the host. In spring, the silkworm spins its cocoon, yet the cocoon binds the body;
in summer, the insect dwells upon ice, yet the ice first robs it of its soul. The sea of burning poison is vast and deep; Mount Cakravāḍa is towering and precipitous.

The four elements manifest strange and wondrous forms, while the single "I" persists with a continuous, subtle pulse. Within the dream of the pillow lies the kingdom of槐 (Huái), where one commands the birds.
Tigers, dragons, and snakes; fire within stone. Distinguishing between the egg-born, womb-born, transformation-born, and moisture-born:
a drop of water in the human realm is difficult to exhaust, yet the journey through the hells is most urgent. With fires two hundred cubits thick, where is the lotus flower?

Blown by the wind for three thousand years, when will one find a secure dwelling? Illnesses are already manifold, and elixirs are ten thousand kinds. [The masters] of the forty-seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven—
Having received the direct transmission from the Medicine Master, the two or three [patriarchs] of the Eastern Land together inherited the authentic lineage of the King of Physicians.

At times, they took the great earth to serve as *i-phu* (vegetarian) offerings to satisfy the hunger and emptiness of others; at other times, they gathered floating clouds to weave into robes of golden thread.

It revives those suffering from the chill of illness; it may kindle incense and lamps, with precious torches illuminating their darkened stupor; it may drive forth the lightning of Dharma and the thunder of wisdom to awaken them from their somnolent slumber;
it may be likened to a flower in the sky or compared to the second month, washing away the nest-like roots of outflows (*āsrava*).
Sometimes he points to the four great elements; sometimes he designates the six sense objects. He rolls back the quilt and pillow of ignorance;

or he manifests the power of *dāna*, such that the Buddha’s bowl may be filled with but a few flowers. Or he erects the banner of *vīrya*, wherein the diamond-like [nature] is not mixed with the cooking of the mundane.
Or he is perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts (*śīla*), emerging pure and white from the mire. Or the water of *samādhi* is deep and clear, returning [to its source].
The True and Eternal gradually permeates [the mind]. Sometimes one restrains the deluded movements of the serpent of anger to avoid burning down the forest of merit.

Sometimes one uses the metaphor of the silkworm cocoon to illustrate the difficulty of conditions, pulling out the brocade of Bodhi. Sometimes one tames the wild elephant by girthing it with a tether.
Some restrain the lost monkey within its cage; some brandish the sword of wisdom to shatter the layered nets of desire;
some row the vessel of *prajñā* across the murky river of craving; some speak of the great ocean of the *gandharva*-city with its boundless towers of dragons and vapors;
some discourse upon the Pure Land with its countless golden and silver lotuses in jeweled ponds; or some reveal...
The three bodies manifest in response; they are neither annihilated nor eternal. Sometimes they reveal a single, perfect realization—neither increasing nor decreasing.
They split open the single flavor of equality, suchness as it is, and produce ten thousand varieties of distinct teachings and schools, sudden and gradual.
Transcending expedient means, one abides in Perfect Enlightenment; ceasing the crying with leaves on a willow branch, one cuts off the cycle of birth and death to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Return! The cataracts before the eyes and the floating flowers in the void pass away in a flash. To burn Mount Sumeru would be as appropriate as using a firefly;
yet to bind empty space relies entirely upon tortoise hair. Pushing aside illusory shadows and drifting light, the jade dragon turns its hooves;

striking against the silver mountain and iron wall, the stone tiger roars. Flowers scatter across the clear sky; the five schools each let fall their rain of fragrance, while waves overturn the vast expanse.
The Ground. Three Gates, a long scroll of silver waves: neither half nor full, neither partial nor round. A single kind of flowerless fruit;
possessing both the provisional and the real, both illumination and function. A solitary bridge without wood;
it drives to death the world’s Zen-seeking monks and confounds the heroes among the world’s Buddhists. The Lion cub roars at the tree.
A headwind binds the sleeves; a rabbit’s horn picks up the moon at the bottom of the pond, hanging it upon the tip of the brow.

The waters of the eight seas are transformed into clarified butter (*sarpis*); there is nothing that is not a poisonous medicine. This perfectly realized treasure of the Dharma is found in this very hair-pore.
This is the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is the dream, the illusion, the shadow, and the bubble. What is there to love? What is there to hate?
Whether cut by a blade or smeared with sandalwood paste, the flavor is one and the same; what is there to grasp and what is there to reject? Śākyamuni and Devadatta both roam in ease.

That which is neither seen nor heard becomes a self-abandonment when approached through intellectual understanding. That which is neither non-existent nor existent gives rise to worldly toil when one stagnates in partiality.
When all things are equal and uniform, to stir even a single thought is to provide nourishment for delusion.
It is originally complete and perfect. If you seek it from others, it only increases your clamor and confusion. It must be like the brilliant clarity of the bright sun;
it must be like the vast emptiness of the great void; it must be like the rapid turning of the wind-wheel;
it must be like the moon over the river illuminating all. One must be such a person to clarify this matter. The light of the precious mirror shines upon a thousand things.
A thousand [times] do not conceal it; strictly avoid looking with the eyes. The sound of the lion’s string is resonant; you must simply gaze upon it. It is like water becoming ice:
this ice is not the water, yet the entirety of the water is ice. It is like gold forming a vessel: this vessel is not the gold, yet the entirety of the gold is the vessel.
Open your eyes and become a Buddha within a dream; only when the six perfections and ten thousand practices are perfected will [this be realized].

One does not act for the sake of accomplishing a single matter; one sets the mind to subdue the demons within the mirror. When the ten sages and six classes of ordinary beings are all sent away, one first realizes that both extremes are identical:
phenomena are principle, and principle is phenomena. The two obstacles are entirely eliminated. Delusion is awakening, and awakening is delusion; the two causes are placed side by side.
To be able to separate the seer from the seen during their separation is called ignorance; once this is realized, there is nothing left.

To thoroughly understand that which is to be understood is what is called "wisdom. It is like a flying serpent gliding through mist; though it dwells in the mist, it is not the void. It is like a wild elephant crossing a river;
though it treads upon the water, it is entirely solid ground. One does not rely on conditions to cultivate realization, nor does one dwell upon appearances when practicing giving.
Like jade-water, it is naturally clear and limpid, leaving the waves and surges to themselves. Like a mountain of gold, it has no fear of being sealed by mud. What need is there for further action?
When one is filled with anger, the Vase of Virtue is struck and yet remains unbroken; this is simply because it encompasses the three thousand worlds.
When one ascends the shore of the Way, one abandons the boat; only then does one truly believe that *nirvāṇa* is non-dual. Indeed, this very thing does not fall into any trap or snare.
Not a single dharma emerges from within it, nor does a single dharma arrive from without. It is luminous before the primordial antiquity and distinct throughout the furthest reaches of the future.
The Great Treasury of Radiant Light is, in its very essence, without dependence; it is primordially pure and naturally so. It is uniquely honored and supremely noble.
It gives birth to humans, it gives birth to beings, and it gives birth to Buddhas. It is devoid of both delusion and truth, transcending all duality. In its differentiation, it is identical;

the four do not depart from the one. In its identity, it is differentiated; the one does not depart from the four. In the One, there is not even one; how could there be four in the four? Subject and object are both extinguished.

Form and emptiness are both entrusted [to this state]; its essence transcends both the ordinary and the sage. The path between "other" and "self" is cut off, leaving not even a single thread of separation.

How could it be something to be kept secret? Fundamentally, there is nothing to be awakened to; we merely give it the forced name "enlightenment. Thus, seeing is severed by the clarity of mind, and clarity becomes limpid through the severance of seeing.
Because seeing is severed, the true and the conventional, the defiled and the pure, do not obstruct the faculty of sight. How could the great trichiliocosm be [an obstacle]?
Discernment: When the mind is luminous, bodhi and afflictions are one path, as are nirvana and samsara; what need is there to seek them through the seven locations?
One pearl enters all pearls, and all pearls enter one pearl; there is no division and no union.

As the single moon universally appears in all waters, the moons in all waters are subsumed within that single moon. Sudden and perfect, sudden and accomplished, it penetrates the three periods of time directly.
It stands upright, extending across the ten directions in great breadth; for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas it remains thus, level in the north, south, east, and west.
This constitutes the vastness of the Avataṃsaka assembly; therefore, through this, infinite life is perfectly luminous.
The Imperial Edict of the Yongqing Prince, the Layman Yuanming:

"In my view, the Chan school has never flourished more than it does today, nor has it ever declined more than it does today. Throughout the provinces, the monasteries and temples stand as numerous as chess pieces..."
As for those who have spread [the Dharma] and held the whisk upon entering the hall, they are beyond counting; indeed, there has never been a time more flourishing than today.
Nevertheless, among the disciples throughout the land, there are few who have not only penetrated the ultimate barrier above, but even those who can break through their fundamental inquiry are rare.
Those who possess right knowledge and vision are likewise not found in great numbers; such is the current state of our tradition, which has truly reached its lowest point today.
Now, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years before finally enabling the Second Patriarch, Huike, to receive the robe.

Even those who employ the wisdom-power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to guide humans and devas waited for the duration of nine years to obtain but a single person. Today, throughout the entire land...
Below this, there are ten thousand monasteries and ten thousand monks; ten thousand monks and ten thousand fly-whisks. The Master transmits in blindness, and the disciples receive in blindness.

Every person proclaims the vehicle of the school, yet each fails to realize their own mind. Does this not cause the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana to hang by a thread?
Although one might say that it cannot necessarily be like the transmission from Bodhidharma to the Second Patriarch, it must nevertheless be so.

True practice and genuine awakening entail possessing correct knowledge and correct view from within oneself; one must receive these from a person who has attained such correct knowledge and correct view.
How could there be such a thing as blind transmission and blind reception, utterly devoid of foundation?

To claim that this constitutes the revitalization of the Buddha-dharma or the continuation of the Buddha’s wisdom-life—how does this differ from destroying the Buddha and extinguishing the Dharma? At worst, with fame and profit corrupting the mind, one commits the great falsehood of false speech.
They boast of having realized the Way whenever they move; they revile Buddhas and scold patriarchs; they hold the precepts in no regard; they deceive one another;

they hawk fly-whisks and robes like commoners in the marketplace; they treat the life-force of the Buddhas and patriarchs as mere worldly sentimentality. Though they claim to possess the Buddha, they are but thieves.
The names of these patriarchs and their descendants lacked the actual substance of being teachers and models for humans and devas.

Figures such as Fǎzàng and Hóngrěn did nothing but cultivate relationships with scholar-officials and rely upon their influence as a means to protect their monastic seats. Among these scholar-officials...
Those who take pride in the title of "lay practitioner" (upāsaka) at home accept such superficiality and compete with one another for reputation.

Although on that day the World-Honored One entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings, ministers, and faithful laypeople to protect and uphold it, he never commanded them to follow a path that deviates from the Way;
how much less so when they fail to observe the retreat (zhì), do not practice incense meditation (zuò xiāng), and instead devote themselves solely to composing poetry and essays to curry favor?
To please the scholar-officials and abandon the fundamental for the trivial—such a disposition of mind, how does it differ from that of a layperson?

If this continues, the Buddha-dharma will be swept away in the future. Indeed, the intended meaning of the Patriarch from the West does not fall within the realm of verbal explanations; the establishment of the various schools [of Chan] was for this purpose.

This is why they distinguish between demons and discern differences. Although they may change their faces when engaging others, they have never intentionally established separate doctrines or diverged from the primary intent of the "Direct Pointing" (dantou).

Yet, many of the present-day followers of our school take the root of consciousness and birth-and-death as their basis, and by the side of words and letters, they pick up the dregs of others' spittle to study.
People are loquacious; questioner and respondent alike confuse the essential principles. Those who strike with the staff or shout with the *katsu* end up merely evading and following along.
Suddenly meeting on the path of understanding, they become like water and milk merging into one, claiming, "This is the secret intent of our school.
If this were so, how would it differ from external paths or demonic delusions? This is truly what is called "one blind man leading a crowd of blind men," pulling each other into the fire.

A pitfall. One carries such a heavy burden oneself; how can one speak of benefiting living beings? With a limited mind, one gives rise to discriminatory views and stirs up the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) toward the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
One fixes the intent according to the literal text and divides the schools by following the words. This causes later students who wish to apply diligent effort and mental power to practice:
alas, thorns are spread across the ground and scorching poison mists the sky, leaving no place to set foot, as they rely on the arising of the mind.
Through the accumulation of karma over months and years, although the number of followers has increased, the core tenets have increasingly faded away—this is truly lamentable.

I hereby issue this clear edict to inform all monasteries: if among the current abbots of the various temples in the provinces there are those who possess self-confidence free from doubt and have already attained the higher stages, and who wish to come and see me, they are to come to the capital. I shall personally [discuss] the Buddha-dharma with them.

I shall receive him. Among those in the deep mountains and remote valleys, there may be some who dwell alone amidst the mists and clouds, refusing to accept the robe and whisk of a blind master—those individuals who possess correct knowledge and correct view themselves.
Such people should reflect that the ancestral style has fallen into decay and must emerge from their seclusion to repay the Buddha’s kindness in kind.
If, in truth, they have traversed the three barriers and their insight transcends all bounds, I shall surely bestow upon them the title of Chan Master.
Decree: I have ordered that [those who come] shall continue to partake of the Dharma-milk of the successive patriarchs above.

Should anyone, however, harbor a mind for fame and profit or give rise to thoughts of seeking fortune, once they arrive before Me, the water will recede and the stones will be revealed. Since they hope for the emergence of glory, I shall immediately cast them into the net of the Dharma.

If, on the other hand, they lack fundamental self-confidence and merely imitate the bottle-gourd (the model), yet claim to be practitioners of Chan, they must simply preach the Dharma. This is the correct course.

Regarding those who hold both the view of Māra and the view of [the Buddha], yet lack both, upon hearing this decree of mine, you should exert all your strength to lead the assembly into the formal retreat (jie-zhi) and sit in meditation (zuo-xiang).

Diligently seek your own fundamental nature (ben-fen). Whether it be striking the bell and withdrawing the wooden board, or casting aside the whisk and discarding the comb, you must redouble your efforts in study and practice, vowing to attain final realization.
Do not again deceive yourselves or mislead others. If great falsehoods are established, then even a virtuous cause will—

Encountering such evil retribution, why is the suffering so great? As for the rest of the monastic community who have not yet received this entrustment, you should contemplate the Buddhas and Patriarchs and preserve this Dharma-gate.
It was originally intended for the life-and-death cycle of sentient beings; if you do not take the ending of birth and death as your primary concern, for what purpose do you don the *kāṣāya*?
To end birth and death, you must clarify the mind-ground. Do not cling to fragmentary knowledge or be satisfied with meager attainment.

It is sufficient. Do not fall into the trap of relying on mere learning and intellectual penetration, nor claim realization when you have not yet attained it. Do not merely scheme for false commissions or lead others astray with your own pretenses.
Do not compromise with worldly ways to seek fame at the cost of your own integrity. This is what is meant by "the karmic consciousness wandering aimlessly, with no foundation to rely upon.
Above, you would fail the profound intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, whose eyebrows trail the ground; below, you would fail your own original nature.
To possess such countenances and yet remain submerged in samsara for a long time, forever dependent on the realms of suffering—this is truly pitiable. How can one not be struck with alarm?

It is fitting that you contemplate this with a sincere heart, seeking ultimate liberation and realization. Only through great awakening and profound penetration can one avoid living a life of drunken delusion and dream-like ignorance.
If you are unable to achieve this, then at the very least, firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts, strictly purify your holy conduct, and do not commit the transgressions of greed and anger.

Foolishness! One must constantly cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom. One must not recklessly claim realization, thereby misleading future students. One should preserve this seed of the Buddha to await the proper conditions.

If one merely transmits false knowledge and wrong views through secret oral instructions—deceiving oneself and others, coveting fame and profit, spreading worldly doctrines, and violating precepts and discipline—then one is worse than a common layperson; how could such a person be considered part of the Dharma-gate?

These matters must be as they ought to be; you must urgently engage in self-reflection to understand the past and cultivate the future, so as not to辜负 (fail) My sincere and earnest intent to protect the Dharma through instruction.
Let the relevant ministries issue a proclamation to the Governors and Viceroys of all provinces, ordering them to inform all Chan monasteries throughout the realm.
